cards.front: Name the four key types of technology the lesson focuses on for business.
cards.answer: E-commerce / Social media / Digital communication / Payment systems

cards.front: Name the four areas of employment law the lesson identifies for small businesses.
cards.answer: Fair recruitment / Pay (minimum wage) / Protection from discrimination / Health and safety requirements

cards.front: How does digital communication help a freelance designer work with clients far away?
cards.answer: It lets them collaborate with a client in another city using only a laptop and internet connection, cutting travel costs and speeding up contact.

cards.front: Why can technology increase a small business's sales?
cards.answer: It reaches a wider customer base online, enables 24/7 trading and allows targeted advertising to specific market segments.

cards.front: Why does boiling point increase as the carbon chain of an alkane gets longer?
cards.answer: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, which need more energy to overcome, raising the boiling point.

cards.front: Why do alkanes not decolourise bromine water?
cards.answer: Alkanes are saturated with no C=C double bond, so bromine cannot add across a double bond.

cards.front: Why is cracking carried out on long-chain hydrocarbons from crude oil?
cards.answer: There is more demand for shorter-chain hydrocarbons like petrol than for longer-chain ones, and cracking also produces useful alkenes.

cards.front: Name the three settings DNA alternates between.
cards.answer: The street / The field / The wood

cards.front: Why do Mark and Jan's street scenes give a detached perspective on events?
cards.answer: Their scenes happen outside the main locations, so they report on events rather than participating in them.

cards.front: How does the field symbolically represent the inner world in DNA?
cards.answer: It shows Leah's moral struggle through her monologues and Phil's emotional blankness through his silence.

cards.front: Why does the title 'Eden Rock' suggest innocence and safety?
cards.answer: It alludes to the Garden of Eden, a paradise before the Fall, suggesting perfection and innocence.

cards.front: How do the mundane domestic details in 'Eden Rock' change how death feels?
cards.answer: Specific details like the 'H.P. Sauce bottle' anchor the memory, making death feel like a safe return rather than the unknown.

cards.front: How does the final line of 'Eden Rock' affect the sense of time?
cards.answer: 'I had not thought that it would be like this' shows time dissolving as past, present and future merge with calm surprise.

cards.front: Name the three poems the lesson groups under the theme of Memory & Time.
cards.answer: Winter Swans / Climbing My Grandfather / Eden Rock

cards.front: Name the three objectives the 19th-century prose extract question assesses.
cards.answer: AO1: personal response backed by quotations / AO2: language, form and structure / AO3: context
items: AO1: personal response backed by quotations

cards.front: Name the four main themes of Jekyll and Hyde that the lesson says interconnect.
cards.answer: Duality / Secrecy/reputation / Science/morality / Nature of evil

cards.front: Why does the novella argue that repressing evil is more dangerous than acknowledging it?
cards.answer: Pretending evil does not exist makes it stronger, while honestly recognising it might allow it to be managed.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson suggest science needs both ambition and restraint?
cards.answer: Lanyon's caution and Jekyll's recklessness are both inadequate, so progress without morality leads to destruction.

cards.front: Name the eight units of data storage the lesson lists, from smallest to largest.
cards.answer: bit / nibble / byte / kilobyte / megabyte / gigabyte / terabyte / petabyte

cards.front: What are the four rules for adding binary digits given in the lesson?
Why does adding 11111111 + 00000001 in 8-bit binary cause an overflow error?
cards.answer: The true answer needs nine bits, but only eight are available, so the leading 1 is lost and the result reads incorrectly.

cards.front: Why was Unicode created when ASCII already existed?
cards.answer: ASCII's 128 characters were not enough for every writing system, so Unicode was made to represent far more characters.

cards.front: Name the five steps of the source utility method for answering an exam question.
cards.answer: Identify the specific enquiry / Examine the source content / Analyse the provenance / Use contextual knowledge to confirm or challenge / Make an overall judgement of usefulness
items: Use contextual knowledge to confirm or challenge
Make an overall judgement of usefulness

cards.front: Name six topics from this unit that a synthesis essay on 'nation of contrasts' could connect.
cards.answer: Immigration restriction and the Red Scare / The KKK and Jim Crow / Farm poverty alongside Wall Street boom / Native American poverty alongside consumer culture / Sacco and Vanzetti's execution alongside democratic ideals / Flappers' limited freedom alongside exclusion of Black and working-class women
items: Immigration restriction and the Red Scare
Farm poverty alongside Wall Street boom
Native American poverty alongside consumer culture
Sacco and Vanzetti's execution alongside democratic ideals
Flappers' limited freedom alongside exclusion of Black and working-class women

cards.front: Why would a KKK recruitment poster's provenance limit its usefulness as a source about the Klan?
cards.answer: It was made by the Klan to recruit members, so it presents its most attractive image and omits its violence and corruption.

cards.front: Why would a 1921 temperance cartoon be less useful for judging whether Prohibition succeeded than for explaining why it was introduced?
cards.answer: It was made by Prohibition supporters as propaganda before problems emerged, and contextual knowledge shows Prohibition actually failed to stop drinking.

title: Terrorism, the War of Attrition and Yom Kippur, 1967–73
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three tools did each side use to try to break the post-1967 stalemate (Egypt, Palestinian groups, Sadat)?
cards.answer: Egypt fought a low-intensity War of Attrition / Palestinian groups turned to international terrorism / Sadat prepared a limited war to force negotiation
items: Egypt fought a low-intensity War of Attrition
Palestinian groups turned to international terrorism
Sadat prepared a limited war to force negotiation

cards.front: Why did Sadat expel around 20,000 Soviet military advisers from Egypt in July 1972?
cards.answer: It cleared the way diplomatically for the US to broker a postwar settlement without Egypt looking like a Soviet client.

cards.front: Why was the Yom Kippur War a political victory for Sadat despite Egypt being militarily outflanked by its end?
cards.answer: He shocked Israel out of its post-1967 confidence, restored Egyptian honour, and forced the US to take Egyptian negotiation seriously.

cards.front: How did the Munich Olympics attack affect international attitudes to the Palestinian cause?
cards.answer: It made the cause globally famous but also globally toxic, turning most Western opinion against terrorism as a tactic.

cards.front: What four things must be labelled on a reaction profile?
cards.answer: Energy level of reactants / Energy level of products / Activation energy / Overall energy change

cards.front: Why is a polystyrene cup used when measuring temperature change in a reaction?
cards.answer: It insulates the reaction, reducing heat loss to the surroundings and giving a more accurate temperature reading.

cards.front: Why is the reaction between H2 and Cl2 to form HCl exothermic?
cards.answer: More energy is released making the H-Cl bonds (862 kJ) than is needed to break the H-H and Cl-Cl bonds (678 kJ).

title: Gibson and Gregory: Two Theories of Perception
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name Gibson's three key terms that are all picked up directly from the environment.
cards.answer: Optic flow / Invariants / Affordances

cards.front: Give the two weaknesses of Haber and Levin's study of size and distance perception.
cards.answer: Relied on subjective verbal estimates / Small unrepresentative sample of 9 male US students
items: Small unrepresentative sample of 9 male US students

cards.front: How does Gibson's theory explain why everyday perception like judging a room's layout is so fast and accurate?
cards.answer: Perception happens directly from rich environmental information rather than through slow, effortful inference.

cards.front: How does Gregory's constructivist theory explain why visual illusions occur?
cards.answer: Illusions occur when the brain's perceptual hypothesis is wrong, such as misapplying size or depth cues learned from experience.

cards.front: Name the five thermosetting polymers the lesson covers.
cards.answer: Urea formaldehyde / Melamine formaldehyde / Phenol formaldehyde (Bakelite) / Epoxy resin / Polyester resin

cards.front: Name the eight thermoforming polymers the lesson covers.
cards.answer: Acrylic (PMMA) / HIPS / HDPE / LDPE / Polypropylene (PP) / PVC / PET / ABS

cards.front: Why is a melamine worktop able to withstand a hot cup without deforming?
cards.answer: Its permanent covalent cross-links cannot be broken by heat, so the material stays rigid instead of softening.

cards.front: Why are all oil-based polymers considered non-renewable?
cards.answer: Because crude oil, the resource they are made from, takes millions of years to form.

title: Factors Influencing Design (2): Standards, Sustainability and Market Forces
subject: cambridge-nationals-engineering-design

cards.front: Name the four higher-value recovery loops the circular economy prioritises before recycling, in order from highest to lowest value.
cards.answer: Repair (product stays in use) / Remanufacturing (core parts refurbished to as-new) / Reuse of components (harvested parts in new assemblies) / Recycling of materials (last resort)
items: Reuse of components (harvested parts in new assemblies)

cards.front: Why is recycling considered the lowest-value recovery option in the circular economy?
cards.answer: Because recycling downgrades materials, such as mixed plastic being recycled into lower-grade products, losing value compared to repair or reuse.

cards.front: How does Kay use enjambment to show the speaker's anxious thoughts in 'Dusting the Phone'?
cards.answer: Enjambment makes lines tumble into each other without control, mimicking how her thoughts spiral without pause.

cards.front: Why does the speaker find both a ringing phone and a silent phone equally frightening?
cards.answer: Both possibilities feel threatening because either could mean disaster, so she cannot escape her fear whatever happens.

title: Education and Capitalism: Bowles and Gintis
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: Name the four ways Bowles and Gintis said schools mirror the workplace.
cards.answer: Hierarchy and authority / External rewards for compliance / Little control over content / Fragmented tasks/subjects

cards.front: Why did Bowles and Gintis think working-class pupils are less likely to achieve high grades despite equal talent?
cards.answer: They face material disadvantages at home, such as cramped housing, lack of resources and parents working long hours.

cards.front: How does the correspondence principle explain why schools fragment subjects into separate lessons?
cards.answer: This mirrors industrial production being divided into separate, specialised tasks, preparing pupils for divided workplace labour.

cards.front: Give the three Spanish verb forms used to describe your house in the present, past and conditional tenses.
cards.answer: hay (there is/are) / tiene (it has) / había/tenía (there was/it had) / tendría/habría (would have/there would be)

cards.front: To get the highest marks describing your home, how should you structure your answer across time-frames?
cards.answer: Describe your home now (present), what it was like before (imperfect), and your ideal home (conditional).

title: Tibet, propaganda and the Mao cult
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four channels through which propaganda operated during the Cultural Revolution.
cards.answer: Personality cult (badges, portraits, rallies) / The Party press / Thought reform sessions / Model campaigns like Dazhai

cards.front: Name the three things Lin Biao did to build the Mao cult.
cards.answer: Mass published the Little Red Book / Organised the 1966 Tiananmen rallies / Made soldiers read Mao's writings daily
items: Mass published the Little Red Book
Made soldiers read Mao's writings daily

cards.front: Why did Lin Biao's death in 1971 damage the credibility of CCP propaganda?
cards.answer: Lin had been praised as Mao's chosen successor but was posthumously denounced as a traitor, exposing propaganda's unreliability.

cards.front: Why were Tibetan monasteries destroyed during the Cultural Revolution?
cards.answer: Red Guards banned religious practice and destroyed hundreds of monasteries as part of enforcing revolutionary ideology across China.

cards.front: Name the five ways each Birling family member fails Eva Smith in the chain of responsibility.
cards.answer: Birling fails as an employer / Sheila fails as a consumer / Gerald fails as a lover / Mrs Birling fails as a charity worker / Eric fails as a man
items: Mrs Birling fails as a charity worker

cards.front: How does Mrs Birling's language about Eva expose class prejudice?
cards.answer: She calls Eva 'a girl of that sort' and 'impertinent', reducing her from a person to a stereotype.

cards.front: The lesson gives three effects created by Kathy's qualifying narration — name them.
cards.answer: Mimics real memory's uncertainty / Reflects the clones' conditioned self-doubt / Makes her an unreliable narrator

cards.front: How does the other children's cruelty towards Tommy foreshadow society's treatment of the clones?
cards.answer: It shows that those who don't conform or produce the 'right' kind of expression are mocked and excluded, just as society excludes the clones.

cards.front: Why does Kathy's calm competence as a carer create tragedy in the novel?
cards.answer: Her quiet competence means she serves and enables the very system that will eventually kill her, without resisting it.

cards.front: Why does Miss Lucy's honesty fail to change anything at Hailsham?
cards.answer: The students are so thoroughly conditioned that even direct truth cannot provoke them to act, so the system continues unchanged.

title: Propaganda, culture and the cult of Hitler
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the five separate chambers set up within the Reich Chamber of Culture.
cards.answer: Press / Film / Music / Theatre / Visual arts

cards.front: Name three Nazi projects or programmes that used Volksgemeinschaft imagery.
cards.answer: Volkswagen project / Strength Through Joy holidays / Hitler Youth

cards.front: Why did the 'Hitler Myth' benefit the Nazi regime politically?
cards.answer: It let Germans blame policy failures on subordinate officials while keeping faith in Hitler, stopping discontent turning into opposition to him.

cards.front: Why did the Nazis stage the Nuremberg Rallies as elaborate spectacles?
cards.answer: The choreographed architecture, lighting, music and scale were designed to create an overwhelming emotional experience of mass devotion and unity.

title: Brown, Montgomery and the early civil rights movement
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Why did President Eisenhower send federal troops to Little Rock in 1957?
cards.answer: He could not allow Governor Faubus to defy a federal court order desegregating Central High School.

cards.front: How did King argue non-violent direct action worked as a strategy?
cards.answer: It showed the movement's moral superiority while forcing authorities into using visible brutality against peaceful protesters, exposing them to the nation.

cards.front: Name the three organisations that shaped the early civil rights movement.
cards.answer: SCLC / NAACP / SNCC

title: Stages of Development, the Brain and Intelligence
subject: psychology-ocr

cards.front: What four things do IQ tests use standardised questions to cover?
cards.answer: Verbal reasoning / Memory / Spatial awareness / Problem-solving

cards.front: Why can a teenager be both a careful reasoner and impulsive at different moments?
cards.answer: The brain's emotional and reward regions mature before the cortex, so emotion outpaces reasoning ability.

cards.front: Why does a newborn baby fail to walk straight away?
cards.answer: The cerebellum, which coordinates movement, needs time and repeated practice to build a smooth movement programme.

cards.front: Why is the interaction between neurons and synapses, not just neuron number, key to brain development?
cards.answer: Frequently used synapses strengthen while rarely used ones are pruned, making the brain more efficient as it develops.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that increase braking distance.
cards.answer: Higher vehicle speed / Greater vehicle mass / Poor road conditions / Poor brake or tyre condition

cards.front: How does ABS braking help a driver, unlike other safety features?
cards.answer: It prevents wheel locking so the driver keeps steering control, and shortens braking distance instead of extending collision time.

cards.front: Why does a greater vehicle mass increase braking distance?
cards.answer: A greater mass gives the vehicle more kinetic energy, which must be removed by the braking force.

cards.front: Why do successful entrepreneurs assess risks before committing, rather than acting recklessly?
cards.answer: They research the market, keep start-up costs low and plan for disappointing sales, then still act despite uncertainty.

cards.front: Why can confidence without competence lead to poor decisions for an entrepreneur?
cards.answer: Confidence makes them act on decisions, but without the underlying ability those decisions may be badly judged.

cards.front: What four causes does the lesson give for turning the Creature violent?
cards.answer: Victor's abandonment at creation / universal human rejection over its appearance / reading Victor's journal calling it an abomination / the De Laceys' violent response to friendship
items: universal human rejection over its appearance
reading Victor's journal calling it an abomination
the De Laceys' violent response to friendship

cards.front: Why does Shelley present the Creature's early sensations as confusing and overwhelming?
cards.answer: To show it experiences the world like a newborn, overwhelmed and without any frame of reference, arguing for its essential innocence.

cards.front: Why does the Creature identify with Satan as well as Adam in Paradise Lost?
cards.answer: Like Adam it was created by one who should have cared for it, and like Satan it has been cast out and burns with rejection and rage.

cards.front: What are the four stages of Odysseus's plan to escape Polyphemus's cave?
cards.answer: Find and sharpen a wooden stake / Harden the tip in the fire / Get Polyphemus drunk on wine / Blind him with the stake, then hide under rams
items: Find and sharpen a wooden stake
Harden the tip in the fire
Blind him with the stake, then hide under rams

cards.front: Name three details Homer uses to show Polyphemus is barbaric.
cards.answer: Lives entirely off his flock, no farming / Dismisses the gods and xenia / Lives alone with no community or law / Eats his guests instead of feeding them / Keeps a messy, disordered cave
items: Lives entirely off his flock, no farming
Lives alone with no community or law
Eats his guests instead of feeding them

cards.front: Why does the 'Nobody' trick work so well as a pun in Greek?
cards.answer: In the grammatical form Polyphemus uses, 'mē tis' (no one) sounds identical to 'mētis' (cunning intelligence), the quality that defeated him.

cards.front: Why does Polyphemus dismiss Odysseus's appeal to xenia when Odysseus invokes Zeus?
cards.answer: Polyphemus says the Cyclopes are stronger than any god, showing he has no concept of the gods or hospitality.

title: Midnight on the Great Western — Thomas Hardy
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name the four poems the lesson compares with 'Midnight on the Great Western'.
cards.answer: Out, Out— (Robert Frost) / Holy Thursday (William Blake) / Baby Song (Thom Gunn) / Theme for English B (Langston Hughes)

cards.front: How does the poem's structure shift between its first two stanzas and its last two?
cards.answer: It moves from simple description of the boy to direct question and address, showing the speaker moving from watching to wondering.

cards.front: How do the uneven line lengths in the poem reflect the train journey?
cards.answer: Short lines interrupt longer ones, mimicking the train's irregular motion and the way the journey interrupts any clear sense of the boy's past or future.

cards.front: Why does the boy show no anxiety about travelling alone at night, according to the poem?
cards.answer: His calm may come from ignorance, or from his soul belonging to a sphere above the corrupt adult world he travels through.

title: Stave 3: The Ghost of Christmas Present
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: How does Dickens use the Cratchit family dinner to argue that wealth is not necessary for happiness?
cards.answer: Despite having almost nothing, the Cratchits transform their modest meal into a celebration through love and togetherness.

cards.front: Why does Dickens link Tiny Tim's illness directly to the Cratchits' poverty?
cards.answer: Because they cannot afford proper food, medical care, or warmth, showing his suffering is preventable if society helps.

cards.front: Why does the Ghost of Christmas Present age and die during Stave 3?
cards.answer: Because he lives for only one Christmas Day, showing that Christmas warmth is temporary unless people choose to carry it forward.

cards.front: Name the three things Lydia's elopement exposes, according to the lesson's Key Fact.
cards.answer: Wickham's predatory nature / Mr Bennet's parental negligence / the precariousness of women's reputations

cards.front: How does the lesson contrast Darcy's first and second proposals?
cards.answer: The first was prideful, mentioned degradation, expected gratitude, and was delivered indoors formally, unlike the humble second.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Bennet's reaction to the three marriages create comic irony?
cards.answer: She reacts only to the money ('Ten thousand a year!'), showing she has learned nothing from the Lydia crisis.

title: Human Life, Sikh Virtues and Mukti
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the five vices (panj chor) that flow from haumai in Sikh teaching.
cards.answer: Lust (kam) / Anger (krodh) / Greed (lobh) / Worldly attachment (moh) / Pride (ahankar)

cards.front: Name the two dimensions of mukti described in Sikh teaching.
cards.answer: Positive: joyful union with God / Negative: release from the cycle of rebirth
items: Negative: release from the cycle of rebirth

cards.front: Why does human life have such moral weight in Sikh teaching?
cards.answer: Because it is the rare, highest form of life in the rebirth cycle, giving the soul its chance to draw close to God, so every thought, word and action affects its journey.

cards.front: How can a soul overcome the weight of its past karma in Sikh teaching?
cards.answer: Through God's grace (nadar or kirpa) and sincere devotion, which can transform even a soul burdened by past actions, since liberation is open to all.

cards.front: Name the three extra structures plant cells have that animal cells lack.
cards.answer: Chloroplasts / Permanent vacuole / Cell wall

cards.front: List the four steps for preparing and viewing a slide under a light microscope.
cards.answer: Place thin sample on slide / Add a drop of stain / Lower coverslip at 45 degrees / Start on lowest magnification then increase
items: Start on lowest magnification then increase

cards.front: Why does the cell wall stop a plant cell bursting when water enters by osmosis?
cards.answer: It is made of cellulose and strengthens and supports the cell, resisting the pressure from water entering.

cards.front: Why are mitochondria so efficient at transferring energy, according to electron microscope images?
cards.answer: Their inner membranes are folded into cristae, which increase the surface area for respiration enzymes.

cards.front: Name the four poetic forms the lesson describes besides free verse.
cards.answer: Sonnet / Dramatic monologue / Ballad / Lyric

cards.front: Why might a poet choose free verse instead of a regular form?
cards.answer: Usually because the content is irregular, unpredictable, or emotionally raw.

cards.front: Why can a sudden breakdown in a poem's regular rhythm be significant?
cards.answer: It might mirror a shift in emotion, an interruption, or a moment of crisis.

cards.front: What effect does a mid-line full stop (caesura) create?
cards.answer: It is particularly dramatic, disrupting the flow of the line to emphasise or isolate a word.

cards.front: The lesson gives three things that drive Enid's fierce protectiveness of her daughters — name them.
cards.answer: An abusive marriage / Her mother's death and their estrangement / Racism as a Windrush immigrant
items: Her mother's death and their estrangement

cards.front: Name the two physical settings used in the exam strategy's list of key moments to prepare for Leave Taking.
cards.answer: The two physical settings / The candle symbolism

cards.front: How does Del become a mother-figure-in-waiting by the end of Leave Taking?
cards.answer: Her pregnancy makes her Mai's successor and Enid's bridge back to her Caribbean heritage.

cards.front: Why does the generational divide in Leave Taking mirror the wider Windrush experience?
cards.answer: The first generation sacrificed everything to build a life in England while the second generation questions the cost of that sacrifice.

cards.front: Name the four measures the lesson gives for reducing social and environmental harm in manufacturing.
cards.answer: Safe working conditions / Reducing pollution / Ethical sourcing / Designing for inclusivity

cards.front: How does the Fairphone show the 'Repair' R of sustainable design?
cards.answer: It has replaceable modules so users can swap a broken screen instead of buying a new phone.

cards.front: Why did the 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse matter for social footprint in design?
cards.answer: It killed over 1,100 garment workers and exposed dangerous conditions in the global textile supply chain.

cards.front: Why is reducing energy use the most effective way to lower a product's ecological footprint?
cards.answer: Because using less energy in the first place cuts impact more than switching sources or offsetting emissions afterwards.

title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah & Angels
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four roles angels perform in Muslim life, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Deliver revelations from Allah to prophets / Record every person's good and bad deeds / Welcome the righteous into paradise / Be present at the Day of Judgement
items: Deliver revelations from Allah to prophets
Record every person's good and bad deeds
Be present at the Day of Judgement

cards.front: Why do Muslims not create images of Allah or Muhammad?
cards.answer: Because Shirk (associating partners with Allah) is the worst sin, so Islamic art uses geometric patterns and calligraphy instead of depictions of God.

cards.front: How does belief in the recording angels encourage moral behaviour in Muslims today?
cards.answer: Knowing an angel is always recording their deeds acts as a deterrent, encouraging honesty and mindfulness in daily life.

cards.front: Why are angels described as central to linking together other articles of Islamic faith?
cards.answer: Without Jibril the Qur'an would not exist, and without the recording angels there would be no account of deeds for the Day of Judgement, linking prophethood, the Qur'an and the afterlife.

cards.front: Name the five settings/objects the lesson says carry symbolic weight in The Woman in Black.
cards.answer: The marshes / The fog / The house / The locked door / The rocking chair

cards.front: How does Hill structure the setting as a series of enclosures around the haunting?
cards.answer: The marshes surround the house, the house contains the nursery, and the nursery contains Jennet's grief.

cards.front: How does the graveyard near Eel Marsh House reinforce the theme of social exclusion?
cards.answer: Its neglected, overgrown state mirrors how Jennet was pushed outside respectable society and left among the forgotten dead.

cards.front: Why does Hill compare the marshes to the town of Crythin Gifford's secrets?
cards.answer: Just as the marsh hides quicksand beneath its surface, the town hides the truth about the curse beneath its silence.

cards.front: Why does dramatic irony in Acts 3-4 intensify the emotional impact of the church scene?
cards.answer: The audience knows about Don John's plot beforehand, so they watch Hero be publicly destroyed while powerless to intervene.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare place the benevolent gulling and Don John's malicious plot side by side?
cards.answer: To show how the same mechanism of tricking people through sight and sound can produce completely opposite outcomes, joy or catastrophe.

title: The Second Crusade and its failure
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Why did Louis VII's French army arrive in the Holy Land much weaker than it started?
cards.answer: It was mauled at the Cadmus mountain pass, then lack of shipping at Adalia meant most foot soldiers were left behind.

cards.front: Why did the crusaders abandon their strong position in the orchards outside Damascus?
cards.answer: They moved to a barren eastern plain with no water or food, possibly after local lords accepted bribes.

title: Performance Interpretation: Hanako Across Twenty Years
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Why should 'release moments' for Hanako be played very short and sudden?
cards.answer: Because the accommodation has become second nature, so the release is only a brief flash showing her hidden self still exists.

cards.front: How do Reiko's proxemic patterns change from early to middle scenes?
cards.answer: Early-grief Reiko moves away and closes off, while middle-scenes Reiko moves toward people, demanding to be taken seriously.

title: Exam Practice: Performer, Director and Designer
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things every performer or designer answer needs, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: A named moment / A named technique / A stated effect on the audience
items: A stated effect on the audience

cards.front: What three-step pattern keeps a design-and-context answer specific?
cards.answer: Name the design element / Name the technique or material / State the effect and link to context
items: State the effect and link to context

cards.front: Why does a thrust configuration suit staging the family reunion in Things I Know to Be True?
cards.answer: It makes the family's proxemics visible from every angle, suiting a play about a family constantly re-forming and separating.

cards.front: Why is naming a feeling like 'sad lighting' not enough in an exam answer?
cards.answer: It describes a feeling rather than naming a specific choice, such as a lantern or state, and its effect on the audience.

cards.front: The lesson gives three examples of Utterson's discretion limiting his investigation as a detective figure — what are they?
cards.answer: Refuses to open Lanyon's sealed letter / Avoids prying into Jekyll's private life / Chooses discretion over truth
items: Refuses to open Lanyon's sealed letter
Avoids prying into Jekyll's private life

cards.front: Why does Stevenson present Lanyon and Jekyll as two contrasting views of science?
cards.answer: Lanyon represents cautious, evidence-based orthodox science while Jekyll represents reckless ambition beyond accepted boundaries, and both approaches fail.

cards.front: How does the maid's reaction to the Carew murder contrast with the male characters?
cards.answer: Her emotional, swooning response contrasts with the male characters' restraint, reflecting Victorian gender expectations.

title: Weltpolitik, the Navy Laws and German society
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three insurance schemes Bismarck introduced to undercut socialism, in order.
cards.answer: Sickness insurance (1883) / Accident insurance (1884) / Old-age pensions (1889)

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson says supported or opposed the Navy Laws domestically.
cards.answer: Ruhr steel barons (Krupp, Thyssen) / Shipyard workers in the north / Patriotic middle-class Navy League members / Farmers/Junkers in the east (opposed)

cards.front: Why did the Kaiser's advisers see Weltpolitik as useful inside Germany, not just abroad?
cards.answer: A confident, imperial Germany would distract working-class voters from socialism and reassure the middle class the monarchy mattered.

cards.front: Why did passing the Navy Laws force the Kaiser to bargain with the Reichstag he distrusted?
cards.answer: The Reichstag controlled the budget, so Tirpitz needed its votes to raise the taxes needed to fund the navy.

cards.front: Name the four key pieces of legislation the lesson gives that have extended legal rights in the UK.
cards.answer: Representation of the People Act / Equal Pay Act 1970 / Race Relations Act 1976 / Human Rights Act 1998

cards.front: Why does criminal law use a higher standard of proof than civil law?
cards.answer: Because a criminal conviction can mean prison, so a higher bar protects defendants from wrongful conviction compared with civil remedies like compensation.

cards.front: Why is judicial independence essential to equality before the law?
cards.answer: Independent courts let individuals challenge state decisions, ensuring government is bound by law rather than above it in practice.

cards.front: Why does the presumption of innocence protect individuals from the power of the state?
cards.answer: Because the burden of proof lies with the prosecution, preventing governments or powerful interests from imprisoning people through accusation alone.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says humans reduce biodiversity.
cards.answer: Fish farming / Introducing non-indigenous species / Eutrophication

cards.front: Name the four abiotic factors the lesson lists as affecting ecosystems.
cards.answer: Temperature / Light / Water / Pollutants

cards.front: How does an increase in predator population lead to a later fall in predator numbers?
cards.answer: More predators eat more prey, so prey numbers fall, leaving less food, so predator numbers then decline too.

cards.front: How does eutrophication lead to fish dying?
cards.answer: Excess nutrients cause an algal bloom that blocks light, killing plants; bacteria decompose them, using up oxygen, so fish suffocate.

title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the five ways the lesson gives for reducing a carbon footprint.
cards.answer: Using renewable energy / Improving energy efficiency / Carbon capture and storage / Reducing meat consumption / Reducing travel

cards.front: Name the four consequences of global warming given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Sea level rise / More extreme weather events / Changes to ecosystems and species distribution / Impacts on agriculture
items: Changes to ecosystems and species distribution

cards.front: How did the ozone layer help more complex life evolve?
cards.answer: As oxygen levels increased, the ozone layer formed and shielded life from harmful UV radiation.

cards.front: How did water vapour in the early atmosphere form the oceans?
cards.answer: As the Earth cooled, water vapour in the atmosphere condensed and formed the oceans.

title: The Last Days of Jesus and the Passion
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What three predictions does Jesus make at the Last Supper in Mark about his disciples?
cards.answer: One of the Twelve will betray him / All of them will fall away / Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows twice
items: One of the Twelve will betray him
All of them will fall away
Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows twice

cards.front: What two questions do the High Priest and Pilate each ask Jesus at his two trials?
cards.answer: Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One? / Are you the king of the Jews?
items: Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?
Are you the king of the Jews?

cards.front: Why did Jesus face two separate trials, before the Sanhedrin and then Pilate?
cards.answer: The Sanhedrin could rule on religious law but had no power to order a death sentence, so it needed Rome to authorise the crucifixion.

cards.front: Why do some Christians see Mark's abrupt ending at 16:8 as deliberate rather than incomplete?
cards.answer: It mirrors the disciples' repeated failure throughout Mark and invites the reader to go to Galilee, tell others, and follow instead.

cards.front: Name the three displacement triggers the lesson identifies for Alvi, Nichols and Adcock.
cards.answer: Objects (clothes and jewellery) / A natural event (the hurricane) / A physical return to a homeland
items: A physical return to a homeland

cards.front: Name the two uncomfortable natural details Adcock notes about Stewart Island.
cards.answer: Sandflies bite the children / A seagull attacks

cards.front: Why does the speaker in 'Presents from my Aunts in Pakistan' feel conflicted about the gifts?
cards.answer: The Pakistani clothes are beautiful but don't suit her English life, as she longed for denim and corduroy instead.

cards.front: Why does Nichols address Caribbean storm gods like Huracan, Oya and Shango in the poem?
cards.answer: To invoke her cultural heritage and spiritual traditions, connecting the English storm to her Caribbean childhood.

title: The Particle Model and States of Matter
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the six changes of state described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Melting / Boiling/evaporation / Condensing / Freezing / Sublimation / Deposition

cards.front: Name the four limitations of the simple particle model given in the lesson. (Higher Tier)
cards.answer: Treats particles as identical spheres / Ignores forces of attraction / Ignores different particle sizes / Cannot explain different melting/boiling points

cards.front: Why does a liquid have a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
cards.answer: Particles stay close together but slide past each other, so they flow to fill the bottom of a container.

cards.front: Why is energy absorbed from the surroundings during melting and boiling?
cards.answer: Energy is needed to break the forces of attraction holding particles together so they can move more freely.

cards.front: Name the three areas of PIES that sickle cell disease is described as affecting.
cards.answer: Physical wellbeing through pain and tiredness / Emotional wellbeing through frustration and anxiety about crises / Social wellbeing through isolation from hospital stays/absences
items: Physical wellbeing through pain and tiredness
Emotional wellbeing through frustration and anxiety about crises
Social wellbeing through isolation from hospital stays/absences

cards.front: What four risk factors does the lesson give for cardiovascular disease (CVD)?
cards.answer: High blood pressure / Smoking / Poor diet / Lack of exercise

cards.front: How does anxiety affect a person's overall PIES development?
cards.answer: It can stop a person socialising, attending work or school, or enjoying daily activities, affecting all PIES areas.

cards.front: Why can sensory impairments lead to social isolation?
cards.answer: They cause challenges in communication, accessing information, and navigating the environment, which can isolate a person without support.

cards.front: Name the three women who appear in Chapters 1-4 of the novella.
cards.answer: The young girl Hyde tramples / The old woman who keeps his Soho rooms / The maidservant who witnesses the Carew murder
items: The old woman who keeps his Soho rooms
The maidservant who witnesses the Carew murder

cards.front: Why does Stevenson make Hyde's ugliness impossible for characters to describe exactly?
cards.answer: It suggests his wrongness is spiritual rather than physical, and that recognising evil is instinct, not rational observation.

cards.front: Name three ways Dickens shows the Ghost of Christmas Present symbolising abundance, openness and peace in Stave 3.
cards.answer: Torch shaped like a cornucopia / Bare 'capacious breast' / Empty, rusted scabbard

cards.front: Why does Dickens have the Ghost say 'beware this boy' about Ignorance most of all?
cards.answer: Because society's wilful blindness to poverty is more dangerous than poverty itself, leading to 'Doom' if unaddressed.

cards.front: How does Dickens use light and darkness in Stave 3 to hint at Scrooge's redemption?
cards.answer: Scrooge's once dark, bare room now blazes with light and warmth, showing him being drawn out of darkness towards truth and change.

cards.front: Why does Dickens describe the Cratchits' small pudding and cheap goose as if they were treasures?
cards.answer: To show that Christmas joy comes from love and togetherness rather than money, despite the family's poverty.

title: Opposition to the Reformation: More, Fisher and Barton
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What did Cromwell's royal injunctions of 1536 and 1538 order every parish to do (three requirements)?
cards.answer: Acquire an English Bible / Teach Pater Noster, Creed and Commandments in English / Keep parish registers of births, marriages, deaths
items: Teach Pater Noster, Creed and Commandments in English
Keep parish registers of births, marriages, deaths

cards.front: Why did Cromwell force Elizabeth Barton to confess publicly at Paul's Cross in November 1533?
cards.answer: To discredit her prophecies as fabricated and stop her visions fuelling Catholic opposition to the annulment.

cards.front: Why was Fisher's execution such a shock across Catholic Europe?
cards.answer: Because it was extremely rare for a sitting bishop and newly created cardinal to be executed in early modern Europe.

cards.front: Why did More's strategy of legal silence over the Oath of Succession ultimately fail?
cards.answer: Because the 1534 Treason Act made denying the supremacy a capital offence, so silence was not accepted as compliance.

cards.front: Name the five characters the lesson says represent different responses to the passion-vs-duty tension.
cards.answer: Jane (balanced synthesis) / Rochester (excessive passion) / St John (excessive duty) / Helen (passive faith) / Bertha (passion denied outlet)

cards.front: Why is Mr Brocklehurst Brontë's sharpest critique of institutional religion?
cards.answer: He starves and humiliates the girls at Lowood while his own family lives in luxury, exposing hypocritical abuse of religious authority.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Fairfax warn Jane about marrying Rochester?
cards.answer: She understands the social reality that gentlemen of Rochester's station do not usually marry their governesses, a gulf Jane's passion overlooks.

cards.front: How does Jane combine passion and principle when she leaves Rochester?
cards.answer: She refuses to suppress her feelings for him but still leaves rather than compromise her morals by becoming his mistress.

cards.front: Why did Gibson's research on pilots landing planes support his direct theory?
cards.answer: It showed perception working accurately in real natural environments, giving the theory high ecological validity.

cards.front: Why does the case of patient S.B. challenge Gibson's direct theory?
cards.answer: S.B. struggled to perceive depth and form after vision was restored, suggesting prior experience is needed for perception.

title: Factors Influencing Design: Energy, Lifespan and Maintenance
subject: engineering-aqa

cards.front: Name the two forms of planned obsolescence the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Functional obsolescence / Aesthetic obsolescence

cards.front: Name three ways of protecting steel components from corrosion given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Galvanising (zinc coating) / Painting / Anodising (aluminium) / Stainless steel / Plastic enclosures

cards.front: Why is biomass energy described as roughly carbon-neutral?
cards.answer: Burning biomass releases CO2, but if it is regrown the carbon is re-absorbed over the growth cycle.

cards.front: Why does designing for a finite engineered lifespan let engineers reduce material use and cost?
cards.answer: They don't need to over-engineer components beyond what the expected service conditions demand for that lifespan.

title: Arguments for the Existence of God
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the three main classical arguments for God's existence covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cosmological argument / Teleological argument / Moral argument

cards.front: What three weaknesses does the lesson give against the cosmological argument?
cards.answer: Hume: universe could be uncaused / Russell: series fallacy / Only proves uncaused cause, not a personal God
items: Only proves uncaused cause, not a personal God

cards.front: Why did Bertrand Russell think the cosmological argument is a fallacy?
cards.answer: Because it wrongly assumes that if every member of a series has a cause, the whole series must have one too.

cards.front: How did Immanuel Kant argue that moral reasoning leads us to postulate God?
cards.answer: Because obligation to seek the highest good requires conditions where virtue and happiness align, implying an afterlife and a God guaranteeing justice.

cards.front: Why does Brontë let Jane win over Blanche Ingram despite Blanche's wealth and title?
cards.answer: To show Jane's moral worth is not dictated by class or gender, unlike the rich but morally empty Blanche.

cards.front: Why is the Gothic setting of the red room and third storey used beyond decoration?
cards.answer: Brontë uses Gothic conventions to make a psychological point about repressed emotion, not just for effect.

title: Election 1994 and the new South Africa
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three main parties and their vote shares in the 1994 South African election.
cards.answer: ANC 62.6 per cent / NP 20.4 per cent / Inkatha Freedom Party 10.5 per cent

cards.front: Why did Joe Slovo argue the ANC should accept the sunset clauses?
cards.answer: He argued the compromise was the necessary price of achieving a peaceful transition to democracy.

cards.front: Why did the TRC offer amnesty instead of prosecuting people for apartheid-era crimes?
cards.answer: It was a deliberate compromise, neither amnesty without accountability nor prosecution without acknowledgement, designed for a society needing to function together.

cards.front: How did the 5 per cent and 20 per cent vote thresholds shape the Government of National Unity's cabinet?
cards.answer: Any party winning at least 5 per cent got cabinet seats, and any party winning 20 per cent could name a Deputy President.

cards.front: Why does Macbeth's mind turn to murder as soon as Ross confirms he is Thane of Cawdor?
cards.answer: The first prophecy has come true instantly, making him believe the throne is also within reach, so he starts thinking of murder.

cards.front: How does Lady Macbeth attack Macbeth's masculinity to persuade him to kill Duncan?
cards.answer: She calls him a coward and claims he was only a man when he 'durst' act, implying his manhood depends on going through with murder.

cards.front: Name the three reasons Macbeth lists against murdering Duncan in his Act 1 Scene 7 soliloquy.
cards.answer: Duncan is his king / Duncan is his kinsman / Duncan is his guest

cards.front: Name the seven main objectives businesses set, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Survival / Profit maximisation / Growth / Market share / Customer satisfaction / Social and ethical objectives / Shareholder value

cards.front: Why do objectives help a business decide what to prioritise when cash is tight?
cards.answer: Objectives answer which project matters most before pressure hits, so the business knows what to cut first.

cards.front: Why did many UK retailers drop growth targets during the 2023 cost-of-living squeeze?
cards.answer: External pressure on cash and customers pushed them back to focusing on survival and keeping existing customers.

cards.front: Why are HDDs slower to access data than SSDs?
cards.answer: HDDs rely on mechanical parts physically moving into position, while SSDs have no moving parts and access data electronically.

cards.front: Why is embedded software typically simpler and more rigorously tested than general-purpose software?
cards.answer: Reliability is critical since a crash could be dangerous or seriously disruptive, so the software has fewer features and less chance of unexpected states.

title: Conflicting Interests in the British Mandate, c1920–45
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three Jewish armed groups that campaigned against British targets after 1945.
cards.answer: Haganah / Irgun / Lehi

cards.front: What three contradictory wartime promises did Britain make about the Middle East?
cards.answer: McMahon-Hussein correspondence to Arab leaders / Sykes-Picot Agreement with France / Balfour Declaration to Zionist leaders

cards.front: Why did the 1936–39 Arab revolt make Britain rethink the Balfour promise?
cards.answer: Crushing the revolt took around 25,000 troops, and the violence forced policymakers to question whether the promise was achievable.

cards.front: Why did Britain lack the will to enforce the 1939 immigration cap after 1945?
cards.answer: Britain emerged from the war economically exhausted, dependent on US loans, and lacking the troops or will to enforce it.

title: Napoleonic wars and Victorian imperial conflicts
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three main effects of the wars with France (1793-1815) on British military organisation and finance, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Army expanded enormously / Navy consumed vast resources / Militia Acts brought compulsory home service
items: Militia Acts brought compulsory home service

cards.front: Why did the name 'Peterloo' cause such outrage in 1819?
cards.answer: It bitterly echoed Waterloo — the men who had defeated Napoleon were being cut down by soldiers on unarmed civilians at home.

cards.front: How did the poor fitness of army recruits in the Second Boer War lead to welfare reform?
cards.answer: Many working-class recruits were too unhealthy to serve, raising questions about the state's duty to maintain public health, feeding into Liberal welfare reforms.

cards.front: Why did Britain reach unprecedented levels of government spending and taxation during the wars with France?
cards.answer: Mass mobilisation of the Army and Navy and compulsory militia service required funding on a scale never seen before.

title: School Rules, Homework and Future Plans
subject: spanish-aqa

cards.front: Name the six Spanish structures for obligation, prohibition and ability given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Se debe (one must) / No se debe (one must not) / Se puede (one can) / No se puede (one cannot) / Tengo que (I have to) / Debo (I must)

cards.front: Name the five irregular future tense stems given in the lesson.
cards.answer: tener → tendr- / hacer → har- / ir → ir- / poder → podr- / querer → querr-

cards.front: Why is 'Los deberes son difíciles' correct rather than 'El deber es difícil'?
cards.answer: Because 'los deberes' (homework) is always plural in Spanish, even though homework is singular in English.

cards.front: How is the simple future tense formed in Spanish?
cards.answer: By adding the endings -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án to the whole infinitive of the verb.

title: Catholic Teaching on Death, the Afterlife and Eschatology
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three sacraments the Catholic Church provides for the dying.
cards.answer: Sacrament of the Sick (anointing) / Confession (Reconciliation) / Viaticum (Eucharist as food for the journey)
items: Viaticum (Eucharist as food for the journey)

cards.front: The lesson gives two foundations for the Catholic rejection of euthanasia. What are they?
cards.answer: Sanctity of human life / Theological significance of suffering

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching say deliberately ending life is unacceptable, even though refusing extraordinary treatment is allowed?
cards.answer: Refusing extraordinary means lets death happen naturally, but euthanasia directly and intentionally causes death, violating the sanctity of life.

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church teach that suffering does not have to be avoided at all costs?
cards.answer: Suffering can be redemptive when united with Christ's own suffering, as developed in Salvifici Doloris.

title: Bhangra and Fusion: Dhol, Chaal and Cross-Cultural Production
subject: music-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four checklist questions the lesson gives for identifying bhangra-fusion features in an unfamiliar extract.
cards.answer: Is there a strong, driving drum pattern like a dhol / Can you hear syncopation suggesting a chaal rhythm / Is there a twangy tumbi or reedy alghoza melodic line / Is the texture layered with acoustic and electronic sounds
items: Is there a strong, driving drum pattern like a dhol
Can you hear syncopation suggesting a chaal rhythm
Is there a twangy tumbi or reedy alghoza melodic line
Is the texture layered with acoustic and electronic sounds

cards.front: Name the four traditional instruments the lesson says feed into bhangra fusion alongside the dhol.
cards.answer: Tumbi / Alghoza / Dholki / Dhol

cards.front: How does the chaal rhythm create its characteristic bouncing, danceable feel?
cards.answer: It uses syncopation, placing accents unevenly on beats and off-beats rather than landing squarely on every beat.

cards.front: How do producers typically layer traditional and electronic elements to create bhangra fusion?
cards.answer: An acoustic traditional layer like dhol, tumbi and Punjabi vocals sits alongside a produced electronic layer of synth bass, programmed beats and samples.

cards.front: Name the four key security risks the lesson gives for IoE devices.
cards.answer: Data interception / Unauthorised device control / Privacy violation / Cascading attacks

cards.front: Name three disadvantages the lesson gives for IoE, besides cyber-security risk and privacy concerns.
cards.answer: Fails without internet connectivity / Interoperability issues between manufacturers / High cost of infrastructure

cards.front: Why do IoE devices create wider attack surfaces than traditional IT systems?
cards.answer: They include devices like smart light bulbs and fridges that were never designed with security in mind, with minimal built-in protection.

cards.front: Why can compromising one IoE device lead to a cascading attack?
cards.answer: Because access to one device gives an attacker a foothold to move across the entire connected network.

title: One God, the Gurus and Sikh Beliefs about Humanity
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the eight qualities of God described in the Mool Mantar (besides being one and known through the Guru's grace).
cards.answer: Truth (satnam) / The creator (kartapurkh) / Without fear (nirbhau) / Without hate (nirvair) / Timeless in form (akal murat) / Beyond birth and death (ajooni) / Self-existent (saibhang)

cards.front: How does a person become a manmukh rather than a gurmukh, according to Sikh teaching?
cards.answer: They become trapped in haumai (ego), leading to attachment, pride and self-interest, which generate bad karma and further rebirth.

cards.front: Why is human birth seen as a precious and crucial opportunity in Sikhism?
cards.answer: The soul passes through many forms of existence, and human life is the stage where it can choose to turn towards God and seek mukti.

cards.front: Why is God described as self-revealing in Sikhism?
cards.answer: Because humans cannot discover God through unaided effort or reason alone, so God reveals himself through grace and the Guru.

title: The Incarnation, the Paschal Mystery, Salvation and Eschatology
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Why must Jesus be both fully divine and fully human, according to Catholic teaching?
cards.answer: He must be fully divine to offer a sacrifice of infinite worth and fully human to represent all humanity in it.

cards.front: Why do Catholics believe the events of the Paschal Mystery actually achieve salvation rather than just symbolise it?
cards.answer: Jesus's suffering and death pay the debt owed by human sin, and his resurrection proves death has been defeated.

cards.front: Why do Catholics pray for the dead, especially at funerals and on All Souls' Day?
cards.answer: Because they believe in purgatory, where those who die in God's grace but aren't fully purified undergo further purification.

cards.front: What three states does Catholic eschatology teach a soul may experience after death?
cards.answer: Heaven / Hell / Purgatory

cards.front: Why does Priestley use Sheila to represent the younger generation?
cards.answer: Because she moves from guilt to genuine understanding, showing the young are capable of learning, changing and building a better society.

cards.front: How does Sheila's character arc begin in the play?
cards.answer: She starts as privileged and shallow, but her response to the Inspector's revelations moves her toward genuine remorse and moral understanding.

title: Core Muslim Beliefs and the Nature of Allah
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four holy books (Kutub) that Muslims believe Allah revealed, with the prophet each was given to.
cards.answer: Qur'an - Muhammad / Tawrat - Musa (Moses) / Zabur - Dawud (David) / Injil - Isa (Jesus)

cards.front: Why do Muslims reject the Christian belief that Jesus is the Son of God?
cards.answer: Islam affirms Isa as a great prophet and the Messiah but says calling him divine violates Tawhid and counts as shirk.

cards.front: Why does the belief in Adalat mean humans have real free will?
cards.answer: Because Allah always acts justly, a just God must leave room for genuine moral choice so humans can be fairly held accountable.

title: Living standards, fashion and the rise of the gentry
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name three changes in middle-class living standards during Elizabeth's reign, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Diet improved with meat and white bread / Pewter replaced wooden tableware / Chairs replaced benches / Feather mattresses replaced straw / Demand grew for books, clocks and mirrors
items: Diet improved with meat and white bread
Demand grew for books, clocks and mirrors

cards.front: Name three Poor Laws passed during Elizabeth's reign, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: 1572 Poor Law / 1576 Poor Law / 1598 Poor Law

cards.front: Why did the growth of London create new problems for the regime?
cards.answer: Its rapid growth to around 200,000 people brought overcrowded slums, plague and visible poverty that alarmed the government.

cards.front: Why do historians see the weak enforcement of sumptuary laws as significant?
cards.answer: Gentry and merchants kept dressing above their rank despite the laws, showing the social hierarchy was becoming blurred.

cards.front: What are the four steps of the method for the close extract analysis task?
cards.answer: Read the extract twice / Select 3-4 key quotations / Identify technique, quote, analyse, explain effect / Keep focus tightly on AO2
items: Identify technique, quote, analyse, explain effect

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare treat Malvolio's social ambition differently from Viola's class transgression?
cards.answer: Viola is noble by birth so her social mobility is accepted, while Malvolio is a servant so his ambition is punished as overreaching.

cards.front: Why does the play suggest love in Twelfth Night is based on projection rather than real knowledge?
cards.answer: Characters love idealised images or fictions of others, like Orsino loving an idealised Olivia and Olivia loving the fiction of Cesario.

cards.front: How does Malvolio's transformation show identity as performative rather than fixed?
cards.answer: Wearing yellow stockings turns him from a stern steward into a grinning fool, showing identity is constructed by appearance and how others see us.

cards.front: Name the four minor/supporting characters the lesson discusses alongside the Boone family and Siobhan.
cards.answer: Mrs Shears / Mrs Alexander / Roger Shears / Reverend Peters

cards.front: Why did Ed's confession about killing Wellington and lying about Judy uniquely devastate his relationship with Christopher?
cards.answer: Christopher's literal commitment to truth means he cannot reframe Ed's lies as protective, so a lie is always just a lie.

cards.front: Why is Siobhan narrating Christopher's book in the play a significant change from Haddon's novel?
cards.answer: In the novel Siobhan only encourages Christopher to write it, but in the play she gives his written voice theatrical presence.

cards.front: How does Mrs Alexander's disclosure about Judy's affair function dramatically, given she isn't malicious?
cards.answer: She assumes Christopher already knows, so her casual disclosure unwittingly triggers his investigation taking a personal turn.

cards.front: Name the four typical speeds given for walking, running, cycling and a car in town.
cards.answer: walking ~1.5 m/s / running ~3 m/s / cycling ~6 m/s / car in town ~13 m/s

cards.front: Why do falling objects and real vehicles experience non-uniform acceleration?
cards.answer: Resistive forces like air resistance increase with speed, reducing the resultant force and therefore the acceleration.

cards.front: How is the instantaneous speed found at a point on a curved distance–time graph?
cards.answer: By drawing a tangent to the curve at that point and calculating its gradient.

cards.front: Why does Richard still obey Phil even though he objects when John Tate threatens him?
cards.answer: Richard's brief objection shows how few people ever refuse, mirroring Milgram's finding that most participants obeyed anyway.

cards.front: How does Kelly's fragmented, overlapping dialogue style reflect the group's guilt?
cards.answer: It creates naturalistic teenage speech but also reflects the group's inability to communicate honestly about what they have done.

cards.front: Name the eight question types described in this unit, from lowest to highest marks.
cards.answer: 2-mark Source Comprehension / 4-mark Describe Two Features / 5-mark Source Utility / 6-mark Cause/Consequence / 8-mark Significance or Change / 10-mark Compare Interpretations

cards.front: Why does the Winter of Discontent (1978-79) count as significant 'over time', not just at the time?
cards.answer: Its images became part of a lasting political narrative justifying Thatcher's union legislation and permanently transformed British industrial relations.

title: Sacraments, the Mass and Catholic Worship
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four places of pilgrimage named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Jerusalem / Lourdes / Rome / Walsingham

cards.front: What are the two parts of the Mass's structure given in the lesson?
cards.answer: Liturgy of the Word / Liturgy of the Eucharist

cards.front: Why is the Eucharist called the 'source and summit' of Catholic life, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It is the source because all sacramental life flows from it, and the summit because all Catholic living is directed towards it.

cards.front: How does the Reformed/memorialist view of the Lord's Supper differ from Catholic teaching on the Eucharist?
cards.answer: Memorialism sees it as a memorial meal recalling Christ's death, with Christ not physically present, unlike Catholic transubstantiation.

cards.front: The title 'Leave Taking' carries at least three meanings in Scene 8 — what are they?
cards.answer: Enid's original departure from Jamaica / the daughters' leave-taking (Del and Viv) / leave-taking from shame

cards.front: Why does the return to Mai's Deptford bedsit for the final scene matter structurally?
cards.answer: It shows the Caribbean spiritual world Enid tried to exclude has not been left behind but hosts the family's key reckoning.

cards.front: Why does Pinnock avoid a neat happy ending in Leave Taking?
cards.answer: Because she does not pretend one conversation can undo decades of suppression, Enid's grief, or the racism that drove her assimilation.

cards.front: Name the four prescribed texts this lesson uses to explore the theme of hospitality.
cards.answer: Ovid's Baucis and Philemon / Ovid's Lycaon / Pliny's letter / Martial's epigram

cards.front: Why does Ovid say Baucis and Philemon's plain earthenware meal still impressed Jupiter and Mercury?
cards.answer: Because what mattered was their generous, willing spirit, not the value of the food or dishes they served.

cards.front: Why did Jupiter destroy Lycaon's house and turn him into a wolf?
cards.answer: Lycaon tried to murder his guest and served him human flesh, so his punishment matched his savage, animal-like crime.

cards.front: How does Pliny's treatment of his freedmen guests contrast with the mean host he describes?
cards.answer: Pliny treats his freedmen as equal fellow diners at table, unlike the host who separated guests by rank into three wine grades.

title: End of the reign: succession, decline and legacy
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five problems the lesson gives that created a mood of uncertainty in Elizabeth's final decade (1593-1603)
cards.answer: Expensive war in Ireland / Continuing conflict with Spain / Harvest failures in the 1590s / Rising prices / Tensions at court / Aging Queen refusing to name a successor
items: Aging Queen refusing to name a successor

cards.front: Why did Essex's rebellion happen after his failure in Ireland?
cards.answer: He made an unauthorised truce with Tyrone, returned without permission, lost his offices and wine licence, and grew desperate, so he tried to raise London against his court enemies.

cards.front: How did the death of Lord Burghley change the dynamic of Elizabeth's court?
cards.answer: Without his steady, cautious hand, factional rivalry intensified between Robert Cecil's cautious group and the aggressive faction around the Earl of Essex.

cards.front: Why does Claudio choose the church, in front of the whole congregation, to reject Hero?
cards.answer: He chooses the most public venue possible to maximise her humiliation, performing his outrage as if he were the victim.

cards.front: Why can Beatrice not challenge Claudio herself and must ask Benedick to act?
cards.answer: The patriarchal system denies women the right to act, so she can only demand a man defend Hero's honour on her behalf.

cards.front: Why does Macbeth arrange Banquo's murder by hiring killers instead of acting himself in Act 3, Scene 1?
cards.answer: He has shifted from reluctant murderer to calculating tyrant, planning coolly and killing without Lady Macbeth's involvement.

cards.front: How does the natural imagery of Macbeth's 'fruitless crown' contrast with Duncan's earlier imagery?
cards.answer: Duncan used growth imagery ('I have begun to plant thee') showing natural order, while Macbeth's barren imagery shows his reign is sterile.

cards.front: Name the six causes of Amazon deforestation given in the lesson (other than cattle ranching and soya farming).
cards.answer: Logging (legal and illegal) / Mineral extraction / Road building / Hydroelectric dams / Settlement and population growth

cards.front: Name the four impacts of Amazon deforestation the lesson describes (besides climate change).
cards.answer: Soil erosion / Water cycle disruption / Biodiversity loss / Indigenous communities losing land and lives
items: Indigenous communities losing land and lives

cards.front: Why does deforestation disrupt the water cycle in the Amazon?
cards.answer: Fewer trees means less transpiration, which reduces rainfall both locally and across the continent.

cards.front: Why is enforcing deforestation laws so difficult in the Amazon?
cards.answer: The Amazon is vast, remote and has few roads, loggers often have political backing, and local people need the income deforestation provides.

title: Brahman, Atman and the Hindu Gods
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why does the Advaita Vedanta school say atman and Brahman are ultimately one and the same?
cards.answer: It teaches the individual soul is not separate from the universal soul, summarised as 'Tat Tvam Asi' (Thou art that).

cards.front: Why does Vishnu descend to earth as an avatar according to the Bhagavad Gita?
cards.answer: He manifests whenever righteousness declines and unrighteousness rises, to restore moral balance in the world.

cards.front: Why does Hindu teaching say Ganesh has an elephant head?
cards.answer: Shiva unknowingly severed Ganesh's head and then replaced it with the first head available, that of an elephant.

title: Nervous System, Reflexes and the Eye
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: What are the five steps of a reflex arc pathway, in order?
cards.answer: Stimulus / Receptor / Sensory neurone / Relay neurone / Motor neurone / Effector

cards.front: The eye has two muscles in the iris that control pupil size in different light levels. What are they and when do they contract?
cards.answer: Circular muscles contract in bright light / Radial muscles contract in dim light
items: Circular muscles contract in bright light
Radial muscles contract in dim light

cards.front: Why are reflexes so much faster than normal conscious responses?
cards.answer: Reflexes bypass the brain and pass through the spinal cord instead, so the brain only learns about it after the response has begun.

cards.front: How does damage to the myelin sheath, as in multiple sclerosis, affect the nervous system?
cards.answer: It removes the insulation around the axon, which slows down impulse conduction.

title: Effect on the Audience: Evaluation Beyond Description
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Why can audience response, like a sudden silence, count as evidence in an evaluation?
cards.answer: Because it is an observable, real collective reaction that confirms whether a specific theatrical choice actually achieved its intended effect.

cards.front: Why did the top-light and slow circling of the ensemble around the kneeling protagonist succeed, according to the worked example?
cards.answer: It communicated the character's willing surrender to forces beyond their control, making them both centre of the world and its prisoner.

cards.front: Name the four landmark laws that transformed women's legal position between 1967 and 1975.
cards.answer: Abortion Act (1967) / Equal Pay Act (1970, in force 1975) / Sex Discrimination Act (1975) / Employment Protection Act (1975)

cards.front: Why did pay gaps persist even after the Equal Pay Act came into force?
cards.answer: Many workplaces were sex-segregated, with men and women doing different jobs on different pay scales, so the Act was hard to enforce.

cards.front: Why did the contraceptive pill matter for women's working lives from 1961?
cards.answer: It gave women reliable control over family planning, enabling more women to stay in or return to work and plan around choices rather than pregnancies.

cards.front: Why was Margaret Thatcher's election as Prime Minister in 1979 seen as debatable for women's progress?
cards.answer: Because it provoked debate over whether one woman reaching the top signified real structural change, given only 19 women MPs existed.

cards.front: Name the three buses on the motherboard that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Data bus / Address bus / Control bus

cards.front: Why is a GPU much faster than a CPU at rendering graphics?
cards.answer: A GPU has thousands of simpler cores working in parallel, letting it do the same pixel calculation on many pieces of data at once.

cards.front: Why does a wider data bus improve system performance?
cards.answer: A wider bus has more parallel wires, so more bits can be transferred between components in one go.

cards.front: What does the control bus carry between the CPU and other components?
cards.answer: Control signals from the CU, such as read or write signals telling RAM whether to accept or send data.

cards.front: Why is T_ON always longer than T_OFF in a standard 555 astable circuit?
cards.answer: The capacitor charges through R1 and R2 in series but discharges through only R2, making charging slower than discharging.

cards.front: How do you find the amplitude of a waveform from an oscilloscope trace?
cards.answer: Count the vertical divisions from the bottom of the waveform to the top of the HIGH level and multiply by V/div.

cards.front: The lesson gives four common exam errors in 555 astable questions. Name them.
cards.answer: Mishandling k and μ multipliers / Multiplying R1 by 2 instead of R2 / Giving amplitude in ms or period in volts / Confusing peak-to-peak and amplitude
items: Multiplying R1 by 2 instead of R2
Giving amplitude in ms or period in volts

cards.front: Why does a 555 astable need a diode to achieve a 1:1 mark-space ratio?
cards.answer: Without a diode R1 always adds extra charging time, so T_ON exceeds T_OFF unless R1 is zero, which would damage the IC.

cards.front: Name the five key drivers of change in family structure identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Secularisation / Feminism and changing status of women / Economic factors / Technology / Immigration and cultural change
items: Feminism and changing status of women

cards.front: Name the Rapoports' five types of family diversity (besides organisational and cohort, already covered).
cards.answer: Organisational / Cultural / Social class / Life cycle / Cohort

cards.front: How did the availability of reliable contraception since the 1960s change family structure?
cards.answer: It separated sex from reproduction, making cohabitation more common and contributing to declining birth rates and smaller families.

cards.front: Why has the age of first marriage risen since the 1970s?
cards.answer: High housing costs and lack of affordable independent housing lead young adults to delay family formation and marriage.

cards.front: Name the six characters Sherriff uses to form his cross-section of the officer class in Journey's End.
cards.answer: Stanhope, the heroic wreck / Osborne, the steady mentor / Raleigh, the innocent newcomer / Trotter, the cheerful pragmatist / Hibbert, the man at breaking point / The Colonel, detached authority
items: Hibbert, the man at breaking point

cards.front: Why does Sherriff choose to kill Osborne, the most universally loved character, during the raid?
cards.answer: To show that war does not spare the good, making Osborne's death the play's emotional turning point.

cards.front: Why does Stanhope threaten to shoot Hibbert instead of showing him sympathy, even though Stanhope feels the same fear?
cards.answer: Because the difference between them is not bravery but that Stanhope's sense of duty is stronger than Hibbert's.

cards.front: How does Raleigh's reaction to Osborne's death reveal the limits of his understanding of front-line life?
cards.answer: His refusal to eat at dinner shows genuine moral feeling but reveals he cannot understand the coping mechanisms soldiers need.

cards.front: Name the three conditions used in the Haber process to make ammonia.
cards.answer: Temperature 450°C / Pressure 200 atmospheres / Iron catalyst

cards.front: Why is 200 atmospheres pressure used in the Haber process?
cards.answer: There are fewer gas moles on the product side, so higher pressure shifts equilibrium forward, increasing ammonia yield.

cards.front: Why does the iron catalyst not change the yield of ammonia in the Haber process?
cards.answer: It speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged.

cards.front: Why is 450°C used in the Haber process instead of a lower temperature?
cards.answer: A lower temperature would give more ammonia but make the reaction rate too slow, so 450°C is a compromise.

title: Derivations and the Short Final Section
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: In the grammar-analysis option, which verb tenses and form are the verbs limited to?
cards.answer: present indicative active / imperfect indicative active / perfect indicative active / present active infinitive

cards.front: Why must you know a Latin word's exact core meaning to answer a derivation question well?
cards.answer: A vague guess at the Latin meaning makes it much harder to justify why the English word means what it does.

cards.front: Name the six stages of Silas's character arc, in order.
cards.answer: Trust / Betrayal / Isolation / Gold-hoarding / Loss / Love (Eppie) and community reintegration

cards.front: Why does Dunsey's theft of Silas's gold end up producing positive events in the novel?
cards.answer: Without the theft Silas would never have been forced out of his isolation, so Eppie's arrival could not become transformative.

cards.front: How does Eliot use Dolly Winthrop's faith to contrast with Lantern Yard's religion?
cards.answer: Dolly cannot explain doctrine but trusts things will work out if people do their best, making her faith flexible and kind unlike Lantern Yard's rigid, manipulable religion.

title: Practitioner Application: Brecht in Russell's Stage Directions
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the five staging conventions of Brecht's epic theatre described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Narrator commenting from outside the action / songs that interrupt to reflect on action / placards announcing events beforehand / visible stage lighting rig / performers stepping outside roles to address audience
items: Narrator commenting from outside the action
songs that interrupt to reflect on action
performers stepping outside roles to address audience

cards.front: Why does the Narrator's spatial position in a thrust or in-the-round staging reinforce his Greek-chorus function?
cards.answer: It lets him move between audience and acting area so the audience never knows whose side he is on, keeping him both storyteller and judge.

cards.front: Why is 'Tell Me It's Not True' described as an act of denial that becomes a lament?
cards.answer: Sung over her sons' bodies, it is so clearly futile that the audience cannot receive it as a prayer, only as grief.

cards.front: How might a lighting designer use a colour wash to signal a song's Brechtian interruption in Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: A whole-stage colour wash removes local realism and places every performer in the same theatrical light, showing the scene has paused for comment.

cards.front: What three symptom groups does the ICD use to classify schizophrenia's clinical characteristics?
cards.answer: Positive symptoms / Negative symptoms / Disorganised speech and behaviour

cards.front: How does an overactive dopamine system lead to positive symptoms in schizophrenia?
cards.answer: Neurons fire more or receptors become oversensitive, so excess dopamine overstimulates brain pathways for perception and thought.
