cards.front: Why did Daniel, Weinberger, Jones et al (1991) give participants amphetamine during the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test?
cards.answer: To increase dopamine release and test whether raising dopamine improved prefrontal blood flow and task performance.

cards.front: Why is it hard to know if social class causes schizophrenia or schizophrenia causes low social class?
cards.answer: Most evidence linking schizophrenia and social class is correlational, so it cannot show which came first.

title: The Atlantic Slave Trade and Plantation Slavery
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three goods did British ships carry back from the Americas on the final leg of the Atlantic trade triangle, according to the lesson's Key Fact?
cards.answer: Sugar / Rum / Tobacco / Rice

cards.front: The lesson gives four differences between indentured servitude and chattel slavery. What made indentured servitude different from chattel slavery?
cards.answer: Time-limited, not lifelong / Voluntary, not forced for life / Ended in freedom / Not inherited by children

cards.front: Why did Chesapeake planters shift from indentured servants to enslaved Africans by the early eighteenth century?
cards.answer: Rising British wages after 1660 cut the supply of indentured servants, and after Bacon's Rebellion elites feared arming poor whites, so they turned to permanent, inheritable enslaved labour.

cards.front: How did the task system on Carolina rice plantations differ in practice from the gang system, despite both being slavery?
cards.answer: Task system workers had a fixed daily quota and could use remaining time for themselves, but this reflected rice farming's rhythm, not any lessening of bondage.

cards.front: Name the three types of field the lesson gives that allow objects to interact at a distance without contact.
cards.answer: Gravitational fields / Magnetic fields / Electrostatic fields

cards.front: Name the two everyday examples the lesson gives of static electricity effects.
cards.answer: Sparks from a door handle after walking on carpet / Lightning from charge building in clouds
items: Sparks from a door handle after walking on carpet
Lightning from charge building in clouds

cards.front: Why is it always electrons that transfer between objects, and never protons?
cards.answer: Protons are locked inside the nucleus by the strong nuclear force, but outer electrons are held weakly and can be dislodged by friction.

cards.front: How does rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth make the rod negatively charged?
cards.answer: Friction transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod, so the rod gains electrons and becomes negatively charged.

title: Anschluss and the Reasons for Appeasement
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six pressures behind Chamberlain's decision to appease Hitler in 1938.
cards.answer: Military weakness / Imperial overstretch / Public pacifism / Lack of strong allies / Dominion opinion against war / Belief Hitler's grievances could be negotiated
items: Belief Hitler's grievances could be negotiated

cards.front: Name the three stages of Anschluss given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Berchtesgaden meeting, 12 February 1938 / Cancelled Austrian plebiscite, 9 March / Wehrmacht entry into Austria, 12 March

cards.front: Why was Britain's military weakness in 1938 a reason for appeasing Hitler?
cards.answer: Rearmament had only begun in 1936-37, so key systems like radar and fighter aircraft were not yet ready, risking defeat in war.

cards.front: Why did the Dominions' attitude push Britain towards appeasement in 1938?
cards.answer: Canada, Australia and South Africa told London they would not fight a European war that looked unjustified to them.

cards.front: Name the four main causes of uneven development given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Colonialism / Trade patterns / Natural resources / Aid

cards.front: Name the five main types of aid described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Bilateral aid / Multilateral aid / Emergency aid / Long-term development aid / NGO aid

cards.front: Why did colonial-era infrastructure fail to help colonies develop after independence?
cards.answer: Roads, railways and ports were built mainly to move raw materials to coastal export points, not to connect colonies internally.

cards.front: Why can tariffs on processed imports like roasted coffee harm LIDCs?
cards.answer: Wealthy countries put tariffs on processed goods but not raw materials, discouraging LIDCs from adding value at home.

title: Revelation, Visions and Miracles as Proof of God
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three ways Catholics believe God has progressively revealed himself throughout history.
cards.answer: Through the natural world / Through the prophets and scriptures of the Old Testament / Most completely through Jesus Christ
items: Through the prophets and scriptures of the Old Testament

cards.front: Why do Humanists say the content of visions cannot prove God exists?
cards.answer: Because a vision is a subjective, unverifiable experience whose content just reflects the visionary's own cultural expectations.

cards.front: How do Catholics respond to Hume's argument that we should always doubt miracle reports?
cards.answer: They say Hume's argument assumes the outcome before examining evidence, and verified Lourdes cases have withstood medical scrutiny.

cards.front: Name the three main left-wing critics of the New Deal mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Huey Long / Father Charles Coughlin / Francis Townsend

cards.front: Which two major New Deal programmes did the Supreme Court strike down in 1935-1936?
cards.answer: NRA (Schechter Poultry case) / AAA (United States v Butler)

cards.front: Why did the Social Security Act fail to help most Black Americans?
cards.answer: It excluded domestic servants and agricultural labourers, the two occupations employing most Black Americans, especially in the South.

cards.front: Why did Roosevelt propose the court-packing plan in 1937?
cards.answer: The Supreme Court had struck down major New Deal programmes, so he proposed adding a new justice for each sitting justice over 70 to protect his reforms.

cards.front: Name the five types of stress covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Tension / Compression / Torsion / Shear / Bending

cards.front: Why do hollow tubes resist bending and torsion better than solid rods of the same cross-sectional area?
cards.answer: Material near the centre contributes little to resisting these forces, so placing it at the outer surface where stress is highest is more efficient.

cards.front: Why are ribs added inside an injection-moulded plastic casing instead of just making the walls thicker?
cards.answer: Ribs resist bending without increasing outer wall thickness, which would cause sink marks and extend cooling time.

cards.front: Why do gussets at frame joints in timber structures prevent racking?
cards.answer: Triangular corner reinforcements resist the shear forces that would otherwise push a rectangular frame into a parallelogram.

cards.front: Name the three advantages of computer networks given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Files shared without physical media / Single internet connection shared across devices / Centralised storage makes backups easier / Users can communicate in real time
items: Single internet connection shared across devices
Users can communicate in real time

cards.front: Name the three disadvantages of computer networks given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cost of hardware setup and maintenance / Risk of spreading malware / Need for security measures
items: Cost of hardware setup and maintenance

cards.front: Why do LANs typically offer higher speeds and lower latency than WANs?
cards.answer: Because devices on a LAN are physically close together with dedicated infrastructure, unlike WANs which depend on third-party links.

cards.front: Why is fibre optic cable used for backbone connections between buildings?
cards.answer: It carries data as pulses of light, achieving very high speeds over long distances with minimal signal degradation.

cards.front: Name Kohlberg's three levels of moral development, in order.
cards.answer: Pre-conventional / Conventional / Post-conventional

cards.front: Why does a pre-operational child say a tall thin glass has 'more water' than a short wide one with the same amount?
cards.answer: They lack conservation, so they judge quantity by appearance rather than understanding it stays the same despite the shape change.

cards.front: How did Kohlberg study people's level of moral development?
cards.answer: He presented moral dilemmas, like the Heinz dilemma, and studied the reasons people gave for their answers, not just the answers.

cards.front: Why must you avoid bridging the central gap on a breadboard when placing an IC?
cards.answer: Bridging the central gap can short-circuit the IC's power pins, since the gap separates the two independent halves of connected rows.

cards.front: How does the middle section of a breadboard connect components electrically?
cards.answer: Holes are joined in short horizontal rows of five, so pushing two leads into the same row of five connects them electrically.

title: Chapters 7–10: The Last Night and Jekyll’s Statement
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why does the window scene in Chapter 7 mirror the door scene from the novel's opening?
cards.answer: Both show Utterson and Enfield witnessing something disturbing at Jekyll's house then silently agreeing not to discuss it, reinforcing Victorian repression.

cards.front: Why did the axe breaking down the laboratory door matter symbolically in Chapter 8?
cards.answer: It symbolises the violent exposure of Jekyll's secret, smashing apart the barriers between his public and private selves.

cards.front: Why did Jekyll originally design his experiment, according to his Chapter 10 confession?
cards.answer: To separate his respectable public self from his hidden, pleasure-seeking private self.

cards.front: How did Jekyll's control over his transformations change over time in Chapter 10?
cards.answer: Hyde grew stronger and more violent while Jekyll grew weaker, until transformations began happening involuntarily without the potion.

cards.front: Name the three daytime symptoms that must occur alongside poor sleep for insomnia to be diagnosed.
cards.answer: Tiredness / Irritability / Poor concentration or low mood

cards.front: How does low orexin lead to the symptoms of narcolepsy?
cards.answer: Low orexin makes the brain's sleep-wake switch unstable, letting REM features like cataplexy and hallucinations intrude into wakefulness.

cards.front: Why does insomnia often become a vicious cycle?
cards.answer: Worrying about not sleeping raises anxiety and arousal at bedtime, making sleep even less likely and causing the next poor night.

cards.front: What is the key difference between insomnia and narcolepsy?
cards.answer: Insomnia is a lack of sleep from the brain staying too alert, while narcolepsy is uncontrolled sleep from an unstable wake-sleep switch.

cards.front: The lesson gives five arguments against capital punishment now held by the Catholic Church — name them.
cards.answer: Dignity of person can't be forfeited / Execution is irreversible, risks killing innocents / Modern incarceration protects society safely / Execution prevents repentance and reform / Deterrent effect not statistically supported
items: Dignity of person can't be forfeited
Execution is irreversible, risks killing innocents

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church say forgiving an offender doesn't remove the need for punishment?
cards.answer: Forgiveness works on the personal, spiritual level, healing the victim, while justice works on the social, legal level for the common good.

cards.front: Why did the Church's teaching on capital punishment shift from acceptable to inadmissible by 2018?
cards.answer: Modern understanding of human dignity (imago Dei) made execution incompatible with the Gospel, since dignity cannot be forfeited.

cards.front: Name three group members whose reactions show cracks appearing when Phil orders Adam's killing.
cards.answer: Richard questions the plan / Lou is uneasy / Brian seems to recognise this is different
items: Brian seems to recognise this is different

cards.front: How does Cathy's willingness to kill Adam differ from reluctant obedience to Phil's order?
cards.answer: Cathy shows enthusiasm and pleasure in violence, volunteering for the worst tasks rather than being forced into it.

cards.front: Why does Kelly show the group treating Adam as a problem rather than a person in Act 3?
cards.answer: It shows their dehumanisation of him — they ask only what to do with him, never how he feels.

cards.front: Name the four unresolved tensions the lesson gives about the play's ending.
cards.answer: Don John captured but not punished / Hero returned to the same system / Claudio shows no real transformation / The honour code remains intact
items: Don John captured but not punished
Hero returned to the same system

cards.front: Why do many critics find Claudio's penance inadequate?
cards.answer: He never apologises to Hero directly, doesn't seek the truth himself, and agrees to marry a stranger sight unseen.

cards.front: How does Beatrice explain her reason for accepting Benedick's marriage proposal?
cards.answer: She claims she accepts him partly to save his life, since she was told he was in a consumption.

cards.front: Name the five main climatic regions described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Tropical (equatorial) / Hot desert / Temperate / Polar / Mediterranean

cards.front: Name the four conditions tropical storms need to develop.
cards.answer: Sea temperature at least 27°C / around 70m of warm water / low wind shear / location 5-30° from the equator

cards.front: How does the Ferrel cell create the UK's typical weather?
cards.answer: It carries air polewards near the surface, forming prevailing south-westerly winds that bring wet, mild weather.

cards.front: How does condensation make a tropical storm stronger as it forms?
cards.answer: Warm moist air rises rapidly and its water vapour condenses, releasing energy that drives the storm harder.

cards.front: How does motivation affect what we notice in a scene?
cards.answer: A strong need or desire makes us more likely to perceive things related to that need, prioritising need-relevant stimuli.

cards.front: How does emotion create a perceptual set?
cards.answer: Emotion directs attention toward mood-congruent information, so an anxious person may perceive ambiguous stimuli as threatening.

cards.front: What was the method used in Gilchrist and Nesberg's study?
cards.answer: Food/water-deprived participants viewed images at fixed brightness, then adjusted darkened images to reproduce the brightness they thought they'd seen.

title: Plant Transport: Xylem, Phloem and Transpiration
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that affect the rate of transpiration.
cards.answer: Light intensity / Temperature / Humidity / Air movement (wind)

cards.front: Name the three leaf adaptations the lesson gives that reduce unnecessary water loss.
cards.answer: Waxy cuticle on upper surface / Stomata mostly on lower surface / Guard cells close stomata when dark or water is scarce
items: Guard cells close stomata when dark/dry

cards.front: How does the cohesion-tension mechanism pull water up through the xylem?
cards.answer: Water evaporating from leaves creates tension, and cohesion between water molecules keeps a continuous column that gets sucked upward.

cards.front: Why does higher temperature increase the rate of transpiration?
cards.answer: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy, increasing evaporation and diffusion of water vapour from the leaf.

title: Aryan ideas, racial policy and the Final Solution
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five stages the lesson gives for the radicalisation of Nazi racial policy.
cards.answer: Boycotts and dismissals (1933) / Legal exclusion under Nuremberg Laws (1935) / Organised violence at Kristallnacht (1938) / Mass shootings by Einsatzgruppen (1941) / Industrial murder coordinated at Wannsee (1942)

cards.front: Name four groups other than Jews that the lesson says were targeted by the Nazi regime.
cards.answer: Sinti and Roma / Disabled Germans / Gay men / Soviet prisoners of war / Polish elites

cards.front: Why did around half of Germany's Jews fail to emigrate by September 1939?
cards.answer: They lacked the visas, money or contacts needed to leave the country.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say concentration camps and death camps should not be treated as the same thing?
cards.answer: Concentration camps held prisoners who died from labour, disease and execution, while death camps were built solely for industrial murder, mainly of Jews.

cards.front: Name the three main employers or sectors that recruited Caribbean and South Asian migrants after 1945, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: NHS (nurses) / London Transport (from 1956) / British textile towns (Bradford, Leicester, Coventry)

cards.front: Why did tens of thousands of Kenyan Asians lose their right to enter Britain freely under the 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Act?
cards.answer: The Act only allowed free entry to those with a parent or grandparent born in Britain, which most Kenyan Asians lacked despite holding British passports.

cards.front: Why did the Learie Constantine case in 1943 fail to change the law on racial discrimination?
cards.answer: Although Constantine won damages, his case attracted attention but did not change the law, which offered no general protection until 1965.

cards.front: Why does Princess go missing before the boycott resolves in Act 3?
cards.answer: She endures racist abuse at school and cuts her hair short as an act of self-transformation expressing distress and refusal.

cards.front: How does Margot's role in sheltering Princess show cross-racial solidarity?
cards.answer: Margot shelters Princess despite never backing the boycott, making the solidarity personal rather than political.

cards.front: What three strange events at Thornfield are blamed on Grace Poole, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: The mirthless laugh from the third floor / A fire in Rochester's bedroom / A violent attack on Mason
items: The mirthless laugh from the third floor

cards.front: Why does Jane leave Thornfield after discovering the truth about Bertha?
cards.answer: She refuses to compromise her moral integrity, not because she stops loving Rochester.

cards.front: Why does Jane find Thornfield both freeing and confining?
cards.answer: She has escaped Lowood's cruelty but remains a dependent, paid, housed and controlled by her employer.

title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that affect the resistance of a wire.
cards.answer: Length of wire / Cross-sectional area / Material / Temperature

cards.front: In a series circuit, what happens to current across the components (as stated in the lesson)?
cards.answer: Current is the same everywhere

cards.front: Why is total resistance in a parallel circuit less than the smallest individual resistance?
cards.answer: Because current can flow through multiple branches at once, giving it more paths and reducing overall resistance.

cards.front: Why don't filament bulbs follow Ohm's law?
cards.answer: They are non-ohmic, meaning their resistance changes with temperature instead of staying constant.

cards.front: Why is high carbon steel hard but not tough?
cards.answer: High carbon steel holds a chisel edge well but is brittle, so it can shatter suddenly if struck sideways instead of bending.

cards.front: Why does stainless steel have low machinability?
cards.answer: Stainless steel work-hardens during cutting, which dulls tools rapidly and forces slower cutting speeds, increasing cycle time and tool costs.

title: Jesus as God Incarnate, Salvation and the Resurrection
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What three gifts did the Magi bring to Jesus in Matthew's birth account?
cards.answer: Gold / Frankincense / Myrrh

cards.front: Name the four events the lesson says together form the Christian 'Gospel' (good news).
cards.answer: The Incarnation / The crucifixion / The Resurrection / The Ascension

cards.front: Why is the virgin birth significant for Christians?
cards.answer: It shows Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit, not a human father, confirming he was uniquely both divine and human from birth.

cards.front: Why did Paul argue that the Resurrection is essential to Christian faith?
cards.answer: Because without the Resurrection, Paul said, Christian faith would be pointless, so it is the foundation of belief.

title: Redemption, the Church and the Mystery of Salvation
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three models the lesson gives for what Christ's death on the Cross accomplished.
cards.answer: Anselm's satisfaction theory / Aquinas's perfect sacrifice / Liberation model

cards.front: Name the four marks of the Church affirmed in the Nicene Creed.
cards.answer: One / Holy / Catholic / Apostolic

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church affirm the reality of hell despite teaching that God's love is unconditional?
cards.answer: Hell is the logical consequence of a person freely and finally refusing the love and mercy God offers, not something God sends.

cards.front: Why is the Church described as 'apostolic'?
cards.answer: It stands in direct succession from the apostles, as bishops succeed the apostles and the Pope succeeds Peter.

cards.front: Name the three sections of a river's course from source to mouth.
cards.answer: Upper course / Middle course / Lower course

cards.front: According to the Bradshaw model, name the four variables that fall as you move downstream.
cards.answer: Gradient / Sediment size / Channel roughness

cards.front: Why do interlocking spurs form in the upper course of a river?
cards.answer: The young river lacks power to cut through ridges of higher land, so it weaves around them.

cards.front: How do levees and floodplains build up in the lower course of a river?
cards.answer: Floodwater spreads over flat ground, slows down and drops sediment, coarsest near the channel, building levees and deepening floodplain soil.

cards.front: Name the six adaptation strategies Australia used after the Millennium Drought.
cards.answer: Water-saving rules in cities / New water sources (desalination plants) / Smarter farming methods / Murray-Darling Basin Plan (2012) / Better ENSO forecasting / Greywater reuse

cards.front: Give three effects the Millennium Drought had on Australia's environment.
cards.answer: Murray-Darling stopped reaching the sea / Wetlands shrank, killing river red gums / Bushfires intensified / Dust storms swept across cities
items: Wetlands shrank, killing river red gums

cards.front: How does El Nino cause drought in Australia and Indonesia?
cards.answer: Trade winds weaken, so the warm water pool shifts eastward, taking the rain that normally falls on the western Pacific with it.

cards.front: Why did Australian farming losses become less severe by the 2015-16 El Nino compared with 2002?
cards.answer: Cities used desalination plants and stricter water rules built after the Millennium Drought, reducing the impact of the later drought.

cards.front: Name the five psychological factors the lesson identifies that affect injury risk.
cards.answer: Motivation / Arousal / Anxiety and stress / Confidence / Aggression

cards.front: How does anxiety and stress increase injury risk in an athlete?
cards.answer: Elevated cortisol impairs immune function and slows healing, while anxiety causes muscle tension that restricts movement and alters gait.

cards.front: How can overconfidence increase injury risk for an athlete?
cards.answer: A highly confident athlete may attempt skills beyond their current ability, exposing them to injury through poor technique or mistimed actions.

cards.front: How can a previous knee injury lead to a new injury elsewhere in the body?
cards.answer: It may cause a footballer to alter their running technique, placing excess stress on the opposite hip and creating a new overuse injury site.

title: The Great American Desert and Manifest Destiny
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three push factors driving Americans west in the 1840s given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Overcrowded cities / The 1837 Panic / Soil exhaustion in the East

cards.front: Name the three older ideas that Manifest Destiny bundled together.
cards.answer: Religious belief God favoured the US / Racial belief in Anglo-Saxonism / Political confidence in republican institutions
items: Religious belief God favoured the US

cards.front: Why did easterners begin to see the Plains as a gateway rather than a barrier in the 1840s?
cards.answer: Missionary reports of fertile Oregon valleys, California's climate and harbours, and gold strikes after 1848 made the risky journey worthwhile.

cards.front: How did Manifest Destiny affect attitudes towards Native nations on the Plains?
cards.answer: It treated the land as empty, legitimising the removal and confinement of the hundreds of thousands of Native people already living there.

title: Exploring the Moon: Origin, Far Side and Apollo
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three key evidence strands supporting the Giant Impact Hypothesis.
cards.answer: Moon's composition matches Earth's mantle / Moon has a disproportionately small iron core / Apollo rock samples share Earth's oxygen isotope ratios
items: Moon has a disproportionately small iron core
Apollo rock samples share Earth's oxygen isotope ratios

cards.front: Name the three missions that revealed the Moon's far side, in order.
cards.answer: Luna 3 (1959) / Apollo 8 (1968) / Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (2009)

cards.front: Why does the Moon have a relatively small iron core compared to its size?
cards.answer: Theia's iron core merged with Earth's core during the impact, so the ejected debris that formed the Moon came only from the mantles.

cards.front: Why is the Moon's far-side crust thicker than the near-side crust?
cards.answer: Earth's heat likely warmed the near side more, delaying its crust solidifying, while the far side cooled and solidified faster into a thicker crust.

title: The Third Crusade: Causes, Acre and Arsuf
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson gives as motives for why English crusaders went on the Third Crusade.
cards.answer: Moved by loss of Jerusalem, wanted indulgence / Hoped for booty and lands / Wanted to escape debts or law-suits / Summoned by feudal duty to their lord
items: Moved by loss of Jerusalem, wanted indulgence
Wanted to escape debts or law-suits
Summoned by feudal duty to their lord

cards.front: Why was the capture of Acre in 1191 such an important victory for the crusaders?
cards.answer: Acre was the gateway to the Holy Land, so its fall reopened the supply line to Europe and gave crusaders a base to march on Jerusalem.

cards.front: Why did Richard's discipline during the march to Jaffa help him win at Arsuf?
cards.answer: He kept the army in three tight blocks with baggage shielded, so knights held ranks under harassment until able to counter-charge and break Saladin's force.

title: Titrations, Chemical Cells and Fuel Cells
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three disadvantages the lesson gives for hydrogen fuel cells.
cards.answer: Hydrogen hard/expensive to store and transport / Most hydrogen made from fossil fuels / Fuel cell technology is expensive
items: Hydrogen hard/expensive to store and transport
Most hydrogen made from fossil fuels

cards.front: Why does a chemical cell made of zinc and copper produce a higher voltage than one made of iron and copper?
cards.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, and a bigger reactivity difference between the two metals gives a higher voltage.

cards.front: Why does electric current flow through the external circuit in a chemical cell?
cards.answer: The more reactive metal is oxidised and loses electrons, which flow through the circuit to the less reactive metal where they are gained (reduction).

cards.front: Name the three forces the lesson gives for rising global water demand.
cards.answer: Growing world population / Richer middle class eating more meat and dairy / Spread of intensive farming
items: Richer middle class eating more meat and dairy

cards.front: Name the five strategies the lesson gives for a sustainable water future.
cards.answer: Efficient drip irrigation / Recycling treated wastewater for industry / Rainwater harvesting in homes / Repairing leaky pipes / Pricing water so heavy users pay more
items: Pricing water so heavy users pay more

cards.front: Why can groundwater over-abstraction cause saltwater to ruin coastal aquifers?
cards.answer: Pumping too much fresh groundwater lowers water tables, letting seawater seep into coastal aquifers and contaminate drinking supplies.

cards.front: Why do big dams like the Three Gorges Dam harm downstream farmland?
cards.answer: Sediment that used to flow downstream and fertilise farms instead collects behind the dam wall.

title: Glorious Revolution and the Hanoverian succession
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the five constitutional landmarks the lesson lists between 1689 and 1714.
cards.answer: Bill of Rights (1689) / Toleration Act (1689) / Act of Settlement (1701) / Act of Union with Scotland (1707) / George I crowned (1714)

cards.front: Name the three effects the Glorious Revolution had within the British Isles outside England, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Williamite War in Ireland followed by Penal Laws / Jacobite rising at Killiecrankie in Scotland collapsed / Scotland pushed towards the Act of Union 1707
items: Williamite War in Ireland followed by Penal Laws
Jacobite rising at Killiecrankie in Scotland collapsed
Scotland pushed towards the Act of Union 1707

cards.front: Why did George I become king in 1714 despite having over 50 closer Catholic blood relatives?
cards.answer: The Act of Settlement barred Catholics from the throne, so religion rather than bloodline now decided who could rule.

cards.front: How did the Bill of Rights shift power away from the Crown towards Parliament?
cards.answer: It stopped the monarch suspending laws, levying taxes or keeping a peacetime army without parliamentary consent, and guaranteed free elections and speech.

cards.front: Name the six categories of security measure covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Identifying staff / Monitoring of keys / Receiving and monitoring visitors / Reporting concerns to line managers / External doors restricting access / Window locks and restraints

cards.front: Name the two emergency procedures the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Fire drill / Evacuation

cards.front: Why is a fire drill carried out regularly in a care setting?
cards.answer: It is a practised rehearsal so all staff know the assembly point and their responsibilities in an evacuation.

cards.front: Why must faulty equipment have a reporting system in a care setting?
cards.answer: So faulty equipment is taken out of service immediately rather than left for another staff member to unknowingly use.

cards.front: What three interlocking plots does Act 1 establish, all driven by money?
cards.answer: Antonio's bond with Shylock / Bassanio's quest to win Portia via the caskets / tension between Christians and Jews in Venice
items: Bassanio's quest to win Portia via the caskets
tension between Christians and Jews in Venice

cards.front: Why does Shylock propose a pound of flesh instead of charging interest on the loan?
cards.answer: It seems like a joke on the surface but hides genuine menace, since Antonio has publicly abused and humiliated Shylock.

cards.front: Why does Portia have no control over who she marries?
cards.answer: She is bound by her dead father's will, which forces suitors to choose correctly between three caskets to win her hand.

title: Girlhood: Representation and the Paris Banlieue
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five key sequences the lesson identifies for micro/representation analysis in Girlhood.
cards.answer: Opening American-football tracking shot / Train-station fight / Hotel-room karaoke 'Diamonds' set piece / Boxing fight in the second act / Closing crossing-the-road sequence
items: Boxing fight in the second act

cards.front: How does Sciamma's use of the Cinemascope frame represent the four friends as a collective rather than individuals?
cards.answer: The wide frame holds all four friends simultaneously so none are cropped or marginalised, presenting Black femininity as a collective, social experience.

cards.front: Why does the opening football-game tracking shot avoid introducing Marieme with an individualising hero shot?
cards.answer: It follows a collective of young Black women already occupying public space, so Marieme emerges from the group rather than being singled out.

title: Votes for Women: Suffragists, Suffragettes, and 1918
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four militant suffragette tactics listed for the period after 1905/1912.
cards.answer: Heckling cabinet ministers / Chaining themselves to railings / Smashing shop windows on Oxford Street / Burning letters in postboxes / Arson attacks on empty country houses / Slashing paintings like the Rokeby Venus
items: Smashing shop windows on Oxford Street
Arson attacks on empty country houses
Slashing paintings like the Rokeby Venus

cards.front: Why did the government introduce force-feeding of imprisoned suffragettes from 1909?
cards.answer: Imprisoned suffragettes went on hunger strike, so the government force-fed them with a tube to stop them dying in custody.

cards.front: Why did excluding women from voting become harder to justify by 1917-18?
cards.answer: Around 1.7 million women were doing vital war work in munitions, transport and agriculture, undermining claims they were 'unfit' for political responsibility.

cards.front: Why did Parliament have to legislate on the franchise during the First World War?
cards.answer: The existing male franchise required residence, so soldiers serving abroad would lose their vote on returning, forcing Parliament to redraw the franchise.

cards.front: Why does Claudio's honour demand public revenge rather than private investigation of Hero?
cards.answer: Because the honour system prioritises public male judgement of female chastity over fairness or truth.

cards.front: Why does love based on appearance fail while love based on connection survives in Much Ado?
cards.answer: Conventional love has no foundation in genuine knowledge, so a single deception destroys it, unlike tested, earned love.

cards.front: Name the four parts of the essay structure this lesson recommends for a Jane Eyre answer.
cards.answer: Introduction (1-2 sentences) / Extract analysis (2-3 paragraphs) / Whole novel (2-3 paragraphs) / Brief conclusion

cards.front: Why does the lesson say you must memorise quotations for the Jane Eyre exam?
cards.answer: The paper is closed book, so you cannot take a copy of the novel in and must reference it from memory.

cards.front: Why should context be embedded inside analysis rather than given its own separate paragraph?
cards.answer: Context should be linked directly to the writer's purpose within the analysis, not bolted on separately.

cards.front: What is the most common mistake students make when structuring their Jane Eyre essay, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Spending too long analysing the extract and neglecting the whole-novel section, instead of aiming for an even split.

cards.front: Name the four staging choices Odimba uses (besides lighting) to shape meaning in Princess & The Hustler.
cards.answer: Flexible set / Sound design / Costume and period detail / Physical storytelling

cards.front: What four structural techniques does the lesson say give the play its distinctive quality?
cards.answer: Cyclical framing / Dual timelines / Episodic scenes / Small cast

cards.front: Why does Odimba use a small cast of only seven characters?
cards.answer: The boycott arrives as news carried into the flat, keeping the play's scope intimate.

cards.front: How does Odimba use episodic scenes with gaps between them?
cards.answer: Short scenes with gaps of weeks or months allow time jumps and tonal shifts without losing momentum.

cards.front: Name the six religious traditions/concepts the lesson gives as key foundations for social justice.
cards.answer: Amos 5:24 (Hebrew prophetic tradition) / Galatians 3:28 (Christian equality) / Tzedek and tikkun olam (Judaism) / Adl (Islamic justice) / Sewa (Sikh service) / Ahimsa (Hindu non-harm)

cards.front: Why did Archbishop Desmond Tutu argue that apartheid was theologically wrong, not just politically wrong?
cards.answer: He drew on the Christian teaching of imago Dei and ubuntu philosophy to show apartheid denied the God-given dignity all people share.

cards.front: How did Martin Luther King Jr justify resisting unjust laws in his 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'?
cards.answer: He argued Christians had a moral duty to resist unjust laws, drawing on the natural-law tradition rooted in Augustine and Aquinas.

title: Cromwell, Government Reform and the Fall, 1534–40
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four new revenue departments Cromwell created to manage royal finance.
cards.answer: Court of Augmentations / Court of First Fruits and Tenths / Court of Wards / Court of General Surveyors
items: Court of First Fruits and Tenths

cards.front: Name the six pieces of Reformation Parliament legislation the lesson lists between 1532 and 1540.
cards.answer: Act in Restraint of Appeals 1533 / Act of Supremacy 1534 / Act of Succession 1534 / two Acts of Dissolution / Statute of Uses 1536 / Act of Six Articles 1539

cards.front: Why was Cromwell able to be condemned without a trial in 1540?
cards.answer: He was condemned by Act of Attainder, the same legal weapon he had previously used against the Nun of Kent and Anne Boleyn.

cards.front: How did the failed Cleves marriage help bring about Cromwell's fall?
cards.answer: It looked like a personal humiliation for Henry, making him willing to listen to the conservative faction's case against Cromwell.

title: Designing Sociological Research and Interpreting Data
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: What are the eight steps in the research design sequence, in order?
cards.answer: Aim / Hypothesis / Operationalisation / Method choice / Sampling / Pilot study / Data collection / Analysis and conclusions

cards.front: The lesson gives four steps for interpreting sociological data correctly. What are they?
cards.answer: Read the axis labels first / Cite specific figures not vague claims / Describe the pattern before explaining it / Consider what data might be missing
items: Cite specific figures not vague claims
Describe the pattern before explaining it
Consider what data might be missing

cards.front: Why must a sampling strategy match the research method chosen?
cards.answer: A random or stratified sample suits a large survey aiming for representativeness, while a snowball sample suits interviews with hard-to-reach groups where depth matters more.

cards.front: Why can different operationalisations of 'social class' produce different research findings?
cards.answer: Because concepts like class can be defined differently (e.g. free school meal eligibility, parental occupation, self-reported class), each measuring something slightly different.

cards.front: Name the three constraints placed on Portia as a woman that the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Cannot choose her own husband (casket test) / Cannot enter a courtroom without disguise / Transfers all her property to Bassanio on marriage
items: Cannot choose her own husband (casket test)
Cannot enter a courtroom without disguise
Transfers all her property to Bassanio on marriage

cards.front: Name the four critical readings of Shylock given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Traditional (comic villain defeated) / Sympathetic (moral centre of the play) / Postcolonial (the scapegoated Other) / Marxist (exposes capitalism's hypocrisy)

cards.front: Why does Antonio's self-description as a "tainted wether" suggest he passively accepts death?
cards.answer: The wether metaphor is self-pitying and sacrificial, suggesting Antonio sees his own life as expendable.

cards.front: How does Jessica's line "never merry when I hear sweet music" show the cost of her elopement?
cards.answer: It indicates persistent sadness and displacement despite gaining a husband and wealth through assimilation.

title: How Rights Have Developed Over Time
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the four rights the lesson lists as protected by the Human Rights Act 1998.
cards.answer: Right to life / Right to a fair trial / Freedom from torture / Freedom of expression

cards.front: Name the four tactics the suffragette movement used in its campaign for women's votes.
cards.answer: Protests / Hunger strikes / Property damage / Arson

cards.front: Why did early trade unions operate illegally before 1871?
cards.answer: Because the Combination Acts of 1799 and 1800 banned workers from organising collectively.

cards.front: Why was taking a human rights case to Strasbourg before 1998 a problem for UK citizens?
cards.answer: Because it was costly and time-consuming to take a case all the way to the European Court of Human Rights.

cards.front: Name the four brutal conditions Hari faces as a lascar, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Long hours / Dangerous cargo / Racial abuse from white sailors / Pay far below British crew

cards.front: Why does Gupta use Hari's exploitation to show injustice was deliberate, not just neglect?
cards.answer: His brutal pay, conditions and abuse show exploitation was active and built into the system, not accidental.

cards.front: How does Gupta structure the play to move from individual suffering to collective resistance?
cards.answer: She converges the ayahs' abandonment, Hari's exploitation and the memory of 1857 to reveal systemic injustice needing collective political action.

cards.front: Why does a Punnett square only show probabilities rather than guaranteeing the outcome for individual offspring?
cards.answer: Inheritance involves random fertilisation, so the ratios are a long-run statistical expectation, not a fixed prediction.

cards.front: Why do genes on the Y chromosome affect sex development in a human embryo?
cards.answer: Genes on the Y chromosome trigger the development of testes during embryo development.

cards.front: Why was Mendel's explanation for inheritance patterns significant, given he didn't know about DNA or chromosomes?
cards.answer: His explanation correctly predicted inheritance patterns we now explain in molecular terms, even without knowledge of DNA or chromosomes.

cards.front: Name the four non-hormonal contraceptive methods described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Barrier methods (condoms/diaphragms) / Spermicidal agents / Surgical sterilisation / Abstinence or natural family planning

cards.front: How do copper IUDs prevent pregnancy?
cards.answer: Copper IUDs are non-hormonal devices in the uterus that prevent implantation.

cards.front: How does IVF help a couple conceive?
cards.answer: The mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate multiple eggs, which are collected, fertilised outside the body, and transferred to the uterus.

title: Early Bolshevik Decrees and the Constituent Assembly
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four headline decrees issued by the Bolsheviks between October and December 1917.
cards.answer: Decree on Peace / Decree on Land / Decree on Workers' Control / Decree on Nationalities

cards.front: Name the three steps the lesson gives towards banning rival parties after October 1917, before the 1921 factions ban.
cards.answer: Kadets outlawed as 'enemies of the people' (Nov 1917) / Left SRs quit Sovnarkom and were shut out of soviets (March 1918) / Right SRs and Mensheviks banned from soviets (summer 1918)
items: Kadets outlawed as 'enemies of the people' (Nov 1917)
Left SRs quit Sovnarkom and were shut out of soviets (March 1918)
Right SRs and Mensheviks banned from soviets (summer 1918)

cards.front: Why did Lenin close down the Constituent Assembly on 6 January 1918?
cards.answer: The Assembly, dominated by the SRs, refused to endorse Sovnarkom's decrees, so the Red Guard locked the doors and Sverdlov declared it dissolved.

cards.front: Why were the Romanovs executed without trial in July 1918?
cards.answer: White and Czech Legion forces were approaching, and as long as the Romanovs lived they remained a rallying point for monarchist resistance.

cards.front: Name the three narrative techniques the lesson says together turn memory into the film's dominant device in Slumdog Millionaire.
cards.answer: Frame narrative (quiz show as present frame) / Dual timeline editing (alternating past and present) / Ellipsis (omitting years between key scenes)
items: Frame narrative (quiz show as present frame)
Dual timeline editing (alternating past and present)

cards.front: How does the opening interrogation sequence use colour to create a tonal shock in Slumdog Millionaire?
cards.answer: It cuts from the warm, saturated orange and gold quiz-show stage to cool, single-source police-station grey, jolting the spectator into the frame.

cards.front: Why does the quiz-show format naturally create suspense in Slumdog Millionaire?
cards.answer: The spectator already understands the game's rules, since each round is a multiple-choice question, making them wait for each answer with Jamal.

cards.front: How does camera stability in Slumdog Millionaire create different meanings for the slum and studio spaces?
cards.answer: Handheld camerawork makes slum scenes feel kinetic and precarious, while locked-off camerawork makes the studio feel exposed and stable.

cards.front: Name the original Seven Commandments of Animalism (in order).
cards.answer: Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy / Whatever goes on four legs or has wings is a friend / No animal shall wear clothes / No animal shall sleep in a bed / No animal shall drink alcohol / No animal shall kill any other animal / All animals are equal
items: Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy
Whatever goes on four legs or has wings is a friend
No animal shall sleep in a bed
No animal shall kill any other animal

cards.front: Name the three rhetorical techniques Old Major uses in his speech.
cards.answer: Tricolon for emotional impact / Rhetorical questions to seem inevitable / A unifying song for collective identity
items: A unifying song for collective identity

cards.front: Why does Orwell make the milk and apples disappear so early in the novella?
cards.answer: To show that corruption begins immediately after revolution rather than developing gradually over time.

cards.front: Why does Orwell suggest the Rebellion happens almost accidentally rather than through planned ideology?
cards.answer: Because Jones forgets to feed the animals, showing revolutions arise from desperation rather than ideology.

title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps: Crisis and Triumph
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four style devices in Livy's Style Toolkit for Passages E to H.
cards.answer: Oxymoron / Hyperbaton / Asyndeton / Antithesis

cards.front: Why did soldiers behind the leading infantry fall through the snow at the cliff in Passage G?
cards.answer: Old hard-packed snow lay under a softer new layer, and once many men and animals had trampled it, the surface broke into slippery slush.

cards.front: How does the ablative absolute 'arboribus circa immanibus deiectis detruncatisque' work grammatically?
cards.answer: It describes a completed background action — the huge trees having already been felled and stripped of branches before the main action.

cards.front: Why did the cavalry report to Hannibal that the cliff path was impassable in Passage G?
cards.answer: A landslide had torn away part of the path, leaving a drop of almost 1,000 feet with nothing to grab onto.

cards.front: Name the five parts a full genetic diagram must include.
cards.answer: Parental phenotypes and genotypes / Gametes produced by each parent / A 2x2 Punnett square / Offspring genotypes with phenotypes stated / Probabilities or ratios

cards.front: Why is there a 50:50 chance of a baby being male or female?
cards.answer: Fathers can pass either an X or a Y chromosome in their sperm, giving an equal chance of XX or XY.

cards.front: Why do actual offspring ratios from a genetic cross sometimes differ from the expected ratio?
cards.answer: The ratios are only probabilities based on chance, so actual results may vary, especially with small samples.

title: African Drumming: Polyrhythm, Master Drummers and Oral Tradition
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the three tones a djembe player can produce on the drum.
cards.answer: Bass / Tone / Slap

cards.front: Give the three sizes of dunun drum by name.
cards.answer: Kenkeni / Sangban / Dundunba

cards.front: Why is African drumming described as belonging to an oral tradition?
cards.answer: It is passed down by ear and imitation, with no written notation, so children learn by watching experienced players.

cards.front: How does texture typically build in a piece like Rhythms of the Malinke?
cards.answer: It opens with a single dunun or bell pattern, then further dunun and djembe parts enter one by one adding ostinato layers.

cards.front: Name the four actions the lesson gives that show Scrooge reversing his cruelty from Stave 1.
cards.answer: Sends the prize turkey anonymously / Donates to charity collectors he rejected / Attends Fred's Christmas party / Raises Bob Cratchit's salary
items: Donates to charity collectors he rejected

cards.front: Why does Dickens make the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come silent throughout Stave 4?
cards.answer: Its silence forces Scrooge to interpret the terrifying visions alone, making the reader share his growing horror.

cards.front: How does Dickens use the contrast between the unnamed dead man and Tiny Tim's death to make his message about greed?
cards.answer: The man dies alone and mocked while Tiny Tim dies mourned by loving family, showing greed leads to an empty death and love creates lasting bonds.

cards.front: The lesson gives four things a business's legal structure affects — what are they?
cards.answer: How much control owners keep / How profits are shared / Where the business can raise money / What happens if things go wrong
items: Where the business can raise money
What happens if things go wrong

cards.front: Why would a lone builder just starting out usually choose to be a sole trader?
cards.answer: It's cheap and simple with no reporting, and the work is low-risk enough to accept unlimited liability.

cards.front: Why is the key difference between an Ltd and a Plc about how they raise money?
cards.answer: An Ltd can only sell shares to people it invites, while a Plc can sell shares to anyone through the stock exchange.

title: The Home Front in the Second World War
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three women's auxiliary services mentioned that women could be conscripted into.
cards.answer: ATS / WRNS / WAAF

cards.front: Why did the government introduce blackout regulations during the war?
cards.answer: To cover all windows after dark so enemy bombers could not identify towns from the air.

cards.front: Why have historians like Angus Calder questioned the 'Blitz spirit' narrative?
cards.answer: Because censorship suppressed panic and looting, and class inequalities like wealthier families leaving cities were glossed over.

cards.front: Why did women's wartime factory work challenge pre-war assumptions?
cards.answer: Because factory managers who doubted women's ability to operate machinery found them capable and productive.

title: The Gunpowder Plot and the start of the Bloody Code
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three items early modern town watchmen carried on patrol.
cards.answer: A lantern / A staff / A rattle

cards.front: Name the four corporal punishments the lesson gives for theft, vagabondage and minor disorder.
cards.answer: Flogging / Branding / Ear-cropping / The pillory and stocks

cards.front: Why did the state rely on public, harsh punishment in the early modern period instead of a police force?
cards.answer: With no professional police, authorities used terrifying public spectacle as deterrence to make onlookers too scared to commit crime.

cards.front: Why did Parliament create so many new capital offences under the Bloody Code?
cards.answer: Fear of crime, lack of an effective police force, and landowners in Parliament wanting to protect property drove its expansion.

title: Creating the Dictatorship: Reichstag Fire to Führer
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three tactics Hitler used to secure a two-thirds majority for the Enabling Act.
cards.answer: Banned the 81 Communist deputies / Used the SA to intimidate opponents / Promised the Centre Party Catholic rights
items: Used the SA to intimidate opponents
Promised the Centre Party Catholic rights

cards.front: Name the three major consequences of the Night of the Long Knives given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Removed the SA as a rival power / Won over the army / Showed Hitler would use murder to keep power
items: Removed the SA as a rival power
Showed Hitler would use murder to keep power

cards.front: Why was Hitler alarmed by Ernst Röhm's ambitions for the SA in 1934?
cards.answer: Röhm wanted the SA to absorb the army and push a socialist 'second revolution', threatening army support and industrialist backing Hitler needed.

cards.front: Why did other political parties fail to resist Hitler's takeover in 1933?
cards.answer: The SA and Gestapo arrested opponents and sent them to camps like Dachau, while many Germans accepted lost democracy for promised stability and recovery.

cards.front: Name the five principal methods for joining polymer components given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Solvent/chemical adhesives / Epoxy adhesives / Plastic welding / Mechanical fixings / Designed-in snap-fit features

cards.front: Name the three plastic welding methods described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Hot gas welding / Ultrasonic welding / Hot plate welding

cards.front: Why can nuts and bolts with washers reduce the risk of cracking a brittle polymer like acrylic?
cards.answer: The washers distribute the clamping force over a larger area instead of concentrating stress at one point.

cards.front: Why does eliminating a painting or plating stage for self-finishing polymers benefit production economically?
cards.answer: It removes the need for capital equipment, material, energy, time and VOC emissions associated with a secondary finishing process.

title: The Six Day War and Its Aftermath, June 1967
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three fronts on which Israel fought during the Six Day War of June 1967.
cards.answer: Southern front against Egypt in Sinai / Eastern front against Jordan in West Bank / Northern front against Syria on Golan Heights
items: Southern front against Egypt in Sinai
Eastern front against Jordan in West Bank
Northern front against Syria on Golan Heights

cards.front: How did the pre-emptive air strike of 5 June 1967 make Israel's rapid ground victories possible?
cards.answer: Destroying about 300 Egyptian aircraft on the ground gave Israel air supremacy on every front from the first morning, enabling the ground campaign.

cards.front: Why did the Khartoum Resolution of September 1967 close off the diplomatic route opened by Resolution 242?
cards.answer: The Arab League's 'three nos' ruled out peace, recognition and negotiation with Israel, blocking immediate progress on land for peace.

cards.front: The lesson pairs four sets of contrasting characters in Romeo and Juliet. Name the four contrasts.
cards.answer: Romeo's idealism vs Mercutio's cynicism / Juliet's decisiveness vs Nurse's earthiness / Tybalt's honour-rage vs Benvolio's peacemaking / Mercutio's fluid energy vs Tybalt's rigid control
items: Mercutio's fluid energy vs Tybalt's rigid control

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Mercutio's death is the clearest demonstration that the feud destroys bystanders?
cards.answer: Because Mercutio belongs to neither the Montagues nor the Capulets, yet still dies because of their feud.

cards.front: How should a performer change Romeo's voice between Act One and Act Three?
cards.answer: From a languid, self-absorbed, meandering pace early on to sudden volume, clipped pace and physical stillness by Act Three.

cards.front: Why does Lord Capulet's staging change so much in Act Three, Scene Five?
cards.answer: Because he shifts from a magnanimous host in Act One to a threatening, physically imposing father when Juliet refuses to marry Paris.

title: Selecting Papers & Boards for a Purpose
subject: design-technology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three types of forces packaging must withstand during manufacture, transit and retail display.
cards.answer: Compressive forces (stacking) / Tensile forces (pulling walls apart when lifted) / Shear forces (at glued joints when dropped)

cards.front: Name the three standard stock forms paper and board are supplied in by merchants.
cards.answer: Sheets / Reams / Rolls

cards.front: Why is solid white board (SWB) the default choice for luxury packaging and cosmetics?
cards.answer: It achieves the highest whiteness and brightness values, making colours appear vivid and conveying premium quality.

cards.front: Why might a designer choose clay-coated board with a water-based barrier instead of foil-lined board?
cards.answer: It gives moisture protection but is recyclable, avoiding foil-lined board's end-of-life recycling problem, though it is a less effective barrier.

cards.front: Name the six future tense endings used for all French verbs, in order (je/tu/il/nous/vous/ils).
cards.answer: -ai / -as / -a / -ons / -ez / -ont

cards.front: Give the four environmental problems named in the lesson's vocabulary list (besides pollution and global warming).
cards.answer: l'effet de serre / la déforestation / les déchets / les espèces menacées

cards.front: How do you form the future tense of a regular -re verb like prendre?
cards.answer: Drop the final -e from the infinitive, then add the future endings, e.g. je prendrai.

cards.front: How does the future tense differ between regular and irregular verbs in French?
cards.answer: Regular verbs use the infinitive as the stem, while irregular verbs use a special stem that must be learned by heart.

cards.front: Name the three barriers used in modern landfill engineering to stop leachate reaching groundwater, from bottom to top.
cards.answer: Geomembrane plastic liner / Compacted clay layer / Drainage pipes collecting leachate to treatment
items: Drainage pipes collecting leachate to treatment

cards.front: Name the three remediation options the lesson gives for cleaning up contaminated groundwater.
cards.answer: Pump-and-treat systems / Permeable reactive barriers / Bioremediation using microorganisms

cards.front: Why does chalk make a good aquifer despite having tiny pores?
cards.answer: Chalk has high porosity but most water moves through its extensive network of fractures and joints instead of the pores.

cards.front: Why must a good aquifer rock be both porous and permeable?
cards.answer: Porosity lets it store water while permeability lets water flow through it fast enough to supply a well.

title: The Gulling Scenes & Don John's Plot
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: What three factors does the lesson give as reasons behind Don John's villainy?
cards.answer: he is illegitimate / he is socially marginalised / he was recently defeated in war by his own brother
items: he was recently defeated in war by his own brother

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare give Beatrice's gulling scene a different tone from Benedick's?
cards.answer: Hero speaks in verse to signal emotional sincerity, so Beatrice's surrender feels dignified rather than comic like Benedick's.

cards.front: How does Don John's plot create dramatic irony for the audience in Acts 2-3?
cards.answer: The audience knows the gulling is benign and Don John's plot is a malicious fabrication, so they feel both comic pleasure and growing dread.

cards.front: Why is Margaret's role in the window scene ambiguous?
cards.answer: Shakespeare never explains whether she knowingly helped Borachio deceive Claudio, and she is never punished for it.

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson gives as gaining from hyperinflation in 1923.
cards.answer: People with debts / Businesspeople and industrialists with physical assets / Foreign visitors with hard currency / Shrewd speculators
items: Businesspeople and industrialists with physical assets

cards.front: Name the three effects of the Ruhr occupation on German society and economy given in the lesson.
cards.answer: 150,000 Germans expelled from homes / Factories and mines seized / German economy ground to a halt
items: German economy ground to a halt

cards.front: How did German government policy during the First World War lay the roots of hyperinflation?
cards.answer: The government borrowed heavily and printed money to fund the war instead of raising taxes, increasing money in circulation without increasing goods.

cards.front: Why did the increase in money supply after the First World War cause prices to rise?
cards.answer: The amount of money in circulation increased massively but the amount of goods available did not, so prices rose.

cards.front: Why does HMS Thunder Child's destruction of two tripods matter, given the tripods' usual power?
cards.answer: It shows individual courage can briefly overcome even overwhelming Martian technology, before the ship is overwhelmed.

cards.front: How does Wells show that class distinctions collapse during the London exodus?
cards.answer: A fine carriage becomes no better than a cart, and the strong take from the weak regardless of wealth.

title: Collectivisation and the War on the Kulaks
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four methods the lesson gives for how peasants resisted collectivisation.
cards.answer: Slaughtered their livestock / Buried grain / Broke tools / Fled to the cities

cards.front: Why did Stalin abandon the NEP and launch the Great Turn in 1928?
cards.answer: The 1927 grain procurement crisis meant peasants were not delivering enough grain, and Stalin needed grain to feed cities and fund industrialisation.

cards.front: How did the famine of 1932-33 come about?
cards.answer: Sown area and grain output collapsed, yet the state raised procurement quotas to fund industrial imports, causing famine.

cards.front: Why did agricultural output remain poor even though collectivisation gave the state political control?
cards.answer: Peasant resistance like livestock slaughter and disrupted farming meant grain output did not regain 1928 levels for decades.

cards.front: Name the four discoveries Galileo made with his telescope from 1609.
cards.answer: Phases of Venus / Four moons of Jupiter / Mountains and craters on the Moon / Sunspots
items: Mountains and craters on the Moon

cards.front: Name three advantages of reflecting telescopes over refractors given in the lesson.
cards.answer: No chromatic aberration / Mirrors can be made much larger / Shorter tube lengths / Lower cost per unit aperture
items: Mirrors can be made much larger

cards.front: Why does the human eye struggle to see faint astronomical objects compared to a telescope?
cards.answer: Its pupil is only about 7 mm wide, limiting light collected, and it cannot accumulate light over time like a camera.

cards.front: Why is there a practical maximum useful magnification for any telescope?
cards.answer: Beyond about 2x the aperture in mm, the image becomes too dim and blurred by atmospheric turbulence to show more detail.

title: Black Power, the Panthers and the 1968 Olympics
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five 'survival programmes' the Black Panthers ran for their communities.
cards.answer: Free Breakfast for Children / Free health clinics / Sickle-cell anaemia testing / Free legal aid / Escort services for the elderly / Liberation Schools

cards.front: Why did SNCC activists break with nonviolent direct action by 1966?
cards.answer: The 1964 and 1965 Acts had not touched ghetto poverty, racist policing or Northern segregation, so activists concluded nonviolence alone could not deliver freedom.

cards.front: How does the relationship between monastics and lay Buddhists sustain Buddhism?
cards.answer: Monastics provide teaching and spiritual merit while lay people provide material support, an interdependence sustaining Buddhism for over 2,500 years.

cards.front: Why must monks remain in their monastery during Vassa?
cards.answer: Vassa runs during the monsoon season so monks can focus on intensive meditation and study without travelling.

cards.front: Why does Sallust describe Sempronia's crimes using the word 'virilis' (manly)?
cards.answer: Because Sallust saw boldness as a male virtue, so he could not simply call her actions bold without marking them as unnatural for a woman.

cards.front: How does Virgil's introduction of Camilla as 'an Amazon' before naming her shape how readers judge her?
cards.answer: It signals immediately that she should be read as a legendary warrior-woman type, not an ordinary woman, before her name is even given.

cards.front: Why does Livy present Tullia driving her chariot over her father's corpse as shocking?
cards.answer: Because she deliberately chose that route over a longer one, showing disregard for family duty and horrifying even her own household gods.

cards.front: According to the lesson, why do Sempronia's talents fail to redeem her in Sallust's account?
cards.answer: Because Sallust judges her against feminine virtues like decus and pudicitia, which she lacked, so her talents become evidence of moral danger instead of praise.

cards.front: Name the five levels in the hierarchy of control measures, from most to least effective.
cards.answer: Elimination / Substitution / Engineering controls / Administrative controls / PPE

cards.front: Name three hazards mentioned during machining operations such as turning, milling and drilling.
cards.answer: Sharp swarf can cut skin / Swarf can enter eyes / Rotating chuck can catch loose clothing
items: Rotating chuck can catch loose clothing

cards.front: Why is risk assessed using both likelihood and severity rather than either alone?
cards.answer: Risk is likelihood multiplied by severity, so a hazard needs both factors judged together to decide how much control it needs.

cards.front: Why should engineering controls and administrative controls be described before PPE when explaining how to reduce a risk?
cards.answer: PPE only protects the wearer and doesn't remove the hazard, so engineering and administrative controls must be tried first as they are more effective.

cards.front: Give the reactivity series of metals listed in the lesson, from most to least reactive (11 items).
cards.answer: Potassium / Sodium / Calcium / Magnesium / Aluminium / Carbon / Zinc / Iron / Hydrogen / Copper / Silver / Gold

cards.front: Why is gold found in the Earth's crust as an uncombined element rather than as an ore?
cards.answer: Gold is very unreactive, so it does not readily react with other substances to form compounds.

cards.front: In the industrial purification of copper by electrolysis, why does the impure copper anode lose mass while the pure copper cathode gains mass?
cards.answer: The impure copper anode dissolves into the solution as ions, while pure copper is deposited onto the cathode.

cards.front: Why does iron displace copper from copper sulfate solution?
cards.answer: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from its salt solution.

title: The First New Deal: Hundred Days and the Alphabet Agencies
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six main alphabet agencies of the First New Deal (by their initials).
cards.answer: CCC / AAA / FERA / TVA / NRA / PWA

cards.front: Which three agencies fall under Roosevelt's 'Relief' and 'Reform' categories in the three Rs grouping?
cards.answer: FERA and CCC (Relief) / TVA (Reform) / FDIC under Glass-Steagall (Reform)

cards.front: Why did Roosevelt declare a four-day bank holiday on taking office in March 1933?
cards.answer: To stop the banking panic by closing every bank so inspectors could check their books before reopening only sound ones.

cards.front: How did the Emergency Banking Act and Glass-Steagall together restore confidence in banks?
cards.answer: They ensured only solvent banks reopened and insured deposits, so people trusted their money would still be there.

cards.front: Name the five physical conditions the lesson gives that push UK rivers towards flooding.
cards.answer: Heavy or prolonged rainfall / Saturated soil / Steep upland slopes / Impermeable rocks / Sparse vegetation cover

cards.front: Name the four human land-use changes the lesson gives that increase flood risk.
cards.answer: Building on a floodplain / Drains moving water to rivers fast / Deforestation in upland catchments / Ploughing fields up and down slopes
items: Drains moving water to rivers fast
Ploughing fields up and down slopes

cards.front: Why does building on a floodplain increase flood risk?
cards.answer: It replaces grass and soil with roofs, roads and concrete, so a city centre rejects 70–90% of rainfall as overland flow that drains reach quickly.

cards.front: Why do UK rivers show higher discharge in winter than in summer?
cards.answer: Low evaporation and saturated soils in winter mean even moderate rain causes high discharge, while summer plants intercept and transpire more water leaving spare soil capacity.

cards.front: Why does the boys' democratic assembly on the island matter for Golding's message?
cards.answer: It mirrors adult society like Parliament, so its collapse into tribal warfare reflects how civilisations throughout history break down.

cards.front: Why did many writers after WWII question whether humanity was capable of progress?
cards.answer: Because two World Wars, the Holocaust and the atomic bombings showed 'civilised' nations committing industrial-scale atrocities.

cards.front: Name the 6Rs framework used to evaluate textile sustainability.
cards.answer: Reduce / Reuse / Recycle / Rethink / Refuse / Repair

cards.front: List the six features designed into a professional cycling jersey described in the sportswear case study.
cards.answer: Polyester-elastane weft-knit panels / Sublimation printing / Flatlock overlocked seams / Silicone gripper banding at hem / UV-protective finish / Recycled polyester construction

cards.front: Why does batch production have lower unit costs than one-off production but still involve downtime?
cards.answer: Set-up costs are spread across the whole batch, but machinery must be reconfigured between different batches, causing downtime.

cards.front: Why does France's Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) scheme drive circular fashion effectively?
cards.answer: It requires brands to fund collection and recycling infrastructure, internalising costs previously pushed onto society and the environment.

title: Enforcing law and order: medieval to early modern
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Why did the Anglo-Saxon tithing system give men an incentive to police their neighbours?
cards.answer: Because if a member committed a crime and could not be produced, the whole tithing was collectively fined.

cards.front: Why did the end of trial by ordeal in 1215 lead to jury trial?
cards.answer: Without the Church's support for ordeal, guilt had to be decided another way, so twelve local men judged cases using knowledge of the accused and circumstances.

cards.front: Name the four non-hormonal contraceptive methods given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Condoms / Diaphragms / Copper IUDs / Surgical sterilisation

cards.front: Name the three functions of healthy kidneys stated in the lesson.
cards.answer: Filter blood and remove waste / Maintain ion balance / Regulate water content

cards.front: How does dialysis remove waste products from the blood?
cards.answer: Blood flows through a membrane into dialysate solution and waste products like urea move across by diffusion.

cards.front: Why is a liver transplant sometimes possible using a living donor, unlike most other organ transplants?
cards.answer: Because the liver can partially regenerate, so a living donor can donate just a segment of it.

cards.front: How does Mrs Hepworth's praise of Willie's boots help Maggie's case for leaving Hobson's shop?
cards.answer: It proves Willie's talent is objectively valuable, not just useful within Hobson's shop, giving Maggie evidence to act on.

cards.front: Why do Alice and Vickey refuse to care for Hobson in Act 4?
cards.answer: Their genteel, respectable values don't extend to real family loyalty, showing they benefit from Maggie's rebellion without her courage.

cards.front: Name three disadvantages (Nachteile) of technology given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cyberbullying (Online-Mobbing) / It can be dangerous / You spend too much time online / Unhealthy to sit long at the screen / You can become addicted / Personal data isn't always safe
items: You spend too much time online
Unhealthy to sit long at the screen

cards.front: Name three advantages (Vorteile) of technology given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Stay in contact with friends / Find information quickly / It is fun / Download music / Practical and useful / Share videos with friends

cards.front: How does a separable verb like 'herunterladen' work in the present tense in German?
cards.answer: The prefix splits off and goes to the end of the clause, e.g. Ich lade Musik herunter.

cards.front: How is 'zu' placed when using the um...zu construction with a separable verb like 'herunterladen'?
cards.answer: Zu goes between the prefix and the stem, e.g. um Fotos herunterzuladen.

cards.front: Why can't a solid ionic compound be electrolysed?
cards.answer: Its ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move to carry the current.

cards.front: Why does electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate produce oxygen rather than chlorine at the anode?
cards.answer: No concentrated halide ions are present, so hydroxide ions are oxidised instead, releasing oxygen gas.

cards.front: Why does extracting aluminium by electrolysis cost a lot of money?
cards.answer: Melting aluminium oxide needs huge amounts of energy and the carbon anodes burn away and must be replaced.

title: Jazz and Blues Ensembles: Roles, Riffs and Improvisation
subject: music-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four rhythm section roles the lesson describes for drums, bass, piano and guitar.
cards.answer: Drums keep swung pulse and add fills / Bass plays walking bass outlining changes / Piano/guitar comp with syncopated chord stabs / All three react to soloist and shape dynamics
items: Drums keep swung pulse and add fills
Bass plays walking bass outlining changes
Piano/guitar comp with syncopated chord stabs
All three react to soloist and shape dynamics

cards.front: How does a walking bass line create swing-style momentum?
cards.answer: It moves in a smooth, mostly stepwise sequence of quarter notes, one per beat, outlining the chord changes and driving the music forward.

cards.front: Why can musicians from different backgrounds improvise together confidently over a 12-bar blues?
cards.answer: Because every musician knows the shared 12-bar chord pattern by ear, allowing the band to play together spontaneously without written parts.

cards.front: How does swing feel differ from straight classical rhythm?
cards.answer: Swing feel plays quaver pairs unevenly, long-short, combined with syncopation, giving forward-leaning energy unlike evenly-divided classical rhythms.

title: Staging and Design: The Garden, the Bulbs and the Lifts
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the two halves the stage was split into by Geoff Cobham's design.
cards.answer: Downstage slippery black floor / Upstage garden with real water pool
items: Upstage garden with real water pool

cards.front: Why was the stage floor built slippery and black downstage?
cards.answer: It was built for sliding furniture and for Frantic Assembly's physical sequences.

cards.front: Why is Pip lit in a tight, isolated lighting state during her autumn announcement?
cards.answer: A narrow warm wash holds her alone against the tree so the audience reads instantly that she is apart from the family.

cards.front: Why did the creative team keep the play's Australian working-class setting when it was remade for a British cast?
cards.answer: They judged the social class, not the Australian setting, was the essential thing to preserve, so nothing was reset.

cards.front: Name the 5 steps in the 5-Minute Planning Template for the anthology comparison question.
cards.answer: Write a one-sentence thesis / Point 1: language feature per poem / Point 2: form/structure per poem / Point 3: context point per poem / Write out chosen poem quotations from memory
items: Write out chosen poem quotations from memory

cards.front: Name the 4 poems suggested as a thematic pairing for 'Social criticism' and 'Displacement' combined.
cards.answer: London / Nothing's Changed / Presents from my Aunts in Pakistan / Hurricane Hits England
items: Presents from my Aunts in Pakistan

cards.front: Why should you learn short quotations of 3-6 words rather than long passages?
cards.answer: Short quotations are easier to memorise accurately and can be embedded smoothly into analytical sentences, showing precise selection.

cards.front: Why does a slightly misquoted word matter in the exam?
cards.answer: Because it can undermine your credibility, so accuracy in quotations is important.

cards.front: Name the three processes the lesson gives that Earth has but the Moon lacks, which destroy impact craters.
cards.answer: Active weathering and erosion by water and wind / Plate tectonics (subduction and mountain building) / Abundant vegetation covering topography
items: Active weathering and erosion by water and wind

cards.front: Why do the lunar highlands have more craters than the maria?
cards.answer: The maria formed later from volcanic eruptions (about 3.9-3.0 billion years ago) which resurfaced the area, burying older craters.

cards.front: How can an ancient impact crater on Earth become a valuable mineral deposit, as at the Sudbury Basin?
cards.answer: The impact melted and redistributed metal-rich rocks, concentrating them into a nickel-copper ore deposit.

title: Other explorers: Diaz, da Gama, Vespucci and Magellan
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What two problems did Vasco da Gama face when he tried to trade at Calicut in 1498?
cards.answer: The Zamorin was unimpressed by Portugal's cloth and trinkets / Arab merchants worked to undermine Portuguese trade
items: The Zamorin was unimpressed by Portugal's cloth and trinkets
Arab merchants worked to undermine Portuguese trade

cards.front: Why did Bartolomeu Dias's 1488 voyage matter even though he didn't reach India?
cards.answer: He proved Africa had an end and that a sea route to the Indian Ocean existed, making da Gama's voyage possible.
