cards.front: Why did Roosevelt shift emphasis to workers' rights and social security in the Second New Deal of 1935?
cards.answer: Because the Supreme Court had struck down the NRA and AAA, so he responded with new legislation on labour rights and social security instead.

title: Gender Equality and the Roles of Women and Men
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson gives four traditional roles in the Theravada Buddhist four-fold hierarchy. What are they?
cards.answer: Monks (bhikkhus) / Nuns (bhikkhunis) / Laymen / Laywomen

cards.front: Why do women not lead Friday prayers over mixed congregations in mainstream Sunni and Shia tradition?
cards.answer: Qur'an 2:228 says men have a degree over women, interpreted in traditional jurisprudence to reserve Friday prayer leadership to men.

cards.front: Why has the bhikkhuni sangha not been fully reinstated in some Theravada countries like Thailand and Sri Lanka?
cards.answer: Some authorities resist full reinstatement because they believe the unbroken ordination lineage for nuns has been lost.

cards.front: Why can women serve as rabbis in Reform Judaism but not in Orthodox Judaism?
cards.answer: Reform grounds this in the Torah's ethical core of full human equality, seeing old restrictions as historically conditioned, unlike Orthodox halakha.

cards.front: Name the five common mistakes in Period Essays given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Storytelling / Shopping list conclusion / Undated evidence / Ignoring the question's concept / Abandoning the thesis at the end
items: Abandoning the thesis at the end

cards.front: Why is writing a 'storytelling' essay a mistake in a Period Essay?
cards.answer: It narrates events in order without analysis, so evidence isn't grouped by argument.

cards.front: Why must you address the question's concept, such as 'how far' or 'change', in every paragraph?
cards.answer: Ignoring the concept means only listing events instead of addressing extent, pace or limits as asked.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for the taiga's low productivity.
cards.answer: Short growing season / Cold soils slow microbial activity / Low-light angle for much of the year
items: Low-light angle for much of the year

cards.front: Name the four types of commercial threat to the taiga the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Softwood logging / Fossil fuel extraction / Mining / HEP dams

cards.front: Why do taiga needles cut water loss and resist frost?
cards.answer: They have a waxy coating instead of broad leaves, which reduces water loss and resists frost.

cards.front: Why does the taiga risk switching from a carbon sink to a carbon source?
cards.answer: As permafrost thaws and fires release stored carbon, the taiga's huge carbon store starts entering the atmosphere instead.

title: Acts 2-3: Hath Not a Jew Eyes?
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Why does Shylock's 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech end by justifying revenge rather than pleading for peace?
cards.answer: Shylock argues Christians preach mercy but practise revenge, so he has learned cruelty from their example and will follow it.

cards.front: How does Antonio's lost ships change Shylock's situation with the bond?
cards.answer: Antonio cannot repay the loan, so the pound of flesh bond becomes enforceable and Shylock can pursue it.

title: Exam Practice: Performer, Director and Designer
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: In the row scene in Act Two Scene One, why might a director remove the underscore and use silence instead of sad music?
cards.answer: Music would soften the insults, so silence keeps the cruelty raw and unaccompanied as Delaney's dialogue intends.

cards.front: How does staging the flat on a thrust stage change the audience's experience compared to a proscenium arch?
cards.answer: On a thrust stage side audiences feel part of the cramped room with no fourth wall, making it feel inescapable, unlike the framed, distanced view a proscenium gives.

cards.front: Why does a calm, private smile from Jo in the final moment make her isolation feel more painful to the audience?
cards.answer: The audience knows Geof has left for good while Jo does not, so her calm contentment creates dramatic irony that sharpens her isolation.

cards.front: Name the four specific design choices the lesson gives for the freezing flat at the start of Act One Scene One.
cards.answer: Damp-stained wallpaper and sagging armchair / Unshaded practical bulb hung low / Distant tugboat horn / Low industrial hum fading in

cards.front: Name the four weaknesses of the Weimar 'Golden Age' recovery given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dependence on American loans / Unemployment stayed above 1 million / Farmers struggled with low prices / Extremist parties still won Reichstag seats
items: Extremist parties still won Reichstag seats

cards.front: Name the four strengths of the Weimar economic recovery given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Industrial output surpassed pre-war levels / Exports rose / New housing was built / Wages increased for many workers

cards.front: Why did Stresemann call off passive resistance in the Ruhr in 1923?
cards.answer: To help end hyperinflation and stabilise the economy, though this angered nationalists as an unpopular decision.

cards.front: Why did right-wing nationalists like Hitler attack the Young Plan of 1929?
cards.answer: They argued Germany should not be paying reparations at all, even though the plan reduced the burden.

title: Characters: The Inspector and Mr Birling
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why does the Inspector show the photograph to only one character at a time?
cards.answer: To stop the characters comparing stories, forcing each to face their guilt individually.

cards.front: Why does the Inspector use graphic language like 'burnt her inside out'?
cards.answer: To shock the characters and audience out of complacency and confront the real human cost of their actions.

cards.front: Why does Cassius's collaborative language ('ourselves', 'we') work so effectively on Brutus?
cards.answer: Brutus would never take orders, but responds to an appeal framed as between honourable equals.

cards.front: Why does Caesar dismiss the soothsayer's warning in Act 1, Scene 2?
cards.answer: His dismissal shows his arrogance and belief that he is above mortal danger.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare use Portia's self-wounding to challenge Elizabethan gender expectations?
cards.answer: It shows her willingness to endure pain and refusal to be dismissed as a weak woman, demanding equal treatment.

cards.front: Name the three parts of the hypocaust heating system used in Roman baths.
cards.answer: Praefurnium (furnace) / Pilae (brick pillars under floor) / Tubuli (hollow wall tiles)

cards.front: Why did bathers often wear wooden-soled sandals in the caldarium?
cards.answer: The hypocaust heated the floor so much that sandals protected bathers' feet from the heat.

cards.front: Why were admission prices for the baths sometimes free?
cards.answer: Local politicians sponsored free bathing days as a form of public generosity, called euergetism, to win popularity.

cards.front: Why is combining literary and material sources the strongest way to study Roman baths?
cards.answer: Literary sources give personal accounts but only from upper-class men, while material remains show layout and heating but not experience or frequency.

cards.front: Name the three character contrasts (foils) the lesson gives as Delaney's dramatic method.
cards.answer: The Boy's tenderness exposes Peter's cruelty / Geof's devoted care exposes Helen's neglect / Jo's directness exposes Helen's evasion
items: The Boy's tenderness exposes Peter's cruelty
Geof's devoted care exposes Helen's neglect

cards.front: Why does Peter's departure at the end of his relationship with Helen confirm the audience's suspicions about him?
cards.answer: He leaves Helen for another woman, proving he was never interested in her as a person, only as a convenience.

cards.front: Why does Geof's departure from the play happen quietly rather than dramatically?
cards.answer: Helen destroys his relationship with Jo through homophobic bullying and Jo does not fight hard enough to keep him, so he leaves without drama.

title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the five steps given for calculating the mass of a substance in a reaction.
cards.answer: Write the balanced chemical equation / Identify the molar ratio from the equation / Calculate moles of the known substance / Use the molar ratio to find moles of unknown substance / Convert moles back to mass using molar mass
items: Identify the molar ratio from the equation
Calculate moles of the known substance
Use the molar ratio to find moles of unknown substance
Convert moles back to mass using molar mass

cards.front: How do you work out the molar mass of a compound like CO₂?
cards.answer: Add up the relative atomic masses of all the atoms present in the compound.

title: Jerusalem Lost, Ransom Paid: Richard's Return and Capture
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name three routes home Richard could not use in October 1192, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Western Mediterranean (Philip controlled southern France) / Through Spain (coasts closed by treaties) / Through Italy (unsafe due to quarrel with Henry VI)
items: Through Italy (unsafe due to quarrel with Henry VI)

cards.front: Name four sources the lesson gives for raising Richard's ransom in England.
cards.answer: Quarter tax on income and moveables / Wool clip of Cistercian and Gilbertine monasteries / Church plate seized from cathedrals / Tallages on the Jewish community
items: Quarter tax on income and moveables
Wool clip of Cistercian and Gilbertine monasteries

cards.front: Why was Philip II's departure from the crusade a strategic disaster for Richard?
cards.answer: It removed part of the army, let Philip plot against Richard's French lands, and destroyed the legitimacy of a joint royal crusade.

cards.front: How did the ransom England paid for Richard shape problems John later inherited?
cards.answer: It exhausted the Treasury, hardened scutage as a substitute for knight service, and taught barons royal demands could escalate without limit.

cards.front: Why does Heaney structure the poem into sixteen lines then eight lines?
cards.answer: The unequal stanzas mirror how briefly the pleasure of picking lasts compared to how long the disappointment of rot stays.

cards.front: Why does Heaney compare the children's hands to Bluebeard's?
cards.answer: It hints that even a childhood pleasure like picking berries carries a shadow of guilt, since Bluebeard's hands were stained with blood.

cards.front: How does Heaney link the children's hunger to the fungus that ruins the fruit?
cards.answer: The fungus is shown 'glutting' on the store, suggesting desire itself can spoil what it seeks, just as the children were greedy.

title: Modern recruitment: conscription, women and the professional army
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four possible outcomes a WW1 or WW2 conscientious objector tribunal could give.
cards.answer: Absolute exemption / Conditional exemption / Non-combatant service in uniform / Refusal leading to court-martial

cards.front: Name the three older forms of compelled military service in Britain mentioned before 1916.
cards.answer: Medieval feudal duty / Eighteenth-century Militia Act ballots / Royal Navy impressment (press gangs)

cards.front: Why did the government introduce the Military Service Act in January 1916?
cards.answer: Casualties on the Western Front, especially at the Somme, outpaced volunteer recruitment, narrowing the government's political room for manoeuvre.

cards.front: Why did public attitudes towards conscientious objectors differ between 1914-18 and 1939-45?
cards.answer: In WW1 the white-feather campaign shamed objectors as cowards, but by WW2 opposition was tolerated more since fighting Nazi Germany was widely seen as morally justified.

title: Family Life: Birth, Bar and Bat Mitzvah, Marriage and Mourning
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four key Jewish life-cycle ceremonies the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Brit Milah / Bar/Bat Mitzvah / Wedding / Shiva and Kaddish

cards.front: Why do mourners cover mirrors and sit on low chairs during shiva?
cards.answer: The focus during shiva is entirely on honouring the deceased and supporting the grieving family, not on normal life or appearance.

cards.front: Why is a minyan needed for saying kaddish?
cards.answer: It draws mourners into the synagogue community and ensures they are surrounded by others while grieving.

cards.front: Why does Judaism hold a baby-naming ceremony (simchat bat) for girls instead of a physical rite?
cards.answer: No equivalent physical rite exists for girls, so communities instead welcome and name the girl before the congregation.

title: The King's Great Matter and the Reformation Parliament
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four key Acts that completed the legislative break from Rome, 1532-1534.
cards.answer: Submission of the Clergy (1532) / Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) / Act of Supremacy (1534) / Treason Act (1534)

cards.front: How did the Submission of the Clergy (1532) weaken the Church's independence?
cards.answer: It made the Church accept it could not make new canon law without royal permission, ending its legislative independence.

cards.front: Why did Thomas Cranmer's appointment as Archbishop allow Henry to marry Anne Boleyn?
cards.answer: Cranmer held an ecclesiastical court that declared Henry's marriage to Catherine void, then confirmed his marriage to Anne valid.

cards.front: Why did Cardinal Wolsey lose his position in 1529?
cards.answer: He failed to secure the Pope's annulment of Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, the 'Great Matter'.

cards.front: The lesson gives six distinct tasks that happen during post-production. Name them.
cards.answer: audio mixing and sound design / music licensing and composition / visual effects and colour grading / motion graphics or animated titles / quality assurance review / final export or delivery

cards.front: Why is it a mistake to say post-production just means 'editing the video'?
cards.answer: Because post-production covers many processes beyond editing, including audio mixing, VFX, colour grading, motion graphics and quality review.

cards.front: Name the four questions the lesson gives for reading a poem's structure.
cards.answer: Where does it begin and end emotionally / Where is the turn / What repeats / How do the final lines land
items: Where does it begin and end emotionally
How do the final lines land

cards.front: Name the terminology the lesson lists as always safe to use on an unseen poem.
cards.answer: Stanza, quatrain, couplet / Refrain, rhyme scheme, half-rhyme / Enjambment, caesura, volta / Free verse, first person, present tense
items: Free verse, first person, present tense

cards.front: Why does a tight, regular rhyme scheme suit a poem making an argument feel proved?
cards.answer: It makes the poem sound settled and inevitable, so the argument feels resolved and certain.

cards.front: Why does a sudden break in a regular rhyme scheme deserve its own sentence in an analysis?
cards.answer: Because the break is a structural event, signalling a shift that needs separate explanation.

title: Your Fieldwork Approach for 2028: Transects and Place
subject: geography-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five kinds of transect enquiry listed in the specification.
cards.answer: Quality of life or environmental quality across an urban area / Micro-climate across a town or up a slope / Patterns of flow and deposition across a river channel / Vegetation patterns across a sand dune or woodland / Slope profiles and sediment sorting up a beach
items: Quality of life or environmental quality across an urban area
Micro-climate across a town or up a slope
Patterns of flow and deposition across a river channel
Vegetation patterns across a sand dune or woodland
Slope profiles and sediment sorting up a beach

cards.front: Name the five kinds of place enquiry listed in the specification.
cards.answer: Coastal features in two locations / River features in two locations / An ecosystem in two locations / Two villages or two urban environments / Quality of life in two neighbourhoods
items: Two villages or two urban environments
Quality of life in two neighbourhoods

cards.front: Why does choosing a wider sampling interval along a transect risk missing important data?
cards.answer: It covers more distance but may miss the point where the biggest change actually happens.

cards.front: Why must a place enquiry collect the same kind of evidence at both locations?
cards.answer: So the comparison between the two contrasting locations is fair.

cards.front: Name the three problems the lesson gives as the fundamental barriers to better medieval public health.
cards.answer: Poverty / Lack of central authority / No scientific understanding of disease spread
items: No scientific understanding of disease spread

cards.front: What three conditions does the lesson say public health involves managing, alongside clean water?
cards.answer: Waste disposal / Housing standards / Food safety

cards.front: Why did life expectancy fall so low in some industrial districts between 1800 and 1850?
cards.answer: Housing was built quickly with no sanitation, so overflowing cesspits and shared privies contaminated rivers used for water.

cards.front: How did removing the Broad Street pump handle change how disease spread was understood?
cards.answer: It showed cholera spread through contaminated water rather than miasma, a major step toward germ theory.

cards.front: Name the three ecological harms of metal extraction given in the lesson.
cards.answer: habitat and topsoil loss from open-cast mining / heavy metals leaching into waterways from tailings / carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide from smelting
items: habitat and topsoil loss from open-cast mining
heavy metals leaching into waterways from tailings
carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide from smelting

cards.front: Name the four non-ferrous metals covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: aluminium / copper / zinc / tin

cards.front: Why is stainless steel used for saucepan handles instead of copper?
cards.answer: Stainless steel is a poorer thermal conductor than copper, so it stays cooler to touch.

cards.front: Why does duralumin suit aircraft frames better than pure aluminium?
cards.answer: Duralumin has tensile strength close to mild steel while keeping aluminium's low density, giving strength without extra weight.

cards.front: Name the four religious changes England went through in the twenty-five years before Elizabeth's 1559 Settlement.
cards.answer: Henry VIII's break with Rome / Henry VIII as Supreme Head / Edward VI's Protestant reforms / Mary I's return to papal obedience
items: Mary I's return to papal obedience

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth retain traditional features like clerical vestments and the crucifix in the Chapel Royal?
cards.answer: To please moderate traditionalists and keep the settlement broadly acceptable, even though it frustrated committed Protestants who wanted plainer worship.

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth's 1559 Religious Settlement prove more stable than earlier religious changes in England?
cards.answer: It was a genuine compromise pleasing no one perfectly, giving workable stability that survived her whole reign without civil war.

cards.front: Name the five marriage models Austen presents in the novel.
cards.answer: Elizabeth and Darcy / Jane and Bingley / Charlotte and Collins / Lydia and Wickham / Mr and Mrs Bennet

cards.front: Why does Elizabeth trust Wickham but distrust Darcy at first?
cards.answer: She judges by surface social performance — charm and openness — rather than evidence, mistaking manners for moral character.

cards.front: Why does Austen give Elizabeth a happy ending but not Charlotte or Lydia?
cards.answer: Austen rewards Elizabeth's combination of merit and luck in marrying up, showing the class system can recognise individual worth but still stands.

title: Karma, Reincarnation, Varna and Hindu Festivals
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four stages of life (ashramas) in Hinduism, in order.
cards.answer: Brahmacharya (student life) / Grihastha (householder) / Vanaprastha (forest-dweller) / Sannyasa (renunciant)

cards.front: Why do many Hindus in northern and western India light lamps and clean their homes at Diwali?
cards.answer: Lakshmi, goddess of wealth and prosperity, is believed to visit clean, well-lit homes.

cards.front: Why does ahimsa lead some Hindu communities into environmental activism, as shown by the Chipko movement?
cards.answer: Ahimsa teaches non-harm to all living beings, so villagers embraced trees to stop loggers cutting them down.

cards.front: How did Vivekananda's teaching challenge the idea that Dalits were spiritually inferior?
cards.answer: He taught that service to humanity was service to God, calling God present in the poor (daridra narayan).

cards.front: Name the ten factors the lesson gives as influencing food choice.
cards.answer: Physical activity level (PAL) / Food availability / Celebration/occasion / Cost and income / Preferences and enjoyment / Healthy eating and lifestyles / Seasonality / Time of day / Time available to prepare/cook

cards.front: Why might someone with a good understanding of nutrition still eat an unhealthy diet, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Structural barriers like cost, lack of time, poor access to fresh food, limited cooking facilities or caring responsibilities can override knowledge.

cards.front: Why does a food desert lead to poor diets even when people understand nutrition?
cards.answer: There is no affordable fresh-food retailer nearby, so people cannot access or afford vegetables even though they know they are nutritious.

cards.front: Why do taste preferences typically differ between young children and adults?
cards.answer: Young children prefer sweeter, milder flavours, while adults develop tolerance for bitterness like coffee and dark chocolate.

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four things do the clones demonstrate their humanity through?
cards.answer: Love (Kathy and Tommy) / Creativity (the Gallery, Tommy's art) / Memory (Kathy's narration) / Suffering (donation and completion)

cards.front: Why does the system in Never Let Me Go refuse to acknowledge the clones' humanity?
cards.answer: Because acknowledging it would make the organ donation programme morally indefensible, so denial is necessary for exploitation to continue.

cards.front: Why did Miss Emily's Gallery campaign to prove the clones' humanity fail?
cards.answer: Society did not want proof clones are human, as acknowledging it would make the organ programme unconscionable.

cards.front: How does Ishiguro show that conformity in the novel does not require force?
cards.answer: Guardians give partial knowledge and Hailsham builds habit and comfort, conditioning the clones to accept their purpose without question.

cards.front: Name the four main effects e-commerce brings for a business, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Wider customer reach / Richer data on customer behaviour / Lower fixed costs per sale / Pressure on prices from easy comparison
items: Pressure on prices from easy comparison

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson gives as examples of after-sales service.
cards.answer: Help lines when something goes wrong / User training for complex products / Servicing like a boiler check or MOT / Easy returns or warranty claims
items: Help lines when something goes wrong
Servicing like a boiler check or MOT

cards.front: Why does free and simple returns work as after-sales service for ASOS?
cards.answer: A confident customer is more likely to order in the first place if returns won't be a hassle.

cards.front: How does good customer service eventually lead to higher profit?
cards.answer: Satisfaction rises, which breeds loyalty, giving repeat business that costs less to win than new customers, raising sales and profit.

cards.front: Name the three benefits of economic growth the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Higher living standards / Improved public services / More business investment and innovation

cards.front: Why does potential growth require more than just using spare resources?
cards.answer: Potential growth needs new investment, better technology or a larger, better-trained workforce to raise the economy's ceiling.

cards.front: Why can GDP per capita rise while the average person is no better off?
cards.answer: If the population grows at the same rate as real GDP, GDP per capita stays flat despite headline growth.

cards.front: Why can a boom lead to overheating in the economic cycle?
cards.answer: Demand outstrips supply so inflation accelerates and debts build up as growth runs above its long-run trend.

title: Observing the Sun and Planets in Motion
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four stages of the observation cycle used when designing a solar or meteor observation.
cards.answer: Design / Make / Analyse / Evaluate

cards.front: Name the four items the lesson says are NOT safe for observing the Sun.
cards.answer: Welding glass below shade 14 / Old CDs / Unexposed film / Unfiltered binoculars or telescopes

cards.front: Why are Venus transits of the Sun so rare?
cards.answer: Venus transits occur in pairs 8 years apart, with the pairs separated by over a century.

cards.front: Why should observers look 45°-90° away from a meteor shower's radiant rather than straight at it?
cards.answer: Looking away from the radiant gives the longest meteor trails to observe.

cards.front: Why does the split chestnut tree still symbolise hope for Jane and Rochester's future?
cards.answer: The two halves stay connected at the roots, showing they are separated by Bertha's revelation but ultimately reconnected.

cards.front: Why does Jane see Rochester's plea to become his mistress as self-serving rather than compassionate?
cards.answer: Staying would make her a dependent mistress with no legal rights, the powerless position she has always fought against.

cards.front: Name the three types of Hindu pilgrimage the lesson gives, with an example site for each.
cards.answer: Sacred river - the Ganges / Sacred city - Varanasi / Deity's childhood place - Vrindavana

cards.front: Why do Hindus perform seva (charity work) through organisations like Sewa UK?
cards.answer: Seva is selfless service expressing karma yoga and bhakti, reflecting the Bhagavad Gita's teaching that service to others is service to God.

cards.front: Why is the Ganges considered able to purify a person's karma?
cards.answer: The Ganges is regarded as the goddess Ganga Mata, whose waters purify karma and bless those who bathe in them.

cards.front: Name the twelve king-becoming graces Malcolm lists to Macduff.
cards.answer: Justice / Verity / Temperance / Stableness / Bounty / Perseverance, mercy, lowliness, devotion, patience, courage, fortitude
items: Perseverance, mercy, lowliness, devotion, patience, courage, fortitude

cards.front: Why does Macbeth order the murder of Lady Macduff and her children?
cards.answer: It is his most gratuitous crime, with no political benefit or threat to neutralise, showing pure tyranny.

cards.front: Why does Lady Macbeth speak in prose rather than verse during her sleepwalking scene?
cards.answer: Verse represents order and control, so switching to disordered prose shows her mind has fractured.

cards.front: Why does Malcolm pretend to be worse than Macbeth when he first meets Macduff?
cards.answer: He is testing Macduff's loyalty before trusting him, since a genuine reaction would prove his honesty.

cards.front: Name the three types of corrective editing done before creative effects are applied to a mix.
cards.answer: Unwanted audio removal / Pitch correction / Rhythmic correction

cards.front: Name the three types of speakers/headphones used for monitoring during mixing.
cards.answer: Headphones / Main speakers / Near-field speakers

cards.front: Why does panning instruments across the stereo field improve a mix?
cards.answer: It creates width and separation between sounds, preventing a cluttered, mono-sounding mix.

cards.front: How does adding reverb make a sound seem further away in a mix?
cards.answer: More reverb versus dry signal increases apparent distance, while a dry, close-miked sound appears right in front of the listener.

cards.front: Name the six factors the lesson gives that decided an enslaved person's status within a familia.
cards.answer: Skill / Education / Cost / Length of service / Gender / Urban or rural location

cards.front: What two rewards did Varro recommend giving a trusted overseer to keep him loyal?
cards.answer: A female companion from other enslaved workers / A peculium (personal fund)
items: A female companion from other enslaved workers

cards.front: Why did Varro warn against buying too many enslaved people of the same nationality?
cards.answer: Because it was very often accustomed to cause domestic quarrels.

cards.front: How did Crassus force Spartacus's army into a final battle?
cards.answer: He built a wall across an isthmus to trap Spartacus's army.

title: The Great Famine and Recovery under Liu and Deng, 1959-65
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four causes the lesson gives for the Great Famine, layered over the same harvest.
cards.answer: Structural: communes destroyed peasant incentives / Scientific: quotas set on inflated yield figures / Personal: no one dared challenge Mao after Lushan / External: Soviet advisers withdrawn in 1960
items: Scientific: quotas set on inflated yield figures
Personal: no one dared challenge Mao after Lushan

cards.front: Name the four things sanzi yibao covered in the 1961-62 recovery reforms.
cards.answer: Private plots restored / Free rural markets reopened / Private sideline industries allowed / Household production contracts

cards.front: Why did grain keep being exported and sent to cities while villages starved during the famine?
cards.answer: Local cadres inflated yield figures out of fear of denunciation, so procurement quotas took grain that villages actually needed to survive.

cards.front: Why did Mao see Liu and Deng's recovery measures as a betrayal justifying the Cultural Revolution?
cards.answer: He viewed them as 'capitalist roaders' restoring the old order under a new label, even though their reforms stayed within socialist language.

cards.front: The lesson names five consequences of guilt that Macbeth and Lady Macbeth suffer. What are they?
cards.answer: Insomnia and nightmares / Paranoia and fear / Social isolation / Mental breakdown / Spiritual damnation

cards.front: What three reasons does Macbeth give in Act 1 Scene 7 for not killing Duncan?
cards.answer: Duncan is his king / Duncan is his kinsman / Duncan is his guest

cards.front: Why does Macbeth keep committing more murders after killing Duncan?
cards.answer: He commits increasingly brutal murders partly to silence his guilty conscience, but each crime only increases his torment.

cards.front: How does Lady Macbeth's early dismissal of guilt make her later breakdown ironic?
cards.answer: She claims water clears the deed, but later realises no perfume can sweeten her hand, showing guilt cannot be washed away.

title: Newspaper Front Pages: The Guardian and The Sun (2025 editions)
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three colours The Guardian's house style uses in its front page design, and what each signals.
cards.answer: Deep sapphire blue - newsstand visibility and brand recognition / Red type near masthead - signals a news story / Yellow - used only for emphasis
items: Deep sapphire blue - newsstand visibility and brand recognition
Red type near masthead - signals a news story

cards.front: Why does the caption on The Guardian's balcony photo count as anchorage?
cards.answer: It explains the family are leaning left to see the flypast, turning an off-guard moment into a relatable, unified family scene.

cards.front: Why is the word 'rethink' used in The Guardian's headline instead of a more aggressive word?
cards.answer: It connotes careful reconsideration rather than panic, reflecting The Guardian's left-leaning sympathy with the Labour government.

cards.front: Why are the letters 'Y' and 'S' printed wonky in The Sun's 'Faulty Powers' headline?
cards.answer: They echo the misspelled hotel sign running joke in Fawlty Towers, implying chaos and incompetence in Britain's infrastructure.

title: Social policies, women and education under Mao
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four activities the All-China Women's Federation carried out.
cards.answer: Ran literacy classes for women / Organised participation in cooperatives and communes / Campaigned for enforcement of Marriage Law / Mobilised women into political participation
items: Organised participation in cooperatives and communes
Campaigned for enforcement of Marriage Law

cards.front: Name the three changes made to higher education in China in 1952.
cards.answer: Technical institutes prioritised over humanities / Universities amalgamated and reorganised / Curricula rewritten around Marxist-Leninist ideology

cards.front: Why can the political education of the 1950s be linked to the Cultural Revolution a decade later?
cards.answer: The generation taught loyalty to Mao and class struggle in the 1950s became the deeply indoctrinated Red Guards of the 1960s.

cards.front: Why do historians caution against accepting the CCP's claim that it fully 'liberated' women?
cards.answer: Legal equality existed on paper, but rural social conservatism, inconsistent enforcement and stigma meant emancipation was partial in practice.

title: Immigration, the Red Scare and nativism
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: What three things did Marcus Garvey's UNIA promote, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Black economic self-sufficiency / pride in African heritage / an independent Black nation in Africa
items: an independent Black nation in Africa

cards.front: Why did the Palmer Raids eventually stop?
cards.answer: Legal challenges, cancelled deportation orders on due-process grounds, and Palmer's failed May Day revolution prediction damaged his credibility.

cards.front: How did the 1919 mail bombs affect action against radicals in the US?
cards.answer: Bombs targeting officials, including Palmer, intensified public demands for action, leading to the Palmer Raids.

cards.front: Why were Sacco and Vanzetti's trial and conviction seen as unfair?
cards.answer: Critics argued prosecution was driven by their immigrant background and anarchist beliefs, and the judge showed prejudice against them.

cards.front: Name the four disadvantages the lesson gives for using a programmable system instead of a hard-wired circuit.
cards.answer: requires programming knowledge / relies on power supply stability / software bugs can cause faults / initial setup more complex

cards.front: Why would a PLC be chosen over a microcontroller to control a bottling plant's conveyor and filling machines?
cards.answer: The PLC must run continuously without failure in a noisy factory environment, which a microcontroller isn't built to withstand.

cards.front: Why is a flowchart system a good choice for a teacher planning the logic of a new control system before coding it?
cards.answer: It lets you map out decision trees and loops visually before writing code, acting as a design document.

title: Engineering Processes — Marking, Cutting, Shaping & Drilling
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four key marking-out tools listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Scriber / Centre punch / Try-square / Vernier calipers and steel rule

cards.front: What five shapes can a centre lathe produce from round bar stock, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Face off a flat end / Turn down a diameter / Drill along the axis / Cut threads / Produce tapers

cards.front: Why must drill speed be reduced when drilling harder materials or using larger drill bits?
cards.answer: To avoid overheating and breaking the drill bit.

cards.front: Why is a bandsaw useful for cutting curved shapes compared to a hacksaw?
cards.answer: It uses a continuous toothed blade loop and can cut thicker material much faster, suiting curved cuts.

cards.front: Name the three personality dimensions in Eysenck's PEN model that he linked to criminality.
cards.answer: High psychoticism / High extraversion / High neuroticism

cards.front: Why does high neuroticism make self-control harder in stressful situations, according to Eysenck?
cards.answer: The ANS reacts too quickly and strongly to stress and the limbic system amplifies fear and anxiety, making self-control harder.

cards.front: Why did Eysenck argue extraverted children take longer to learn moral restraint?
cards.answer: Because they are chronically under-aroused, their anxiety response is weaker, so punishment does not condition them as effectively.

cards.front: Why does Heaven's (1996) study only offer limited support for Eysenck's theory?
cards.answer: Psychoticism predicted delinquency at the same time but was a weak predictor of delinquency two years later.

cards.front: Name the four state symbols used in chemical equations and what they mean.
cards.answer: (s) solid / (l) liquid / (g) gas / (aq) dissolved in water

cards.front: Why does Al2O3 have the formula Al2O3 rather than AlO for aluminium oxide ions Al3+ and O2-?
cards.answer: Two Al3+ ions (total +6) balance three O2- ions (total −6) so the overall charge is zero.

cards.front: Why must a coefficient be added instead of changing a subscript when balancing an equation?
cards.answer: Changing a subscript would change the ratio of atoms and so change the identity of the substance.

cards.front: How do you find the number of moles in 44g of CO2 (Mr = 44)? (Higher)
cards.answer: Divide the mass by the relative formula mass: 44 ÷ 44 = 1 mole.

cards.front: How does a microwave oven heat food?
cards.answer: Microwaves cause water molecules in the food to vibrate, which heats it.

cards.front: Why can long wave radio signals travel around hills but short wave signals reach distant places via the sky?
cards.answer: Long wave can diffract around hills, while short wave reflects off the ionosphere for long-distance communication.

cards.front: Name the three biographical facts the lesson gives about Dickens that shaped his writing.
cards.answer: His father was imprisoned for debt / He worked in a blacking factory as a child / He used fiction as a weapon for social change
items: His father was imprisoned for debt
He worked in a blacking factory as a child
He used fiction as a weapon for social change

cards.front: Why did the Victorian wealthy believe poverty was a moral failing?
cards.answer: They believed if you were poor it was because you were lazy or immoral, letting them ignore suffering with a clear conscience.

cards.front: Why did Dickens deliberately set A Christmas Carol at Christmas?
cards.answer: Christmas was linked to rising traditions of generosity and family, so it connected his message of social responsibility to readers already thinking about goodwill.

cards.front: How does Marley's chain reflect the Gothic theme in A Christmas Carol?
cards.answer: It shows the Gothic idea that past sins have the power to curse your future.

cards.front: What five demands does Hari's notice in Scene Two make for lascar crewmates?
cards.answer: Equal pay with white sailors / Equal food and water rations / No more beatings / Rest periods between heavy labour / Recognition as members of the human race
items: Recognition as members of the human race

cards.front: Why does the royal household force Victoria to retract Abdul's higher honour in 1897?
cards.answer: The Prince of Wales insists the Munshi is not their equal and refuses to travel with him unless she backs down.

cards.front: Why is Dadabhai disillusioned and packing to return to India by 1900?
cards.answer: Years of believing in British fairness were undone by famine and plague in India and the Boer War's concentration camps.

cards.front: Why does Priestley place Birling's confident speeches immediately before the Inspector's arrival?
cards.answer: So the audience already sees Birling's views as wrong and are primed to side with the Inspector against him.

cards.front: Why does the Inspector pause and look hard at people before speaking?
cards.answer: It gives him power over the conversation by forcing the Birlings to wait in uncomfortable silence.

cards.front: Why does Sheila's reaction to sacking Eva differ from her father's reaction to sacking Eva?
cards.answer: Sheila feels immediate genuine remorse and accepts responsibility, while Birling tries to justify his actions, showing the generational divide.

cards.front: Why does Priestley keep Eva Smith absent from the stage throughout the play?
cards.answer: So the audience focuses on judging the Birlings' guilt rather than pitying Eva as an individual victim.

cards.front: Name the four types of barriers to inclusion in care settings given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Physical (no wheelchair access) / Communicative (no BSL interpreter) / Attitudinal (staff assumptions about age/ethnicity) / Systemic (referral pathways excluding those without fixed address)
items: Systemic (referral pathways excluding those without fixed address)

cards.front: Why does exclusion from services harm an individual's well-being, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Excluded individuals experience worse health outcomes, greater isolation and lower levels of well-being.

cards.front: How does being included in the community support a positive self-concept?
cards.answer: Being included in their community makes an individual feel valued, which supports a positive self-concept.

cards.front: Name the five metal ions and the flame colours the lesson gives for flame tests.
cards.answer: Lithium - crimson / Sodium - yellow / Potassium - lilac / Calcium - red-orange / Copper - blue-green

cards.front: Why can flame tests only tell you which metal is present, not how much?
cards.answer: Flame tests are qualitative tests, so they identify the metal ion present but give no information about its quantity.

cards.front: In fractional distillation, why do lower boiling point liquids get collected first?
cards.answer: Liquids with lower boiling points travel further up the fractionating column and are collected first.

cards.front: Name the four key twentieth/twenty-first century public health interventions the lesson lists, each tackling a different problem.
cards.answer: Clean Air Act 1956 (air pollution) / Smoking ban 2007 (tobacco disease) / Change4Life 2009 (obesity and inactivity) / Sugar tax 2018 (childhood obesity and diabetes)

cards.front: Why did the government initially respond cautiously to the 1950 evidence linking smoking to lung cancer?
cards.answer: Partly because tobacco generated significant tax revenue for the government.

cards.front: How did new council housing built after the 1919 Addison Act improve living conditions for working-class families?
cards.answer: It gave families homes with gardens, indoor sanitation and proper ventilation, unlike overcrowded Victorian slums.

cards.front: Why was the NHS vaccination programme launched in December 2020 significant?
cards.answer: It was the most rapid mass vaccination programme in British history, with most adults getting a dose by mid-2021.

cards.front: Name the eight pieces of information UK food labels must legally carry.
cards.answer: Product name / Ingredients list by weight / Allergen information in bold / Net quantity / Date mark / Storage conditions / Manufacturer name and address / Country of origin for certain foods

cards.front: Name the four preservation methods the lesson describes for extending shelf life.
cards.answer: Freezing / Jam-making / Pickling / Bottling and vacuum packing

cards.front: Why does chilling a sliced apple slow enzymic browning?
cards.answer: Chilling inhibits the enzyme polyphenol oxidase so it reacts more slowly with oxygen, slowing browning.

cards.front: Why can frozen food be stored safely for weeks or months at −18°C?
cards.answer: Micro-organisms cannot reproduce at this temperature and enzyme activity slows dramatically, though the organisms do not die.

title: Responding to Sports Injuries: First Aid (SALTAPS & PRICE)
subject: cambridge-nationals-sport-science

cards.front: Name the five steps of DRABC, the emergency first-aid checklist for an unresponsive performer.
cards.answer: Danger / Response / Airway / Breathing / Circulation

cards.front: Why should ice never be applied directly to the skin during PRICE therapy?
cards.answer: Direct contact with ice can cause an ice burn, so it must be wrapped in a damp cloth or ice bag first.

cards.front: How can a first aider tell if a bandage applied during Compression is too tight?
cards.answer: If the performer's fingers or toes become pale, cold or numb, the bandage is too tight and must be loosened.

title: Enslavement and the Lives of the Enslaved
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five routes into slavery the lesson gives for the Roman world.
cards.answer: Capture in war / Seizure by pirates / Birth to an enslaved mother / Punishment for crime or debt / Abandonment as an infant

cards.front: Where were Rome's two dedicated slave markets located?
cards.answer: Beside the Temple of Castor in the Forum / In the Campus Martius
items: Beside the Temple of Castor in the Forum

cards.front: Why did emperor Trajan rule that free-born infants raised as slaves should not have to buy their freedom?
cards.answer: Because he decided anyone who could prove free birth should be able to claim it without paying back their upbringing costs.

cards.front: Why did public slaves such as the artisans at New Carthage have a better chance of freedom?
cards.answer: Because officials like Scipio promised freedom to public slaves who worked hard providing equipment for war.

cards.front: Name the six phrases the lesson gives, from most positive to most negative, for saying you like or dislike something (excluding the strongest and weakest).
cards.answer: Me gusta mucho / Me mola / It's cool / I really like it / Me gusta bastante / I quite like it / No me gusta / No me interesa / I don't like it / Me aburre / Me molesta / No soporto / I can't stand it
items: No me gusta / No me interesa
Me aburre / Me molesta / No soporto

cards.front: Why does the lesson use 'encantan' instead of 'encanta' in the sentence 'me encantan las películas de acción'?
cards.answer: Because with verbs like gustar the thing liked is the subject, and 'las películas' is plural so the verb must be plural.

cards.front: Why must the adjective 'divertida' end in -a when describing 'una comedia' in the model paragraph?
cards.answer: Because adjectives in Spanish must agree with the noun, and a feminine singular noun takes the -a ending.

title: Nazi-Soviet Pact, Poland and the Outbreak of War
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four hinge events of August-September 1939 given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Anglo-French-Soviet talks failed (mid-August) / Nazi-Soviet Pact signed (23 August) / Germany invaded Poland (1 September) / Britain and France declared war (3 September)
items: Britain and France declared war (3 September)

cards.front: Which territories did the secret protocol assign to the USSR?
cards.answer: Eastern Poland / Estonia / Latvia / Finland / Bessarabia

cards.front: Why did the Blitzkrieg tactics used against Poland prove so effective?
cards.answer: Armoured columns combined with close air support and motorised infantry overwhelmed the Polish army, which was poorly equipped to face this combination.

cards.front: Why did Hitler need the Nazi-Soviet Pact before invading Poland?
cards.answer: He needed his eastern flank secured, and the pact removed the eastern obstacle that might otherwise have deterred him.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says British Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi.
cards.answer: Akhand paths beforehand / Nagar kirtan processions / Kirtan in the gurdwara / Langar

cards.front: Why is Naam Karan not the same as Amrit Sanskar?
cards.answer: Naam Karan is a birth ceremony of thanksgiving with no vows, while Amrit Sanskar is a voluntary adult initiation into the Khalsa's code of conduct.

cards.front: Why do Sikhs and Hindus celebrate Divali for different reasons?
cards.answer: Hindus mark Lord Rama's return from exile, while Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, Guru Hargobind's release from Gwalior Fort with 52 princes.

cards.front: Why did the congregation cheer with lights when Guru Hargobind returned to Amritsar?
cards.answer: Crowds celebrated his release and that of the 52 Hindu princes with lights, starting the tradition of lighting the gurdwara at Divali.

cards.front: Name four examples of individual sports the lesson gives that suit introverts.
cards.answer: Archery / Long-distance swimming / Cycling / Singles tennis

cards.front: Name four team sports the lesson gives that suit extroverts.
cards.answer: Rugby / Football / Basketball / Volleyball

cards.front: Why is a fast bowler bouncing the ball at a batsman's head classed as indirect aggression rather than direct aggression?
cards.answer: Because the aggression is intentional but directed through an object, the ball, rather than physical contact with the opponent.

cards.front: Why can overusing extrinsic rewards harm a performer's motivation long-term?
cards.answer: The performer becomes dependent on rewards, so if they are removed motivation and participation can drop sharply (the overjustification effect).

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson gives for talking about pain in German.
cards.answer: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen (I have a headache) / Ich leide an Zahnschmerzen (I suffer from toothache) / Ich habe mir den Finger gebrochen (I broke my finger) / Ich habe mir das Bein verletzt (I injured my leg)
items: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen (I have a headache)
Ich leide an Zahnschmerzen (I suffer from toothache)
Ich habe mir den Finger gebrochen (I broke my finger)
Ich habe mir das Bein verletzt (I injured my leg)

cards.front: Name the four modal verbs the lesson gives for talking about health advice.
cards.answer: müssen (must/have to) / sollen (should) / dürfen (may/allowed to) / können (can/able to)

cards.front: How do you decide whether to use haben or sein in the German perfect tense?
cards.answer: Use sein for verbs involving a change of location like going, swimming, running or hiking, and haben for everything else.

cards.front: How do you use 'um … zu …' to explain why you do a healthy activity in German?
cards.answer: Put 'um' before the reason and 'zu' plus the infinitive at the end, e.g. Ich schwimme, um fit zu bleiben.

cards.front: Name the five legal reforms of the 'permissive society' brought in under Home Secretary Roy Jenkins.
cards.answer: Abortion Act 1967 / Sexual Offences Act 1967 / Divorce Reform Act 1969 / Suspension/abolition of capital punishment (1965/1969) / Abolition of theatre censorship (1968)

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why young people gained new spending power in the early 1960s.
cards.answer: Rising wages / Near-full employment / Cheap credit

cards.front: Why did many Commonwealth migrants end up concentrated in specific areas like Notting Hill and Brixton?
cards.answer: Because they wanted to keep their cultural identity but were also pushed into these areas by discrimination in housing.

cards.front: Why do historians question how far the 'permissive society' really changed Britain in the 1960s?
cards.answer: Because outside London's educated urban minority, working-class life changed little, church attendance stayed significant and conservative values remained strong.

cards.front: Name the five types of evidence the lesson gives for past climate change.
cards.answer: Ice cores / Tree rings / Pollen analysis / Historical records / Thermometer records

cards.front: Name the three human activities the lesson gives as causes of climate change.
cards.answer: Burning fossil fuels / Agriculture / Deforestation

cards.front: How do tree rings act as evidence of past climate?
cards.answer: Wide rings show warm wet years and narrow rings show cool dry years, giving a year-by-year record over thousands of years.

cards.front: Why does a small rise in methane matter as much as a larger rise in CO2?
cards.answer: Methane traps about 28 times more heat than CO2 over a century, so even modest increases have a big warming effect.

title: Engineering Drawing, CAD/CAM and the Impact of Modern Technology
subject: engineering-aqa

cards.front: Why does 3D printing reduce material waste compared to traditional manufacturing?
cards.answer: It builds near-net-shape, adding only the material needed layer by layer, so there are no off-cuts.

cards.front: Why does CNC machining produce more consistent parts than manual machining?
cards.answer: Cutting tools follow programmed paths precisely, giving high precision and repeatable tolerances every time.

cards.front: Name the three views commonly built from a 3D CAD model (isometric, oblique and one other), each used for a different purpose.
cards.answer: Isometric — realistic view without perspective distortion / Oblique — front face true, depth at 45°, simpler but less realistic / Exploded view — parts separated to show assembly relationships
items: Isometric — realistic view without perspective distortion
Oblique — front face true, depth at 45°, simpler but less realistic
Exploded view — parts separated to show assembly relationships

cards.front: Why does increasing pressure shift equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas?
cards.answer: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas moles, opposing the increase in pressure.

cards.front: Why does adding a catalyst help equilibrium be reached faster without changing the yield?
cards.answer: A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged.

cards.front: What four paragraphs make up a typical high-scoring Section B Part 1 response?
cards.answer: Introduction with thesis / Paragraph 2: comparative point / Paragraph 3: comparative point / Final comparison/conclusion linking to thesis

cards.front: What three-step order should you follow within a comparison paragraph to integrate AO2 and AO3?
cards.answer: Analyse the named poem / Compare with your chosen poem / Add context for one or both
items: Add context for one or both

cards.front: Why should you underline key words in the Section B Part 1 question before answering?
cards.answer: So everything you write connects to the specified focus, avoiding the mistake of writing everything you know without answering the actual question.

cards.front: Why is 'Poem A then Poem B' structure discouraged in a poetry comparison?
cards.answer: It makes it harder to compare and often results in retelling rather than analysis.

cards.front: Name the six elements a complete storyboard frame should include.
cards.answer: a sketch of the scene / shot type and camera angle / duration of the shot / any camera movement / transition to the next shot / audio notes

cards.front: Name the five items a video production script typically includes.
cards.answer: speaker's name before each line / narration or voiceover descriptions / sound effect and music cues / scene headings / stage directions

cards.front: Why must a work plan include contingency time?
cards.answer: Because without a buffer for problems like equipment failure or reshoots, any delay causes the final deadline to be missed.

cards.front: How does a bird's-eye view camera angle differ from a worm's-eye view?
cards.answer: A bird's-eye view is directly overhead looking down, while a worm's-eye view is directly below looking up.

title: Synthesis: Factors Across 850 Years — Cracking the 16-Mark Essay
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What are the five steps of the five-minute essay plan for a 16-mark factors essay?
cards.answer: Name the factor / List two examples supporting it / List two examples suggesting another factor mattered more / Choose a defensible judgement / Choose two contrasting factors to weigh against it
items: List two examples suggesting another factor mattered more
Choose two contrasting factors to weigh against it

cards.front: What four pitfalls recur in weak factors-essay answers, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Single-period coverage / Listing factors instead of judging them / Ignoring the named factor / Treating individuals as isolated causes
items: Listing factors instead of judging them

cards.front: Why does the lesson say religion was more the frame than the underlying cause in 1381?
cards.answer: John Ball's preaching gave the Peasants' Revolt religious framing, but the grievances were actually rooted in the economy.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say chance made the 1381 Peasants' Revolt possible?
cards.answer: The Black Death disrupted labour and society, creating the conditions that allowed the revolt to happen.

cards.front: Name the three strengths of FPTP given in the lesson (besides stability).
cards.answer: Usually produces a clear result / Direct link between MP and constituency / Simple to understand and quick to count
items: Direct link between MP and constituency
Simple to understand and quick to count

cards.front: Name the three weaknesses of FPTP given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Large majorities from a minority of votes / Many votes are wasted in safe seats / Smaller parties win few seats despite support
items: Large majorities from a minority of votes
Many votes are wasted in safe seats
Smaller parties win few seats despite support

cards.front: Why can FPTP produce a large parliamentary majority from a minority of the national vote?
cards.answer: Votes for losing candidates in each constituency contribute nothing to the final seat count, so seats don't match vote share.

cards.front: Why does the Additional Member System produce a more proportional result than plain FPTP?
cards.answer: Regional list seats are allocated to correct for the disproportionality produced by the FPTP constituency results.

cards.front: How does John Reed's treatment of Jane represent patriarchal power at Gateshead?
cards.answer: He is male, wealthy and cruel, and the adults around him allow his bullying to continue unchecked.

cards.front: Why does Jane's outburst against Mrs Reed have both a cost and a reward?
cards.answer: Speaking truth to power gets Jane sent away, but she also feels 'the strangest sense of freedom.'

cards.front: How did Brontë's own life inspire Helen Burns's death at Lowood?
cards.answer: Her sisters Maria and Elizabeth caught tuberculosis at the harsh Cowan Bridge school and died at home, like Helen.

cards.front: Why does Brontë emphasise that Jane's Lowood education matters for her future?
cards.answer: It gives her the means to support herself as a governess, a radical achievement for a penniless Victorian orphan girl.

cards.front: Name the four things the Long Parliament did within months of assembling in November 1640 to dismantle Personal Rule.
cards.answer: Impeached Strafford / Abolished the Court of Star Chamber / Abolished the Court of High Commission / Passed the Triennial Act
items: Abolished the Court of Star Chamber
Abolished the Court of High Commission

cards.front: Why did the narrow 159-148 vote on the Grand Remonstrance matter?
cards.answer: It showed Parliament was fracturing, as some MPs like Edward Hyde felt it had gone too far and began moving towards the King.

cards.front: How did the attempted arrest of the Five Members affect opinion in Parliament?
cards.answer: It united parliamentary opinion against Charles more effectively than any speech, convincing wavering MPs he could not be trusted within constitutional limits.

cards.front: Why did the Grand Remonstrance divide Parliament?
cards.answer: It was addressed to the people rather than the King, which traditional MPs saw as wrong, and it raised fears about abolishing bishops.

title: Synovial Joints and Movement at Joints
subject: physical-education-ocr

cards.front: Name the four key components of a synovial joint that the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Synovial fluid / Articular cartilage / Ligaments / Tendons

cards.front: How does synovial fluid help protect the joint during sustained aerobic exercise?
cards.answer: It lubricates the joint, reducing friction and wear on the cartilage surfaces.

cards.front: How does articular cartilage help prevent injury when landing from a jump?
cards.answer: It absorbs the compressive impact forces from landing, protecting the ends of the bones.

title: Themes: Class, Fate, Nature versus Nurture
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four theatrical layers the lesson says stage the class divide in Blood Brothers.
cards.answer: Set / Costume / Vocal register / Proxemics

cards.front: Why might a director position the Narrator upstage and elevated throughout Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: So he becomes a watching presence the other characters seem to move beneath, making fate feel literally looming.

cards.front: How does costume design communicate the nature-versus-nurture theme in Blood Brothers?
cards.answer: Twins wear similar costumes as children showing shared nature, then diverge completely as adults showing nurture overwriting nature.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Lyons's use of the shoes-on-the-table superstition matter thematically, not just as a quirky detail?
cards.answer: She exploits Mrs Johnstone's genuine fear as a mechanism of control, showing how the powerful exploit the powerless's beliefs.

cards.front: Name the four anthology poems this lesson compares with 'Cold Knap Lake'.
cards.answer: The Bluebell / My First Weeks / Venus's-flytraps / Out, Out—

cards.front: How does the question 'Was I there?' change the structure of 'Cold Knap Lake'?
cards.answer: It breaks the confident storytelling of the opening stanzas, collapsing certainty into doubt about whether the memory is real.

cards.front: Why is the poem's final phrase 'the poor man's daughter' deliberately ambiguous?
cards.answer: It could mean the rescued child, whose poverty is shown by 'a poor house', or blur into the speaker herself since the memory's owner is unclear.

cards.front: How does the circular structure of 'Cold Knap Lake' suggest memory is hard to recover?
cards.answer: It moves from a definite, witnessed event to an uncertain closing image of things buried under 'closing water', showing memory sinking further away.

title: Profit Calculations and Average Rate of Return
subject: business-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three limitations of ARR given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Ignores timing of cash flows / Relies on forecasted figures that may be inaccurate / Does not account for inflation
items: Relies on forecasted figures that may be inaccurate

cards.front: Why does ARR treating £30,000 in year one the same as £30,000 in year four cause problems?
cards.answer: It ignores the timing of cash flows, but receiving money earlier is more valuable than receiving it later.

title: Détente and the end of the Cold War, 1970-1991
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three events/decisions the lesson gives that ended the détente era by 1980-81.
cards.answer: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, Dec 1979 / Carter's withdrawal from 1980 Moscow Olympics / US Senate refusal to ratify SALT II
items: US Senate refusal to ratify SALT II

cards.front: How did Gorbachev's reforms end up undermining the Soviet system instead of saving it?
cards.answer: Perestroika and glasnost were meant to save the Soviet system but unleashed demands for greater freedoms that fatally undermined it.

cards.front: Why did both superpowers have an incentive to pursue détente in the early 1970s?
cards.answer: Both had enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other many times over, and wanted to limit the costly arms race, while the Vietnam War had drained American confidence and resources.

cards.front: What was glasnost, introduced by Gorbachev in the mid-1980s?
cards.answer: Gorbachev's policy of openness and greater freedom of expression, introduced alongside perestroika to address Soviet economic stagnation.

cards.front: Name the four things every character in the play is searching for but never fully achieves, according to the Belonging & Loneliness theme.
cards.answer: A stable home and caring parent (Jo) / Financial security and companionship (Helen) / Connection before sailing away (the Boy) / Acceptance as he is (Geof)
items: A stable home and caring parent (Jo)

cards.front: Why does the play suggest Helen may struggle to properly mother Jo?
cards.answer: Motherhood is a skill Helen never learned because nobody modelled it for her, raising the question of how she can mother Jo.

cards.front: How does Delaney use the Boy's character to challenge her 1958 audience's racist assumptions?
cards.answer: She presents him as the kindest, most genuine character in the play, directly challenging the racist assumptions of her audience.

cards.front: Name the three key areas of disagreement the lesson identifies between religious and non-religious worldviews.
cards.answer: The basis of morality / Life after death / The nature of the universe

cards.front: Name three practical humanist ceremonies described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Naming ceremonies / Weddings / Funerals

cards.front: Why is an atheist's position different from an agnostic's, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: An atheist makes a claim about reality (there is no God), while an agnostic makes a claim about knowledge (God's existence is unknowable).

cards.front: Why does the lesson say humanism is not simply the negation of religion?
cards.answer: Humanism makes positive commitments (reason, empathy, hope, dignity, humanity) that many religious people also share, not just anti-religious claims.

cards.front: Name the four interlocking tactics the Vietcong used to neutralise US firepower.
cards.answer: Ambush from jungle cover / Booby traps and punji pits / Tunnel networks like Cu Chi / Integration with the peasant population

cards.front: What three things was Operation Rolling Thunder meant to achieve?
cards.answer: Break Hanoi's political will / Cut supply lines down the Ho Chi Minh Trail / Reassure the Saigon government
items: Cut supply lines down the Trail

cards.front: Why was the search-and-destroy tactic a strategic defeat despite winning most battles?
cards.answer: US forces killed Vietcong but did not hold ground, so villages produced refugees and resentment that fed the insurgency instead of building South Vietnamese legitimacy.

cards.front: Why couldn't the Vietcong be neutralised even in areas the US had 'cleared'?
cards.answer: They lived among the peasant population wearing peasant clothes and using tunnel networks, so they were almost never visible until they fired.

cards.front: Name the three types of genetic testing described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Carrier testing / Predictive testing / Diagnostic testing

cards.front: Name three risks or concerns raised about PGD in the lesson.
cards.answer: IVF carries medical risks for the woman / Unused embryos are destroyed / Risk of 'designer baby' selection / Implies lives with conditions are less valuable
items: IVF carries medical risks for the woman
Implies lives with conditions are less valuable

cards.front: Why could herbicide-resistant GM crops lead to 'superweeds'?
cards.answer: Modified genes could spread to wild plant relatives through cross-pollination, creating herbicide-resistant weeds.

cards.front: Why do regulatory bodies deciding on technologies like PGD include ethicists and lay members, not just scientists?
cards.answer: Because the decision involves values, personal beliefs and social priorities alongside scientific evidence, not science alone.

cards.front: Name the four main limitations of Pompeii and Herculaneum as evidence, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Frozen at AD 79 only / Pompeii disrupted by AD 62 earthquake / Both provincial Italian towns, not Rome / Poor and transient population under-represented
items: Both provincial Italian towns, not Rome

cards.front: Name the four literary sources the lesson says historians use alongside the physical evidence from Pompeii and Herculaneum.
cards.answer: Pliny's letters / Juvenal's Satire 3 / Petronius's Satyricon / Horace's Satires

cards.front: Why was Herculaneum buried under far more volcanic material than Pompeii?
cards.answer: Herculaneum, closer to the volcano, was engulfed by fast-moving pyroclastic surges rather than falling ash and pumice like Pompeii.

cards.front: How do the Pompeii election notices (programmata) show wide participation in local politics?
cards.answer: One set records endorsements from bakers, fruit-sellers, gold-smiths and other trades, showing many commercial groups took part in elections.

cards.front: Name the four main sociological perspectives on stratification given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Functionalist / Marxist / Weberian / Feminist

cards.front: According to Davis and Moore, what two essential tasks does stratification perform for society?
cards.answer: Effective role allocation / Performance linked to rewards

cards.front: Why do critics argue the UK class system is not fully open despite being meritocratic in theory?
cards.answer: Privately educated individuals are over-represented in top professions, showing ascribed status still shapes outcomes independently of talent.

cards.front: Why, according to Walby, do female-dominated jobs like care work and teaching receive lower rewards?
cards.answer: Reward levels reflect gender power relations under patriarchy, not lower functional importance of the work.

title: Hitler’s Early Career & the Munich Putsch 1923
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three roles did the SA (Brownshirts) perform for the Nazi Party?
cards.answer: Protect Nazi meetings / Disrupt rival parties' meetings / Intimidate opponents

cards.front: What three crises hit Germany in late 1923 that made Hitler think the time was right to seize power?
cards.answer: Hyperinflation destroying the economy / French occupation of the Ruhr / The government appeared weak

cards.front: Why did the failure of the Munich Putsch lead Hitler to change his strategy for gaining power?
cards.answer: The putsch proved violent revolution would fail as the army and police would crush it, so he switched to winning power through legal, democratic means.

cards.front: Why did the Nazis have only limited support between 1924 and 1928?
cards.answer: Stresemann's economic recovery made most Germans reasonably content, so the Nazis' message of anger and humiliation had less appeal.

title: The Great Cause and the Conquest of Scotland, 1290-1296
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four steps of Edward I's 1296 invasion of Scotland after Balliol's alliance with France, in order.
cards.answer: Sack of Berwick, 30 March / Battle of Dunbar, 27 April / Deposition of Balliol at Montrose, 8 July / English administration left under John Warenne
items: Deposition of Balliol at Montrose, 8 July
English administration left under John Warenne

cards.front: Why did Edward I insist candidates in the Great Cause accept him as overlord before he judged their claims?
cards.answer: By locking in overlordship first, he ensured the new king of Scots could be summoned to English courts, demanded military service, and overruled in his own kingdom.

cards.front: Why did Edward I invade Scotland in 1296?
cards.answer: Balliol's nobles refused Edward's demand for troops and sealed the auld alliance with France, which Edward saw as open rebellion.

cards.front: How did Edward I symbolically end Scottish kingship at Montrose in July 1296?
cards.answer: He ritually stripped Balliol of his royal regalia, leaving him in an empty surcoat, earning him the nickname Toom Tabard.

cards.front: Name the three factors that increase the size of an induced EMF, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Moving the conductor faster / Using a stronger magnet / Adding more turns to the coil
items: Adding more turns to the coil

cards.front: How does a dynamo produce direct current instead of alternating current?
cards.answer: A split-ring commutator swaps the connections to the circuit every half-turn, so the output voltage always points the same way.

cards.front: How does an alternator produce an alternating voltage?
cards.answer: As the coil rotates, the angle between coil and field lines constantly changes, changing the rate of cutting field lines and reversing the voltage.

cards.front: How does a transformer transfer energy between its primary and secondary coils without a direct electrical connection?
cards.answer: The changing magnetic field from the primary coil passes through the shared iron core and induces an alternating EMF in the secondary coil.

title: Saddam, WMD and the Road to the 2003 Invasion
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three formal moments and one non-event the lesson identifies on the road to the 2003 invasion.
cards.answer: UN Resolution 1441 (Nov 2002) / Blix's January/March 2003 reports / The 15 February 2003 global protests / The second UN resolution never secured
items: The second UN resolution never secured

cards.front: Why did the Bush administration treat the inspectors' findings as evidence Iraq was hiding WMD?
cards.answer: Inspectors had not found WMD but also had not concluded none existed, and this absence of certainty was treated as proof of concealment.

cards.front: Why did the post-Saddam planning by the Bush administration create problems for Iraq's Sunni minority?
cards.answer: Plans assumed Shia and Kurds would welcome liberation but paid little attention to displaced Sunnis once the army and Ba'ath party were dissolved.

title: Natural Selection, Evolution and Genetic Engineering
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three levels of scientist/discovery given for human fossil evidence of evolution (fossil finder or investigator for each).
cards.answer: Tim White's team found Ardi / Donald Johanson found Lucy / Richard Leakey led East African finds of Homo erectus
items: Richard Leakey led East African finds of Homo erectus

cards.front: How does increasingly complex stone tool-making provide evidence for human cognitive evolution?
cards.answer: Tool-making became more sophisticated (from basic Oldowan flakes to refined Acheulean hand axes) as brain size increased over time.

cards.front: Why is it important to complete a course of antibiotics and avoid overusing them?
cards.answer: Overuse lets resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, spreading resistance genes and speeding up antibiotic resistance.

cards.front: Why is the giraffe's long neck a common misconception about evolution?
cards.answer: Giraffes did not grow longer necks in their lifetime; variation already existed and longer-necked individuals survived and reproduced more, increasing average neck length over generations.

title: Faith and Learning: The Church, Universities and Roger Bacon
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the seven liberal arts studied by medieval university students.
cards.answer: Grammar / Rhetoric / Logic / Arithmetic / Geometry / Music / Astronomy

cards.front: Why did Edward I outlaw clergy who refused to pay taxes after the 1296 bull Clericis Laicos?
cards.answer: He was deep in war with France and Scotland and needed royal finance, so he defied Rome and forced clergy to pay.

cards.front: Why did friars deliberately settle in the rough, growing parts of England's cities?
cards.answer: Unlike enclosed monks, friars lived among lay people, begging for bread and preaching in the open air to ordinary townsfolk.

cards.front: Why is Charles Booth's survey extract considered reliable evidence for understanding poverty in London?
cards.answer: Booth was a wealthy businessman with no financial interest in exaggerating poverty, which increases the reliability of his findings.

cards.front: Why did Ferguson's revisionist view of the First World War differ from the traditional view partly because of when he wrote?
cards.answer: Ferguson wrote in the 1990s post-Cold War era when empire and military intervention were being reassessed, unlike earlier historians.

cards.front: Name the three long-term effects of the Cuban Missile Crisis given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Washington-Moscow hotline opened / Partial Test Ban Treaty signed / Khrushchev removed from power in 1964

cards.front: Why did Kennedy withhold US air support during the Bay of Pigs invasion?
cards.answer: He feared direct American military involvement would be exposed.

cards.front: Why did the Bay of Pigs invasion push Khrushchev toward bolder Soviet moves against the US?
cards.answer: It convinced him Kennedy might be too inexperienced to respond to bolder Soviet actions.

cards.front: Why did Khrushchev's removal in 1964 come about partly because of the missile crisis?
cards.answer: The crisis had exposed Soviet missile weakness, damaging his standing with Politburo colleagues.

title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the four environmental/economic benefits the lesson gives for recycling metals.
cards.answer: Saves energy / Reduces use of limited ore resources / Reduces landfill waste / Reduces environmental damage from mining and emissions
items: Reduces use of limited ore resources
Reduces environmental damage from mining and emissions

cards.front: Why is carbon used to extract metals like iron from their metal oxides?
cards.answer: Carbon is cheaper and more reactive than these metals, so it removes the oxygen from the metal oxide.

cards.front: [HIGHER] In a displacement reaction, why is the more reactive metal described as being oxidised?
cards.answer: Because the more reactive metal loses electrons, and oxidation is the loss of electrons.

cards.front: What are the three different consequences of idealised love shown by Keats, Byron and Barrett Browning?
cards.answer: Destruction (Keats) / Reverence (Byron) / Devotion (Barrett Browning)

cards.front: Why does the cyclical structure of 'La Belle Dame Sans Merci' matter?
cards.answer: It traps the knight in his loss by beginning and ending in the same barren scene, showing he can never escape the memory.

cards.front: Why does Keats include the vision of 'pale kings and princes' in the knight's dream?
cards.answer: It shows these are past victims of the belle dame, proving that power or status cannot protect a man from destructive desire.

cards.front: How does the structure of Sonnet 43 mirror the overwhelming nature of Barrett Browning's love?
cards.answer: It escalates from everyday, simple love to a transcendent claim of loving even after death.

cards.front: Name the three pre-war crises (1905-1911) that shook the alliance system, in order.
cards.answer: First Moroccan Crisis (1905-06) / Bosnian Annexation Crisis (1908-09) / Second Moroccan/Agadir Crisis (1911)

cards.front: Name the four countries that made up the Balkan League that attacked the Ottoman Empire in October 1912.
cards.answer: Serbia / Bulgaria / Greece / Montenegro
