cards.answer: Rapid economic change has drawn tens of millions of people from farms to cities as jobs shifted to industry and services.

cards.front: How has India's demographic profile changed as its economy has developed?
cards.answer: Fertility fell from 5.4 to 2.0 and life expectancy rose from 41 to 70 as the country urbanised and grew economically.

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say shaped the real Salem witch trials, besides superstition?
cards.answer: Land disputes between families / Social tensions between settlers and newcomers / Vulnerability of people at the social margins
items: Social tensions between settlers and newcomers
Vulnerability of people at the social margins

cards.front: How did Puritan theology make the witch trials logically coherent within the community's own belief system?
cards.answer: Puritans believed one sinner could bring divine punishment on everyone, so private behaviour became a legitimate public concern.

cards.front: Why did Miller use a small number of specific historical details rather than a fully period-accurate set for The Crucible?
cards.answer: A fully period-specific design risks letting the audience distance themselves historically instead of seeing the pattern across time.

cards.front: How did Puritan dress visually reinforce the community's culture of conformity and surveillance?
cards.answer: Puritan dress was deliberately plain and uniform, so in a community where everyone looked alike, any deviation became visible.

cards.front: Why does deforming a solid always need at least two forces?
cards.answer: A single force just accelerates the object; changing its shape needs two opposite forces acting on it.

cards.front: Why can a stretched spring return to its original shape when the force is removed?
cards.answer: Stretching pulls particles apart, increasing attractive forces, which restore the original arrangement if not overstretched.

cards.front: Why does bending a paperclip until it stays bent show plastic deformation?
cards.answer: The force is large enough that particles permanently slip past each other into new positions and don't return.

cards.front: Name the two precautions the lesson gives for accurately investigating Hooke's law.
cards.answer: Use a set square or pointer at eye level to reduce parallax error / Remove loads gently afterwards to check for permanent deformation
items: Use a set square or pointer at eye level to reduce parallax error
Remove loads gently afterwards to check for permanent deformation

cards.front: Why does incongruence lead to low self-esteem, according to Rogers?
cards.answer: A large gap between self-image and ideal self causes anxiety and low self-worth, blocking self-actualisation.

cards.front: Why might a child with an anxious temperament and critical upbringing develop especially low self-esteem?
cards.answer: Their innate anxious nature and repeated criticism from experience reinforce each other, lowering self-esteem further.

cards.front: Why must the existential self develop before the categorical self?
cards.answer: A child cannot categorise itself until it first understands it exists as a separate self to be categorised.

title: Form and Methods: Monologue, Movement and Season
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four children whose monologues open a seasonal section, and where each is set.
cards.answer: Rosie in Berlin / Pip in the garden / Mark remembering the gum tree / Ben remembering his parents dancing

cards.front: Name the six seasonal sections in the order given by the world premiere's printed synopsis.
cards.answer: Winter (London) for Rosie / Summer (Adelaide) as the family gathers / Autumn for Pip / Winter for Mark / Spring for Ben / final Summer in which Rosie leaves and Fran dies
items: final Summer, Rosie leaves and Fran dies

cards.front: Why did Bovell write the four children's monologues instead of naturalistic dialogue scenes?
cards.answer: Because collaborating with physical theatre company Frantic Assembly meant monologues suited a more physical, abstract, movement-based staging better.

cards.front: How did the production use a harness to stage the opening midnight phone call knocking Bob off balance?
cards.answer: A hidden harness let the performer fall slowly forward at about forty-five degrees and return upright, as if the earth tilted.

cards.front: Name the seven types of low-rise building given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Residential / Commercial / Industrial / Agricultural / Community / Religious / Recreational

cards.front: What four design priorities does the lesson give for industrial buildings?
cards.answer: Large clear floor areas / High eaves heights / Heavy-duty floor slabs for forklifts and racking / Good loading facilities like dock levellers and roller shutter doors
items: Heavy-duty floor slabs for forklifts and racking
Good loading facilities like dock levellers and roller shutter doors

cards.front: Why can a single building fall into more than one building-type category, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Buildings often combine uses, like a hotel that is commercial but also has recreational and community facilities within it.

cards.front: Why has the UK housing shortage created strong demand for residential construction?
cards.answer: Population growth, longer life expectancy and more single-person households increase demand while planning restrictions, land costs and worker shortages limit supply.

cards.front: Name the three developments the lesson gives that deepened American disillusionment with the Vietnam War.
cards.answer: Television coverage of the war / The Tet Offensive (1968) / The My Lai massacre revelation (1969)

cards.front: Why did the Korean War (1950-53) count as a direct application of containment?
cards.answer: UN forces, mainly American, fought to stop communist North Korea from conquering South Korea, resisting communist expansion by force.

cards.front: Why was NATO founded in April 1949?
cards.answer: To formalise Western defence by committing members to treat an attack on any one member as an attack on all.

cards.front: Name the five stratigraphic principles used together to build a sequence of geological events.
cards.answer: Superposition / Original horizontality / Lateral continuity / Cross-cutting relationships / Included fragments

cards.front: Name three way-up structures the lesson gives for working out which way up a tilted rock sequence originally was.
cards.answer: Graded bedding / Cross-bedding / Mudcracks

cards.front: Why can mudcracks be used to tell which way up a rock sequence originally formed?
cards.answer: Mudcracks only form at an exposed surface, so they show which side of the bed was on top.

cards.front: Why does uniformitarianism let geologists interpret rocks formed millions of years ago using processes seen today?
cards.answer: Because the laws of physics and chemistry do not change, past processes followed the same rules as present-day ones.

title: Photosynthesis, Limiting Factors and the Inverse Square Law
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four ways leaves are adapted to maximise photosynthesis, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Broad, flat surface area for light / Thin leaf so CO2 diffuses short distance / Network of veins for water and glucose transport / Waxy cuticle that is transparent and waterproof
items: Broad, flat surface area for light
Thin leaf so CO2 diffuses short distance
Network of veins for water and glucose transport
Waxy cuticle that is transparent and waterproof

cards.front: Name the five uses of glucose in plants given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Respiration for energy / Converted to starch for storage / Producing cellulose for cell walls / Making amino acids and proteins with nitrates / Producing lipids for storage
items: Making amino acids and proteins with nitrates

cards.front: Why does the waxy cuticle on a leaf's upper surface being transparent help photosynthesis?
cards.answer: Being transparent lets light pass through it so it can still reach the chloroplasts.

cards.front: Why should you repeat each distance measurement at least three times in the light intensity core practical?
cards.answer: Repeating and calculating a mean reduces the effect of anomalous results.

cards.front: Name the four groups Michael Harrington identified as living in poverty amidst plenty in 1950s America.
cards.answer: Rural poor of Appalachia / Elderly Americans on fixed incomes / African Americans excluded from the boom / Urban workers left behind by change
items: African Americans excluded from the boom
Urban workers left behind by change

cards.front: Why did the GI Bill end up reinforcing racial segregation in housing?
cards.answer: Banks refused mortgages and universities denied admission to Black veterans, so white veterans alone gained access to all-white suburbs.

cards.front: How did the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956 change American life?
cards.answer: It built over 41,000 miles of motorway linking cities, deepening car dependency and shifting retail and jobs to the suburbs.

cards.front: Why did unemployment disappear in the USA during the Second World War?
cards.answer: Millions of Americans joined the armed forces while defence industries absorbed the rest of the workforce.

cards.front: Name the three main differences the lesson gives between the Roman matrona and the Athenian kyria.
cards.answer: attended dinner parties with husbands / could receive academic education / greater legal independence under sine manu
items: greater legal independence under sine manu

cards.front: Why did Lucretia stab herself even though she was raped against her will?
cards.answer: Because in Roman thinking her chastity belonged to her male relatives, so her violation had to be cleansed by death despite her innocence.

cards.front: Why does the Laudatio Turiae complicate the simple picture of Roman women as passive and voiceless?
cards.answer: It shows a real wife exercising loyalty, bravery and practical influence, publicly valued and praised by her husband.

cards.front: Name the six religious traditions covered in this lesson's teaching on sexual ethics and contraception.
cards.answer: Christianity / Judaism / Islam / Hinduism / Sikhism / Buddhism

cards.front: Why does an agunah in Orthodox Judaism remain unable to remarry?
cards.answer: Because Orthodox divorce requires the husband to issue the get and a woman cannot obtain one unilaterally, so refusal leaves her chained.

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching in Humanae Vitae reject artificial contraception?
cards.answer: Because it breaks the God-given link between the unitive and procreative dimensions of sex, which must remain open to new life.

cards.front: Why is natural family planning permitted by the Catholic Church while artificial contraception is not?
cards.answer: Because tracking fertility cycles works with the body's natural processes rather than against them, unlike artificial contraception.

title: The League's 1920s Record: Successes and Failures
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three 1920s disputes the lesson lists as League successes.
cards.answer: Aaland Islands (1921) / Upper Silesia (1921) / Bulgaria (1925)

cards.front: Name four humanitarian achievements of League agencies in the 1920s described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Nansen passports for stateless refugees / Repatriating about 425,000 prisoners of war / Fighting typhus and cholera epidemics / ILO securing 17 labour conventions

cards.front: Why could the League resolve the Aaland Islands and Upper Silesia disputes but not Vilna or Corfu?
cards.answer: Aaland and Upper Silesia involved small, cooperative states, while Vilna and Corfu involved a great power or one backed by a great power, which the League couldn't force to comply.

cards.front: Why did the League's agencies' humanitarian work survive into the 1945 United Nations even though the League's political system failed?
cards.answer: Agencies like the refugee commission, Health Committee and ILO achieved durable practical results, so they outlived the political League and formed the UN's foundation.

cards.front: Name the five strong structural points the lesson lists for writing about structure in the exam.
cards.answer: The three unities / The lighting shift / The doorbell / The act-ending cliffhangers / The cyclical ending

cards.front: How does Act 1 end on a cliffhanger?
cards.answer: It ends with the Inspector beginning to question Gerald, keeping the audience engaged into the next act.

cards.front: Why is Mrs Birling's demand to 'make an example' of Eva's child's father dramatically ironic?
cards.answer: Because the father she is unknowingly condemning is her own son, Eric.

cards.front: Why is the audience's knowledge of the two world wars a form of dramatic irony in the play?
cards.answer: The 1945 audience knows the Birlings' confident 1912 world will be destroyed, undercutting their assertions that all is well.

title: Space Physics: The Solar System and Beyond
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four types of small bodies (other than the planets) listed as part of our solar system.
cards.answer: Dwarf planets / Moons / Asteroids / Comets

cards.front: What are the two independent pieces of evidence given for the Big Bang theory?
cards.answer: Red-shift of distant galaxies / Cosmic microwave background radiation

cards.front: Why does a comet move fastest at perihelion (closest to the Sun)?
cards.answer: Because the gravitational pull from the Sun is strongest when the comet is closest to it.

cards.front: Why do scientists think dark matter exists in galaxies?
cards.answer: Stars at the edges of galaxies rotate faster than expected, suggesting galaxies contain much more mass than we can see.

cards.front: Name the four persuasion techniques Lady Macbeth uses on Macbeth in Act 1, Scene 7.
cards.answer: Questions his manhood / Accuses him of cowardice / Presents a practical plan / Uses the image of killing her own child
items: Uses the image of killing her own child

cards.front: Name the three things a wife was expected to do in Jacobean England, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Obey her husband / Manage the household / Bear children

cards.front: Why is Lady Macbeth's manipulation of Macbeth so effective?
cards.answer: She exploits the Jacobean equation of masculinity with violence, appealing only to his pride and shame, not reason or morality.

cards.front: Why would Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me here' speech have unsettled a Jacobean audience?
cards.answer: Women were expected to be gentle, obedient and maternal, so her rejection of femininity for cruelty seemed deeply unnatural.

title: The Depression and the rise of the Nazis, 1928-1932
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What did Hitler offer to the six different audiences he appealed to, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Unemployed: jobs, food, dignity / Middle class: protection from Communism, order / Farmers: subsidies and protectionism / Industrialists: end to union militancy, rearmament / Nationalists: revision of Versailles / Everyone: Volksgemeinschaft
items: Middle class: protection from Communism, order
Industrialists: end to union militancy, rearmament

cards.front: Why did the Wall Street Crash cause a severe economic collapse in Germany specifically?
cards.answer: American banks called in loans that had funded German industry under the Dawes Plan, reversing the flow of borrowed US capital almost overnight.

cards.front: Why did Bruning's deflation policy make the Depression worse rather than better?
cards.answer: Cutting wages, benefits and spending while six million were unemployed caused more starvation, which fuelled more political extremism.

cards.front: Why were middle-class Germans willing to vote Nazi even though many did not love Hitler?
cards.answer: Fear of a Bolshevik revolution, fuelled by Bruning's austerity, SA street violence and the rising KPD, made an authoritarian regime seem the only way to restore order.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson gives to increase the strength of an electromagnet.
cards.answer: Increasing the current / Increasing the number of turns in the coil / Using a soft iron core
items: Increasing the number of turns in the coil

cards.front: Name four applications of electromagnets given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Scrapyard cranes / Electric bells / Relays / Loudspeakers / MRI scanners

cards.front: Why is an induced magnet always attracted to the permanent magnet that magnetises it, never repelled?
cards.answer: Because the induced poles always form so that unlike poles face the permanent magnet, causing attraction.

cards.front: How does a split-ring commutator keep a DC motor spinning continuously?
cards.answer: It reverses the current direction through the coil every half turn, keeping the forces pushing in the same rotational direction.

cards.front: Name the three laws the lesson calls the legal spine of apartheid.
cards.answer: Population Registration Act (1950) / Group Areas Act (1950) / Bantu Education Act (1953)

cards.front: Why did the apartheid government create the Bantustans and strip citizenship via the 1970 Act?
cards.answer: It let the government claim it wasn't oppressing South African citizens, since black residents were legally citizens of foreign homelands instead.

cards.front: How was the Suppression of Communism Act (1950) used to silence opposition to apartheid?
cards.answer: It defined 'communist' broadly to include anyone advocating racial equality, letting the government ban the ANC, unionists and liberals as criminals.

title: Magna Carta and the emergence of Parliament 1199-1399
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Why did King John face rebellion from his barons by 1215?
cards.answer: He raised taxes beyond feudal custom, took hostages, manipulated royal courts and lost Normandy, damaging baronial estates.

cards.front: Why did John seek papal annulment of Magna Carta soon after sealing it?
cards.answer: He wanted to escape its limits on his power, so he had Pope Innocent III annul it in August 1215.

cards.front: How did Edward I's Model Parliament of 1295 shape later constitutional practice?
cards.answer: By requiring representative consent for taxation, it built the convention that taxation needed approval from a representative body.

cards.front: Why is Richard II's deposition in 1399 constitutionally significant?
cards.answer: Parliament formally approved it, showing kingship could be conditional on good governance rather than absolute.

cards.front: Name the three men who destroy Hero at the wedding, with the phrase each uses.
cards.answer: Claudio - 'rotten orange' / Don Pedro - 'common stale' / Leonato - 'Do not live'

cards.front: Why does Friar Francis plan to announce Hero has died?
cards.answer: To make Claudio feel remorse and, if the truth emerges, allow Hero to be restored; if not, hidden in a convent.

cards.front: Why does Beatrice say 'O God, that I were a man!' instead of confronting Claudio herself?
cards.answer: As a woman she cannot challenge Claudio to a duel, so gendered constraints force her to rely on Benedick to act.

cards.front: Why does Leonato's shift in Act 5 Scene 1 not undo the damage of his earlier reaction?
cards.answer: His initial wish for Hero's death cannot be unsaid, showing patriarchal reflexes are destructive even when later regretted.

cards.front: Name the six fundamental operations that flowchart programs can implement.
cards.answer: Input/output / Counting / Branching / Testing a condition / Time delay / Loop

cards.front: In the pedestrian crossing flowchart, list the steps in order from START to the loop back point.
cards.answer: Turn GREEN LED on / Is button pressed? / Turn GREEN LED off, RED LED on / Wait 5000 ms / Turn RED LED off
items: Turn GREEN LED off, RED LED on

cards.front: Why does a light-sensor circuit include a Schmitt inverter before the microcontroller input pin?
cards.answer: Without it, a slowly-rising LDR voltage could put the input pin at an ambiguous logic level, causing unpredictable behaviour.

cards.front: How does a flowchart implement a counting operation?
cards.answer: A process block increments or decrements a variable each time the program passes through it, and a decision block tests if it reached a target.

title: The Periodic Table and Its Patterns
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the three uses of noble gases given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Argon in welding (shields weld from oxygen) / Helium in balloons and airships / Neon in lighting
items: Argon in welding (shields weld from oxygen)

cards.front: Give the four coloured transition metal compounds/ions named in the lesson and their colours.
cards.answer: Copper compounds are blue or green / Iron(II) compounds are pale green / Iron(III) compounds are orange-brown
items: Copper compounds are blue or green

cards.front: How does chlorine water added to potassium bromide solution show a displacement reaction?
cards.answer: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from the salt, turning the solution orange.

cards.front: Why do elements in the same period of the periodic table differ from each other despite being neighbours?
cards.answer: Periods share the same number of electron shells, but each element has a different number of outer electrons, giving different properties.

title: Signed Binary, Addition, Subtraction and Shifts
subject: computer-science-eduqas

cards.front: How does a processor perform binary subtraction (A − B) without a separate subtraction circuit?
cards.answer: It adds A to the two's complement of B, turning subtraction into addition.

cards.front: What does a logical shift right do to the MSB, and why is this different from an arithmetic shift?
cards.answer: It always inserts 0 into the MSB, not preserving sign, since it's used for unsigned numbers.

title: Effectiveness, Opposition and the Second New Deal
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three directions from which opposition to the New Deal came.
cards.answer: The Supreme Court / Congressional Republicans / Radical critics

cards.front: Name the three parts of the Second New Deal package of 1935.
cards.answer: Wagner Act (union rights) / Social Security Act (pensions, insurance, aid) / WPA (work for 8.5 million)

cards.front: Why did Roosevelt propose the 1937 court-packing plan?
cards.answer: Because the Supreme Court had struck down the NRA and AAA, so he wanted extra justices to outvote the conservative bloc blocking New Deal laws.

cards.front: Why did political pressure push Roosevelt to launch the Second New Deal in 1935?
cards.answer: Court strikes against the NRA and AAA, radical critics' popularity, and the approaching 1936 election convinced Roosevelt he needed bolder, more redistributive reforms.

cards.front: Why does Golding have Roger throw stones to miss in Chapter 4 but kill Piggy in Chapter 11?
cards.answer: It shows Roger's progression from restrained by civilisation's taboo to committing deliberate murder once that taboo is destroyed.

cards.front: Why does Piggy still carry the conch to Castle Rock even though the tribe no longer respects it?
cards.answer: Piggy believes the conch still commands authority, showing his continued faith in rules and democracy even as they collapse.

cards.front: What three things does Ralph weep for at the novel's end (three things named in the lesson)?
cards.answer: The end of innocence / The darkness of man's heart / The fall through the air of the true, wise friend called Piggy
items: The fall of the wise friend Piggy

title: Stars, Galaxies and the Big Bang
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the four types of object the lesson says space telescopes can detect that ground telescopes can't (blocked by Earth's atmosphere).
cards.answer: Infrared / Ultraviolet / X-ray / Microwave

cards.front: Why does gravity provide a centripetal force for orbiting planets without changing their speed?
cards.answer: Gravity continuously changes a planet's direction of travel, keeping it in a circular path, but doesn't change its speed.

cards.front: How does a cloud of gas and dust heat up enough to start nuclear fusion when a star forms?
cards.answer: Gravity compresses the cloud, doing work on it so particles collide more forcefully, raising the core temperature until fusion begins.

cards.front: Why can't a massive star's core release energy once it has fused elements up to iron?
cards.answer: Iron cannot release energy through fusion, so the core can no longer balance gravity and collapses catastrophically.

title: From Diem to Tonkin: US Steps into Vietnam, 1954-64
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: According to the domino theory, which four Southeast Asian states would fall to communism in sequence after South Vietnam?
cards.answer: Laos / Cambodia / Thailand / Burma

cards.front: Name three features of Diem's government that made it structurally weak in rural South Vietnam.
cards.answer: Reversed land reform for landlords / Catholic-Mandarin regime alienated Buddhist peasants / Nepotistic rule via brother Nhu's secret police / Preferential treatment for Catholic refugees
items: Nepotistic rule via brother Nhu's secret police

cards.front: Why did Diem's reversal of land reform help the Vietcong recruit peasants?
cards.answer: Bringing back fled landlords and reimposing rents on tenant farmers gave the Vietcong a ready-made recruitment programme among angry peasants.

cards.front: Why did the 1963 self-immolation of Thich Quang Duc damage Diem internationally?
cards.answer: Photographs of the monk's protest against Buddhist repression were printed on front pages worldwide, destroying Diem's remaining international standing.

cards.front: Name the four things Athena does to help Odysseus in the Odyssey.
cards.answer: Engineers his release from Calypso's island / Guides Telemachus on his journey / Gives Odysseus his beggar's disguise / Intervenes in the battle of Book 22
items: Engineers his release from Calypso's island
Intervenes in the battle of Book 22

cards.front: Name the three things Poseidon does to stop Odysseus getting home.
cards.answer: Destroys his ships / Strands him on distant islands / Stirs up deadly storms

cards.front: Why is Polyphemus presented as the worst possible host in the Odyssey?
cards.answer: He eats his guests instead of feeding them, dismisses the gods who protect xenia, and ignores reciprocal obligation.

cards.front: Why does Homer treat Circe's hospitality as improving over time?
cards.answer: Odysseus's resistance transforms her from a hostile host into a genuine one who gives a year of hospitality, restores his crew and vital information.

cards.front: What four things does ATP energy power in cells, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Muscle contraction / Nerve impulse transmission / Protein synthesis / Active transport

cards.front: The lesson describes three stages in how mitochondria's function was discovered over time — name them in order.
cards.answer: Observation of structure under light microscopes / Experimental isolation to find function / Detailed biochemical analysis of reaction steps
items: Observation of structure under light microscopes
Detailed biochemical analysis of reaction steps

cards.front: Why do cristae increase the rate of aerobic respiration in mitochondria?
cards.answer: The cristae are folds in the inner membrane that increase the surface area for aerobic respiration reactions to take place.

cards.front: Why must yeast fermentation avoid having too much oxygen present?
cards.answer: Too much oxygen switches yeast to aerobic respiration, which reduces the ethanol yield.

cards.front: Name the four types of erosion the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Abrasion / Hydraulic action / Attrition / Solution

cards.front: Name the four types of transport the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Traction / Saltation / Suspension / Solution

cards.front: Why does freeze-thaw weathering break rock apart?
cards.answer: Water seeps into cracks, freezes overnight, expands by about 9%, and prises the rock apart.

cards.front: Why do hard rocks like those in the Pennines stand higher than surrounding land?
cards.answer: Harder rocks such as limestone and Millstone Grit resist weathering more, so they weather slower and stand higher.

title: The Alliance System and Splendid Isolation
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three bilateral agreements the lesson says formed the Triple Entente.
cards.answer: Franco-Russian Alliance (1894) / Entente Cordiale (1904) / Anglo-Russian Convention (1907)

cards.front: Why did Italy's commitment to the Triple Alliance stay shallow?
cards.answer: Many Italians saw Austria-Hungary as the hereditary enemy for controlling Italian-speaking lands like Trento and Trieste.

cards.front: How did the alliance system raise, rather than lower, the risk of war by 1914?
cards.answer: Once both blocs were locked in, a small incident could trigger a chain reaction as mobilisation timetables left diplomacy only days to defuse crises.

cards.front: Name the four categories that hospitality and catering provision is split into.
cards.answer: Commercial residential / Commercial non-residential / Non-commercial residential / Non-commercial non-residential

cards.front: Name the four examples the lesson gives of non-commercial residential provision.
cards.answer: Hospitals, hospices and care homes / Boarding schools, colleges and university residences / Prisons / Armed forces
items: Boarding schools, colleges and university residences

cards.front: Why can achieving a Michelin star or AA rosettes be expensive for a restaurant to maintain?
cards.answer: Staff must be highly trained, ingredients must be top quality, and facilities must be immaculate.

cards.front: Why does a higher hotel or restaurant rating often let a business charge more?
cards.answer: Ratings give customers confidence in quality, so a higher rating attracts wealthier clientele willing to pay more.

title: SQL: Retrieving Data with SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the six comparison operators the lesson gives for use in a WHERE clause.
cards.answer: = (equal) / <> (not equal) / (greater than) / = (greater than or equal to)

cards.front: Why must you write Students.student_name instead of just student_name in a two-table query?
cards.answer: TableName.ColumnName notation avoids ambiguity when the same column name appears in both tables.

cards.front: Why does the WHERE clause in a two-table query set Students.student_id = Enrolments.student_id?
cards.answer: This matches the primary key in one table to the foreign key in the other, effectively joining the tables.

title: Performance Interpretation: Playing Mickey at Seven and Twenty-Five
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four physical vocabulary choices the lesson gives for playing the adult Mickey at twenty-five.
cards.answer: Higher, contracted posture with shoulders forward / Slower, heavier gait / Reduced range of gesture / Vacancy behind the eyes
items: Higher, contracted posture with shoulders forward

cards.front: Why does invading personal space signal childhood when playing Mickey at seven?
cards.answer: Children are not yet socialised into adult rules about personal space, so leaning in close reads instantly as childlike to an audience.

cards.front: How does adult Edward's clear, measured, authoritative vocal delivery affect Mickey even though Edward means only warmth?
cards.answer: It marks Edward's class privilege, making Mickey feel excluded and patronised despite Edward's genuine affection for him.

cards.front: Name the three sterilisation methods the lesson gives for treating potable water.
cards.answer: Chlorine / Ozone / Ultraviolet (UV) light

cards.front: Name the five stages of sewage treatment described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Screening and grit removal / Primary sedimentation / Biological treatment / Secondary sedimentation / Final filtration and sterilisation

cards.front: Why is chlorine most commonly used to sterilise water in the UK?
cards.answer: It is effective, cheap, and continues to kill bacteria as water travels through the distribution network.

cards.front: Why is desalination essential in arid countries but not usually needed in the UK?
cards.answer: Desalination uses lots of energy and is expensive, whereas the UK has enough rainfall for cheaper fresh water treatment.

cards.front: Name the seven operations the lesson says cover the whole string/random topic.
cards.answer: .length / .substring(x, i) with .left(i) and .right(i) / .upper / .lower / + for joining / ASC(...) and CHR(...) / random(min, max)

cards.front: Why does random(1,7) or random(0,6) break a six-sided dice program instead of causing an error?
cards.answer: Because random is inclusive of both ends, so those ranges give seven possible outcomes instead of six, silently giving wrong results.

cards.front: How can arithmetic on a character code shift a letter along the alphabet?
cards.answer: Because character codes run in order, adding to a code with ASC and converting back with CHR moves to the next letter.

cards.front: Why does word.substring(3,4) on 'Programming' give 'gram' rather than stopping at index 4?
cards.answer: Because the second argument is a count of characters taken from the start index, not a stopping index, so it takes indexes 3 to 6.

title: Cinema, TV and screen entertainment from 1920
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three Ealing comedy films the lesson gives as examples from the late 1940s and early 1950s.
cards.answer: Passport to Pimlico (1949) / Kind Hearts and Coronets (1949) / The Lavender Hill Mob (1951)

cards.front: Why did British cinema admissions fall so sharply between 1946 and 1970?
cards.answer: Television was free at the point of use, available at home, and offered a growing range of content, making it more convenient than cinema.

cards.front: How did cinema survive despite losing audiences to television?
cards.answer: It differentiated itself with large screens, better sound, and blockbuster films that could not be replicated at home.

title: Cold War, IRA and the wars on terror
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four IRA attacks described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Guildford pub bombings (1974) / Birmingham pub bombings (1974) / Brighton hotel bomb (1984) / Canary Wharf bomb (1996)

cards.front: Name the four key figures involved in the Good Friday Agreement given in the lesson.
cards.answer: John Hume (SDLP) / Gerry Adams (Sinn Féin) / David Trimble (Ulster Unionist Party) / Mo Mowlam (Secretary of State)

cards.front: Why did the Army's relationship with nationalist areas in Northern Ireland deteriorate after 1969?
cards.answer: Troops initially welcomed as protection against loyalist attacks saw relations with nationalist communities rapidly worsen after deployment.

cards.front: Why did the 7/7 bombings prompt debate about British foreign policy?
cards.answer: The bombers were inspired by al-Qaeda ideology, raising questions about links between the Iraq War and domestic terrorist recruitment.

title: Fort Laramie 1851 and the Indian Wars 1862-1867
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four pressures the lesson gives for why the 1851 Fort Laramie concentration policy failed.
cards.answer: Senate cut annuity from fifty to ten years / no Plains nation was a single political body / growing settler pressure from Pike's Peak gold rush / 1861 Treaty of Fort Wise stripped Cheyenne/Arapaho land
items: Senate cut annuity from fifty to ten years
no Plains nation was a single political body
growing settler pressure from Pike's Peak gold rush
1861 Treaty of Fort Wise stripped Cheyenne/Arapaho land

cards.front: Name the three consequences the lesson gives for the 1862-67 Indian Wars.
cards.answer: trust between Plains nations and government collapsed / US Army grew to 25,000 men west of the Mississippi by 1869 / eastern public opinion split over Sand Creek
items: trust between Plains nations and government collapsed
US Army grew to 25,000 men west of the Mississippi by 1869
eastern public opinion split over Sand Creek

cards.front: Why did the 1862 Dakota War break out in Minnesota?
cards.answer: Annuity payments were months late, the harvest had failed, and starving Dakota were told to eat grass, so four young men killed settlers, sparking a wider uprising.

cards.front: How did Fetterman's Trap happen on 21 December 1866?
cards.answer: Fetterman's detachment chased a Lakota decoy party led by Crazy Horse over a ridge into an ambush of 1,500-2,000 warriors, killing all 81 men.

title: Tests for Ions, Gases and Chromatography
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four hydroxide precipitate colours the lesson gives for identifying metal ions with sodium hydroxide (excluding aluminium).
cards.answer: Copper - blue precipitate / Iron(II) - green precipitate / Iron(III) - brown (rust-coloured) precipitate / Calcium - white precipitate

cards.front: How can you distinguish an aluminium hydroxide precipitate from a magnesium hydroxide precipitate using excess sodium hydroxide?
cards.answer: Excess sodium hydroxide dissolves the aluminium hydroxide precipitate but does not dissolve the magnesium hydroxide precipitate.

cards.front: In paper chromatography, why do some components travel further up the paper than others?
cards.answer: Components that are more soluble in the solvent travel further up the paper.

cards.front: How is ammonia gas detected in the test for ammonium ions?
cards.answer: Damp red litmus paper held near the gas turns blue because ammonia is an alkaline gas.

title: The Dignity of Human Life and Religious Freedom
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six humanitarian organisations the lesson gives as examples of religious groups acting on human dignity.
cards.answer: World Jewish Relief and HIAS / Islamic Relief and Muslim Aid / Ramakrishna Mission / Khalsa Aid / Karuna Trust / Christian charities and advocacy organisations

cards.front: How did Sikh legal cases in Britain illustrate tension with Article 18 of the UDHR?
cards.answer: Cases over wearing the kara and turban in schools and workplaces tested religious freedom against institutional rules, mostly resolved in favour of accommodation.

cards.front: Why do Humanists argue that human rights should not be based on religion?
cards.answer: They ground dignity in every person's capacity to reason, feel, and flourish, so rights don't depend on religious belief and must be universal.

cards.front: Why is Article 18 of the UDHR especially significant for Jewish people, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because Jewish history is shaped by persecution, making the protection of religious freedom particularly resonant for Jews.

title: Sedimentary Rocks and Environments of Deposition
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four clastic sedimentary rocks in order from coarsest to finest grain size.
cards.answer: Breccia / Conglomerate / Sandstone / Shale

cards.front: In the Carboniferous cyclothem, name the repeating sequence of beds from bottom to top.
cards.answer: Limestone / Shale / Sandstone / Seat earth (fossil soil) / Coal

cards.front: Why do well-rounded, frosted sandstone grains suggest a desert (aeolian) origin?
cards.answer: Grains are rounded and frosted by long transport and constant collisions carried by wind in a desert environment.

cards.front: Why does grain size in a graded bed fine from base to top?
cards.answer: A turbidity current drops its sediment load as it slows, so heaviest grains settle first and finer particles settle last.

title: Lanfranc and the Reform of the English Church
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three functions Lanfranc's Church reforms created or revived: synods, archdeacons and Church courts.
cards.answer: Revived regular synods / Developed the office of archdeacon / Separated Church courts from secular courts
items: Separated Church courts from secular courts

cards.front: Why did Lanfranc replace almost all Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans by 1080?
cards.answer: To put Norman voices in royal council, shire courts and coronations, giving political control alongside doctrinal reform.

cards.front: Why did the 1075 Council of London move sees like Sherborne and Selsey into towns?
cards.answer: Because bishops belonged where Norman castles, courts and markets were concentrated, not remote Anglo-Saxon religious sites.

cards.front: Why were the new Norman cathedrals politically significant as well as religious?
cards.answer: Their huge size and Romanesque style made Norman authority visible from miles away, like castles asserting conquest.

cards.front: Name the three muscle roles the lesson says OCR requires for movement analysis.
cards.answer: Agonist / Antagonist / Fixator

cards.front: Why must every joint be controlled by at least two muscles working in opposite directions?
cards.answer: Muscles can only pull, not push, so an opposing muscle is needed to reverse or allow the movement.

cards.front: Why do the roles of the biceps and triceps reverse during elbow extension in a press-up?
cards.answer: The triceps becomes the agonist by contracting to extend the elbow, while the biceps becomes the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening.

cards.front: Why do muscle fibres contain lots of mitochondria?
cards.answer: Mitochondria produce ATP through aerobic respiration, supplying energy for sustained muscular contraction during exercise.

cards.front: Name Merton's five modes of adaptation to strain.
cards.answer: Conformity / Innovation / Ritualism / Retreatism / Rebellion

cards.front: Why does Merton's strain theory say working-class people are more likely to turn to crime?
cards.answer: They share the same success goals as everyone else but face greater structural barriers to legitimate means, creating strain to deviate.

cards.front: How does Cohen's status frustration explain non-instrumental crime like vandalism?
cards.answer: Boys who fail by mainstream standards form subcultures that invert mainstream values, gaining status and prestige rather than material reward.

cards.front: Why did Durkheim believe a society with no crime at all would be unhealthy?
cards.answer: It would have become so rigid and repressive that even minor non-conformity would be treated as a serious offence.

title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three uses of noble gases given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Helium in balloons and airships / Neon in advertising signs / Argon in light bulbs and welding
items: Argon in light bulbs and welding

cards.front: Name the three properties of transition metals given in the lesson that alkali metals do not typically share.
cards.answer: High melting points / High density / Coloured compounds and can be catalysts
items: Coloured compounds and can be catalysts

cards.front: How do sodium and water react to form sodium hydroxide?
cards.answer: Sodium reacts with water to produce sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

cards.front: Why did chemists arrange elements by atomic weight before atomic number was known?
cards.answer: Protons and neutrons had not yet been discovered, so atomic weight was the property used to order elements.

cards.front: Name the three types of visitors Scrooge rejects in Stave 1.
cards.answer: His nephew Fred / Two charity collectors / Marley's ghost (warning him)

cards.front: Why does Dickens keep the office 'cold, bleak, biting' and give Cratchit only a tiny fire?
cards.answer: It shows Scrooge's miserliness causing real suffering to real people, not just atmosphere.

cards.front: Why does Dickens allude to Hamlet at the start of the novella?
cards.answer: Just as Shakespeare's audience must believe the old king is dead before his ghost appears, readers must accept Marley's death for the ghost's appearance to work.

cards.front: Why does Dickens make Scrooge such a repellent character by the end of Stave 1?
cards.answer: So the reader actively wants him to change, making his later redemption arc satisfying.

cards.front: Give the order of the 12 key metals (and reference elements) in the reactivity series, most to least reactive.
cards.answer: Potassium (K) / Sodium (Na) / Calcium (Ca) / Magnesium (Mg) / Aluminium (Al) / Carbon (C) / Zinc (Zn) / Iron (Fe) / Hydrogen (H) / Copper (Cu) / Silver (Ag) / Gold (Au)

cards.front: What two changes can you observe when iron is placed into copper sulfate solution?
cards.answer: Iron becomes coated with reddish-brown copper / Blue colour of the solution fades
items: Iron becomes coated with reddish-brown copper
Blue colour of the solution fades

cards.front: Why is limestone added to a blast furnace?
cards.answer: Limestone removes acidic impurities like silica by forming molten slag.

cards.front: How does bioleaching recover metal from the leachate produced by bacteria?
cards.answer: Scrap iron is added to the leachate to displace the less reactive metal, such as copper, from solution.

cards.front: Name the four types of strategy used to balance development and conservation in cold environments.
cards.answer: Technology / Governments / International agreements / Conservation groups

cards.front: Give the three reasons the lesson gives for the wilderness value of cold environments.
cards.answer: Scientific value / Aesthetic value / Ethical value

cards.front: Why is infrastructure so expensive to build and maintain in Svalbard's permafrost landscape?
cards.answer: Heat from buildings or pipelines melts permafrost ice, turning solid ground into unstable mud (thermokarst), causing subsidence and costly repairs.

cards.front: How does the 1920 Svalbard Treaty create tension between Norway's development goals and conservation?
cards.answer: It gives Norway sovereignty but grants all signatory nations equal commercial rights, so Norway cannot unilaterally end other nations' operations like Russian coal mining.

cards.front: Why does the discovery of Dunsey's skeleton force Godfrey to confess to Nancy?
cards.answer: The skeleton confirms Dunsey stole the gold and links the crime back to Godfrey's hidden past, forcing his secret marriage and Eppie's parentage into the open.

cards.front: How does Eliot use language differences to show the class divide between Eppie and Godfrey?
cards.answer: Eppie speaks in working-class dialect while Godfrey speaks formally and educatedly, showing her identity is rooted in her upbringing, not blood.

cards.front: Why is the Holocaust scene morally uncomfortable in The History Boys?
cards.answer: It exposes that Irwin's contrarian method produces smart answers on demand rather than genuine belief, applied to a subject that resists inversion.

cards.front: How does Bennett use the motorbike crash to deny the audience moral closure?
cards.answer: Hector's death freezes him as a beloved teacher, avoiding questions about prosecution, while Irwin survives diminished, preventing a clear judgement.

cards.front: Why does the Headmaster force Hector out once he discovers the abuse?
cards.answer: He exploits it as a pretext because he cannot measure the value of general studies, not out of concern for the boys.

cards.front: How does Irwin respond when Scripps challenges his relativism in the Holocaust lesson?
cards.answer: He avoids defending truth and instead tells them to distance themselves, saying 'this is history'.

title: Sources of Data on Crime and the Dark Figure
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three types of crime the lesson gives as examples of invisible crime.
cards.answer: Domestic abuse / Environmental crime / White-collar and corporate crime in private settings
items: White-collar and corporate crime in private settings

cards.front: Name the two main reasons the lesson gives for why the dark figure of crime exists.
cards.answer: Crimes are not reported to police / Reported crimes are not always recorded
items: Crimes are not reported to police
Reported crimes are not always recorded

cards.front: Why does the Crime Survey for England and Wales usually record higher crime levels than police-recorded statistics?
cards.answer: It captures crimes experienced by victims even when they were never reported to the police.

cards.front: Why is environmental crime considered invisible crime?
cards.answer: It lacks obvious individual victims who can report it to the police.

cards.front: Name the four structures blood/urine pass through in order from the kidney to leaving the body (via the renal vein and ureter/bladder/urethra route).
cards.answer: Renal artery into kidney / Ureter to bladder / Bladder stores urine / Urethra expels urine

cards.front: Why do large molecules like proteins and red blood cells stay in the blood during ultrafiltration?
cards.answer: They are too big to pass through the capillary walls into the Bowman's capsule.

cards.front: How does dialysis fluid prevent useful substances like glucose being lost from the blood?
cards.answer: Dialysis fluid has the same concentration of glucose and mineral ions as normal blood, so none diffuses out.

cards.front: Why does drinking a lot of water lead to large volumes of dilute urine? (Higher tier)
cards.answer: Osmoreceptors detect diluted blood, less ADH is released, tubules become less permeable, so less water is reabsorbed.

cards.front: Why does Claudio believe Don John's lie at the masked ball so easily?
cards.answer: His trust is fragile and built on surfaces, so one sentence from a known villain destroys it instantly.

cards.front: How does Benedick's failed love poem in Act 5 Scene 2 show his change?
cards.answer: He switches from prose to clumsy verse, comically but genuinely trying to express love in an unnatural language.

cards.front: Name the two parallel tracks of deception Shakespeare establishes by the end of Act 2.
cards.answer: Benign deceptions leading to love / Malicious deceptions leading to destruction

title: Business Ownership and Sources of Capital
subject: cambridge-nationals-enterprise-and-marketing

cards.front: Name the six sources of start-up capital the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Own savings / Friends and family / Loans / Crowdfunding / Grants / Business angels

cards.front: What four factors determine which source of capital an entrepreneur should choose?
cards.answer: How much capital is needed / How quickly it is needed / How much control they'll give up / What obligations come with the money
items: How much control they'll give up
What obligations come with the money

cards.front: Why do banks see sole traders as higher risk when lending?
cards.answer: Because sole traders have unlimited liability and limited access to finance, making banks less willing to lend.

cards.front: Why might one partner in a standard partnership be forced to pay a debt they had no involvement in creating?
cards.answer: Because standard partners share unlimited liability, so all partners are personally responsible for any debt any partner creates.

title: Dietary Laws and Rites of Passage
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: What four features make land animals, fish and birds kosher or not, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: split hooves and chew the cud (land animals) / fins and scales (fish) / birds of prey forbidden, domestic birds permitted / all insects prohibited
items: split hooves and chew the cud (land animals)
birds of prey forbidden, domestic birds permitted

cards.front: Name the four steps in Jewish burial rites described in the lesson.
cards.answer: washing and purifying the body (tahara) / dressing in simple white shrouds / burial within 24 hours / seven-day mourning period (shiva)

cards.front: How does a shochet slaughter an animal to make it kosher?
cards.answer: A trained shochet uses a single, swift cut to the throat with a perfectly smooth blade to minimise suffering and ensure rapid blood loss.

cards.front: Why does Judaism insist on burial rather than cremation?
cards.answer: Out of respect for the body created in G-d's image and in anticipation of bodily resurrection.

cards.front: Name the three characters the lesson gives as examples of managing their public reputation in The Crucible.
cards.answer: Reverend Parris (as minister) / Danforth (as incorruptible judge) / Abigail (as chosen witness of God)

cards.front: How might a director use tableau to stage the moment Abigail points and accuses in Act 3?
cards.answer: Freeze the whole cast in a fixed image at the point of accusation, showing the court collapsing into one collective response rather than individuals.

cards.front: How might a lighting designer use colour contrast to stage the hypocrisy theme across court and private scenes?
cards.answer: Use cold blue-white light for court scenes to feel institutional and inhuman, and warm amber side-light for private moments to feel human.

cards.front: Why might a Brechtian director use direct address in the courtroom scenes of The Crucible?
cards.answer: To force the audience to recognise themselves as the jury of history rather than passively watching, keeping critical distance instead of emotional immersion.

title: Energy in Motion — Crumple Zones and Momentum
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the three vehicle safety features the lesson says work by increasing collision time (other than crumple zones).
cards.answer: Airbags / Seatbelts / Cycle helmets and padded sports equipment
items: Cycle helmets and padded sports equipment

cards.front: Why does braking distance increase with the square of speed?
cards.answer: Because kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, so more energy must be removed by braking as speed rises.

cards.front: Why do sudden braking forces on vehicle occupants become very large during a crash?
cards.answer: Large deceleration means large negative acceleration, and since F = ma, this produces a very large force.

cards.front: In the worked example where a 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s collides and sticks to a stationary 1 kg trolley, why does kinetic energy fall from 9 J to 6 J? (HT)
cards.answer: The 3 J difference converts to thermal energy and sound, even though momentum stays conserved.

cards.front: The lesson gives four broad themes of rights covered by the UNCRC. Name all four.
cards.answer: Survival rights / Development rights / Protection rights / Participation rights

cards.front: According to the lesson, who do the Geneva Conventions protect?
cards.answer: Wounded and sick soldiers / Prisoners of war / Civilians in occupied territories

cards.front: Why did the Human Rights Act 1998 make it easier for UK citizens to challenge human rights violations?
cards.answer: Before 1998 citizens had to take cases all the way to the Strasbourg court, which was slow and expensive, but the Act allows cases to be heard in UK courts.

cards.front: Why do critics argue that international human rights agreements are not always effective?
cards.answer: They rely on states' willingness to comply, powerful states can resist enforcement, and the UN Security Council veto can block action against allies.

title: The Nature of God and the Trinity
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four 'omni' attributes the lesson gives to describe God's nature.
cards.answer: Omnipotence / Omnibenevolence / Omniscience / Omnipresence

cards.front: Name the three persons of the Trinity the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Father / Son / Holy Spirit

cards.front: Why do Christians say humans have inherent dignity that cannot be taken away by poverty, failure or sin?
cards.answer: Because every person is made in the image of God (imago Dei), so all human life has inherent dignity.

cards.front: How does the Trinity provide a model for human relationships, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Since God exists as three persons in loving community, humans made in his image are fundamentally relational too.

cards.front: Name the four specific animals Clarke lists as victims of the Gulf oil spill in 'Lament'.
cards.answer: Green turtle / Cormorant / Dugong and dolphin / Whale

cards.front: How does the structure of 'Lament' widen as the poem progresses?
cards.answer: It moves from a single turtle, through named and unnamed people, to wider groups of animals and the whole scorched landscape.

cards.front: Why does Clarke name only the civilian Ahmed while leaving combatants unnamed in 'Lament'?
cards.answer: Giving one civilian a name while leaving soldiers, gunsmiths and armourers anonymous shifts sympathy toward those displaced rather than those fighting.

cards.front: Why does Clarke include figures like the 'boy fusilier' and 'farmer's sons' in the litany of 'Lament'?
cards.answer: They show war draws in the naive and unwilling for ordinary reasons, complicating who deserves blame.

cards.front: Name the seven main characters examined in this lesson on Coram Boy.
cards.answer: Meshak / Otis Gardiner / Alexander Ashbrook / Aaron / Melissa / Thomas Ledbury / Sir William Ashbrook

cards.front: Why does Thomas Ledbury's death during the rescue of Aaron and Toby matter to the novel?
cards.answer: It is one of the novel's most shocking moments, and his reliable decency throws the dysfunction of other characters into sharp relief.

cards.front: How does the pairing of Melissa and Mrs Lynch develop Gavin's themes?
cards.answer: Both are women caught in systems that exploit them, yet Melissa is a victim while Mrs Lynch is a willing accomplice, testing themes from multiple angles.

title: Explaining Depression: Genes and Cognitive Theory
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Why does having a negative attribution style make setbacks feel permanent and unavoidable?
cards.answer: It blames setbacks on internal, stable and global causes, so the person feels it's their fault, will always happen, and ruins everything.

cards.front: Why does twin study evidence suggest genes play a role in depression?
cards.answer: Identical twins, who share all their genes, are more likely to both develop depression than non-identical twins, who share only some genes.

cards.front: Why is Caspi et al. (2003) only correlational evidence rather than proof genes cause depression?
cards.answer: It only identifies a relationship between the gene, stress and depression, so it cannot prove the gene causes it.

title: Formatting Output: .format, Alignment, Width and Precision
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four common mistakes with formatted output that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Too few values for placeholders raises IndexError / Forgetting the colon after the opening brace / Using type d on a real number / Expecting quotation marks to appear in printed output
items: Too few values for placeholders raises IndexError
Forgetting the colon after the opening brace
Using type d on a real number
Expecting quotation marks to appear in printed output

cards.front: Why does right-aligning a fixed-width numeric column keep the digits lined up under each other?
cards.answer: Right-aligning within a fixed width means every value ends at the same column, whatever the number of digits it has.

cards.front: Why is a format placeholder with .2f safer than round() for displaying money?
cards.answer: A .2f placeholder always shows exactly two digits, whereas round() does not force a trailing zero to appear.

cards.front: Name the several factors the lesson gives for why Cabinet support for Thatcher collapsed so rapidly in 1990.
cards.answer: Poll Tax made Conservatives deeply unpopular / MPs in marginal seats feared losing seats / European question created ministers willing to act against her / Howe's speech made dissent respectable / individual consultations revealed private willingness for her to go
items: Poll Tax made Conservatives deeply unpopular
MPs in marginal seats feared losing seats
European question created ministers willing to act against her
individual consultations revealed private willingness for her to go

cards.front: Why did Geoffrey Howe's resignation speech accelerate Thatcher's political collapse?
cards.answer: It broke the convention of Cabinet loyalty, made dissent respectable, and directly prompted Heseltine's leadership challenge within days.

cards.front: Why did Thatcher decide not to contest the second ballot of the 1990 leadership election?
cards.answer: After consulting Cabinet ministers individually, she found most believed she could not win a second round.

cards.front: Why was the Community Charge widely seen as unfair?
cards.answer: It charged every adult the same flat amount regardless of income, so a wealthy owner paid the same as a low-paid worker.

cards.front: Name the seven main anti-hooliganism strategies the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: All-seater stadia / Segregation of fans / Alcohol restrictions / Early kick-offs / Improved security and CCTV / Banning orders / Education and campaigns

cards.front: Why do the home team win more often than the away team in football?
cards.answer: Players feed off crowd energy, officials may be subconsciously influenced, and away teams face the psychological burden of hostile noise.

cards.front: How does deliberate crowd hostility disrupt an away penalty-taker?
cards.answer: Abuse from the crowd is a form of deliberate psychological disruption designed to increase pressure and harm performance.

cards.front: What four levels does the Inspector function on in the play?
cards.answer: A detective figure uncovering truth / A moral judge forcing confrontation with guilt / A mouthpiece for Priestley's socialist beliefs / A supernatural or symbolic presence
items: A moral judge forcing confrontation with guilt
A mouthpiece for Priestley's socialist beliefs

cards.front: Why does Priestley make Mrs Birling's rejection of Eva especially damning?
cards.answer: She chairs the Brumley Women's Charity Organisation, so the person meant to help the vulnerable is the one who turns Eva away.

cards.front: How does Eric's family environment contribute to his weakness?
cards.answer: His family values respectability over honesty, so he cannot be honest with his father when in trouble.

cards.front: Why is Birling's line about minding his own business important to Priestley's message?
cards.answer: It represents the capitalist creed of selfish individualism that Priestley wants to dismantle through the play.

cards.front: Name the 6 conditional tense endings used for -ar, -er and -ir verbs.
cards.answer: -ía / -ías / -ía / -íamos / -íais / -ían

cards.front: Name the 8 irregular verbs the lesson gives with irregular stems in the conditional tense.
cards.answer: tener / poder / querer / hacer / ir / ser / salir / poner

cards.front: How is the conditional tense formed for regular verbs like hablar, comer and vivir?
cards.answer: Add the endings -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían directly to the infinitive.

cards.front: How do irregular verbs like tener and poder change in the conditional tense?
cards.answer: They drop the -e- or -i- from the infinitive, sometimes adding -d-, before adding the normal conditional endings.

title: Types and Causes of Sports Injuries
subject: cambridge-nationals-sport-science

cards.front: Name the four types of acute skin damage covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Abrasions (grazes) / Cuts and lacerations / Contusions (bruises) / Blisters

cards.front: Why must a suspected fracture or dislocation not be manipulated in the field?
cards.answer: Because handling by non-experts risks further damage, so the injury must be immobilised and the athlete referred straight to emergency services.

cards.front: Why do contact sports like rugby union and American football have strict return-to-play protocols after concussion?
cards.answer: Because repeated concussive and sub-concussive blows are linked to Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy, so no athlete with suspected concussion should return in the same session.

cards.front: Name the five components of fitness tested by speed, power, agility, balance and reaction time tests, along with their test names.
cards.answer: Speed - 30-metre sprint / Power - vertical jump/Sargent jump / Agility - Illinois agility run / Balance - stork stand / Reaction time - ruler drop test

cards.front: Why is the one-rep max test hard to standardise safely?
cards.answer: The participant must lift to their absolute maximum, raising injury risk, and testers may judge 'full range of motion' differently.

cards.front: Why can the ruler drop test give a falsely fast reaction time score?
cards.answer: If the tester gives a visual cue like a finger movement before releasing, the participant reacts to the cue rather than the drop.

cards.front: Why must testing conditions be standardised before comparing results to normative data tables?
cards.answer: Any change in warm-up, equipment, time of day or examiner technique threatens reliability, which then makes the comparison invalid.

cards.front: Name the four musical elements the lesson says composers manipulate to build character and tension.
cards.answer: Instrumentation / Dynamics / Harmony / Rhythm

cards.front: What quick test does the lesson give for telling if music in a film is source (diegetic) music?
cards.answer: Character on screen could hear it / Character might react to it / e.g. dancing to it / e.g. turning down a radio
items: Character on screen could hear it

cards.front: Why does a gradual crescendo build tension before a climax or jump scare?
cards.answer: It controls dynamics directly, building anticipation as the sound gets louder towards the dramatic moment.

cards.front: How does the minor key and heavy brass in the Imperial March create a sense of menace?
cards.answer: The minor key, heavy low brass, simple repeated rhythmic motif and loud dynamic combine to represent power and menace.

title: Civil Wars in England, Scotland and Ireland 1642-1651
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four ways ordinary communities were burdened during the Wars of the Three Kingdoms.
cards.answer: Sieges / Requisitioning / Heavy taxation / Quartering of soldiers

cards.front: How did the Scottish Bishops' Wars lead directly to the English Civil War?
cards.answer: Charles I's prayer book triggered war with Scotland, forcing him to recall Parliament, which then challenged his power and caused the English conflict.

cards.front: Why was the New Model Army's cavalry discipline decisive at Naseby?
cards.answer: It was trained to maintain formation after charging instead of galloping off to plunder like earlier Parliamentary horse.

cards.front: Why did Colonel Pride's soldiers exclude Presbyterian MPs from Parliament in December 1648?
cards.answer: Army leaders were convinced Charles would never accept a lasting settlement, so they purged MPs likely to negotiate with him, leaving the Rump Parliament to try him.

title: Exoplanets, Habitable Zones and the Search for Life
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three Solar System moons the lesson gives as potential life candidates.
cards.answer: Europa / Enceladus / Titan

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson states astrometry and radial velocity together can determine about a planet.
cards.answer: Minimum mass (radial velocity) / True mass (astrometry) / Full 3D orbit (astrometry)

cards.front: Why does the radial velocity method only give a planet's minimum mass rather than its true mass?
cards.answer: It measures the star's wobble along our line of sight, so it cannot directly determine the planet's radius or true mass.

cards.front: Why do red dwarf stars have habitable zones located very close to the star?
cards.answer: Because red dwarfs are cooler and less luminous, so the zone where liquid water can exist lies much nearer to the star.

title: The Five Year Plans and Soviet Society
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What were the three core aims Stalin set out for industrialisation?
cards.answer: Build heavy industry / Achieve autarky / Prepare for war

cards.front: Name the three ways Soviet workers' lives were controlled or made harsher under the Plans.
cards.answer: Lateness over 20 minutes criminalised / Internal passports restricted movement / Wages tied to output via piece-rates
items: Wages tied to output via piece-rates

cards.front: Why is the Stakhanov coal-cutting record described as 'engineered' rather than a fair record?
cards.answer: He had teams clearing the coal away for him, making the output look like one man's work.

cards.front: Why do historians say the Five Year Plans were a triumph of headline numbers but a failure of living standards?
cards.answer: Tonnage and output soared, but quality was poor, quotas were falsified, and consumer goods stayed scarce throughout the 1930s.

cards.front: Name the four functions of political parties in a democracy given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Give voters clear policy choices / Recruit and train politicians / Organise debate in Parliament / Provide an organised Opposition

cards.front: Name the two main policies Reform UK has campaigned on, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Lower taxes / Stricter immigration controls

cards.front: Why do left-wing and right-wing parties disagree on economic policy?
cards.answer: Left-wing parties favour state intervention and redistribution while right-wing parties favour free markets, lower taxes and personal responsibility.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say political parties and pressure groups are the same thing?
cards.answer: Parties field candidates and seek to win elections and govern, while pressure groups try to influence government without seeking power themselves.

cards.front: Name the four stages in the sequence from 1950 redistribution to 1956 collective ownership.
cards.answer: 1950 redistribution to poor peasants / 1951–52 voluntary Mutual Aid Teams / 1953–54 lower-stage cooperatives / 1955–56 higher-stage cooperatives

cards.front: Why did Mao accelerate cooperation with his 1955 'Socialist High Tide' speech?
cards.answer: He believed the masses were ready, feared a return of rich-peasant power, and wanted higher grain output for industry.

cards.front: How did land reform bind peasants to the CCP through more than just receiving land?
cards.answer: Speak bitterness meetings made peasants denounce and often help kill landlords, creating shared guilt as well as shared gain.

title: Case Study: A Dynamic UK City (Birmingham)
subject: geography-edexcel-b

cards.front: Name the four zones in Birmingham's urban structure, from centre outwards.
cards.answer: CBD / Inner city / Suburbs / Urban-rural fringe

cards.front: What three migrant groups does the lesson identify as shaping Birmingham's population since 1948?
cards.answer: Caribbean families from 1948 / South Asian families from the 1960s / EU migrants after 2004

cards.front: Why do land values fall so sharply from Birmingham's CBD to its suburbs?
cards.answer: Retail and business demand for space is highest in the centre, so competition pushes rents and land values down with distance from the CBD.

cards.front: How did the closure of factories in Birmingham's inner city help cause inequality with the suburbs?
cards.answer: Factory closures like Longbridge removed most jobs from the inner ring, while suburbs gained new jobs from car-friendly retail and tech parks.

title: The Nature of Allah, Tawhid and the Qur'an
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three dimensions of tawhid in Islamic theology.
cards.answer: Tawhid al-rububiyya (oneness of lordship) / Tawhid al-uluhiyya (oneness of right to worship) / Tawhid al-asma wa-l-sifat (oneness of names and attributes)
items: Tawhid al-uluhiyya (oneness of right to worship)
Tawhid al-asma wa-l-sifat (oneness of names and attributes)

cards.front: Name four occasions when the Shahadah is spoken, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Whispered to a newborn at birth / Recited in the call to prayer / Spoken by converts entering Islam / Ideally the last words before death
items: Whispered to a newborn at birth
Recited in the call to prayer
Ideally the last words before death

cards.front: Why does Islamic art favour calligraphy and geometric patterns instead of figurative images?
cards.answer: Because the prohibition on images, rooted in tawhid, stops any object being associated with Allah, guarding against shirk.

cards.front: Why is shirk considered the most serious sin in Islam?
cards.answer: Because it directly violates tawhid and is the one sin the Qur'an indicates cannot be forgiven if not repented.

title: From Wall Street Crash to Depression America
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four main causes the lesson gives for the Depression slump.
cards.answer: Over-production by industry / Under-consumption from 1920s inequality / Speculation on the stock market / Bank failures

cards.front: Name the four Depression-era nicknames or terms the lesson gives for poverty and Hoover-blaming.
cards.answer: Hoovervilles / Hoover blankets / Hoover flags / Okies

cards.front: Why did falling share prices in 1929 lead to a spiral of factory layoffs?
cards.answer: When share-buyers stopped spending, factories cut production and laid off workers, so unemployed workers stopped buying and more factories cut production.

cards.front: Why was 1929's stock market crash able to drag down the whole economy rather than staying contained?
cards.answer: Most Americans had little spare cash due to inequality, and over-production, bank failures and the Hawley-Smoot Tariff all multiplied the damage.

cards.front: Name the four ways German school life differs from the UK, according to the lesson's Kulturzone section.
cards.answer: No school uniform / Classes last 45 minutes / Pupils stay in same room, teachers move / Must repeat year if you fail two subjects
items: Pupils stay in same room, teachers move
Must repeat year if you fail two subjects

cards.front: Why does 'halb sechs' mean 5:30 and not 6:30 in German?
cards.answer: Because halb means 'half to' the next hour, not 'half past', so it counts down to six.

cards.front: Why does the verb come straight after 'Montags' in 'Montags habe ich Englisch'?
cards.answer: Because German follows the verb-second rule, so the verb stays in position 2 even when a time phrase starts the sentence.

cards.front: Why do 'du' and 'er/sie' forms of finden add an extra e, as in 'du findest'?
cards.answer: Because finden's stem ends in -d, so an extra e is added before the ending.

cards.front: The lesson names four types of imagery pattern used across the Relationships poems. What are they?
cards.answer: Pathetic fallacy / Sensory imagery / Domestic imagery / Natural imagery

cards.front: Why does the enjambment in 'My Last Duchess' disguise the rhyme of the heroic couplets?
cards.answer: It makes the speech sound natural while keeping poetic control, mirroring the Duke's smooth exterior hiding his violent interior.

cards.front: Why does the shortened fourth line in each stanza of 'La Belle Dame Sans Merci' matter?
cards.answer: It creates a halting, incomplete rhythm that mirrors the knight's interrupted happiness.

cards.front: Name the three main rites of the Lupercalia described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Goats sacrificed at the Lupercal / Noble boys touched with bloodied knife then wiped clean, forced to laugh / Luperci running near-naked striking bystanders with goat-hide strips
items: Noble boys touched with bloodied knife then wiped clean, forced to laugh
Luperci running near-naked striking bystanders with goat-hide strips

cards.front: Why did young married women let the Luperci strike them during the Lupercalia?
cards.answer: They believed the blows would help them conceive and deliver safely.

cards.front: Why did some Roman men view the December Bona Dea rite with suspicion?
cards.answer: Because upper-class women met at night to drink wine and dance unsupervised, without men present.

cards.front: Why did Julius Caesar divorce his wife after the 62 BC Bona Dea scandal?
cards.answer: Because a man had disguised himself as a woman to infiltrate the secret rite at his house, and it was ruled sacrilege.

title: Cell Structure and How We Know It
subject: science-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the three internal structures revealed by electron microscopy that light microscopes could not resolve.
cards.answer: Mitochondrial cristae / Structure of ribosomes / Double membrane of the nucleus

cards.front: Why does the folded inner membrane of the mitochondrion make aerobic respiration more efficient?
cards.answer: The folds (cristae) greatly increase the surface area available for respiration enzymes, speeding up energy transfer.

cards.front: Why can the cell wall stop a plant cell bursting when water enters by osmosis?
cards.answer: It provides structural strength around the cell membrane, keeping the cell turgid instead of bursting.

cards.front: Why does the nuclear membrane keep pores to let genetic instructions out to the ribosomes?
cards.answer: It keeps genetic material separate from the cytoplasm while still allowing DNA instructions to be copied and sent to ribosomes for protein synthesis.

cards.front: Name the three things that are true about a reaction at dynamic equilibrium.
cards.answer: Forward rate equals reverse rate / Concentrations of reactants and products stay constant / Reaction has not stopped
items: Concentrations of reactants and products stay constant

cards.front: Why is the temperature used in the Haber process a compromise?
cards.answer: Lower temperature would give a higher yield but the reaction rate would be too slow.

cards.front: How does an iron catalyst affect the yield of ammonia in the Haber process?
cards.answer: It speeds up the reaction without changing the yield.

cards.front: How does Victor's failure to protect Elizabeth mirror his failure with the Creature?
cards.answer: In both cases his self-absorption blinds him to an obvious threat, leading to destruction.

cards.front: Why does Walton turn the ship back at the end of the novel?
cards.answer: His crew demand it, and he yields, heeding the warning Victor gave but could not follow himself.

cards.front: Name the four motives the lesson gives for Iago's actions against Othello.
cards.answer: Professional jealousy over Cassio's promotion / Sexual jealousy over suspected cuckolding / Racial hatred / General Schadenfreude

cards.front: Name the four techniques the lesson gives for how Iago manipulates others.
cards.answer: Soliloquy sharing plans with audience / Insinuation without direct accusation / Weaponising truth / Exploiting each character's weakness

cards.front: How does Othello's suicide give him back a kind of agency, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: He becomes judge, executioner and condemned in one gesture, refusing to let Venetian justice define his ending.

cards.front: Why does Roderigo keep helping Iago despite his suspicions, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: His desire for Desdemona overrides his judgment every time, despite flickering awareness he is being manipulated.

cards.front: Name the three steps of Iago's method for destroying Cassio and Othello, as given in the lesson's Key Fact.
cards.answer: Get Cassio drunk and disgraced / Advise Cassio to seek Desdemona's help / Present their innocent meetings as an affair
items: Advise Cassio to seek Desdemona's help
Present their innocent meetings as an affair

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why Othello accepts the handkerchief as 'ocular proof'.
