cards.front: Why did settlers and Plains nations clash along the trails in the years before 1851?
cards.answer: They competed over wood, water and grazing, and settlers brought disease and disturbed the buffalo herds.

cards.front: Why did US policy shift from separation to concentration by 1851?
cards.answer: Migration, new territory from Guadalupe Hidalgo, and the Gold Rush made the Permanent Indian Frontier unworkable, so reservations replaced separation.

cards.front: Name the four key properties used to describe any wave.
cards.answer: Amplitude / Wavelength / Frequency / Period

cards.front: Why can light travel through a vacuum but sound cannot?
cards.answer: Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium, but sound is mechanical and needs particles of a medium to travel.

cards.front: Why does sound diffract noticeably around corners but light does not?
cards.answer: Sound's wavelength (0.1–10 m) is similar to gaps like doorways, while light's wavelength is millions of times smaller than everyday gaps.

cards.front: Why does a wave bend towards the normal when it enters a denser medium?
cards.answer: Refraction occurs because the wave slows down when it enters a denser medium, causing it to change direction towards the normal.

title: Radio: Desert Island Discs — Industry and Audience
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four gratifications the lesson gives for why audiences listen to Desert Island Discs.
cards.answer: Entertainment / Information / Social interaction / Personal identity

cards.front: Name the four things a Desert Island Discs castaway personally chooses (aside from the automatic Bible and Shakespeare).
cards.answer: Eight pieces of music / One book / One luxury item

cards.front: Why is the BBC classed as a conglomerate?
cards.answer: It owns commercial subsidiaries like BBC Studios alongside its public service divisions, operating across different markets.

cards.front: How does Desert Island Discs show radio converging with online platforms?
cards.answer: Over 2,400 episodes are available as podcasts via BBC Sounds or the BBC website, letting listeners access it on-demand.

cards.front: What three parts should a well-structured conclusion from retail data have?
cards.answer: Reference to specific figures / A reason explaining the trend or change / The business implication going forward
items: A reason explaining the trend or change

cards.front: Why should a retailer investigate an anomaly rather than ignore it?
cards.answer: Because it is an unexpected data point breaking the trend, so it may signal a specific cause like a competitor sale or closure needing explanation.

cards.front: Why does recognising seasonal patterns matter for a retail business?
cards.answer: It helps the business plan staffing, stock levels and promotions appropriately around predictable busy or quiet periods.

cards.front: Name the five reasons the lesson gives for why Catholics go on pilgrimage.
cards.answer: To be closer to God / To seek healing or forgiveness / To pray for others / To deepen their faith / To fulfil a vow

cards.front: Why did the Catholic Church historically prefer burial over cremation?
cards.answer: Burial more clearly symbolised the resurrection of the body and followed the example of Jesus, who was buried in a tomb.

cards.front: Why do priests wear white or gold vestments rather than black at a Catholic funeral?
cards.answer: The white or gold vestments reflect the resurrection hope at the heart of Catholic funerals, rather than mourning.

cards.front: Why do pilgrims walk the final mile to Walsingham barefoot?
cards.answer: It is a penitential act of devotion, following the example of medieval pilgrims and countless generations of believers.

title: The Royal Society, Pepys and the New Science
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four buildings the lesson says Christopher Wren designed alongside his scientific work.
cards.answer: Royal Observatory at Greenwich / Royal Hospital at Chelsea / Trinity College Library, Cambridge / New buildings at Kensington Palace and Hampton Court
items: New buildings at Kensington Palace and Hampton Court

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the Royal Society was not a government department?
cards.answer: Royal patronage gave it prestige only; fellows funded it themselves through weekly subscriptions, with no Treasury money involved.

cards.front: Why did Hooke and Newton clash bitterly in the 1680s?
cards.answer: Hooke believed Newton had used his earlier ideas about gravity's inverse-square law without giving him credit.

cards.front: Why did the Royal Society require fellows to repeat each other's experiments?
cards.answer: Because the Society held that scientific claims must be reproduced by others before being accepted as true.

cards.front: Name the three characters the lesson says experience internal conflict, and what each is torn between.
cards.answer: Romeo: love vs honour after Mercutio's death / Juliet: loyalty to Romeo vs grief for Tybalt / Friar: helping the lovers vs risk of his secret plans
items: Romeo: love vs honour after Mercutio's death
Juliet: loyalty to Romeo vs grief for Tybalt
Friar: helping the lovers vs risk of his secret plans

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present family love in Verona as actually being about control?
cards.answer: Capulet demands Juliet's obedience rather than asking what she wants, showing love is conditional on compliance.

cards.front: How does the feud corrupt relationships throughout the play, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It stops Romeo and Juliet being open, kills Mercutio, forces the Friar into secrecy, and turns Capulet into a tyrant.

title: Themes: Race, Power, Love Across Lines
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the seven themes the lesson lists as running through Noughts and Crosses.
cards.answer: Racial hierarchy and its reversal / invisibility of privilege / segregation and systemic power / terrorism versus resistance / love across enforced lines / family loyalty versus political loyalty / education as gatekeeping

cards.front: Why did Blackman invent words like 'Cross', 'nought' and 'blanker' rather than using real racial terms?
cards.answer: To make the audience experience the language of hierarchy as a structural system rather than as a personal insult.

cards.front: How might a director use proxemics to show the change in Sephy and Callum's relationship over the play?
cards.answer: Early scenes show them moving freely into each other's space with childhood ease; later scenes charge the same movements with caution and risk.

cards.front: Why does Cooke's play refuse to simply endorse the Liberation Militia's violence?
cards.answer: Because the violence arises from genuine systematic oppression yet is also morally costly since innocent people are harmed, making it political tragedy not propaganda.

cards.front: Name the three contingent events the lesson gives for the shift from reconciliation to independence.
cards.answer: George III's refusal to receive the Olive Branch Petition / The Prohibitory Act of December 1775 / Publication of Paine's 'Common Sense' in January 1776
items: George III's refusal to receive the Olive Branch Petition
Publication of Paine's 'Common Sense' in January 1776

cards.front: Name the three things Paine's 'Common Sense' did that no previous patriot writer had done.
cards.answer: Attacked monarchy itself, not just ministers / Framed independence as common sense for a continent / Wrote in plain English for ordinary people
items: Attacked monarchy itself, not just ministers
Framed independence as common sense for a continent
Wrote in plain English for ordinary people

cards.front: Why did many colonists see the Prohibitory Act of December 1775 as the moment independence became inevitable?
cards.answer: It stopped trade with the colonies and authorised seizing American ships, putting them outside the king's protection.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to treat the Revolution as inevitable from 1765 onwards?
cards.answer: Because reconciliation efforts like the Declaration of Rights and Grievances, Galloway's near-successful plan and the Olive Branch Petition show reconciliation was still the majority position deep into 1775.

cards.front: Name the three main types of chemical bond covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Ionic bonding / Covalent bonding / Metallic bonding

cards.front: Give the four examples of simple covalent molecules used in this lesson.
cards.answer: H2 (single bond) / O2 (double bond) / N2 (triple bond) / H2O and CO2

cards.front: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved but not when solid?
cards.answer: In solid ionic lattices the ions are fixed in position, but when molten or dissolved they are free to move and carry charge.

cards.front: Why are ionic compounds brittle?
cards.answer: Layers of ions shift under force so ions of the same charge line up and repel each other, shattering the lattice.

cards.front: Name the three dramatic effects the lesson gives for The Empress's episodic structure.
cards.answer: Prevents settling into one perspective / Mirrors the fragmented historical record / Creates pace and energy

cards.front: How does blending historical and fictional characters serve Gupta's purpose in The Empress?
cards.answer: Historical figures give the play authority and credibility, while fictional characters let her explore emotions the historical record doesn't capture.

cards.front: How does the contrast between staging spaces communicate theme in The Empress?
cards.answer: The cramped, dark spaces of Indian characters against Victoria's grand palace visualises the power imbalance at the heart of the play.

cards.front: Name the four main reasons the first day of the Somme went so wrong.
cards.answer: Bombardment failed to cut wire / Bombardment failed to destroy dugouts / Infantry advanced slowly at walking pace, heavily loaded / Creeping barrage used inconsistently
items: Infantry advanced slowly at walking pace, heavily loaded

cards.front: Why did Pétain rotate divisions through Verdun using the noria system?
cards.answer: So that no single unit was completely destroyed, allowing about three quarters of the French army to serve there without collapse.

cards.front: How did the launch of the Somme offensive affect the German attack at Verdun?
cards.answer: It forced Germany to thin out its Verdun assault by sending divisions north, weakening the bleeding strategy.

cards.front: Why is the significance of the Somme not seen as pure futility despite huge losses?
cards.answer: It drew German divisions from Verdun, helped remove Falkenhayn, and taught the British lessons used in 1917-18.

title: The Four Aims of Life, Dharma and Human Concerns
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the four principal yamas described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Ahimsa (non-violence) / Daya (compassion) / Dama (self-control) / Dana (generosity/giving)

cards.front: Name the four duties the Bhagavad Gita (XVI 1-3) assigns to each varna.
cards.answer: Brahmins cultivate purity and wisdom / Kshatriyas show courage and leadership / Vaishyas engage in trade and agriculture / Shudras serve the other varnas
items: Vaishyas engage in trade and agriculture

cards.front: How does Hindu teaching explain suffering through karma?
cards.answer: Suffering is the natural consequence of past actions working themselves out, not divine punishment or random cruelty, and should inspire compassion.

cards.front: Why do Hindu thinkers say the four Purusharthas are not really in tension?
cards.answer: Dharma regulates the pursuit of artha and kama so wealth and pleasure don't become ends in themselves, guiding life gradually towards moksha.

title: Evaluating Human Rights and Final Exam Skills
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three mistakes the lesson says cost the most marks on the 15-mark evaluation question.
cards.answer: Giving only one side / Using bullet points / Failing to reach a clear justified conclusion
items: Failing to reach a clear justified conclusion

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four things must be checked for accurate writing in the exam?
cards.answer: Use full sentences / End each sentence with a full stop / Capital letters for proper nouns / Be consistent with religious terms
items: End each sentence with a full stop

cards.front: Why does the lesson say bullet points hurt a 15-mark evaluation answer?
cards.answer: Bullet points leave no room for the evaluative language needed to reach higher marks.

cards.front: Why does the lesson recommend writing your conclusion first if you are running short on time?
cards.answer: An answer with a conclusion but a thin body scores higher than a detailed first paragraph with no conclusion.

cards.front: Name the seven consequences of a sedentary lifestyle given in the lesson.
cards.answer: overweight/obesity / coronary heart disease / high blood pressure / type 2 diabetes / osteoporosis / loss of muscle tone and poor posture / depression/anxiety
items: loss of muscle tone and poor posture

cards.front: Why does a diet high in saturated fat and refined sugar increase risk of coronary heart disease?
cards.answer: It raises LDL cholesterol, which contributes to atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease.

cards.front: How does long-term heavy alcohol consumption harm an athlete's fitness?
cards.answer: It damages the liver, raises blood pressure, causes weight gain and disrupts sleep, worsening recovery and fitness over time.

cards.front: Why is an overfat person not always the same as someone who is overweight?
cards.answer: Overweight is based on BMI, but a heavily muscled athlete can have a high BMI without having excess body fat.

cards.front: Why does Antony dismiss Lepidus as 'a slight unmeritable man, / Meet to be sent on errands'?
cards.answer: Antony sees Lepidus as a useful tool rather than an equal partner in the triumvirate.

cards.front: How does the formal farewell between Brutus and Cassius before Philippi contrast with their earlier quarrel?
cards.answer: Its calm formality shows their bond has survived the bitter strain of the Sardis quarrel.

title: The Glorious Revolution and parliamentary monarchy
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Why did William III need to call Parliament every year after 1688?
cards.answer: He needed Parliament's money to fund his wars against Louis XIV of France.

cards.front: How did Robert Walpole hold power as First Lord of the Treasury without a formal Prime Minister title?
cards.answer: He managed Parliament through patronage, persuasion and political organisation rather than relying on royal favour.

cards.front: Why did Catholics and Jacobites see the events of 1688 as not 'glorious'?
cards.answer: It was the violent overthrow of the legitimate king by a foreign army funded by Dutch commercial interests.

cards.front: Name the two Palestinian factions the lesson gives as part of the PLO umbrella body.
cards.answer: Fatah, led by Arafat / the Marxist-Leninist PFLP

cards.front: Why did the Rabat resolution of 1974 matter for future negotiations over the West Bank?
cards.answer: It made the PLO the sole legitimate representative of Palestinians, so any Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank had to be negotiated with the PLO, not Jordan.

cards.front: Why was Hezbollah able to displace the PLO as the main symbol of resistance to Israel after 1982?
cards.answer: The 1982 invasion removed the PLO's mini-state and fighters from Lebanon, leaving a vacuum that Iranian-backed Hezbollah filled with attacks Israel had not anticipated.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to treat 'the PLO' and 'the Palestinians' as the same thing?
cards.answer: The PLO was an Arab-state-funded leadership based in Lebanon, not a government chosen by Palestinians in the West Bank or Gaza.

cards.front: Name the three causes the lesson gives for the 2021 UK supply chain crisis.
cards.answer: Covid factory closures / shortage of shipping containers / Suez Canal blockage (Ever Given) / HGV driver shortages

cards.front: Name the three effects the lesson gives of high unemployment on UK businesses.
cards.answer: Sales fall as customers spend less / wage costs drop from more competition for jobs / government benefit spending rises
items: Sales fall as customers spend less
wage costs drop from more competition for jobs

cards.front: Why are luxury brands like Burberry hit hard when consumer income falls?
cards.answer: Their products are non-essential, so customers cut them first when money is tight.

cards.front: How did the 2021 global supply chain crisis affect UK car production?
cards.answer: A shortage of computer chips from Taiwan meant car makers could not get parts, stalling production.

cards.front: Why does the theft of Piggy's glasses symbolise more than just losing an object?
cards.answer: It represents the theft of rational thought and technology, as fire and power now belong entirely to Jack.

cards.front: Why does the conch shattering at Piggy's death matter symbolically?
cards.answer: Piggy and the conch represent belief in reason and self-government, so both being destroyed shows democracy has been annihilated.

cards.front: Why is the naval officer's rescue of Ralph described as deeply ironic?
cards.answer: He expects brave British boys but finds painted savages and murderers, showing the adult world he belongs to is equally uncivilised.

cards.front: Why does Ralph lose his innocence, according to the lesson's reading of the ending?
cards.answer: Not because he witnessed violence, but because he took part in it and realised he was capable of it himself.

cards.front: Give the six stages of Othello's verse-to-prose arc across the play, in order.
cards.answer: Controlled iambic pentameter (Acts 1–2) / Increasingly disturbed verse (Act 3) / Fragmented prose (Act 4) / Epileptic collapse (Act 4) / Restored verse in murder scene (Act 5) / Restored verse in final speech (Act 5)

cards.front: Name the six stages of the handkerchief's journey through different hands in Othello.
cards.answer: Desdemona drops it / Emilia finds it / Iago takes it / Cassio has it planted on him / Bianca copies it / Othello sees it as proof
items: Cassio has it planted on him

cards.front: How does the eavesdropping staging in Act 4 Scene 1 create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: Iago places Othello where he can see but not hear Cassio joking about Bianca, so Othello wrongly believes Cassio is laughing about Desdemona.

cards.front: Why does Iago speak prose with Roderigo but verse with Othello?
cards.answer: Iago adapts his register to each audience, lowering himself to Roderigo's level and matching Othello's noble speech to manipulate them both.

cards.front: Name the four sources of tension the lesson identifies building in Act 2.
cards.answer: Economic pressure / Family conflict / Racial hostility / Junior's radicalisation

cards.front: Why does Lorna face a crisis of belonging in Act 2?
cards.answer: As Wendell's mixed-race daughter, she is neither fully Black nor fully white and feels she does not belong anywhere.

cards.front: Why does Princess destroy her beauty pageant costumes in Act 2?
cards.answer: After racist bullying, it rejects white beauty standards and marks her loss of innocence as her ambition cannot survive contact with racism.

cards.front: Name the three Hobson daughters introduced in Act 1.
cards.answer: Maggie / Alice / Vickey

cards.front: Why does Brighouse present Hobson's authority as absurd from the start of Act 1?
cards.answer: Hobson lectures his daughters on respectability then goes drinking, showing he cannot manage his own behaviour despite claiming authority.

cards.front: Why is Mrs Hepworth's visit a pivotal moment in Act 1?
cards.answer: She publicly recognises Willie's talent and gives him her calling card, giving Maggie evidence that Willie's skill is being exploited.

cards.front: How does Willie first directly challenge Hobson's power in Act 1?
cards.answer: He warns Hobson that if he uses the belt, Willie will take Maggie and the two will set up on their own.

title: Themes: change and continuity in health and medicine
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name three examples of continuity given in the lesson that persisted across all three eras of British medical history.
cards.answer: Quarantine used against outbreaks / Herbal and alternative medicine / Reactive government response to crises / Health inequalities between rich and poor
items: Health inequalities between rich and poor

cards.front: Why did Lister's antiseptic surgery, despite being based on Pasteur's germ theory, face years of resistance from surgeons?
cards.answer: Germ theory was published in 1861 but established surgeons resisted applying it in practice for years afterwards.

cards.front: How did the printing press speed up the spread of Vesalius's corrections to Galen?
cards.answer: It allowed medical knowledge to spread rapidly, making Vesalius's corrections widely known within years rather than decades.

cards.front: Why does Gerald leave to be alone for a while after confessing about Eva?
cards.answer: So he can avoid witnessing Mrs Birling's interrogation, meaning distance stops him truly being changed by the experience.

cards.front: Why does the Inspector let Mrs Birling demand harsh punishment for the father before revealing it is Eric?
cards.answer: So her own class prejudice traps her into publicly condemning her son, delivering dramatic justice she cannot retract.

cards.front: Name the three Norfolk events/moments that build its symbolic weight in Never Let Me Go.
cards.answer: The failed search for Ruth's possible / Tommy finding the replacement tape / Kathy at the wire fence in the final scene
items: The failed search for Ruth's possible
Kathy at the wire fence in the final scene

cards.front: Why does the loss and replacement of the Judy Bridgewater tape reinforce the novel's message?
cards.answer: The original held Kathy's real childhood feelings, but the replacement only holds the memory of them, showing what is lost cannot be truly recovered.

cards.front: Why does Ishiguro present Hailsham as both a paradise and a prison?
cards.answer: It gave the clones friendship and safety while conditioning them to accept organ donation, showing how people can feel nostalgic for institutions that harmed them.

cards.front: Why did the Gallery's campaign to prove the clones' humanity fail?
cards.answer: Because proof of humanity means nothing to a society that has decided it doesn't want to think about the clones' treatment.

title: The League of Nations in the 1920s
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four main bodies of the League of Nations' structure.
cards.answer: The Assembly / The Council / The Permanent Court of International Justice / The Secretariat
items: The Permanent Court of International Justice

cards.front: Give three areas of humanitarian or technical work the League achieved success in during the 1920s.
cards.answer: Refugee work via the Nansen passport / Improving working conditions (ILO) / Coordinating typhus outbreak responses / Monitoring slavery in territories
items: Refugee work via the Nansen passport

cards.front: Why was the Mosul Settlement of 1925 considered a success for the League?
cards.answer: The League settled the border dispute between Turkey and British-controlled Iraq over the oil-rich Mosul region by awarding it to Iraq.

cards.front: Why did the Corfu incident reveal a critical weakness in the League's authority?
cards.answer: The League had moral authority but no military force to compel powerful states like Mussolini's Italy to obey its rulings.

cards.front: Why did the Montgomery bus boycott put serious pressure on the city's bus company?
cards.answer: Black passengers provided around 70 per cent of its revenue, so their boycott caused serious financial losses.

cards.front: Why was Emmett Till's mother's decision to hold an open-casket funeral so significant?
cards.answer: It let published photographs of his body show the brutal reality of racial violence, shocking and energising the movement.

cards.front: Name the three ways the Montgomery Bus Boycott was significant beyond Montgomery, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Showed organised non-violent protest could succeed / Launched Martin Luther King Jr. as a national figure / Provided a model of protest copied across the South
items: Showed organised non-violent protest could succeed
Launched Martin Luther King Jr. as a national figure
Provided a model of protest copied across the South

cards.front: Name the six stages of designing a piece of sociological research, in order.
cards.answer: Aim/hypothesis / Operationalise key concepts / Choose method / Choose sampling strategy / Run a pilot study / Address ethical issues

cards.front: Name the five main sampling methods covered for studying school exclusion.
cards.answer: Random / Systematic / Stratified / Quota / Snowball

cards.front: Why might a researcher choose participant observation to study excluded pupils rather than a questionnaire?
cards.answer: Because the group is hard to reach and unlikely to respond to surveys, so observation generates rich qualitative data on natural behaviour.

cards.front: How does using mixed methods increase the validity of a study's findings?
cards.answer: Combining two methods allows triangulation, checking whether findings from one method are supported or contradicted by another.

cards.front: Name the three anti-heroes/villains covered in this part of the Heroes and Villains theme.
cards.answer: Sejanus, ambitious adviser (Tacitus) / Mezentius, cruel Etruscan king (Virgil) / Sempronia, dangerous noblewoman (Sallust)

cards.front: Name the three crimes Sallust lists for Sempronia using asyndeton.
cards.answer: Betrayed trust / Denied a debt under oath / Was party to murder

cards.front: Why does the villa Spelunca rockfall episode make Sejanus hard to judge as simply a villain?
cards.answer: His genuine physical bravery in shielding Tiberius sits uneasily alongside Tacitus's portrait of his secret ambition and flattery elsewhere.

cards.front: Why does Virgil use a rhetorical question instead of listing all of Mezentius's crimes?
cards.answer: It lets Virgil imply endless, unspeakable cruelty without needing to catalogue every crime in full.

cards.front: Name the four groups in the class pyramid of Russian society in 1894.
cards.answer: Nobility (about 1%) / Middle class (about 1.5%) / Urban proletariat (about 4%) / Peasants (over 80%)

cards.front: Name the three methods Witte used to fund and drive industrial growth.
cards.answer: Borrowed heavily from French banks / Introduced the gold standard in 1897 / High tariffs protecting Russian industry / High indirect taxes on vodka, sugar and matches
items: High indirect taxes on vodka, sugar and matches

cards.front: Why was modern farming almost impossible under the mir system?
cards.answer: Land was divided into narrow, scattered strips to share good soil fairly, blocking efficient modern farming methods.

cards.front: Why were Russia's new industrial cities a natural recruiting ground for revolutionary parties?
cards.answer: Workers faced brutal conditions, illegal trade unions, harsh policing by the Okhrana, and violent responses to organising, breeding resentment.

title: Vocal Music: Meeting Purcell and Queen
subject: music-edexcel

cards.front: Why does Purcell use long melismas in Music for a While?
cards.answer: To let the voice imitate the sustained, hypnotic effect of music charming pain away, especially on words about eternity, suffering or enchantment.

cards.front: How does multitrack recording let Queen build a denser texture than Purcell's live continuo?
cards.answer: It lets separate vocal and instrumental performances be recorded on individual tracks and combined, creating layers impossible in one live take.

cards.front: How does Brian May's guitar solo in Killer Queen create an orchestral tone?
cards.answer: By recording layered guitar tracks that combine to sound almost brass-like rather than a single guitar line.

title: Themes: Motherhood, Class, Race and Sexuality
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four everyday things Geof does that show him practically mothering Jo.
cards.answer: Cleans / Cooks / Pays rent / Sews a maternity dress

cards.front: How does the play's circular structure reinforce the theme of motherhood?
cards.answer: It opens with Helen and Jo arriving together and closes with Jo alone in the same flat, suggesting the pattern of neglect repeats.

cards.front: Why did the Lord Chamberlain's Office demand cuts to the language used about Geof?
cards.answer: Because every play had to be licensed before performance, and sex between men was a criminal offence at the time.

title: The Hate U Give: Issue-Led Indie
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five sequences the lesson identifies for micro-analysis in The Hate U Give.
cards.answer: Opening kitchen-table 'the talk' scene / Traffic-stop police-shooting sequence / Protest-and-tear-gas sequence / Kitchen confrontation with King / Closing house-fire and recovery sequence

cards.front: How does the framing at Williamson Prep dramatise Starr's code-switching, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: The camera frames Starr with more space around her and cooler light, keeping her at a slight remove from the other students to show displacement before she speaks.

cards.front: How does Tillman use the formal grammar of the opening kitchen-table scene to contain its political content?
cards.answer: Warm palette, close hand-held framing and ordinary diegetic sound with no score create domestic warmth that holds the politically weighty conversation, making it feel personal.

cards.front: Why does the lesson argue The Hate U Give's YA register itself counts as a political choice?
cards.answer: Tillman and Thomas deliberately chose accessibility to reach audiences that more formally challenging or prestige-positioned films could not.

cards.front: Name the three responses Hoover made to the Depression, according to the lesson's key fact.
cards.answer: 1930 Hawley–Smoot Tariff / 1932 Reconstruction Finance Corporation / Continued belief in rugged individualism

cards.front: Name the three academics in Roosevelt's 'Brain Trust' during the 1932 campaign.
cards.answer: Raymond Moley / Rexford Tugwell / Adolf Berle

cards.front: Why did the Hawley–Smoot Tariff backfire on American farmers?
cards.answer: Twenty-five trading partners retaliated with their own tariffs, so farmers lost overseas export markets while crop prices collapsed at home.

cards.front: Why did the nicknames 'Hoovervilles' and 'Hoover blankets' damage Hoover politically?
cards.answer: They turned an economic crisis into a personal verdict on Hoover, attaching his name directly to people's misery.

cards.front: Name the three techniques Byron uses in 'When We Two Parted' to present heartbreak as inescapable and permanent.
cards.answer: Pathetic fallacy (cold dew) / Metaphor (cold kiss = dead love) / Cyclical structure (ending repeats beginning)

cards.front: How does the personification in the final lines of 'Love's Philosophy' work as an argument for love?
cards.answer: It makes nature itself ('sunlight clasps', 'moonbeams kiss') act out love, so nature argues that the beloved should kiss the speaker too.

cards.front: Why does the final word 'me' at the end of each stanza in 'Love's Philosophy' disrupt the poem's smooth, song-like rhyme scheme?
cards.answer: It breaks the flow because the speaker's personal desire suddenly interrupts the natural philosophy he has been building.

cards.front: How does Barrett Browning complicate the vine metaphor in Sonnet 29?
cards.answer: She asks the beloved to 'burst, shattered, everywhere' the vines, showing she wants the real person, not just her idealised thoughts of him.

cards.front: Name the three poems the lesson covers under 'Inner Conflict & Anger'.
cards.answer: A Poison Tree by William Blake / Extract from The Prelude 'Boating' by William Wordsworth / Cousin Kate by Christina Rossetti
items: A Poison Tree by William Blake
Extract from The Prelude 'Boating' by William Wordsworth

cards.front: Why does Blake describe watering the tree with tears and sunning it with smiles?
cards.answer: The nurturing natural imagery is ironic, showing how the speaker's dishonest kindness secretly feeds his toxic hidden anger.

cards.front: How does the boy's confidence change during the boat journey in The Prelude extract?
cards.answer: His joyful confidence is destroyed when the huge peak seems to pursue him, leaving him terrified and permanently haunted by nature's power.

cards.front: How does the lord's language show he treats the speaker as property in Cousin Kate?
cards.answer: Rossetti uses possessive similes like 'wore me like a silken knot' to show the lord treating her as a disposable object, not a person.

cards.front: What three purposes does Meena's lying serve in the novel?
cards.answer: To get attention / To fit in / To protect herself from a painful reality
items: To protect herself from a painful reality

cards.front: Why does Papa's statement 'We are the British' matter in the novel?
cards.answer: It is factually true since the Kumars are British citizens, and also a quiet act of resistance against exclusion.

cards.front: Why is what Meena envies in Anita actually an illusion?
cards.answer: Anita's freedom is really neglect and her confidence is bravado masking insecurity, while her home life is loveless.

cards.front: How does the food contrast between the Kumar and Rutter households support the novel's themes?
cards.answer: Mama's rich, ritual-filled cooking shows warmth and cultural pride, while Anita's processed, joyless food reveals emotional neglect.

cards.front: Name the eight A8 countries that joined the EU in May 2004.
cards.answer: Poland / Czech Republic / Slovakia / Hungary / Slovenia / Estonia / Latvia and Lithuania

cards.front: Why did the July 2005 London bombings intensify criticism of multiculturalism?
cards.answer: Three of the four bombers were British-born men of Pakistani heritage, fuelling arguments that 'parallel lives' had replaced integration.

cards.front: Why was the genuine refugee/economic migrant distinction used in 1990s asylum debates seen as legally uncertain?
cards.answer: Many people fleeing poverty were doing so because their states had failed to protect them from violence.

cards.front: How did Britain's approach to A8 migration differ from Germany and France, and what was the result?
cards.answer: Britain, Ireland and Sweden imposed no transitional restrictions, causing large, rapid migration mainly from Poland.

title: Modern Britain: Wars, Empire's End and the Law, c1900–present
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four major migrant streams that shaped modern Britain, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: World War refugees / Commonwealth migrants (Caribbean, South Asia, East Africa) / EU migrants after 2004 / Asylum seekers throughout
items: Commonwealth migrants (Caribbean, South Asia, East Africa)

cards.front: Name the four Race Relations/anti-discrimination laws or bodies the lesson says developed alongside restriction laws.
cards.answer: 1965 Race Relations Act / 1968 Race Relations Act / 1976 Race Relations Act / Commission for Racial Equality

cards.front: Why did Caribbean migration to Britain grow steadily through the 1950s?
cards.answer: London Transport, the new NHS and British Rail actively recruited workers from Barbados, Jamaica and Trinidad.

cards.front: Why did the state gain more discretion over who could enter Britain between 1905 and 1939?
cards.answer: Wartime laws like the 1914 Aliens Restriction Act gave sweeping powers over 'enemy aliens', later extended into peacetime and visa requirements.

title: Peasant discontent: long and short-term causes
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three long-term causes the lesson gives for the Peasants' Revolt.
cards.answer: Continued enforcement of serfdom / Statute of Labourers reversing wage gains / Decades of resentment over legal status vs economic reality
items: Statute of Labourers reversing wage gains
Decades of resentment over legal status vs economic reality

cards.front: Why did tension build between peasants and lords in the decades after the Black Death?
cards.answer: Peasants felt their labour had earned them freedom, but lords used the courts to keep enforcing serfdom against them.

cards.front: Why did ordinary taxation in this period fall especially heavily on the poorest?
cards.answer: Parliamentary subsidies were assessed on moveable goods, so poorer property-owners paid while the richest paid proportionally less.

title: The Classical Concerto: Balance, Dialogue and the Rise of the Public Concert (1750-1820)
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the four instrument groups the lesson says were added to the Classical orchestra beyond Baroque strings and continuo.
cards.answer: Oboes / Bassoons / Horns / Timpani

cards.front: Why did the rise of public, ticketed concerts change how composers wrote for orchestras?
cards.answer: Bigger, mixed audiences and larger halls demanded music that could impress a paying public, so orchestras grew larger and more varied in timbre.

cards.front: Why do Classical concerto melodies typically end with an imperfect cadence followed by a perfect cadence?
cards.answer: Melodies use an antecedent phrase ending on an imperfect cadence balanced by a consequent phrase ending on a perfect cadence, like a question and answer.

cards.front: How do Classical dynamics differ from Baroque terraced dynamics in concertos?
cards.answer: Instead of sudden loud/soft blocks, Classical orchestras use gradual crescendos and diminuendos, giving phrases shape and drama within themselves.

cards.front: During a football kick, name the four muscle actions the lesson describes happening in sequence.
cards.answer: Hip flexors swing thigh forward / Quadriceps extend the knee / Gastrocnemius plantar-flexes the ankle / External obliques rotate the trunk

cards.front: Why can cardiac muscle keep contracting without ever fatiguing, unlike skeletal muscle?
cards.answer: Its cells are interconnected so electrical signals spread instantly across the whole heart wall, producing a coordinated contraction resistant to fatigue.

cards.front: Why is smooth muscle non-striated while cardiac muscle is striated?
cards.answer: Cardiac muscle has the overlapping actin-myosin filament arrangement for fast, high force, while smooth muscle's filaments are irregular, giving slower, sustained contraction.

title: The end of prosperity: the Wall Street Crash, 1929
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Why did unequal distribution of wealth make overproduction worse in the 1920s?
cards.answer: The top 5% got a third of income, so tens of millions of farmers and unskilled workers had little money to buy the goods being produced.

cards.front: How did margin buying turn falling share prices into a self-reinforcing crash?
cards.answer: Falling prices triggered margin calls, forcing investors to sell shares to repay loans, which pushed prices down further.

cards.front: How did the Wall Street Crash lead to mass unemployment in America?
cards.answer: Banks facing ruin called in loans to businesses, which cut production and laid off workers, collapsing consumer spending.

cards.front: Name the four pathetic fallacy examples the lesson gives across the anthology.
cards.answer: Byron: cold dew = grief / Hardy: white sun = drained love / Sheers: storm = discord, calm = reconciliation / Shelley: sunlight/moonbeams personified as lover

cards.front: How does the loose, irregular form of 'Singh Song!' support its meaning?
cards.answer: The playful, varying line lengths and phonetic dialect mirror the joy and spontaneity of the relationship it describes.

cards.front: Name the three features of a sperm cell that adapt it for its function.
cards.answer: Acrosome with enzymes to penetrate egg / Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy / Long flagellum tail for swimming
items: Acrosome with enzymes to penetrate egg
Midpiece packed with mitochondria for energy

cards.front: Name the two features of a muscle cell that adapt it for contraction.
cards.answer: Large numbers of mitochondria for ATP / Actin and myosin proteins that slide past each other
items: Large numbers of mitochondria for ATP
Actin and myosin proteins that slide past each other

cards.front: Why do root hair cells have long thin extensions?
cards.answer: To dramatically increase surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.

cards.front: Why can undifferentiated stem cells be risky if transplanted into a patient?
cards.answer: They could divide uncontrollably after transplantation, forming tumours.

cards.front: Name the three 'common mistakes' the lesson lists for comparison essays other than retelling the poem.
cards.answer: Writing about each poem separately / Dropping in context without connecting it / Choosing a poem you barely know
items: Dropping in context without connecting it
Choosing a poem you barely know

cards.front: Why should you prepare a comparison grid before the exam?
cards.answer: It lets you choose your comparison poem within 30 seconds of reading the question, leaving more time for writing.

cards.front: How should AO2 and AO3 be combined in a strong comparison essay?
cards.answer: They should be woven together in the same sentence, showing context explains why a poet makes a language choice.

cards.front: Name the four common sample rates given in the lesson, with their uses.
cards.answer: 8,000 Hz - telephone / 22,050 Hz - radio quality / 44,100 Hz - CD audio / 48,000 Hz - professional video

cards.front: Why does a low sample rate like 8,000 Hz make audio sound tinny or robotic?
cards.answer: The measurements are too sparse to faithfully reproduce high frequencies in the original wave.

cards.front: How does increasing bit depth reduce quantisation error?
cards.answer: More bits give more possible amplitude levels, making the stored 'staircase' approximation finer and closer to the true value.

cards.front: Why does increasing the sample rate above 44,100 Hz give diminishing returns for human listeners?
cards.answer: Human hearing tops out around 20,000 Hz, and 44,100 Hz already captures frequencies up to about 22,050 Hz, above that limit.

title: Growth, Stem Cells and Plant Hormones
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the three research uses being investigated for stem cell therapy other than bone marrow transplants.
cards.answer: Replacing insulin-producing cells in type 1 diabetes / Restoring nerve function after spinal cord injury / Repairing heart muscle after a heart attack
items: Replacing insulin-producing cells in type 1 diabetes
Restoring nerve function after spinal cord injury
Repairing heart muscle after a heart attack

cards.front: Why do roots grow downwards in response to gravity?
cards.answer: Auxin builds up on the lower side of the root, and high auxin concentrations inhibit elongation there, so the upper side elongates more and the root bends down.

cards.front: How can gardeners grow a new, genetically identical plant from a cutting?
cards.answer: A cut stem contains meristem tissue that can divide by mitosis and differentiate into roots, letting the cutting develop into a full plant.

cards.front: Why do most cells not divide by mitosis until each chromosome has been copied?
cards.answer: During interphase the cell copies all its DNA so each chromosome exists in duplicate, ensuring each daughter cell gets a full set.

cards.front: What four factors should be considered when weighing benefits against risks of radioactive materials?
cards.answer: Type and dose of radiation / Likely duration of exposure / Whether exposure is deliberate or accidental / Whether precautions can reduce risk
items: Whether exposure is deliberate or accidental

cards.front: Why is the moderator's role in a nuclear reactor different from the control rods' role?
cards.answer: The moderator slows neutrons to make further fission more likely, while control rods absorb excess neutrons to limit the reaction.

cards.front: Why is a long half-life chosen for the source in an industrial thickness gauge?
cards.answer: So the source lasts years without replacement and gives a stable count rate for comparison.

cards.front: Why is rotating the radiotherapy beam around the patient used to treat tumours?
cards.answer: Healthy tissue gets a lower dose from each angle, while the tumour receives a concentrated combined dose, reducing damage.

title: The Versailles Settlement: Terms and Diktat
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five blocks or themes the Treaty of Versailles is structured around, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Blame (war guilt) / Money (reparations) / Military restrictions / Territorial changes / League of Nations covenant

cards.front: Name the four territories or areas the lesson says Germany lost or had restricted in the east and west (excluding colonies).
cards.answer: Alsace-Lorraine to France / Eupen and Malmedy to Belgium / North Schleswig to Denmark / Posen and West Prussia to Poland
items: Posen and West Prussia to Poland

cards.front: Why did most Germans feel the war guilt clause was especially unjust?
cards.answer: They believed responsibility for the war was shared across Europe, since Germany had simply been defending itself after Russia mobilised.

cards.front: Why did John Maynard Keynes warn that reparations would harm more than just Germany?
cards.answer: He argued reparations were so heavy they would wreck the German economy, and through trade damage the wider European economy too.

cards.front: Name the three types of people most ordinary people relied on for medical care during the Renaissance, besides herbal remedies.
cards.answer: Apothecaries / Barber surgeons / Physicians (few and expensive)

cards.front: How did the printing press help spread Vesalius's ideas across Europe?
cards.answer: It let books like Fabrica be reproduced quickly and distributed widely, unlike slow, error-prone hand-copied manuscripts.

cards.front: Why did anatomy theatres get built at universities during this period?
cards.answer: Influenced by Vesalius, universities included human dissection in training so students could observe real bodies instead of just reading Galen.

cards.front: What three types of displacement do the poems in this comparison show, one per poet?
cards.answer: Nichols: physical migration with sensory memories / Zephaniah: violent displacement by conflict / Chingonyi: cultural displacement from Zambian traditions
items: Nichols: physical migration with sensory memories
Chingonyi: cultural displacement from Zambian traditions

cards.front: Why does Zephaniah use simple, accessible language and a rhetorical style in 'We Refugees'?
cards.answer: To argue persuasively, like a speech, that refugees are human beings with stories rather than criminals or statistics.

cards.front: How does Nichols use colour contrast to show the Island Man's split sense of belonging?
cards.answer: She contrasts the warm blue Caribbean surf with London's cold grey traffic, showing his body is in London but his belonging stays with the island.

title: Standard Algorithms: Bubble Sort, Merge Sort, Linear and Binary Search
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four standard algorithms covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Linear search / Binary search / Bubble sort / Merge sort

cards.front: Why is linear search a good choice for a school register that changes daily?
cards.answer: Re-sorting after every change would cost more time than just scanning the unsorted list linearly.

cards.front: Why does binary search need far fewer comparisons than linear search for large datasets?
cards.answer: It halves the search area with every comparison, discarding the half that cannot contain the target.

cards.front: How does bubble sort decide whether to swap two adjacent items during a pass?
cards.answer: It compares each adjacent pair and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.

cards.front: Name the three decisive military engagements of the Williamite War in Ireland (1689-1691).
cards.answer: Siege of Derry / Battle of the Boyne / Battle of Aughrim

cards.front: Why did the Siege of Derry become such a defining moment in Ulster Protestant memory?
cards.answer: The garrison held out 105 days against famine and disease before Williamite ships broke the boom, seen as providential deliverance.

cards.front: How did the Battle of the Boyne affect James II's cause even though it did not end the war?
cards.answer: It shattered Jacobite morale and forced James to flee to France permanently, ending his hopes of restoration.

cards.front: Why did the Protestant Ascendancy come to dominate Ireland after 1691?
cards.answer: Military defeat, the broken promises of the Treaty of Limerick, and the Penal Laws combined to lock Catholics out of political and economic power.

title: Forces and Their Effects: Moments, Levers and Gears
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three real-world lever examples the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Crowbar / Wheelbarrow / Pair of scissors

cards.front: Name the four common forces shown on a free-body diagram (Higher tier).
cards.answer: Weight / Normal contact force / Friction / Tension

cards.front: Why does a tall, narrow object like a double-decker bus topple more easily than a wide, low object?
cards.answer: Its centre of mass is higher and its base is narrower, so it moves outside the base more easily when tilted.

cards.front: Why must a heavier child sit closer to the pivot on a see-saw to balance a lighter child further away?
cards.answer: Because moment equals force times distance, so a smaller distance can balance a larger force to keep clockwise and anticlockwise moments equal.

cards.front: Name the five digital methods (besides CAD drawings) the lesson gives for communicating design outcomes.
cards.answer: Rendered 3D images / Animations and fly-through videos / Virtual reality and augmented reality / Digital presentation tools (slides, PDFs) / Simulation software (FEA/CFD)

cards.front: Why can a power cut or software failure be a serious problem when using CAD?
cards.answer: CAD is dependent on electricity and technology, so access to drawings is lost unless paper backups exist.

title: Suez 1956 and the Arab Nationalist Surge
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three reasons Israel had for joining the secret Sèvres plan against Egypt in 1956.
cards.answer: Ending fedayeen raids from Gaza / Reopening the Straits of Tiran for shipping to Eilat / Degrading Nasser's new Soviet weapons before they were absorbed
items: Reopening the Straits of Tiran for shipping to Eilat
Degrading Nasser's new Soviet weapons before they were absorbed

cards.front: Name the three steps agreed in the secret Sèvres Protocol plan for Suez.
cards.answer: Israel invades Sinai / Britain and France issue an ultimatum for both sides to withdraw / Britain and France 'intervene' to seize the Canal Zone
items: Britain and France issue an ultimatum for both sides to withdraw
Britain and France 'intervene' to seize the Canal Zone

cards.front: Why did Nasser turn to Czechoslovakia for weapons in 1955 instead of the West?
cards.answer: The US and Britain refused to sell Egypt modern weapons for fear of upsetting Israel, so Nasser bought Soviet-bloc arms instead.

cards.front: Why was Egypt's nationalisation of the Suez Canal Company legally justified according to international lawyers?
cards.answer: A sovereign state had the right to nationalise companies on its territory as long as it paid compensation, which Egypt offered.

cards.front: Name the three levels on which Meena's code-switching operates.
cards.answer: Dialect (Black Country vs standard English) / Language (English vs Punjabi) / Register (childish enthusiasm vs adult reflection)

cards.front: Name the three structural phases of the novel's bildungsroman arc.
cards.answer: Bright, comic early chapters / Darkening middle section as racism surfaces / Reflective, elegiac final chapters
items: Darkening middle section as racism surfaces

cards.front: Why does Meena use humour as a 'shield' in the village?
cards.answer: Making people laugh controls how others see her, so being funny stops her being seen as the 'different' one.

cards.front: How does the seasonal structure of the novel reinforce Meena's coming-of-age journey?
cards.answer: The novel moves through the seasons, with winter's approach symbolising the end of childhood, making her growth feel natural and inevitable.

title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the five steps in the process for calculating masses in reactions.
cards.answer: Write the balanced chemical equation / Identify the molar ratio from the equation / Calculate moles of the known substance / Use the molar ratio to find moles of unknown substance / Convert moles back to mass using molar mass
items: Identify the molar ratio from the equation
Calculate moles of the known substance
Use the molar ratio to find moles of unknown substance
Convert moles back to mass using molar mass

cards.front: How do you identify the limiting reactant in a reaction?
cards.answer: Calculate the moles of each reactant and compare to the molar ratios in the balanced equation; the one used up first is limiting.

cards.front: Why does Stephens end the play on a question rather than the novel's declaration?
cards.answer: Because Christopher hasn't reached full confidence and needs Siobhan's validation of what he's beginning to believe about himself.

cards.front: Why does Stephens stage the post-curtain maths scene as a celebration rather than a printed proof?
cards.answer: To show mathematics as Christopher experiences it — clarity, certainty and delight — not a dry exercise, celebrating his way of engaging with the world.

cards.front: Name the five days of Diwali in order.
cards.answer: Dhanteras / Choti Diwali / Naraka Chaturdashi / Diwali / Lakshmi Puja / Govardhan Puja / Padwa / Bhai Dooj

cards.front: What three theological themes does the lesson say Holi expresses?
cards.answer: Renewal and the transition from winter to spring / Triumph of dharma over adharma / Equality of all people before God
items: Equality of all people before God

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Diwali has a more formal religious character than Holi?
cards.answer: Diwali centres on puja, lamps and prayers for prosperity, while Holi's religious side sits alongside more exuberant, popular colour and play celebrations.

cards.front: Why is lighting diyas and decorating homes at Diwali significant for British Hindu families like Meena's?
cards.answer: It symbolises divine light entering and blessing the household while bringing the family together, keeping them connected to Hindu identity in England.

cards.front: Name the four marketing methods the lesson gives for influencing food choice.
cards.answer: BOGOF and special offers / Meal deals / Media and advertising / Point of sale marketing

cards.front: Name the ten mandatory pieces of information required on all pre-packed food in the UK.
cards.answer: Name of the food / List of ingredients / Allergen information / Net quantity / Date marking / Storage conditions and instructions for use / Name and address of manufacturer, packer or seller / Country of origin for specific foods / Nutrition declaration
items: Storage conditions and instructions for use

cards.front: Why might drinks in a supermarket meal deal add more sugar to someone's diet than they realise?
cards.answer: The drink offered in a meal deal is rarely water and is usually a sugary juice or fizzy drink.

cards.front: Why does 'no added sugar' on packaging not mean a food is low in sugar?
cards.answer: It only means no sugar was added during production, but the product may still contain naturally occurring sugars that add to total sugar intake.

cards.front: Name the four major revolts William faced between 1067 and 1071, with their locations.
cards.answer: Kent (Eustace of Boulogne, 1067) / Exeter (south-west, 1068) / The North (Edwin and Morcar, then Danish-backed rising, 1069) / Ely (Hereward and the Fens, 1070-71)
items: The North (Edwin and Morcar, then Danish-backed rising, 1069)

cards.front: Why did William come so close to losing his throne in the 1069 northern revolt?
cards.answer: It combined a foreign Danish invasion fleet, the legitimate claimant Edgar Atheling, and the northern nobility, plus revolts elsewhere, all at once.

cards.front: How did William's response to revolt change after 1068?
cards.answer: Conciliation collapsed and he increasingly removed English nobles, replaced them with Normans, and centralised land among a few trusted tenants-in-chief.

cards.front: Why did William build so many castles during the 1067-71 revolts?
cards.answer: Castles were a direct strategic response to each revolt, creating permanent military infrastructure to make repeat uprisings impossible.

cards.front: Which three roles does the Chorus perform in Henry V?
cards.answer: Narrator / Apologist / Propagandist/stage manager

cards.front: Why is Henry's transformation from Prince Hal described as both admirable and disturbing?
cards.answer: He becomes the ideal public king by killing the private man, rejecting Falstaff and executing Bardolph.

cards.front: How does Pistol's capture of a French soldier in Act 4 Scene 4 expose the reality of war?
cards.answer: It shows he talks of profit and ransom while Henry talks of honour, revealing war's mercenary side.

title: Plot and Structure: Eight Actors, Eighty Days
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: The lesson gives the order of geographical episodes Verne organised his novel around, starting in London — name the eleven locations in sequence.
cards.answer: London / Paris / Suez / Bombay / Calcutta / Hong Kong / Yokohama / San Francisco / New York / Liverpool / London again

cards.front: Why must each scene transition in Around the World in 80 Days be rapid rather than slow?
cards.answer: Because episodic structure relies on momentum, so performers must quickly signal a change of continent without slowing the pace.

cards.front: Why does Eason use a narration device where performers step out to address the audience directly?
cards.answer: It frames the action, stops the audience losing themselves in pure empathy, and invites them to watch the storytelling as storytelling.

cards.front: Why is treating this play as a costume drama with a realistic Victorian set a misreading of the form?
cards.answer: Because the play's aesthetic is built on performers' and audience's imagination creating the world, not literal scenery.

title: Deng's Four Modernisations and economic reform
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: How did the Household Responsibility System increase agricultural output in the early 1980s?
cards.answer: It replaced collective obligation with private incentive, letting households sell surplus produce after meeting state quotas.

cards.front: Why did the CCP set up Special Economic Zones instead of opening the whole economy to market forces?
cards.answer: To import foreign technology and management expertise in controlled areas without exposing the whole Chinese economy to market forces at once.

cards.front: Why did the dismantling of collective communes create hardship for some rural families?
cards.answer: It eroded the welfare safety net, so healthcare and education once collectively organised now required cash some families couldn't afford.

cards.front: How did the Democracy Wall closure and Wei Jingsheng's arrest show the limits of Deng's reforms?
cards.answer: They showed market economics would coexist with one-party rule, with no equivalent political reform on offer.

title: The Great Awakening and the Enlightenment
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three institutions Benjamin Franklin founded to spread public learning in Philadelphia.
cards.answer: Library Company of Philadelphia (1731) / American Philosophical Society (1743) / What became the University of Pennsylvania (1749)
items: What became the University of Pennsylvania (1749)

cards.front: How did the split between Old Lights and New Lights help prepare colonists for later political dissent?
cards.answer: It taught ordinary believers to choose between competing ministers, so judging clergymen made judging governors thinkable.

cards.front: Why did Whitefield preach in fields and on village greens rather than in churches?
cards.answer: He was refused some pulpits because of his emotional preaching style.

title: The Catholic threat: Northern Earls, plots and Mary Queen of Scots
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives that caused the Northern Rebellion of 1569 to collapse.
cards.answer: Elizabeth moved Mary further south / Expected Spanish support from Philip II never came / Southern England did not rise in support
items: Expected Spanish support from Philip II never came
Southern England did not rise in support

cards.front: Name the three Catholic plots against Elizabeth between 1571 and 1586.
cards.answer: Ridolfi Plot (1571) / Throckmorton Plot (1583) / Babington Plot (1586)

cards.front: How did the papal bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570) harden the government's response to Catholics?
cards.answer: By releasing Catholics from obedience to Elizabeth, it turned recusancy into potential treason, making every Catholic a suspect.

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth refuse to execute Mary Queen of Scots after the Ridolfi Plot despite Parliament's demands?
cards.answer: She argued that executing a fellow anointed monarch would set a dangerous precedent that could be used against herself.

cards.front: Why does violence erupt in public spaces rather than dark alleys in Jekyll and Hyde?
cards.answer: Stevenson shows evil doesn't stay hidden in darkness; it breaks through the surface of civilised, respectable public life.

cards.front: Why is the exact nature of Jekyll's 'undignified pleasures' never specified?
cards.answer: Stevenson's deliberate vagueness makes Jekyll's sins universal rather than naming one specific vice.

cards.front: Why is Victorian characters' language of concealment significant in the novella?
cards.answer: It mirrors Victorian society's defence mechanism of hiding its dual nature behind propriety and refusing to name uncomfortable truths.

cards.front: Name the five most important characters in The Empress examined in this lesson.
cards.answer: Rani / Abdul / Hari / Susan Matthews / Dadabhai Naoroji

cards.front: Why does Gupta show Queen Victoria being served an egg in a golden egg cup right after showing Rani with nowhere to sleep?
cards.answer: The contrast dramatises how power operates, offering a direct dramatic commentary on inequality between ruler and ruled.

cards.front: Why does Gupta present Susan Matthews as ordinary rather than an extreme villain?
cards.answer: To show that racism does not require malice, only a system that normalises inequality, making it more disturbing.

title: Doing Research: Experiments, Self-Report and Observations
subject: psychology-ocr

cards.front: Name the three independent dimensions that observations vary along, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Setting: naturalistic or controlled / Participant awareness: overt or covert / Researcher involvement: participant or non-participant

cards.front: Why is it hard to be sure the IV caused any difference found in a natural experiment?
cards.answer: Because participants cannot be randomly allocated to conditions, unlike in lab or field experiments.

cards.front: Why might participants change their behaviour in an overt observation?
cards.answer: Because they know they are being watched, so their awareness of being observed can affect how they act.

title: Origins of the Universe, the Sanctity of Life and Abortion
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three views on abortion the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Catholic pro-life position (no circumstance justifies abortion) / Christian pro-choice view weighing mother's circumstances using situation ethics / Non-religious pro-choice view based on a woman's right over her body
items: Catholic pro-life position (no circumstance justifies abortion)
Christian pro-choice view weighing mother's circumstances using situation ethics
Non-religious pro-choice view based on a woman's right over her body

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching reject treating the universe purely as a commodity?
cards.answer: Because the universe belongs to God, not humanity, so exploiting it goes against God's intention for creation.

cards.front: How did Pope Francis explain that evolution and belief in God as Creator are not in competition?
cards.answer: Evolution requires living things to already exist, so evolution describes the process while God remains the reason anything exists to evolve.

cards.front: Why is the Catholic view on abortion considered a divergent position?
cards.answer: Because other Christians and non-religious thinkers hold different views, such as pro-choice positions based on circumstances or personal rights.

cards.front: Name the roles a detective, criminal, senior officer, forensics expert and partner play when Propp's functions are applied to a crime drama.
cards.answer: Detective = hero / Criminal = villain / Senior officer assigning case = dispatcher / Forensics expert = donor / Partner/junior colleague = helper

cards.front: Why do producers keep repeating a genre's conventions while also adding variation?
cards.answer: Repetition lets audiences recognise a genre instantly, while variation stops products feeling stale, letting genres evolve gradually.

cards.front: How does hybridity help a producer reach a wider audience?
cards.answer: Blending conventions from more than one genre, like a sitcom with romantic drama elements, appeals to fans of both forms at once.

cards.front: Why does an intertextual reference, like a poster echoing a classic film, benefit a new product?
cards.answer: It rewards audiences who recognise it, borrows the earlier product's reputation, and signals the new product's genre identity.

title: Risalah, Holy Books, Angels and Predestination
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: The Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam include belief in angels (Malaikah) as the second. Name four qualities the lesson gives that describe angels.
cards.answer: Created from divine light / Have no free will / Do not eat or sleep / Neither male nor female

cards.front: The lesson names four things a hadith says an angel records about a person before birth. What are they?
cards.answer: Their provision / Their lifespan / Their deeds / Whether fortunate or unfortunate

cards.front: How do most Sunni Muslims explain al-Qadr alongside human free will?
cards.answer: Allah knows in advance what people will choose, but His knowing does not cause the action, so humans genuinely choose and remain accountable.

cards.front: Why is the number 25 mentioned in relation to prophets, but Muslims still believe in many more?
cards.answer: The Qur'an names 25 prophets, but Muslim tradition holds Allah sent prophets to every nation, so there were many more than those named.

title: Kenilworth Castle in the Civil War
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Why did Kenilworth Castle never experience a prolonged siege in the Civil War?
cards.answer: Parliament held it continuously from late 1642 and Royalist attempts to retake Warwickshire failed, so it was never besieged.

cards.front: Why did Hyde not restore Kenilworth Castle after receiving the estate in 1665?
cards.answer: The lesson shows the castle was left as a ruin worked as a farm, with its stone stripped for reuse rather than rebuilt.

cards.front: Name the eight energy stores the lesson lists that energy can be transferred between.
cards.answer: Kinetic / Gravitational potential / Elastic potential / Chemical / Thermal / Magnetic / Electrostatic / Nuclear

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson gives for engineers to reduce wasted energy in machines.
cards.answer: Lubrication / Streamlining / Thermal insulation / More efficient technologies e.g. LED lighting
items: More efficient technologies e.g. LED lighting

cards.front: Why does pushing a box across a rough floor make the box and floor warm up?
cards.answer: Work is done against friction, transferring kinetic energy into thermal energy stores of the box and floor.

cards.front: Why does a car's braking distance increase so sharply as its speed increases?
cards.answer: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples KE, requiring four times the braking distance.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says Street Pastors offer to vulnerable people at night.
cards.answer: Water / Flip-flops to those barefoot / Warm clothing / A listening ear

cards.front: Name the three activities the lesson gives for how CAFOD works to tackle poverty and injustice.
cards.answer: Emergency relief after disasters / Funding long-term development projects / Campaigning for justice

cards.front: Why do churches provide volunteers and premises for food banks?
cards.answer: Because Jesus taught that helping the hungry is the same as serving God, so churches put this faith into practical action.

cards.front: Why do street pastors not preach or try to convert people while patrolling?
cards.answer: Because their role is to demonstrate Christian love through practical care rather than to spread the faith directly.

cards.front: Name the five flowchart shapes covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Oval / rounded rectangle (terminator) / Rectangle (process) / Parallelogram (input/output) / Diamond (decision) / Rectangle with double side bars (subroutine call)
items: Rectangle with double side bars (subroutine call)

cards.front: Why should you avoid writing prose (plain English sentences) instead of pseudocode in an exam algorithm answer?
cards.answer: Prose has no control structure keywords, so it cannot be traced step by step.

cards.front: Why is pseudocode often better to use than real code like Python in exam conditions?
cards.answer: A syntax slip in real code can hide the logic, and pseudocode is faster to write without worrying about syntax errors.

cards.front: Why is Simon killed before he can reveal the truth about the parachutist?
cards.answer: Golding suggests truth-tellers are destroyed by the very society they try to save.

cards.front: How does the dead parachutist physically block the boys' chance of rescue?
cards.answer: It lands on the mountain, sitting on the signal fire's path and blocking it, so the adult world's war prevents rescue.

title: Yield, Atom Economy, Molar Concentrations and Gas Volumes
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why percentage yield is less than 100%.
cards.answer: reaction is reversible (equilibrium) / product lost during transfer or separation / side reactions produce unwanted by-products
items: product lost during transfer or separation

cards.front: Why do substitution and elimination reactions have lower atom economy than addition reactions?
cards.answer: They produce by-products alongside the desired product, whereas addition reactions put all atoms into a single product.

cards.front: How do you convert a volume from cm³ to dm³ when calculating concentration?
cards.answer: Divide the volume in cm³ by 1000 to get the volume in dm³.

cards.front: Name the three phases the lessons group Leon's dated chapters into.
cards.answer: Domestic / Institutional / Political

cards.front: Why does De Waal write the whole novel in the present tense?
cards.answer: So events feel as though they are happening now, beside Leon, rather than being recounted afterwards.

title: China in 1945: A Country at the Crossroads
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four strengths the Guomindang had on paper in 1945.
cards.answer: Around 4.3 million soldiers / Control of major cities / A UN Security Council seat / Steady American aid

cards.front: Name the four weaknesses hidden beneath the Guomindang's strong surface in 1945.
cards.answer: Hyperinflation / Widespread corruption / Brutal conscription / A hollowed-out countryside

cards.front: Why did Soviet forces in Manchuria hand captured Japanese weapons to the CCP instead of the Guomindang?
cards.answer: Soviet forces controlled Manchuria after Japan's surrender and chose to arm the CCP's Eighth Route Army there rather than the GMD.

cards.front: Why did the Marshall Mediation of 1945-46 ultimately fail to prevent civil war?
cards.answer: Zhou Enlai played for time, Chiang doubted Marshall's promises and used the lull to position troops, so fighting never really stopped.

cards.front: Name the three parts of Leon's character development traced in the lesson.
cards.answer: Part 1: protector, capable and adult / Part 2: identity struggle and deterioration / Part 3: defiant, purposeful, matured by riots
items: Part 3: defiant, purposeful, matured by riots

cards.front: How does the riots experience mature Leon's understanding in Part 3?
cards.answer: He experiences a fusion of personal and political anger, which gives his quest for Jake direction and matures him.

cards.front: Why does De Waal show Carol through Leon's loving memories rather than an objective view?
cards.answer: It prevents the reader from writing Carol off as simply a bad parent, since Leon remembers good times and affection.

cards.front: Why is Salma's bureaucratic language, like 'permanency planning', significant?
cards.answer: It obscures what is really happening, showing how institutional language can be a form of violence that denies children clarity.

cards.front: Name the five core reasons the lesson gives for engineering companies implementing quality systems.
cards.answer: Early intercept of production problems / Reducing waste and its costs / Ensuring consistency of finished products / Meeting conformity requirements of standards/regulations / Reducing customer issues (returns, warranty, reputation)

cards.front: Why must the tolerances of two mating parts, like a shaft and a bearing housing, be compatible?
cards.answer: If the shaft's maximum diameter exceeds the housing's minimum bore, the parts will not assemble at all.

cards.front: Why would an engineer choose a micrometer over a go/no-go gauge for inspecting a part?
cards.answer: A micrometer records the actual dimension, allowing tool wear to be tracked so maintenance happens before parts go out of tolerance.

title: We Lived Happily during the War
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name the three other anthology poems this poem is compared with on the theme of guilt or blindness to conflict.
cards.answer: Vergissmeinnicht by Keith Douglas / Flag by John Agard / What Were They Like? by Denise Levertov
items: What Were They Like? by Denise Levertov

cards.front: Why does the poem's use of 'we' from the very first line implicate the reader?
cards.answer: The title runs straight into the opening line, so the collective pronoun 'we' draws the reader in before any context is given.

cards.front: How does the poem's central idea of complicity differ from the guilt shown in Douglas's Vergissmeinnicht?
cards.answer: Kaminsky's speaker feels wider civilian guilt for doing nothing while war happened elsewhere, unlike Douglas's soldier's specific guilt over a dead enemy.

title: Divorce and the Roles of Men and Women
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the three ways the Catholic Church's position on divorce and remarriage plays out, as given in the lesson's comparison of Christian denominations?
cards.answer: Divorce not recognised for valid sacramental marriage / Annulment is possible instead / Remarriage without annulment bars a person from Communion
items: Divorce not recognised for valid sacramental marriage
Remarriage without annulment bars a person from Communion

cards.front: Why can the Catholic Church not recognise divorce as ending a marriage?
cards.answer: Because it teaches that valid sacramental marriages are indissoluble, so divorce cannot end one.

cards.front: Why do many theologians reject 1 Timothy 2:11-14 as a rule restricting women's leadership today?
cards.answer: They argue it addresses a specific local situation in Ephesus rather than being a universal rule.

cards.front: Why do non-religious perspectives see divorce as sometimes necessary despite the pain it causes?
cards.answer: Because the harm principle means remaining in a damaging or abusive marriage can cause greater harm than ending it.

cards.front: Name six services that local councils provide, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Rubbish collection / Roads and parks / Planning permission / Social care for elderly/vulnerable / Housing / Libraries and leisure facilities

cards.front: Why does central government retain significant influence over what councils can afford to do?
cards.answer: Because most council funding comes as grants from central government, not from council tax alone.

cards.front: Why do critics argue English Votes for English Laws (EVEL) is problematic?
cards.answer: It creates a two-tier Parliament, complicates voting on the same bill, and risks deepening divisions between UK nations.

title: The End of the Mandate and the Creation of Israel, 1945–48
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three armed Jewish underground groups active in Palestine by 1945.
cards.answer: Haganah / Irgun / Lehi (Stern Gang)

cards.front: What were the two plans contained in the September 1947 UNSCOP report?
cards.answer: Majority plan: partition into Jewish and Arab states / Minority plan: single federal state
items: Majority plan: partition into Jewish and Arab states

cards.front: Why did the King David Hotel bombing push Britain towards withdrawal from Palestine?
cards.answer: It showed insurgents could strike British rule's heart, meaning holding the Mandate meant endless costly counter-insurgency Britain no longer wanted to fund.

cards.front: Why did the Deir Yassin attack accelerate the Palestinian exodus in 1948?
cards.answer: News of the killing of around 100 villagers spread rapidly, causing Palestinian civilians near the fighting to flee in fear.

cards.front: Name the seven types of EM wave in order of decreasing wavelength.
cards.answer: Radio waves / Microwaves / Infrared / Visible light / Ultraviolet / X-rays / Gamma rays

cards.front: Why can long wave radio signals travel around hills but short wave signals reach distant places differently?
cards.answer: Long wave diffracts around hills, while short wave reflects off the ionosphere for long-distance communication.

cards.front: How does the danger of EM radiation change as frequency increases?
cards.answer: Danger generally increases with frequency, from low-risk radio waves and microwaves to cell-damaging X-rays and gamma rays.

title: The Nature of God and the Trinity
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the three persons of the Trinity and their roles, as given in the lesson's Key Fact.
cards.answer: God the Father - creator and sustainer / God the Son - Jesus, incarnate redeemer / God the Holy Spirit - counsellor and guide
items: God the Father - creator and sustainer
God the Son - Jesus, incarnate redeemer
God the Holy Spirit - counsellor and guide
