cards.front: Why do Evangelical and Pentecostal Christians often emphasise God's immanence?
cards.answer: They stress his closeness, availability and power to act in daily life.

cards.front: Why does the Trinity matter for how Christians understand love?
cards.answer: Because God is three persons in relationship within himself, love is not added later but is what he eternally is.

cards.front: Why do Unitarian Christians like the Christadelphians reject the doctrine of the Trinity?
cards.answer: They believe God is strictly one person, the Father alone, and argue the Trinity was a later addition not found in scripture.

title: Believers, Creation and Humanity as Khalifah
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: The lesson gives three groups of people described at the start of Surah al-Baqarah. What are they?
cards.answer: Believers / Disbelievers / Hypocrites

cards.front: Why does the Qur'an treat hypocrisy as more dangerous than open disbelief?
cards.answer: Because hypocrites claim to believe but do not, and this corrupts the community from within.

cards.front: How does the khalifah concept lead to Islamic environmental ethics?
cards.answer: As Allah's steward on earth, humanity is a trustee not an owner, so environmental destruction is a betrayal of that trust.

title: End of the war and its international legacy
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three legacies the lesson gives for the USA of the Vietnam War (besides the death toll)
cards.answer: Exposed the limits of American military power / Damaged public trust in government / Produced a generation of veterans with physical and psychological injuries
items: Exposed the limits of American military power
Produced a generation of veterans with physical and psychological injuries

cards.front: Name the three schools of interpretation of appeasement given in the lesson
cards.answer: Guilty Men / A.J.P. Taylor's revisionist reading / R.A.C. Parker's reply

cards.front: Why did Congress pass the War Powers Act in 1973?
cards.answer: It was a direct response to the way the President had bypassed congressional approval throughout the Vietnam War.

cards.front: How did A.J.P. Taylor's revisionist reading of appeasement differ from the Guilty Men view?
cards.answer: Taylor argued appeasement reflected a genuine popular desire to avoid another catastrophic war, rather than culpable naivety.

title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the four environmental factors that affect the rate of transpiration.
cards.answer: Temperature / Humidity / Air movement / Light intensity

cards.front: Name the five main plant tissues described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Epidermal tissue / Palisade mesophyll / Spongy mesophyll / Xylem / Phloem

cards.front: How does spongy mesophyll tissue help gas exchange in a leaf?
cards.answer: It has air spaces that let carbon dioxide and oxygen diffuse easily through the leaf.

cards.front: How does transpiration cause water to move up through the xylem?
cards.answer: Water evaporates and diffuses from the leaf surface, creating a transpiration stream that pulls water up through the xylem.

title: Ways of Living: The Four Margas
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the four margas (paths to liberation) in Hinduism.
cards.answer: Jnana yoga (knowledge) / Bhakti yoga (devotion) / Karma yoga (selfless action) / Raja yoga (meditation)

cards.front: Name the eight stages of raja yoga outlined in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.
cards.answer: Yama (ethical restraint) / Niyama (personal observance) / Asana (posture) / Pranayama (breath control) / Pratyahara (withdrawal of senses) / Dharana (concentration) / Dhyana (meditation) / Samadhi (absorption)

cards.front: Why do actions performed through karma yoga not tie a person to samsara?
cards.answer: Because they are performed without craving reward or fearing failure, so they do not generate karmic residue.

cards.front: Why is jnana considered the highest path within Advaita Vedanta?
cards.answer: Because it directly confronts and dissolves the ignorance (avidya) that perpetuates samsara.

title: Electronic Systems: Sensors, Logic and Components
subject: engineering-aqa

cards.front: Name the three passive/component symbols the lesson says students commonly confuse, and their correct identity.
cards.answer: Resistor = box or zigzag / Transistor = three connections with arrow on emitter / Diode = triangle pointing to a bar
items: Transistor = three connections with arrow on emitter
Diode = triangle pointing to a bar

cards.front: Why does an analogue sensor need an ADC to work with a microcontroller?
cards.answer: Because most sensors produce continuous analogue voltages, but a microcontroller can only read digital binary numbers, so an ADC converts between them.

cards.front: How does an LDR's resistance change between bright light and darkness, and what effect does this have on current?
cards.answer: In bright light resistance is low giving high current; in the dark resistance is high giving low current.

title: Treating disease: medieval medicine to anaesthetics
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three main types of treatment used in medieval medicine.
cards.answer: Bloodletting / Herbal medicines / Surgery by barber surgeons

cards.front: Why was speed the most valued skill for a surgeon before 1847?
cards.answer: Surgery was performed on conscious patients, so a fast surgeon reduced the pain and shock the patient suffered.

cards.front: Why did the medical establishment initially resist Simpson's use of chloroform in childbirth?
cards.answer: Some believed pain in childbirth was natural and biblically ordained, so easing it was seen as wrong.

cards.front: Name the four Gothic conventions the lesson identifies in the novella.
cards.answer: The doppelgänger / The mad scientist / The discovered manuscript / Atmosphere of dread

cards.front: How does the discovered manuscript convention work in the novella?
cards.answer: The truth is revealed through found documents like Lanyon's letter and Jekyll's statement, creating a sense of authenticity.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson make Hyde animalistic rather than simply morally bad?
cards.answer: It suggests evil is a biological reality lurking inside everyone, not just a moral failing.

cards.front: Name the seven spectral types in order from hottest to coolest.
cards.answer: O / B / A / F / G / K / M

cards.front: Why does a star's spectral type reveal its surface temperature?
cards.answer: The dominant absorption lines depend on which elements are ionised or excited, which is determined by surface temperature.

cards.front: How does Wien's displacement law explain why hotter stars look blue and cooler stars look red?
cards.answer: Hotter stars peak in the ultraviolet and appear blue, while cooler stars peak in the infrared and appear red.

title: The Peasants' Revolt: events of May-June 1381
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What three additional demands did Wat Tyler present at Smithfield on 15 June 1381?
cards.answer: Distribution of Church wealth / Abolition of all lordship except the king's / Equality before the law
items: Abolition of all lordship except the king's

cards.front: Why did the rebels burn John of Gaunt's Savoy Palace instead of looting it?
cards.answer: Rebels forbade looting, turning the act into a symbolic political statement about who they blamed for their condition, rather than theft.

cards.front: Why did the rebel army disperse after Wat Tyler was killed at Smithfield?
cards.answer: With Tyler dead and no leader, and after Richard II claimed authority over them, the rebels lost cohesion and the revolt collapsed.

title: Scenes 1–3: Enid, Del & the Obeah Woman
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why does Enid's rejection of her Caribbean heritage create a gap between her and her daughters in Leave Taking?
cards.answer: Because her assimilation strategy means she rarely speaks about Jamaica, so her daughters sense a heritage they cannot name.

cards.front: Why is Mai significant to Del in Leave Taking?
cards.answer: Mai represents Jamaica and the old ways Enid rejected, and recognises Del's potential as her spiritual successor.

cards.front: How does Brod's experience in England contrast with Enid's in Leave Taking?
cards.answer: Brod embodies disillusionment and gave up everything for England, showing a Windrush experience Enid has refused to allow herself.

title: The Respiratory System and Gas Exchange
subject: physical-education-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four features that maximise diffusion at the alveoli.
cards.answer: Large surface area / Thin membrane / Rich blood supply / Steep concentration gradients

cards.front: During inhalation, what two muscle actions increase the volume of the thoracic cavity?
cards.answer: Diaphragm contracts and flattens / External intercostals contract and lift ribcage
items: External intercostals contract and lift ribcage

cards.front: Why does air rush into the lungs during inhalation?
cards.answer: Thoracic volume increases, lowering pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air moves down the pressure gradient into the lungs.

cards.front: Why does breathing rate stay high after a 100m sprint even though the race has finished?
cards.answer: Elevated breathing continues to repay the oxygen debt, supplying extra oxygen needed to remove lactic acid and restore the body's pre-exercise state.

title: Gorbachev & the Collapse of the Soviet Union
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What four problems did Gorbachev recognise were facing the Soviet Union when he became leader?
cards.answer: Stagnating economy / War in Afghanistan draining resources / Cripplingly expensive arms race / Shortages of basic goods

cards.front: Name the three Cold War summit meetings between Gorbachev and Reagan mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Geneva Summit, November 1985 / Reykjavik Summit, October 1986 / INF Treaty signing, December 1987

cards.front: Why did the 1986 Reykjavik Summit talks collapse?
cards.answer: Reagan refused to abandon his proposed space-based missile defence system, SDI.

cards.front: How did Gorbachev's reforms end up destroying the Soviet system he wanted to save?
cards.answer: Glasnost let people criticise the government and demand independence, while perestroika failed to improve the economy, fuelling frustration and nationalist movements.

cards.front: Name the two elements of asthma treatment during sport given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Reassurance / Inhalers or nebulisers

cards.front: Why does wearing a scarf or sports buff over the mouth help an asthmatic performer in cold weather?
cards.answer: It warms and humidifies the inhaled air, reducing the exercise-induced asthma trigger.

cards.front: Why should a coach make sure a Type 1 diabetic's reliever items, like glucose tablets, are kept immediately accessible during sport?
cards.answer: Exercise significantly increases the risk of a hypo, so fast-acting carbohydrates must be to hand during activity.

cards.front: Why does the body produce symptoms like increased thirst and frequent urination in diabetes?
cards.answer: The body tries to dilute excess blood sugar by drawing water from cells and kidneys filter the excess glucose through urine.

cards.front: Name the four risks the lesson gives of starting a business.
cards.answer: Losing savings invested / Giving up a guaranteed salary / Mortgaging a home to raise finance / Long hours replacing evenings and weekends
items: Mortgaging a home to raise finance
Long hours replacing evenings and weekends

cards.front: Name the three common causes the lesson gives for start-ups failing in the first three years.
cards.answer: Under-estimating time to win customers / Over-estimating profit margins / Taking on unaffordable personal debt

cards.front: Why did Pasta Evangelists trial its subscription in London before going nationwide?
cards.answer: Starting small before scaling reduces risk while keeping the potential reward intact if the idea works.

cards.front: How did Sir James Dyson's vacuum story show both risk and reward?
cards.answer: He remortgaged his house and was rejected by five retailers, risking everything, before Japan's stocking led to a billion-pound company.

cards.front: Name the three wartime resisters against Nazi Germany given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Hans and Sophie Scholl (White Rose) / Claus von Stauffenberg (July Plot) / Dietrich Bonhoeffer (anti-Nazi theologian)

cards.front: Name the six countries Germany overran in rapid succession in the first two years of the war.
cards.answer: Poland / Denmark / Norway / France / the Low Countries / Yugoslavia

cards.front: Why did the German advance into the Soviet Union stall before reaching Moscow?
cards.answer: Soviet resistance stiffened, German supply lines became over-extended, and the Russian winter halted the advance.

cards.front: Why did Germany surrender unconditionally on 8 May 1945?
cards.answer: Soviet forces had encircled Berlin and Hitler killed himself on 30 April 1945, leading to Germany's collapse.

cards.front: Name the four sub-problems given for decomposing an online GP appointment booking system.
cards.answer: Patient login / Show available slots / Book a slot / Send confirmation

cards.front: How does breaking a program into subprograms reduce complexity for a developer reading the code?
cards.answer: It shows short, clearly-named blocks instead of one huge sequence, hiding detail inside each subprogram.

cards.front: Why does decomposing the GP appointment system into four sub-problems cut development time?
cards.answer: Each sub-problem is small enough to be designed, coded and tested independently, so a team can work on them simultaneously.

title: The Battle of the Cowshed & Snowball's Leadership
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why does Napoleon oppose Snowball's windmill plan?
cards.answer: Not because it's a bad idea, but because he opposes Snowball having the credit for it.

cards.front: What did Snowball's windmill plan promise to do for the animals?
cards.answer: It would bring electricity and reduce the animals' workload to three days a week.

cards.front: Name the three brain areas the lesson says brain imaging has shown volume/activity differences in for schizophrenia.
cards.answer: Frontal lobes / Hippocampus / Temporal lobes

cards.front: Why is psychotherapy for schizophrenia usually given alongside anti-psychotic medication rather than instead of it?
cards.answer: Symptoms often need to be biologically stabilised first before a patient can engage fully with talking therapy.

cards.front: Why can psychotherapy for clinical depression sometimes be used alone, unlike for schizophrenia?
cards.answer: It can be used alone for milder cases, only combined with anti-depressants for severe or treatment-resistant depression.

cards.front: Why might symptoms return after a person stops taking biological treatment for a mental health problem?
cards.answer: Because biological treatments change brain chemistry rather than the underlying thoughts or life circumstances causing symptoms.

cards.front: Name the four steps for preparing a light microscope slide, given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Place a thin sample on a clean slide / Add a drop of stain / Lower a coverslip at 45° / Focus on lowest magnification first, then increase
items: Place a thin sample on a clean slide
Focus on lowest magnification first, then increase

cards.front: Why is the cell wall able to stop a plant cell bursting when water enters by osmosis?
cards.answer: It is made of cellulose which strengthens and supports the cell, preventing it from bursting as water enters.

cards.front: Why are mitochondria so efficient at transferring energy?
cards.answer: Their inner membranes are folded into cristae, which increase the surface area for respiration enzymes.

cards.front: Why does iodine stain make plant cell structures easier to see under a light microscope?
cards.answer: Iodine stains plant cell walls and nuclei yellow-brown, making otherwise colourless structures visible.

cards.front: How can PIES impacts of a lack of safeguarding link together in one service user?
cards.answer: Emotional distress can cause social withdrawal, which reduces intellectual stimulation and leads to physical decline through loss of appetite.

cards.front: Why might a person with a sensory impairment struggle to get help if they are being harmed?
cards.answer: Limited access to information and reduced ability to raise the alarm makes it harder for them to seek support.

cards.front: Name the four things safeguarding training ensures all staff can do.
cards.answer: Recognise possible signs of harm or abuse / Know the setting's reporting procedures / Understand their personal duty to report / Know who the DSL is and how to contact them
items: Recognise possible signs of harm or abuse
Understand their personal duty to report
Know who the DSL is and how to contact them

title: The Designers' Toolkit: Set, Lighting, Sound, Costume
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four design fundamentals that apply to every theatre design discipline.
cards.answer: Scale / Shape / Colour / Texture

cards.front: Name the four core design disciplines in theatre.
cards.answer: Set design / Lighting design / Sound design / Costume design

cards.front: Why does light from directly above (top light) make a face look gaunt or threatening?
cards.answer: Top light creates hard shadows under the eyes, distorting the face to look gaunt or threatening.

cards.front: Why does a design answer naming only 'dark lighting to show sadness' score poorly?
cards.answer: It is vague: it doesn't name the specific element, effect, or connect the choice to a named moment.

title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the six things the Bible says God created in order in Genesis 1.
cards.answer: Light / Sky / Land / Plants / Animals / Humans

cards.front: Why do many non-literal Christians see no conflict between Genesis and the Big Bang theory?
cards.answer: Because the Genesis order of light, sky, land, plants, animals and humans broadly matches the scientific order of events.

cards.front: Why do creationists reject the Big Bang theory?
cards.answer: It contradicts a literal reading of Genesis, and cannot explain what existed before or caused the explosion, suggesting a creator.

cards.front: Why do most Muslims reject the idea that humans evolved from apes?
cards.answer: Because the Qur'an describes Adam's special creation from clay, so most believe Allah directly created Adam as the first human.

title: Sources and interpretations of Elizabeth's reign
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three main historical interpretations of Elizabeth I given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Whig/traditional Golden Age view / Revisionist troubled reign view / Feminist view of negotiating power

cards.front: Why do feminist historians say Elizabeth used the Gloriana myth?
cards.answer: It was a clever adaptation to the real limitations placed on women in power in a male-dominated political culture.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say royal portraits are not reliable evidence of Elizabeth's real appearance?
cards.answer: They were official propaganda constructed to project power, purity and authority rather than painted from life.

cards.front: Name the three costs of out-of-town retail parks given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Higher CO2 emissions and air pollution from car use / Independent high-street shops lose footfall and close / Farmland or scrub permanently sealed under tarmac
items: Higher CO2 emissions and air pollution from car use
Independent high-street shops lose footfall and close
Farmland or scrub permanently sealed under tarmac

cards.front: Name three types of shop the lesson says are filling gaps left on UK high streets.
cards.answer: Charity shops / Vape shops / Chain coffee outlets

cards.front: Why did rising car ownership help out-of-town retail parks grow?
cards.answer: Around 80% of households own a car, making parking the most important convenience out-of-town parks offer over the high street.

cards.front: How did technology allow out-of-town retail parks to stock more products than high-street shops?
cards.answer: Large warehouses with refrigeration and stock-control software let one site hold far more product lines than a small high-street shop.

cards.front: Name the three effector responses the body uses when it is too hot.
cards.answer: Vasodilation / Sweating / Body hairs lying flat

cards.front: Name the three effector responses the body uses when it is too cold.
cards.answer: Vasoconstriction / Shivering / Body hairs standing on end

cards.front: How does shivering warm the body when it is cold?
cards.answer: Skeletal muscles contract rapidly and repeatedly, and the increased metabolic activity generates heat.

cards.front: Why is Type 2 diabetes often preventable while Type 1 is not?
cards.answer: Type 2 is linked to obesity and lifestyle so it can be managed by diet and exercise, but Type 1 is autoimmune destruction of beta cells.

cards.front: Name the three types of solar eclipse the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Total solar eclipse / Annular solar eclipse / Partial solar eclipse

cards.front: Name the five key distances/sizes the lesson gives for the Sun, Earth and Moon system.
cards.answer: Sun diameter ~1.4 million km / Earth diameter ~13 000 km / Moon diameter ~3 500 km / Earth-Moon distance ~384 000 km / Earth-Sun distance ~150 million km (1 AU)

cards.front: Why does a total solar eclipse only occur when the Moon is closer to Earth in its orbit?
cards.answer: Being closer makes the Moon's angular size large enough to completely cover the Sun's photosphere, unlike near apogee.

cards.front: Why does the Sun affect Earth's tides only about 46% as strongly as the Moon, despite being far more massive?
cards.answer: The Sun's much greater distance reduces its differential gravitational effect, outweighing its greater mass.

cards.front: Name the three causes of diseconomies of scale given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Poor communication / Coordination issues / Reduced staff motivation

cards.front: Name the six typical sections a business plan includes, as listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Business idea and aims / Target market / Marketing plan / Operations plan / Management and staff details / Financial forecasts

cards.front: Why does spreading fixed costs over more units lower the average cost per loaf?
cards.answer: Fixed costs stay the same as output rises, so dividing the same fixed cost across more loaves reduces the cost per loaf.

cards.front: How can a business use the extra profit margin gained from economies of scale?
cards.answer: It can cut prices, raise profit margins, or invest the difference back into the business.

cards.front: Name the three common mistakes to avoid, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Plot retelling / Bolted-on context / Missing AO2 (no named techniques)

cards.front: Name the two question type choices for the Pride and Prejudice exam question.
cards.answer: Extract-based question linked to whole novel / Discursive question
items: Extract-based question linked to whole novel

cards.front: Why should context be embedded within analysis rather than given its own paragraph?
cards.answer: Bolting on context as a separate paragraph is a common mistake; context should be woven into analysis, not separated out.

cards.front: Why should a student memorise short embedded quotations rather than long passages?
cards.answer: Short embedded quotations are more effective than long passages, so 2-3 per theme should be memorised and woven into analytical sentences.

cards.front: Name the three phrases the lesson gives describing Scrooge's coldness in Stave 1.
cards.answer: His own low temperature always about with him / Iced his office in the dog-days / No warmth could warm him
items: His own low temperature always about with him
Iced his office in the dog-days

cards.front: Why does Dickens insist so firmly at the start that Marley is dead?
cards.answer: So that when Marley's ghost later appears, the supernatural event carries its full shocking weight.

cards.front: How do Bob Cratchit and Fred together establish the novella's moral standard in Stave 1?
cards.answer: They show happiness doesn't need wealth, since Bob has nothing but is content and Fred is joyful, unlike miserable, wealthy Scrooge.

cards.front: How does the cold imagery in Stave 1 link to Scrooge's isolation?
cards.answer: The cold symbolises how Scrooge has frozen out all human connection, cutting himself off from other people.

cards.front: What are Darwin's five observations that make up the theory of natural selection?
cards.answer: Individuals show variation in characteristics / Organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support / Best-adapted individuals more likely to survive and reproduce / These individuals pass on advantageous alleles to offspring / Advantageous allele becomes more common over generations
items: Organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support
Best-adapted individuals more likely to survive and reproduce
These individuals pass on advantageous alleles to offspring
Advantageous allele becomes more common over generations

cards.front: What are the two processes that create genetic variation within a population?
cards.answer: Mutations / Sexual reproduction

cards.front: Why does sexual reproduction increase genetic variation?
cards.answer: Fusion of gametes from two parents, plus random allele mixing in meiosis and random fertilisation, gives each offspring a unique allele combination.

cards.front: How can speciation occur when populations become geographically isolated?
cards.answer: Separated groups face different environments, so different characteristics are favoured, and over time they change too much to interbreed.

cards.front: Name the three wires in a UK three-pin plug and their colours.
cards.answer: Live wire (brown) / Neutral wire (blue) / Earth wire (green and yellow stripes)

cards.front: Why must fuses and circuit breakers be wired into the live wire, not the neutral wire?
cards.answer: The live wire carries the alternating potential difference, so breaking it stops voltage reaching the appliance and makes it safe.

cards.front: Why does stepping up the voltage with a transformer force the current to decrease?
cards.answer: Because power in equals power out in an ideal transformer (VpIp = VsIs), so increasing voltage must proportionally decrease current.

cards.front: How does Mercutio's Queen Mab speech make his death more tragic?
cards.answer: He is a rationalist who rejects fate and dreams, so dying cursing both families is especially senseless.

cards.front: Why does the Friar call Romeo's threat of suicide 'womanish'?
cards.answer: Elizabethan society expected men to bear suffering stoically, so Romeo's emotional intensity showed a lack of self-control.

cards.front: How does Juliet resolve her conflict between loving Romeo and mourning Tybalt?
cards.answer: She reasons logically that her husband lives while Tybalt would have killed him, so she chooses Romeo.

title: Black America in 1954: Segregation, Voting and the NAACP
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four deliberate barriers the lesson gives that stopped Black Southerners voting by 1954.
cards.answer: Literacy tests / Poll taxes / White-only primaries / Grandfather clauses

cards.front: Name the three pressures the lesson says were converging on Jim Crow by the early 1950s.
cards.answer: Returning Black soldiers refusing segregation / Northern migration giving Black voters political weight / Cold War making segregation a propaganda gift to the USSR
items: Northern migration giving Black voters political weight
Cold War making segregation a propaganda gift to the USSR

cards.front: Why was 'separate but equal' in reality unequal for Black Americans in the South?
cards.answer: Black schools, teachers, hospitals and buses received far less funding and worse treatment than white equivalents despite the law's promise of equality.

cards.front: Why was the NAACP harassed and banned in some Southern states by 1956?
cards.answer: White supremacists saw its legal strategy as a real threat, so states demanded membership records and banned it, like in Alabama.

cards.front: Name the four steps of Kennedy's non-military response to the Berlin Wall going up.
cards.answer: Sent Johnson and Clay to West Berlin / Sent a US battle group up the autobahn / Deployed US tanks at Checkpoint Charlie / Gave the 'Ich bin ein Berliner' speech in 1963
items: Sent Johnson and Clay to West Berlin
Sent a US battle group up the autobahn
Deployed US tanks at Checkpoint Charlie
Gave the 'Ich bin ein Berliner' speech in 1963

cards.front: Why did Khrushchev order the Berlin Wall to be built rather than issue another ultimatum?
cards.answer: The Vienna ultimatum had not moved the West, so Khrushchev needed a way to stop refugees fleeing without starting a war.

cards.front: Why did Kennedy accept the Berlin Wall instead of trying to tear it down?
cards.answer: He had no good military options, since removing the wire would mean troops firing on East German conscripts and risking nuclear escalation.

cards.front: How did the Berlin Wall help stabilise the Cold War in the short term?
cards.answer: It removed Berlin as an immediate flashpoint, letting both leaders turn their attention to other issues.

title: Context: 1981 Britain, Race & the Care System
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: What three things caused the Handsworth riots to break out, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Racial discrimination / Aggressive policing / Mass unemployment in Black communities

cards.front: What immediate event triggered the violence in Handsworth on 10 July 1981?
cards.answer: A well-known police superintendent was attacked / He was trying to calm rumours of a National Front march
items: A well-known police superintendent was attacked
He was trying to calm rumours of a National Front march

cards.front: Why does de Waal's 2016 retrospective viewpoint help show structural racism in the novel?
cards.answer: It lets readers see, through Leon's child perspective, things that were invisible to many white people at the time.

cards.front: How did underfunding affect children's experience of the 1980s care system?
cards.answer: Overworked social workers managed enormous caseloads, so children's emotional needs were often secondary to bureaucratic processes.

title: US involvement in Iran, Iraq and the Gulf War
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What two reasons did Saddam Hussein give for invading Kuwait in 1990?
cards.answer: Claimed Kuwait was historically part of Iraq / Resented Kuwait's oil overproduction depressing prices
items: Claimed Kuwait was historically part of Iraq
Resented Kuwait's oil overproduction depressing prices

cards.front: Why did the US support for Iraq during the Iran-Iraq War later prove embarrassing?
cards.answer: The USA had armed and supported Saddam Hussein, who then invaded Kuwait less than two years later, forcing the USA to mobilise against him.

cards.front: How did the USA's response to the USS Stark incident in 1987 show its priorities in the Iran-Iraq War?
cards.answer: It treated the Iraqi attack that killed 37 sailors with restraint, showing it prioritised containing Iran over confronting Iraq.

cards.front: Name four factors the lesson says have shaped how cuisines evolve over time.
cards.answer: Climate / Trade routes / Migration and cultural exchange / Industrialisation, food technology and globalisation

cards.front: Name the four regional British cuisines the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Scottish cuisine / Welsh cuisine / Northern English cuisine / West Country cooking

cards.front: Why are many traditional British dishes cooked as one-pot or slow-cooked meals?
cards.answer: To make the most of cheaper cuts of meat, which become tender through long, moist cooking.

cards.front: Why is fusion cuisine wrongly seen as less authentic, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because no cuisine is static — ingredients like tomatoes and chillies only reached Italy and India in the 16th century, showing authenticity means internal consistency, not pure origins.

cards.front: Name the eight energy stores given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Kinetic / Thermal / Chemical / Elastic potential / Gravitational potential / Electrostatic / Magnetic / Nuclear

cards.front: Name the four energy transfer pathways given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Mechanically (by forces) / Electrically (by currents) / By heating / By radiation

cards.front: Why does a ball thrown upwards momentarily stop at the top of its flight?
cards.answer: All of its kinetic energy has transferred into the gravitational potential store, leaving none for movement.

cards.front: Name the four features of every Newton's third law pair.
cards.answer: Act on two different objects / Are the same size / Act in opposite directions / Are the same type of force
items: Are the same type of force

cards.front: How does a rocket accelerate forwards even though Newton's third law forces are equal and opposite?
cards.answer: The rocket pushes gas backwards and the gas pushes the rocket forwards, but these forces act on different objects so the rocket can still move.

cards.front: Why does a skydiver reach a new, lower terminal velocity after the parachute opens?
cards.answer: Air resistance suddenly increases above weight causing deceleration, until the reduced speed makes air resistance balance weight again.

cards.front: Name the four things Native American boarding school children were forbidden to do at school.
cards.answer: Speak their native languages / Wear traditional clothing / Practise their religions / Keep their hair and given names
items: Keep their hair and given names

cards.front: Why were death rates high in Native American boarding schools?
cards.answer: Partly due to disease spreading in crowded conditions, and partly due to inadequate care.

cards.front: Why does the lesson call the 1920s boom a 'nation of contrasts' for Native Americans?
cards.answer: While Wall Street boomed, reservations remained in deep poverty, showing prosperity did not reach Native Americans.

cards.front: How did the Dawes Act's allotment system damage tribal life beyond taking land?
cards.answer: It destroyed communal economic and social structures without providing meaningful support for individual farming.

cards.front: Why does the gap between Siobhan's narration and Christopher's performance create meaning in the play?
cards.answer: Siobhan's compassionate reading of Christopher's stark, logical words reveals the emotional weight he cannot express himself.

cards.front: How did Stephens theatrically replace the novel's printed diagrams, maps and mathematical proofs?
cards.answer: He used video projections on the graph-paper set and had the ensemble physically enact Christopher's spatial reasoning.

cards.front: Why did Haddon present Christopher's perspective as the novel's lens in 2003?
cards.answer: To challenge readers to see neurotypical behaviour as strange rather than normal, against the deficit model of autism common then.

cards.front: Name the five groups the lesson says are exempt from fasting during Ramadan.
cards.answer: Children / The elderly / Pregnant or nursing women / Travellers / Those who are seriously ill

cards.front: Name the five key rituals of Hajj the lesson lists as re-enacting Ibrahim's trials.
cards.answer: Wearing ihram / Circling the Ka'bah / Walking between Safa and Marwa / Standing at Arafat / Stoning the devil at Mina

cards.front: Why do pilgrims walk seven times between Safa and Marwa during Hajj?
cards.answer: It re-enacts Hajar's search for water for her son Isma'il.

cards.front: How is Khums split between recipients according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Half goes to needy descendants of the Prophet (sayyids) and half goes to the Imam or his representatives.

cards.front: What two threats does Macbeth identify about Banquo in Act 3, Scene 1?
cards.answer: Witches prophesied his descendants would be kings / He has a 'royalty of nature' and 'dauntless temper'
items: Witches prophesied his descendants would be kings
He has a 'royalty of nature' and 'dauntless temper'

cards.front: How does Macbeth manipulate the murderers he sends after Banquo?
cards.answer: He tells them Banquo is their enemy, manipulating them just as Lady Macbeth once manipulated him.

cards.front: Why does Fleance's escape devastate Macbeth even though Banquo is dead?
cards.answer: It keeps the witches' prophecy that Banquo's descendants will be kings possible, shattering his sense of security.

cards.front: Why does Lady Macbeth's attempt to cover for Macbeth at the banquet fail to restore order?
cards.answer: His public outburst at the ghost exposes his guilt in front of the nobles and destabilises his authority.

title: Looking at Your Hands — Martin Carter
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name the six key phrases the lesson says to learn exactly for 'Looking at Your Hands'
cards.answer: dear friend / looking at your hands / a room without a light / walking in the sun / fire / dream to change the world

cards.front: Why does Carter use participles in three successive lines of stanza three?
cards.answer: To suggest that dreaming of change and working for change are ongoing, unfinished processes rather than one-off gestures.

cards.front: How does the shift from stanza two to stanza three change the poem's sense of time?
cards.answer: It moves the poem out of memory of the past into a more immediate, ongoing present, mirroring change as continuous.

cards.front: Name the four stages in the chain of scientists (hypothesis, observation, law, theory) that led from geocentric to heliocentric astronomy, in order.
cards.answer: Copernicus proposed a simpler heliocentric framework / Brahe provided precise observational data / Kepler found laws fitting the data using ellipses / Newton explained why those laws hold
items: Copernicus proposed a simpler heliocentric framework
Kepler found laws fitting the data using ellipses
Newton explained why those laws hold

cards.front: Why does a planet move faster near perihelion than near aphelion?
cards.answer: Kepler's Second Law means the Sun-planet line sweeps equal areas in equal times, so the planet must move faster when closer to the Sun.

cards.front: Why do Northern Hemisphere winters last slightly less time than summers?
cards.answer: Earth is near perihelion in January and moves faster there, so it covers that part of its orbit more quickly than the aphelion arc in summer.

cards.front: What happens to a satellite's orbit if its speed is too low or too high for its orbital radius?
cards.answer: Too slow and gravity pulls it inward so it spirals in or falls; too fast and it escapes gravity on a parabolic or hyperbolic path.

title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
subject: english-literature-eduqas

cards.front: Why does the memory of the daffodils matter more than the original sighting in the poem?
cards.answer: Because the mind stores the moment and can replay it later to lift the speaker's spirits when tired or low.

cards.front: How does the simile 'lonely as a cloud' shape our first impression of the speaker?
cards.answer: It suggests he drifts freely and passively through the landscape, detached and alone, until the daffodils interrupt him.

cards.front: Why does Wordsworth compare the daffodils to the waves on the lake in stanza three?
cards.answer: To show the daffodils 'out-did' the sparkling waves in glee, proving they dominate the scene completely.

cards.front: Name the three anthology poems this lesson pairs with 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud' for comparison.
cards.answer: Heaney's 'Blackberry Picking' / Clarke's 'Catrin' / Blake's 'The Schoolboy'

title: British & International Cuisine and Sensory Evaluation
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: Name the five senses involved in tasting food.
cards.answer: Taste / Smell (aroma) / Sight / Touch and texture / Aroma

cards.front: Name the three types of grading test used in sensory evaluation.
cards.answer: Ranking test / Rating test / Profiling test

cards.front: Why does food taste bland when you have a blocked nose from a cold?
cards.answer: The olfactory receptor cells cannot detect the aromatic compounds in food, and smell contributes hugely to flavour.

cards.front: Why is asking a few friends 'what do you think?' not valid sensory evaluation?
cards.answer: Friends are socially biased, the sample is too small, conditions are uncontrolled, and the question is too vague for useful data.

title: Film Music: Borrowed Classics and Video Game Scores
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the three named game composers/teams from the lesson and one game each is linked with.
cards.answer: Koji Kondo – Super Mario Bros./Zelda / Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori – Halo / Jesper Kyd – Assassin's Creed
items: Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori – Halo

cards.front: Name the two main forms of adaptive/dynamic scoring described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Vertical layering / Horizontal re-sequencing

cards.front: Why do game composers write music in short repeatable loops and layers rather than one fixed cue?
cards.answer: Because the player controls pacing, so a composer never knows exactly when an event will happen or how long it lasts.

cards.front: How does the Halo theme's musical style suggest Master Chief's character?
cards.answer: Its Gregorian-style chant and ritualistic timbre over a rolling string ostinato suggest ancient duty and sacrifice, fitting the soldier-hero.

title: The Importance & Impact of Effective Communication
subject: health-social-care-ocr

cards.front: Name the four rights the lesson says are most directly protected by good communication.
cards.answer: Choice / Confidentiality / Consultation / Protection from abuse and harm

cards.front: Name the four specific impacts of poor communication given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Misunderstanding / Errors or danger to health / Distress if patronised / Failing to retain information when speech is too fast
items: Failing to retain information when speech is too fast

cards.front: Why does being well-informed make a service user safer, using the pharmacist example?
cards.answer: Explaining how to take medication, side effects and when to return means the patient understands and can manage their care safely.

cards.front: How can poor communication lead to a chain of PIES harms, using the discharge instructions example?
cards.answer: Speech too fast means instructions aren't understood, medication is taken incorrectly, health deteriorates, causing distress and then withdrawal from appointments.

cards.front: What is the typical three-step sequence of neurons when the body responds to a stimulus?
cards.answer: sensory neuron / relay neuron / motor neuron

cards.front: Why does too much excitation in the nervous system cause a seizure?
cards.answer: The nervous system depends on a balance between excitation and inhibition, and too much excitation over-stimulates neural activity, causing a seizure.

cards.front: How do SSRIs affect serotonin levels at the synapse?
cards.answer: SSRIs block the reuptake of serotonin, so it stays in the synapse longer and keeps stimulating the post-synaptic receptor.

cards.front: What is a weakness of Hebb's theory relating to when it was proposed?
cards.answer: Hebb proposed it before technology existed to observe synapses in living brains, so it was initially only theoretical.

cards.front: Name the three components involved in all homeostatic control systems.
cards.answer: Receptors / Coordination centres / Effectors

cards.front: Name the three organs the lesson gives as coordination centres.
cards.answer: Brain / Spinal cord / Pancreas

cards.front: Why does a shorter distance in the ruler drop test mean a faster reaction time?
cards.answer: The ruler falls for less time before being caught, so less distance means the person reacted quicker.

cards.front: Why is a stable internal environment essential for cells?
cards.answer: Cells need the right conditions to function properly, particularly for enzymes to work.

title: Pillow Talk and When Harry Met Sally: The Romantic Comedy
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why did the seductions in Pillow Talk have to be entirely verbal rather than physical?
cards.answer: The Hays Code prohibited explicit sexual content and required transgression to be punished, so desire was displaced into dialogue and split-screen choreography.

cards.front: How does the static two-shot framing in the Katz's Delicatessen scene affect representation of Sally?
cards.answer: It keeps both characters in frame together throughout, giving Sally equal screen presence rather than privileging Harry's reaction.

cards.front: Why does the camera movement change during Harry's run through Manhattan at the New Year's Eve climax?
cards.answer: The handheld urgency breaks the film's previously static visual register, signalling emotional urgency before returning to stillness for sincerity.

cards.front: What three elements does the lesson say every comparative paragraph needs, to avoid 'parallel description'?
cards.answer: A matched moment / A named difference / A contextual reason

cards.front: What four stages describe Antony's transformation across the play?
cards.answer: Apparent hedonism (Act 1) / Genuine grief (Act 3, Scene 1) / Devastating rhetoric (Act 3, Scene 2) / Ruthless political calculation (Act 4, Scene 1)

cards.front: Why does Caesar dismiss the threat he identifies in Cassius?
cards.answer: Because he believes himself invulnerable, so his insight into Cassius's danger is undermined by his own arrogance.

cards.front: Why is Octavius's final speech and rise to power ironic for an Elizabethan audience?
cards.answer: Because they knew Octavius became Augustus, showing the assassination destroyed the republic it was meant to save.

cards.front: How does Portia try to prove her constancy to Brutus?
cards.answer: She wounds herself to demonstrate she can bear pain and be trusted with his secret.

cards.front: Name the seven elements of non-verbal communication listed in the specification for care settings.
cards.answer: Adapting type/method to needs / Eye contact / Facial expressions / Gestures / Positioning (space, height, personal space) / Positive body language / Sense of humour

cards.front: Why must a practitioner's facial expressions be consistent with the tone of a service user's conversation?
cards.answer: Consistent, genuine expressions build trust, while mismatched ones (like smiling during distress) confuse and unsettle the service user.

cards.front: Why can overusing gestures during a conversation with a service user be a problem?
cards.answer: Exaggerated or theatrical gestures can feel condescending to the service user rather than supportive.

title: The Buddha, the Dhamma and the Three Marks of Existence
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Why did Siddhattha Gotama choose the Middle Way rather than luxury or extreme asceticism?
cards.answer: He found neither luxury nor extreme self-denial led to liberation, so he chose a balanced path between the two.

cards.front: Why does understanding dependent origination (paticca-samuppada) help end suffering?
cards.answer: If suffering arises from conditions, changing those conditions can end suffering, which is the logic behind Buddhist practice.

cards.front: How does the chariot analogy show that persons exist conventionally but not ultimately?
cards.answer: Removing each part leaves no chariot, showing 'chariot' and 'person' are labels for changing collections, not fixed eternal entities.

title: Family Life, Shabbat, Festivals and the Synagogue
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three stages of Jewish mourning described in the lesson.
cards.answer: shiva (seven days) / avelut (30 days then first year) / yahrzeit (annual memorial)

cards.front: Name the four synagogue features the lesson's Key Fact lists besides the ner tamid.
cards.answer: Ark (houses Torah scrolls, faces Jerusalem) / bimah (raised reading platform) / yad (Torah pointer) / menorah (seven-branched lampstand)

cards.front: Why is a glass broken at the end of a Jewish wedding ceremony?
cards.answer: It recalls the destruction of the Temple, showing that even joy is tempered by remembrance of loss.

cards.front: Why do Orthodox synagogues mark a girl's Bat Mitzvah differently from a boy's Bar Mitzvah?
cards.answer: Orthodox synagogues do not let women read the Torah, so it is marked with a talk or a ceremony outside the main service.

title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What three things happen during the 'iddah waiting period after talaq?
cards.answer: Couple typically continues living under same roof / Husband continues financial support / Reconciliation is actively encouraged
items: Couple typically continues living under same roof

cards.front: What three rights did revelation at the time of Muhammad give women, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Right to inherit / Right to consent to their own marriage / Right to own property
items: Right to consent to their own marriage

cards.front: Why do mainstream scholars extend the 'azl reasoning to modern reversible contraception like the pill or condom?
cards.answer: Because the same underlying principle applies: spacing pregnancies for the health of the mother and stability of the family.

cards.front: Why is abortion treated more restrictively than reversible contraception in Islam?
cards.answer: It is not accepted as a method of contraception, and strict conditions apply after ensoulment, allowing termination only if the mother's life is at risk.

cards.front: What three false identities does the lesson identify as performances in Great Expectations?
cards.answer: Pip performing the gentleman / Estella performing the lady / Miss Havisham performing the jilted bride
items: Miss Havisham performing the jilted bride

cards.front: What three parts does the lesson say a strong analytical response needs?
cards.answer: A clear opening addressing the question / Analytical paragraphs with point, evidence, analysis, context / A brief conclusion returning to the question
items: A clear opening addressing the question
Analytical paragraphs with point, evidence, analysis, context
A brief conclusion returning to the question

cards.front: Why does the lesson say Pip is not a true gentleman despite Magwitch's money?
cards.answer: Magwitch's money bought clothes, education and manners but could not buy character, which comes only from within.

cards.front: How does guilt drive the plot of Great Expectations, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Guilt makes Pip help Magwitch escape, sends him back to the forge, and shapes his remorseful narration.

cards.front: Why does Dickens make the Ghost of Christmas Past's appearance ambiguous, with a child's face but white hair?
cards.answer: It reflects how memories of the past can be both clear and uncertain, joyful and painful.

cards.front: Why does Scrooge weep when he sees his lonely younger self at school?
cards.answer: It shows his childhood hope and imagination still exist within him, waiting to be reawakened.

cards.front: What three main medical uses does the lesson give for genetic testing?
cards.answer: Informing family planning / Assessing individual disease risk / Enabling personalised medicine

cards.front: How do GM mosquitoes reduce wild mosquito populations that spread malaria and dengue?
cards.answer: Male GM mosquitoes carrying a self-limiting gene mate with wild females, so offspring inheriting the gene do not survive to reproduce.

cards.front: Why did human insulin production using bacteria replace extracting insulin from animals?
cards.answer: Animal-sourced insulin sometimes caused immune reactions in patients, so genetically modified bacteria producing human insulin were used instead.

cards.front: Why can a genetic carrier of a recessive disease allele still have an affected child?
cards.answer: A carrier has one copy of the recessive allele and is unaffected, but can pass it on to a child who inherits two copies.

cards.front: Name the four short quotable phrases the lesson says to learn exactly for 'Colonization in Reverse'.
cards.answer: de motherlan / bag an baggage / loyalty / tun history upside dung

cards.front: Name the three poems the lesson pairs with 'Colonization in Reverse' besides Flag and Papa-T.
cards.answer: Partition by Sujata Bhatt / Songs for the People by Frances E. W. Harper / We Lived Happily during the War by Ilya Kaminsky
items: Songs for the People by Frances E. W. Harper
We Lived Happily during the War by Ilya Kaminsky

cards.front: Why does Bennett use humour rather than anger to criticise empire in 'Colonization in Reverse'?
cards.answer: She lets the comedy of reversed history do the criticism, since Jamaican dialogue's nature is comedy and laughing stops people weeping.

cards.front: How does the structure of the poem build up to its punchline about reversed history?
cards.answer: Rhetorical pairing sets up comic opposites, exclamations in the fourth stanza speed up the excitement, building to 'tun history upside dung'.

title: The Nature of God & the Trinity
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four Christian responses to the problem of evil given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Free will / Life as a test / Part of God's plan / The Devil

cards.front: What are the three persons of the Trinity and their roles?
cards.answer: Father - creator and sustainer / Son - Jesus, became human to save humanity / Holy Spirit - God's presence active in the world
items: Son - Jesus, became human to save humanity
Holy Spirit - God's presence active in the world

cards.front: How does the free will response try to explain moral evil?
cards.answer: God gave humans freedom to choose how to live, and some choose to do wrong, causing moral evil.

cards.front: How does the story of Job explain suffering as part of Christian belief?
cards.answer: It shows God allows suffering to test whether people remain faithful, rewarding those who do.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives for why Hitler became Chancellor.
cards.answer: Failure of other chancellors (Brüning, von Papen, von Schleicher) / Von Papen's scheming and desire for revenge / Hindenburg's exhaustion with political instability / Nazis were the largest party in the Reichstag
items: Failure of other chancellors (Brüning, von Papen, von Schleicher)
Von Papen's scheming and desire for revenge
Nazis were the largest party in the Reichstag

cards.front: Why did von Schleicher's attempt to stay in power fail?
cards.answer: He tried to split the Nazis by offering Strasser a post, and Hindenburg refused his request to rule by decree, so he resigned.

title: What Were They Like? — Denise Levertov
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Why does Levertov use enjambment, e.g. 'There is an echo yet / of their speech which was like a song'?
cards.answer: It keeps images incomplete until the next line resolves them, echoing how the culture has been left unfinished.

cards.front: How does the structure of the poem's two halves change its pace?
cards.answer: Six hopeful questions crowd the opening, then six calm flat answers follow, shifting the pace from curiosity to horror.

cards.front: Why does the adjective 'burned' in 'laughter is bitter to the burned mouth' matter?
cards.answer: It turns a gentle image of laughter into a wound, showing how war has corrupted something once peaceful.

cards.front: Why does addressing the answers to 'Sir' create guilt in the reader?
cards.answer: It puts the reader in the questioner's position, someone who assumed a culture could be reduced to a checklist of facts.

title: Cortes and the Conquest of Mexico
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What six factors does the lesson give for what actually defeated the Aztec Empire?
cards.answer: Tlaxcalan alliance provided warriors and intelligence / Smallpox killed the Aztec leadership / Tribute system alienated subject peoples / Spanish steel, horses, crossbows and brigantines / La Malinche's linguistic and political skill / Cortes's leadership
items: Tlaxcalan alliance provided warriors and intelligence
Spanish steel, horses, crossbows and brigantines
La Malinche's linguistic and political skill

cards.front: Why did the Tlaxcalans agree to ally with Cortes against the Aztecs?
cards.answer: They were not Aztec subjects and resented Aztec tribute demands, so they saw Cortes as a way to fight Aztec rule.

cards.front: How did smallpox help the Spanish coalition win the war against the Aztecs?
cards.answer: It killed the new emperor Cuitlahuac and much of the Aztec leadership and army, buying the coalition time to regroup before the siege.

cards.front: Why did Cortes scuttle his ships at Vera Cruz?
cards.answer: To strand his men on the mainland so they could not change their minds and sail back to Cuba.

title: Comparing Films: Genre, Narrative, Context Side by Side
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three matched moments this unit uses for its comparative film pairs.
cards.answer: Genre conflict announced (Pillow Talk / When Harry Met Sally) / Rebellion staged for the spectator (Rebel Without a Cause / Ferris Bueller) / Alien first encountered (Invasion of the Body Snatchers / E.T.)
items: Genre conflict announced (Pillow Talk / When Harry Met Sally)
Rebellion staged for the spectator (Rebel Without a Cause / Ferris Bueller)
Alien first encountered (Invasion of the Body Snatchers / E.T.)

cards.front: Why is 'Invasion of the Body Snatchers has dark lighting but E.T. has warm lighting' too weak to count as a named difference?
cards.answer: It names a tonal contrast but not a specific technique, sequence or effect that could be analysed.

cards.front: Why did Nicholas Ray frame teen rebellion in Rebel Without a Cause as existentially costly?
cards.answer: The 1950s moral-panic context drove him to use CinemaScope dwarfing and dissonant scoring to show rebellion as costly.

cards.front: How should contextual knowledge be used in a comparative essay, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It should support the comparison within paragraphs, not be listed separately at the start or end.

cards.front: Name the four key considerations the lesson gives for choosing a distribution platform.
cards.answer: Target audience / File formats the platform accepts / Cost to creator and audience / Accessibility

cards.front: Name the four accessibility features the lesson gives for digital distribution.
cards.answer: Subtitles or closed captions / Alt text for images / Colour contrast standards / Transcripts for audio content

cards.front: Why is app store distribution best suited to interactive products rather than videos or podcasts?
cards.answer: Because app stores are designed to distribute software-based interactive products like games and apps, not passive media.

cards.front: Why does an app often need two separate versions when distributed through app stores?
cards.answer: Because the app must be built to meet the different technical requirements of iOS and Android platforms.

cards.front: Why were Jews permitted to live in Venice despite being confined to a ghetto?
cards.answer: Their financial services were essential to Venice's economy, so the city depended on them despite hostility towards them.

cards.front: Why does Shylock's anger at Antonio go beyond just the economic rivalry?
cards.answer: Antonio has personally abused Shylock, calling him 'misbeliever, cut-throat dog' and spitting on his gaberdine.

title: Elizabeth's accession in 1558: a difficult inheritance
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four overlapping problems Elizabeth inherited in 1558.
cards.answer: Questions about her legitimacy and gender / Crown debt of around £300,000 / Deep religious division / Hostile France with troops in Scotland
items: Questions about her legitimacy and gender
Hostile France with troops in Scotland

cards.front: Name the four religious changes England went through in the twenty-five years before Elizabeth's accession.
cards.answer: Catholic under Henry VIII / Protestant under Edward VI from 1547 / Firmly Catholic again under Mary I from 1553 / Protestant again under Elizabeth
items: Firmly Catholic again under Mary I from 1553

cards.front: Why was marriage seen as the obvious solution to Elizabeth's succession problem, yet still dangerous?
cards.answer: Marriage could produce an heir and a male partner, but a foreign Catholic prince risked making England a satellite of Spain or France, while an English noble would unbalance the court.

cards.front: Why did the loss of Calais in 1558 matter so much to Elizabeth's new reign?
cards.answer: It proved France could push England back militarily and showed the war Mary I fought for Philip II had cost England territory for nothing.

title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Why is the live wire dangerous even when an appliance switch is off?
cards.answer: Because the live wire is still at 230 V relative to earth, so touching it makes current flow through your body.

cards.front: Why must a switch always be connected in the live wire rather than the neutral wire?
cards.answer: So that when the switch is off, no current can reach the appliance at all.

cards.front: Name the three wires found in a UK three-pin plug.
cards.answer: Live wire / Neutral wire / Earth wire

cards.front: Name the four main stages of genetic engineering described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cut out the desired gene / Open the vector / Insert the gene into the vector / Transfer to host organism
items: Insert the gene into the vector

cards.front: How does the same restriction enzyme allow a gene to be inserted into a vector?
cards.answer: Using the same enzyme on both the gene and vector creates complementary sticky ends that pair up together.

cards.front: Why does inbreeding increase health problems in animals like flat-faced dog breeds?
cards.answer: Breeding only similar organisms narrows the gene pool, reducing genetic variation and causing health problems such as breathing difficulties.

cards.front: Why has genetically modified bacteria replaced pig or cow insulin for treating diabetes?
cards.answer: GM bacteria produce human insulin cheaply and reliably, avoiding the allergic reactions sometimes caused by animal insulin.

cards.front: Name the three UK/government approaches used to reduce regional differences in the UK.
cards.answer: Enterprise Zones / Transport investment (HS2, Crossrail, Northern Powerhouse Rail) / Regional development funding
items: Transport investment (HS2, Crossrail, Northern Powerhouse Rail)

cards.front: Name the three ways migration has reshaped the UK's population geography over the past 50 years.
cards.answer: Internal migration / International migration / Changing immigration policy

cards.front: Why did the UK become one of the world's largest destinations for foreign direct investment (FDI) from the 1980s onwards?
cards.answer: UK policy from the 1980s favoured free trade, privatisation of nationalised industries, and openness to foreign investment.

cards.front: Why do more people live in London than in the Scottish Highlands, according to population density figures?
cards.answer: London is part of the job-rich urban core with over 5,500 people per km2, while the Highlands are rural periphery with under 10.

cards.front: Name the four holy books (Kutub) that Muslims believe Allah revealed, in the order given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Qur'an / Torah (Tawrat) / Psalms (Zabur) / Gospel (Injil) / Scrolls of Abraham (Suhuf Ibrahim)

cards.front: Why does the story of Ibrahim being commanded to sacrifice Isma'il matter in Islam?
cards.answer: It showed Ibrahim's total faith and willingness to obey Allah completely, so Allah provided a ram instead.

cards.front: How does the Imamate show a key difference between Sunni and Shi'a Islam?
cards.answer: Shi'a Muslims believe leadership passed to divinely appointed, infallible Imams from Muhammad's family, while Sunnis followed elected caliphs and scholarly consensus.

cards.front: Why do Muslims treat the physical Qur'an with such great respect?
cards.answer: Because it is believed to be the literal, unchanged word of Allah, so it is kept on the highest shelf and hands are washed before reading it.

cards.front: Why does rising onto your toes (plantar flexion) lift the whole body with relatively little calf muscle effort?
cards.answer: It is a second class lever with the effort arm longer than the load arm, giving mechanical advantage greater than 1.

cards.front: Why does a bicep curl need much more muscular effort than the weight being lifted?
cards.answer: The effort arm (elbow to biceps insertion) is much shorter than the load arm (elbow to hand), giving mechanical advantage less than 1.

cards.front: How do you work out which class a lever belongs to when labelling a diagram?
cards.answer: Find the joint (fulcrum) first, then the load, then where the muscle pulls (effort); whichever sits in the middle decides the class.

cards.front: Why does Rosa use a quieter, warmer tone with Caitlin, who has an eating disorder?
cards.answer: A warm, quiet tone signals a safe space and avoids clinical formality that could feel dehumanising.

cards.front: Why can 'adapting communication' mean using more technical language, not simpler language?
cards.answer: Adaptation means meeting the person where they are, so oversimplifying can feel condescending to someone with a professional background.

cards.front: Give the number of shared electron pairs and molecule example for the three types of covalent bond described (single, double, triple).
cards.answer: Single bond - one shared pair (H2) / Double bond - two shared pairs (O=O) / Triple bond - three shared pairs (N≡N)

cards.front: Why do ions formed by ionic bonding end up stable?
cards.answer: Both ions gain full outer electron shells after electrons are transferred, making them stable.

cards.front: How does metallic bonding hold a metal structure together?
cards.answer: Delocalised electrons form a moving sea that creates strong electrostatic attraction to the positive metal ions.

cards.front: Why does Bennett link Hector's teaching method to his own coping mechanism?
cards.answer: Hector cannot express his feelings directly, so he channels his loneliness and failure through poetry and quotation instead.

cards.front: Why is Mrs Lintott's description of herself as 'confided in by all parties' significant?
cards.answer: It is an understatement showing she sees everyone's secrets but remains invisible and powerless in the male-dominated drama.

cards.front: Why does the Headmaster call Hector's abuse 'the odd grope'?
cards.answer: The euphemism minimises sexual abuse into a trivial inconvenience, showing he processes everything through institutional self-interest.

cards.front: Why is Posner's declaration 'I'm a Jew...I'm fucked' so powerful?
cards.answer: Its short, simple sentences gain power because they contrast with his usual hesitant, quiet register.

title: Themes across the period: continuity and change
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the seven major turning points the lesson identifies across 1929-2000.
cards.answer: 1933 New Deal / 1941 Pearl Harbor / 1954 Brown v Board / 1963-68 civil rights legislation / 1974 Nixon resignation / 1980-81 Reagan revolution / 1991 Gulf War/USSR dissolved

cards.front: Name the four political scandals the lesson describes as recurring features of the period.
cards.answer: Teapot Dome scandal / Watergate / Iran-Contra affair / Clinton's impeachment

cards.front: Why did Watergate mark a significant turning point in US politics?
cards.answer: It resulted in the first presidential resignation, testing whether constitutional checks could limit presidential power.

cards.front: How did the Second World War change American unemployment compared to the New Deal?
cards.answer: It delivered full employment the New Deal had not achieved, with unemployment below 2 per cent by 1944.

cards.front: Why can't newborn babies walk straight after birth?
cards.answer: The cerebellum, which coordinates movement and balance, continues developing into early childhood.

cards.front: Why does the brain develop in a bottom-up order, with survival structures first?
cards.answer: This reflects evolution prioritising survival over sophisticated cognition, so life-sustaining structures form before thinking structures.

cards.front: Why does a skilful movement in a chain like a javelin throw break down if one body part fires too early?
cards.answer: Different body parts must work together in the correct timed sequence, so an early or late link disrupts the co-ordination.

cards.front: Why is a gymnastics floor routine classed as a closed skill even though it is very complex?
cards.answer: Closed depends on the environment being predictable and controlled, not on how difficult or complex the skill's movements are.

cards.front: Name the three main functions Kenilworth Castle served across its history, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Military fortress and defence / Aristocratic/royal residence / Administrative and political centre

cards.front: What four things did Colonel Joseph Hawkesworth's 1649-50 slighting of Kenilworth involve?
cards.answer: Breaching part of the Norman keep / Stripping lead from roofs / Cutting the causeway dam / Draining the Great Mere permanently
items: Breaching part of the Norman keep

cards.front: How did John of Gaunt change Kenilworth's function after inheriting it in 1361?
cards.answer: He transformed it from a military fortress into a palatial residence with state apartments, a great hall and an administrative centre for his estates.

cards.front: Why did Robert Dudley spend so lavishly on the 1575 royal entertainment at Kenilworth?
cards.answer: It was political theatre designed to show Dudley's fitness as a royal consort and persuade Elizabeth I to marry him.

cards.front: Name the three key techniques Berry uses in 'On an Afternoon Train from Purley to Victoria, 1955'.
cards.answer: Documentary precision / Free verse and everyday language / Four stanzas marking conversation stages

cards.front: Name the three key techniques Dharker uses in 'A Century Later'.
cards.answer: War imagery in a peaceful setting / Enjambment across a stanza break / Free verse with no fixed stanza pattern
items: War imagery in a peaceful setting
Free verse with no fixed stanza pattern

cards.front: How does Berry's plain, unmetaphorical tone make the woman's racism in the poem more disturbing?
cards.answer: It shows the casual racism as ordinary and unremarkable, built into everyday life rather than exceptional.

cards.front: How does Robinson's use of imperatives like 'trace', 'smell' and 'hum' support the poem's idea of home?
cards.answer: They ask the reader to use their senses, showing cultural memory is embodied in the body, not just the mind.

title: McCarthyism and the Red Scare of the 1950s
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four events that triggered the second Red Scare.
cards.answer: Soviet atomic bomb (Aug 1949) / Communist victory in China (Oct 1949) / Conviction of Alger Hiss (Jan 1950) / Outbreak of the Korean War (June 1950)

cards.front: Name four groups of people affected by McCarthyism beyond the entertainment industry, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Marxist academics sacked by universities / Books removed from public libraries / Left-wing officers purged from trade unions / China experts lost from the State Department
items: Left-wing officers purged from trade unions
China experts lost from the State Department

cards.front: Why did Hollywood studios issue the Waldorf Statement in November 1947?
cards.answer: Studios were terrified of losing audiences, so they announced they would not employ Communists.

cards.front: Why did Eisenhower drop his planned defence of General Marshall during his 1952 campaign in Wisconsin?
cards.answer: McCarthy had become electorally dangerous, so Eisenhower avoided confronting him rather than defend his friend Marshall.

title: Lenin in Power: Brest-Litovsk, Cheka and Civil War
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why the Reds won the Civil War.
cards.answer: Geography: held the central core with railways and people / Leadership: Trotsky built a disciplined five-million-strong Red Army / Unity: single command and clear cause / Propaganda: cast Whites as agents of foreign capital
items: Geography: held the central core with railways and people
Leadership: Trotsky built a disciplined five-million-strong Red Army
Unity: single command and clear cause
Propaganda: cast Whites as agents of foreign capital

cards.front: Name the four White generals mentioned in the lesson and where they operated.
cards.answer: Denikin in the south / Kolchak in Siberia / Yudenich near Petrograd / Wrangel in Crimea

cards.front: Why was the Bolshevik government forced to accept the harsh Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918?
cards.answer: Trotsky tried delaying tactics but a renewed German advance forced Russia to accept the treaty to honour the Decree on Peace.

cards.front: Why did the Bolsheviks order the murder of the Romanov family in July 1918?
cards.answer: As White forces approached Ekaterinburg, killing the family closed off any restoration of the dynasty and removed a rallying point.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare show that mercy is not a neutral virtue in the play?
cards.answer: Mercy is a form of power, as the person with authority gets to define what mercy means.

cards.front: Why might Shylock's cruelty be seen as the product of his treatment rather than his nature?
cards.answer: Christian prejudice despised and abused him for so long that it created the 'monster' they feared.

cards.front: For whole-play Shakespeare tasks, how widely should quotations be drawn?
cards.answer: Quotations should be drawn from at least three different scenes.

cards.front: Why does Shylock agree to lend Antonio money despite Antonio's abuse of him?
cards.answer: Lending gives Shylock power over Antonio for the first time, making it strategy rather than generosity.

cards.front: How does Antonio's use of 'the devil' against Shylock reveal his own hypocrisy?
cards.answer: Antonio uses religious language to justify himself while denying Shylock the right to do the same.

cards.front: Name the three sources of evidence the lesson gives for what Earth's early atmosphere was like.
cards.answer: Chemical composition of ancient rocks / Volcanic emissions today / Comparison with other planets like Mars and Venus
items: Comparison with other planets like Mars and Venus

cards.front: Why does the absence of oxidised iron minerals in very ancient rocks suggest little free oxygen existed then?
cards.answer: Ancient rocks show what gases were present when they formed, so no rust-like oxidised iron suggests there was little or no free oxygen.

cards.front: Why can't ice cores tell us about Earth's very early atmosphere?
cards.answer: Ice cores only preserve trapped air from up to around 800,000 years ago, far too recent to sample the early atmosphere.

cards.front: Why have carbon dioxide levels risen significantly since industrialisation?
cards.answer: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon that had been locked away for millions of years back into the atmosphere.

cards.front: Name the three unities of drama that An Inspector Calls observes.
cards.answer: Unity of time / Unity of place / Unity of action

cards.front: How does the Inspector's plain, direct language give him moral authority over the Birlings?
cards.answer: His short, simple sentences cut through the Birlings' evasions, unlike their more elaborate, self-serving speech.

cards.front: How does dramatic irony give the 1945 audience moral superiority over the Birlings?
cards.answer: The audience knows Birling's confident predictions about the Titanic and war are wrong, so they reject his worldview.

cards.front: How does Sheila's changing language across the play show her moral growth?
cards.answer: She moves from shallow exclamations like “Oh — how horrible!” to measured, thoughtful sentences showing real understanding.

cards.front: Name the six key structures found inside a synovial joint.
cards.answer: Joint capsule / Synovial membrane / Synovial fluid / Articular cartilage / Ligaments / Bursae/menisci

cards.front: Name the three types of blood vessel in the cardiovascular system.
cards.answer: Arteries / Veins / Capillaries

cards.front: Why does the left ventricle have much thicker walls than the right ventricle?
cards.answer: Because it must generate higher pressure to pump blood around the entire body, not just to the lungs.

cards.front: How does the structure of capillaries allow efficient gas and nutrient exchange?
cards.answer: They are only one cell thick with a tiny diameter, so red blood cells pass in single file, maximising contact time for exchange.

cards.front: What four features must be true of a Newton's Third Law pair of forces?
cards.answer: Equal in size / Opposite in direction / Same type of force / Act on different objects

cards.front: Why does a spacecraft drifting in deep space keep moving at the same velocity forever?
cards.answer: There is no friction or air resistance, so there is no resultant force to change its motion.

cards.front: Why does doubling a car's speed quadruple its braking distance?
cards.answer: Braking distance is proportional to speed squared, so doubling speed multiplies braking distance by four.

cards.front: Why does a book resting on a table stay stationary?
cards.answer: The normal contact force from the table exactly balances the book's weight, giving zero resultant force.

cards.front: Name the three main ways the lesson says consumer law impacts businesses.
cards.answer: Damage to reputation / Cost of returns and refunds / Cost of product recalls

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says businesses do to stay ahead of consumer law.
cards.answer: Build quality assurance into production / Train staff to handle returns politely / Use clear labelling and honest advertising / Track customer feedback to spot problems early
items: Train staff to handle returns politely
Use clear labelling and honest advertising
Track customer feedback to spot problems early

cards.front: Why did the 2013 Tesco horsemeat scandal wipe £300 million off its stock market value?
cards.answer: Customers switched to rivals after Tesco was exposed selling beef with horse DNA, breaching the 'as described' test.

cards.front: How did the Volkswagen 2015 emissions scandal breach consumer law principles?
cards.answer: Its diesel cars' official emissions data did not match their real performance, so they were not 'as described'.

cards.front: Name the three effects acid rain has, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Corrodes limestone/marble buildings / Kills trees / Acidifies lakes

cards.front: Name the four alternative approaches the lesson gives for reducing pollution.
