cards.answer: Switch to renewable energy sources / Use electric or hydrogen-powered vehicles / Improve fuel efficiency / Develop carbon capture and storage technologies
items: Develop carbon capture and storage technologies

cards.front: How does flue gas desulfurisation remove sulfur dioxide from power station emissions?
cards.answer: It reacts SO2 with calcium oxide or calcium carbonate, producing calcium sulfate.

cards.front: Why do soot particles cause global dimming?
cards.answer: Soot particles block sunlight from reaching the Earth's surface.

cards.front: Why did the AIDS crisis intensify prejudice against homosexuality in 1980s Britain?
cards.answer: Tabloid newspapers labelled AIDS a 'gay plague', deepening stigma against homosexuality from 1981 onwards.

cards.front: How does Winterson's setting show class intersecting with religion in the novel?
cards.answer: In a working-class northern community lacking material wealth, the church provides structure, meaning and social connection instead.

cards.front: Why does the church give Jeanette's mother power she wouldn't have elsewhere?
cards.answer: The church gives women like the mother a platform for authority they would not have in secular society.

cards.front: How should context like Section 28 be used when answering the prose exam question?
cards.answer: It must be embedded naturally within analysis of language and evidence, not written as a standalone bolt-on paragraph.

title: The Problem of Suffering in Islam
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: The lesson gives three atheist/humanist challenges to the 'life as test' response — name them.
cards.answer: Scale of suffering is disproportionate / Some predestined to fail the test by birth / Future paradise makes injustice ethically irrelevant
items: Some predestined to fail the test by birth
Future paradise makes injustice ethically irrelevant

cards.front: How do Muslims respond to the atheist challenge that the scale of suffering is too disproportionate for a fair test?
cards.answer: They argue the Day of Judgement is the ultimate measure of justice, and Allah's mercy and wisdom extend beyond human perception of any case.

cards.front: Why does prayer (du'a) help Muslims cope with suffering, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It lets Muslims bring their pain and needs directly to Allah, trusting he hears and may respond in ways serving their ultimate good.

cards.front: Why is charity considered a practical response to suffering rather than just accepting it?
cards.answer: Charity redistributes wealth, addressing the conditions that produce poverty and inequality rather than merely accepting the suffering they cause.

title: Profit Margins & Average Rate of Return
subject: business-ocr

cards.front: Name the two strengths of the ARR method the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Simple to calculate and explain / Uses the full life of a project
items: Uses the full life of a project

cards.front: Name the two weaknesses of the ARR method the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Ignores timing of returns / Ignores risk and relies on forecasts
items: Ignores risk and relies on forecasts

cards.front: Why does ARR treat a project paying profits in year 1 the same as one paying them in year 5?
cards.answer: Because ARR averages profit over the whole project, ignoring when the returns actually arrive.

cards.front: Why might a small high-street shop have a large gap between gross and net margin?
cards.answer: Because expensive shop rents and many staff create high overheads that eat into gross profit.

title: Form and Methods: Direct Address, Music and Comedy
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: How should an actor physically play one of Helen's asides to the audience?
cards.answer: With a clear turn towards the audience, a shift in eye-line away from other characters, and a conspiratorial, dry vocal tone.

cards.front: Why does calling A Taste of Honey 'straightforwardly naturalistic' miss half the picture?
cards.answer: Because its content feels realistic but it is staged through openly theatrical devices like songs, live music and direct address.

cards.front: Why did Delaney give her characters Standard English instead of phonetic dialect?
cards.answer: To challenge the stereotype that working-class characters must sound uneducated, letting sharp wit and pace carry the comedy.

cards.front: Why does a director stage the Act Two Scene One time-jump with dance rather than dialogue?
cards.answer: Because the stage directions mark the passing weeks through movement, letting the audience read time passing and domestic routine without words.

cards.front: Why does Meena reshape reality as a narrator instead of telling events straight?
cards.answer: She copes with the gap between who she is and who she wants to be by turning to mythology when she lacks history.

cards.front: Why does Syal present Anita as more than just a villain?
cards.answer: Anita's neglect, poverty, and dysfunctional family have shaped her into a survivor who uses toughness and manipulation as defence mechanisms.

cards.front: Why is Sam Lowbridge dangerous beyond just holding racist views?
cards.answer: He has charismatic authority among Tollington's young people, meaning he can mobilise others to act on his views.

cards.front: How does Mama Kumar typically respond to racism?
cards.answer: She responds with quiet dignity rather than confrontation, modelling a resilience Meena eventually learns to admire.

cards.front: Name the three inputs/outputs a D-type flip-flop has (2 outputs, 1 data input, plus clock).
cards.answer: D (data) input / CLK (clock) input / Q output / Q-bar output

cards.front: Why does Q1 toggle on the falling edge of Q0 in a 2-bit counter, not on Q0's rising edge?
cards.answer: Q1 is clocked by Q0's Q-bar output, and Q-bar rises (triggering Q1) exactly when Q0 falls.

cards.front: How does connecting Q-bar back to D make a D-type flip-flop toggle every clock cycle?
cards.answer: At each rising edge Q copies D, which is the opposite of Q, so Q flips to the opposite value every cycle.

cards.front: Why is a sensor's brief pulse better captured using a D-type flip-flop as a data latch?
cards.answer: The flip-flop latches onto D's value at the rising clock edge and holds it, so the brief pulse isn't lost before it can be read.

title: The Plains Nations: Beliefs and Way of Life
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name six distinct Plains nations mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Lakota Sioux / Cheyenne / Arapaho / Comanche / Crow / Pawnee

cards.front: Give four things Plains nations made from parts of the buffalo.
cards.answer: Meat for food / Sinew for bowstrings / Bone for tools / Bladder turned into water-skin

cards.front: Why did the spread of the horse in the 1700s transform Plains life?
cards.answer: It let nations that had once walked ride hundreds of miles, follow buffalo herds far more effectively and outrun rivals.

cards.front: Why did the Plains belief that land was shared clash with American settlers?
cards.answer: Settlers saw land as a fenced, owned rectangle to be claimed and inherited, while Plains nations used territory in common with no ownership.

cards.front: Name the six comparison operators SQL can use in a WHERE condition.
cards.answer: equal to = / not equal to <> / less than / less than or equal to =

cards.front: Name the five common mistakes the lesson lists when writing a query.
cards.answer: forgetting quotes around text / putting quotes around a number / writing clauses out of order / naming a field that doesn't exist / using > instead of >= for 'at least'
items: naming a field that doesn't exist

cards.front: Why does WHERE genre = Drama (without quotes) cause an error?
cards.answer: Without quotes the database reads Drama as a field name rather than a text value, so it can't compare it properly.

cards.front: Why does an OR condition always return the same number of records or more than an AND condition on the same two tests?
cards.answer: OR keeps a record if at least one condition is true, while AND needs both true, so OR is easier to satisfy.

title: Hosting a Major Event — During & After (Legacy)
subject: cambridge-nationals-sport-studies

cards.front: Name the five negative impacts the lesson gives for during a major sporting event.
cards.answer: Transport congestion / Noise and litter / Security costs / Terrorism risk / Displacement of local residents

cards.front: Why did grassroots cycling participation gains from London 2012 not last in the long term?
cards.answer: Funding cuts to grassroots sport in subsequent years undermined the participation gains inspired by Team GB's medal success.

cards.front: Why did most Athens 2004 venues become white elephants within a decade?
cards.answer: Greece's financial crisis made maintaining the expensive facilities impossible, so they fell into disrepair or sat empty.

cards.front: Why did Ed keep lying rather than admit he killed Wellington?
cards.answer: Admitting it would force him to explain why, and that explanation would destroy his version of reality.

cards.front: How does the play's staging show that Swindon feels safe for Christopher?
cards.answer: Through contained ensemble movement, familiar domestic projections, and Christopher moving with confidence.

title: Act 3: Hath Not a Jew Eyes?
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why does Shylock say he will be cruel to the Christians?
cards.answer: He argues Christians taught him cruelty, so he will copy and even improve on their example.

cards.front: Why is the 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech considered ambiguous?
cards.answer: It can be read as a plea for human sympathy or as a villain justifying revenge, and Shakespeare leaves both open.

cards.front: Why does hearing Shylock's grief through Solanio complicate our sympathy for him?
cards.answer: Solanio openly mocks Shylock, so his pain is filtered through the contempt of someone enjoying his suffering.

cards.front: How does the ring Portia gives Bassanio set up later events in the play?
cards.answer: She warns that parting with it will ruin their love, and Bassanio's vow never to remove it sets up Act 5's ring subplot.

cards.front: Name the five parts of the PECLC paragraph structure for comparison essays.
cards.answer: Point / Evidence (Poem 1) / Comment on method / Link to Poem 2 / Context

cards.front: Why should you pick a comparison poem with a contrasting approach rather than a very similar one?
cards.answer: Similarities give connection points but differences give analytical depth, so greater contrast makes the comparison richer.

cards.front: Why must AO2 be discussed alongside AO1 in the comparison essay?
cards.answer: AO2 (methods) is equally weighted with AO1 (ideas), so discussing methods is needed to access the top band.

cards.front: Name the four scientists (in order) whose models developed our understanding of atomic structure.
cards.answer: Dalton (solid sphere) / Thomson (plum pudding) / Rutherford (nuclear model) / Bohr (electron shells)

cards.front: Name the four natural sources of background radiation given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Radon gas from the ground / Cosmic rays / Food and drink / Building materials

cards.front: Why did Rutherford conclude the atom has a dense positive nucleus from the gold foil experiment?
cards.answer: A very few alpha particles bounced straight back, showing they hit something small, dense and positively charged.

cards.front: How did Bohr's model explain why atoms emit and absorb specific frequencies of radiation?
cards.answer: Electrons orbit only in fixed, specific energy levels, so energy changes occur in set amounts producing set frequencies.

title: Cnut, Emma & the North Sea Empire
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four rival claimants to the English throne after Edward the Confessor died childless in 1066.
cards.answer: Harold Godwinson / Edgar Aetheling / Harald Hardrada of Norway / William of Normandy

cards.front: Why did Aethelred's Danegeld payments fail to buy lasting peace from Viking raiders?
cards.answer: Each payment showed the Danes that raiding worked, encouraging a fresh fleet to come back for more.

cards.front: Why did Cnut govern England through Anglo-Saxon laws and English earls rather than as a foreign conqueror?
cards.answer: He cultivated the public image of a Christian English king, confirming Edgar's laws and endowing monasteries, while keeping Danish housecarls as his guard.

cards.front: Why was a personal union like Cnut's North Sea Empire fragile?
cards.answer: It depended on one life, so when Cnut died his sons squabbled and the empire fell apart within seven years.

cards.front: Name the four main actions Ariel performs for Prospero, as listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Creates the storm / Leads Ferdinand to Miranda with a song / Appears as a harpy to terrify the nobles / Stages the wedding masque
items: Leads Ferdinand to Miranda with a song
Appears as a harpy to terrify the nobles

cards.front: Name the three character foil pairs the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Ferdinand vs Caliban / Gonzalo vs Antonio / Ariel vs Caliban

cards.front: Why does Ariel's line about becoming 'tender' shame Prospero into showing mercy?
cards.answer: A non-human spirit shows more compassion than Prospero, reminding him what humanity should mean and pushing him to choose virtue over vengeance.

cards.front: Why does Caliban's line 'my profit on't is I know how to curse' encapsulate the colonial dynamic?
cards.answer: The coloniser's 'gift' of language becomes the weapon the colonised person turns back against them.

cards.front: Name the four environmental impacts of business activity given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Traffic congestion / Noise and air pollution / Waste sent to landfill / Use of scarce resources

cards.front: Why did the Volkswagen dieselgate scandal cost the firm so much long-term?
cards.answer: It cost over thirty billion dollars in fines and lost sales and damaged its brand for years.

cards.front: Name the two biblical texts most frequently cited by Christians opposing same-sex relationships.
cards.answer: Leviticus 20:13 / 1 Timothy 1:8-10

cards.front: Why do critics argue Leviticus 20:13 should not be simply applied to same-sex relationships today?
cards.answer: The same Holiness Code forbids things like eating shellfish, so consistency requires reading it in its ancient context.

cards.front: Why do some Hindus see same-sex relationships as conflicting with dharma?
cards.answer: Traditional teaching links the householder ashrama to sexual activity aimed at procreation and continuing family lineage, part of one's dharma.

cards.front: Why does Reform Judaism affirm same-sex relationships despite Leviticus prohibitions?
cards.answer: It grounds its position in human dignity (kavod ha-beriyot) and the commandment to love one's neighbour, reinterpreting tradition accordingly.

title: Akhirah: Life After Death and the Day of Judgement
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four features of the Day of Judgement described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Deeds recorded by Kiraman Katibin / Mizan weighs good and bad deeds / Record given in right or left hand / Sirat bridge crossed over hell
items: Mizan weighs good and bad deeds
Record given in right or left hand

cards.front: How does entry to Jannah work according to Islamic teaching?
cards.answer: Entry to Jannah is by Allah's mercy, not deeds alone — deeds only indicate faith, but Allah makes the final decision.

cards.front: Why do Sunni scholars generally believe Jahannam is not eternal for all its inhabitants?
cards.answer: Non-believers remain permanently, but sinning believers may be punished temporarily before entering Jannah by Allah's mercy.

title: Selma and the Voting Rights Act, 1965
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four devices the lesson gives that kept Black Americans off the electoral roll in the Deep South.
cards.answer: Arbitrary literacy tests / Poll taxes / Requirement to bring a registered voter to vouch for you / Threat of being sacked, evicted or beaten
items: Requirement to bring a registered voter to vouch for you
Threat of being sacked, evicted or beaten

cards.front: Why did the killing of Jimmie Lee Jackson lead to the Selma to Montgomery march?
cards.answer: Out of grief and anger at Jackson's death, the SCLC announced a march from Selma to Montgomery to deliver a petition to Governor Wallace.

cards.front: Why did the deaths of Jimmie Lee Jackson and James Reeb generate such different reactions?
cards.answer: Reeb's death, unlike Jackson's, produced national headlines and presidential condolences, a contrast King spoke about with honesty.

cards.front: Why did the third Selma to Montgomery march in March 1965 go ahead successfully?
cards.answer: Federal Judge Frank Johnson lifted the restraining order and the march was legally protected by federalised National Guard and US Army troops.

cards.front: Name the four occupation zones Germany was divided into in 1945.
cards.answer: American zone / British zone / French zone / Soviet zone

cards.front: Why did Stalin impose the Berlin Blockade in June 1948?
cards.answer: He saw the West's new Deutschmark currency in West Berlin as a threat and wanted to force the West to abandon Berlin or accept Soviet terms.

cards.front: Why was the mass emigration of East Germans in the 1950s a serious problem for the GDR?
cards.answer: It drained skilled workers and professionals, threatening the economy and stability, which led to the decision to build the Berlin Wall.

cards.front: Name the four natural methods of pain relief the lesson gives that carry no medical risk.
cards.answer: Water (birthing pool) / Breathing and relaxation techniques / Massage / Hypnobirthing

cards.front: Why might a caesarean section be planned in advance rather than done as an emergency?
cards.answer: It is planned when there is a known risk, such as placenta praevia or a breech presentation.

cards.front: Why can forceps rotate a baby's head but ventouse cannot be used in some positions?
cards.answer: Forceps are metal instruments that cup the head and can rotate it, while ventouse relies on suction so cannot be used for very premature babies or certain positions.

cards.front: Name the five OCR activity settings where hazards must be identified for injury prevention.
cards.answer: Sports hall / Fitness centre / Playing field / Artificial outdoor areas / Swimming pool

cards.front: Why does bending at the waist with a rounded back increase the risk of lower-back injury when lifting equipment?
cards.answer: It transfers compressive force directly to the intervertebral discs and lumbar vertebrae, increasing the risk of disc herniation.

cards.front: Why is a spotter needed when performing a heavy lift like the bench press in a fitness centre?
cards.answer: Without a spotter there is no one to assist if the lifter fails, increasing the risk of injury from an uncontrolled heavy weight.

title: Functionalist and Subcultural Theories of Crime
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name Merton's five modes of adaptation to strain.
cards.answer: Conformity / Innovation / Ritualism / Retreatism / Rebellion

cards.front: Why did Merton say working-class people face greater strain than others?
cards.answer: They are socialised into the same success goals as everyone else but face greater structural barriers to legitimate means of achieving them.

cards.front: How does Cohen explain why working-class boys form delinquent sub-cultures?
cards.answer: Cultural deprivation and poor educational prospects cause status frustration, so boys collectively invert mainstream values to gain status instead.

cards.front: Why is Cohen's theory seen as adding something Merton's theory lacks?
cards.answer: It explains non-instrumental crime committed for status, thrill or group belonging rather than for economic gain.

title: Carpetbaggers, the Klan and the End of Reconstruction
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three groups Congress passed the Enforcement Acts against, and what did each act (1870, Feb 1871, April 1871) do?
cards.answer: 1870: made interfering with voting a federal crime / Feb 1871: put federal supervisors over congressional elections / April 1871 (KKK Act): allowed troops, suspended habeas corpus, allowed conspiracy charges
items: 1870: made interfering with voting a federal crime
Feb 1871: put federal supervisors over congressional elections
April 1871 (KKK Act): allowed troops, suspended habeas corpus, allowed conspiracy charges

cards.front: Why did federal will to protect Black civil rights in the South fade after 1873?
cards.answer: An economic depression sharpened Northern concern about taxes, turning Republican voters against further Southern intervention, alongside the Slaughter-House Cases ruling.

cards.front: How did the collapse of federal enforcement lead to the Jim Crow system?
cards.answer: With federal troops withdrawn after 1877, Southern state legislatures used literacy tests, poll taxes and grandfather clauses to disfranchise and segregate Black voters.

cards.front: Name the four workshop tools/methods described for cutting different materials (scalpel, foam board, corrugated card, circles).
cards.answer: Scalpel with metal safety rule for straight lines / Long blade or foam-board cutter for foam board / Strong craft knife for corrugated card / Circle/compass cutter for circular cuts
items: Scalpel with metal safety rule for straight lines
Long blade or foam-board cutter for foam board
Strong craft knife for corrugated card

cards.front: Why must a steel safety rule be used instead of a plastic rule when cutting board with a scalpel?
cards.answer: Cutting against a plastic rule risks the blade jumping into the fingers, so a steel rule is mandatory for safe, accurate cuts.

cards.front: Why is corrugated card cut with a craft knife rather than scissors?
cards.answer: The fluted core compresses under scissor pressure, producing a ragged edge, so a strong craft knife gives a cleaner cut.

cards.front: Name the three main terms the Statute of the Jewry of 1275 imposed on Jews.
cards.answer: Ban on lending at interest / Order to take up trade or crafts / Larger yellow felt badge from age seven
items: Order to take up trade or crafts
Larger yellow felt badge from age seven

cards.front: Why did Edward I no longer need Jewish moneylenders by the 1270s?
cards.answer: He turned to Italian bankers like the Riccardi, who could lend on a far larger scale and were not seen as religiously suspect.

cards.front: Why did Parliament agree to the expulsion of the Jews in 1290?
cards.answer: Edward offered removal of a resented community in exchange for a huge taxation grant of about £116,000.

title: Source skills for Spitalfields and Empire
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four successive uses of the Brick Lane Jamme Masjid building.
cards.answer: Huguenot chapel (1743) / Methodist chapel / Synagogue (c.1897) / Mosque (1976)

cards.front: Why is Charles Booth's poverty map data not fully objective evidence of poverty in Spitalfields?
cards.answer: The maps reflect Booth's own assumptions, mixing admiration for Jewish immigrants' industry with Victorian class prejudices.

cards.front: Why is Henry Mayhew's journalism valuable despite being shaped by his own perspective?
cards.answer: It gives voice to individuals like Irish costermongers and casual labourers who left no other written record.

title: End of French Rule: Dien Bien Phu and Geneva
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the six key terms of the Geneva Accords, July 1954.
cards.answer: France withdraws from Indochina / Vietnam divided at 17th parallel / Vietminh regroup north under Ho Chi Minh / Non-communist forces regroup south / Cambodia and Laos become independent neutral kingdoms / Reunification elections held by July 1956
items: Vietminh regroup north under Ho Chi Minh
Cambodia and Laos become independent neutral kingdoms

cards.front: Why did Navarre choose Dien Bien Phu for his 1953 operation against the Vietminh?
cards.answer: He wanted to lure the Vietminh into open battle where French firepower would prevail, assuming Giap could not bring artillery to the hills.

cards.front: How did the Vietminh manage to bombard the French base at Dien Bien Phu?
cards.answer: Porters carried Chinese-supplied artillery through the jungle and dug it into reverse slopes hidden from French air power.

title: Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century crime: highwaymen, smugglers and protest
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What four changes does the lesson give for the collapse of highway robbery by the 1830s-1840s?
cards.answer: Better-lit, busier turnpike roads / Banking reforms (notes and cheques) / Mounted patrols from Bow Street Runners / Railways moving traffic off roads
items: Mounted patrols from Bow Street Runners

cards.front: Why were the Tolpuddle Martyrs prosecuted under an old 1797 oath law rather than for forming a union?
cards.answer: Trade unions had been legal since 1824, so the government used the obscure Unlawful Oaths Act, aimed at naval mutineers, to prosecute them instead.

cards.front: Why did local communities in coastal counties often support smugglers despite the law?
cards.answer: High customs duties made smuggled tea, brandy and tobacco cheaper, so whole villages benefited and saw it as dodging unfair taxation.

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that cause wage differentials between jobs.
cards.answer: Skill and qualifications / Responsibility and decision-making / Danger and unpleasant conditions / Experience

cards.front: Name the four factors the lesson gives that shift the supply of labour.
cards.answer: Size of the working population / Skills and qualifications needed / Non-wage factors like job security / Trade union membership

cards.front: Why might a minimum wage set well above equilibrium in a highly competitive labour market cause unemployment?
cards.answer: Firms face higher labour costs, so they reduce their workforce, cut hours, or delay hiring in response.

cards.front: Why do some jobs like teaching or social work attract workers even at lower wages?
cards.answer: They offer non-wage benefits such as social status, interesting work, flexible hours, or job security.

title: North vs South: the Road to the Civil War
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four key dates the lesson gives on the path to civil war.
cards.answer: 1820 Missouri Compromise / 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act / 1857 Dred Scott decision / 1860 election and 1861 Fort Sumter

cards.front: Why did the Mexican Cession of 1848 create a problem for the Missouri Compromise?
cards.answer: It added a vast new territory that the 1820 Compromise, written only for the Louisiana Purchase, could not cover.

cards.front: Why did Lincoln's election in November 1860 trigger southern secession?
cards.answer: He won without carrying a single southern state, showing the South had lost political power, so South Carolina seceded within six weeks.

cards.front: Name the four functions the lesson gives for the Narrator's role in the play.
cards.answer: Foreshadowing / Dramatic irony / Moral commentary / Atmosphere

cards.front: Why does Russell present Mrs Lyons as both a victim and a perpetrator?
cards.answer: Her desire for a child and loneliness are genuine, but her wealth lets her manipulate and exploit Mrs Johnstone without facing consequences.

cards.front: How does Eddie's kindness relate to his class privilege?
cards.answer: Eddie can afford to be generous and helpful to Mickey and Linda because he has never had to struggle financially.

cards.front: Why does Russell use Sammy's violence and crime in the play?
cards.answer: To show what happens when working-class young people have no opportunities, no guidance, and no hope.

cards.front: Name the seven sacraments recognised by Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
cards.answer: Baptism / Confirmation / Eucharist / Penance (Reconciliation) / Anointing of the Sick / Holy Orders / Matrimony

cards.front: What six things does the structure of the Lord's Prayer include?
cards.answer: Address to God as Father in heaven / Hallowing of his name / Petition for God's kingdom to come / Request for daily bread / Request for forgiveness / Protection from temptation and evil

cards.front: Why do Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox Christians baptise infants rather than waiting for a declaration of faith?
cards.answer: Because in their theology baptism washes away original sin and incorporates the person into the Body of Christ regardless of age.

cards.front: Why is Christian worship strikingly different from Islamic Salah in style?
cards.answer: Salah is highly ritualised with fixed times, postures and Arabic recitation, while Christian worship varies from Pentecostal free-flowing to formal Catholic Mass.

cards.front: What conditions did the Petrograd Soviet demand before it would not oppose the new Provisional Government?
cards.answer: Civil liberties / Amnesty for political prisoners / Democratic elections

cards.front: Why did Nicholas II abdicate for his son Alexei as well as himself?
cards.answer: Because he could not bear to be parted from his haemophiliac son.

cards.front: Why did the front commanders advise Nicholas II to abdicate on 1 March 1917?
cards.answer: They told him the army would not keep fighting for a regime that had lost the capital.

cards.front: Why did the killings at Znamenskaya Square on 26 February 1917 end up breaking the regime rather than stopping the protests?
cards.answer: Troops firing on protesters sickened soldiers, leading regiments like the Volynsky to mutiny instead of obey.

title: Global Non-English-Language Film: Representation in Focus
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five non-English-language films studied for representation, with their countries.
cards.answer: Tsotsi - South Africa / The Wave - Germany / Wadjda - Saudi Arabia / Girlhood - France / The Farewell - China/US

cards.front: How does Wadjda give its protagonist agency as a 'subject who looks' rather than an object of the gaze?
cards.answer: Point-of-view shots, like her looking at the bicycle in the shop window, and low-angle observation shots show her actively looking at the world.

cards.front: How does the framing and editing in The Wave's classroom 'unity' sequence represent fascist conformity as seductive?
cards.answer: The frame tightens into close-ups, the palette warms, and editing quickens as the class conforms, drawing the spectator into the energy before dangers are clear.

cards.front: Why does Lulu Wang use slow static takes in warm interior light in The Farewell?
cards.answer: To hold family tensions inside a single room and let the spectator sit inside the dynamics rather than being rushed through by plot.

title: Selection, Combination and the Construction of Reality
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: How does camera angle in a news photograph shape meaning, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Eye level implies equality, while a low angle implies power.

cards.front: Why might audiences decode a tabloid front page differently from its preferred meaning?
cards.answer: Audiences bring their own experience, values and knowledge to reading, so they don't always accept the intended meaning.

cards.front: How does a broadsheet's coverage of a demonstration differ from a tabloid's, according to the worked example?
cards.answer: The broadsheet selects a wide crowd shot with an academic quote, while the tabloid selects a close-up confrontation with a politician's warning.

cards.front: Name the three processes the lesson says shape the meanings audiences take from media products.
cards.answer: Selection / Combination / Exclusion

title: Ethical Behaviour, Festivals and Sangha Practice
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four items placed on a Buddhist home shrine mentioned in the lesson, besides the Buddha image.
cards.answer: Candles / Incense / Flowers / Water offerings

cards.front: Name the three sections of the Eightfold Path that sila forms part of.
cards.answer: Morality (sila) / Wisdom (panna) / Meditation (samadhi)

cards.front: Why might a committed Buddhist avoid a job like weapons manufacturing or slaughterhouse work?
cards.answer: Because the first precept of non-harming (ahimsa) means avoiding occupations that cause harm to living beings.

cards.front: Why does living by the Five Precepts present a daily challenge for Triratna Buddhists in Western culture?
cards.answer: Because Western consumer culture normalises alcohol, meat-eating and sexual permissiveness, conflicting with the precepts.

title: Life After Death and the Messiah
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: According to the lesson's Key Fact, what three ideas are at the centre of Jewish teaching on life after death?
cards.answer: Soul's continued existence in olam ha-ba / Judgement by God according to deeds / Future resurrection when the Messiah comes
items: Soul's continued existence in olam ha-ba
Judgement by God according to deeds
Future resurrection when the Messiah comes

cards.front: Name three criteria the lesson says a personal Messiah must fulfil according to Orthodox Judaism.
cards.answer: Rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem / Gather all Jews to the land of Israel / Bring an era of universal peace
items: Gather all Jews to the land of Israel
Bring an era of universal peace

cards.front: Why does belief in judgement encourage Jews to live ethically?
cards.answer: Because knowing that actions matter to God and have consequences beyond this life motivates people to behave morally.

cards.front: Why does Orthodox Judaism see the resurrection of the body as God's ultimate vindication of the righteous?
cards.answer: Because it means those who suffered unjustly in this world will be restored by God.

cards.front: Name the four escalating acts of bullying the group did to Adam before the fall.
cards.answer: Made him eat leaves / Hit him / Burned him with cigarettes / Made him steal vodka

cards.front: How does Phil's cover-up plan use an innocent postman to protect the group?
cards.answer: Cathy gets a postman to handle Adam's jumper so his DNA is on it, and he is then arrested and picked out by Brian.

cards.front: Why does Mark and Jan's retelling of Adam's fall come out fragmented and contradictory?
cards.answer: Their broken, interrupting speech mirrors the group's inability to process the horror because they cannot face what it means.

title: The Origin and Development of Life
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four groups of vertebrates in the order they first appear in the fossil record (fish first, then three more).
cards.answer: Fish / Amphibians / Reptiles / Mammals and birds

cards.front: What are the two pieces of evidence found at Lucy's skeleton that show both upright walking and tree-climbing?
cards.answer: Shape of knee and pelvis / Curved finger bones

cards.front: Why has the deep-ocean black smoker hypothesis for the origin of life gained support over surface hydrothermal pools?
cards.answer: Early Earth had no ozone layer, so intense UV radiation hit the surface, while deep-sea environments were protected.

cards.front: Why doesn't finding a new fossil that extends a group's known range further back in time contradict evolution?
cards.answer: It fills a gap that was always expected to exist, since the fossil record always underestimates biodiversity.

cards.front: Name the four rubric errors on the poetry paper that cap an answer regardless of writing quality.
cards.answer: Answering on only one poem in part (a) / Choosing a part (b) poem from a different cluster / Re-using the part (a) poem in part (b) / Comparing poems in part (b)
items: Answering on only one poem in part (a)
Choosing a part (b) poem from a different cluster
Re-using the part (a) poem in part (b)

cards.front: What are the four weekly drills in the timed practice plan for the poetry hour?
cards.answer: Untimed grid practice on an unfamiliar poem / Thirty minutes on part (a) alone, twice / Thirty minutes on part (b) alone, twice / The full poetry hour, both parts, twice
items: Untimed grid practice on an unfamiliar poem
Thirty minutes on part (a) alone, twice
Thirty minutes on part (b) alone, twice
The full poetry hour, both parts, twice

cards.front: Why is grid practice described as the highest-value drill for the poetry paper?
cards.answer: Because filling a comparison grid against a cluster poem builds the skill both parts of the paper depend on.

cards.front: Why should quotations on this paper be kept short and embedded rather than long?
cards.answer: Four well-placed words prove more than a copied stanza and leave room for analysis that earns the mark.

title: After Victory: Frontier and Tax Tensions, 1763–64
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Why did General Amherst's actions help spark Pontiac's Rebellion?
cards.answer: Amherst stopped the French custom of giving diplomatic gifts and let settlers push aggressively into former French forts.

cards.front: Why did frontier and tax grievances reinforce each other after 1763?
cards.answer: The Proclamation Act stopped westward settlement, the army enforcing it was funded partly by the Sugar Act, so each grievance made the other look worse.

cards.front: Why did the Sugar Act hit New England merchants harder despite halving the molasses duty?
cards.answer: It tightened enforcement, requiring detailed paperwork and moving smuggling trials to vice-admiralty courts, ending the old habit of evading tax entirely.

cards.front: What two decisions did British ministers make after 1763 that later looked like provocations to colonists?
cards.answer: Stationing 10,000 troops in the colonies / Taxing colonial trade more vigorously

cards.front: What are the three strands the 19th-century novel question assesses (AO1, AO2, AO3)?
cards.answer: Critical response with well-chosen references / Analysis of Dickens's methods (language, structure, form) / Understanding of Victorian context
items: Analysis of Dickens's methods (language, structure, form)

cards.front: What four parts make up the essay structure for a Great Expectations extract question?
cards.answer: Introduction stating your argument / Extract paragraphs analysing language and structure / Whole-novel paragraphs with wider references / Brief conclusion linking to Dickens's purpose
items: Extract paragraphs analysing language and structure
Brief conclusion linking to Dickens's purpose

cards.front: How does the conditional structure in Pip's 'If I could have kept him away by paying money' show calculated intent?
cards.answer: The 'If I could have… I certainly would have' structure shows this was a considered willingness, not a passing thought.

cards.front: Why does Dickens make the reader feel Joe's hurt alongside Pip's embarrassment in the Joe's Visit scene?
cards.answer: To force the reader to judge a class system that makes people ashamed of their own families.

title: Religious Experience, the Design Argument and the Cosmological Argument
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What are Aquinas's First Three Ways, in order?
cards.answer: Argument from motion / Argument from causation / Argument from contingency

cards.front: What three features of the natural world does the design argument say point to an intelligent designer?
cards.answer: Order / Complexity / Beauty

cards.front: Why do Humanists say bad design in nature challenges the design argument?
cards.answer: Vestigial organs, disease, predation and extinction suggest that if there is a designer, they are not all-loving and all-powerful.

cards.front: How do Catholics respond to Dawkins's claim that evolution removes the need for a designer?
cards.answer: Evolution is compatible with Catholic teaching, and the predictable laws governing it still point to a rational mind, a lawgiver, behind nature.

cards.front: Name the seven sacraments recognised by Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
cards.answer: Baptism / Confirmation / Eucharist / Penance (Reconciliation) / Anointing of the Sick / Holy Orders / Matrimony

cards.front: What six elements does the structure of the Lord's Prayer include, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Address to God as Father / Hallowing of his name / Petition for God's kingdom / Request for daily bread / Request for forgiveness / Protection from temptation and evil

cards.front: Why do Catholics and Anglicans baptise infants while Baptists baptise only believers?
cards.answer: Catholics/Anglicans see baptism as washing away original sin, while Baptists require a personal declaration of faith first.

cards.front: Why do some Christians prefer non-liturgical worship over liturgical worship?
cards.answer: Because it has no fixed script, allowing the Spirit to guide the service rather than following a predetermined order.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says coasts erode.
cards.answer: Hydraulic action / Abrasion / Attrition / Solution

cards.front: Name the sequence of five landforms the lesson gives from headland erosion, ending offshore.
cards.answer: Crack / Cave / Arch / Stack / Stump

cards.front: Why do bays and headlands form along coasts with alternating bands of hard and soft rock?
cards.answer: Where bands of hard and soft rock meet the sea at right angles, soft rock erodes faster forming bays, leaving hard rock as headlands.

cards.front: Why does a spit like Spurn Head curve into a recurve at its end?
cards.answer: Longshore drift keeps carrying material past a sudden change in the coastline, and wind/wave direction changes bend the tip landward.

title: Investigative Geology: Maps, Fieldwork and Practical Skills
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: What four appearances of a boundary crossing a valley does the rule of Vs describe?
cards.answer: V points upstream, sharper than contours (dip upstream) / V follows contours pointing upstream (horizontal strata) / V points downstream (dip downstream) / No V, straight line (vertical strata)
items: V points upstream, sharper than contours (dip upstream)
V follows contours pointing upstream (horizontal strata)

cards.front: Why do alternating sandstones and mudstones in a graphic log suggest a fluctuating energy environment like a tidal flat?
cards.answer: Because the changing rock types record changing energy conditions during deposition, such as a tidal flat or delta margin.

cards.front: Why might a rose diagram with four petals suggest two conjugate joint sets?
cards.answer: Because four petals show measurements clustering in two opposite pairs of directions, indicating two joint sets linked to a tectonic stress field.

cards.front: Name the three significant acts Scrooge performs in Stave 5 that reverse his Stave 1 failures.
cards.answer: Buys the largest turkey for the Cratchits / Gives to the charity collectors he refused / Goes to Fred's Christmas dinner
items: Buys the largest turkey for the Cratchits
Gives to the charity collectors he refused

cards.front: Why does Dickens make the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come silent, only pointing?
cards.answer: The silence forces Scrooge and the reader to interpret the visions themselves, making the horror feel personal and inescapable.

cards.front: Why does Dickens show thieves stealing from the dead man's body at Old Joe's shop?
cards.answer: To show the ultimate degradation of a life devoted only to money, where even your possessions are stripped away by people who care nothing for you.

cards.front: Why is Scrooge's gravestone the climax of his transformation in Stave 4?
cards.answer: Seeing his own name makes Scrooge beg to change, showing genuine repentance and commitment to a new way of living, not just a Christmas promise.

cards.front: Why is a reaction exothermic overall in terms of bond energy?
cards.answer: More energy is released when new bonds form than is needed to break the original bonds.

cards.front: Why is a reaction endothermic overall in terms of bond energy?
cards.answer: More energy is needed to break the original bonds than is released when new bonds form.

cards.front: Name the three townspeople in Crythin Gifford whose strange reactions build the 'wall of silence' around Kipps.
cards.answer: Mr Jerome, the land agent / Sam Daily, the local businessman / The landlord at the inn

cards.front: Why does hardly anyone attend Mrs Drablow's funeral?
cards.answer: Because Mrs Drablow was feared or avoided by the community, showing she was an unpopular or dreaded figure.

cards.front: How does pathetic fallacy build unease as Kipps travels to Crythin Gifford?
cards.answer: The train journey shifts from comfort to unease as the bleak, flat marshes, grey sky and biting wind foreshadow the horror awaiting him.

cards.front: Why does the community's silence make the townspeople complicit in the Woman in Black's deaths?
cards.answer: Their fear leads them never to warn outsiders like Kipps, so their silence allows each new death to happen.

cards.front: Name the five imperfect tense verbs given in the lesson for describing what celebrities used to be like.
cards.answer: era (used to be) / tenía (used to have) / llevaba (used to wear) / hacía (used to do) / iba (used to go)

cards.front: Name four positive influence phrases the lesson gives for describing a celebrity's good influence.
cards.answer: tiene buenos valores / ayuda a los pobres / dona dinero a buenas causas / habla sobre problemas de salud mental
items: habla sobre problemas de salud mental

cards.front: How do you justify saying a celebrity is a good role model in Spanish, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Use porque plus a personality adjective plus evidence, e.g. 'porque es generosa y dona dinero a buenas causas'.

cards.front: Why might some people think celebrities are a bad influence on young people, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because they can promote an unrealistic image, encourage materialism and only care about money.

cards.front: Why did Miss Emily say Hailsham's experiment ultimately failed?
cards.answer: Society did not want to give up its cure for illness, so it refused to treat clones as fully human despite Hailsham's aims.

cards.front: How does Kathy's final reflection about 'the people we save' challenge the reader?
cards.answer: She suggests clones' limited, loss-filled lives differ from normal human lives only in degree, not kind, forcing readers to recognise themselves in her.

cards.front: Name the nine vocal skills the specification gives for performers' vocal interpretation of character.
cards.answer: Accent / Volume / Pitch / Timing / Pace / Intonation / Phrasing / Emotional range / Delivery of lines

cards.front: Name the eight physical skills the specification gives for performers' physical interpretation of character.
cards.answer: Build / Age / Height / Facial features / Movement / Posture / Gesture / Facial expression

cards.front: Why must a pause be explained in terms of what it communicates at that specific moment, not just as creating tension?
cards.answer: A pause is a deliberate choice that can show guilt, calculation, fear or contempt, so its meaning must be specified.

cards.front: How does facing full-back to the audience usually function in proscenium staging?
cards.answer: It is rare and usually signals a powerful dramatic moment of withdrawal or concealment.

title: Glacial Deposition & a Glaciated Upland: The Lake District
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four main types of moraine described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Lateral moraine / Medial moraine / Terminal moraine / Recessional moraine

cards.front: Name three sources of rock debris a glacier collects and carries, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Fragments shattered by freeze-thaw / Blocks ripped out by plucking / Material scraped off by abrasion / Rock falls onto the glacier's surface
items: Rock falls onto the glacier's surface

cards.front: Why does a glacier deposit the material it is carrying?
cards.answer: When the glacier melts, at its snout or as the climate warms, it loses the energy needed to carry its load.

cards.front: How does medial moraine form?
cards.answer: Two valley glaciers merge, so their lateral moraines meet and form a dark streak of debris down the centre of the combined glacier.

cards.front: Name the four types of buildings the lesson gives that stood around the Pompeii forum besides the Temple of Jupiter.
cards.answer: Colonnaded walkway / Basilica / Comitium / Offices for magistrates

cards.front: Name the three Italian towns the lesson uses as evidence for Roman city life.
cards.answer: Pompeii / Herculaneum / Ostia

cards.front: Why is Ostia useful evidence for Roman town planning even though it wasn't destroyed like Pompeii?
cards.answer: Because Ostia kept being occupied and altered, it shows how a Roman city evolved and grew over time.

cards.front: How did most ordinary residents of Pompeii get their water?
cards.answer: They collected it from public fountains placed at regular intervals along the streets, fed by the aqueduct system.

title: Context: Tudor Propaganda & the History Play
subject: english-literature-eduqas

cards.front: Why did Shakespeare add the Archbishop's long Salic Law speech, which isn't in Holinshed's account?
cards.answer: To make the Archbishop look self-serving, rather than presenting Henry's claim to France as straightforward.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare change Holinshed's account of the battle of Agincourt to add ambiguity?
cards.answer: He adds the common soldiers' doubts and Henry's agonised soliloquy the night before, unlike Holinshed's clear victory.

cards.front: Name the four anthology poems this lesson connects to 'Dusting the Phone'.
cards.answer: Poem for My Love (June Jordan) / The Perseverance (Raymond Antrobus) / Warming Her Pearls (Carol Ann Duffy) / Looking at Your Hands (Martin Carter)

cards.front: Why does Kay repeat 'Sirens' at the end of both lines about the phone ringing and staying silent?
cards.answer: The epistrophe makes both ringing and silence feel equally alarming, showing logic has broken down for the anxious speaker.

cards.front: How does the use of tercets and enjambment together reflect the speaker's state of mind?
cards.answer: The tercets suggest control, but enjambment lets thoughts spill past line breaks, mirroring her racing, uncontrollable thoughts.

cards.front: Name the four examples the lesson gives of duality beyond Jekyll himself (including Jekyll's own claim).
cards.answer: Jekyll's own split nature / Utterson's austere yet tolerant character / London respectable by day, sinister by night / The narrative's mystery concealing a confession
items: London respectable by day, sinister by night
The narrative's mystery concealing a confession

cards.front: Name the four secrets/silences the lesson lists as saturating the novella.
cards.answer: Jekyll hides Hyde / Utterson hides his suspicions / Enfield hides what he saw / Lanyon's letter sealed until death

cards.front: Why does Hyde emerge with such explosive, disproportionate violence?
cards.answer: Decades of suppressed impulse compressed desire instead of eliminating it, so it erupts violently when released.

cards.front: How does Stevenson use the sample paragraph's evidence to link Hyde's body to Darwinian anxiety?
cards.answer: Hyde's simian imagery and 'fury' suggest evolutionary regression, expressing Victorian fear that a primitive animal self lies beneath civilised behaviour.

cards.front: Name the three tiers of oarsmen on a trireme, from lowest to highest bank.
cards.answer: Thalamites (lowest bank) / Zygites (middle bank) / Thranites (upper bank)

cards.front: Name the two main trireme attack techniques the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Diekplous (through the line, then ram) / Periplous (round the flank/rear)

cards.front: How did Themistocles trick Xerxes into sending his fleet into the strait at Salamis?
cards.answer: He sent a false message via a slave saying the Greeks were fleeing, prompting Xerxes to order his fleet to block the strait overnight.

cards.front: Why couldn't the Persian fleet manoeuvre effectively once trapped in the strait at Salamis?
cards.answer: The strait was too narrow for their large numbers to deploy, and their rowers were exhausted from rowing all night while the Greeks had rested.

title: Nazi social policy — women, youth, churches
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four Nazi youth organisations that divided German children by age and sex.
cards.answer: Jungvolk (boys 10-14) / Hitler Youth (boys 14-18) / Jungmadel (younger girls) / BDM (girls 14-18)

cards.front: Name the three elite Nazi school networks set up for training future leaders.
cards.answer: Napola schools / Adolf Hitler Schools / Ordensburgen castles

cards.front: Why were women pushed out of the professions such as teaching, medicine and the civil service after 1933?
cards.answer: Nazi ideology said women's role was motherhood and domestic life, so they were squeezed out of professional jobs by law.

cards.front: How did the Reich Church try to Nazify Protestant Christianity?
cards.answer: It merged regional Lutheran churches under Nazi influence, removed the Old Testament, and replaced crosses with swastikas in some services.

cards.front: What four things do managers use revenue, cost and profit figures for, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Set prices sensibly / Spot problems early / Talk credibly to lenders and investors / Decide which product lines to keep
items: Talk credibly to lenders and investors
Decide which product lines to keep

cards.front: Why does a market-stall sandwich seller face a low-fixed/high-variable cost structure?
cards.answer: Stall rent is low but bread, fillings and packaging cost real money per sandwich sold.

cards.front: Why can a business with £1 million revenue still be making a loss?
cards.answer: Revenue is the gross figure before costs are deducted, so if costs exceed revenue the business loses money.

cards.front: Why did Oakleaf Coffee's profit turn into a loss when sales dropped from 800 to 400 lattes?
cards.answer: Variable costs fell with lower sales but fixed costs stayed at £1,200, so revenue no longer covered total costs.

title: Context: Bovell, Frantic Assembly and Suburban Australia
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the six ordinary objects the lesson gives for the Price family's garden.
cards.answer: a shed / a wading pool / rose bushes / a lemon tree / a garden hose / a wheelbarrow

cards.front: Name the three places, besides the Hallett Cove garden, that the action of the play travels to.
cards.answer: a railway platform in Berlin / Vancouver / the airport

cards.front: Why did Bovell write four children's monologues even though Graham told him not to write for movement?
cards.answer: Bovell recognised that a more physical theatre realisation would suit the Price children, so he wrote monologues for Graham to respond to.

cards.front: Why does the play use the gum tree and Bob's rose bushes as a contrast?
cards.answer: The gum tree is native, untended and permanent, while Bob's roses are cultivated, fragile and demanding, so the contrast recurs in design and staging.

cards.front: Name the three instances of eavesdropping that drive the plot of Much Ado, given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Gulling scenes tricking Benedick and Beatrice / Claudio and Don Pedro witnessing the window scene / The Watch overhearing Borachio's confession
items: Gulling scenes tricking Benedick and Beatrice
Claudio and Don Pedro witnessing the window scene

cards.front: How does the play's title pun connect to its theme of unreliable perception?
cards.answer: It puns on nothing/noting, showing characters trust what they see over what they know, making language and perception unreliable.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare give Dogberry and the Watch a dual comic function in the play?
cards.answer: They make the audience laugh while creating agonising irony, since the truth is known but not yet delivered.

cards.front: Name the five tools the lesson gives for sustainably managing coral reefs.
cards.answer: Marine Protected Areas / Mooring buoys / Visitor caps / Education briefings / Tourist taxes

cards.front: How does wetland restoration at the Great Fen reduce flood risk downstream?
cards.answer: Rewetted peat and reedbeds create deeper, slower water that holds back rainfall, providing flood storage that protects towns downstream.

cards.front: Why does building hotels on mangrove coastlines increase storm damage to beaches?
cards.answer: Removing mangroves takes away the natural buffer that had protected those beaches from storms.

cards.front: How does ecotourism income in Borneo help protect the rainforest?
cards.answer: Payments from tourists give villagers a reason to keep the forest standing rather than sell it for palm oil.

cards.front: Why does modelling and simulation help during NEA 2.3, rather than testing only at the end?
cards.answer: It lets you find problems while they are still cheap and quick to fix, before the prototype is nearly finished.

cards.front: Why must feedback in NEA 2.5 be weighed against the specification rather than just copied?
cards.answer: Explaining why feedback was accepted or rejected is what separates a described change from a properly evaluated one.

cards.front: Why should you consider the design as a whole in NEA 2.3, not just separate parts?
cards.answer: Because a well-designed part is no use if it does not fit the rest of the product.

cards.front: Why must technical detail in NEA 2.3 state a tolerance?
cards.answer: Because no manufacturing process cuts a component to an exact size every time, so tolerance shows acceptable variation.

cards.front: Why do cardiovascular adaptations reverse faster than muscle mass when training stops?
cards.answer: Cardiovascular adaptations like lower resting heart rate reverse within weeks, while muscle mass is lost more slowly.

cards.front: Why does overtraining increase injury risk?
cards.answer: Training too hard without enough rest causes fatigue, declining performance and increased injury risk.

cards.front: Name the eight key events in the timeline of tension in Europe from 1931 to 1939.
cards.answer: Manchuria (1931) / Abyssinia invaded (October 1935) / Rhineland remilitarised (March 1936) / Anschluss with Austria (March 1938) / Munich Agreement over Sudetenland (September 1938) / Nazi-Soviet Pact (23 August 1939) / Germany invades Poland (1 September 1939) / Britain and France declare war (3 September 1939)

cards.front: Why did Britain and France not respond militarily when Germany remilitarised the Rhineland in 1936?
cards.answer: French commanders needed full mobilisation which the government would not order, and British leaders thought Germany had legitimate grievances not worth war over.

cards.front: How did the Abyssinian Crisis push Mussolini closer to Hitler?
cards.answer: League sanctions and the Hoare-Laval scandal showed Britain and France would avoid confronting Italy, encouraging Mussolini to align with Germany instead.

cards.front: Why did Stalin agree to the Nazi-Soviet Pact in August 1939?
cards.answer: He grew frustrated with Britain and France's slow talks lacking real military commitment, so he aligned with Germany instead.

title: Global English-Language Film: Narrative in Focus
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five global English-language films and the country each was produced in (5 films).
cards.answer: Slumdog Millionaire - UK/India / District 9 - South Africa / The Babadook - Australia / The Breadwinner - Ireland / Jojo Rabbit - New Zealand

cards.front: Name the five structural narrative approaches the lesson gives, one for each of the five global English-language films.
cards.answer: Slumdog Millionaire: frame narrative with cross-cut flashbacks / District 9: mockumentary-into-conventional narration / The Babadook: domestic realism accumulating dread / The Breadwinner: animated embedded narrative / Jojo Rabbit: child's-eye-view satirical narration with anachronistic music
items: Slumdog Millionaire: frame narrative with cross-cut flashbacks
The Babadook: domestic realism accumulating dread
Jojo Rabbit: child's-eye-view satirical narration with anachronistic music

cards.front: How does District 9's shift from news footage to handheld camera affect the spectator's position?
cards.answer: It signals a loss of institutional control and pulls the spectator into the protagonist's isolated personal perspective.

cards.front: How do The Breadwinner's storybook insets let the protagonist deal with her trauma?
cards.answer: The embedded storybook tale lets her process trauma obliquely, so the spectator understands more than the in-film characters do.

cards.front: Name the four shapes/lines seen on a distance-time graph and what each means.
cards.answer: Horizontal line: stationary / Straight diagonal line: constant speed / Curve getting steeper: accelerating / Curve getting shallower: decelerating

cards.front: Why does an object moving in a circle at constant speed still count as accelerating?
cards.answer: Its velocity is changing because its direction is constantly changing, even though its speed stays the same.

cards.front: How can you find the speed at one instant on a curved distance-time graph?
cards.answer: Draw a tangent to the curve at that point and calculate the gradient of the tangent.

cards.front: Why does a skydiver reach a first terminal velocity before opening their parachute?
cards.answer: As speed increases drag increases until it equals weight, giving zero resultant force so speed stays constant.

cards.front: Name the four causes the lesson gives for a Domesday village being marked 'waste' besides direct destruction
cards.answer: No taxable value at survey / Tenants had fled / Lord could not produce records / Estate deliberately reorganised by Normans

cards.front: How did the Harrying change landholding in the North by 1086?
cards.answer: Surviving Anglo-Saxon thegns lost their estates, which were redistributed to a small group of trusted Normans who garrisoned the region.

title: Settler Pressure: Railroads, Cattle, Gold and the Indigenous Plains
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three settler pressures (plus the underlying fourth) that combined to destroy Plains Indigenous life.
cards.answer: Railroads splitting herds and carrying hunters / Cattle industry taking grass and water / Gold strikes breaking treaty lines / US government reservation policy
items: Railroads splitting herds and carrying hunters
Cattle industry taking grass and water

cards.front: Name the three gold strikes that broke treaty lines with Plains nations.
cards.answer: Pike's Peak strike 1858-59 / Bozeman Trail goldfields 1862-63 / Black Hills strike 1874

cards.front: How did the completion of the First Transcontinental Railroad in 1869 damage the bison population?
cards.answer: It physically split the great buffalo herd into northern and southern populations that never recombined, making them easier to wipe out separately.

cards.front: Why did hunger from bison loss lead to a repeating cycle of conflict for reservation nations?
cards.answer: Hunger pushed nations off reservations to hunt on cattle land, that hunting caused conflict with ranchers and the army, and conflict justified further restrictions.

cards.front: Name the four things the UK Equality Act 2010 relates to that are mentioned in the lesson (grounds, protected characteristics count, and race/religion examples)
cards.answer: Makes discrimination illegal / Based on nine protected characteristics / Race is one protected characteristic / Religion is one protected characteristic

cards.front: Why did Dr B.R. Ambedkar convert to Buddhism in 1956?
cards.answer: He argued Buddhism rejected caste and offered genuine equality, unlike Hinduism's caste structures which he was critical of.

cards.front: How does the langar in a gurdwara express Sikh teaching on equality?
cards.answer: It is open to all regardless of background, practically showing that no one is superior to another in God's eyes.

cards.front: Why did Martin Luther King argue that unjust laws need not be obeyed?
cards.answer: Because unjust laws degrade human personality and contradict natural and divine law, as he argued in his Letter from Birmingham Jail.

title: Investigating the Ripper: detection, sources and the press
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three detective methods police used in the 1888 Whitechapel investigation.
cards.answer: Door-to-door witness interviews / Police sketches from descriptions / Photographing bodies at crime scenes

cards.front: Name the four things missing from detective work in 1888 that would exist later.
cards.answer: Fingerprinting / Blood-typing / Central database of suspects / Anything beyond a paper record system
items: Anything beyond a paper record system

cards.front: Why did door-to-door interviews in Whitechapel often fail to produce reliable evidence?
cards.answer: Residents in the lodging houses moved frequently, so witnesses could become untraceable within a week.

cards.front: Why is a Punch cartoon useful for a historian studying public attitudes to the police in 1888, despite being biased?
cards.answer: Its bias reflects public mood, which is exactly what an enquiry into attitudes towards the Met needs to capture.

title: The Eternal Self, Samsara and Karma
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Why does maya keep the atman trapped in samsara, according to Shankara's rope-and-snake illustration?
cards.answer: Maya makes people mistake the material world for ultimate reality, causing attachment that binds the atman to the cycle of rebirth.

cards.front: Why does the Vishishtadvaita school teach that moksha is loving union with a personal God rather than realising identity with Brahman?
cards.answer: Vishishtadvaita holds the individual self is real and distinct from Brahman, so liberation means union, not dissolving into one reality.

title: Energetics, Reaction Profiles and Bond Energies
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Why does using a polystyrene cup give a more accurate reading when measuring energy changes in reactions?
cards.answer: It acts as an insulator, reducing heat loss to the surroundings.

cards.front: Why is the reaction between hydrogen and chlorine to form HCl exothermic?
cards.answer: More energy is released making the H–Cl bonds than is needed to break the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds.

title: Cells and Control: Mitosis, Stem Cells and the Brain
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four main phases of mitosis, in order.
cards.answer: Prophase / Metaphase / Anaphase / Telophase and cytokinesis

cards.front: Name the three therapeutic uses of stem cells given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Replacing damaged nerve cells in spinal injuries / Producing insulin-secreting cells for diabetes / Growing replacement tissue for burns patients
items: Replacing damaged nerve cells in spinal injuries
Growing replacement tissue for burns patients

cards.front: Why can plant cells differentiate throughout life while most animal cells cannot?
cards.answer: Plants have meristem tissue at root and shoot tips that keeps dividing and differentiating, unlike most animal cells which lose this ability after embryonic development.

cards.front: Why is the outer layer of the cerebral hemispheres deeply folded?
cards.answer: The folding of the cerebral cortex increases its surface area.

cards.front: How does Dickens use pathetic fallacy to show Scrooge's inner coldness in Stave 1?
cards.answer: The cold 'froze his old features, nipped his pointed nose, shrivelled his cheek', showing his inner coldness physically shapes his appearance.

cards.front: Why does Dickens have Fred act as a foil to Scrooge in Stave 1?
cards.answer: Fred's warmth and generosity, despite being poorer, make Scrooge's coldness and greed appear even more obvious by contrast.

cards.front: Why does Marley say his own chain was forged 'link by link, and yard by yard'?
cards.answer: The repetition emphasises the chain was built gradually over years through many small, selfish choices rather than one act.

cards.front: Why is it significant that Scrooge asks charity collectors 'Are there no prisons? And the Union workhouses?'?
cards.answer: It shows Scrooge believes prisons and workhouses are already sufficient provision for the poor, excusing him from helping further.

title: Wave Behaviour and the Wave Equation
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four measurable properties used to describe all waves.
cards.answer: Amplitude / Wavelength / Frequency / Period

cards.front: Why does sound travel faster in solids than in gases?
cards.answer: Particles in solids are more tightly bonded, so they can transmit compressions more rapidly than in gases.

cards.front: Why does a mechanical wave like sound need a medium to travel, unlike light?
cards.answer: Sound relies on particles vibrating to pass energy on, while electromagnetic waves like light need no particles to travel.

cards.front: How is the period of a wave related to its frequency?
cards.answer: Period and frequency are reciprocals, so period equals one divided by frequency.

cards.front: Name the four steps the lesson gives that Hitler used methodically to consolidate power from 1933-1934.
cards.answer: Reichstag Fire pretext to arrest communists / Enabling Act for legal dictatorship / Gleichschaltung dismantled independent institutions / Night of the Long Knives eliminated rivals and secured army loyalty
items: Reichstag Fire pretext to arrest communists
Night of the Long Knives eliminated rivals and secured army loyalty

cards.front: How did Hitler achieve the two-thirds majority needed to pass the Enabling Act?
cards.answer: He had communist deputies arrested and surrounded the Reichstag with SA stormtroopers to intimidate the remaining members.

cards.front: Why did the Night of the Long Knives secure the loyalty of the German army to Hitler?
cards.answer: It destroyed the SA's threat to the army and showed Hitler would protect the generals' institutional interests, so they accepted it.

cards.front: Why did Hitler pursue a 'legal revolution' rather than relying on raw force to seize power?
cards.answer: The failed Munich Putsch of 1923 taught him force alone was insufficient, so he used constitutional legitimacy to neutralise conservative resistance.

cards.front: What are the five stages of the tragic five-act structure in Macbeth?
cards.answer: exposition (Act 1) / rising action (Act 2) / climax (Act 3, banquet) / falling action (Act 4) / catastrophe (Act 5)

cards.front: How does Shakespeare use metre to show Macbeth's psychological state in Act 5?
cards.answer: Macbeth increasingly breaks from regular iambic pentameter, signalling his psychological fragmentation.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare have the witches speak in trochaic tetrameter instead of iambic pentameter?
cards.answer: Its stressed-unstressed, four-beat rhythm sounds jagged and unnatural, like a chant or spell, unlike noble characters' controlled speech.

cards.front: How does the changing attitude to blood between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: Macbeth sees blood as permanent while Lady Macbeth thinks it easily washed away, but their positions reverse by Act 5.

cards.front: Name the three Rivers siblings who live at Moor House and take Jane in.
cards.answer: St John / Diana / Mary

cards.front: Why does St John suppress his feelings for Rosamond Oliver?
cards.answer: He believes she is not 'suitable' for missionary work, so he denies his love for religious duty.

cards.front: How does Moor House differ from both Thornfield and Lowood for Jane?
cards.answer: It offers a middle ground, giving Jane equal female friendship and financial independence, unlike Thornfield's passion or Lowood's coldness.

cards.front: Why is St John's self-denial described as a form of violence rather than virtue?
cards.answer: He suppresses his own and Jane's natural feelings for religious duty, harming both their true natures.

title: Jewish Practices: Worship, Shabbat and Kashrut
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What are the four Shabbat rituals the lesson gives for ushering in and observing the day?
cards.answer: Lighting two candles / Reciting Kiddush over wine / Sharing a double portion of challah bread / Synagogue attendance, family meals and rest
items: Sharing a double portion of challah bread
Synagogue attendance, family meals and rest

cards.front: What two rules does the lesson give for an animal's meat to be kosher?
cards.answer: Chews the cud and has split hooves / Slaughtered by shechitah with blood fully drained
items: Chews the cud and has split hooves
Slaughtered by shechitah with blood fully drained

cards.front: Why do observant Jewish households keep two separate sets of crockery and cutlery?
cards.answer: Because the Torah repeats three times that a kid must not be boiled in its mother's milk, requiring complete separation of meat and dairy.

cards.front: Why do Orthodox Jews observe kashrut according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because it is commanded by God in the Torah, needs no further justification, and sanctifies eating as an act of obedience.

cards.front: Name the four musical elements the lesson says composers manipulate to build character and tension.
cards.answer: Instrumentation / Dynamics / Harmony / Rhythm

cards.front: How does the lesson say you can tell if a piece of music in a film is source music (diegetic)?
cards.answer: If a character on screen could plausibly hear the music and react to it, such as dancing or turning down a radio.

cards.front: Why does dark, low brass instrumentation suggest menace to an audience?
cards.answer: Low brass and dark string writing are chosen by composers because that timbre suggests menace or power.

cards.front: How do John Williams's Imperial March and Force theme use contrasting musical elements to represent opposite characters?
cards.answer: The Imperial March uses minor key, heavy brass and loud dynamics for menace, while the Force theme uses major key, strings and a rising melody for heroism.

title: Factors Affecting Achievement: Class, Ethnicity and Gender
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four material deprivation examples the lesson gives for working-class pupils.
cards.answer: overcrowded housing with no quiet study space / unable to afford uniform or equipment / needing a part-time job that reduces study time / parents unable to pay for private tuition
items: overcrowded housing with no quiet study space
unable to afford uniform or equipment
needing a part-time job that reduces study time
parents unable to pay for private tuition

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for girls' improved performance since the 1990s.
cards.answer: changes in female aspirations / growth in service-sector employment for women / curriculum reforms moving away from male-dominated content
items: growth in service-sector employment for women
curriculum reforms moving away from male-dominated content

cards.front: How does the crisis of masculinity explain some working-class boys' underachievement?
cards.answer: De-industrialisation removed traditional male manual jobs, so some boys saw academic effort as incompatible with masculine identity, associating it with femininity and passivity.

cards.front: How do Willis's 'lads' reproduce their class position through counter-school culture?
cards.answer: Working-class boys develop anti-school peer cultures that value manual labour over academic work, limiting their own qualifications despite appearing to choose freely.

cards.front: Name the two everyday uses of static electricity given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Electrostatic paint sprayers / Laser printers and photocopiers

cards.front: Name the two safety measures the lesson gives for dealing with static hazards.
cards.answer: Earthing fuel tankers before transfer / Wearing anti-static wristbands

cards.front: Why do fuel tankers get earthed before fuel is transferred?
cards.answer: Earthing connects the tanker to the ground via a conducting cable, letting built-up static charge flow away safely instead of sparking near flammable vapour.

cards.front: Why does a jumper crackle when you pull it over your head?
cards.answer: Different fabrics rub together, transferring electrons and creating regions of opposite charge, which attract and cause rapid discharge as small sparks and sounds.

cards.front: Name the seven areas of the catering kitchen workflow in order.
cards.answer: Delivery area / Staffing area / Wash area / Storage area / Preparation and cooking area / Serving area (the pass) / Washing/cleaning area

cards.front: In a restaurant, what six steps does the front of house workflow follow, from arrival to leaving?
cards.answer: Customer arrives at reception / Shown to their table / Receives menus / Places an order / Served food and drinks / Pays the bill

cards.front: Why do front of house and back of house staff have different dress codes?
cards.answer: Front of house wear smart uniforms to look professional and reflect the brand, while back of house wear protective clothing for hygiene and safety.

cards.front: Why can well-kept documentation help a business during an Environmental Health Officer inspection?
cards.answer: Records demonstrate legal compliance, which can help the business avoid prosecution or closure.

cards.front: Name the five paragraphs of the recommended structure for a comparison essay.
cards.answer: Introduction with argument / Comparative point paragraph 2 / Comparative point paragraph 3 / Comparative point paragraph 4 / Conclusion on which poem is more effective
items: Conclusion on which poem is more effective

cards.front: List the four common mistakes the lesson warns against in comparison essays.
cards.answer: Writing about each poem separately / Superficial comparison / Context dump / Choosing a weak comparison poem

cards.front: Why does the integrated structure usually score higher than the block structure?
cards.answer: It weaves between both poems within each paragraph, making the comparison explicit rather than describing each poem separately.

cards.front: Why is context best woven into analysis rather than given its own paragraph?
cards.answer: Because context must serve the argument by explaining why poets took different approaches, not sit as unconnected biography or history.

cards.front: Name the three barriers to Jane and Rochester's union that the Thornfield fire destroys.
cards.answer: Legal barrier: Bertha dies / Social barrier: Rochester's power reduced by blindness / Class barrier: Jane's inheritance gives financial independence
items: Social barrier: Rochester's power reduced by blindness
Class barrier: Jane's inheritance gives financial independence

cards.front: Why does Rochester partially regain his sight at the end of the novel?
cards.answer: Some critics read it as a reward for his repentance, having learned humility, honesty and dependence after the fire.

title: The Collapse of the League: Manchuria and Abyssinia
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Why did Britain and France refuse to impose oil sanctions on Italy during the Abyssinian Crisis?
cards.answer: They were unwilling to push Mussolini into an alliance with Hitler, so excluded the materials Italy needed most.

cards.front: Why couldn't the League impose economic sanctions on Japan over Manchuria?
