cards.answer: Japan was a permanent Council member, and the unanimity rule meant Japan would have had to vote to sanction itself.

cards.front: What three foreign policy moves did Hitler make within a year of the Abyssinian collapse?
cards.answer: Remilitarised the Rhineland (March 1936) / Formed the Rome-Berlin Axis (October 1936) / Concluded the League was a paper tiger
items: Concluded the League was a paper tiger

cards.front: Name five key facts the lesson gives about Britain's condition by 1918.
cards.answer: Women over 30 could vote / House of Lords lost its absolute veto / Old age pensions and national insurance existed / Britain had fought its most costly war / Boer War had exposed cracks in imperial confidence
items: House of Lords lost its absolute veto
Old age pensions and national insurance existed
Britain had fought its most costly war
Boer War had exposed cracks in imperial confidence

cards.front: How did the Second Boer War change British attitudes to empire?
cards.answer: Concentration camps, humiliating early defeats and the cost in lives and money exposed the gap between imperial rhetoric and reality, sparking a pro-Boer movement.

cards.front: Why was the Representation of the People Act 1918 only a 'partial victory' for women?
cards.answer: The age of 30 and property requirement excluded most young working-class women, precisely those who had contributed most in munitions factories.

cards.front: Why did the Parliament Act 1911 matter for what governments could achieve?
cards.answer: It confirmed the elected Commons was supreme over the hereditary Lords, allowing controversial legislation to pass without a permanent Lords veto.

cards.front: Name the five stages of Scrooge's arc that a strong essay tracks across the novella.
cards.answer: Hard-hearted capitalist (Stave 1) / Grieving the lost boy (Stave 2) / Awakened to others (Stave 3) / Confronted with death (Stave 4) / Active giver (Stave 5)

cards.front: Name the four briefly sketched women in the novella and the narrow moral slot each occupies.
cards.answer: Fan, the loving sister / Mrs Cratchit, the loyal wife / The laundress at Old Joe's, a cynical thief / The charwoman, a cynical thief
items: The laundress at Old Joe's, a cynical thief

cards.front: Why does Dickens have Tiny Tim's 'God bless us, every one!' line recycled as the novella's final line?
cards.answer: It links Tim directly to the novella's moral message, making him the test of Scrooge's humanity.

cards.front: Why is Fred's role important even though essays often overlook him?
cards.answer: He opens and closes Scrooge's transformation, stating Dickens's thesis on Christmas and modelling forgiveness by inviting Scrooge despite refusal.

cards.front: Name the three techniques the lesson says advertisers use with schema-consistent cues to shape memory
cards.answer: Familiar cues linked to viewer's schema / Repeating key images or messages / Avoiding information overload
items: Familiar cues linked to viewer's schema

cards.front: How can a leading question distort a witness's memory of a car crash?
cards.answer: Asking how fast the car was going when it 'smashed' rather than 'what happened' can make them recall the crash as more severe than it was.

cards.front: Name the five common mistakes the lesson warns against in 19th-century novel responses.
cards.answer: Only writing about the extract / Retelling the story instead of analysing / Bolting on context without linking it / Spending time on presentation / Not using literary terminology
items: Retelling the story instead of analysing
Bolting on context without linking it

cards.front: What four steps does the lesson recommend planning for each of your 3–4 key points about an extract?
cards.answer: What technique or language Dickens uses / What it reveals about character/theme / How it connects to the wider novella / Relevant context
items: What technique or language Dickens uses
How it connects to the wider novella

cards.front: Why should context be integrated rather than bolted on in an extract response?
cards.answer: Because bolted-on context just lists facts, while integrated context links context to Dickens's method and purpose, showing deeper analysis.

cards.front: Why does the lesson suggest treating the extract as a 'window' rather than a 'destination'?
cards.answer: Because the extract gives close textual evidence, but the argument should range across the whole novella to make wider connections.

cards.front: Name the three natural archives (besides ice cores) the lesson gives for reconstructing past climate.
cards.answer: Tree rings / Pollen records in lake sediments / Historical sources like harvest records and paintings
items: Historical sources like harvest records and paintings

cards.front: Name the three main sources of human greenhouse gas emissions the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Burning fossil fuels / Agriculture (cattle, rice, fertilisers) / Tropical deforestation

cards.front: Why did the 1815 Tambora eruption cause a 'year without a summer' in 1816?
cards.answer: Ash and sulphur particles from the eruption reflected sunlight back into space, cooling the planet.

cards.front: Why does tropical deforestation add to climate change in two ways?
cards.answer: Burning trees releases stored carbon, and fewer trees reduce the planet's ability to absorb future emissions.

title: Jojo Rabbit: Narrative and Comic Distance
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why does the editing of Jojo Rabbit treat the imaginary Hitler scenes the same as real scenes?
cards.answer: It uses the same shot-reverse-shot cutting rhythm, forcing the spectator to inhabit Jojo's credulous view while recognising its absurdity.

cards.front: Why does the public-square hanging sequence use the same warm palette and framing as the comic scenes?
cards.answer: The formal continuity shows fascist violence was embedded in ordinary community life and did not look different to those inside it.

cards.front: Why is the camera in Jojo Rabbit mounted at Jojo's eye level, roughly waist-height on an adult?
cards.answer: This low angle makes the imaginary Adolf slightly over-large and distorted, sustaining a child's-eye view where the adult world seems imposing and absurd.

cards.front: Name the four conditions the lesson says homeostasis controls in the body.
cards.answer: Body temperature / Blood glucose concentration / Water levels / Ion levels

cards.front: Name the six steps in the pathway of a normal nervous response, from stimulus to response.
cards.answer: Stimulus / Receptor / Sensory neurone / Relay neurone (in CNS) / Motor neurone / Effector

cards.front: Which brain region is responsible for consciousness, thought and memory?
cards.answer: The cerebral cortex.

cards.front: In the ruler drop test, what does a shorter drop distance tell you about reaction time?
cards.answer: A shorter distance means the person reacted faster.

title: There's a Certain Slant of Light
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Why does Dickinson's poem never explain what causes the 'Heavenly Hurt'?
cards.answer: She presents despair as something that simply arrives like weather, not the result of any human decision.

cards.front: How does Dickinson's use of dashes affect the poem's language?
cards.answer: The dashes interrupt each line, forcing pauses that mimic hesitation as the speaker struggles for words.

cards.front: Why does the poem isolate the speaker's suffering from others?
cards.answer: It insists the state cannot be shared or taught, and there is no enemy to identify or action to end it.

title: Two world wars and total war 1914-1945
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the five 'giants' the Beveridge Report (1942) said the welfare system should attack.
cards.answer: Want / Disease / Ignorance / Squalor / Idleness

cards.front: Which four items were rationed comprehensively during the Second World War?
cards.answer: Food / Clothing / Petrol / Furniture

cards.front: Why did Britain introduce conscription in 1916 despite the earlier success of voluntary recruitment?
cards.answer: Catastrophic losses like the Somme meant volunteers alone could no longer replace army casualties fast enough.

cards.front: How did total war experience during the Second World War create conditions for post-war welfare reform?
cards.answer: Shared suffering from bombing and rationing built social solidarity, making voters expect the state to provide healthcare, education and housing after the war.

cards.front: Name the ten main aims of retail businesses given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Survival/break-even / Profit maximisation / Increase sales / Increase market share / Customer satisfaction / Diversification / Be ethical / Environmental awareness / Social responsibility / Retail-specific aims

cards.front: Why might a furniture chain run a Bank Holiday sale even if it reduces profit margins?
cards.answer: It deliberately prioritises increasing sales volume, accepting temporarily reduced margins to boost turnover.

cards.front: How can pursuing market share through price matching conflict with the aim of profit maximisation?
cards.answer: Heavily discounting prices to increase market share can reduce profit margins in the short term, so the aims conflict.

cards.front: What is different about the aim of a charity shop compared with a profit-making retailer?
cards.answer: Charity shops aim to raise funds for a cause while covering running costs, rather than maximise profit for owners.

title: Allah in the Qur'an: Al-Fatiha, Tawhid and the 99 Names
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three things al-Fatiha establishes as a summary of the whole Qur'an
cards.answer: Who Allah is (the Lord, the Merciful) / What the human relationship with Allah should be (worship and dependence) / What the goal of human life is (guidance to paradise)
items: Who Allah is (the Lord, the Merciful)
What the human relationship with Allah should be (worship and dependence)
What the goal of human life is (guidance to paradise)

cards.front: Why do Muslims say Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim both come from a root linked to the womb?
cards.answer: Because the root r-h-m suggests mercy as fundamental and enveloping as a mother's care for a child.

cards.front: How does belief in Tawhid shape how Muslims see human authority?
cards.answer: Tawhid means ultimate loyalty belongs to Allah alone, so no human authority can override divine command.

cards.front: What three inscriptions appear on Portia's three caskets (gold, silver, lead)?
cards.answer: Gold: 'shall gain what many men desire' / Silver: 'shall get as much as he deserves' / Lead: 'must give and hazard all he hath'
items: Gold: 'shall gain what many men desire'
Silver: 'shall get as much as he deserves'
Lead: 'must give and hazard all he hath'

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare present Shylock's bond as more than unprovoked villainy?
cards.answer: Antonio has spat on Shylock, called him 'dog', kicked him, and damaged his business by lending without interest, so the bond responds to real persecution.

cards.front: How does Arragon's choice of the silver casket fail the appearance-versus-reality test?
cards.answer: He chooses by outward show rather than looking beyond surfaces, and finds a fool's head inside instead of the prize.

cards.front: Why does Shylock's 'merry bond' harden into a genuine desire for revenge?
cards.answer: It is only after Jessica's betrayal and Antonio's continued abuse that Shylock's wish for revenge becomes determined rather than a joke.

cards.front: Name the four things international standards govern in engineering, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dimensions (interchangeable parts) / Material properties / Test methods / Quality management systems / Environmental management

cards.front: Why did UK manufacturing employment fall sharply in the 1980s and 1990s?
cards.answer: Industries relocated production to countries where wages were a fraction of UK rates, a process called offshoring.

title: Population & Urban Change in the UK
subject: geography-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson gives three types of factors behind falling UK birth rates. Name them.
cards.answer: Economic factors / Political factors / Social factors

cards.front: Name the four consequences of an ageing UK population the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Pressure on NHS and social care / Rising pension spending / Workforce shortages / Positive contributions from older people
items: Pressure on NHS and social care

cards.front: Why has the UK's average life expectancy risen to about 81 years?
cards.answer: Better healthcare, falling smoking rates and improved diets have raised average life expectancy.

cards.front: Why do workforce shortages appear in jobs like nursing, teaching and engineering?
cards.answer: The over-65 group is leaving work faster than school leavers can replace them.

title: The Great Depression and the New Deal
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Why did the Wall Street Crash lead to widespread bank collapses?
cards.answer: Banks had invested depositors' money in shares, so when share prices collapsed banks failed and savings were wiped out.

cards.front: Why did Hoover refuse to give direct federal relief during the Depression?
cards.answer: He believed in rugged individualism, fearing government handouts would make Americans dependent on the state.

cards.front: Why was the National Recovery Administration struck down in 1935?
cards.answer: The Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional.

cards.front: Why did farmers in the Midwest suffer a 'double blow' during the Depression?
cards.answer: Banks repossessed their farms while drought turned the Great Plains into a Dust Bowl, driving many west.

cards.front: Name the ten school facilities vocabulary words given in the lesson.
cards.answer: una biblioteca - a library / una cantina - a canteen / un gimnasio - a gym / un laboratorio de ciencias - a science lab / una piscina - a swimming pool / un patio - a playground
items: un laboratorio de ciencias - a science lab

cards.front: Name the seven days of the week in Spanish given in the lesson.
cards.answer: lunes / martes / miércoles / jueves / viernes / sábado / domingo

cards.front: Why do you say 'es la una' but 'son las dos' when telling the time in Spanish?
cards.answer: Es la una is singular because it is one o'clock, but son las is used with all other numbers because they are plural.

cards.front: How do adjectives describing teachers change to agree, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: They change for gender and number, e.g. estrictos for masculine plural and estrictas for feminine plural, but -e adjectives like paciente stay the same.

title: Imperial Policy: Trade Monopoly, Slavery and the Missionaries
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three layers of Spain's trade monopoly with the Indies.
cards.answer: Only Castile could trade with the Indies / Only Seville (later also Cadiz) could send/receive ships / Only licensed Spanish ships and crews could sail
items: Only Castile could trade with the Indies
Only Seville (later also Cadiz) could send/receive ships
Only licensed Spanish ships and crews could sail

cards.front: Name the four pillars of Spanish imperial policy described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Trade monopoly / Encomienda labour system / Licensed African slave trade / Catholic mission

cards.front: Why did the Crown keep such tight control over Atlantic shipping through the Casa de Contratacion?
cards.answer: To capture the royal fifth of all gold and silver returning from the Indies and to keep out Portuguese, French and English ships.

cards.front: Why was Montesinos's 1511 sermon such a shock to the Spanish colonists?
cards.answer: Because he was attacking the moral story Spain told about itself, that encomenderos were performing a Christian service.

cards.front: Name the three acts of eavesdropping/noting the lesson gives as structuring the play.
cards.answer: Gulling scenes (benevolent trick into love) / Window scene (malevolent trick into rage) / Watch overhearing Borachio's confession (accidental truth)

cards.front: Name the four performances/disguises the lesson lists as saturating the play with theatricality.
cards.answer: The masked ball / Don Pedro impersonating Claudio to woo Hero / Margaret impersonating Hero at the window / Hero's staged 'death'
items: Don Pedro impersonating Claudio to woo Hero
Margaret impersonating Hero at the window

cards.front: Why does Claudio use verse when he denounces Hero at the altar?
cards.answer: Verse gives his denunciation rhetorical power, lending his cruelty a public, ceremonial quality.

cards.front: How does the play's structure show that observation is never neutral?
cards.answer: The same device of noting produces different outcomes depending on what characters already expect to see.

title: Types of Reaction: Redox, Acids and Neutralisation
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the fourteen metals in the reactivity series, from most to least reactive.
cards.answer: Potassium / Sodium / Calcium / Magnesium / Aluminium / Zinc / Iron / Tin / Lead / Hydrogen / Copper / Silver / Gold / Platinum

cards.front: Name the three types of acid reaction given, other than with an alkali, and their products.
cards.answer: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen / Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide / Acid + metal oxide → salt + water
items: Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide

cards.front: Why does copper sulfate solution fade from blue to colourless when zinc is added?
cards.answer: Zinc displaces copper, forming colourless zinc sulfate as the copper ions are reduced and deposited as copper metal.

cards.front: Why can zinc displace copper from copper sulfate solution but copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulfate?
cards.answer: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

cards.front: The lesson compares three types of bonding. What type of atoms combine to form each: ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding?
cards.answer: Ionic: metal + non-metal / Covalent: non-metal + non-metal / Metallic: metal atoms

cards.front: Why do both ions become stable after an ionic bond forms, such as in sodium chloride?
cards.answer: Because losing or gaining electrons gives both ions full outer electron shells.

title: The Charge of the Light Brigade & Bayonet Charge
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: In 'The Charge of the Light Brigade', what three directions surround the soldiers in the cannon repetition?
cards.answer: Cannon to right of them / Cannon to left of them / Cannon in front of them

cards.front: Why does Tennyson's final quotation 'Honour the charge they made! / Honour the Light Brigade' use the imperative 'Honour'?
cards.answer: It directly instructs the reader to remember and respect the soldiers, turning the poem into a memorial.

cards.front: How does the casualty toll of the real Battle of Balaclava show the scale of the disaster behind Tennyson's poem?
cards.answer: Around 110 of the 600 soldiers were killed, 160 wounded, and 375 horses destroyed due to a miscommunication in orders.

title: The Five Pillars, Ten Obligatory Acts & Shahadah
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the six extra duties in the Ten Obligatory Acts beyond the four shared Pillars.
cards.answer: Khums (20% tax on surplus income) / Jihad (striving in the way of God) / Amr bil ma'ruf (commanding good) / Nahi anil munkar (forbidding evil) / Tawalla (loving the Ahl al-Bayt) / Tabarra (dissociating from their enemies)
items: Jihad (striving in the way of God)

cards.front: Why is Khums considered particularly important in Shi'a Islam?
cards.answer: Because the money is partly given to descendants of Muhammad, supporting the religious scholars who guide the Shi'a community.

cards.front: How does believing in Tawhid shape a Muslim's daily life?
cards.answer: If Allah alone is God, only He deserves worship, so Muslims must not place money, status or people above Him.

cards.front: Name the four ingredients of a top-band thematic change essay given in the lesson.
cards.answer: evidence from all three eras / clear argument about change AND continuity / explanation of why things changed / substantiated overall judgement in conclusion
items: clear argument about change AND continuity

cards.front: Name the four things a strong essay paragraph should do, according to the lesson's pattern.
cards.answer: make a point / support with specific evidence / explain what it shows about change or continuity / link back to the question
items: explain what it shows about change or continuity

cards.front: Why does an essay covering only the modern period cap itself in the middle band?
cards.answer: Because it misses evidence from the medieval and early modern eras, and the essay must cover all three eras to access the top bands.

cards.front: Why does writing 'sport changed because football was codified in 1863' only earn a description mark, not an explanation mark?
cards.answer: Because it states what happened without explaining the causes, such as public schools, railways, the Saturday half-holiday and urban growth.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why beginners should avoid outcome goals.
cards.answer: Winning may be unrealistic against experienced opponents / Repeated failure can demotivate / Shifts focus away from technique development onto the scoreboard
items: Winning may be unrealistic against experienced opponents
Shifts focus away from technique development onto the scoreboard

cards.front: Why can outcome goals still be useful for a highly experienced performer like an elite rower?
cards.answer: An outcome goal like winning a final sharpens focus and intensity, especially when combined with controllable performance goals for daily targets.

title: How Materials, Smart Technologies & Microelectronics Changed Everyday Life
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Name four products the lesson gives as only possible because of miniaturisation.
cards.answer: Implantable pacemakers / In-ear hearing aids / GPS chips in children's shoes / Wrist-worn fitness trackers

cards.front: Why is stainless steel used for kitchen utensils, sinks and medical instruments?
cards.answer: It is an alloy of iron with chromium added to resist corrosion, giving the hygiene and durability those uses need.

cards.front: Why did Wi-Fi let engineers design new products without planning for cable routing?
cards.answer: A single router gives every device internet access wirelessly, so engineers could assume connectivity without running network cables.

title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church forbid artificial contraception but allow natural family planning?
cards.answer: Artificial contraception deliberately separates the unitive and procreative purposes of sex, while natural family planning works with the body's natural process.

cards.front: Why do Christians who use situation ethics say a strict no-divorce rule can be wrong?
cards.answer: Because remaining in a loveless or harmful marriage cannot be the most loving outcome for the couple or their children.

cards.front: Name the three different approaches to remarriage after divorce found among Christian groups in this lesson.
cards.answer: Catholic annulment instead of divorce / Church of England discretionary remarriage since 2002 / Orthodox penitential remarriage through oikonomia
items: Church of England discretionary remarriage since 2002

cards.front: Name the three changes the lesson gives for why coastal flood risk is increasing.
cards.answer: Rising sea levels / More powerful and frequent storms / Continued building on the coast

cards.front: Why does a sea wall at Bridlington cause the beach in front of it to erode?
cards.answer: The wall reflects wave energy back, scouring away the beach in front of it.

cards.front: How does dune restoration at Studland Bay protect the coast?
cards.answer: Marram grass is planted to bind and trap sand, and fenced walkways keep walkers off the dunes.

cards.front: How does the Medmerry realignment scheme protect land further inland?
cards.answer: The sea wall was breached to flood farmland, creating salt marsh that absorbs wave energy and defends land behind.

title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four benefits of recycling metals given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Saves energy / Reduces use of limited ore resources / Reduces landfill waste / Reduces environmental damage from mining and emissions
items: Reduces use of limited ore resources
Reduces environmental damage from mining and emissions

cards.front: Name the three metals the lesson says react with cold water.
cards.answer: Potassium / Sodium / Lithium

cards.front: Why does carbon reduction work to extract metals like iron from their oxide ores?
cards.answer: Carbon is more reactive than iron, so it removes the oxygen from the metal oxide, reducing it to the metal.

cards.front: In a displacement reaction, why is the less reactive metal ion reduced?
cards.answer: Because it gains electrons from the more reactive metal, and gaining electrons is reduction.

title: Wave Behaviour and the EM Spectrum
subject: science-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the three uses of infrared given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Remote controls / Thermal imaging / Optical fibre communication / radiant heaters

cards.front: Name the three properties of a wave that stay unchanged during reflection.
cards.answer: Speed / Frequency / Wavelength

cards.front: Why does sound diffract around a doorway but visible light does not?
cards.answer: Sound wavelengths are similar in size to doorways, while visible light wavelengths are millions of times shorter.

cards.front: Why do higher-frequency EM waves like UV and gamma rays tend to be more hazardous to living tissue?
cards.answer: They carry more energy per photon and are more ionising, which can damage DNA.

cards.front: Why does Dickens have the ghost repeat Scrooge's own words about the death of Tiny Tim?
cards.answer: It forces Scrooge to hear the cruelty of his own Malthusian language applied to a real, innocent child.

cards.front: Why does the Ghost of Christmas Present age and die within one day?
cards.answer: It shows that opportunities for generosity are fleeting, creating urgency because a missed chance may never return.

cards.front: Why were the English ships better suited to fighting the Armada in the Channel than the Spanish ships?
cards.answer: English ships were smaller, faster and more manoeuvrable with longer-range guns, while Spanish ships were large and built for boarding.

cards.front: Why was the Armada unable to return to Calais to rendezvous with Parma's army after Gravelines?
cards.answer: Its formation was broken and the wind had changed, forcing it to sail north around Scotland and Ireland instead.

cards.front: Why did Mary Queen of Scots' execution in 1587 give Philip extra motivation for the Armada, even though it could no longer put her on the throne?
cards.answer: The Armada could instead avenge her death and break England's interference in his empire.

cards.front: Name the five sections a typical business plan contains, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Executive summary / Market section / Operations section / Finance section / People section

cards.front: How does writing a business plan reduce risk before launch?
cards.answer: Writing down sales, costs and cash flow forces the entrepreneur to check research and prices, revealing problems while they are still cheap to fix.

cards.front: Why does a written plan help a founder get finance from a bank?
cards.answer: Banks almost always require a plan with a realistic cash flow forecast, and clear numbers and evidence make the idea more credible than a verbal pitch.

cards.front: Name the five actions employers must take under COSHH to control hazardous substances.
cards.answer: Identify hazardous substances used / Assess the risks / Provide protective equipment / Train staff in safe handling / Store chemicals correctly / Keep records

cards.front: What four things must a completed HACCP document record?
cards.answer: The hazard / The critical control point / The control measure / The corrective action

cards.front: Why do the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 require trolleys and lifting training in kitchens?
cards.answer: To reduce the risk of injury when staff move heavy boxes, hot pans, and catering equipment that cannot be avoided.

cards.front: Why must deaths, specified injuries and dangerous occurrences be reported to the HSE without delay under RIDDOR?
cards.answer: Because these are the most serious reportable incidents, so employers must notify the Health and Safety Executive immediately.

cards.front: Name the four solutions the lesson gives for dealing with non-biodegradable polymer waste.
cards.answer: Mechanical recycling / Chemical recycling (cracking) / Incineration for energy recovery / Biodegradable bioplastics

cards.front: Name the three variables the lesson says must be controlled in the enthalpy of combustion practical.
cards.answer: Mass of water / Draught conditions / Distance between flame and calorimeter

cards.front: Why can fermentation not produce ethanol concentrations above about 12–15%?
cards.answer: Higher ethanol concentrations kill the yeast, stopping fermentation.

cards.front: Why is the experimental value from the alcohol combustion practical lower than the true enthalpy of combustion?
cards.answer: Heat loss to surroundings, incomplete combustion, and evaporation of alcohol all reduce the measured energy value.

cards.front: Why does Dickens repeat the word 'his own' four times at the start of Stave 5?
cards.answer: It shows Scrooge reclaiming control of his life after being a passive observer in the previous three staves.

cards.front: Why does Dickens mix comedy and emotion when Scrooge wakes, like the 'Laocoön' stockings image?
cards.answer: The humour signals that genuine transformation has occurred, showing Scrooge is now joyfully, messily human rather than cold and calculating.

cards.front: Name three changes glasnost brought to Soviet media and public life.
cards.answer: Previously banned books published / Newspapers criticised government policies / TV showed reality of Afghanistan / Stalinism's crimes discussed openly

cards.front: Name three economic problems perestroika caused according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Inflation from relaxed price controls / Disrupted supply chains / Wages rose without productivity gains / Economic output fell

cards.front: Why did the Chernobyl disaster become a symbol of Soviet institutional failure?
cards.answer: The government tried to conceal the accident but glasnost meant journalists reported the truth, exposing the gap between official claims and crumbling reality.

cards.front: Why did Gorbachev's reforms spiral out of his control?
cards.answer: Glasnost exposed Soviet failures without improving living conditions, so people demanded political freedom and independence, squeezing Gorbachev between conservatives and reformers.

cards.front: Name the three Chamberlain-Hitler meetings that made up the Sudeten Crisis.
cards.answer: Berchtesgaden (15 September) / Bad Godesberg (22 September) / Munich Conference (29-30 September)

cards.front: Why did Henlein keep raising his demands even after Beneš offered concessions in 1938?
cards.answer: Hitler had instructed Henlein to make demands the Czech government could never accept, so agitation would continue regardless of concessions.

cards.front: Why did Chamberlain and Daladier decide to leave Czechoslovakia out of the Munich Conference?
cards.answer: They reasoned the alternative was war, and Czechoslovakia's consent was unobtainable but unnecessary since Britain and France would not fight for it.

cards.front: Why did Munich's failure to secure lasting peace only become clear in March 1939?
cards.answer: Hitler's seizure of the rump Czech lands in March 1939, not Munich itself, ended Czech independence and British appeasement.

cards.front: Name the eight key techniques the lesson lists as part of Brecht's approach.
cards.answer: Verfremdungseffekt / gestus / direct address / placards / songs that interrupt the action / visible stage machinery / episodic structure / narrators who comment on the action

cards.front: Why did Brecht want his audience to think rather than feel, unlike Stanislavski?
cards.answer: He believed emotional immersion made audiences passive, lulling them into accepting the world as it was.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception that Brechtian performance means deliberately bad or robotic acting?
cards.answer: Brecht wanted skilled performers; the alienation effect comes from theatrical framing like narrators, songs and placards, not poor acting.

cards.front: Name the four line shapes on a distance-time graph and what each means, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: horizontal line = stationary / straight diagonal line = constant speed / curve getting steeper = accelerating / steeper line = faster object

cards.front: Name the three lines on a velocity-time graph and what each means, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: horizontal line = constant velocity / line sloping upwards = acceleration / line sloping downwards = deceleration

cards.front: In the required practical, why does plotting force against acceleration show F = ma?
cards.answer: Varying force while keeping total mass constant gives a straight line through the origin, showing force and acceleration are proportional.

cards.front: What does a negative value of acceleration mean?
cards.answer: The object is decelerating, meaning it is slowing down.

title: Civil Rights, 1955-1970: King, Malcolm X and legislation
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three US cities where urban rebellions broke out in the 1960s, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Watts, Los Angeles (1965) / Detroit (1967) / Newark (1967)

cards.front: What two things did the Black Panther Party combine, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Armed self-defence patrols / Community programmes like free breakfasts for children
items: Community programmes like free breakfasts for children

cards.front: Why did President Kennedy call for federal civil rights legislation after Birmingham in 1963?
cards.answer: Televised footage of Bull Connor's fire hoses and police dogs used against peaceful protesters, including children, shocked and outraged the nation.

cards.front: Why did President Johnson push for the Voting Rights Act after Bloody Sunday in 1965?
cards.answer: Televised scenes of state troopers beating marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge shocked Johnson into acting on voting rights.

title: Santo Domingo, Smallpox and the Caribbean Settlements
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What three reasons does the lesson give for why Santo Domingo was sited on the south coast of Hispaniola instead of La Navidad's location?
cards.answer: Safer harbours / Closer to gold-bearing rivers / Away from alienated caciques' territory

cards.front: What four things does the lesson say happened to Tainos on Hispaniola under Spanish forced labour and violence?
cards.answer: Fields left untended / Villages broken up / Family structures destroyed by sexual violence / Resisters enslaved or killed
items: Family structures destroyed by sexual violence

cards.front: Why did the Taino settlers at La Navidad end up killed within a year?
cards.answer: The garrison quarrelled among themselves, kidnapped Taino women and turned on Guacanagarí's rivals, who then wiped them out.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say smallpox and Spanish conquest cannot be treated as separate disasters?
cards.answer: Forced labour, malnutrition, dispossession and warfare had already weakened Taino communities, making them far more vulnerable when smallpox arrived.

cards.front: Name the five examples the lesson gives of appearance concealing reality in the play.
cards.answer: Shylock's 'merry sport' hides a deadly trap / Portia's disguise hides her intelligence / Antonio's calm hides sadness / Venice's fair reputation hides prejudice / Bassanio's charm hides recklessness
items: Shylock's 'merry sport' hides a deadly trap

cards.front: Name the two exam tasks the lesson describes for Shakespeare questions and their focus.
cards.answer: Extract task: close reading of language and structure within printed lines / Whole-play task: discuss the theme across the whole play using memorised quotations and context
items: Extract task: close reading of language and structure
Whole-play task: theme across the play with memorised quotations

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare use money and commerce to shape relationships in The Merchant of Venice?
cards.answer: Because money mediates love, justice, mercy and revenge in Venice, shown through Bassanio's courtship, the bond, usury and the casket test.

cards.front: How does the play show that prejudice in Venice is structural rather than just individual?
cards.answer: Prejudice appears across institutions and characters, from the alien statute to insults from Antonio, Solanio, Salerio, Gratiano and Portia.

cards.front: Why can depression return when antidepressant medication is stopped?
cards.answer: Antidepressants only treat brain chemistry and do not address the underlying thought patterns that maintain depression.

cards.front: How does CBT use behavioural activation to treat depression?
cards.answer: It gradually reintroduces activities the person has withdrawn from, helping build healthier patterns of behaviour.

cards.front: Name the four measures the Long Parliament used in 1640-41 to limit royal power.
cards.answer: Abolished ship money / Outlawed the Personal Rule's courts / Passed the Triennial Act / Passed the Attainder of Strafford

cards.front: Why did Personal Rule collapse in 1640?
cards.answer: Charles's attempt to impose a Prayer Book on Scotland provoked the Bishops' Wars, forcing him to call Parliament to fund an army.

cards.front: Why did the Parliamentarians ultimately win the Civil War?
cards.answer: They had the superior financial resources of London and the south-east and reorganised their military into the New Model Army.

title: Foods of Rich and Poor Households
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four foods from Juvenal's farmhouse dinner alongside the young kid, as listed in the poem.
cards.answer: wild asparagus / warm eggs in hay / preserved grapes / pears and apples

cards.front: Why did the Licinian law set exact limits on dried meat and pickled fish but not on fruit and vegetables?
cards.answer: Meat and fish had to be bought and showed off wealth, while homegrown produce cost nothing and did not display wealth.

cards.front: Why does Juvenal say the senate's old-fashioned meal now seems contemptible even to a ditch-digger?
cards.answer: Roman standards of luxury had risen so much that what was once a luxurious senate meal is now seen as beneath contempt.

cards.front: How does Petronius use Trimalchio's dinner to mock hosts who show off their wealth?
cards.answer: He exaggerates the luxury, like dormice on soldered bridges and fake century-old wine, to mock using food to advertise wealth rather than honour guests.

cards.front: Name the sections included in a complete business plan (8 given in the lesson).
cards.answer: Business idea / Aims and objectives / Target market / Forecast revenue, costs and profit / Cash-flow forecast / Sources of finance / Planned location / Marketing mix

cards.front: How can a cash-flow forecast help a café owner avoid running out of cash before opening?
cards.answer: It reveals in advance, such as month three, when cash will run short, letting her arrange an overdraft beforehand.

cards.front: Name the three generations through which the pilot's story passes in 'Kamikaze'.
cards.answer: The father who lived it / The daughter recounting it to her children / The readers, who receive it second-hand
items: The daughter recounting it to her children
The readers, who receive it second-hand

cards.front: Why does the pilot turn his plane around in 'Kamikaze'?
cards.answer: The overwhelming beauty and movement of the natural world, like the fish and fishing boats, pulls him back to life over duty.

cards.front: How does shame spread through the pilot's family in 'Kamikaze'?
cards.answer: His children, who first chattered and laughed around him, eventually learn to be silent, spreading rejection to a generation who never witnessed the mission.

cards.front: How does the poem's structure mirror the conflict between the pilot's freedom and the code he is trapped in?
cards.answer: Free, unpunctuated, enjambed sentences flow against a rigidly regular shape of seven six-line stanzas, mirroring the pilot's rigid code.

cards.front: Name the three limited options the lesson says were available to working-class women like Helen in the 1950s.
cards.answer: Marriage / Factory work / Dependence on men

cards.front: Why does the lesson say poverty is more than just background detail in A Taste of Honey?
cards.answer: Poverty is the defining force shaping the characters' lives, trapping Jo and Helen in their cramped, comfortless flat and each other's company.

cards.front: Why can context still help a drama answer even though it earns no marks by itself?
cards.answer: It can help explain a moment in the play if kept short and embedded within analysis, rather than a separate paragraph.

cards.front: What three prevention measures did the government enforce during the Great Plague of 1665?
cards.answer: Quarantine of infected houses for 40 days / Watchmen posted to stop people leaving / Killing of dogs and cats / Bodies collected by dead carts / Large gatherings banned
items: Quarantine of infected houses for 40 days
Watchmen posted to stop people leaving

cards.front: What three continuities does the lesson give between the Black Death (1348) and the Great Plague (1665)?
cards.answer: Blamed on miasma / Blamed on God's punishment / Blamed on the humours / Same ineffective treatments used / No effective cure existed

cards.front: How did Harvey's ligature experiment prove blood flows in one direction through veins?
cards.answer: Veins below the ligature swelled, showing blood couldn't return to the heart, while veins above emptied, showing blood had already passed through.

cards.front: Why did many physicians reject Harvey's theory of blood circulation?
cards.answer: They trusted Galen's ancient authority and thought a doctor disagreeing with Galen must be unreliable, so some lost patients.

title: Singin' in the Rain and Grease: The Hollywood Musical
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three named sequences from Singin' in the Rain (1952) used for micro-analysis in this lesson.
cards.answer: The title number on the rain-soaked back lot / The 'Make 'Em Laugh' solo / The 'Good Morning' three-hander
items: The title number on the rain-soaked back lot

cards.front: Why does the title number in Singin' in the Rain use a long, locked-off master shot instead of cutting away?
cards.answer: It insists the body itself is the spectacle, refusing the implication that the performance needs cinematic assistance to be impressive.

cards.front: Why is the 'Greased Lightnin'' garage number in Grease edited with rapid cuts every two to three seconds?
cards.answer: To prioritise the sensation of energy and spectacle over letting the audience see any one performer's full movement clearly.

cards.front: What is the most common error the lesson identifies when comparing Singin' in the Rain and Grease?
cards.answer: Writing all of one film then all of the other, with a transitional sentence, instead of relating the two films within each paragraph.

cards.front: Why does Macbeth order Banquo's murder without telling Lady Macbeth?
cards.answer: He fears Banquo's noble nature and the prophecy that Banquo's descendants, not his, will be kings.

cards.front: How does the escape of Fleance affect the play's outcome?
cards.answer: The prophecy that Banquo's descendants will be kings remains intact, so Macbeth's murder achieves nothing.

cards.front: How does Macbeth manipulate the murderers he hires to kill Banquo?
cards.answer: He challenges their masculinity by questioning whether they are too pious to act against Banquo, copying Lady Macbeth's tactic.

title: The Northern Rebellion, excommunication and the missionary threat
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What three grievances drove the earls to launch the Northern Rebellion, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Resented the 1559 religious settlement / Lost influence to southern Protestants / Plan to marry Mary to Duke of Norfolk
items: Plan to marry Mary to Duke of Norfolk

cards.front: Name the three Catholic plots against Elizabeth that the lesson says the 1570 bull fed into.
cards.answer: Ridolfi Plot (1571) / Throckmorton Plot (1583) / Babington Plot (1586)

cards.front: Why did Regnans in Excelsis turn English Catholics into a national-security problem for the regime?
cards.answer: It released Catholics from their oath of allegiance, so any recusant could now be seen as a potential traitor.

cards.front: Why did the 1585 Act make it treason for foreign-trained priests just to be in England?
cards.answer: After the bull, the regime assumed any secretly entering priest was working towards the queen's deposition.

title: Common Medical Conditions: Epilepsy & Sudden Cardiac Arrest
subject: cambridge-nationals-sport-science

cards.front: Name the three symptom areas of the body affected by an epileptic seizure, as listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Eyes / Mouth / Limbs

cards.front: What immediate steps should you take if a performer has a seizure?
cards.answer: Protect them from injury / Do not restrain them / Place in recovery position once convulsions stop / Stay with them / Call 999 if seizure lasts over 5 minutes or no consciousness
items: Place in recovery position once convulsions stop
Call 999 if seizure lasts over 5 minutes or no consciousness

cards.front: Why can intense physical activity trigger sudden cardiac arrest in some athletes?
cards.answer: It places extreme demand on an already abnormal heart in those with undetected underlying heart conditions.

cards.front: Why must you never put anything in the mouth of a performer having a seizure?
cards.answer: Because swallowing the tongue is not actually possible, so it is unnecessary and could cause harm.

title: Government, the Prime Minister and Cabinet
subject: citizenship-aqa

cards.front: Name the four mechanisms the lesson gives for holding government accountable.
cards.answer: Parliament (questions, debates, select committees) / National Audit Office checking public spending / Courts using judicial review / Elections removing an unpopular government
items: National Audit Office checking public spending

cards.front: Name the three cabinet positions the lesson gives as examples, with their areas of responsibility.
cards.answer: Chancellor of the Exchequer (economic policy and budget) / Home Secretary (policing, immigration, national security) / Foreign Secretary (international relations)
items: Chancellor of the Exchequer (economic policy and budget)

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the Prime Minister's role is hard to define legally?
cards.answer: Because the role has grown by convention rather than statute, with no single law defining it.

cards.front: Why is the separation between ministers and civil servants an important constitutional safeguard?
cards.answer: Ministers set policy while civil servants impartially implement it, keeping government running neutrally regardless of who is in power.

title: Sorting Algorithms: Bubble Sort and Merge Sort
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three advantages of bubble sort given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Simple to understand and implement / Sorts in place (no extra memory) / Can detect an already-sorted list early
items: Can detect an already-sorted list early

cards.front: Name the two advantages of merge sort given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Much faster for large datasets / Consistent performance regardless of initial order
items: Consistent performance regardless of initial order

cards.front: During a merge step in merge sort, how does the algorithm decide which item to place next?
cards.answer: It compares the first elements of the two sub-lists and picks the smaller one.

cards.front: Why is merge sort harder to implement than bubble sort?
cards.answer: It is more complex, using divide-and-conquer with splitting and merging, and needs extra memory for sub-lists.

cards.front: Name the three poems studied in this lesson on Memory & Loss, with their poets.
cards.answer: 'Where the Picnic was' by Hardy / 'First Flight' by Fanthorpe / 'Absence' by Jennings

cards.front: How does Hardy's stanza structure in 'Where the Picnic was' reflect the speaker's emotion?
cards.answer: The short, clipped lines and shrinking stanzas give a controlled, restrained quality, showing the speaker holding back deeper emotion.

cards.front: How does the final stanza's 'earthquake tremor' work in Jennings's 'Absence'?
cards.answer: It breaks the poem's calm tone, showing the speaker's own thought about the absent person shaking the still scene.

cards.front: Why does Fanthorpe's shift in perspective in 'First Flight' end with 'At this height nothing lives'?
cards.answer: As the plane climbs, the familiar place becomes abstract and impersonal, ending in a distance where nothing recognisable remains.

title: The Second World War and American Recovery
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four home-front groups the lesson describes as being drawn into new roles or restrictions during the war (besides African-Americans and women).
cards.answer: Japanese-Americans interned under Executive Order 9066 / Mexican-American workers under the Bracero Programme / Native Americans including Navajo Code Talkers / Households under rationing
items: Mexican-American workers under the Bracero Programme
Native Americans including Navajo Code Talkers

cards.front: Why does the lesson argue that war spending ended the Depression when New Deal spending could not?
cards.answer: War spending reached $98 billion in 1944, about twenty times the New Deal's peak, and conscription removed 12 million men from the unemployment count.

cards.front: Why did A. Philip Randolph's threatened march on Washington in 1941 lead Roosevelt to act?
cards.answer: Randolph threatened the march unless Roosevelt banned discrimination in defence industries, so Roosevelt issued Executive Order 8802 to prevent it.

cards.front: Why were women's wartime job gains described as partial and contested?
cards.answer: Female wages were only around 60% of men's, and about 4 million women were dismissed after 1945 to make way for returning servicemen.

cards.front: Why does excess demand for a new games console (like the £300 launch) push its price up?
cards.answer: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so shoppers bid up the price until demand contracts and supply extends to restore equilibrium.

cards.front: Why does a rise in house prices lead to more homes being built over time?
cards.answer: High profits give construction firms an incentive to build, so resources flow into housebuilding until increased supply moderates the price rise.

cards.front: Name the six categories of performance-enhancing drugs the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Stimulants / Anabolic steroids / Narcotic analgesics / Peptide hormones (EPO/GH) / Diuretics / Beta blockers

cards.front: Name the four consequences of doping scandals for a sport described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Damaged public trust in results / Sponsors withdraw funding / Governing bodies divert resources to anti-doping / Clean athletes disadvantaged and harmed
items: Governing bodies divert resources to anti-doping

cards.front: Why do narcotic analgesics carry a risk of injuries worsening undetected?
cards.answer: They block pain signals, allowing athletes to keep training or competing on injuries without realising the damage is worsening.

cards.front: Why is the Biological Passport used instead of just testing for specific substances?
cards.answer: It monitors an athlete's blood values over time and flags abnormal fluctuations, catching doping methods that specific substance tests miss.

cards.front: Name the five sources of support the lesson identifies for coping with life events.
cards.answer: Family, friends, neighbours, partners / Professional carers and services / Community, voluntary and faith-based organisations / Multi-agency working / Multidisciplinary working

cards.front: Name the three types of life event the lesson groups events into.
cards.answer: Health and wellbeing events / Relationship changes / Life circumstances

cards.front: In Carol's bereavement case study, why is professional emotional support especially important for her?
cards.answer: Her low self-esteem means she may not believe she can cope alone, so professional emotional support is vital.

cards.front: Why does Carol's negative disposition affect the type of support she needs?
cards.answer: Because she focuses on problems rather than solutions, she needs encouragement to see progress from her daughter and church group.

cards.front: Why does a car's environmental impact come mainly from its use rather than its manufacture?
cards.answer: A car emits far more carbon dioxide over its driving lifetime than was released during manufacture.

cards.front: Why do minimum energy performance standards (MEPS) drive engineering innovation?
cards.answer: Governments set limits on appliance power consumption, forcing manufacturers to redesign motors, insulation and control systems to meet them.

cards.front: Give three malapropisms Dogberry uses in the play.
cards.answer: 'dissembly' for assembly / 'everlasting redemption' for damnation / 'aspicious' for suspicious

cards.front: Why does Leonato's belated challenge to Claudio raise uncomfortable questions?
cards.answer: It only comes after he already believes Hero is dead, following his own failure to defend her during the church scene.

cards.front: How does Claudio's reaction to learning the truth about Hero reveal his love is still superficial?
cards.answer: He speaks of Hero's 'image' and 'semblance' rather than expressing personal anguish, showing he still thinks in terms of appearance.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare's title 'Much Ado About Nothing' work as ironic commentary on the ending?
cards.answer: The characters treat the resolution as if nothing happened, but the audience knows the fractures the play exposed were never truly healed.

cards.front: Name the seven main biomes described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Tropical rainforest / Hot desert / Temperate forest / Tundra / Polar regions / Boreal forest (taiga) / Grasslands

cards.front: How does fertiliser runoff cause fish to suffocate in a pond ecosystem?
cards.answer: It causes an algal bloom that blocks sunlight, killing deeper plants, whose decomposition uses up oxygen, suffocating fish.

cards.front: Why does the global pattern of biomes follow latitude, such as rainforest at the equator and desert at 30°?
cards.answer: Because biomes are determined by climate, and climate follows the global atmospheric circulation system.

cards.front: How do nutrients return to the soil after plants and animals die?
cards.answer: Bacteria and fungi decompose the dead bodies chemically, releasing nutrients back into the soil as inorganic compounds.

cards.front: Name the five components the lesson describes I–V characteristics for.
cards.answer: Fixed resistor / Filament lamp / Diode / Thermistor / LDR

cards.front: Why does a filament lamp not obey Ohm's law as current increases?
cards.answer: As current increases the filament heats up, which increases its resistance, so the I-V graph curves and flattens.

cards.front: Why does a diode's I-V graph show almost no current in reverse bias?
cards.answer: A diode only allows current to flow in one direction, so in reverse bias essentially no current flows.

cards.front: Why is the I-V graph for a fixed resistor a straight line through the origin?
cards.answer: Current is directly proportional to potential difference because the resistor's resistance stays constant, obeying Ohm's law.

cards.front: What three types of response to catastrophe does each main character represent in The War of the Worlds?
cards.answer: Practical endurance (narrator) / Religious collapse (curate) / Empty rhetoric (artilleryman)

cards.front: Why does Wells make the narrator write his account retrospectively?
cards.answer: It combines the immediacy of first-person experience with the authority of hindsight, creating tension between terror and calm analysis.

cards.front: Why is the narrator described as morally ambiguous rather than heroic?
cards.answer: He kills or knocks out the curate and struggles with cowardice, showing an ordinary man surviving rather than a traditional heroic protagonist.

cards.front: Why does the artilleryman's talk of selecting the 'able-bodied, clean-minded' feel disturbing?
cards.answer: It echoes Social Darwinist and eugenic thinking about dividing humanity into strong and weak, shown as seductive but hollow since he never acts.

title: Act 4: The Friar’s Plan and the Sleeping Potion
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the four steps of the Friar's plan to reunite Juliet and Romeo.
cards.answer: Juliet drinks a potion to fake death / Family places her in the Capulet tomb / Friar sends word to Romeo / Romeo rescues her and they flee to Mantua
items: Juliet drinks a potion to fake death
Family places her in the Capulet tomb
Romeo rescues her and they flee to Mantua

cards.front: Name the three adults who fail Juliet before she turns to the Friar.
cards.answer: Lord Capulet / Lady Capulet / The Nurse

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare create suspense around the Friar's plan in Act 4?
cards.answer: The plan is fragile and depends on perfect timing, so the audience, knowing the lovers will die, sees exactly how it can fail.

cards.front: Why does Lady Capulet refuse to help Juliet even though she may sympathise?
cards.answer: As a woman trapped by the same patriarchal system, she cannot oppose her husband publicly even if she privately sympathises.

cards.front: Name the three family relationships described as having failed or collapsed in the lesson's family theme.
cards.answer: Ed's marriage collapsed / Judy left Christopher and moved to London / Ed's relationship with Mrs Shears collapsed
items: Judy left Christopher and moved to London
Ed's relationship with Mrs Shears collapsed

cards.front: Why does discovering Ed's lies harm Christopher more than the truth would have?
cards.answer: Because Christopher values truth absolutely, so learning his father lied leads him to logically conclude his father might harm him.

cards.front: Why does Anne Brontë's own life as a governess matter for understanding 'The Bluebell'?
cards.answer: Her real experience of working away from home explains why the speaker's 'toilsome life' far from loved ones feels so heartfelt.

cards.front: How does the poem's word choice show the contrast between childhood and adult life?
cards.answer: Childhood is described with soft, warm words like 'kindred hearts', while the present uses hard, negative words like 'heartless' and 'thankless'.

cards.front: How does the structure of 'The Bluebell' move from general idea to personal memory?
cards.answer: The first two stanzas make a general statement about flowers, then 'Yet I recall not long ago' pivots into a specific narrated memory.

cards.front: Name the three other poems the lesson compares 'The Bluebell' with in the cluster.
cards.answer: Cold Knap Lake / Theme for English B / Happy Birthday Moon / Tea With Our Grandmothers

title: Planet Earth: Shape, Structure and Atmosphere
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five named parallels of latitude given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Equator (0°) / Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N) / Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S) / Arctic Circle (66.5° N) / Antarctic Circle (66.5° S)

cards.front: Why is the magnetosphere important for observers on Earth?
cards.answer: It deflects the solar wind, which would otherwise strip away Earth's atmosphere and expose the surface to harmful charged particles.

cards.front: Why does the magnetosphere have an asymmetrical teardrop shape?
cards.answer: Solar wind compresses it on the dayside facing the Sun and stretches it into a long magnetotail on the night-side.

cards.front: Why does the sky turn red and orange at sunset instead of staying blue?
cards.answer: The low Sun's light passes through a much thicker layer of atmosphere, scattering away nearly all the blue light and leaving reds and oranges.

title: The Civil War: Impact on Civilians
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four pieces of legislation the lesson gives that expanded federal power during the Civil War.
cards.answer: 1861 Revenue Act / 1862 Legal Tender Act / 1863 National Banking Act / Homestead Act and Pacific Railroad Act (1862)
items: Homestead Act and Pacific Railroad Act (1862)

cards.front: Name the three battles/turning points the lesson identifies as mattering most for civilians.
cards.answer: Antietam (September 1862) / Gettysburg (July 1863) / Vicksburg (July 1863)

cards.front: Why did working-class Northerners see conscription as a 'rich man's war and a poor man's fight'?
cards.answer: Because a wealthy man could pay $300 to avoid service or hire a substitute, while poorer men could not.

cards.front: Why did Sherman's March to the Sea target railroads, plantations and livestock rather than just Confederate armies?
cards.answer: His 'total war' strategy aimed to break Confederate civilian morale by destroying the economy and showing the war could reach them directly.

title: Nutritional Needs, Life Stages and Diet Planning
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: Name the four life stages the lesson covers in detail for changing nutritional needs.
cards.answer: Young children (1-5 years) / Teenagers / Adults / The elderly

cards.front: Name the five practical ways the lesson gives to reduce the cost of a balanced diet.
cards.answer: Planning meals in advance / Writing a shopping list / Using seasonal ingredients / Buying own-brand products / Avoiding food waste

cards.front: Why are elderly adults at higher risk of dehydration?
cards.answer: The sense of thirst becomes less reliable with age, so they may not notice they need fluids.

cards.front: Why should young children's meals be nutritionally dense rather than bulky?
cards.answer: Their stomachs are small but they need relatively high energy, protein, calcium and vitamin D for rapid growth.

cards.front: Name the five main types of data retail businesses collect.
cards.answer: Sales revenue/turnover / Footfall / Stock/inventory data / Customer/loyalty data / Profit data

cards.front: Why might a retail manager use qualitative data alongside quantitative data when sales figures show a problem?
cards.answer: Quantitative data shows what is happening, but qualitative data like reviews or focus groups explains why, allowing a solution to be designed.

cards.front: Why is monitoring profit important, not just sales revenue, for a retail manager?
cards.answer: Profit shows what is left after costs, telling managers whether the business is genuinely succeeding rather than just busy.

title: Stolypin, the Dumas and Reform to 1914
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three structural problems the lesson gives for why the Dumas failed as parliaments.
cards.answer: State Council could veto Duma laws / Tsar controlled the army/navy/court budget / Deputies had no control over ministers
items: State Council could veto Duma laws
Deputies had no control over ministers

cards.front: Why did Nicholas II dissolve the Second Duma in June 1907?
cards.answer: He used a fabricated charge that Social Democrat deputies were plotting against him.

cards.front: How did the new electoral law after 1907 make the Third Duma one Stolypin could work with?
cards.answer: It gave one landlord vote the same weight as 260 peasant votes and 543 workers' votes, favouring the propertied classes.

cards.front: Why did Stolypin's land reform fail to fully solve peasant land hunger?
cards.answer: The poorest peasants often sold their consolidated plots and drifted back to the cities as proletarian recruits.

cards.front: Name the four impacts on sustainability that the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Transportation costs / Demand on natural resources / Pollution / Waste generated

cards.front: Name the four scales of production described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Batch production / Continuous production / One-off production / Mass production

cards.front: Why does crowd funding reduce financial risk for a designer compared with a bank loan?
cards.answer: It tests demand by collecting pledges before manufacturing, so money is only spent once demand is proven.

cards.front: How does just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing cut costs?
cards.answer: It orders stock only when needed for production, cutting the cost of storing large amounts of material.

cards.front: Name the four levels at which duality operates in the novella.
cards.answer: Character (Jekyll/Hyde) / Setting (respectable front/decayed laboratory) / Narrative (multiple perspectives) / Title ('Strange Case')

cards.front: Why did Jekyll's experiment to split good and evil ultimately fail?
cards.answer: Because good and evil are not separable — they are woven into the fabric of every person.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson's novella suggest science should be limited in exploring human nature?
cards.answer: Because although the chemistry works, it is the moral cost of ignoring boundaries that destroys Jekyll.

cards.front: Name the two themes the lesson gives for Ozymandias besides the power of art.
cards.answer: Power of nature over human power / Transience of political power
items: Power of nature over human power

cards.front: Why does the sibilance in 'Half sunk, a shattered visage lies' matter?
cards.answer: It creates a sense of violent destruction, showing time has erased even the most powerful figures.

cards.front: Why is 'the hand that mocked them' ambiguous?
cards.answer: 'Mocked' can mean the sculptor imitated the king's expressions or ridiculed him, enriching the poem's exploration of power.

cards.front: How does Ozymandias compare to London in exploring power?
cards.answer: Both criticise abuse of power, Shelley through the ancient tyrant and Blake through Georgian London's institutions, showing oppressive power is destructive.

cards.front: Name the seven stages Doyle uses to structure the pacing of The Sign of Four.
cards.answer: Slow beginning / Mystery builds / Revelation / Shock / Investigation / Climax / Resolution

cards.front: Why does Doyle use real Victorian fog symbolically in The Sign of Four?
cards.answer: Fog obscures, distorts and confuses, representing the appearance versus reality theme that nothing is what it first seems.

cards.front: Why does the Agra treasure ending up in the Thames suit the novel's themes?
cards.answer: The treasure is swallowed by the same waterway that connects London to the empire it was stolen from.

cards.front: Name the three caskets Portia's suitors must choose between.
cards.answer: Gold / Silver / Lead

cards.front: What two grievances does Shylock have against Antonio, beyond religion and money?
cards.answer: publicly humiliated by Antonio / daughter Jessica betrayed him / cultural identity under constant assault

cards.front: Why does Shylock hate Antonio?
cards.answer: Antonio is a Christian who has humiliated him publicly, and he lends money for free, undercutting Shylock's livelihood.

cards.front: Why do the Prince of Morocco and Prince of Arragon both fail the casket test?
cards.answer: They are guided by surface appearances and self-importance rather than true worth, choosing gold and silver over lead.

cards.front: What three specific charitable actions does Scrooge take at the start of Stave 5?
cards.answer: Buys the prize turkey for the Cratchits / Donates generously to the charity collectors / Goes to Fred's for dinner
items: Buys the prize turkey for the Cratchits
Donates generously to the charity collectors

cards.front: Why does Dickens refuse to show the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come's face or form?
cards.answer: By describing it only in the negative, Dickens denies the reader reassurance, making it the most frightening spirit.

cards.front: Why does seeing his own name on the gravestone affect Scrooge more than the earlier warnings?
cards.answer: It moves the abstract idea of death into sensory, undeniable reality, forcing him to speak the pledge of change himself.

cards.front: How does the novella's cyclical structure support Dickens's argument that people can change?
cards.answer: The ending circles back to the Christmas-story frame, moving Scrooge from mean to generous, arguing change is possible for anyone.

cards.front: Why is a trained 5,000 m runner racing at full pace still working aerobically, even though the intensity is high?
cards.answer: Because oxygen delivery keeps pace with demand throughout the multi-minute race, so it can be sustained aerobically.

cards.front: Why is a basketball player's overall fitness classed as predominantly aerobic despite frequent explosive sprints and jumps?
cards.answer: Because most of the match is spent jogging and walking, even though critical moments demand anaerobic bursts.

cards.front: Why does a designer use both sketching and modelling when generating ideas, rather than just one?
cards.answer: Sketching is fast and cheap for exploring many forms, but modelling reveals fit, proportions and interference that sketching cannot show.

cards.front: Why does the iterative cycle restart if a manufactured prototype does not meet the specification?
cards.answer: The designer returns to the design stage to modify the idea and make a revised prototype until it meets all criteria.

cards.front: How does a model differ from a prototype in the iterative design process?
cards.answer: A model tests specific aspects like proportions before full manufacture, while a prototype is a working version evaluated against the whole brief and specification.

title: DNA Structure, Cloning and the History of Genetics
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four steps of genetic engineering used to make a genetically modified organism.
cards.answer: Cut out desired gene with restriction enzymes / Insert gene into a vector / Vector carries gene into target cells / Target organism expresses new gene, makes protein
items: Cut out desired gene with restriction enzymes
Vector carries gene into target cells
Target organism expresses new gene, makes protein

cards.front: Name the four steps of adult cell cloning used to create Dolly the sheep.
cards.answer: Nucleus from adult cell removed / Nucleus inserted into enucleated egg cell / Electric shock stimulates egg to divide / Embryo implanted into surrogate mother
items: Nucleus inserted into enucleated egg cell
Electric shock stimulates egg to divide

cards.front: Why was Mendel's work on inheritance not recognised until the early 1900s?
cards.answer: Because the mechanism of inheritance, chromosomes and DNA, had not yet been discovered when he published his work.

cards.front: Why does plant tissue culture cloning produce genetically identical plants?
cards.answer: Small groups of cells taken from a plant are grown in a sterile medium with nutrients and hormones, so each develops into an identical copy.

cards.front: Name the five steps of the systematic fault-finding approach described in the lesson, in order.
cards.answer: Visually inspect the circuit / Check the power supply with a multimeter / Use a continuity tester on connections / Measure voltage stage by stage / Use an oscilloscope on waveforms
items: Check the power supply with a multimeter
Use a continuity tester on connections

cards.front: How must a multimeter's probes be connected to measure voltage across a component?
cards.answer: The probes are placed across (in parallel with) the component being measured.

cards.front: Why can't a multimeter be used to test rapidly changing or high-frequency AC signals?
cards.answer: A multimeter cannot capture rapidly changing signals, so an oscilloscope is needed instead.

cards.front: How do you find the peak-to-peak voltage of a waveform from an oscilloscope trace?
cards.answer: Count the vertical divisions from the lowest to highest point of the wave and multiply by the volts/div setting.

cards.front: Why does alpha decay only happen in large, heavy nuclei?
cards.answer: Because the nucleus is too big to remain stable, so it ejects an alpha particle to become more stable.

cards.front: Why is gamma radiation often emitted after alpha or beta decay?
cards.answer: The daughter nucleus is left in an excited energy state and releases the excess energy as gamma radiation.

cards.front: In nuclear equations, what must balance on both sides?
cards.answer: The total mass number on both sides must match, and the total atomic number on both sides must match.

title: Spitalfields: Irish, Jewish and Bangladeshi communities
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three main types of work Irish migrants did in Spitalfields.
cards.answer: Dock labourers / Street sellers / Casual labouring trades

cards.front: Name the four trades/occupations Jewish migrants worked in around Spitalfields.
cards.answer: Garment trade / Furniture-making / Cabinet-making / Market traders

cards.front: Why did Irish migrants in Spitalfields face hostility from English workers?
cards.answer: Irish workers competed with English labourers for scarce casual work in the East End docks.

cards.front: Why is the repeated conversion of the Brick Lane building (chapel to synagogue to mosque) significant to historians?
cards.answer: It shows the physical layering of different migrant communities succeeding one another in the same building.

cards.front: Name the three types of paper named in the specification.
cards.answer: Copier paper / Cartridge paper / Tracing paper

cards.front: Name the three working properties used to compare papers and boards.
cards.answer: Flexibility / Printability / Biodegradability

cards.front: Why does folding boxboard crease cleanly without cracking?
cards.answer: It is a lightweight multi-layer board with a bulky mechanical-pulp core between two bleached chemical-pulp liners, giving stiffness at low weight.

cards.front: How does plywood become strong in every direction?
cards.answer: It is built from thin veneer layers glued with the grain of each layer running at right angles to the next.

cards.front: Name the six key methods the lesson lists as applied to crime and stratification research.
cards.answer: Official crime statistics / Crime Survey for England and Wales / Self-report studies / Ethnographic observation / Surveys (e.g. Townsend on poverty) / Longitudinal studies
items: Crime Survey for England and Wales

cards.front: Why does the Crime Survey for England and Wales still under-represent some crimes despite capturing more offending than official statistics?
cards.answer: It misses crimes with no individual victim like corporate crime and drug supply, and crimes victims can't or won't disclose, like domestic violence.

cards.front: Why did Townsend's questionnaire findings on poverty raise questions about validity?
cards.answer: Critics questioned whether the absence of certain foods or activities showed real deprivation or just personal choice or cultural difference.

cards.front: Why is Fiona Devine's return to Luton considered a restudy rather than a true longitudinal study?
cards.answer: She interviewed a fresh sample of workers rather than following the same people over time, so it shows change without tracking individuals.

title: Particle Model: Density, States and the Gas Laws
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three steps for measuring the density of a liquid in the core practical.
cards.answer: Measure mass of empty container / Add liquid and measure combined mass / Pour liquid into measuring cylinder to find volume
items: Add liquid and measure combined mass
Pour liquid into measuring cylinder to find volume

cards.front: Why does increasing the temperature of a gas increase its pressure?
cards.answer: Particles move faster and hit the container walls harder and more often.

cards.front: Why does decreasing the volume of a gas increase its pressure, according to the kinetic model?
cards.answer: Particles collide with the walls more frequently because they travel shorter distances between collisions.

cards.front: Name the four tenses the Spanish specification expects you to use when discussing technology.
cards.answer: present / preterite / imperfect / future

cards.front: Give the three disadvantages of technology listed about signal, cost and safety.
cards.answer: A veces la señal puede ser débil / Puede ser cara / Hay sitios peligrosos
items: A veces la señal puede ser débil

cards.front: How do you form the perfect tense in Spanish for regular -ar verbs like comprar?
cards.answer: Use haber plus the past participle, formed by changing -ar to -ado, e.g. he comprado.

cards.front: How can you structure a balanced argument about technology in Spanish?
cards.answer: Use por un lado… por otro lado… (on one hand… on the other hand…) to present both sides.

title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three steps in the practical to make a pure, dry salt from an acid and an insoluble base.
cards.answer: Add excess base or metal oxide to the acid / Filter off the excess solid / Evaporate water from the filtrate to leave crystals
items: Add excess base or metal oxide to the acid
Evaporate water from the filtrate to leave crystals

cards.front: Why is an excess of insoluble base or metal oxide added to the acid when making a salt?
cards.answer: To make sure all the acid reacts, so no acid is left in the final salt solution.

cards.front: What are the four combinations of reinforcement and punishment in operant conditioning?
cards.answer: Positive reinforcement / Negative reinforcement / Positive punishment / Negative punishment

cards.front: Why might approval from a peer group keep a young offender's criminal behaviour going?
cards.answer: It acts as a powerful secondary reinforcer, giving learned rewards like praise and status that reinforce the behaviour.

cards.front: Why might a younger sibling copy an older sibling's shoplifting without being rewarded themselves?
cards.answer: Vicarious reinforcement means seeing someone else rewarded for a behaviour makes the observer more likely to copy it.

cards.front: Why is it a weakness that the Bobo doll study used a doll rather than a real victim?
cards.answer: The artificial setting means findings may lack validity when generalised to real aggressive or criminal behaviour outside the laboratory.

title: The Trinity and the Nicene Creed
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three persons of the Trinity and the role the lesson gives each.
