cards.answer: Father - creator and sustainer of all things / Son - incarnate Word who redeems humanity / Holy Spirit - presence of God active in the world
items: Father - creator and sustainer of all things
Son - incarnate Word who redeems humanity
Holy Spirit - presence of God active in the world

cards.front: Why did the Council of Constantinople (381 CE) refine the Nicene Creed?
cards.answer: To add a fuller statement on the Holy Spirit, reaching the form Catholics recite at Mass today.

cards.front: Why does the play's non-linear structure create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: The audience learns future outcomes, like Irwin's wheelchair and Hector's death, before the characters live through them.

cards.front: How does Posner use the song 'Bewitched, Bothered, and Bewildered' to express himself?
cards.answer: He channels his unrequited love for Dakin through the song's lyrics about helpless infatuation, since he cannot say it directly.

cards.front: Name Macbeth's five character stages across the play, as the lesson traces his arc.
cards.answer: Act 1: celebrated warrior with dangerous ambition / Act 2: reluctant murderer consumed by guilt / Act 3: paranoid king who plans murder alone / Act 4: tyrant who massacres innocents / Act 5: nihilistic, despairing figure who dies fighting
items: Act 1: celebrated warrior with dangerous ambition
Act 2: reluctant murderer consumed by guilt
Act 3: paranoid king who plans murder alone
Act 5: nihilistic, despairing figure who dies fighting

cards.front: Why does Banquo's caution about the witches' prophecies not make him a simple moral paragon?
cards.answer: He suspects Macbeth of foul play after the murder but does nothing to act on his suspicions, and thinks about his own descendants becoming kings.

cards.front: Why does Malcolm test Macduff by pretending to be lustful, greedy and lacking every kingly virtue?
cards.answer: It is political shrewdness to check Macduff's loyalty before trusting him, showing Malcolm's careful judgement.

title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps: The March
subject: latin-eduqas

cards.front: According to Passage A, what two reasons does Livy give for the Second Punic War being the most memorable war ever fought?
cards.answer: Both sides equally strong in resources and manpower / The two nations fought with unusual hatred
items: Both sides equally strong in resources and manpower
The two nations fought with unusual hatred

cards.front: Why does Livy include the story of Hannibal's childhood oath?
cards.answer: It explains Hannibal's lifelong hostility to Rome as instilled in childhood and foreshadows that he will never turn back.

cards.front: How does the hyperbaton in Passage E, delaying 'montani' to the last word, create suspense?
cards.answer: It stops the reader knowing who threatens the column until the final word, recreating the soldiers' own fear as danger appears above them.

cards.front: Why did veteran soldiers believe 'Hamilcarem iuvenem redditum esse sibi' when they saw Hannibal?
cards.answer: Because Hannibal's face and manner were so like his father's that it felt as if a young Hamilcar had been given back to them.

cards.front: Name the six key themes the lesson identifies in My Name is Leon.
cards.answer: Racism and the care system / Family and separation / Identity and belonging / Childhood, neglect and innocence / Class and poverty / The 1981 riots — resistance and voice

cards.front: Why does De Waal draw a parallel between Leon and the Black community in the riots theme?
cards.answer: Both are silenced — Leon by a system that doesn't listen to children, the community by a state that doesn't listen to citizens.

cards.front: How does De Waal use Leon's identity to make a political point?
cards.answer: Mixed-race children placed with white families who couldn't build a positive racial identity often felt they belonged nowhere.

cards.front: What two joining words does the lesson say you should use to give a reason after an opinion in French?
cards.answer: parce que (because) / car (as/because)

cards.front: Name the two French school stages given in the lesson, with their age ranges.
cards.answer: le collège (ages 11-15) / le lycée (ages 15-18)

cards.front: Why must the adjective change between 'Le prof est strict' and 'La prof est stricte'?
cards.answer: Because adjectives must agree in gender with the noun they describe.

cards.front: Why do French students have a longer lunch break than English students, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because French law requires a lunch break of at least 90 minutes.

title: Cattle's End, the Range Wars and Frontier Law and Order
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four developments the lesson gives that turned the High Plains into a wheat-growing region within a decade.
cards.answer: Mechanical reaper and combine harvester / John Deere's steel plough / Refrigerated railcars / Bonanza farms of the Dakotas

cards.front: Why did British investors pull their money out of Wyoming and Montana ranching within months of spring 1887?
cards.answer: The spring thaw revealed valleys filled with rotting cattle carcasses, showing the Big Die-Up had devastated their herds.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the OK Corral gunfight was not simply a case of law versus lawlessness?
cards.answer: It was a fight inside the law, between Earp's town marshals and the Clantons' rural cattle interests, not an absence of law.

cards.front: Name the three forces the lesson says drove twentieth-century medical advances.
cards.answer: New scientific discoveries like radiation and antibiotics / Industrial-scale research and manufacturing from WWII / Expansion of public healthcare
items: New scientific discoveries like radiation and antibiotics
Industrial-scale research and manufacturing from WWII

cards.front: Name the four modern cancer treatment advances the lesson describes beyond radiotherapy and chemotherapy.
cards.answer: Keyhole surgery / Genetic research into cancer genes / Stem cell therapy / Targeted drug therapy

cards.front: Why did Marie Curie's research on radioactivity matter for cancer treatment?
cards.answer: She discovered that radioactive substances could destroy living tissue, laying the foundation for radiotherapy to treat tumours.

cards.front: Why did Albert Alexander die despite improving after his 1941 penicillin treatment?
cards.answer: The limited supply of penicillin ran out before he was fully cured, so he was not treated for long enough.

cards.front: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
cards.answer: Many strong electrostatic forces act in all directions between ions, needing lots of energy to break.

cards.front: Why is graphite soft and slippery?
cards.answer: Its layers are held together by weak forces, so they can slide over each other.

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson gives for controlling extraneous variables.
cards.answer: Standardised procedures / Counterbalancing / Randomisation / Single/double-blind techniques

cards.front: Why does counterbalancing help control order effects in a study with two conditions?
cards.answer: Half complete Condition A then B, and half complete B then A, spreading practice or fatigue effects evenly across both conditions.

cards.front: How does a double-blind technique reduce bias compared to a single-blind one?
cards.answer: Neither participants nor the researcher running the session know which condition is being tested, removing the researcher's own expectations from influencing treatment.

title: The Destruction of Sennacherib — Lord Byron
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Why does Byron's use of similes before the destruction make the army's defeat more shocking?
cards.answer: Each simile builds the army up as beautiful, vast and unstoppable, so its sudden destruction contrasts sharply.

cards.front: How does the poem's rhythm create a strong contrast after the army is destroyed?
cards.answer: The same insistent galloping rhythm continues but now describes stillness and silence instead of movement, sharpening the contrast.

cards.front: Name the three physical or emotional details Byron gives after the Angel of Death passes, moving from one body to a nation.
cards.answer: Horse's foam turning cold / Rider lying distorted and pale / Widows of Ashur wailing / Idols broken in temple of Baal
items: Idols broken in temple of Baal

cards.front: What were the three constitutional experiments Cromwell tried between 1653 and 1658?
cards.answer: Barebone's Parliament / Instrument of Government / Rule of the Major-Generals / Humble Petition and Advice

cards.front: What three areas were the Major-Generals responsible for in their districts?
cards.answer: Security (suppressing Royalism) / Taxation (10% tax on Royalist incomes) / Moral reform (alehouses, bear-baiting, Sunday observance)

cards.front: Why did Cromwell refuse the crown offered by the Humble Petition and Advice in 1657?
cards.answer: He believed God had visibly 'blasted' the title of king by executing Charles I, so he could not accept what providence had condemned.

cards.front: Why could the Protectorate never find a stable civilian settlement?
cards.answer: Its legitimacy rested on military power, but Cromwell's godly minority lacked enough electoral support to govern without the army.

title: Reversible Reactions, Equilibrium and the Haber Process
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Why does increasing pressure shift the Haber process equilibrium to the right?
cards.answer: High pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gas, and ammonia has fewer moles.

cards.front: Why is 200 atmospheres used in the Haber process rather than a much higher pressure?
cards.answer: Very high pressures give better yields but are too expensive and dangerous to maintain, so 200 atm is a practical compromise.

cards.front: Why are unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen recycled in the Haber process?
cards.answer: Because the yield per pass is only around 15–25%, so unreacted gases are separated and pumped back into the reactor.

cards.front: What three factors does the lesson say can shift a system at equilibrium?
cards.answer: Temperature / Concentration / Pressure (for gases)

cards.front: Name the three main Mycenaean-world sites the lesson identifies (besides Troy) as key sites.
cards.answer: Mycenae / Tiryns / Pylos

cards.front: What four things happened across Greece during the Mycenaean collapse, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Palaces were burned / Linear B writing disappeared / Population levels fell sharply / Trade networks broke down

cards.front: Why do most scholars now see the Mycenaean collapse as a 'systems collapse' rather than one single event?
cards.answer: Because interconnected palace economies broke down together, with each site falling for locally specific reasons within a wider regional crisis.

cards.front: Why do scholars think Homer's epics are a 'layered blend' rather than a pure record of Mycenaean life?
cards.answer: Because some details match Bronze Age archaeology, but the Odyssey also shows later Iron Age features like iron tools.

cards.front: Name the three control variables in the pH and enzyme activity investigation.
cards.answer: Temperature / Concentration of enzyme and starch / Volume of solutions

cards.front: What are the four things needed to calculate energy content using calorimetry (Q = mcΔT)?
cards.answer: Mass of water / Specific heat capacity of water / Temperature rise / Heat from burning food sample

cards.front: Why does raising temperature towards the optimum increase enzyme reaction rate?
cards.answer: Molecules have more kinetic energy, collide more frequently, and form enzyme-substrate complexes faster.

cards.front: Why does extreme pH stop an enzyme working?
cards.answer: It alters the bonds holding the enzyme's 3D shape, changing the active site so the substrate can't bind.

title: Enterprise and the Dynamic Business Environment
subject: business-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why businesses fail even with a good idea.
cards.answer: Poor financial management / Underestimating competition / Failing to understand what customers want / Bad timing
items: Failing to understand what customers want

cards.front: Why did the rise of smartphones create whole new industries?
cards.answer: New technology opened new possibilities, creating demand for apps, cases, chargers and repair services that barely existed before.

cards.front: Why do smartphone manufacturers release updated versions on a regular cycle?
cards.answer: This is planned obsolescence, a deliberate strategy to encourage customers to keep upgrading to newer versions.

cards.front: How did an ageing UK population create new business opportunities?
cards.answer: Demographic change increased demand for mobility aids, retirement financial services and age-appropriate leisure activities.

cards.front: Name the three specific ways the lesson says a business benefits from motivated employees.
cards.answer: Attracting employees / Retaining employees / Productivity

cards.front: Why can a bonus create problems even though it rewards achievement?
cards.answer: Bonuses can create pressure and may cause employees to cut corners to hit targets quickly.

cards.front: Why is promotion considered one of the most powerful motivators?
cards.answer: It gives a long-term incentive for consistent performance and also brings status and new challenges, not just money.

cards.front: Why can micromanaging demotivate skilled employees?
cards.answer: It removes their autonomy, making them feel their expertise is not respected.

title: Rivers: Long Profile, Cross Profile & Processes
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four processes the lesson gives for how a river transports its load.
cards.answer: Traction / Saltation / Suspension / Solution

cards.front: Name the four features the lesson lists as forming in a river's cross profile across the three courses.
cards.answer: Interlocking spurs / Meanders / Flood plains / Levees

cards.front: Why does the long profile of a river flatten out from a steep source to a gentle gradient near the mouth?
cards.answer: Near the source energy fights friction on the rough bed so goes into vertical erosion, but downstream the smoother channel needs less energy for friction, letting the river carry more load with a gentler slope.

cards.front: Why does a river drop larger material first while the finest particles travel furthest downstream?
cards.answer: Larger material needs more energy to carry, so it is deposited as soon as the river slows, while fine particles stay carried until energy drops further.

title: Time Series, Index Numbers and Rates of Change
subject: statistics-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three named index numbers the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: RPI (Retail Price Index) / CPI (Consumer Price Index) / GDP (Gross Domestic Product)

cards.front: How do you choose how many points to use in a moving average? (Higher)
cards.answer: Match the number of points to the cycle length in the data, e.g. 4-point for quarterly, 7-point for weekly, 3-point for a 3-period cycle.

cards.front: Why do RPI and CPI give housing a bigger weight than entertainment? (Higher)
cards.answer: Because households spend far more of their income on housing, so it should have more influence on the overall index.

cards.front: How do you predict a future value using a trend line and seasonal effect?
cards.answer: Take the trend line's value at that point in time, then adjust it using the average seasonal effect for that period.

title: Chapters 1–3: The Door, the Will and Dr Jekyll
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the three key structural and language methods established in Chapters 1–3.
cards.answer: Mystery and withholding / Setting as symbolism / Fog and darkness

cards.front: Why do Enfield and Utterson agree never to speak of the trampling incident again?
cards.answer: It reflects a very Victorian response, prioritising discretion over truth.

cards.front: How does the fog in London link to the story's themes?
cards.answer: The fog symbolises the obscured truth and moral confusion at the heart of the story.

cards.front: Why does Utterson's rational perspective limit what the reader can understand?
cards.answer: He cannot understand Jekyll's experiment because it is beyond rational explanation.

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four parts should each main essay paragraph make when analysing Anita and Me?
cards.answer: A specific claim / A supporting quotation / Analysis of Syal's language and methods / Embedded relevant context
items: Analysis of Syal's language and methods

cards.front: Why does Meena tolerate Anita's cruelty for so long in their friendship?
cards.answer: Her willingness to tolerate it reveals the depth of her desire to belong, since the friendship is never between equals.

cards.front: Why is the eventual breakdown of the Meena-Anita friendship presented as a positive step?
cards.answer: It shows Meena learning that real friendship cannot be built on inequality and the suppression of identity.

cards.front: How should context (AO3) be used across an essay on Anita and Me, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It must be woven into every analytical paragraph and always linked to Syal's purpose, not bolted on separately.

cards.front: What three reasons does Mrs Birling give for rejecting Eva's charity appeal?
cards.answer: Eva used the name 'Mrs Birling' / Sybil disliked her manner / Eva refused stolen money from the father
items: Eva refused stolen money from the father

cards.front: How does Gerald's behaviour in Act 3 undermine his moment of genuine feeling for Daisy in Act 2?
cards.answer: He recovers quickly and leads efforts to prove the Inspector was a hoax, restoring the status quo instead of changing.

cards.front: Why is Mrs Birling's demand that the father be publicly shamed an example of dramatic irony?
cards.answer: She unknowingly demands her own son Eric be publicly humiliated, since he is the father of Eva's child.

cards.front: Name the four men who kill the suitors together in Book 22.
cards.answer: Odysseus / Telemachus / Eumaeus / Philoetius

cards.front: Name the two loyal servants who help Odysseus and are contrasted with the disloyal ones in the homecoming books.
cards.answer: Eumaeus the swineherd / Philoetius the cowherd

cards.front: Why must Odysseus stay disguised as a beggar when he first returns to Ithaca?
cards.answer: Over a hundred suitors have taken his palace, so he would be killed if recognised before he could prepare.

cards.front: How does the moral case built across the poem justify Odysseus killing the suitors in Book 22?
cards.answer: They were repeatedly warned, violated xenia, dishonoured his household, and the gods disapproved and sanctioned the punishment.

cards.front: What three quotations should you learn for each poem in your cluster?
cards.answer: One for the central idea / One for the strongest image / One from the ending

cards.front: How does a shift from 'you' to 'they' in a poem's pronouns reveal attitude?
cards.answer: It shows the speaker stepping back from the subject, distancing themselves from it.

cards.front: How does using the present tense affect how an old wound feels in a poem?
cards.answer: It makes the old wound feel current, whereas a sudden shift to past tense pushes the feeling safely out of reach.

cards.front: Why is misquotation costly in part (b) answers?
cards.answer: It stops responses reaching the higher bands, especially for analysis of method.

title: Changes in tactics and strategy: medieval to early modern
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson lists four dominant weapon/arm types across British warfare, in order. What are they?
cards.answer: Infantry (shield wall) / Cavalry (Norman knight) / Missile (longbow) / Firearm (musket and rifle)

cards.front: Why was Viking raiding hard for Saxon England to defend against?
cards.answer: Longships let Vikings strike coastal and river targets fast, plunder, and withdraw before a defensive force could be gathered.

cards.front: Why could cavalry charges by armoured knights fail against disciplined infantry?
cards.answer: Cavalry struggled against disciplined pikemen, prepared defensive terrain, and especially the English longbow.

cards.front: What single factor does the lesson say stayed constant from the shield wall to the musket line?
cards.answer: Discipline: disciplined soldiers consistently outperformed undisciplined ones whatever formation or weapon they used.

cards.front: Name the three events the lesson gives that cause Elizabeth's growth.
cards.answer: Darcy's letter reveals her errors / Pemberley shows Darcy's true character / the Lydia crisis proves Darcy's love
items: the Lydia crisis proves Darcy's love

cards.front: Name the four qualities the lesson says Darcy's pride conceals.
cards.answer: loyal / generous / honest / responsible

cards.front: How does the pun on 'prided' in Elizabeth's self-recognition quotation work?
cards.answer: It shows her realising that her prejudice was actually a form of pride in her own judgement.

cards.front: Why is the Wickham/Darcy pairing described as the most important foil in the novel?
cards.answer: Wickham looks like a gentleman but isn't, while Darcy looks unfriendly but truly is one, showing appearance and reality rarely align.

title: Reading Data — Graphs, Histograms & Pie Charts
subject: engineering-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four graph types the lesson describes and their main use.
cards.answer: Bar chart — discrete categories / Histogram — continuous data intervals / Line graph — trends over time / Pie chart — proportions of a whole
items: Pie chart — proportions of a whole

cards.front: In the component diameter histogram, why does the tall central bar (120 out of 200 within tolerance) suggest good process control?
cards.answer: Most components cluster near the target diameter with only a few significantly over- or under-size, showing a roughly symmetrical distribution.

cards.front: How should you decide whether a histogram's bar height shows frequency or frequency density?
cards.answer: Check the vertical-axis label, since area (not always height) represents frequency unless class widths are equal.

cards.front: Name the four levels of colonial society's social hierarchy, from top to bottom.
cards.answer: Colonial gentry / Middling sort / Tenant farmers, labourers, indentured servants / Enslaved people

cards.front: Name the three sources of tension between groups in colonial society described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Tidewater elites vs backcountry farmers / Religious dissent between Puritans, Quakers and Anglicans / Urban tradesmen vs merchants over prices
items: Religious dissent between Puritans, Quakers and Anglicans
Urban tradesmen vs merchants over prices

cards.front: Why did backcountry farmers resent the tidewater-dominated colonial assemblies?
cards.answer: Assemblies ignored their petitions for protection from frontier raids and gave the backcountry too few seats.

cards.front: Why were the Middle colonies more ethnically and religiously diverse than New England or the South?
cards.answer: Religious toleration, fertile soil and the busy port of Philadelphia attracted a wider mix of nationalities and faiths.

cards.front: What three social layers make up the class hierarchy in Raveloe?
cards.answer: Squire Cass and his sons / respectable villagers like farmers and tradespeople / labourers and outsiders like Silas
items: respectable villagers like farmers and tradespeople

cards.front: Why did Eliot set Silas Marner in an earlier period than when she published it?
cards.answer: To capture a pre-industrial rural world that her readers were losing to factories, railways and migration.

cards.front: How does Eppie's final choice show female agency in the novel?
cards.answer: She chooses to stay with Silas rather than accept Godfrey's wealth, acting on her own will despite limited women's rights.

title: Social & Emotional Development — Bowlby, Ainsworth & Burke
subject: health-social-care-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three attachment types Ainsworth identified in the Strange Situation.
cards.answer: Secure attachment / Insecure-avoidant attachment / Insecure-resistant (ambivalent) attachment

cards.front: What social and emotional changes does the lesson say later adulthood brings?
cards.answer: Retirement changing identity and purpose / More frequent bereavement of partners/friends / Shrinking social networks / Increased physical dependency affecting self-esteem / Loneliness risk

cards.front: Why does Bowlby's internal working model shape a person's future relationships?
cards.answer: The primary attachment figure gives the infant a mental template of what relationships are like, which shapes expectations of all later relationships.

cards.front: Why might a teenager copy a behaviour they see a peer being praised for, according to Bandura?
cards.answer: Through vicarious reinforcement, seeing someone else rewarded for a behaviour makes the teenager more likely to imitate it themselves.

title: Charles II: The King and His Court
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three items the East India cities/territories part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry included alongside cash and trading rights.
cards.answer: City of Bombay / City of Tangier / Trading rights in Brazil and East Indies
items: Trading rights in Brazil and East Indies

cards.front: Why did who got near Charles II's mistresses matter politically?
cards.answer: Court mistresses were channels of patronage, so being close to them could win jobs, contracts and titles.

cards.front: Why was reaching Charles II's bedchamber the surest sign of political favour?
cards.answer: Access to the king moved by stages from public rooms to the bedchamber, admitting only a handful of trusted courtiers.

cards.front: How did the Earl of Danby use court patronage to manage Parliament?
cards.answer: As Lord Treasurer he distributed Crown money and offices, with an estimated 200 MPs receiving payments in some form.

title: Electric Circuits, Ohm's Law and I-V Characteristics
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three rules that apply to a series circuit.
cards.answer: Same current everywhere / Voltages add up / Resistances add up

cards.front: In the core practical for I-V characteristics, name three things you must do to get a reliable graph.
cards.answer: Record at least six evenly spaced values / Repeat readings to check anomalies / Allow cooling time between filament lamp readings
items: Record at least six evenly spaced values
Allow cooling time between filament lamp readings

cards.front: Why does an LDR's resistance fall as light intensity increases?
cards.answer: A light-dependent resistor's resistance falls as light intensity increases, giving low resistance in bright conditions and high resistance in darkness.

cards.front: Why does adding more branches to a parallel circuit decrease the total resistance?
cards.answer: Each extra branch gives current another path to flow through, so adding more branches decreases the total resistance.

title: Information Processing, Forgetting and the Brain
subject: psychology-ocr

cards.front: Why can retrieval failure make a memory feel completely lost even though it still exists?
cards.answer: Without the correct retrieval cue, stored information cannot be accessed, even though it has not decayed or been displaced.

cards.front: Why does shallow, surface-level encoding tend to produce weaker memories?
cards.answer: Repeating information without thinking about its meaning fades quickly, unlike linking it to something already known.

cards.front: Name the three ways encoding can happen, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Visually (as an image) / Acoustically (as a sound) / Semantically (by meaning)

title: The Great Society, Feminism and Roe v Wade
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three programmes created by the 1964 Economic Opportunity Act.
cards.answer: Job Corps / Head Start / Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA)

cards.front: What four things did Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign claim the amendment would cause?
cards.answer: Force women into the military draft / End alimony / Abolish single-sex bathrooms / Undermine the family
items: Force women into the military draft

cards.front: Why did the Vietnam War undermine the Great Society?
cards.answer: Military spending rose from $100 million to $20 billion a year, diverting money that could have funded anti-poverty programmes.

cards.front: Why did many married women oppose the Equal Rights Amendment in the 1970s?
cards.answer: They benefited from alimony, presumed custody and draft exemption, and feared losing those legal protections.

cards.front: Name the three types of technical textile used in buildings, homes and sport, as described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Construction textiles / Domestic textiles / Sports textiles

cards.front: Name the six modern/smart materials the lesson says react to a stimulus rather than staying fixed.
cards.answer: Shape-memory alloys / Nanomaterials / Reactive glass / Piezoelectric materials / Temperature-responsive polymers / Conductive inks

cards.front: Why is plywood strong in more than one direction and less likely to split?
cards.answer: It is made of glued wood veneer layers with the grain of each layer rotated, spreading strength in multiple directions.

cards.front: Why are shape-memory alloys useful in self-adjusting fittings without motors or switches?
cards.answer: They snap back to their original shape when heated past a set temperature, changing shape automatically without electronics.

cards.front: Name the three most useful structural terms the lesson says you should learn to identify.
cards.answer: Enjambment / Caesura / Volta

cards.front: Why might a stanza break in a poem about a relationship represent a change in mood?
cards.answer: The gap between stanzas can mark a shift in time, perspective or mood, like a moment of emotional change.

cards.front: How does regular rhyme breaking down across a poem mirror emotional change?
cards.answer: Full rhyme breaking down in the final stanza structurally mirrors a shift from happiness to loss.

cards.front: Why do short lines create a sense of control or tension in a poem?
cards.answer: Short lines feel abrupt and controlled, while long lines suggest expansiveness or overwhelming emotion.

title: Data Structures: Arrays, Records and File Design
subject: computer-science-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three data structures the lesson says you need to understand for GCSE.
cards.answer: One-dimensional array / Two-dimensional array / Record

cards.front: The lesson lists four fields in the example student file design. What are they?
cards.answer: StudentID / Surname / Forename / YearGroup

cards.front: Why are arrays efficient for storing data?
cards.answer: All elements are the same type and size, so the computer can jump directly to any index in one step.

cards.front: Why is a file needed instead of just a single record when storing data on thousands of patients?
cards.answer: A file stores many related records together permanently on secondary storage, whereas a record only represents one entity.

cards.front: Name four ways the lesson says religious believers work for justice and reconciliation.
cards.answer: Interfaith dialogue between conflicting communities / Organisations like the Corrymeela Community / Prison chaplaincy and restorative justice programmes / Charitable work addressing causes of conflict / Prayer for those affected by violence
items: Prison chaplaincy and restorative justice programmes
Charitable work addressing causes of conflict
Prayer for those affected by violence

cards.front: Name three arguments the lesson gives for why forgiveness is not always desirable.
cards.answer: Quick forgiveness minimises the wrong done / True forgiveness needs genuine repentance / Premature forgiveness can silence victims
items: Quick forgiveness minimises the wrong done

cards.front: Why might reconciliation built on injustice be considered a 'false peace'?
cards.answer: Because true peace is said to be impossible without justice, so peace without justice will eventually break down.

cards.front: Why did Martin Luther King Jr say Christians were obligated to oppose racial segregation?
cards.answer: Because he argued segregation was a form of social injustice that Christians had a duty to challenge.

cards.front: Name the three wires in a UK three-pin plug, with their colours.
cards.answer: Live - brown / Neutral - blue / Earth - green and yellow striped

cards.front: Why is the live wire always dangerous even when an appliance is switched off?
cards.answer: Because it remains connected to the mains supply at about 230 V.

cards.front: How do the earth wire and fuse work together to protect against a fault?
cards.answer: If live touches the casing, a surge of current flows through the earth wire, blowing the fuse and cutting the supply.

cards.front: Why don't double-insulated appliances need an earth wire?
cards.answer: The plastic casing is an insulator so it can't become live, so there's no shock risk even with a wiring fault.

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for counter-urbanisation in the UK.
cards.answer: Better roads (M25, M6, M62) / Electronic working, especially since 2020 / Perceived crime in cities / Rising house prices pushing families out
items: Rising house prices pushing families out

cards.front: The lesson names four historical factors that determined where UK Industrial Revolution cities grew. What are they?
cards.answer: Access to coal / Access to iron ore / Fast water for early mills / Port access for trade

cards.front: Why do cities in emerging and developing countries often develop informal settlements like favelas?
cards.answer: Because cities grow faster than housing supply, leaving migrants without enough affordable homes.

cards.front: Why do birth rates spike within rapidly urbanising cities, beyond migration itself?
cards.answer: Because young migrants moving to cities are typically of childbearing age, causing natural increase.

title: The League of Nations: Structure and Membership
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four specialist agencies or commissions of the League described in the lesson (besides its main political bodies).
cards.answer: International Labour Organization / Health Committee / High Commission for Refugees / Slavery Commission / Mandate Commissions

cards.front: Why did the US Senate's refusal to ratify the Treaty of Versailles matter for the League?
cards.answer: It meant the USA, despite Wilson designing the League, never joined it.

cards.front: How did Eric Drummond shape the League's Secretariat?
cards.answer: He built it into a genuinely international civil service, recruiting staff loyal to the League rather than their home states.

cards.front: Why could the League do little when a great power was the aggressor and willing to accept sanctions?
cards.answer: It had no army of its own and members had no obligation to send troops, leaving only economic threats.

cards.front: How does Walby say 'the state' structure of patriarchy restricts women's power?
cards.answer: The state does little to protect women from patriarchal power — women are under-represented in office and equal pay laws are weakly enforced.

cards.front: How does patriarchal culture, according to Walby, control women's behaviour?
cards.answer: Cultural norms and media impose double standards on men's and women's behaviour, so women who challenge them face ridicule or stigma.

cards.front: According to the lesson, why does the social model of disability say disabled people have limited power in society?
cards.answer: Because of social barriers like inaccessible buildings, discriminatory attitudes and lack of support, not the impairment itself.

cards.front: Name the six factors, besides gender, the lesson identifies as producing unequal power relationships.
cards.answer: Social class / Sexuality / Race and ethnicity / Age / Disability / Religion and beliefs

title: The Five Life Stages & Their Developmental Milestones
subject: health-social-care-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four PIES milestones a nursery key-worker would expect to see in a 5-year-old, one from each domain.
cards.answer: Can dress themselves and use scissors accurately / Vocabulary growing rapidly with theory of mind developing / Comparing self to peers, sensitive to praise or criticism / Play becoming cooperative with friendships based on shared interests
items: Can dress themselves and use scissors accurately
Vocabulary growing rapidly with theory of mind developing
Comparing self to peers, sensitive to praise or criticism
Play becoming cooperative with friendships based on shared interests

cards.front: Why is forming an attachment bond so significant during infancy?
cards.answer: It is an infant's most significant emotional development and forms the foundation for emotional security later in life.

cards.front: Why do many older adults face a higher risk of loneliness in later adulthood?
cards.answer: Social networks may shrink because mobility reduces and peers die, increasing the risk of isolation.

cards.front: Why does Austen use Mrs Reynolds's praise of Darcy to change Elizabeth's view of him?
cards.answer: As a servant with nothing to gain, her praise is more credible than anything Darcy could say about himself.

cards.front: How does Darcy's behaviour at Pemberley show he has changed since his first proposal?
cards.answer: He shows change through actions like asking permission to introduce Georgiana and treating the Gardiners with warmth, rather than declaring it.

cards.front: How does Georgiana Darcy's near-elopement with Wickham parallel Lydia's situation?
cards.answer: Both were targeted by Wickham, but Georgiana was rescued by Darcy's wealth and protection while Lydia's family cannot save her.

cards.front: How was Mr Bennet partly responsible for Lydia's elopement?
cards.answer: He let Lydia go to Brighton despite Elizabeth's warnings and retreated into his books instead of confronting the problem.

title: Runnymede 1215: Magna Carta and the First Barons' War
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six broad areas covered by Magna Carta's provisions.
cards.answer: Feudal incidents / Taxation / Justice / The Church / Royal forests, weights and measures / Treatment of foreign mercenaries

cards.front: What three different things did the rebel barons at Runnymede want, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Customary law of Henry I over feudal incidents / Personal redress for royal extortion / A constitutional principle that the king is under the law
items: Customary law of Henry I over feudal incidents
A constitutional principle that the king is under the law

cards.front: Why did John destroy the south-east tower of Rochester Castle during the siege?
cards.answer: His miners undermined the tower and set the timbers alight by burning forty fat pigs in the mine, collapsing the foundation.

cards.front: Why did the rebel barons offer the English throne to Prince Louis of France in 1216?
cards.answer: They had run out of moderate options once the Pope became their enemy, so needed an alternative ruler with continental resources to match John's mercenaries.

cards.front: Name the five central themes of The Empress covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Empire and exploitation / Identity and belonging / Belonging and exclusion (then and now) / Racism / Gender / Resistance and agency

cards.front: Name the three gendered vulnerabilities the lesson gives for the ayahs.
cards.answer: Employed as carers, traditionally female work / More economically dependent on employers / Danger of being women alone in a foreign country
items: Employed as carers, traditionally female work
Danger of being women alone in a foreign country

cards.front: Why does Gupta present the ayahs as sources of strength, not just victims?
cards.answer: Their solidarity, mutual care, and cultural practices represent a specifically female form of resistance to oppression.

cards.front: Why do strong essay answers on The Empress need to range across the whole play?
cards.answer: Because the most common mistake is writing about only one part, so answers should cover different acts and characters to show breadth.

cards.front: Name the remaining animal-to-real-world mappings in Animal Farm (not counting Old Major, Napoleon, Snowball, Squealer, Boxer or Moses)
cards.answer: Benjamin = cynical intellectuals / Mollie = the bourgeoisie / the dogs = secret police (NKVD) / the sheep = citizens who repeat propaganda / Mr Jones = Tsar Nicholas II / Frederick = Hitler, Pilkington = Western powers
items: The sheep = citizens who repeat propaganda

cards.front: Why does Napoleon ban the song 'Beasts of England' once he consolidates power?
cards.answer: Because the song represented the original revolutionary dream, and keeping it alive would expose how far the new reality had fallen from that promise.

cards.front: Why does Napoleon let Moses stay and give him a daily ration of beer?
cards.answer: It parallels Stalin rehabilitating the Russian Orthodox Church in WWII, showing totalitarian regimes co-opt any institution that helps maintain control.

cards.front: How does the repeated destruction and rebuilding of the windmill support Orwell's message about promises of a better future?
cards.answer: Each cycle costs the animals more suffering while delivering less benefit, showing the promised future never actually arrives for ordinary citizens.

title: Ethics in Daily Life: Precepts and Perfections
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the six qualities that make up the Mahayana Six Perfections.
cards.answer: Generosity (dana) / Morality / Patience (khanti) / Energy/Diligence (viriya) / Meditation (dhyana) / Wisdom (prajna)

cards.front: Why do most Theravada Buddhists extend the first Precept beyond just not killing humans?
cards.answer: Because all beings experience suffering (dukkha), so harming any sentient being contradicts the Buddhist path, linking the Precept to karuna.

cards.front: Why is kamma not the same as fate, according to Buddhist teaching?
cards.answer: Intentional actions create conditions for the future, but the practitioner retains free will to choose wisely in each moment.

cards.front: Name the four poems in the Conflict anthology that explore social conflict and identity.
cards.answer: Half-caste (Agard) / No Problem (Zephaniah) / The Class Game (Casey) / Belfast Confetti (Carson)

cards.front: Why does Agard write Half-caste without punctuation or standard capitalisation?
cards.answer: The rejection of conventional English grammar mirrors his rejection of the social conventions that label him "half."

cards.front: How does the form of Belfast Confetti reflect the effect of the violence on the speaker?
cards.answer: The poem's fragmented form, with interrupting dashes, mirrors the fragmentation of the speaker's mind and city caused by the violence.

cards.front: Why does Agard use colloquial Caribbean dialect instead of standard English in Half-caste?
cards.answer: Using standard English would mean accepting the hierarchy that labels him as inferior, so his dialect becomes an act of resistance.

cards.front: Why did the USA fear South Vietnam's collapse under the domino theory?
cards.answer: Because if South Vietnam fell to communism, neighbouring states like Laos, Cambodia and Thailand might follow.

cards.front: Why did Diem's anti-Buddhist policies weaken his government in 1963?
cards.answer: They triggered large-scale protests, adding to unpopularity from his authoritarian, corrupt rule in rural areas.

cards.front: Why did the USA feel unable to abandon South Vietnam by the mid-1960s?
cards.answer: Having pledged to defend South Korea, abandoning South Vietnam would signal US security guarantees could not be trusted.

cards.front: Name the three actions given to reduce the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
cards.answer: Doctors only prescribe antibiotics when necessary / Patients complete the full course / Restrict agricultural use of antibiotics
items: Doctors only prescribe antibiotics when necessary

cards.front: Why are double-blind trials used when testing new drugs?
cards.answer: So that neither patient nor doctor knows who has the real drug or placebo, eliminating bias.

cards.front: Name the four things the play's stage ending does NOT include, which the exam only credits for the stage version.
cards.answer: No reconciliation / No returning fiance / No birth / No Geof or Helen on stage at the end
items: No Geof or Helen on stage at the end

cards.front: Why does Geof choose to leave the flat quietly after Helen returns in Act Two Scene Two?
cards.answer: Helen makes his position in the flat impossible, so he leaves rather than cause Jo distress.

cards.front: Why does Jo react violently when Geof gives her a baby doll to practise with?
cards.answer: Because she says she does not want the baby, does not want to be a mother, and does not want to be a woman.

cards.front: How does Helen's concealment about Geof create dramatic irony at the end of the play?
cards.answer: Helen lets Jo believe Geof is not back yet, so the audience knows he has gone for good but Jo does not.

cards.front: What three groups did the 1601 Poor Law divide the poor into, and how was each treated?
cards.answer: Impotent poor: given outdoor relief / Able-bodied unemployed: set to work / Idle poor/sturdy beggars: punished

cards.front: Why did sumptuary laws restrict certain colours and fabrics to the highest ranks in Elizabethan England?
cards.answer: Dress was a public statement of rank, so laws reserved things like purple silk and cloth of gold for royalty to show status.

cards.front: Why were Elizabethan fashions like the ruff and farthingale deliberately impractical?
cards.answer: They were expensive and time-consuming to maintain, advertising that the wearer did not need to do physical work.

cards.front: Name the five non-specific defences the human body uses to stop pathogens entering.
cards.answer: Skin as physical barrier / Mucus and cilia in airways / Stomach acid / Lysozyme in tears and saliva / Gut bacteria competing with pathogens

cards.front: Name the five common routes given for how pathogens spread between hosts.
cards.answer: Airborne droplets / Direct contact / Contaminated food or water / Bodily fluids / Animal vectors

cards.front: How does stomach acid help protect the body from pathogens?
cards.answer: It has a very low pH that kills most ingested pathogens.

cards.front: How do lymphocytes help destroy a pathogen once it enters the body?
cards.answer: They produce antibodies that bind to antigens on the pathogen's surface, disabling it or marking it for destruction.

cards.front: How does the word 'really' in 'Elizabeth, feeling really anxious, was determined to go' show free indirect discourse at work?
cards.answer: It feels like Elizabeth's own thought inserted into the narrator's sentence, blending her voice with the narrator's.

cards.front: Why does the reader recognise Elizabeth's misjudgement of Wickham before she does?
cards.answer: The narrator's gentle irony signals the error, giving readers insight her limited perspective cannot provide.

cards.front: Why does the natural imagery of fish in "Kamikaze" matter to the pilot's decision?
cards.answer: The fish flashing silver and turning towards the sun represent life, beauty and freedom, reminding him what he would lose by dying.

cards.front: Why are the pilot's memories of "grandfather's boat" significant in "Kamikaze"?
cards.answer: They show the ordinary personal life and human connection he is being asked to give up for his mission.

cards.front: Name the two things the comparison between Garland and Rumens says both poems suggest.
cards.answer: Both explore conflict between identity and society / Both speakers face an impossible choice / Both use light imagery / Personal memory can outweigh politics or ideology
items: Both explore conflict between identity and society
Both speakers face an impossible choice
Personal memory can outweigh politics or ideology

cards.front: How does the personified city in "The Emigrée" contrast with the speaker's present reality?
cards.answer: Her remembered city 'dances' with her in joy and freedom, unlike her current 'city of walls' full of barriers and hostility.

title: The Brain, the Eye and Temperature Control
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three methods the lesson gives for studying brain function.
cards.answer: Studying patients with brain damage / Electrical stimulation during surgery / MRI scanning

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives why brain surgery and treating brain disorders is difficult.
cards.answer: The brain is extremely complex / Neurones in the brain can't easily regenerate / Damage to one area may cause unpredictable knock-on effects
items: Neurones in the brain can't easily regenerate
Damage to one area may cause unpredictable knock-on effects

cards.front: How does sweating help cool the body down when it's too hot?
cards.answer: Sweat evaporates from the skin surface, transferring heat energy from the body to the environment.

cards.front: Why does the eyeball shape in myopia cause distant objects to appear blurry?
cards.answer: The eyeball is too long or the lens too curved, so light focuses in front of the retina instead of on it.

title: Food Choices — Religion, Culture, Ethics and Medical Needs
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: Name the five ethical factors affecting food choice covered in this lesson.
cards.answer: Animal welfare / Fairtrade / Local produce / Organic food / Genetically modified (GM) foods

cards.front: Name the seven religions covered in this lesson's food choices.
cards.answer: Buddhism / Christianity / Hinduism / Islam / Judaism / Rastafarianism / Sikhism

cards.front: Why do Sikhs following the Khalsa code avoid halal or kosher-slaughtered meat?
cards.answer: Both methods involve prayers said during slaughter, which is seen as objectionable.

cards.front: Why can even a trace of nuts trigger a severe reaction in someone with a nut allergy?
cards.answer: The body's immune system wrongly recognises the harmless protein as a threat and mounts a rapid, systemic response causing anaphylaxis.

cards.front: What four stages make up Meena's bildungsroman journey in Anita and Me?
cards.answer: Trying to fit into white Tollington / Confronting the limits of acceptance / Reconnecting with her heritage / Achieving a synthesis of both identities
items: Trying to fit into white Tollington
Achieving a synthesis of both identities

cards.front: Why does the novel's ending stay ambiguous rather than fully happy?
cards.answer: Meena's individual growth is hopeful, but Tollington's racism and prejudice remain unchanged, showing structural problems persist.

cards.front: Why does Meena finally walk away from Anita after the fete?
cards.answer: Anita's failure to stand up for Meena during Sam Lowbridge's attack shatters Meena's illusions, revealing Anita as unable to be a real friend.

cards.front: How did Tollington shape Meena despite its cruelties?
cards.answer: The village's racism forced her to confront her identity, and its cruelties taught her resilience and what genuine connection is not.

cards.front: Why is Mrs Johnstone terrified when she finds Mickey and Eddie playing together?
cards.answer: Not disapproval but superstition — she fears the twins will learn the truth if they stay close.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Lyons slap Edward for playing with Mickey?
cards.answer: She fears exposure of Edward's true origins, not superstition, showing her paranoia turning violent.

cards.front: Name the four dune types from youngest (nearest the sea) to oldest (furthest inland).
cards.answer: Embryo dunes / Yellow dunes / Grey dunes

cards.front: Why do headlands form on a discordant coast?
cards.answer: Soft rock bands erode faster than hard bands, leaving the hard rock sticking out as headlands while soft rock erodes into bays.

cards.front: Why does a cliff retreat and leave a wave-cut platform behind it?
cards.answer: Waves cut a notch at the cliff base, undermining the rock above until it collapses, so the cliff steps back leaving a flat platform.

cards.front: Why does a spit form where the coastline suddenly changes direction, such as at a river mouth?
cards.answer: Longshore drift keeps carrying sediment in its original direction past the bend, building a ridge out into the sea.

cards.front: Name the six alkali metals in Group 1.
cards.answer: Lithium / Sodium / Potassium / Rubidium / Caesium / Francium

cards.front: Name the three uses of noble gases the lesson gives, with their applications.
cards.answer: Helium in balloons/airships / Neon in advertising signs / Argon in light bulbs and welding
items: Argon in light bulbs and welding

cards.front: Why do noble gases have no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons?
cards.answer: They already have full outer electron shells, which gives them great stability.

cards.front: Why do halogen boiling points increase going down Group 7?
cards.answer: The molecules get larger, so intermolecular forces between them become stronger.

cards.front: Why does Stevenson make Hyde's evil hard for characters to describe?
cards.answer: By making Hyde's evil indefinable, Stevenson makes it feel universal rather than a specific type of villain.

cards.front: How does the maidservant's vertical viewpoint during the Carew murder reflect Victorian society?
cards.answer: Watching from an upstairs window down to the street mirrors respectability living 'upstairs' while violence happens below.

cards.front: Why does nobody speak to Jekyll directly in the first four chapters?
cards.answer: The web of second-hand narration mirrors Victorian secrecy, where gentlemen avoid asking uncomfortable questions directly.

cards.front: What three qualities does Carew's description emphasise, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Age / Beauty / Courtesy/politeness

cards.front: Why does Josh attack Adam at the climax, despite being his secret boyfriend?
cards.answer: Logan forces Josh to prove he isn't gay, and Josh chooses violence to protect his public identity.

cards.front: Why does Dante's climactic act of reporting his friends connect him to journalism?
cards.answer: It is an act of truth-telling regardless of social cost, echoing the journalist he wanted to become.

cards.front: Name the two crises that Tyler responds to in the novel.
cards.answer: Emma's arrival / the attack on Adam

cards.front: Name the five key themes the lesson says every exam question on Never Let Me Go connects to.
cards.answer: Identity / Mortality / Hope vs Acceptance / Art and Creativity / Conformity and Compliance

cards.front: Why did Ishiguro have Miss Emily say the Gallery was created to test whether the clones had souls?
cards.answer: It shows societies define certain groups as less than human to justify exploiting them, as with slavery, colonialism and class oppression.

cards.front: How does the lesson explain why the clones never rebel against their fate?
cards.answer: Their conformity is not cowardice but the product of systematic conditioning that raised them to obey.

cards.front: For a comparison task on Never Let Me Go, how should each paragraph be structured?
cards.answer: As a direct comparison using linking phrases, analysing language and linking to context, rather than covering one text then the other.

cards.front: Name the four gas tests needed for Combined Science, one gas each.
cards.answer: Hydrogen - burning splint gives squeaky pop / Oxygen - glowing splint relights / Carbon dioxide - turns limewater milky / Chlorine - bleaches damp litmus paper white
items: Hydrogen - burning splint gives squeaky pop
Chlorine - bleaches damp litmus paper white

cards.front: In the systematic analysis of an unknown ionic compound, what are the steps in order?
cards.answer: Dissolve the sample in water / Flame test to identify metal ion / NaOH precipitate test to confirm metal ion / Test for the negative ion with the right reagent
items: Flame test to identify metal ion
NaOH precipitate test to confirm metal ion
Test for the negative ion with the right reagent

cards.front: Why does damp litmus paper turn red then bleach white near chlorine gas?
cards.answer: Chlorine is acidic so first turns litmus red, then bleaches it white as it is a powerful bleaching agent.

cards.front: How can you tell apart the white precipitates given by aluminium ions and magnesium ions with NaOH?
cards.answer: Aluminium's white precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution, but magnesium's does not.

title: Mary, Queen of Scots: plots, trial and execution
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Give the four reasons the lesson gives for why Elizabeth held back from executing Mary.
cards.answer: Would set a dangerous precedent / Risked war with France and Spain / Would damage her merciful image / Would martyr Mary, making her more dangerous
items: Risked war with France and Spain
Would martyr Mary, making her more dangerous

cards.front: Why did Elizabeth choose house arrest instead of killing or releasing Mary in 1568?
cards.answer: Killing an anointed queen was politically impossible, but releasing her risked her becoming a Catholic figurehead abroad, so house arrest seemed the safest option.

cards.front: How did Walsingham's agents uncover the Babington Plot?
cards.answer: A brewer smuggling Mary's ciphered letters in beer barrels at Chartley Hall was working for Walsingham, so every letter was intercepted and copied.

cards.front: Why was Mary's written approval of the Babington Plot so important legally?
cards.answer: It became the evidence used to justify putting her on trial and executing her for complicity in plotting Elizabeth's death.

title: The Nazi Police State, Propaganda & Opposition
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What four ways did the Nazis change the legal system to destroy judicial independence?
cards.answer: Sacked judges who opposed the regime / Made political opposition a criminal offence / Intimidated defence lawyers in political cases / Set up the People's Court with hand-picked Nazi judges
items: Sacked judges who opposed the regime
Made political opposition a criminal offence
Intimidated defence lawyers in political cases
Set up the People's Court with hand-picked Nazi judges

cards.front: What three things did the Swing Youth do to reject Nazi culture, besides listening to jazz?
cards.answer: Danced in clubs / Adopted non-conformist fashion / Socialised with Jewish people

cards.front: Why was the Gestapo able to control Germany with only around 32,000 officers?
cards.answer: Ordinary Germans informed on neighbours, colleagues and family, creating a climate of fear where people censored themselves.

cards.front: Why did the Nazis want to control the Christian Churches in Germany?
cards.answer: The Churches were the only organisations with the loyalty and reach to potentially challenge the regime.

cards.front: Name the five pollutants the lesson gives from burning fossil fuels, with the problem each causes.
cards.answer: CO2 - greenhouse gas, climate change / CO - toxic, binds to haemoglobin / Soot - breathing problems / SO2 - acid rain from sulfur impurities / NOx - acid rain, formed at high temperatures
items: SO2 - acid rain from sulfur impurities
NOx - acid rain, formed at high temperatures

cards.front: Name the four disadvantages the lesson gives for using hydrogen as a car fuel.
cards.answer: Difficult to store safely / Highly flammable and explosive / Mostly made from fossil fuels, releasing CO2 / Fuel cells and stations expensive and rare
items: Mostly made from fossil fuels, releasing CO2
Fuel cells and stations expensive and rare

cards.front: Why can carbon monoxide poisoning go unnoticed in homes with gas appliances?
cards.answer: Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless, so it cannot be detected without a detector fitted.

cards.front: Why is burning hydrogen considered cleaner than burning petrol at the point of use?
cards.answer: The only product of burning hydrogen is water, with no CO2, CO, soot or SO2 released.

cards.front: Name the four lines of evidence scientists look for to move from correlation to causation.
cards.answer: Plausible biological mechanism / Dose-response relationship / Consistency across studies / Temporality (exposure before disease)

cards.front: Why does a severely blocked coronary artery lead to a heart attack?
cards.answer: The blockage starves the heart muscle of oxygen because blood flow is reduced.

cards.front: Why is peer review important before scientists accept a study's findings on lifestyle and health?
cards.answer: Results from a single study aren't treated as definitive until scrutinised by independent scientists and replicated.

cards.front: Why does Mickey mask his pain with jokes in speech but reveal envy in song like 'That Guy'?
cards.answer: Song lets Russell show interiority — Mickey's real feelings that he cannot express in ordinary dialogue.

cards.front: Why does Russell show poverty following the Johnstones after their move to Skelmersdale?
cards.answer: Overspill schemes gave better housing but failed to provide jobs, transport or community infrastructure, so moving house did not change class.

cards.front: Why does Russell present Sammy's criminal path as a warning rather than pure villainy?
cards.answer: Sammy is shown as a product of the same poor environment that shaped Mickey, showing crime is a consequence of poverty not an inherent choice.

cards.front: Why does Meena's growing awareness of racism matter for her development in Anita and Me?
cards.answer: It marks her coming of age, as she learns surface friendliness isn't acceptance and her parents' silence is a survival strategy.

cards.front: What does Syal's structuring of Nanima's arrival with Meena's lowest point achieve?
cards.answer: It offers Meena a path back to her heritage right when she is rejected by both cultures, enabling an integrated identity.

title: Design Strategies and Avoiding Design Fixation
subject: design-technology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three strategies the lesson gives for breaking design fixation.
cards.answer: Random input / Reverse brainstorming / Analogous inspiration

cards.front: Name the four phases of the Double Diamond in order.
cards.answer: Discover / Define / Develop / Deliver

cards.front: How does reverse brainstorming help generate genuine improvements?
cards.answer: By asking how the product could fail or be made worse, then reversing those answers into improvements.

cards.front: Why is iterative design like Dyson's 5,000+ prototypes effective?
cards.answer: Each failed version reveals a specific reason for failure, which informs and improves the next attempt.

title: Themes: Empire, Race, Education and Solidarity
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four main themes that run through The Empress.
cards.answer: Empire and its human cost / Race and prejudice / Education as a route to freedom / Female solidarity
items: Education as a route to freedom

cards.front: How does Dadabhai's parliamentary speech in Act Two Scene Eleven expose the cost of empire?
cards.answer: He names the famine and plague sweeping India alongside the Diamond Jubilee, calling her 'the Empress of Famine and the Queen of Black Death.'

cards.front: Why do three English women refuse to hire Rani at the docks in Act One Scene Eight before Georgina takes her on?
cards.answer: It shows quiet, everyday prejudice against Rani because of her race, before Georgina finally offers her work.

cards.front: How does structural juxtaposition in Act One Scene Fifteen connect Victoria and Rani's stories even though they never meet?
cards.answer: It cuts between Victoria's Hindi lesson with Abdul and Rani abandoning her newborn, letting the audience compare their situations though the characters cannot.

cards.front: Name the four events of the Paschal Mystery, in order.
cards.answer: Suffering (the passion and crucifixion) / Death (Jesus dies on the cross) / Resurrection (Jesus rises on the third day) / Ascension (Jesus returns to the Father)
items: Resurrection (Jesus rises on the third day)

cards.front: Why do Catholics believe grace is necessary for salvation, according to the Catechism?
cards.answer: Because human beings cannot save themselves through good works alone; faith and grace together orient people towards God.

cards.front: Why does Paul say faith is 'futile' if Christ has not been raised (1 Corinthians 15:17)?
cards.answer: Because the resurrection is the foundation of Christian faith and proclamation, not just a vision or metaphor.

cards.front: Name the two chart types the lesson gives for showing discrete data.
cards.answer: Bar charts / Pictograms

cards.front: Why are bar charts for discrete data drawn with gaps between the bars, unlike histograms for continuous data?
cards.answer: Discrete data only takes specific separate values, so gaps show the values are distinct, unlike continuous data which has no gaps.

cards.front: Why does merging small survey categories (like commute times) make charts easier to read?
cards.answer: Combining very small categories into bigger ones avoids charts being hard to read and comparisons being unreliable, though detail is lost.

cards.front: According to the Key Fact, name the five things the Messiah is expected to do.
cards.answer: Be descended from King David / Be a political and spiritual leader / Bring world peace / Rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem / Gather the Jewish people from exile
items: Be a political and spiritual leader
Gather the Jewish people from exile

cards.front: How does the Covenant at Sinai differ from the Covenant with Abraham in who it makes responsible for keeping G-d's commands?
cards.answer: The Covenant at Sinai makes the whole Israelite people, not just their leaders, responsible for keeping G-d's commands.

cards.front: Why do Jews leave a cup of wine and open the door at Passover?
cards.answer: As a symbolic expression of Messianic hope, welcoming Elijah who will return to announce the Messiah's arrival.

cards.front: Name the three poems studied in 'Complicated Love' that show love failing, with their poets.
cards.answer: A Complaint - Wordsworth / Neutral Tones - Hardy / One Flesh - Jennings

cards.front: What are the three stanzas of structure in Wordsworth's 'A Complaint', in order?
cards.answer: Past (the fountain) / Present (the well) / Reflection

cards.front: Why does Wordsworth's regular metre and rhyme in 'A Complaint' contrast with its content?
cards.answer: The controlled, measured form keeps Wordsworth's composure even as he mourns, contrasting with the emotional pain beneath.

cards.front: How does the mundane opening of 'One Flesh' show the couple's separation?
cards.answer: The couple lie in separate beds, he with an unread book and she dreaming of childhood, showing physical and mental distance.

title: Myth as a Symbol of Power
subject: classical-civilisation-ocr

cards.front: Name the three main figures/scenes shown on the Ara Pacis relief panels.
cards.answer: Aeneas making a sacrifice / the goddess Roma seated on captured weapons / a mother goddess with children, animals and grain
items: the goddess Roma seated on captured weapons
a mother goddess with children, animals and grain

cards.front: Why did the Lapiths and Centaurs both represent the same 'combat' theme as the Amazons in Greek temple art?
cards.answer: Both mapped Greek victory over a monstrous or barbaric 'other' onto the Greek experience of the Persian Wars, celebrating the rightness of Greek order.

cards.front: How did placing the Centauromachy and Amazonomachy on sacred temples strengthen their political message?
cards.answer: Because the battles appeared on buildings dedicated to gods, they implied divine approval, suggesting the gods endorsed the Greek defeat of chaos.

cards.front: Name the five common errors that come up again and again in working drawing questions.
cards.answer: Omitting the third-angle projection symbol / Placing the plan view below the front view (first-angle) / Using thick continuous line for hidden detail / Writing dimensions in inches or mixing units / Omitting tolerances on a critical fitting dimension
items: Placing the plan view below the front view (first-angle)
Using thick continuous line for hidden detail
Writing dimensions in inches or mixing units
Omitting tolerances on a critical fitting dimension

cards.front: How is a chamfer shown on a working drawing?
cards.answer: A chamfer, an angled cut at the end of a shaft or hole edge, is shown with angled lines at the relevant corner.

cards.front: Name the eight 'king-becoming graces' Malcolm lists as ideal royal qualities.
cards.answer: Justice / Verity / Temperance / Mercy / Devotion / Patience / Courage / Fortitude

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare make Duncan a near-perfect king?
cards.answer: To maximise the horror of his killing, since his only flaw, excessive trust, allows his murder.

cards.front: How does Lady Macbeth's fear of darkness by Act 5 show her psychological collapse?
cards.answer: She once called on 'thick night' to hide the murder but now keeps light by her continually, fearing the dark.

cards.front: Why is Banquo's silence about Duncan's murder morally ambiguous?
cards.answer: He suspects Macbeth but says nothing, perhaps protecting himself or waiting for his own prophecy about his descendants to come true.

title: Modelling Methods & Evaluating a Design Outcome
subject: cambridge-nationals-engineering-design

cards.front: Name the three methods the lesson gives for evaluating a design outcome after manufacture.
cards.answer: Quantitative comparison against the specification / User testing / Identifying potential modifications and improvements

cards.front: Name the four pieces of equipment used to measure dimensions and performance during quantitative comparison.
cards.answer: Vernier callipers / Micrometers or steel rules / CMM (coordinate measuring machine) / Multimeter or oscilloscope

cards.front: Why can a virtual 3D CAD model test stress and clearance before any material is used?
cards.answer: It is a digital representation that can be simulated for loading and interference, so no physical model needs to be made.

cards.front: Why must features that fail a quantitative check be redesigned?
cards.answer: Because they fall outside the tolerance stated in the specification, so they must be changed to bring them within tolerance.

title: Poverty as a Social Issue: Townsend and Murray
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: Name the seven variables Townsend included in his deprivation index.
cards.answer: Diet / Fuel / Clothing / Housing conditions / Health / Education / Social activities

cards.front: Why did Townsend argue relative deprivation is a more meaningful measure of poverty than absolute poverty?
cards.answer: Because poverty is always experienced within a social and cultural context, not just biological survival, so social participation matters.

cards.front: Why did Murray believe welfare benefits created an underclass?
cards.answer: He argued welfare made it rational for people, especially single parents and young unemployed, to depend on benefits rather than seek work.

cards.front: Why can relative poverty rise even when absolute living standards improve for the poor?
cards.answer: Because relative poverty depends on the income gap, so if society gets wealthier but inequality widens, relative poverty can increase.

title: Riots, Kerner and King's Last Year, 1965-68
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four Northern conditions the lesson gives that the 1964-65 civil rights legislation had not addressed.
cards.answer: Poverty from lost manufacturing jobs / Housing segregation from redlining / Schools segregated by housing / Racist, almost all-white police forces

cards.front: Why did the Kerner Report conclude the 1965-67 riots did not discredit the civil rights movement?
cards.answer: It found rioters were a representative cross-section provoked by specific police violence, and that the causes were structural conditions, not individual failings.

cards.front: Why did King's Chicago campaign fail to end Northern housing segregation?
cards.answer: White residents in Marquette Park attacked marchers with bricks, and Mayor Daley's settlement was vague, unenforceable and largely ignored.

cards.front: Why did King's Riverside Church speech condemning Vietnam cost him support?
cards.answer: It angered white liberals, the Johnson administration and parts of the SCLC board, who feared losing federal allies.

title: The Wider War: Gallipoli and Other Fronts
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: What four reasons does the lesson give for why Gallipoli failed?
cards.answer: Poor intelligence on Ottoman strength / Loss of surprise after failed naval attack / Difficult terrain and disease / Skilled Ottoman defence under Kemal and Sanders
items: Loss of surprise after failed naval attack
Skilled Ottoman defence under Kemal and Sanders

cards.front: Why did the failed naval attack on 18 March 1915 make the later land landings harder?
cards.answer: It removed all surprise from the land landing, giving the Ottomans five weeks to prepare their defences.

cards.front: How did the Eastern Front's collapse in 1917 affect Germany's plans in the west?
cards.answer: It freed German divisions, which were then used for the 1918 Spring Offensive on the Western Front.

cards.front: Why did Russia's defeats and hardships on the Eastern Front matter for its government?
cards.answer: The huge casualties and food shortages undermined Tsar Nicholas II and contributed to the 1917 revolutions.

cards.front: Name the three key geological factors the lesson gives for dam siting.
cards.answer: Foundation rock must be strong and impermeable / Dip of strata must not create seepage pathways / Faults and joints must be identified and sealed by grouting
items: Foundation rock must be strong and impermeable
Dip of strata must not create seepage pathways
Faults and joints must be identified and sealed by grouting

cards.front: Name the three steps of a UK geotechnical site investigation described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Review existing BGS maps and borehole records / Walkover survey for surface outcrops and geohazards / Drilling boreholes or trial pits for subsurface samples
items: Review existing BGS maps and borehole records
Walkover survey for surface outcrops and geohazards
Drilling boreholes or trial pits for subsurface samples

cards.front: Why are beds that dip upstream (into the reservoir) favourable for a dam?
cards.answer: Water entering a bedding plane travels down the dip, away from the dam, reducing seepage beneath it.

cards.front: Why can tunnelling through permeable rock below the water table cause surface subsidence?
cards.answer: The tunnel acts as an underground drain, letting groundwater flow in and lowering the water table above it.

cards.front: Name the four Gothic elements at Thornfield that foreshadow the revelation of Bertha Mason.
cards.answer: Locked third floor / Strange nighttime laughter / Dark corridors / Fire in Rochester's bedroom

cards.front: How does Rochester's fall from his horse reverse the usual master-governess power dynamic?
cards.answer: He is injured and depends on Jane's help, so they meet as equals outside Thornfield's social hierarchy.

cards.front: Why does Rochester interrogate Jane and confide his past to her during their developing relationship?
cards.answer: He needs genuine honesty, which he cannot find among high-society women who perform femininity rather than express truth.

cards.front: Name the three motives the lesson gives for Henry II's interest in Ireland.
cards.answer: Papal bull Laudabiliter gave religious cover / controlling barons like Strongbow already there / personal union model made expansion easy
items: Papal bull Laudabiliter gave religious cover
controlling barons like Strongbow already there
personal union model made expansion easy

cards.front: Name the three languages used in Henry II's multilingual court, and who used each.
cards.answer: Norman French for king and barons / Latin for clergy and government documents / English for the great majority of the population
items: Norman French for king and barons
Latin for clergy and government documents
English for the great majority of the population

cards.front: Why did Henry II's royal justice grow stronger in England even though he spent most of his time in France?
cards.answer: To govern in his absence he expanded the exchequer, sent justices in eyre on circuits, and pushed jury trial, building institutions that ran without him present.

cards.front: Why did the loss of Normandy in 1204 change how the English aristocracy identified themselves?
cards.answer: It forced Norman nobles to choose between English and Normandy estates, ending cross-Channel landholding so English politics turned inward and identity shifted to England.

title: Time: Sidereal vs Solar Days and the Equation of Time
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Why does the apparent solar day get shorter around early January?
cards.answer: Earth moves faster near perihelion, so the Sun appears to move more quickly along the ecliptic, shortening the apparent solar day.

cards.front: Why does the earliest sunset not fall on the same date as the latest sunrise around the December solstice?
cards.answer: The Equation of Time is falling quickly then, so apparent solar noon slips about half a minute later each day, separating the dates.

cards.front: How does a shadow stick reveal true north?
cards.answer: A line through the stick's base and the point of minimum shadow length, which occurs at local noon, points true north.

cards.front: What two features of a sidereal day let it be used to track a star's position, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: measures Earth's true rotation relative to stars / stars treated as fixed reference points
items: measures Earth's true rotation relative to stars
stars treated as fixed reference points

cards.front: Name the three poets studied in the Identity & Heritage lesson, with their poems.
cards.answer: Raman Mundair — Name Journeys / Seni Seneviratne — A Wider View / Grace Nichols — Like an Heiress

cards.front: Which three techniques does Nichols use in 'Like an Heiress'?
cards.answer: Simile in the title / Personification of the ocean's moodswings / A sonnet written in free verse
items: A sonnet written in free verse

cards.front: How does Seneviratne's 'A Wider View' use the Dark Arches to link past and present?
cards.answer: The Dark Arches, finished in 1869, appear in both timelines, so past and future generations arc between the speaker and her ancestor.

cards.front: Why is writing in English itself a form of reclamation for these three poets?
cards.answer: They are women of colour using the coloniser's language to celebrate colonised cultures English tried to suppress.

cards.front: Why can prison increase reoffending through social learning?
cards.answer: Offenders can learn further criminal behaviour from other prisoners, sometimes called prison being a 'school for crime'.

cards.front: Why did Charlton et al. suggest television had little effect on St Helena children's behaviour?
