cards.answer: The strong community structure, including close adult supervision, may have limited any effect of television.

cards.front: What three techniques does anger management teach offenders to use, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Notice anger triggers / Recognise physical signs of anger / Use relaxation or stepping away

title: Columbus's Sponsorship and the First Voyage of 1492
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three motives the lesson gives for why Isabella finally sponsored Columbus.
cards.answer: Religious: spread Christianity and fund a crusade / Economic: gold to refill the treasury / Political: match Portugal's exploration lead
items: Religious: spread Christianity and fund a crusade
Economic: gold to refill the treasury

cards.front: Name the two smaller ships (not the flagship) that sailed with Columbus in 1492.
cards.answer: Pinta / Niña

cards.front: Why did Luis de Santángel's intervention succeed in getting Isabella to back Columbus in 1492?
cards.answer: He argued the cost was small, the reward huge, and letting Columbus go to France was too politically risky, appealing to all her motives.

cards.front: Why can't Columbus's original journal be trusted as straightforward evidence?
cards.answer: The original is lost; surviving versions come from Las Casas and Columbus's son Ferdinand, both writing with their own agendas.

cards.front: Why does a warm-up increase the speed of muscle contraction?
cards.answer: Elevated body temperature increases the speed at which nerve impulses travel, improving muscle contraction speed.

cards.front: How does lactic acid get converted back to glucose after exercise?
cards.answer: Maintained blood flow during cool-down transports lactic acid to the liver, where the Cori cycle converts it to glucose.

cards.front: Give the four stages of the conch's journey the lesson traces from Chapter 1 to Chapter 11.
cards.answer: Found and establishes order / Gradually ignored / Restricted to one end of the island / Destroyed alongside Piggy
items: Restricted to one end of the island

cards.front: Name the five symbols the lesson says together map the collapse of civilisation, with their direction of decline.
cards.answer: Conch: democracy to destroyed / Glasses: intellect to stolen / Fire: hope to destructive / Beast: external fear to internal evil / Face paint: identity to deindividuation
items: Beast: external fear to internal evil

cards.front: Why is the ship's failure to rescue the boys in Chapter 4 ironic given what happens in Chapter 12?
cards.answer: The signal fire that could have brought rescue went out, but rescue finally comes from the destructive blaze Jack's tribe sets to kill Ralph.

cards.front: How does the beast show that fear creates the very evil it fears, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Boys project their own savage impulses onto an external monster, avoiding the truth about themselves, which Jack exploits for power.

title: Internal Energy, SHC and Latent Heat
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the five key changes of state described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Melting / Freezing / Evaporation/boiling / Condensation / Sublimation

cards.front: In the specific heat capacity practical (PAG P5), what equipment or steps are used to find the SHC of a metal block?
cards.answer: Drill two holes for thermometer and heater / Measure mass with a balance / Record starting temperature / Switch on heater and record energy with joulemeter / Record final temperature
items: Drill two holes for thermometer and heater
Switch on heater and record energy with joulemeter

cards.front: Why does mass stay the same when a substance changes state?
cards.answer: The same particles are present before and after; only their arrangement and spacing change, not their number.

cards.front: Why is the main source of error in the SHC practical reduced by wrapping the block in insulating material?
cards.answer: Lagging reduces heat lost to the surroundings, so less energy escapes without heating the block.

cards.front: Name the three ways form reinforces content across Brontë, Bridges and Landon's nature poems.
cards.answer: Brontë's short lines/hymn-like metre show spiritual intensity / Bridges's regular rhyme scheme mirrors the steady stream / Landon's expansive flowing structure reflects the vastness of the sea
items: Brontë's short lines/hymn-like metre show spiritual intensity
Bridges's regular rhyme scheme mirrors the steady stream
Landon's expansive flowing structure reflects the vastness of the sea

cards.front: Why does Bridges use a regular rhyme scheme and gentle rhythm in 'Clear and Gentle Stream'?
cards.answer: To mirror the steady flow of the water, reinforcing the idea of nature as calm and unchanging.

cards.front: How does Landon use imaginative play to create a sense of belonging in 'Captain Cook'?
cards.answer: The children turn the garden pond into the South Seas and water lilies into islands, anchoring their shared memory.

cards.front: How does the ending of 'Captain Cook' show nature marking loss as well as joy?
cards.answer: The garden is ploughed up and the closeness with her brother fades, so the imagined world is destroyed too.

title: John versus the Pope: The Interdict and Its Aftermath
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What four crises threatened John simultaneously by 1212-13, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: French invasion fleet / papal deposition sentence / baronial assassination plot / loss of religious legitimacy from Interdict
items: loss of religious legitimacy from Interdict

cards.front: How did John raise money for the Crown during the Interdict?
cards.answer: He seized bishops' lands and revenues, extorted fines from clergy, tallaged Cistercian monasteries, and imposed the Bristol Tallage on Jews.

cards.front: Why did John's 1213 submission to the Pope remove the threat of French invasion?
cards.answer: Because England was now a papal fief, Philip's invading fleet would be attacking land under the Pope's protection.

cards.front: Name the five main methods of sound creation covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Physical props / Environmental sounds / Sound synthesis / Digital sample manipulation / Effects libraries

cards.front: Name the three main sources of an effects library given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Commercial libraries / Online libraries / DAW loops

cards.front: Why are environmental recordings edited to loop seamlessly?
cards.answer: So a short recording can be used as a continuous ambience track throughout a production.

cards.front: How does mapping and looping turn a single violin sample into a playable instrument?
cards.answer: The sample is imported, mapped across the keyboard at different pitches, and looped so it can sustain indefinitely.

title: Performance Interpretation: Sephy and Callum's First Confrontation
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Why might a performer playing Callum move upstage while Cross characters stay downstage?
cards.answer: To create a visual grammar the audience reads as social exclusion, showing his learned habit of not taking up space.

cards.front: How might a performer show Sephy's growing awareness of her own privilege during a conversation?
cards.answer: By speeding up in enthusiasm then abruptly slowing when she realises she has said something revealing her privilege.

cards.front: Why do directors use maximum physical proximity, fully facing, in the hostage scene and Hadley garden exchanges?
cards.answer: To show moments of genuine connection between Sephy and Callum, with the vulnerability that full openness entails.

cards.front: What makes a performer's stillness under interrogation communicate control or fear rather than nothing at all?
cards.answer: Small involuntary movements like a swallow or tightening around the eyes betray the interior state beneath deliberate stillness.

title: Themes: continuity and change in Soviet history
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four social changes the lesson lists for the Soviet Union 1924-1991.
cards.answer: Mass literacy achieved / Life expectancy rose / Urbanisation transformed society / Women entered the workforce in large numbers
items: Women entered the workforce in large numbers

cards.front: Why did superpower status conceal serious weaknesses in the Soviet Union by 1991?
cards.answer: Matching US military spending meant neglecting consumer industries, satellite states were held by force, and the Afghan War exposed military limits.

cards.front: Name the three common waveform shapes shown on a voltage-time graph for amplifier signals.
cards.answer: Sine wave / Square wave / Triangular wave

cards.front: Name the three ways to prevent clipping in an amplifier circuit.
cards.answer: Reduce the input amplitude / Reduce the gain / Increase the supply voltage

cards.front: Why does clipping produce a harsh, buzzing sound in audio amplifiers?
cards.answer: The flat tops of the clipped wave contain many high-frequency harmonic components not present in the original sine wave.

cards.front: Why do high-gain amplifiers only suit applications needing a narrow band of frequencies, like a single radio station?
cards.answer: Because the gain-bandwidth product is fixed, so increasing gain automatically narrows the bandwidth available.

cards.front: Name the three tragedians whose plays survive from the City Dionysia.
cards.answer: Aeschylus / Sophocles / Euripides

cards.front: What three things happened during the Lupercalia ritual, from sacrifice to the run around the Palatine?
cards.answer: Goats and a dog sacrificed in the Lupercal cave / Priests called Luperci ran near-naked around the Palatine Hill / They struck people with strips of animal skin
items: Goats and a dog sacrificed in the Lupercal cave
Priests called Luperci ran near-naked around the Palatine Hill
They struck people with strips of animal skin

cards.front: Why did Pericles use the Panathenaia and the rebuilding of the Acropolis?
cards.answer: To assert Athenian supremacy over the Delian League, showing power as well as religious devotion.

cards.front: Why is the ritual inversion of norms during the Saturnalia described as 'controlled'?
cards.answer: Because it reinforced normal hierarchy by making the reversal a temporary holiday rather than a permanent change.

title: Sea Power, the Navigation Acts and the Dutch Wars
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four things mercantilist theory said a nation must do to prosper.
cards.answer: Export more than it imports / Hoard bullion / Found colonies for raw materials / Protect trade with monopoly companies

cards.front: What three things did Samuel Pepys reform in the navy after 1668?
cards.answer: Naval victualling / Pay / Shipbuilding contracts

cards.front: Why did England go to war with the Dutch in 1665?
cards.answer: Trade rivalry, the seizure of New Amsterdam the year before, and skirmishes off West Africa caused the Second Dutch War.

cards.front: How did Parliament's response to the Third Dutch War affect royal power?
cards.answer: Parliament used its control of money to force Charles into peace, so he never again pushed an open alliance with France.

title: The Story: Winter to the Last Summer
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Why does the physical theatre company stage Mark's arrival on top of the shed in the rain?
cards.answer: To create a single naturalistic image linking his tree-top monologue directly to the news he is about to deliver.

cards.front: Why does Bob feel lost during his spring anniversary confession to Fran?
cards.answer: He took redundancy from the car factory in his fifties and has never replaced work with a new sense of purpose.

cards.front: Why did Fran keep her savings hidden from Bob?
cards.answer: She needed to know she could leave Bob if she ever had to.

cards.front: Why does the phone call framing device make the audience fear for one of Bob's children?
cards.answer: It trains the audience to expect bad news about a child, so Fran's death is never considered a possibility.

cards.front: What are the four types of base an acid can react with, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Metal / Metal oxide / Metal hydroxide / Metal carbonate

cards.front: Name the six steps given for preparing pure, dry copper sulfate crystals.
cards.answer: Warm dilute sulfuric acid / Add excess copper oxide, stir / Filter off excess copper oxide / Pour solution into evaporating basin / Heat on water bath until crystals form / Pat dry with filter paper
items: Heat on water bath until crystals form

cards.front: Why is excess insoluble reactant added when making a soluble salt this way?
cards.answer: The excess base ensures all the acid has reacted, so it can be filtered off leaving just the salt solution.

cards.front: How does the test for hydrogen work?
cards.answer: A burning splint is held near the gas and it burns with a squeaky pop if hydrogen is present.

title: The Loss of Normandy: Château Gaillard and 1204
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three rulers and their competing aims over Normandy that the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Richard I wanted to recover lost ground and fortify the frontier / John wanted recognition as lawful heir at almost any price / Philip II wanted to absorb Normandy into the French crown
items: Richard I wanted to recover lost ground and fortify the frontier
John wanted recognition as lawful heir at almost any price
Philip II wanted to absorb Normandy into the French crown

cards.front: Name the five causes the lesson gives for why Normandy fell in 1204.
cards.answer: Baronial loyalty drained by Arthur's murder and Lusignan affair / John refused to commit decisively in the field / Philip concentrated his force on one decisive point / Richard's ransom and crusade had drained the treasury / Château Gaillard could not hold without outside relief
items: Baronial loyalty drained by Arthur's murder and Lusignan affair
John refused to commit decisively in the field
Philip concentrated his force on one decisive point
Richard's ransom and crusade had drained the treasury
Château Gaillard could not hold without outside relief

cards.front: Why did the Lusignan appeal of 1202 give Philip II his trigger for war?
cards.answer: Because John's French lands were technically held in vassalage to Philip, so the appeal let Philip's court legally declare John's fiefs forfeit.

cards.front: Why does the lesson argue the loss of Normandy was not inevitable?
cards.answer: The Angevin Empire was larger and richer than France in 1199, and specific decisions like Arthur's murder and the Lusignan affair, not Channel geography, triggered the loss.

title: Analysing Design: Set, Lighting, Sound, Costume
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four design disciplines the lesson says a review should cover.
cards.answer: Lighting / Sound / Set / Costume

cards.front: Why does back lighting on a character suggest mystery or loss of identity?
cards.answer: Back lighting creates a silhouette, hiding the individual's features and suggesting mystery or loss of identity.

cards.front: Why might a small figure on an enormous set suggest the individual is overwhelmed?
cards.answer: The contrast in scale between the tiny performer and the huge set reads as the individual overwhelmed by forces beyond their control.

cards.front: Why is 'the lighting was atmospheric' not a strong piece of design analysis?
cards.answer: It is too general because it does not name the lantern, colour, direction or effect, so it shows no real understanding of how design communicates meaning.

cards.front: Why does Lady Macbeth lose her sanity in the sleepwalking scene, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: She suppressed natural feelings like guilt and remorse, which drove them underground until they resurfaced and destroyed her mind.

cards.front: How does the light and darkness motif reverse between the start of the play and the sleepwalking scene?
cards.answer: Characters who once called on darkness to hide their crimes, like Lady Macbeth, now cling desperately to light out of fear.

title: Whiplash: Cutting, Sound and Pursuit of Greatness
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: How did Whiplash's $3 million budget shape its visual style?
cards.answer: Limited resources meant Chazelle focused visual energy on controlled interior spaces like rehearsal rooms and jazz venues.

cards.front: Why does the opening solo-drumming sequence cut to Fletcher standing still in the doorway?
cards.answer: The juxtaposition of Andrew's kinetic energy against Fletcher's stillness establishes the film's central power dynamic before dialogue begins.

cards.front: How does Whiplash use diegetic music as its score?
cards.answer: The music characters perform is foregrounded as subject matter and emotional driver, fusing aesthetic pleasure with moral stakes.

cards.front: According to Bordwell's concept of narration, how does the closing sequence position the spectator?
cards.answer: Chazelle withholds moral resolution, so spectacular form creates exhilaration exactly when the moral reading feels most uncomfortable.

cards.front: What four restrictions did Mississippi's Black Codes and similar laws place on freedpeople, as given in the lesson?
cards.answer: Limits on movement / Limits on changing jobs / Ban on owning property in towns / Ban on testifying in court against white men
items: Ban on owning property in towns
Ban on testifying in court against white men

cards.front: Why did Northerners come to see the Black Codes as recreating slavery under another name?
cards.answer: Because they restricted freedpeople's movement, jobs, property and legal rights, and used vagrancy laws to force Black people into forced labour for white employers.

cards.front: How did the 1867 Reconstruction Acts force change in the South?
cards.answer: They divided the South into five military districts, suspended existing state governments, and required new constitutions guaranteeing Black male suffrage before rejoining the Union.

cards.front: Why did most freedpeople end up trapped in poverty despite gaining legal freedom?
cards.answer: Because Johnson rescinded land redistribution, so freedpeople became sharecroppers whose debt and crop failures kept them poor for life.

title: NATO, Warsaw Pact and the Berlin Wall
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the eight founding member countries the lesson gives for the Warsaw Pact.
cards.answer: USSR / Poland / Czechoslovakia / Hungary / East Germany / Romania / Bulgaria / Albania

cards.front: Why did the Warsaw Pact give the USSR real military control over Eastern Europe, not just an alliance on paper?
cards.answer: Soviet commanders held the top military posts and Soviet forces could legally be stationed in member states.

title: The Problem of Evil and Catholic Responses
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What three attributes of God create the logical tension in the problem of evil (sometimes called the Epicurean trilemma)?
cards.answer: Omnipotent (all-powerful) / Omniscient (all-knowing) / All-loving

cards.front: Why did Augustine argue that God gave humans free will despite the risk of evil?
cards.answer: Because love that is freely chosen is infinitely more valuable than love that is compelled.

cards.front: How does Irenaeus's idea of 'epistemic distance' explain why God remains hidden?
cards.answer: So humans can freely choose to trust God rather than being overwhelmed into belief by his direct presence.

title: Hormones, the Menstrual Cycle and Plant Hormones
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four non-hormonal contraception methods the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Condoms / Diaphragms / Copper IUDs / Surgical sterilisation

cards.front: Name the four types of hormonal contraception the lesson lists.
cards.answer: Combined pill / Mini-pill / Implants / Injections

cards.front: Why does thyroxine stay at a stable level in the body?
cards.answer: Negative feedback: high thyroxine reduces TSH release from the pituitary, and low thyroxine increases TSH, controlling thyroid output.

cards.front: How does oestrogen control the timing of ovulation in the menstrual cycle?
cards.answer: Oestrogen inhibits further FSH production and stimulates the release of LH, whose surge around day 14 triggers ovulation.

cards.front: Give the three reasons the lesson states for why Shakespeare keeps Duncan's murder offstage.
cards.answer: Showing an anointed king murdered would offend a Jacobean audience / Forces audience to focus on psychological consequences not violence / Maintains sympathy for Macbeth
items: Showing an anointed king murdered would offend a Jacobean audience
Forces audience to focus on psychological consequences not violence

cards.front: How does the reversal of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth's reactions to guilt develop between Act 2 and Act 5?
cards.answer: In Act 2 Macbeth is guilt-ridden while Lady Macbeth is calm, but by Act 5 Macbeth is numb to violence while she is destroyed by guilt.

cards.front: What does the Porter's joke about an 'equivocator' connect to in the play?
cards.answer: It connects to the play's theme of deception, as an equivocator lies by telling half-truths.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says redemption requires before Scrooge can genuinely change.
cards.answer: Self-awareness (confronting the past) / Empathy (understanding others' suffering) / Fear of consequences (facing death)

cards.front: Name the five steps the lesson gives for the wider-text strategy.
cards.answer: Don't repeat the extract task / Plan by thinking about each stave / Use memorised quotations / Remember context isn't assessed / Link to Dickens's purpose
items: Plan by thinking about each stave

cards.front: How does Dickens show that Scrooge's redemption is genuine rather than just words?
cards.answer: Scrooge acts through atonement — sending the turkey, donating to charity, attending Fred's party and raising Cratchit's salary.

cards.front: Why does the extract task reward only AO2 while the wider-text task rewards only AO1?
cards.answer: The extract task tests analysis of language, form and structure, while the wider-text task tests your own argument across the whole novella using quotations.

cards.front: What three stages make up Pip's Bildungsroman character arc?
cards.answer: Innocence / Corruption / Redemption

cards.front: Why does Estella's true parentage undermine the class distinction between her and Pip?
cards.answer: It reveals the girl who called Pip 'common' is herself the daughter of a convict, showing class is a social construction, not biological.

cards.front: How does Magwitch serve as a foil to both Miss Havisham and Compeyson?
cards.answer: He earned his money through hard labour and used it for good, unlike Miss Havisham's inherited wealth and revenge, and unlike Compeyson's deceitful gentlemanly appearance.

cards.front: Why does Dickens present Joe as his ideal of a true gentleman despite his lack of education?
cards.answer: Joe is kind, honest, loyal and shows unconditional love, proving true worth is moral rather than social.

cards.front: Name the three gas tests used in the electrolysis of aqueous solutions practical.
cards.answer: Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop / Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper / Oxygen relights a glowing splint
items: Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop

cards.front: In aqueous electrolysis, how do you know whether a halogen or oxygen forms at the anode?
cards.answer: If a halide ion is present the halogen is produced; if not, oxygen is produced from hydroxide ions.

title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the six changes of state described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Melting / Freezing / Evaporation/Boiling / Condensation / Sublimation / Deposition

cards.front: Why do aircraft need low-density materials while ship anchors need high-density materials?
cards.answer: Aircraft need low density to reduce weight, while anchors need high density to sink effectively.

cards.front: Why does a substance's density usually change when it changes state?
cards.answer: The particles become more or less tightly packed, changing the volume while the mass stays the same.

cards.front: Name the three unnatural events Ross and the Old Man describe after Duncan's murder in Act 2 Scene 4.
cards.answer: Sun blocked by dark night / Falcon killed by an owl / Duncan's horses turn wild and eat each other
items: Duncan's horses turn wild and eat each other

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson says Macbeth flatters King James I.
cards.answer: Set in Scotland, James's homeland / Based on Holinshed's Chronicles, a source James knew / Traces Banquo's descendants as future kings of Scotland
items: Based on Holinshed's Chronicles, a source James knew
Traces Banquo's descendants as future kings of Scotland

cards.front: Why did Shakespeare write Macbeth as a play about Scottish witchcraft and regicide?
cards.answer: To please King James I, who was fascinated by witchcraft, and to warn against the dangers of regicide.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare use the witches' language to make them seem unnatural?
cards.answer: The witches speak in trochaic tetrameter instead of the iambic pentameter used by noble characters, making them sound otherworldly.

title: The Revolt of the Northern Earls, 1569–70
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four causes the lesson gives for why the Northern Earls rebelled.
cards.answer: Loss of noble power under Elizabeth / Religious grievance over the 1559 settlement / Mary, Queen of Scots' arrival in 1568 / The Norfolk marriage scheme
items: Loss of noble power under Elizabeth
Mary, Queen of Scots' arrival in 1568

cards.front: Name the four consequences the lesson says the revolt triggered.
cards.answer: 1570 papal bull excommunicating Elizabeth / 1571 Treasons Act / Harsher recusancy fines / Rise of plots centred on Mary
items: Rise of plots centred on Mary

cards.front: How did Elizabeth's loss of noble power contribute to the revolt?
cards.answer: Elizabeth had taken back Crown lands from northern lords, promoted 'new men' like Cecil, and cut the old Council of the North's role, angering the Earls.

cards.front: Why did the failure of the Northern Rebellion change the type of threat Elizabeth faced afterwards?
cards.answer: Open military rebellion had failed, so Catholic resistance moved underground into secret plots like Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington.

cards.front: Name the four soft engineering methods for flood management given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Tree planting in upper catchments / Restoring straightened meanders / Beach nourishment with imported sand / Managed realignment

cards.front: Name the two reasons the lesson gives for rising flood risk in the UK.
cards.answer: Climate change bringing more intense rainfall / Urban growth paving over absorbent fields
items: Climate change bringing more intense rainfall
Urban growth paving over absorbent fields

cards.front: Why did house prices rise so much relative to earnings in the Lake District?
cards.answer: Second-home conversions pushed average house prices to over 11 times local earnings, driving young workers away.

cards.front: How did the Pickering 'Slowing the Flow' scheme reduce flooding in the town?
cards.answer: Planting trees, building leaky dams and a storage reservoir slowed run-off, cutting peak river flow by 15-20%.

title: Promoting Health & Well-being — Role, Purpose & Supporting Individuals
subject: health-social-care-eduqas

cards.front: Why is providing information alone rarely enough to change someone's lifestyle behaviour?
cards.answer: Individuals also need to feel the changes are achievable and relevant to their own lives.

cards.front: Why is a generic leaflet less effective than culturally appropriate, personalised information?
cards.answer: Information at the right literacy level and in a person's first language is more likely to enable behaviour change.

cards.front: Why does Shylock refuse to show mercy in the trial scene?
cards.answer: He has never received mercy himself, so he refuses to grant it to others.

cards.front: How does the casket test's moral lesson get contradicted by the wider play?
cards.answer: It teaches humility over appearance, yet Bassanio still needs borrowed money to reach Belmont.

cards.front: Name the four key themes the lesson identifies in The Merchant of Venice.
cards.answer: Prejudice and anti-Semitism / Mercy versus justice / Wealth, commerce and value / Identity and appearance

cards.front: Why is each boy fascinated by the other's language and vocabulary?
cards.answer: Eddie envies Mickey's rough slang and swear words, while Mickey is impressed by Eddie's confidence and knowledge, showing each envies what the other has.

cards.front: Why does Russell use the twins' childhood friendship to make a political point about class?
cards.answer: At seven they see no class barriers and like each other for who they are, showing class division is socially constructed by adults, not natural.

cards.front: What three things does Shelley say the abandoned Creature is denied, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Parental guidance / Love / Language

cards.front: Why does Shelley use pathetic fallacy in the opening line of the creation scene?
cards.answer: The 'dreary' night signals that the creation is a catastrophe, not a triumph, undercutting Victor's sense of achievement.

cards.front: Why does Shelley describe the Creature as both beautiful and horrifying at once?
cards.answer: The contrast creates an uncanny effect, close enough to human to be recognisable but different enough to be disturbing.

cards.front: How does Victor's illness after the creation reflect his psychological state?
cards.answer: His nervous fever is a physical manifestation of the guilt his mind cannot process after abandoning the Creature.

cards.front: Name the four types of data the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Quantitative (numbers) / Qualitative (words/descriptions) / Primary (collected first-hand by this researcher) / Secondary (collected previously by someone else)

cards.front: Why is the mean sensitive to outliers?
cards.answer: Because the mean uses all the data, so a single extreme value can pull it up or down significantly.

cards.front: Why is a weakness of using secondary data in a study?
cards.answer: The data may not perfectly match the current research question, and the researcher cannot control its quality.

cards.front: Why is the normal distribution important in psychology?
cards.answer: Many statistical tests assume data is normally distributed, and it acts as a benchmark for judging how typical a score is.

cards.front: Name the four essential interior features every synagogue contains.
cards.answer: The Ark (Aron Kodesh) / The Bimah / The Ner Tamid / The Sefer Torah

cards.front: Name four ways Jews worship or pray at home, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Fixing a mezuzah to the doorpost / Lighting Shabbat candles on Friday evening / Reciting blessings over wine and bread / Teaching children to pray
items: Fixing a mezuzah to the doorpost
Lighting Shabbat candles on Friday evening
Reciting blessings over wine and bread

cards.front: Why is the yad used when reading from the Sefer Torah?
cards.answer: So the sacred text is never touched directly by bare fingers.

cards.front: Why were local synagogues seen as having religious authority even though the Temple was destroyed?
cards.answer: Ezekiel had described G-d as a 'little sanctuary' for the people in exile, giving authority to local prayer places.

cards.front: Why does Aaron have no sense of true identity at the Foundling Hospital?
cards.answer: He was given a new name, has no surname, and possesses no token linking him to his real parents.

cards.front: How does Aaron's musical gift connect him to his father Alexander?
cards.answer: Aaron inherits an extraordinary singing voice from Alexander, an invisible thread linking father and son without either knowing it.

cards.front: Name the four comfortless details of the flat where Jo and Helen live, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Broken heating / Leaking roof / One bed to share / A view of a slaughterhouse

cards.front: Name the three instruments in the live jazz trio used in Theatre Workshop's original production.
cards.answer: Cornet / Guitar / Double bass

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to call A Taste of Honey simply 'naturalistic'?
cards.answer: Its dialogue and content are realist, but its original staging used direct address, songs, dance and a live band, which are stylised devices.

cards.front: Why was sex between men in 1958 a key context for Geof's character throughout the play?
cards.answer: Sex between men was illegal under an 1885 law, making Geof's private life a criminal offence for the entire play.

cards.front: Name the three ways the lesson describes cities reshaping themselves internally (besides growth).
cards.answer: Suburbanisation / Counter-urbanisation / Re-urbanisation

cards.front: Name the four push factors the lesson gives for rural-urban migration.
cards.answer: Rural poverty / Mechanisation reducing farm labour needs / Drought or land degradation / Limited access to schools or hospitals
items: Limited access to schools or hospitals

cards.front: Why does migration to cities accelerate urban growth even further over time?
cards.answer: Migrants are typically young adults of working age, so once they arrive they have children, boosting natural increase.

cards.front: Why do developed countries now have slow or slightly negative urban growth?
cards.answer: They are already 80% or more urban and people are retiring to the coast or countryside instead.

cards.front: Why does Miller's formal, controlled stage language make John and Elizabeth Proctor's unspoken feelings more powerful in the linen scene?
cards.answer: Because the surface language is so controlled and formal, the subtext beneath it becomes more powerful and noticeable.

cards.front: Why does dramatic irony in the courtroom scenes carry political weight for Miller's 1953 audience?
cards.answer: Audiences were living through McCarthyism, where accusation counted as proof and telling the truth was dangerous, just as in the play.

cards.front: Why does Proctor tear up the signed confession in the final act instead of saving his life?
cards.answer: Because surrendering his name would betray his integrity, and Miller stages this as showing integrity is the only response to a system built on lies.

cards.front: Why is treating The Crucible like a novel (discussing only metaphors and themes) considered a mistake in analysing it?
cards.answer: Drama is a performance art, so Miller's intentions only matter if explained through how staging, vocal and physical choices realise them.

title: The Catholic Question: Popish Plot and Rye House Plot
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three existing fears the lesson gives that made the country primed to believe the Popish Plot.
cards.answer: Louis XIV's dominant Catholic France / Charles II's secret Treaty of Dover with French money / James, Duke of York's open conversion to Catholicism
items: Charles II's secret Treaty of Dover with French money
James, Duke of York's open conversion to Catholicism

cards.front: Why did Edward Coleman's letters make Oates's fabricated story seem believable?
cards.answer: The letters were genuinely incriminating about wider Catholic plans, so seizing them seemed to confirm Oates's claims even though Coleman knew nothing of the assassination story.

cards.front: How did the Rye House Plot allow Charles II to weaken Whig power in borough corporations?
cards.answer: The government used quo warranto writs to challenge corporation charters, forcing boroughs to surrender them and accept new charters giving the Crown veto power.

title: The Five Pillars and Ten Obligatory Acts
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam.
cards.answer: Shahadah / Salah / Zakah / Sawm / Hajj

cards.front: What four Hajj rites does the lesson describe?
cards.answer: Tawaf (circling Ka'aba seven times) / Walking between Safa and Marwa / Standing on the plain of Arafat / Stoning the devil
items: Standing on the plain of Arafat

cards.front: How does Hajj create a sense of equality among pilgrims?
cards.answer: Male pilgrims all wear the same plain white ihram and women wear simple modest dress, erasing distinctions of wealth and rank.

cards.front: Why is Shahadah not included among the Ten Obligatory Acts in Shi'a Islam?
cards.answer: Shi'a Islam places belief in the oneness of Allah among the Five Roots instead of the Ten Obligatory Acts.

cards.front: Name the four quarters of the planning method for the anthology comparison question, in order.
cards.answer: Read question and named poem, underline/circle / Choose comparison poem sharing the theme / Jot 2-3 quotations with technique and effect / Write one-sentence thesis and paragraph plan
items: Read question and named poem, underline/circle
Choose comparison poem sharing the theme
Jot 2-3 quotations with technique and effect
Write one-sentence thesis and paragraph plan

cards.front: Name the five common pitfalls listed for the anthology comparison essay.
cards.answer: Feature-spotting without analysis / Retelling the poem / Writing about poems separately / Ignoring form and structure / Vague context

cards.front: Why must every paragraph in the anthology comparison answer discuss both poems together?
cards.answer: Because writing about poems separately is a listed pitfall — the task requires genuine comparison, not description of each poem alone.

cards.front: Why is naming a specific historical event or biographical detail better than saying a poem 'was written a long time ago'?
cards.answer: Because vague context earns nothing, whereas specific movements, events or biographical details show precise contextual understanding.

cards.front: Name the three responses to mortality the three guardians represent in Never Let Me Go.
cards.answer: Miss Emily: justification / Madame: guilt / Miss Lucy: rebellion/truth-telling

cards.front: Why does Kathy's narration count as an act of resistance despite her calm tone?
cards.answer: By telling her story and memorialising Tommy, Ruth and Hailsham, she asserts her humanity even though she was conditioned not to rage.

cards.front: Why does Madame cry when she sees Kathy dancing to 'Never Let Me Go'?
cards.answer: Her tears suggest deep, conflicted emotion — she is repulsed by clones yet secretly compassionate towards them.

cards.front: Name the four sustainable UK transport options the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Electric vehicles / Rail electrification / Active travel infrastructure / Bus franchising

cards.front: Name the three ways the Lake District National Park Authority responds to tourism pressure.
cards.answer: Footpath repair / Sustainable farming grants under Environmental Land Management schemes / Limits on second-home conversions in some parishes

cards.front: Why has footpath erosion become a problem at popular Lake District peaks like Helvellyn?
cards.answer: High visitor numbers, around 18 million a year, wear down footpaths at popular peaks through constant foot traffic.

cards.front: Why was HS2 scaled back in 2023 seen as a setback for sustainable transport?
cards.answer: It was reduced to just a London-Birmingham line, leaving northern England feeling short-changed on rail investment.

cards.front: Name the three definitions of history given in the play.
cards.answer: Performance and entertainment (Irwin) / Commentary on male failure (Mrs Lintott) / Cultural inheritance between generations (Hector)

cards.front: Why are Posner and Mrs Lintott the only characters who do not perform?
cards.answer: Posner is painfully honest about his identity and Mrs Lintott sees through everyone else's performances, showing Bennett links authenticity to being marginalised.

cards.front: In extract-based exam questions, why is background context not enough on its own?
cards.answer: Background may sharpen a point but only close analysis of quotations, language and structure in the extract is credited.

cards.front: Name the four key erosional landforms produced by glacial plucking and abrasion in upland areas.
cards.answer: Corries / Arêtes / Pyramidal peaks / U-shaped glacial troughs

cards.front: Give the three ways people use UK glaciated uplands today, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Sheep farming / Conifer forestry plantations / Settlement and tourism in valleys / Reservoirs for water supply

cards.front: Why do truncated spurs form when a glacier flows down a valley?
cards.answer: The glacier widens, deepens and straightens the valley, shearing off the interlocking spurs of the original river valley.

cards.front: How does a terminal moraine form at the end of a glacier?
cards.answer: Rock debris piles up at the glacier's snout because ice melts as fast as it advances, forming a curved ridge.

title: Sources and interpretations: how 1951-79 has been remembered
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four pieces of evidence the Thatcherite narrative emphasises about 1951-1979.
cards.answer: IMF crisis of 1976 / Winter of Discontent 1978-79 / Slow growth vs West Germany and France / High inflation of the mid-1970s
items: Slow growth vs West Germany and France

cards.front: Name the four groups whose experiences oral history has recovered for this period.
cards.answer: Caribbean migrants arriving 1940s-50s / Women in women's liberation campaigns / Miners in the 1972 and 1974 strikes / Catholic families in early Troubles

cards.front: Why did Andy Beckett challenge the dominant memory of the 1970s as a decade of gloom?
cards.answer: He argued the decade also had genuine creativity and change, like punk, feminism, gay liberation and environmentalism, showing the Thatcherite narrative caricatured it.

cards.front: Why can't oral testimony from 2005 about events in 1968 be taken as a simple record of 1968?
cards.answer: Memory is fallible and testimony may be shaped by later experiences, so it can reflect as much about 2005 as 1968.

cards.front: The lesson names four site features that explain the Armada's fate through chains of feature and consequence. What are they?
cards.answer: Missing deep-water port / Open roadstead at Calais / Sandbanks off Zeeland / Beacon chains and home ports / North-about route home

cards.front: Why was the English fleet able to react faster to the Armada's movements than Philip's planners could?
cards.answer: Chains of hilltop beacons carried the alarm across southern England in hours, while Philip's planners worked on months-old information.

cards.front: Why did the Armada almost get wrecked on the Zeeland sandbanks off Gravelines?
cards.answer: The wind pushed the battered fleet towards shoaling water with no sea room, and only a last-moment wind shift let it escape.

cards.front: Why did cutting anchor cables to escape the fireships at Calais cause so many wrecks weeks later?
cards.answer: Ships without anchors could not hold themselves off the storm coasts of Scotland and Ireland during the autumn gales.

title: Empire, Slavery and the End of the Reign 1685
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three chartered companies that drove English overseas expansion under Charles II.
cards.answer: East India Company / Royal African Company / Hudson's Bay Company

cards.front: What did Catherine of Braganza's 1662 dowry give England, besides £300,000 in cash?
cards.answer: Bombay / Tangier / trading rights in Brazil / trading rights in the Portuguese East Indies
items: trading rights in the Portuguese East Indies

cards.front: Why did planters in Jamaica and Barbados turn to enslaved African labour rather than European workers for sugar production?
cards.answer: A sugar mill needed many workers continuously, but indentured European labour was scarce, expensive and unwilling to do field work in tropical heat.

cards.front: How did the Royal African Company's slave trading differ from earlier English slaving voyages?
cards.answer: It flowed through a royally chartered company with the Crown itself as a shareholder, a major escalation from earlier private voyages.

title: Robert Peel and the birth of the Metropolitan Police
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four recruitment standards required of Peel's new police officers.
cards.answer: Under 35 years old / At least 5 feet 7 inches tall / Literate / Of good character

cards.front: Why did Peel's police wear a blue coat instead of military red and carry only a truncheon?
cards.answer: To make the force look deliberately civilian and reassure a public fearful of a French-style state spying force.

cards.front: Why did Peel's constables patrol fixed beats rather than investigate crimes after they happened?
cards.answer: So the public knew which officer to expect and the officer learned the local people, aiming for prevention through visible presence.

cards.front: Why did Peel reform the Bloody Code before setting up the Metropolitan Police?
cards.answer: Harsh laws were more enforceable when paired with proportionate punishment, preparing the ground for a police force.

cards.front: Why does Boxer's loyalty make him especially vulnerable to Napoleon's control?
cards.answer: His genuine trust means he cannot imagine someone he trusts would betray him, so he never questions Napoleon.

cards.front: How does the changed commandment about beds show Orwell's point about education and manipulation?
cards.answer: The animals cannot read well enough to challenge the subtle change, showing uneducated populations are vulnerable to manipulation.

cards.front: Name the three golf etiquette customs the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Repair divots / Rake bunkers / Maintain silence when others are playing
items: Maintain silence when others are playing

cards.front: Name the three gamesmanship examples the lesson gives from different sports.
cards.answer: Excessive ball bouncing before serving in tennis / Lying on wrong side of ruck in rugby / Changing gloves to break bowler's rhythm in cricket
items: Excessive ball bouncing before serving in tennis
Lying on wrong side of ruck in rugby
Changing gloves to break bowler's rhythm in cricket

cards.front: Why does the contract to compete matter for fair play in sport?
cards.answer: Without it, sport would allow any unethical tactic as long as it helped a competitor win.

cards.front: How does a fielding side in cricket traditionally show etiquette towards a batsman?
cards.answer: By applauding a departing batsman who has played well, even though this is not required by the rules.

title: Sea Level Change and Drowned Forests
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name three pieces of evidence used to confirm Doggerland once existed as inhabited dry land.
cards.answer: Worked flint tools dredged up / Animal bones dredged up / Land bridge exposed at low sea level 120m below present
items: Land bridge exposed at low sea level 120m below present

cards.front: Why is southern England slowly sinking relative to sea level while Scotland is rising?
cards.answer: Southern England is further from the centre of ice loading, so it is tilting downward as the crust readjusts, unlike Scotland which is rebounding upward.

cards.front: How does radiocarbon dating of peat beneath British drowned forests support the theory of post-glacial sea level rise?
cards.answer: Dating gives ages of roughly 4,000–8,000 years, showing the land was submerged during early Holocene sea level rise after ice retreat.

cards.front: Name the three main causes of the doubling of global water demand since 1975.
cards.answer: Population growth / Rising affluence / Industrialisation in emerging economies

cards.front: What are the two drawbacks of desalination given in the lesson, besides high cost?
cards.answer: Heavy energy use, often fossil-fuel-powered / Salty brine discharged into coastal waters
items: Salty brine discharged into coastal waters

cards.front: Why does agricultural water use take up a much bigger share of total water in developing countries than in developed ones?
cards.answer: Irrigation is essential to feed growing populations and earn foreign currency from food exports, while developed countries often import food instead.

cards.front: Why does waterborne disease kill so many children in poorer countries?
cards.answer: Rivers are polluted by untreated sewage, factory waste and fertiliser run-off, and many lack access to treated drinking water at home.

cards.front: Name the three musculo-skeletal long-term adaptations to training given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Muscle hypertrophy / Increased bone density / Stronger ligaments and tendons

cards.front: Why does a trained athlete's heart rate recover faster after exercise than an untrained person's?
cards.answer: Their higher resting stroke volume means the cardiovascular system achieves adequate oxygen delivery even at lower heart rates.

cards.front: Why does hypertrophy require adequate rest to occur?
cards.answer: Muscle fibres are damaged by training, and satellite cells repair and grow them during rest, not during the session itself.

cards.front: How does Harri's immigrant experience create both opportunity and vulnerability in Pigeon English?
cards.answer: His family came to London for a better life, but estate life falls far short of that dream, exposing him to danger.

cards.front: Why does every paragraph of a Modern Text essay need to answer 'what is Kelman doing here, and why?'
cards.answer: So the essay analyses authorial method and purpose rather than just narrating the plot.

title: Igneous Rocks: Texture, Mineralogy and Classification
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four igneous rock types classified in this lesson.
cards.answer: Peridotite / Basalt / Andesite / Granite

cards.front: What three rock names must you avoid writing because they are outside the four spec igneous rocks?
cards.answer: Gabbro / Dolerite / Rhyolite

cards.front: Why do coarse-grained igneous rocks form?
cards.answer: They cool slowly deep underground, giving crystals time to grow larger than 3 mm.

cards.front: How does the colour of an igneous rock relate to its mineral content?
cards.answer: Colour reflects mineral make-up: dark minerals are iron- and magnesium-rich, pale minerals are silica- and aluminium-rich.

cards.front: Why does Piggy's denial that Simon's death was murder matter thematically?
cards.answer: It shows even the most rational character uses self-deception when confronted with moral horror.

cards.front: Why is the fire that leads to Ralph's rescue ironic?
cards.answer: It was lit to kill Ralph, so destruction rather than civilisation is what brings the rescue.

cards.front: The lesson breaks Ralph's final tricolon into three meanings — what are they?
cards.answer: The end of innocence / The darkness of man's heart / The fall through the air of Piggy
items: The fall through the air of Piggy

title: Workers' Rights: General Strike to Thatcher, 1926-1990
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three key Thatcher trade union reforms the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: 1980 Employment Act narrowed picketing / 1982 Act let employers sue unions and restricted closed shop / 1984 Trade Union Act required secret ballots before strikes
items: 1982 Act let employers sue unions and restricted closed shop
1984 Trade Union Act required secret ballots before strikes

cards.front: How did returning to the gold standard in 1925 help trigger the miners' dispute that led to the General Strike?
cards.answer: It over-valued the pound, pricing coal exports out of world markets, so owners demanded wage cuts and longer hours which miners refused.

cards.front: Why did the 1926 General Strike ultimately fail?
cards.answer: The TUC was divided over industrial versus political aims, government preparation via the OMS kept services running, and it lost the propaganda battle with no plan beyond day nine.

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why quality matters to a business.
cards.answer: Protect the reputation of the business / Gain and retain customers / Reduce product returns and recalls
items: Protect the reputation of the business

cards.front: Why did the Toyota 2009–2010 recalls damage the company so heavily?
cards.answer: About 9 million cars across many models were recalled, costing an estimated $2 billion.

title: Dramatic Methods: Verse, Prose and the Sonnet
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: How is the shared sonnet's fourteen lines divided between Romeo and Juliet at the Capulet feast?
cards.answer: Romeo speaks the first quatrain / Juliet answers with the second quatrain / they share the third quatrain between them / the rhyming couplet crowns the exchange
items: Juliet answers with the second quatrain
they share the third quatrain between them
the rhyming couplet crowns the exchange

cards.front: How might a director stage the shared sonnet to show Romeo and Juliet becoming rhythmically coupled?
cards.answer: Have the lovers' proxemics slowly close as the sonnet progresses, so they become close enough to kiss by the couplet.

cards.front: Why must a Drama student translate iambic pentameter into performance decisions rather than just literary analysis?
cards.answer: Because a Drama exam requires the form to become a physical choice, like a pause or dropped gaze, not just a label.

cards.front: How might lighting differ between a direct-address soliloquy and a private, naturalistic one?
cards.answer: Direct address gets a pool of light isolating the character with the rest fading; private delivery gets a warmer, tighter special with a quieter voice.

title: I Wouldn't Thank You for a Valentine
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Name six commercial Valentine's gifts the speaker rejects before the final twist in Lochhead's poem.
cards.answer: Red-padded satin hearts / Interflora red roses / Singing telegrams / Pints of Chanel Five / A solitaire / An orchid

cards.front: How does Lochhead use clashing registers to create the poem's main joke?
cards.answer: She mixes formal romantic vocabulary like 'promises solemn' with slang and Scots phrasing, undercutting grand language with a bored, sarcastic voice.

cards.front: Why is the postcard with three Xs able to succeed where diamonds and orchids failed?
cards.answer: Because it told her how her partner genuinely felt, showing she wants sincerity rather than expensive spectacle.

cards.front: How do you decide whether to use jouer à or faire de for a sport in French?
cards.answer: Use jouer à if it's a ball or team sport, otherwise use faire de for individual sports and activities.

cards.front: How does the past participle change when a subject using être is feminine plural in the passé composé?
cards.answer: Add -es to the past participle to agree with the feminine plural subject.

cards.front: Name the four ways the past participle can change to agree with the subject when using être in the passé composé.
cards.answer: no extra letter (masculine singular) / add -e (feminine) / add -s (masculine plural) / add -es (feminine plural)

title: Wallace, Bruce and the 'Hammer of the Scots', 1297-1307
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four turning points of the First War of Scottish Independence given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Stirling Bridge, September 1297 / Falkirk, July 1298 / Campaign of 1303-04 ending at Strathord / Methven, June 1306

cards.front: Name the three harsh English policies the lesson gives for provoking the 1297 Scottish risings.
cards.answer: Forcing lords to swear loyalty on the Ragman Roll / Taxing Scottish trade for Edward's war chest / Trying to conscript Scots for the French campaign
items: Forcing lords to swear loyalty on the Ragman Roll
Taxing Scottish trade for Edward's war chest
Trying to conscript Scots for the French campaign

cards.front: How did Wallace and Murray win the Battle of Stirling Bridge?
cards.answer: They let the English cross the narrow bridge two abreast, then charged when only half the army had crossed, cutting the vanguard to pieces as the bridge collapsed.

cards.front: How did the English defeat the Scottish schiltrons at Falkirk?
cards.answer: Cavalry charges failed against the schiltrons, so Edward used longbowmen to pour arrows into the static formations until they crumbled, then charged with cavalry.

title: The impact of the First World War on Germany
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five main terms the Treaty of Versailles imposed on Germany.
cards.answer: War guilt (Article 231) / Reparations of £6.6 billion / Loss of 13% of territory / Rhineland demilitarised / Army limited to 100,000 men

cards.front: Why did the use of the Freikorps to crush the Spartacist Rising damage the Weimar Republic?
cards.answer: Ebert used right-wing ex-soldiers to kill left-wing revolutionaries, permanently alienating the German left from his government.

cards.front: Why was the German army seen as a 'state within the state' under Weimar?
cards.answer: It remained largely loyal to the old imperial order and was never fully committed to supporting democratic government.

title: Red Terror, the Cheka and the Kronstadt Mutiny
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: What five demands did the Kronstadt sailors' fifteen-point resolution include (name four)?
cards.answer: Fresh elections to soviets by secret ballot / Freedom of speech and press for socialist parties / Release of political prisoners / End to grain requisitioning / Right of peasants to farm freely
items: Fresh elections to soviets by secret ballot
Freedom of speech and press for socialist parties
Right of peasants to farm freely

cards.front: What three groups did the Cheka target during the Red Terror?
cards.answer: Whites / The bourgeoisie and clergy / The Kadets

cards.front: Why did the Kronstadt Mutiny shock the Bolsheviks so much?
cards.answer: Because it came from sailors who had been the 'pride and glory' of the 1917 revolution, showing the Bolsheviks' own base had turned against them.

cards.front: Why did the Tenth Party Congress both ban factions and launch the New Economic Policy in March 1921?
cards.answer: Kronstadt showed peasant discontent was dangerous, so Lenin tightened party control while loosening grain requisitioning to ease peasant anger.

cards.front: Why does Hailsham's kindness act as a form of control over the students?
cards.answer: By giving students a good childhood, the guardians make them less likely to question their fate.

cards.front: Why was Miss Lucy dismissed from Hailsham?
cards.answer: She broke the unspoken rule by telling the students their fate directly instead of letting them only sense it.

cards.front: Name the four stages in Roger's arc from restraint to cruelty across the novel.
cards.answer: Throws stones near Henry, deliberately missing / Becomes one of Jack's loyal followers / Levers a boulder onto Piggy, killing him / Sharpens a stick at both ends
items: Throws stones near Henry, deliberately missing
Becomes one of Jack's loyal followers
Levers a boulder onto Piggy, killing him
Sharpens a stick at both ends

cards.front: Why does Jack encourage the boys' fear of the beast even though he claims fear can't hurt them?
cards.answer: He exploits fear as a political tool, offering himself as protector through hunting to consolidate his own power.

cards.front: How does Golding use Castle Rock's geography to represent political systems?
cards.answer: The open, exposed beach fosters debate and democracy, while the defensible, exclusive Castle Rock fosters tyranny.

cards.front: Name the five senses covered by sensory imagery in poetry analysis.
cards.answer: Sight (visual) / Sound (auditory) / Touch (tactile) / Smell (olfactory) / Taste (gustatory)

cards.front: How does the connotation of 'swallowed' create sympathy in 'the city swallowed him whole'?
cards.answer: It suggests consumption and destruction, presenting the city as a predator and the person as prey, making the reader sympathise with the vulnerable individual.

cards.front: How does pathetic fallacy work in poetry?
cards.answer: Weather or landscape reflects the character's emotion, such as a storm during anger or sunshine during joy, mirroring the speaker's inner state.

cards.front: Why is a simile described as more distanced than a metaphor?
cards.answer: A simile acknowledges the comparison using 'like' or 'as', whereas a metaphor asserts the two things are identical.

cards.front: Name the five demands the 1381 rebels made, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: End to serfdom / Abolition of the poll tax / Death of 'traitors' like John of Gaunt / Dissolution of corrupt landlordism / New relationship between king and people
items: Death of 'traitors' like John of Gaunt
New relationship between king and people

cards.front: Name the five AQA factors the lesson says converged to cause the 1381 revolt.
cards.answer: Chance (Black Death) / The economy (poll tax) / Communication (preachers like John Ball) / Role of the individual (Tyler and Ball) / Government (weak boy-king regime)
items: Role of the individual (Tyler and Ball)

cards.front: How did the Black Death give peasants real bargaining power over wages?
cards.answer: It killed about 40% of the population, causing a labour shortage, so lords had to compete for workers and pay higher wages.

cards.front: Why was John of Gaunt so unpopular in the years before the revolt?
cards.answer: He held real power as young Richard II's uncle and was loathed for corruption and links to a costly, unsuccessful war with France.

cards.front: The lesson gives three sources that shaped most Elizabethans' understanding of Judaism — name them.
cards.answer: Crude stereotypes / Religious teachings blaming Jews for Christ's crucifixion / Sensationalised stories like the Lopez case
items: Religious teachings blaming Jews for Christ's crucifixion
Sensationalised stories like the Lopez case

cards.front: Why was Venice's commercial law system ironic for the trial scene's outcome?
cards.answer: Venice's laws promised impartial justice, yet the law was twisted to strip Shylock of his wealth and force his conversion, serving Christian interests.

cards.front: Why did money-lending become one of the few jobs open to Jewish people in medieval Europe?
cards.answer: The Christian Church banned usury as sinful, but Jewish law allowed charging interest to non-Jews, while Jews were barred from most other trades and guilds.

cards.front: How does the contrast between Venice and Belmont support the play's theme of appearance versus reality?
cards.answer: Venice seems ruled by fair law but is full of prejudice, while Belmont seems harmonious but is funded by exploitative Venetian wealth and Portia's racism.

cards.front: Give the seven adverbios de frecuencia (frequency adverbs) listed in the lesson, from always to never.
cards.answer: siempre (always) / a menudo (often) / normalmente (normally) / a veces (sometimes) / de vez en cuando (from time to time) / raramente (rarely) / nunca (never)
items: de vez en cuando (from time to time)

cards.front: What are the six present tense endings for -AR verbs like jugar (yo to ellos)?
cards.answer: juego (yo) / juegas (tú) / juega (él/ella) / jugamos (nosotros) / jugáis (vosotros) / juegan (ellos)

cards.front: How should you structure a Spanish opinion sentence to make it stronger, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Follow an opinion phrase with porque (because) and a reason, e.g. me gusta nadar porque es relajante.

cards.front: How can you make your writing about hobbies sound more varied instead of always saying 'me gusta'?
cards.answer: Use alternative phrases like 'lo que más me gusta es', 'lo paso bomba cuando', or 'me resulta divertido'.

cards.front: Name the three sections the Amidah prayer is divided into.
cards.answer: Praise of God (three opening blessings) / Petitions (thirteen blessings) / Thanksgiving (three closing blessings)

cards.front: Name the two most significant differences between Orthodox and Reform synagogues.
cards.answer: The role of women / The language of prayer

cards.front: Why is the Amidah shortened on Shabbat and festivals?
cards.answer: The thirteen petitions are replaced with a single blessing for the special holiness of the day, shortening the service.

cards.front: Why are musical instruments not used in Orthodox services on Shabbat?
cards.answer: Playing instruments is not permitted on the day of rest, so Orthodox services use unaccompanied cantorial singing (chazanut).

title: The arrival and immediate impact of the Black Death
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the six factors the lesson gives for why the Black Death spread so fast in England.
cards.answer: Population density in towns / Poor sanitation / Trade routes and pilgrim roads / Monasteries and hospitals concentrating the sick / Malnutrition among poorer peasants / No understanding of how disease spread
items: Monasteries and hospitals concentrating the sick
No understanding of how disease spread

cards.front: Why did monasteries and hospitals, meant to help the sick, actually speed up the spread of plague?
cards.answer: They concentrated infected people together in one place, which inadvertently accelerated transmission of the disease.

cards.front: Why did the combination of bubonic and pneumonic plague make the epidemic so hard to stop?
cards.answer: Bubonic spread via fleas and rats while pneumonic spread through the air without needing them, so the epidemic had virtually no natural brake.

cards.front: Why did religious responses to the Black Death, such as mass prayer gatherings and pilgrimages, often make things worse?
cards.answer: They brought large numbers of people together, which may have actively spread the disease further.

cards.front: Name the three means of salvation the lesson identifies.
cards.answer: Law / Grace / Spirit

cards.front: Give the three different understandings of atonement described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Substitutionary atonement / Satisfaction theory / Moral example

cards.front: How does the Holy Spirit help Christians live a holy life, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: It guides them to recognise sin, turn to God, resist temptation, brings comfort, strengthens faith and empowers them to share the gospel.

cards.front: Why do some liberal Christians see Jesus's death as a 'moral example' rather than a payment for sin?
cards.answer: They see it as a supreme act of self-sacrificing love that inspires Christians to live selflessly for others.

title: Earth's Resources: Water, Pollution and Sustainability
subject: separate-sciences-ocr

cards.front: Name the four stages of sewage treatment described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Screening / Primary sedimentation / Biological treatment / Final clarification and sterilisation

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says chemistry contributes to sustainable development.
cards.answer: Higher atom economy processes / Renewable and biodegradable materials / Improved recycling technology / More energy-efficient production routes

cards.front: Why is chlorine used more commonly than ozone or UV light for sterilising UK drinking water?
cards.answer: Chlorine is effective, relatively cheap, and its residual effect keeps killing bacteria as water travels through the distribution network, unlike ozone or UV.

cards.front: Why must industrial waste water receive specialised treatment before release?
cards.answer: It may contain heavy metals or toxic organic compounds that need specific treatment before being safely released.

cards.front: What three things does the lesson say unite all Christian views on visions despite differing on channels and authority?
cards.answer: God can communicate with humans / Debate is about the channels used / Debate is about authority they carry
items: Debate is about the channels used
Debate is about authority they carry

cards.front: Why do Humanists say belief in miracles can be harmful?
cards.answer: It encourages people to reject medicine and science in favour of prayer and superstition.

cards.front: How do Christians respond to Hume's argument against miracles?
cards.answer: They say it assumes the conclusion before examining evidence and would dismiss real but surprising historical events.

cards.front: Name the three quenching media used in hardening, and the order of their cooling speed.
cards.answer: Brine (fastest) / Water / Oil (slowest)

cards.front: List the three shared stages of all heat-treatment processes for carbon steel.
cards.answer: Heat to soaking temperature / Hold at temperature (soaking) / Cool at a controlled rate

cards.front: Why does slow furnace cooling in annealing produce a softer, more ductile metal than air cooling?
cards.answer: Slow cooling gives atoms time to form large, coarse grains with very few dislocations, maximising ductility.

cards.front: Why must full through-hardening be avoided for a gear tooth?
cards.answer: It would make the tooth too brittle to withstand bending loads, so it would snap rather than deform.

title: Themes: Family, Truth, Identity and Love
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the four children whose monologues open each season in Things I Know to Be True.
cards.answer: Rosie in Berlin / Pip in the garden / Mark in the gum tree / Ben remembering his parents dancing

cards.front: Why does the connecting-hands staging moment matter to the family theme?
cards.answer: The family joins hands at the exact same instant, showing they stay connected however far apart they scatter.

cards.front: Why is Fran's secret bank account significant to the truth-telling theme?
cards.answer: She kept it secretly so she would know she could leave Bob if she ever needed to.

cards.front: How does Bovell use dramatic irony around Bob's comment about Mark becoming a woman?
cards.answer: Bob names becoming a woman as the one thing that would shock them, not realising this is exactly what is about to happen.

cards.front: Name the five types of German secondary/primary school mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: das Gymnasium / die Realschule / die Hauptschule / die Gesamtschule / die Grundschule

cards.front: Name the three modal verbs the lesson gives for expressing school rules with 'man'.
cards.answer: man muss / man soll / man darf

cards.front: Why does the word order change in 'In der Pause esse ich in der Kantine' compared to starting with the subject?
cards.answer: Because of verb-second word order: starting with a time phrase forces the subject and verb to swap places.

cards.front: Why is school uniform a good discussion topic for German exam tasks, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because German students don't wear school uniform, so you can compare the British and German systems.

cards.front: What four physical adaptations does regular physical activity cause to the body, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Improved cardiovascular fitness / Increased muscular strength and endurance / Improved flexibility / Improved body composition

cards.front: Why can sports like gymnastics, rowing or wrestling contribute to disordered eating?
cards.answer: Because pressure to achieve a particular body image for weight or aesthetic judging can push athletes towards unhealthy eating habits.

title: Film Music: Writing About an Unfamiliar Cue and Composing to a Brief
subject: music-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four musical choices the lesson suggests for scoring a chase scene.
cards.answer: Fast tempo / Driving string or brass ostinato / Syncopated rhythms / Gradual crescendo and thickening texture

cards.front: Why does the opening semitone ostinato in the Jaws theme sound unsettling?
cards.answer: Because it uses a narrow, repetitive interval played quietly in low strings and tuba, creating dread through simplicity and repetition.

cards.front: How does the Psycho shower scene cue create terror using only strings?
cards.answer: High shrieking violin figures use rapid repeated bowing and sharp accents to imitate stabbing, over dissonant, tightly-spaced harmony.

cards.front: Why should a film music answer describe features stage by stage rather than as a list?
cards.answer: Because describing the time-course shows understanding of the whole cue's journey, not just isolated random details.

title: Contemporary UK Film: Aesthetic Style in Focus
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five contemporary UK films studied for aesthetic style, with their aesthetic category.
cards.answer: Submarine - indie/art-house / Attack the Block - genre/urban science fiction / Skyfall - blockbuster spectacle / Rocks - social realism / Blinded by the Light - musical drama
items: Attack the Block - genre/urban science fiction
Blinded by the Light - musical drama

cards.front: What four aesthetic choices in the Rocks school-corridor scene create its social-realist feel?
cards.answer: Natural light / Handheld camera / Semi-improvised performance / Retention of imperfect dialogue

cards.front: How does the handheld, following camera in Rocks's corridor scene affect the spectator's experience?
cards.answer: It moves with the girls rather than ahead of them, placing the spectator behind the action so it feels like watching something happening rather than performed.

cards.front: How does the Born to Run lyric-overlay sequence in Blinded by the Light show the protagonist's inner experience?
cards.answer: Song lyrics are superimposed as floating typographic text on screen, making his interior emotional response to the music visible rather than just heard.

cards.front: Name the three tones the lesson gives for Tennyson, Owen and Hardy in these war poems.
cards.answer: Tennyson: elevated, heroic register / Owen: bleak, cold and despairing / Hardy: conversational and darkly ironic

cards.front: How does Owen's use of hallucination show the soldiers' state in Exposure?
cards.answer: Soldiers hallucinate about home ('Slowly our ghosts drag home'), suggesting they are already psychologically dead.

cards.front: Why does the repeated 'because' sound unconvincing in The Man He Killed?
cards.answer: The speaker repeats 'because' as though he does not believe his own reasoning for killing a stranger.

cards.front: How does Hardy's simple ballad form affect the impact of The Man He Killed's subject matter?
cards.answer: The neat, deceptively simple ballad stanzas contrast with the killing, making the moral complexity more shocking.

cards.front: Name the four Spanish daily meals given in the lesson, in order through the day
cards.answer: el desayuno (breakfast) / la comida (lunch) / la merienda (afternoon snack) / la cena (dinner)

cards.front: Name the three Latin American cultural traditions the lesson describes
cards.answer: la quinceañera / el carnaval / la sobremesa

cards.front: Why do many shops and businesses in Spain still close between about 2pm and 5pm?
cards.answer: Because of the tradition of the siesta, an afternoon rest taken after lunch, especially in southern Spain.

cards.front: Why is Spanish dinner usually later and lighter than in the UK?
cards.answer: Because lunch is the main meal in Spain, so dinner around 9-10pm is a smaller, later meal by comparison.

title: Eschatological Beliefs: Death, Judgement and the Afterlife
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the three views on the nature of hell described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Conscious eternal separation from God / Annihilation (ceasing to exist) / Universalism (all reconciled to God)

cards.front: Why did Paul insist resurrection is essential to Christian faith in 1 Corinthians 15?
cards.answer: Because if Christ did not rise, then 'your faith is futile', so belief in the afterlife depends on his resurrection.

cards.front: Why does Matthew 25:31-46 show that judgement is based on actions rather than religious profession?
cards.answer: Because Jesus identifies himself with the poor, saying whatever was done for 'the least of these' was done for him, so judgement is ethical.

cards.front: Why does Ruth constantly copy behaviour she has seen on TV at the Cottages?
cards.answer: The clones have no genuine models for adult life, so they construct identities from fragments of popular culture to feel human.

cards.front: Why does Ruth manoeuvre herself into a relationship with Tommy at the Cottages?
cards.answer: Partly because she genuinely cares for him, and partly to stop Kathy from having him.

title: Place and the Integrated Marketing Mix
subject: business-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four Ps of the marketing mix.
cards.answer: Product / Price / Promotion / Place

cards.front: Why do physical products like furniture or fresh food often benefit from selling through a retailer rather than an e-tailer?
cards.answer: Customers want to see, touch or try these products before buying, which a retailer allows.

cards.front: Why might a premium chocolate brand selling through a budget supermarket need to change its product packaging?
cards.answer: Because the packaging might look cheap next to discount products, undermining the brand image.

title: Poem for My Love — June Jordan
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Why does Jordan write the poem's opening questions without question marks?
cards.answer: It makes them read as statements of wonder rather than genuine doubt, as if the speaker already knows the answer.

cards.front: Why does the poem's thirteen-line form (one short of a sonnet) suit its theme of love as 'possibility'?
cards.answer: It echoes the sonnet's link with love poetry while refusing to complete the shape, matching love that feels unfinished.

cards.front: How do the poem's shifting pronouns affect who seems to be speaking?
cards.answer: They unsettle who is speaking and being spoken to, widening the poem beyond a single private exchange.

cards.front: Why does the poem's uncertain addressee help it work as a love poem for any reader?
cards.answer: Since nobody knows who it addresses, it stands as a general love poem rather than a private message to one person.

title: Earthquakes in Contrasting Wealth: Nepal & New Zealand
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four secondary effects of the Nepal 2015 earthquake given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Avalanches killed 19 climbers / Nearly 8 million people affected / 3 million made homeless / Cholera and dysentery outbreaks in camps
items: Cholera and dysentery outbreaks in camps

cards.front: Name the three long-term responses to the Christchurch earthquake given in the lesson.
cards.answer: CERA set up to coordinate rebuild / Central business district demolished and rebuilt to higher standards / Building code reviewed and tightened / Earthquake education in schools strengthened
items: CERA set up to coordinate rebuild
Central business district demolished and rebuilt to higher standards

cards.front: Why did the CTV building in Christchurch kill so many people despite New Zealand's strict building codes?
cards.answer: It was built in the 1980s but later investigation found design flaws, showing codes only work if enforced and inspected.

cards.front: Why was Nepal's death rate so much higher than Christchurch's even though the size difference only partly explains it?
cards.answer: Building quality was the bigger reason: brick and mud-mortar buildings collapsed while flexible reinforced concrete and timber-frame buildings survived.

cards.front: What four things should each paragraph include in an essay on the extract and whole novel?
