cards.answer: A point about Doyle's presentation / A quotation from extract or novel / Analysis of language or structure / A contextual link
items: A quotation from extract or novel

cards.front: Why does Holmes reach for cocaine when Watson announces his engagement?
cards.answer: This juxtaposition shows Holmes is indifferent to love and highlights what each character values and lacks.

title: Elizabeth, Spain and the new world
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the three stages of the English attack on the Armada described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Harried up the Channel / Fireships caused panic off Calais / Attacked scattered ships at Gravelines

cards.front: Why did England end up in conflict with Spain by the 1560s?
cards.answer: Religious conflict between Catholic Philip II and Protestant Elizabeth combined with commercial rivalry over Atlantic trade routes.

cards.front: Why did the Spanish Armada lose so many ships trying to return to Spain?
cards.answer: It tried to sail home around Scotland and Ireland, and storms wrecked many ships on that route.

cards.front: How did attacking Spanish treasure fleets help England's war against Spain?
cards.answer: It disrupted the money supply funding Philip II's armies in the Netherlands and his plans to invade England.

cards.front: Name the five key contextual areas the lesson gives for analysing Blood Brothers.
cards.answer: 1980s Liverpool deindustrialisation / The class system / Russell's working-class background / Housing policy and slum clearance / Russell's purpose as social commentary

cards.front: Name the three sections of a strong Blood Brothers essay's main body, in order.
cards.answer: Opening/Act 1 paragraph / Middle/Development paragraph / Climax/Ending paragraph

cards.front: Why should context be woven into analysis rather than written as a separate paragraph?
cards.answer: A separate context paragraph earns few marks; context must be embedded into analytical paragraphs to score well.

cards.front: How should you use the quotation given at the top of an essay question?
cards.answer: Engage with it as a springboard and reference it, then range across the whole play rather than ignoring it.

cards.front: What three types of argument does Mrs Lyons use to persuade Mrs Johnstone to give up a twin?
cards.answer: Practical logic: a better life / Emotion: she'll see him every day / Guilt: too many children already
items: Emotion: she'll see him every day

cards.front: Why is Mrs Lyons presented as Mrs Johnstone's foil?
cards.answer: She contrasts in wealth, class and temperament, highlighting the power imbalance between them.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Johnstone find it almost impossible to refuse Mrs Lyons's request for a twin?
cards.answer: Mrs Lyons's wealth makes her Mrs Johnstone's employer, and the class dynamic gives her power over her.

cards.front: How does the Narrator's ambiguous identity contribute to the play's sense of tragedy?
cards.answer: By never clarifying if he is character, chorus, fate or the devil, Russell shows forces characters cannot escape.

title: Early Government Policy and the Permanent Indian Frontier
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four hammer blows the lesson gives for why the Permanent Indian Frontier collapsed in the 1840s.
cards.answer: Pioneer migration on Oregon/California Trails from 1841 / Manifest Destiny doctrine / 1846 Oregon Treaty and 1848 Mexican Cession land gains / 1848 California Gold Rush
items: Pioneer migration on Oregon/California Trails from 1841
1846 Oregon Treaty and 1848 Mexican Cession land gains

cards.front: Name the five nations forced off their lands under the Indian Removal Act.
cards.answer: Cherokee / Chickasaw / Choctaw / Creek / Seminole

cards.front: Why did the 1848 California Gold Rush undermine the Permanent Indian Frontier?
cards.answer: It sent about a quarter of a million migrants overland, carving trails through 'Indian country' that killed buffalo and spread cholera into Plains camps.

cards.front: Why is the 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty described as a move to 'concentration' rather than a genuine peace policy?
cards.answer: It stripped vast territory from nations who had not lost a war and forced them into areas defined by Washington, not true peace.

cards.front: Name the three separation techniques the lesson gives for separating mixtures.
cards.answer: Filtration / Distillation / Chromatography

cards.front: Why does adding a glowing splint to a gas confirm it is oxygen?
cards.answer: The splint relights because oxygen supports combustion.

cards.front: Why does bubbling carbon dioxide through limewater make it turn milky?
cards.answer: Calcium carbonate, which is insoluble, precipitates when carbon dioxide reacts with the calcium hydroxide.

cards.front: Why must you acidify with dilute nitric acid before testing for halide ions with silver nitrate?
cards.answer: To prevent interference from carbonate or sulfate ions giving a false precipitate.

title: Interactionist Theory of Crime: Becker and Labelling
subject: sociology-aqa

cards.front: According to Becker, name the three factors the lesson says decide whether a deviant label sticks to someone.
cards.answer: Social characteristics of the actor (class, ethnicity, age, gender) / Discretion of those with formal power (police, teachers, courts) / The social context of the act
items: Social characteristics of the actor (class, ethnicity, age, gender)
Discretion of those with formal power (police, teachers, courts)
The social context of the act

cards.front: Name the three criticisms of labelling theory given by the lesson's Key Fact box.
cards.answer: Marxists: doesn't explain why labels fall on the working class / Feminists: gender shapes labelling and its consequences / Not everyone labelled accepts or acts on the label
items: Marxists: doesn't explain why labels fall on the working class
Feminists: gender shapes labelling and its consequences
Not everyone labelled accepts or acts on the label

cards.front: How can being given a master status lead to a self-fulfilling prophecy?
cards.answer: Rejection from jobs, education and conventional networks makes conventional life harder, so the person identifies with the label and joins deviant groups.

cards.front: According to Heidensohn's chivalry thesis, why might female offenders be treated more leniently by the criminal justice system?
cards.answer: Because they conform to feminine stereotypes, though women who deviate from expected gender roles may be judged more harshly.

cards.front: Name the three structural patterns Hill establishes in Chapters 1-4 of The Woman in Black.
cards.answer: Warning and dismissal / Approach and retreat / Sensory intensification

cards.front: Why is the church almost empty at Mrs Drablow's funeral?
cards.answer: It emphasises Mrs Drablow's isolation and the town's fear of anything connected to Eel Marsh House.

cards.front: Why does Hill use the townspeople's refusal to speak about Eel Marsh House?
cards.answer: Their silence signals a secret too terrible to name, building suspense before Arthur ever arrives there.

cards.front: How does the frame narrative create dramatic irony from the opening pages?
cards.answer: We see the older Arthur unable to tell his story, so we know his cheerful younger self's confidence will be destroyed.

cards.front: Name the three ideological positions shared by Nazi Germany, fascist Italy and militarist Japan.
cards.answer: Opposed parliamentary democracy / Opposed communism / Opposed 'international finance'

cards.front: Why was Britain reluctant to confront Germany over the Rhineland in March 1936?
cards.answer: Britain was preoccupied with the Abyssinian Crisis and its public leaned toward accepting a 'reasonable' settlement after memories of 1914-18.

cards.front: Why did the loss of the demilitarised Rhineland weaken France's alliance system in eastern Europe?
cards.answer: Without the buffer zone, France could no longer credibly threaten to march into Germany to defend Czechoslovakia or Poland.

cards.front: Why did the British claim that Germany was 'only going into its own back garden' miss the strategic point?
cards.answer: The zone existed not because the land was disputed but to stop German forces attacking France or threatening its eastern allies.

title: The North-South Divide & the UK in the Wider World
subject: geography-aqa

cards.front: Name the four strategies the lesson gives for resolving the north-south divide.
cards.answer: Northern Powerhouse / Devolution deals / Enterprise zones / Levelling Up Fund

cards.front: Name the four areas through which the UK's global links run, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Trade / Culture / Transport links / Political links

cards.front: Why did deindustrialisation hit the north, Midlands, south Wales and central Scotland hardest?
cards.answer: Because that is where coal, steel and shipbuilding industries were concentrated.

cards.front: Why does the EU still matter to UK trade even after Brexit?
cards.answer: It is the closest large market and supply chains built up over forty years cannot easily be redirected.

title: Act 2: Geof, Helen's Return & the Ending
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Why does Delaney present Geof's everyday domestic tasks as a form of love?
cards.answer: His mundane, unglamorous care — folding nappies, cooking, tidying — is shown as the closest thing to genuine love Jo has experienced since the Boy left.

cards.front: Why is Geof's departure described as the play's cruellest structural repetition?
cards.answer: It repeats the cycle of abandonment: just as the Boy left Jo then Helen failed her, Jo does not fight hard enough to keep Geof, so the one caring relationship is destroyed.

cards.front: How does Delaney use Jo and Geof's household to question what 'family' means?
cards.answer: Helen is Jo's biological mother but fails at every maternal duty, while Geof has no blood tie yet provides care, stability and selfless love.

cards.front: Name the two homophobic insults Helen and Peter use against Geof to question his fitness to be around a child.
cards.answer: An arty little freak / A bloody little pansy

title: The Falklands War and the Miners' Strike
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five factors the lesson gives for why the miners lost the 1984-85 strike.
cards.answer: Meticulous government preparation with coal stockpiles / Unprecedented police coordination / No national ballot removed legal protection / Nottinghamshire miners kept working, dividing the union / NUM funds sequestrated by courts
items: Meticulous government preparation with coal stockpiles
No national ballot removed legal protection
Nottinghamshire miners kept working, dividing the union

cards.front: Why did Galtieri think Britain would not respond militarily to the Falklands invasion?
cards.answer: He calculated that Britain, with a Conservative government cutting defence spending, would not fight to retake distant islands.

cards.front: How did the Falklands victory affect Thatcher's political standing before the 1983 election?
cards.answer: It transformed her from an unpopular, poll-trailing leader into a national hero, boosting Conservative support dramatically.

cards.front: Why was the Argentine invasion of the Falklands controversial for Britain to respond to militarily?
cards.answer: The sinking of the General Belgrano on 2 May, killing 323, was the most controversial act of the conflict.

cards.front: Name the three categories of emigrant from the British Isles (1688–c.1730).
cards.answer: Voluntary settlers / Indentured servants / Transported prisoners

cards.front: Why did indentured servants completing their term contribute to colonial instability, as shown by Bacon's Rebellion (1676)?
cards.answer: Freed servants often could not obtain promised land grants, creating a large class of frustrated, landless free men.

cards.front: How did the experience of transported prisoners differ from voluntary settlers in the colonies?
cards.answer: Transported prisoners had no choice of destination, no legal protections, no resources, and faced hard labour as punishment.

cards.front: Name the three revision strategies the lesson gives for preparing for the anthology comparison essay.
cards.answer: Quotation cards / Comparison grids / Practice under timed conditions

cards.front: What three things should you decide during the 5-minute planning stage before writing the comparison essay?
cards.answer: Note three comparative points / Choose quotations from both poems / Decide your evaluative conclusion

cards.front: Why should you prepare 3-4 flexible pairings of poems before the exam?
cards.answer: Because the exam names one poem and you choose the comparison, so pairings ready in advance guarantee a strong comparison whatever is named.

cards.front: Why does the lesson say speed in the exam comes from knowing your quotations well?
cards.answer: Because if you already know what to quote, you only need to think about how to use it, saving time.

title: Energy Resources and the Domestic Power Equation
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: What four factors should you consider when comparing energy resources?
cards.answer: Reliability / Environmental impact / Cost / Scalability

cards.front: Name the four main disadvantages of nuclear power given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Radioactive waste storage / High construction costs / High decommissioning costs / Public perception of safety risk

cards.front: Why does using more variable renewables like wind and solar make it harder for the National Grid to balance supply and demand?
cards.answer: Their output depends on weather and daylight rather than demand, so energy storage like pumped-storage hydro is needed to balance supply.

cards.front: Why is hydroelectric power considered highly reliable and able to meet peaks in demand?
cards.answer: Water stored behind a dam can be released to drive turbines whenever extra electricity is needed.

cards.front: Name the four responsibilities of the contracts manager and site manager together.
cards.answer: Coordinate construction site activities / Manage progress and run site meetings / Organise labour, plant and materials / Responsible for health and safety and worker welfare
items: Manage progress and run site meetings
Responsible for health and safety and worker welfare

cards.front: Why does the balance of professional involvement shift once construction begins on site?
cards.answer: The contracts manager and site manager take the lead running the site, while the architect and engineer only make periodic quality-check visits.

cards.front: Why is holding chartered status important for an individual professional if a project goes wrong?
cards.answer: It shows they followed accepted standards and codes of conduct, which matters greatly in legal proceedings.

title: Britain & Europe: From EEC to Brexit
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three answers Britain considered for what kind of country to be after empire.
cards.answer: The United States (special relationship) / The Commonwealth / Europe

cards.front: Name the five sectors that became structurally dependent on East European labour before the 2016 referendum.
cards.answer: Agriculture / Hospitality / Construction / Transport / Food processing

cards.front: Why did Britain choose to stay outside the EEC when it was founded in 1957?
cards.answer: Britain preferred to bet on the Commonwealth and the 'special relationship' with the United States instead.

cards.front: Why did net migration reach record highs after free movement ended in 2020, despite Brexit aiming to cut immigration?
cards.answer: A global recruitment drive for the NHS and care sector, plus visa schemes for Hong Kongers and Ukrainians, drove numbers up.

title: The Origins of the Korean War
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five stacked causes of the Korean War by June 1950 given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Korean nationalist division / two rival regimes under Kim and Rhee / 1949 communist victory in China / Acheson speech excluding Korea from US defence / Stalin's green light after lobbying
items: two rival regimes under Kim and Rhee
Acheson speech excluding Korea from US defence

cards.front: Why did Stalin and Mao eventually agree to let Kim Il Sung invade South Korea?
cards.answer: They believed the Americans would not fight for Korea, especially after Acheson's speech excluding it from the defence perimeter.

title: Blinded by the Light: Aesthetic and Musical Realism
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: What are the three aesthetic registers the lesson identifies in Blinded by the Light?
cards.answer: Lyric-text overlay and superimposition in musical set-pieces / Warm autumnal ambers and golds in domestic/high-street scenes / Colder greyer palette in National Front and New Jersey scenes
items: Lyric-text overlay and superimposition in musical set-pieces
Warm autumnal ambers and golds in domestic/high-street scenes
Colder greyer palette in National Front and New Jersey scenes

cards.front: How does the National Front street-confrontation scene avoid glamourising racism?
cards.answer: The threat and imagery appear at the edges of a wider-focus frame rather than centre, making racism ambient rather than a dramatic centrepiece.

cards.front: Why does Chadha keep the camera in the cramped bedroom during Javed's first Springsteen listen?
cards.answer: So the music transforms the ordinary space Javed already occupies rather than transporting him somewhere spectacular.

cards.front: How does close mid-shot framing in the Khan family kitchen link to the film's themes?
cards.answer: It compresses the family together, linking the claustrophobic space to the intergenerational pressure the Springsteen songs represent an escape from.

title: The Statistical Enquiry Cycle: Reviewing the Whole Investigation
subject: statistics-aqa

cards.front: Why can describing what an investigation did lose marks in a Statistical Enquiry Cycle evaluation?
cards.answer: Description alone doesn't explain why it's a weakness or matters for the conclusion, so it only scores Developing at best.

cards.front: Why does a vague hypothesis at the Initial Planning stage cause problems later in the enquiry?
cards.answer: A vague hypothesis leads to ambiguous data, since decisions at this stage affect every other stage of the cycle.

cards.front: Why might a lurking variable weaken the reliability of a statistical finding?
cards.answer: It could offer an alternative explanation for the pattern seen, rather than the one concluded from the data.

cards.front: Name the three human behaviours the pigs adopt by living in the farmhouse, besides walking on hind legs and carrying whips.
cards.answer: Sleep in beds / Wear clothes / Move into Mr Jones's farmhouse

cards.front: Name the three reasons the lesson gives for why the animals fail to stop the pigs' tyranny.
cards.answer: They cannot read / They trust blindly / They let pigs monopolise information

cards.front: Why is Boxer's collapse and disposal so devastating to the reader?
cards.answer: He gave everything through genuine dedication, but the regime valued him only for labour and discarded him once he could no longer produce.

cards.front: Why does propaganda still work on the animals even though their lives are clearly worse under Napoleon?
cards.answer: Propaganda does not need to be believed to be effective, it just needs to be the only narrative the animals have access to.

cards.front: What tasks did barefoot doctors carry out in rural communes, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Carried a basic kit of medicines / Taught hygiene / Delivered vaccinations / Ran family-planning clinics
items: Carried a basic kit of medicines

cards.front: What did education include in Chinese primary schools before 1966, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Arithmetic / Passages of Mao's thought / Agricultural work experience / Industrial work experience

cards.front: How did simplified characters and Pinyin together speed up mass literacy in China?
cards.answer: Simplified characters cut the strokes needed to write common words while Pinyin gave a Roman-letter system for teaching pronunciation, cutting time to functional literacy.

cards.front: Why did rural healthcare improve so much under the barefoot doctor system despite uneven results overall?
cards.answer: Around one million trained paramedics were dispatched to communes, delivering vaccinations, hygiene teaching and family planning where clinics had never existed before.

title: Reflection, Sound Waves and Waves for Detection
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three things that can happen when a wave hits a boundary between two materials.
cards.answer: Reflected / Absorbed / Transmitted

cards.front: What are the three key differences between P-waves and S-waves given in the lesson?
cards.answer: P-waves longitudinal, S-waves transverse / P-waves travel through solids and liquids, S-waves only solids / P-waves faster and arrive first
items: P-waves travel through solids and liquids, S-waves only solids

cards.front: Why does specular reflection produce a clear image but diffuse reflection does not?
cards.answer: On smooth surfaces the normal is the same everywhere so reflected rays stay parallel, but on rough surfaces the normal differs at every point so rays scatter.

cards.front: How do scientists use P-wave behaviour as evidence for density changes at the mantle-core boundary?
cards.answer: P-waves are refracted as they pass through different layers, which shows density changes at the mantle-core boundary.

title: Scenes 1–3: Enid, Viv & the Obeah Woman
subject: english-literature-ocr

cards.front: Why does Enid distance herself from her Caribbean heritage?
cards.answer: She believes respectability and English education will protect her daughters from the racism she has experienced.

cards.front: Why does Mai take a special interest in Del?
cards.answer: Mai recognises Del's potential as her spiritual successor in Obeah from the start.

cards.front: The lesson gives three things about Brod's life in England. What are they?
cards.answer: Serious drinking problem / Wife and children still in Jamaica / Deeply disenchanted with life in England
items: Wife and children still in Jamaica
Deeply disenchanted with life in England

cards.front: Why does Enid advise sending money to Cynthia even though she suspects exaggeration?
cards.answer: It is Mai who advises Enid to send the money anyway, despite Enid's suspicion Cynthia is exaggerating.

cards.front: Name the four costs of maintaining quality the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Staff training / Inspection costs / Product recalls / Bad publicity hit

cards.front: Name the three benefits of maintaining quality the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Better image and reputation / Additional sales / Higher price customers accept

cards.front: Why does a quality failure cost a business more than just the refund bill?
cards.answer: It also causes fewer repeat purchases, weaker brand image and falling market share, which are much bigger costs.

cards.front: Why does outsourcing make it harder for a business to maintain consistent quality?
cards.answer: A different company makes part of the product using its own standards and culture, which head office cannot fully control.

cards.front: Name the three ways ordinary English people felt the impact of the Hundred Years' War, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Heavy taxation to fund campaigns / Disruption to the wool trade / Losses of families with men sent abroad
items: Losses of families with men sent abroad

cards.front: Why did Henry V position his army between two woods at Agincourt?
cards.answer: To force the French to advance along a narrow muddy field, which negated their numerical advantage.

cards.front: Why was the indenture system better than the feudal levy for long campaigns abroad?
cards.answer: Paid soldiers could serve indefinitely, unlike feudal levies who were only obligated to serve forty days a year.

cards.front: How did chevauchée raids help the English against France?
cards.answer: They destroyed French tax revenues and forced the French to fight battles, though they devastated civilians too.

cards.front: Name the four practical benefits of reprogrammable microcontroller systems given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Flexibility / Firmware updates / Reduced component count / Faster prototyping

cards.front: Name the four limitations of programmable components (microcontrollers) given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Programming expertise required / Higher unit cost for simple tasks / Power consumption / Software dependency
items: Higher unit cost for simple tasks

cards.front: Why does an analogue sensor connected to a microcontroller need an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC)?
cards.answer: Because it converts the continuously varying voltage from the sensor into a number the processor can use.

cards.front: Why can a single microcontroller-based washing machine PCB run different wash programmes instead of needing separate boards?
cards.answer: Because the same hardware can be reprogrammed with different software settings for each wash programme.

title: Postnatal Care of the Mother & Conditions for Development
subject: cambridge-nationals-child-development

cards.front: What four things does the six-to-eight week postnatal GP check cover?
cards.answer: Physical recovery / Pelvic floor health / Contraception / Emotional wellbeing

cards.front: What treatments may be offered if postnatal depression is identified?
cards.answer: Talking therapies (CBT or counselling) / Antidepressant medication / Peer support groups / Referral to perinatal mental health team
items: Referral to perinatal mental health team

cards.front: Why are newborns especially vulnerable to hypothermia without warmth and appropriate clothing?
cards.answer: Because newborns cannot regulate their own body temperature.

cards.front: Why can untreated postnatal depression harm a child's emotional development?
cards.answer: Because it can disrupt attachment between mother and baby, affecting the child's emotional development.

title: Worship in the Gurdwara, Langar and Sikh Initiation
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four steps that happen to a Sikh during the Amrit Sanskar ceremony.
cards.answer: Drinks amrit five times / Has amrit sprinkled on eyes and hair / Repeats the Mool Mantar five times / Commits to the Rehat Maryada and Five Ks
items: Has amrit sprinkled on eyes and hair
Repeats the Mool Mantar five times
Commits to the Rehat Maryada and Five Ks

cards.front: Why does the langar meal express Sikh belief in equality?
cards.answer: Everyone sits together on the floor in rows sharing the same free food, so people of all backgrounds and social positions are made equal.

cards.front: How is a Sikh baby named in the Naam Karan ceremony?
cards.answer: A passage is chosen at random from the Guru Granth Sahib and the baby is given a name starting with the first letter of its first word.

cards.front: How does Rochester's blindness reverse the power dynamic between him and Jane?
cards.answer: He can no longer judge Jane by her appearance and must value her entirely for her inner qualities.

cards.front: Why does Brontë set Jane and Rochester's reunion at Ferndean rather than a grand house?
cards.answer: Its natural, secluded setting reflects the Romantic ideal that truth and happiness are found away from the corruption of civilisation.

cards.front: Why does Elizabeth initially refuse to visit Pemberley?
cards.answer: She fears an awkward encounter with Darcy, and only agrees once she learns he is away.

cards.front: Why does Mrs Reynolds's praise of Darcy carry more weight than public opinion of him?
cards.answer: Servants see their masters without social masks, so her daily private observation is more trustworthy than public performance.

title: Climate Models and Earth's Energy Balance
subject: separate-sciences-ocr-b

cards.front: Name three sources of methane given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Livestock digestion / Rice paddies / Landfill sites / Leaks from natural gas systems

cards.front: Why is water vapour's concentration not directly controlled by human activity, unlike carbon dioxide?
cards.answer: Water vapour's concentration is controlled mainly by temperature rather than directly by human activity.

cards.front: Why do scientists give a range of warming values instead of one precise figure?
cards.answer: Climate models simplify complex systems like clouds, ocean currents and feedback loops, producing uncertainty in the exact magnitude of change.

cards.front: How does the enhanced greenhouse effect shift Earth's energy balance?
cards.answer: Human activities have increased carbon dioxide concentration, trapping more infrared radiation and driving global warming.

cards.front: Name the three observations from electrolysing copper sulfate solution with inert (carbon) electrodes.
cards.answer: Copper metal deposits at the cathode / Cathode gains mass / Oxygen gas produced at the anode / Solution becomes paler
items: Copper metal deposits at the cathode
Oxygen gas produced at the anode

cards.front: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis instead of reduction with carbon?
cards.answer: Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon.

cards.front: How would you test the gas produced at the anode in copper sulfate electrolysis with inert electrodes to confirm it is oxygen?
cards.answer: A glowing splint would relight if the gas is oxygen.

cards.front: In aqueous electrolysis, why does hydrogen gas form at the cathode instead of a metal like sodium or zinc?
cards.answer: Because these metals are more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen is discharged at the cathode instead of the metal.

cards.front: According to Rousseau-influenced philosophy in the novel, why does the Creature become violent?
cards.answer: It begins innocent but turns violent only after repeated rejection, cruelty, and isolation from society.

cards.front: How does the gap between Victor's expectation and the reality of creation criticise him?
cards.answer: Victor expected a beautiful creation but is horrified by the result, showing he planned the creation but not its aftermath.

cards.front: Why does the novella argue that Jekyll's experiment ends in catastrophe?
cards.answer: Because good and evil are not separate entities but inseparable parts of the same person.

cards.front: How does Stevenson's own life connect to the theme of duality in the novella?
cards.answer: He grew up in Edinburgh, split between respectable New Town and vice-ridden Old Town, and knew of Deacon Brodie's double life.

title: Audience Interpretation and Hall's Reception Theory
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three reading positions in Hall's encoding-decoding model.
cards.answer: Dominant/preferred reading / Negotiated reading / Oppositional reading

cards.front: Why can the same media text produce very different responses in different audiences, according to Hall's model?
cards.answer: Social variables like class, ethnicity and age mean audiences bring different knowledge and experience, so they decode texts differently.

cards.front: Why does Hall's model depend on texts being polysemic?
cards.answer: If a text had only one possible meaning there would be no room for negotiated or oppositional readings to exist.

cards.front: Name the seven fractions collected during fractional distillation of crude oil, from top to bottom of the column.
cards.answer: Petroleum gases / Petrol (gasoline) / Naphtha / Kerosene (jet fuel) / Diesel / Fuel oil / Bitumen (residue)

cards.front: What three properties change as hydrocarbon chain length increases in fractional distillation?
cards.answer: Boiling point increases / Viscosity increases / Flammability decreases

cards.front: Why does shorter-chain hydrocarbon collect near the top of the fractionating column?
cards.answer: Shorter-chain hydrocarbons have lower boiling points, so they stay as vapour until they reach the cooler top of the column, where they condense.

cards.front: Why does burning fuel with a sulfur impurity or at high temperature contribute to acid rain?
cards.answer: Sulfur impurities burn to form sulfur dioxide, and high combustion temperatures make nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitrogen oxides, both causing acid rain.

cards.front: Name the three main dimensions of educational achievement studied in GCSE Sociology.
cards.answer: Social class / Gender / Ethnicity

cards.front: Name the two steps for reading and describing patterns in an attainment table or chart.
cards.answer: Identify the overall pattern / Describe a trend over time

cards.front: Why has the class attainment gap remained even though overall GCSE results have risen since 1988?
cards.answer: Despite decades of educational policy, FSM pupils remain substantially behind non-FSM peers, so the gap has not closed significantly.

cards.front: Why do ethnic attainment gaps show a more complex trend than the class or gender gaps?
cards.answer: Some minority ethnic groups like Indian and Chinese pupils have improved rapidly, while others like Black Caribbean and White working-class boys have progressed more slowly.

cards.front: What number of covalent bonds does each of these molecules have: H2, O2, H2O, CH4, NH3?
cards.answer: H2 – one single bond / O2 – one double bond / H2O – two single bonds / CH4 – four single bonds / NH3 – three single bonds plus a lone pair
items: NH3 – three single bonds plus a lone pair

cards.front: Why are metals malleable and ductile?
cards.answer: Because the layers of positive metal ions can slide over each other in the metallic lattice.

cards.front: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
cards.answer: Because many strong electrostatic attractions between ions must be overcome simultaneously to melt them.

cards.front: Why do simple covalent molecules like water have low boiling points?
cards.answer: Because it is the weak intermolecular forces, not the strong covalent bonds, that break during boiling.

cards.front: Name the four key dramatic techniques the lesson gives for Macbeth
cards.answer: Soliloquies / Dramatic irony / Pathetic fallacy / Foreshadowing

cards.front: Name the two structural symmetries the lesson gives between the play's first and second halves
cards.answer: Lady Macbeth dominates then disappears / Macbeth is manipulated then becomes the manipulator
items: Macbeth is manipulated then becomes the manipulator

cards.front: Why does dramatic irony create tension when Duncan praises Macbeth's castle's 'pleasant seat'?
cards.answer: The audience knows Duncan will be murdered there, creating a gap between character and audience knowledge.

cards.front: Why do Macbeth's soliloquies matter to the play's tragic effect?
cards.answer: They create intimacy with the audience, so we share his doubts and guilt and cannot simply condemn him.

cards.front: Name the four key exam question types on the Crusades and their marks.
cards.answer: Source utility (5 marks) / Compare interpretations (10 marks) / Evaluate an interpretation (12 marks) / Period essay (16 marks)

cards.front: Name three things a strong Crusades period essay should draw on, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Power of the papacy and reform ideology / Urban II's specific promises / Individual motivations / Role of the military orders / Strategic failures of the Second Crusade
items: Power of the papacy and reform ideology
Strategic failures of the Second Crusade

cards.front: Why is the Gesta Francorum limited for showing the full range of crusader motivations?
cards.answer: Its purpose was to celebrate the crusade as God's work, so it emphasises religious devotion over material or secular motives.

cards.front: Why does a period essay that tells a detailed story of events without an argument only reach the developing band?
cards.answer: Because it describes events rather than building a line of argument with a substantiated judgement weighing the evidence.

cards.front: What four things should a strong essay plan include, according to the 5-minute plan?
cards.answer: Thesis / 3–4 paragraph topics / Key references / Context links

cards.front: Name the four common mistakes to avoid in the modern text essay.
cards.answer: Retelling the story / Bolting on context / Technique-spotting / Only writing about one part of the play
items: Only writing about one part of the play

cards.front: Why does naming a device (e.g. 'Kelly uses a metaphor') earn no credit on its own?
cards.answer: AO2 rewards analysis of the effect a choice creates, not just spotting that a device is used.

cards.front: Why must you show knowledge of at least three different parts of the play in your essay?
cards.answer: You must show knowledge of the whole text, not just one part, so reference events from at least three different parts.

cards.front: Name the four bases found in DNA nucleotides.
cards.answer: Adenine (A) / Thymine (T) / Cytosine (C) / Guanine (G)

cards.front: Name the three organisms the lesson gives as examples of asexual reproducers.
cards.answer: Bacteria / Strawberry plants (runners) / Hydra

cards.front: How does crossing over during the first division of meiosis lead to genetic variation?
cards.answer: Genetic material is shuffled between homologous chromosomes, making all four resulting cells genetically different from each other and the parent.

cards.front: Why is genetic variation important for a species facing a changing environment?
cards.answer: Individuals with alleles better suited to the new conditions are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those alleles on.

title: Industrial Britain: Irish, Empire and Refugees, c1700–c1900
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four migrant streams that the lesson says shaped 18th- and 19th-century Britain.
cards.answer: Irish famine migrants from 1845 / Lascars, ayahs and African seafarers from the Empire / Political and economic refugees from Europe / Formerly enslaved Africans who became abolitionists
items: Lascars, ayahs and African seafarers from the Empire
Political and economic refugees from Europe
Formerly enslaved Africans who became abolitionists

cards.front: Why did Manchester and Liverpool pull in such large numbers of migrant workers by the mid-19th century?
cards.answer: The Industrial Revolution turned them into booming factory and port cities, creating huge demand for labour.

cards.front: Why did hostility grow towards Italian street musicians and German or Eastern European workers from the 1880s?
cards.answer: Economic competition pinched and the popular press campaigned against them as a threat to wages and jobs.

cards.front: How did Ayahs sometimes end up needing support once they reached Britain?
cards.answer: They travelled with British colonial families to care for children but were sometimes abandoned in London afterwards.

title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the six changes of state given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Melting / Freezing / Evaporation/boiling / Condensation / Sublimation / Deposition

cards.front: Why does water's solid form (ice) take up more space than its liquid form?
cards.answer: When water freezes, molecules arrange into a hexagonal crystal structure that takes up more space than the liquid arrangement.

cards.front: Why do aircraft need low-density materials?
cards.answer: Low-density materials reduce the weight of the aircraft.

cards.front: How does density usually change when a substance changes state?
cards.answer: Particles become more or less tightly packed, changing the volume while the mass stays the same.

title: Earth Structure and the Development of Plate Theory
subject: geology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four main lines of physical evidence for plate tectonics given in the summary (excluding fossils, jigsaw fit and geology matches).
cards.answer: Sea-floor spreading (age increases from ridges) / Magnetic stripes on ocean floor / Earthquake and volcano distribution matching boundaries / GPS measurements of plate velocities
items: Earthquake and volcano distribution matching boundaries

cards.front: List the Earth's four layers from outermost to innermost.
cards.answer: Crust / Mantle / Outer core / Inner core

cards.front: Why does subduction happen when an oceanic plate meets a continental plate?
cards.answer: The denser oceanic crust sinks beneath the lighter, less dense continental crust.

cards.front: How do magnetic stripes on the ocean floor form?
cards.answer: As new basalt solidifies at the ridge, iron minerals align with the Earth's current magnetic field, recording each reversal as it happens.

title: The Church, sanctuary and trial by ordeal
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the two choices a fugitive had after forty days in sanctuary.
cards.answer: Surrender and stand trial / Abjure the realm (swear to leave the kingdom)
items: Abjure the realm (swear to leave the kingdom)

cards.front: Why did Church courts matter so much to accused criminals in medieval England?
cards.answer: Because Church courts could not impose the death penalty, so trial there instead of a royal court could save a person's life.

cards.front: In the ordeal of hot iron, how was guilt or innocence decided?
cards.answer: The accused carried a red-hot bar, the wound was bandaged, and three days later a clean wound meant innocence but a festering wound meant guilt.

title: Sitcom Option: Man Like Mobeen and Friends
subject: media-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three recurring locations used as setting and iconography in 'Wifey Riddim'.
cards.answer: The family home / The local shop / The market outside the mosque

cards.front: Name the four characters shown sitting together on a sofa outside in the final scene of 'Wifey Riddim'.
cards.answer: Mobeen / Aqsa / Eight / Nate

cards.front: Why does 'Wifey Riddim' use split screen in the supermarket scene?
cards.answer: To show Aqsa texting Mobeen and his phone receiving the message at the same time, creating comedy through editing.

cards.front: How does 'Wifey Riddim' challenge stereotypes of masculinity through Mobeen's character?
cards.answer: He is shown as a maternal, caring figure, working as a care-worker and called 'highly domesticated' by his uncle.

cards.front: Why does Wells set the Martian invasion in Surrey rather than a distant or fictional place?
cards.answer: Setting it in the comfortable middle-class heart of England makes the horror of invasion personal and immediate for readers.

cards.front: How does the novel force Victorian readers to empathise with colonised peoples?
cards.answer: By making the Martians treat humans as inferior beings to be displaced or destroyed, exactly as Europeans treated colonised peoples.

title: Political developments: Liberals, Lords and Labour
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What four new taxes did Lloyd George propose in the 1909 People's Budget?
cards.answer: Super-tax on high incomes / Increased death duties / 20% tax on land value increases / Increased income tax

cards.front: What three changes did the Parliament Act 1911 make?
cards.answer: Lords couldn't reject or amend money bills / Lords could only delay other laws two years / Elections held every five years, not seven
items: Lords couldn't reject or amend money bills
Lords could only delay other laws two years
Elections held every five years, not seven

cards.front: Why did King George V agree to threaten creating up to 500 new Liberal peers?
cards.answer: To force the Conservative-dominated Lords, who would be outnumbered, to capitulate and pass the Parliament Bill.

cards.front: Why did Lloyd George frame the 1909 budget as a class confrontation, attacking hereditary landowners?
cards.answer: To unite Liberal and Labour support behind the budget, though it angered Conservative and aristocratic opponents.

cards.front: Name the three values the lesson gives that underpin sporting behaviour.
cards.answer: Fair play / Respect / Tolerance

cards.front: Name the four positive spectator behaviours the lesson gives.
cards.answer: Cheering your team / Applauding great play from either side / Staying within designated areas / Following ground regulations
items: Applauding great play from either side

cards.front: How do all-seater stadia help reduce football-related disorder?
cards.answer: They give every fan an assigned seat, reduce crowd surges, and let stewards more easily monitor and remove troublemakers.

cards.front: Why did the shift to all-seater grounds change the culture of watching football?
cards.answer: Individual ticketing reduced anonymity that could mask troublemakers, made CCTV easier to use, and formalised crowd segregation.

title: Materials, Corrosion, Haber Process and Fertilisers
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the three metals mixed together to make stainless steel.
cards.answer: Iron / Chromium / Nickel

cards.front: Name the three raw materials NPK fertiliser production uses to provide N, P and K.
cards.answer: Ammonia and nitric/sulfuric acid for nitrogen / Phosphate rock and acid for phosphorus / Potassium chloride or sulfate for potassium
items: Ammonia and nitric/sulfuric acid for nitrogen
Phosphate rock and acid for phosphorus
Potassium chloride or sulfate for potassium

cards.front: How does electroplating protect a metal from corrosion?
cards.answer: Electrolysis is used to coat the metal with a thin layer of a less reactive or more attractive metal, such as chromium on car parts.

cards.front: Why is 200 atmospheres used in the Haber process instead of a much higher pressure?
cards.answer: Very high pressures would give a higher yield but are too expensive and dangerous, so 200 atm is a compromise.

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says survive in each of the three poems.
cards.answer: A skill survives, passed father to son (Parker) / Fear survives, the memory of being cornered at thirteen (Femi) / A sentence survives, carried from grandfather to stranger (Antrobus)
items: A skill survives, passed father to son (Parker)
Fear survives, the memory of being cornered at thirteen (Femi)
A sentence survives, carried from grandfather to stranger (Antrobus)

cards.front: Why does the lesson describe Femi's 'Thirteen' as closer to an elegy than a fond memory?
cards.answer: Because it mourns a lost sense of safety rather than celebrating youth, as the boy learns his own street sees him as a threat.

cards.front: Why does the last line of 'The Jewellery Maker' suggest the jewellery means more to the maker than the buyer?
cards.answer: Because 'warming the metal his hands caress' shows his personal care and connection to the work, beyond its value to whoever buys it.

cards.front: How does Elizabeth's judgement of Wickham show her prejudice?
cards.answer: She trusts his charm and judges harshly by appearance rather than character, misjudging him.

cards.front: Why does Austen not reject the class system entirely in the novel?
cards.answer: She values taste, education and responsibility, but argues these are not exclusive to any one class.

title: Post-war Prosperity, Consumerism and the American Dream
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says the post-war boom rested on.
cards.answer: Cheap oil / Mass car ownership / Federal housing finance / Spending power of the GI Bill
items: Spending power of the GI Bill

cards.front: Name the four groups the lesson says made up the 22% of Americans still in poverty in 1960.
cards.answer: Rural African-Americans / Mexican-Americans / Native Americans on reservations / Elderly Americans without Social Security

cards.front: Why could suburbs like Levittown only work once cars became widely owned?
cards.answer: Suburbs were built away from city centres, so residents needed cars to reach jobs, shops and services.

cards.front: How did federal housing policy stop black families sharing in suburban prosperity?
cards.answer: The FHA redlined mixed-race neighbourhoods and refused to insure mortgages there, denying subsidies that built white suburban wealth.

cards.front: Name the three everyday examples the lesson gives of exothermic reactions.
cards.answer: Combustion (burning fuels) / Neutralisation between acids and alkalis / Oxidation of metals

cards.front: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
cards.answer: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react at a given temperature.

cards.front: Why does a match need to be used to light methane gas, even though burning it is exothermic overall?
cards.answer: Even exothermic reactions need an initial energy input (activation energy) to break the first bonds and start the reaction.

cards.front: Name the five animal and insect fibres the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Wool / Cashmere / Mohair / Angora / Alpaca

cards.front: Name the four plant fibres the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Cotton / Linen (flax) / Hemp / Jute

cards.front: Why does wool shrink and felt when agitated in warm water?
cards.answer: The microscopic scales on each wool fibre interlock when agitated in warm water, causing shrinkage and felting.

cards.front: Why is fibre recovery for recycling difficult with blended yarns?
cards.answer: Blended yarns mix two or more fibre types together so tightly that they are impossible to separate.

cards.front: Why does a 100-metre sprinter need very little aerobic endurance?
cards.answer: The race lasts under 11 seconds, so ATP-PC and anaerobic energy systems dominate rather than the aerobic system.

cards.front: Why does a striker in football prioritise speed and agility?
cards.answer: Strikers need to outrun defenders and change direction quickly in tight spaces to create scoring chances.

cards.front: Name the four fitness tests the lesson gives for measuring balance, coordination, reaction time and agility.
cards.answer: Stork stand test (balance) / Alternate hand throw test (coordination) / Ruler drop test (reaction time) / Illinois agility test (agility)

cards.front: What were Murdock's (1962) method details, in his serial position curve study?
cards.answer: Participants heard word lists / Typically 20 words / Presented at one word per second / Recalled in any order immediately after
items: Presented at one word per second
Recalled in any order immediately after

cards.front: Why does the primacy effect happen?
cards.answer: Early words face little competition in short-term memory so get rehearsed a lot, transferring them into long-term memory.

cards.front: Why does the recency effect disappear if participants do a distracting task before recall?
cards.answer: The distracting task means the short-term memory trace of the last words fades before recall can happen.

cards.front: How does Murdock's study support the multi-store model of memory?
cards.answer: Primacy items being recalled from LTM and recency items from STM shows these are separate, limited stores, as the model predicts.

cards.front: Name the seven episodes that structure The War of the Worlds, in order.
cards.answer: The landing / The Heat-Ray / The tripods / Flight / Entrapment / Survival / Resolution

cards.front: Why does each episode in the novel's structure matter for the narrator's confidence?
cards.answer: Each episode escalates the threat and strips away another layer of the narrator's confidence.

title: The Concerto Through Time: The Baroque Era (1650-1750)
subject: music-ocr

cards.front: Name the five features the lesson gives to check together when identifying an unfamiliar extract as Baroque.
cards.answer: Small string orchestra with audible harpsichord continuo / Ritornello form with returning tutti theme / Terraced rather than gradual dynamics / Decorative, ornamented, sequential solo/concertino writing / Clear diatonic tonality without Romantic chromatic drama
items: Small string orchestra with audible harpsichord continuo
Ritornello form with returning tutti theme
Clear diatonic tonality without Romantic chromatic drama

cards.front: Name the five instrument sections that made up a typical Baroque string orchestra.
cards.answer: First violins / Second violins / Violas / Cellos / Double basses (plus keyboard for harmony)

cards.front: Why does terraced dynamics rather than gradual crescendo happen in Baroque music?
cards.answer: The harpsichord's volume is fixed by its plucking mechanism, and Baroque texture favours alternating small and large groups rather than blending them.

cards.front: Why did Baroque orchestras stay small compared to later periods?
cards.answer: They were written for small venues like chapels, court chambers or a cardinal's salon, so patrons' budgets and spaces did not need large wind, brass or string forces.

cards.front: Name the three ways to increase the induced potential difference in a coil, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Move the magnet (or conductor) faster / Use a stronger magnet / Increase the number of turns on the coil
items: Increase the number of turns on the coil

cards.front: Name the two causes of energy loss in a real transformer given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Heat in the coils due to resistance / Eddy currents and magnetisation losses in the core
items: Heat in the coils due to resistance
Eddy currents and magnetisation losses in the core

cards.front: Why does an alternator produce a sinusoidal (wave-shaped) output?
cards.answer: The coil rotates in the magnetic field so the induced potential difference reverses direction every half turn.

cards.front: How does a step-up transformer at a power station help reduce energy loss in the National Grid?
cards.answer: It increases the voltage for transmission, which lowers the current and reduces heat lost in the cables.

cards.front: Name the three remaining poems the lesson uses to enrich the cross-period picture of belonging.
cards.answer: Antrobus's Jamaican British / Hardi's My Mother's Kitchen / Rumens's The Émigrée

cards.front: Name the three key contrasts the lesson gives between Romantic and contemporary belonging.
cards.answer: Source of belonging / Stability / Individual vs collective

cards.front: Why does Hood's 'I Remember, I Remember' still connect to Romantic ideas but feel different in mood?
cards.answer: It keeps Romantic themes of childhood and nature but its dominant mood is Victorian melancholy, a sense the world has grown worse.

cards.front: Why is belonging never automatic for the contemporary poets in the anthology?
cards.answer: They write in a world shaped by globalisation, migration and empire's legacy, so identity is rarely singular and belonging is contested.

cards.front: Name the three human causes of drought given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Over-extraction for agriculture / Unsustainable dam-building upstream / Large-scale deforestation

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says drought is hazardous to people.
cards.answer: Crop failure and food price spikes / Livestock deaths from failed grassland / Water rationing closing industries / Wildfires in dry vegetation
items: Crop failure and food price spikes

cards.front: Why did the Dust Bowl drought of the 1930s cause permanent migration?
cards.answer: The long drought made farming impossible on the Great Plains, forcing 2.5 million people to abandon the land.

cards.front: Why did the 2017-19 Australian drought cause a low death toll despite AU$8 billion in losses?
cards.answer: Australia's wealth allowed water trucks, emergency loans and psychological support to be sent to affected towns and farms.

cards.front: Name the five most important themes in The War of the Worlds for the exam.
cards.answer: Imperialism and colonisation / Evolution and survival / Fragility of civilisation / Limits of technology / Humanity's place in the universe

cards.front: Name the four aspects of Victorian society the novel shows collapsing quickly.
cards.answer: The army fails / The class system dissolves / Crowds become mobs / Religious faith crumbles

cards.front: Why does Wells describe the Martians in purely biological terms (large brains, no digestive system, budding reproduction)?
cards.answer: They represent what humanity might evolve into after millions of years — pure intellect without emotion, showing evolution as amoral.

cards.front: Why do the telegraph and railway failing matter so much to Victorian society in the novel?
cards.answer: These communication and transport networks held the Empire together, so without them society cannot coordinate any response.

title: Homesteaders: The Homestead Act and the Timber Culture Act
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three groups the lesson says were explicitly made eligible under the broad terms of the Homestead Act.
cards.answer: Women heads of households / Freed Black families after 1865 / Migrants intending to become citizens

cards.front: Name four immediate obstacles (besides low rainfall) that broke down Plains homesteading families, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Almost no timber / Wells dug by hand / Grasshopper plagues and prairie fires / Blizzards and isolation

cards.front: Why was 160 acres often not enough for a family farm on the High Plains?
cards.answer: It was designed for well-watered eastern farms, but Plains rainfall was much lower, so dry years without irrigation could destroy crops and ruin families.

cards.front: How did railroad companies undermine the goal of the Homestead Acts, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: They received far more public Plains land than homesteaders through separate land grants and used it to set freight rates that squeezed farmers.

cards.front: Name the three things Elizabethan fathers based their choice of husband on for their daughters, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Wealth / Rank / Family alliances

cards.front: Why does Beatrice's outspokenness make sense within Elizabethan patriarchal society, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Elizabethan society was patriarchal and controlled women through obedience, so Beatrice's outspokenness is a rebellion against that framework.

cards.front: How does the setting of Messina as a port city help create the play's plot?
cards.answer: As a place of arrivals, departures, strangers and soldiers, its transient quality enables rapid courtship, mistaken identity and social disruption.

cards.front: Why does the darker material in Much Ado About Nothing push the comedy close to tragedy before its resolution?
cards.answer: Don John's villainy and Hero's public humiliation nearly destroy innocent lives before the comic ending restores order.

cards.front: Name the five main stakeholder groups covered in the lesson.
cards.answer: Owners / Employees / Customers / Suppliers / Local community

cards.front: Name three levers owners/shareholders can use to influence a business.
cards.answer: Vote at annual general meetings / Replace directors / Refuse further investment

cards.front: Why might raising staff wages still cause stakeholder conflict?
cards.answer: Employees welcome the rise, but owners see profits dip and customers face higher prices as costs are passed on.

cards.front: How can a supermarket cut costs with self-checkouts while limiting harm to staff?
cards.answer: It redeploys staff into personal shopping roles rather than making them redundant.

title: Life After Death, Euthanasia and the Natural World
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Name the six kinds of evidence people point to for life after death.
cards.answer: Remembered lives / Paranormal experiences / Logic / Reward / Comfort / Hope of meeting loved ones again
items: Hope of meeting loved ones again

cards.front: Name the four common non-religious objections to belief in life after death.
cards.answer: Only a psychological comfort / No scientific evidence / Contact with dead is fraudulent / Judgment invented for social control

cards.front: Why do Catholics say suffering can have meaning rather than needing euthanasia?
cards.answer: Suffering can have meaning when united to Christ's own suffering, and hospice care addresses the underlying pain and fear.

cards.front: Why do Catholics treat pollution and overuse of resources as a moral failure, not just a practical problem?
cards.answer: Because the earth belongs to God and is shared by all people and future generations, wasteful use is a failure of stewardship.

cards.front: Name the two fields in a packet header that identify sender and receiver.
cards.answer: Source IP address / Destination IP address

cards.front: Why is packet switching more robust than circuit switching?
cards.answer: Packets can be automatically rerouted around a congested or broken path, whereas circuit switching reserves one fixed dedicated path for the whole call.

cards.front: Why does the receiving device sometimes need TCP to request a packet be resent?
cards.answer: Packets can arrive out of order or go missing, so TCP requests any missing packet be resent to complete the file.

cards.front: Why can dynamic routing recover from a network failure faster than static routing?
cards.answer: Routers share information and automatically update their routing tables when the network changes, finding an alternative path within seconds.

cards.front: Why does a fixed mindset tend to lower self-efficacy?
cards.answer: Because believing ability is fixed makes a student interpret failure as a ceiling on what they can ever achieve.

cards.front: According to Willingham, why should content decide whether information is taught visually or verbally?
cards.answer: Because some information is inherently spatial (best shown visually) and other information is inherently verbal, regardless of learner preference.

title: Sunspots, the Solar Cycle and the Solar Wind
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five effects of space weather on Earth's technology given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Power grid disruption from induced currents / Satellite damage from high-energy particles / Unreliable GPS and radio communications / Increased radiation on polar flight routes / Astronauts sheltered during solar particle events
items: Power grid disruption from induced currents
Increased radiation on polar flight routes
Astronauts sheltered during solar particle events

cards.front: Why does the penumbra of a sunspot look lighter than the umbra?
cards.answer: Its magnetic field is inclined rather than vertical, so convection is only partially inhibited, keeping it hotter than the umbra.

cards.front: How does the 11-year solar cycle actually work?
cards.answer: The Sun's magnetic field winds and tangles due to differential rotation, then resets as opposite polarities reconnect, repeating every 11 years.

cards.front: Why do comets have two separate tails?
cards.answer: The dust tail curves along the orbit due to radiation pressure, while the ion tail is blown straight away from the Sun by the solar wind.

cards.front: Name the two cruelties described at Lowood School besides burnt porridge and thin bread.
cards.answer: Two-mile walk to church in bitter wind / Punishment for small rule breaches
items: Two-mile walk to church in bitter wind

cards.front: How many years does Jane spend at Lowood, and in what roles?
cards.answer: Eight years in all: six as a pupil, then two as a teacher.

cards.front: Why does Jane decide to leave Lowood and advertise for the Thornfield governess job?
cards.answer: When Miss Temple leaves to marry, Jane feels the calm of Lowood leave with her too.

cards.front: How does Helen Burns's model of patience later affect Jane's behaviour towards Rochester?
cards.answer: Helen's example of forbearance helps Jane later leave Rochester without fury and return on her own terms.

title: Act 3: Eric, the Inspector's Speech & the Twist
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: Why does Priestley have the Inspector's speech shift from persuasion to threat?
cards.answer: To suggest collective responsibility is not optional but inevitable, warning that people will be 'taught' the lesson if they refuse to learn it.

cards.front: How does the phone call twist at the end of Act 3 act as a test rather than a relief?
cards.answer: It separates those who genuinely learned (Sheila and Eric) from those who revert to selfishness once the pressure is removed (Birling, Mrs Birling, Gerald).

cards.front: How does J.W. Dunne's theory of time connect to the play's ending?
cards.answer: Dunne argued time can loop rather than run in a straight line, so the cyclical ending suggests the Birlings' failure to learn means the suffering will happen again.

cards.front: What are the three theories the lesson gives for interpreting the play's cyclical ending?
cards.answer: Inspector was a supernatural warning / time is circular and Birlings are trapped in a loop / message that responsibility cannot be escaped
items: time is circular and Birlings are trapped in a loop
message that responsibility cannot be escaped

title: Brown v. Topeka 1954: A Legal Earthquake
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Why did Earl Warren insist on a unanimous 9-0 decision in Brown?
cards.answer: He believed a unanimous ruling would carry greater authority than a split court, so he spent months persuading reluctant Southern justices.

cards.front: Why is it a mistake to say Brown v. Topeka 'ended segregation' in 1954?
cards.answer: The ruling only created a legal opening; real desegregation needed troops, lawsuits and a decade of activism before it happened on the ground.

cards.front: Why did President Eisenhower send troops to Little Rock in 1957?
cards.answer: He had to federalise the Arkansas National Guard and send the 101st Airborne to enforce school integration against local resistance.

cards.front: Name the four events the lesson gives as part of the movement that made Brown's words matter beyond paper.
cards.answer: Emmett Till's funeral / the Montgomery boycott / the Little Rock Nine / Birmingham

cards.front: Why does Dickens describe London as dirty and menacing when Pip first arrives?
cards.answer: To undercut Pip's romantic expectations, showing London is not the elegant paradise he imagined but a place where wealth and crime coexist.

cards.front: Why does Pip begin to see Joe's simplicity as embarrassing after moving to London?
cards.answer: Absorbing London manners makes Pip ashamed of his humble origins, so he starts viewing Joe's plainness as shameful rather than admirable.

title: The American Revolution and 'No Taxation Without Representation', 1763-1783
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the five steps the lesson lists in the build-up to the American Revolution.
cards.answer: Stamp Act 1765 / Townshend Duties 1767 / Boston Massacre 1770 / Boston Tea Party 1773 / Coercive Acts 1774

cards.front: Name the four countries the lesson says joined or entered the war against Britain, 1778-1780.
cards.answer: France (1778) / Spain (1779) / the Dutch (1780)

cards.front: Why did Parliament argue the American colonists should help pay off Britain's war debt after 1763?
cards.answer: Because the colonists had been protected from the French at British expense, so Parliament reasoned they should share the cost.

cards.front: Why was the French alliance after 1778 decisive in Britain losing the war?
cards.answer: French money, ships and troops at Yorktown ended any realistic chance of British military victory.

title: Hitler's dictatorship — Reichstag Fire to Fuhrer
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four things Article 2 of the Enabling Act was used to do within four months, in the order the lesson gives them.
cards.answer: Outlaw trade unions / Ban the SPD / Dissolve all other political parties / Declare a one-party state

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says Hitler used to turn a coalition Chancellor into unchallenged dictator by August 1934.
cards.answer: Law / State violence / Contingency

cards.front: Why did the Reichswehr (army) accept the purge of the SA in the Night of the Long Knives?
cards.answer: Blomberg had agreed the army would back Hitler as Hindenburg's successor if he removed the SA threat.

cards.front: Why did Rohm's SA come into conflict with the Reichswehr generals in 1934?
cards.answer: Rohm wanted the SA to absorb the army and become a revolutionary force, which the generals refused to accept.

cards.front: The lesson says every paragraph in a top-band answer should ideally contain which four elements?
cards.answer: A quotation / A named technique / Analysis of its effect / A contextual link

cards.front: Name the two steps the lesson gives for structuring a drama extract answer.
cards.answer: Analyse the printed extract closely / Widen out to the rest of the play
items: Widen out to the rest of the play

cards.front: Why does Delaney present the Boy as the kindest, most genuine character in the play?
cards.answer: To directly challenge the racist assumptions her 1958 audience would have held.

cards.front: Why can Helen not properly mother Jo, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because motherhood is a skill Helen never learned, as nobody modelled it for her.

cards.front: List the 14 substances in the reactivity series from most to least reactive, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Potassium / Sodium / Lithium / Calcium / Magnesium / Aluminium / Carbon / Zinc / Iron / Hydrogen / Copper / Silver / Gold / Platinum
items: Zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold, platinum

cards.front: Why is carbon reduction of iron oxide called a redox reaction?
cards.answer: The iron oxide is reduced as it loses oxygen, while the carbon is oxidised as it gains oxygen.

cards.front: How can you work out a metal's reactivity by testing it in dilute acid?
cards.answer: Faster fizzing and more heat produced show the metal is more reactive.

cards.front: How does bioleaching extract metal from ore? [HIGHER]
cards.answer: Bacteria produce acidic solutions that dissolve metal compounds from the ore, which can then be extracted by displacement or electrolysis.

cards.front: Name the six fractions collected from crude oil, in order from top to bottom of the fractionating column.
cards.answer: Gases / Petrol / Kerosene / Diesel oil / Fuel oil / Bitumen

cards.front: Name the four defining features of a homologous series given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Same general formula / Differ by CH2 each time / Gradual variation in physical properties / Similar chemical properties

cards.front: Why do hydrocarbons with high boiling points condense near the bottom of the fractionating column?
cards.answer: The column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top, so high boiling point hydrocarbons condense before rising far.

cards.front: Why does ease of ignition decrease as hydrocarbon molecules get larger?
cards.answer: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, making them harder to ignite than smaller molecules.

cards.front: Name the six key extracts the lesson says to prepare for The War of the Worlds.
cards.answer: Opening chapter with Tasmanian reference / Heat-Ray scene on Horsell Common / The London exodus / HMS Thunderchild's destruction / Narrator trapped with the curate / The bacteria ending

cards.front: Name the five common mistakes the lesson warns against in War of the Worlds exam answers.
cards.answer: Retelling the plot instead of analysing methods / Only discussing the extract, not the wider novel / Listing context without linking to purpose / Writing so loosely the point disappears / Not using literary terminology
items: Retelling the plot instead of analysing methods
Only discussing the extract, not the wider novel
Listing context without linking to purpose
Writing so loosely the point disappears

cards.front: Why does the lesson say the retrospective framing in the opening chapter creates dramatic irony?
cards.answer: Because the narrator tells the story looking back, so readers sense the coming horror before it happens.

cards.front: Why does the lesson treat the bacteria ending as anti-climactic?
cards.answer: Because it rejects heroic conventions, with humans saved by humble bacteria rather than human action, ironically undercutting human pride.

title: Wealth, Poverty and the Uses of Money
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the five religious giving duties the lesson gives, one per tradition.
cards.answer: Zakat (Islam) / Tzedakah (Judaism) / Dasvandh (Sikhism) / Dana (Buddhism) / Stewardship (Christianity)

cards.front: Name the four UK religious charities the lesson describes with their founding tradition.
cards.answer: Christian Aid / Islamic Relief / World Jewish Relief / Khalsa Aid

cards.front: Why does Islamic teaching prohibit riba (charging interest)?
cards.answer: Because charging interest exploits those in financial difficulty and concentrates wealth unjustly.

cards.front: How did Zacchaeus's story show the change Jesus's teaching on wealth was meant to bring?
cards.answer: On meeting Jesus, the wealthy tax collector gave half his possessions to the poor and repaid those he had cheated fourfold.

cards.front: Name the four 'loose threads' left unresolved at the end of The Merchant of Venice.
cards.answer: Antonio remains alone / Shylock is absent and destroyed / Jessica's happiness is uncertain / Classical allusions suggest love is fragile
items: Classical allusions suggest love is fragile

cards.front: How does the ring trick show that Portia holds real power in her marriage?
cards.answer: She gave the ring, retrieved it disguised as Balthazar, and controls when the truth about Bassanio's broken oath is revealed.

cards.front: Why might Shylock's dislike of music (Act 2, Scene 5) matter for how Act 5's music speech works?
cards.answer: Since music represents harmony and civilisation in Belmont, Shylock's dislike of it marks him as excluded and 'uncivilised' by the Christian community.

cards.front: Name the four physical features of Inchon that made the landing so risky, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: 9-metre tidal range / harbour a mud-flat outside tidal windows / narrow channels under Wolmido's guns / no beaches, only sea walls to climb
items: harbour a mud-flat outside tidal windows
no beaches, only sea walls to climb

cards.front: List the five stages of the UN advance from Pusan to the Yalu, with the lesson's dates.
cards.answer: Inchon, 15 September / Seoul, 28 September / 38th parallel, 1 October / Pyongyang, 19 October / sight of the Yalu, late November
items: sight of the Yalu, late November

cards.front: Why did the North Korean army collapse after the Inchon landings?
cards.answer: Caught between MacArthur's landing in the west and the Eighth Army's Pusan breakout, their supply lines collapsed and whole units surrendered.

cards.front: Why did the gap MacArthur left between X Corps and Eighth Army matter as they advanced towards the Yalu?
cards.answer: The wide gap in the mountainous interior made supply easier but left the two columns unable to support each other if attacked.

cards.front: Name the six noble gases (Group 0) listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Helium / Neon / Argon / Krypton / Xenon / Radon

cards.front: Name the four properties the lesson gives for transition metals compared with Group 1 metals.
cards.answer: Much less reactive / Higher melting points / Harder and denser / Form coloured compounds

cards.front: Why did the scientific community accept Mendeleev's periodic table?
cards.answer: Because elements like gallium and germanium were later discovered with properties closely matching his predictions.

cards.front: Why do boiling points increase going down Group 0?
cards.answer: The atoms become larger, giving stronger intermolecular forces between them.

cards.front: Name the three conditions that are met at equilibrium.
cards.answer: Forward rate equals reverse rate / Concentrations of reactants and products stay constant / Both reactions still occurring at molecular level
items: Concentrations of reactants and products stay constant
Both reactions still occurring at molecular level

cards.front: Name the three industrial conditions used in the Haber process.
cards.answer: About 450°C / About 200 atm pressure / Iron catalyst

cards.front: Why does heating cooled ammonium chloride cause it to break down into ammonia and hydrogen chloride gas?
cards.answer: The forward reaction is endothermic, so heating supplies the energy needed to decompose the solid into gases.

cards.front: Why is unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen gas recycled in the Haber process?
cards.answer: Only about 15% converts to ammonia per pass, so recycling the unreacted gases increases overall yield over time.

cards.front: Why does an ionic compound shatter when a force is applied, unlike a metal?
cards.answer: Layers of ions shift so ions of the same charge are forced next to each other, and they repel.

cards.front: Why does graphite make a good lubricant?
cards.answer: The weak forces between its layers of hexagons allow the layers to slide over each other.

cards.front: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points?
cards.answer: The intermolecular forces between molecules are weak and need little energy to overcome.

cards.front: Why do polymers have higher melting points than simple molecular substances?
cards.answer: Because polymer molecules are large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong.

cards.front: Name the seven food poisoning bacteria named in the lesson.
cards.answer: Bacillus cereus / Campylobacter / Clostridium perfringens / E. coli / Listeria / Salmonella / Staphylococcus aureus

cards.front: What four things must UK food labelling laws show on all pre-packaged food?
cards.answer: Clear ingredients list / 14 allergens highlighted / Use-by or best-before date / Nutritional information

cards.front: Why can Clostridium perfringens survive and grow in stews and gravies?
cards.answer: It is found in soil and animal intestines and grows in large batches of food cooked slowly and not cooled quickly enough.

cards.front: Why is E. coli food poisoning especially serious for young children and the elderly?
cards.answer: E. coli, found in raw or undercooked beef and contaminated water, can cause very serious illness in these groups.

title: Representing Algorithms: Pseudo-code, Flowcharts and Trace Tables
subject: computer-science-aqa

cards.front: Name the four standard flowchart shapes and what each represents.
cards.answer: Oval/rounded rectangle - start or stop / Rectangle - process or action / Diamond - decision with yes/no exits / Parallelogram - input or output

cards.front: Name the three standard ways to represent an algorithm.
cards.answer: Pseudo-code / Flowcharts / Actual program code

cards.front: Why does a REPEAT...UNTIL loop always run its body at least once, unlike WHILE?
cards.answer: REPEAT...UNTIL checks its condition after the body runs, whereas WHILE tests the condition first.

cards.front: Why are trace tables safer than visual inspection for nested loops or complex conditions?
cards.answer: Trace tables record every variable's value at each step, avoiding mistakes from just reasoning about complex logic in your head.

title: Effects on Wellbeing When Person-Centred Values Are NOT Applied
subject: health-social-care-ocr

cards.front: Name the four intellectual effects the lesson lists when person-centred values are not applied.
cards.answer: Lack of progress or skills development / Failure to achieve potential / Loss of concentration / Lack of mental stimulation
