items: Lack of progress or skills development

cards.front: Why does not consulting Margaret about activities lead to her becoming withdrawn?
cards.answer: She isn't told about activities like the reminiscence group, so she loses social interaction, her conversational skills weaken and she withdraws.

cards.front: How does ignoring dignity cause Margaret to develop low self-esteem?
cards.answer: Being addressed by a disliked nickname or discussed in front of others strips her dignity, making her feel humiliated and inadequate.

cards.front: Name the four qualities the lesson gives that never change in Joe Gargery.
cards.answer: Loyalty / Kindness / Forgiveness / Honesty

cards.front: Why does Dickens present Miss Havisham as both a villain and a victim?
cards.answer: She manipulates Pip and weaponises Estella, yet she herself was defrauded and betrayed by Compeyson and consumed by monomania and remorse.

cards.front: How does Magwitch's life story change how readers see him by the end of the novel?
cards.answer: His orphaned, starved past shows Victorian society created the criminal it punished, revealing his genuine, selfless love for Pip.

cards.front: Why is Joe's discomfort in London described as integrity rather than inferiority?
cards.answer: He refuses to pretend to be something he is not, staying true to himself despite feeling out of place.

cards.front: How does Jane's reserved nature nearly cost her the relationship with Bingley?
cards.answer: Her reserve stops her showing her feelings openly, letting Darcy convince Bingley she is indifferent.

cards.front: How does Bingley's openness make him vulnerable compared to Darcy's reserve?
cards.answer: His openness means he is easily manipulated by his sisters and Darcy, unlike Darcy who conceals deep feeling.

title: Atomic Structure and Models Through Time
subject: science-ocr-b

cards.front: Name the four atomic models covered in the order they developed, from earliest to Bohr's.
cards.answer: Dalton's solid sphere model / Thomson's plum pudding model / Rutherford's nuclear model / Bohr's model with fixed energy levels
items: Bohr's model with fixed energy levels

cards.front: Name the two observations from the alpha particle scattering experiment on gold foil.
cards.answer: Most particles passed straight through / Some bounced back sharply

cards.front: Why does losing an electron produce a positive ion?
cards.answer: Losing electrons means there are now more protons than electrons, giving an overall positive charge.

cards.front: Why does Bohr's model explain emission spectra better than Rutherford's model?
cards.answer: Electrons occupy fixed energy levels and release light of set energies when they fall back to a lower shell, which Rutherford's model couldn't account for.

title: Interpretations: was 1381 a failed revolution or a turning point?
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Why does the conservative reading conclude 1381 was not a turning point?
cards.answer: Because very little changed in law: the revolt was crushed, leaders executed and promises revoked.

cards.front: Why does Christopher Dyer see 1381 as important but not uniquely transformative?
cards.answer: Because it was one episode in a longer process of peasant agency already changing rural society since the Black Death.

title: Food, the Environment and Food Security
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-aqa

cards.front: Name the four practical strategies the lesson gives for reducing household food waste.
cards.answer: Meal planning / Correct food storage / Creative use of leftovers / Freezing food before it spoils

cards.front: Name four essential functions of food packaging given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Protects food from contamination / Extends shelf life / Provides labelling information / Enables safe transport

cards.front: Why can plastic film on a prepared salad be justified environmentally, despite being single-use plastic?
cards.answer: It extends shelf life and prevents food waste, potentially saving more environmental damage than the plastic causes if recycled.

cards.front: Why does wasted food represent more than just wasted food?
cards.answer: It also wastes the energy, water and labour used to produce it, and rotting food releases methane in landfill.

cards.front: Name the four development opportunities the lesson gives for hot deserts (besides indigenous land rights).
cards.answer: Mineral extraction / Energy (solar farms) / Farming with irrigation / Tourism

cards.front: Name the three challenges of development in hot deserts given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Extreme temperatures limiting working hours / Water supply constraints / Inaccessibility

cards.front: How does a camel's blood let it survive severe dehydration?
cards.answer: Its oval-shaped red blood cells keep flowing even when the blood thickens with dehydration.

cards.front: How does letting its body temperature vary help a camel survive in the desert?
cards.answer: Its temperature can rise from 34°C to 41°C, avoiding the energy cost of sweating until absolutely necessary.

title: The Potion, the Tomb & the Ending
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three impossible circumstances Juliet faces at the start of Act 4, Scene 3.
cards.answer: Father has arranged marriage to Paris / Already secretly married to Romeo / Nurse betrayed her by advising she marry Paris
items: Father has arranged marriage to Paris
Nurse betrayed her by advising she marry Paris

cards.front: Why is Romeo's act of defiance against fate ultimately futile?
cards.answer: His decision to buy poison and rush to the tomb is exactly what fate needs to fulfil the Prologue's promise of death.

cards.front: How does Shakespeare create dramatic irony in Romeo's final speech at the tomb?
cards.answer: Romeo notices Juliet's lips and cheeks are still crimson but tragically reads this as death failing to mar her beauty, not as a sign of life.

title: The Trinity, Creation and Human Nature
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the roles of the three persons of the Trinity given in the lesson (Father, Son, Holy Spirit).
cards.answer: Father: creator and sustainer of all things / Son: incarnate Word who redeems humanity / Holy Spirit: presence of God active in the world and believers
items: Father: creator and sustainer of all things
Son: incarnate Word who redeems humanity
Holy Spirit: presence of God active in the world and believers

cards.front: Why do Catholics say Genesis 1 and 2 should not be read as science?
cards.answer: The Church understands them as theological accounts revealing truths about God and human beings, not scientific explanations.

cards.front: How does Catholic teaching say humans should exercise dominion over creation?
cards.answer: True dominion is exercised as stewardship, caring for the earth as God's creation rather than exploiting it carelessly.

title: Act 5: The Tomb and the Tragedy
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: Name the three young men killed by the feud in the play, in order.
cards.answer: Mercutio / Tybalt / Paris

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare give the play a circular structure, ending with the Prince as it began?
cards.answer: It reinforces that the tragedy was inevitable, as the Prologue already told us the lovers would die.

cards.front: How does Romeo's hamartia of impulsiveness cause his death in Act 5?
cards.answer: He rushes to buy poison and ride to Verona without pausing or checking Balthasar's report, missing the Friar's letter.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare include Paris's death at the tomb?
cards.answer: To show the feud's destruction spreads beyond the two families, killing an entirely innocent third young man.

title: Lady Bird: Coming-of-Age and Greta Gerwig's Direction
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four key formal signatures of Gerwig's direction in Lady Bird.
cards.answer: Persistent two-shot for mother-daughter scenes / Hard cut vignette structure / Warm Sacramento palette vs cooler New York / Needle-drop soundtrack as temporal anchor
items: Warm Sacramento palette vs cooler New York

cards.front: Why does the musical-theatre-audition sequence use warmer lighting and hand-held close-ups than the exterior school shots?
cards.answer: It codes the drama room as intimate and emotionally significant, a space where Lady Bird can author herself, unlike the school's hierarchies.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to call Lady Bird simply 'realistic' or 'naturalistic'?
cards.answer: Only the dialogue is naturalistic; the cinematography, colour palette, vignette structure and needle-drop score are deliberate aesthetic choices shaping the spectator's experience.

cards.front: What three conditions must the police tell a person once they have been arrested?
cards.answer: The reason for their arrest / Their right to legal advice

cards.front: Why do critics argue that stop and search can be harmful?
cards.answer: It has been applied disproportionately against certain communities, undermining trust in police without reliably reducing crime.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception that judges decide guilt in a Crown Court trial?
cards.answer: The jury decides guilt after hearing all evidence; the judge only rules on law and sets the sentence.

cards.front: Why can a legal adviser support magistrates in court?
cards.answer: Magistrates are ordinary members of the public, not legally qualified judges, so they need advice on points of law.

cards.front: Why can identical twins end up with different body weight even though they share the same genotype?
cards.answer: Because characteristics depend on genes and the environment interacting, so different environments produce different phenotypes despite identical genotypes.

cards.front: Why can a mutation in a non-coding region of DNA still change an organism's phenotype? (Higher tier)
cards.answer: It can alter gene expression, switching a gene on or off, which changes the phenotype without changing any protein's sequence.

title: Wolsey's Domestic Policy and the Justice System
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: According to the lesson, what four areas of domestic policy did Wolsey work on as Lord Chancellor?
cards.answer: Justice (Chancery and Star Chamber) / Enclosure (1517 Commission) / Finance (the subsidy) / The royal household (Eltham Ordinances)

cards.front: Why did Wolsey's Star Chamber and Chancery system eventually run into trouble in the longer term?
cards.answer: Courts became swamped with cases, common-law judges resented the encroachment, and Wolsey's personal style invited accusations of bias.

cards.front: Why did the 1517 enclosure commission fail to produce lasting change on the ground?
cards.answer: Prosecutions dragged on for years and many landowners simply paid fines and carried on enclosing land.

cards.front: Why did Wolsey have to abandon enforcement of the enclosure commission by 1523?
cards.answer: He compromised to win Parliament's support for granting war taxation.

cards.front: Why is the windmill's real purpose in Chapter 10 a betrayal of Snowball's original promise?
cards.answer: It is used to mill corn for profit rather than to ease the animals' workload as promised.

cards.front: Why does Orwell end the novella with the pigs looking indistinguishable from the humans?
cards.answer: To show the revolution has failed and one oppressor has simply been replaced by another.

cards.front: How does Orwell suggest power corrupts regardless of ideology in the final chapters?
cards.answer: Both capitalist Jones and communist Napoleon end up exploiting the working class the same way.

cards.front: Name the two organs that together carry out the digestive functions of churning food, producing enzymes and making bile.
cards.answer: Stomach churns food and adds acid / Pancreas produces enzymes / Liver makes bile
items: Stomach churns food and adds acid

cards.front: How does extreme temperature or pH stop an enzyme working?
cards.answer: It causes denaturation, permanently changing the active site's shape so the substrate no longer fits.

cards.front: What colour change shows a positive result in the Sudan III test for lipids?
cards.answer: A red layer forms if lipids are present.

cards.front: Name the four things tested in the urine sample at the booking appointment.
cards.answer: Protein / Glucose / Bacteria

cards.front: Name the four groups of women offered amniocentesis or CVS testing, as given in the lesson.
cards.answer: High-risk screening result / Over 35 / Known family history of a chromosomal or genetic condition / Offered, not required, to any of these women
items: Family history of a genetic condition

cards.front: Why is a high-risk result from the dating scan's screening test not enough to confirm a chromosomal condition like Down's syndrome?
cards.answer: Because it is a screening test giving a statistical risk level, not a diagnostic test analysing the baby's own cells.

cards.front: Why does an obstetrician take over or share care in some pregnancies instead of the midwife?
cards.answer: Because the pregnancy is classified as high-risk, for example due to diabetes, high blood pressure, multiple pregnancy or a history of complications.

cards.front: Name the three quotations the lesson recommends learning as exact short quotes from 'Love and Friendship'.
cards.answer: wild rose-briar / holly-tree / which will bloom most constantly? / deck thee with the holly's sheen
items: deck thee with the holly's sheen

cards.front: Why does Bronte use seasonal imagery across the poem's three stanzas?
cards.answer: It gives the argument natural inevitability, showing love fades because everything that blooms in spring must face winter.

cards.front: How does the poem's structure mirror its growing certainty?
cards.answer: The rhyme tightens from a loose sound in stanza one to a fully alternating, firm rhyme in the final stanza, matching the argument's growing confidence.

cards.front: Why is friendship valued over love according to the poem's argument?
cards.answer: Friendship lacks glamour and does not compete with love's early appeal, but it survives winter when love's beauty cannot.

title: Widescreen, Steadicam and the Push for Spectacle: 1948-1990s
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why did Hollywood studios push for spectacle like widescreen after 1948?
cards.answer: Losing cinema chains under the Paramount decree and losing audiences to television meant studios used bigger, wider, more immersive technology to draw people back.

cards.front: Why did a widescreen frame change how directors composed shots compared to the old near-square frame?
cards.answer: The sides of the frame became active, letting directors place characters in spatial tension or dwarf them with environment, not just center subjects.

cards.front: Why did Kubrick's use of the Steadicam in The Shining feel different from handheld or dolly shots?
cards.answer: It glided smoothly at the child's height, feeling inhuman, patient and predatory, unlike a mechanical dolly or an urgent handheld camera.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to credit the Steadicam's invention to a studio like Panavision or ILM?
cards.answer: It was developed and patented by independent inventor Garrett Brown, then licensed to the industry, not created inside a studio's R&D department.

cards.front: Why must a value from input() be converted with int() or float() before doing arithmetic on it?
cards.answer: Because input() always returns a string, and arithmetic cannot be performed on strings.

cards.front: Why must a program call close() after finishing reading or writing a file?
cards.answer: The lesson states you must close the file once you have finished reading or writing to it.

cards.front: Name the six steps in the worked example for reading a CSV file line by line.
cards.answer: Open file in read mode / readline() to skip header / for line in f to loop rows / strip() to remove newline / split(',') into fields / close() the file
items: for line in f to loop rows

title: The need for social reform: Booth, Rowntree and Liberal reforms
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three key Liberal reforms and the group each targeted.
cards.answer: School Meals Act 1906 (children) / Old Age Pensions Act 1908 (elderly) / National Insurance Act 1911 (sick and unemployed workers)
items: National Insurance Act 1911 (sick and unemployed workers)

cards.front: Name three limitations of the Liberal reforms mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Pension age of 70 excluded most workers / National Insurance Part 1 didn't cover dependants / School meals and treatment weren't universal or free
items: Pension age of 70 excluded most workers
National Insurance Part 1 didn't cover dependants
School meals and treatment weren't universal or free

cards.front: Why did Rowntree's idea of 'primary poverty' undermine the Victorian view that poverty was a personal failing?
cards.answer: It proved some families were poor even if they spent perfectly, because they simply did not earn enough money.

cards.front: Why did the Boer War add urgency to calls for social reform?
cards.answer: Recruiters found many urban volunteers too unhealthy to serve, alarming politicians worried about defending the empire.

title: The Prophets: Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail and Yusuf
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: What virtue does each of the four prophets (Nuh, Ibrahim, Ismail, Yusuf) mainly teach Muslims to imitate?
cards.answer: Nuh: perseverance and gratitude despite rejection / Ibrahim: courage, rational faith and total submission / Ismail: patient obedience across generations / Yusuf: moral integrity, patience and forgiveness
items: Nuh: perseverance and gratitude despite rejection
Ibrahim: courage, rational faith and total submission
Yusuf: moral integrity, patience and forgiveness

cards.front: Why did Ibrahim destroy the idols of his people but leave the largest one standing (Surah 21:57-58)?
cards.answer: So people would have to ask who did it, forcing them to think critically about what they were worshipping.

cards.front: Why do Muslims honour the prophets but not worship them?
cards.answer: Prophets were human, not divine, and only Allah is worthy of worship; worshipping a prophet would be shirk.

title: The Thatcher Years: economy and society
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four major industries privatised between 1979 and 1990 mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: British Telecom (1984) / British Gas (1986) / British Airways (1987) / British Steel (1988)

cards.front: What three criticisms does the lesson give of privatising utilities like water and gas?
cards.answer: Natural monopolies shouldn't be run for profit / Services worsened in poorer areas / Sale prices were often too low
items: Natural monopolies shouldn't be run for profit
Sale prices were often too low

cards.front: Why did Thatcher's monetarist policies of 1979-81 cause a deep recession?
cards.answer: Sharp interest rate rises and public spending cuts to control inflation caused manufacturing output to fall and unemployment to soar.

cards.front: Why did regulators like Ofwat and Ofgem need to be created after utility privatisation?
cards.answer: Privatised utilities had no real competition, so regulation was needed to substitute for the market pressure that didn't exist naturally.

title: Sources of Wisdom and Forms of Expression in Catholic Christianity
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three sacred vessels used in the Mass, mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Chalice (cup for the wine) / Paten (plate for the bread) / Ciborium (vessel for communion hosts)

cards.front: Name the four Vatican II documents named in the lesson, in order of year.
cards.answer: Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963) / Lumen Gentium (1964) / Dei Verbum (1965) / Gaudium et Spes (1965)

cards.front: Why do Catholics use a crucifix rather than a bare cross in their churches?
cards.answer: Because the crucifix shows Christ's body on the cross, emphasising his sacrifice, unlike the bare cross used in many Protestant churches.

cards.front: Why does Catholic teaching say scripture cannot be interpreted alone, without the Church?
cards.answer: Because the Bible must be interpreted through the magisterium and the living Tradition of the Church to be properly understood.

title: Diplomacy Outside the League: Locarno and Kellogg-Briand
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three concrete objectives Stresemann pursued through reconciliation diplomacy.
cards.answer: End the Ruhr occupation / Lift the burden of reparations / Bring Germany into the League of Nations
items: Bring Germany into the League of Nations

cards.front: Name the three immediate consequences that flowed from Locarno.
cards.answer: Germany joined the League as Council member / French troops left the Rhineland early / Locarno spirit led to Young Plan and Kellogg-Briand
items: Germany joined the League as Council member
French troops left the Rhineland early
Locarno spirit led to Young Plan and Kellogg-Briand

cards.front: Why did Germany's eastern border ambiguity at Locarno matter later, in 1938-39?
cards.answer: By leaving eastern frontiers open, Locarno let Hitler later use the Sudetenland and Polish Corridor as flashpoints for revision.

cards.front: How did Stresemann pursue rearmament while publicly following reconciliation diplomacy?
cards.answer: He quietly continued secret rearmament cooperation with the Soviet Union under the 1922 Treaty of Rapallo alongside his public policy.

cards.front: Name the four government strategies the lesson gives for narrowing the UK regional economic gap.
cards.answer: Northern Powerhouse / Levelling Up Fund / Freeports / HS2 (transport investment)

cards.front: Name three drawbacks of building on brownfield sites given in the lesson.
cards.answer: high cost of cleaning contaminated soil / complex demolition / gentrification pricing out long-time residents
items: high cost of cleaning contaminated soil

cards.front: Why did net migration to the UK peak at around 944,000 in the year to March 2023?
cards.answer: It was driven by Ukrainian and Hong Kong resettlement schemes, international students, and NHS and care worker visas.

cards.front: Why are UK migration statistics from 2020–22 considered particularly unreliable?
cards.answer: The small International Passenger Survey was suspended in 2020 due to COVID, making estimates for that period uncertain.

cards.front: In DNA Act 4, what three coping methods does the lesson give for how group members handled events?
cards.answer: Denial (John Tate turning to religion) / Chemical numbness (Brian on medication) / New allegiance (following Cathy)

cards.front: Why does Leah disappear from the group by Act 4?
cards.answer: Because her pleas for connection were constantly ignored by Phil, so her conscience eventually fell silent.

title: The Covenant at Sinai, Pikuach Nefesh, the Mitzvot and Life After Death
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Talmud Yoma 83-84 gives three examples of breaking Shabbat to save a child. What are they?
cards.answer: Pulling a child from the sea with a net / Digging free a child trapped in a pit / Breaking open a locked door to reach a frightened child
items: Pulling a child from the sea with a net
Digging free a child trapped in a pit
Breaking open a locked door to reach a frightened child

cards.front: Why do Orthodox and Reform Jews apply Pikuach Nefesh differently?
cards.answer: Orthodox Jews apply it case by case only for genuine immediate threats to life, while Reform Jews extend it more broadly to mental health and long-term wellbeing.

cards.front: Why does Judaism teach that human life has infinite worth?
cards.answer: Because every human life is created by the Almighty, so saving one life is treated as equivalent to saving an entire world.

cards.front: How does Orthodox Jewish belief about resurrection differ from Christian belief about resurrection?
cards.answer: Orthodox resurrection is tied to a future Messianic age for the Jewish people as a whole, while Christian resurrection is linked to individual faith in Jesus's own resurrection.

cards.front: Name four things the Cottages students lack despite having a version of freedom.
cards.answer: Money / Family / Career prospects / Any future beyond donations

cards.front: Why does Ruth react defensively when Kathy confronts her about the copied arm-tap gesture?
cards.answer: Her constructed identity is fragile and cannot survive scrutiny because it is borrowed, not authentic.

cards.front: Why does the failed search for Ruth's possible strip away her hope?
cards.answer: It was really a search for human worth, and its failure denies her the chance that her original was 'somebody'.

title: Religious worship under Henry and Edward
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the six doctrines reaffirmed by the Act of Six Articles (1539).
cards.answer: Transubstantiation / Withholding the communion cup from laity / Celibacy of priests / Private masses / Auricular confession / Vows of chastity
items: Withholding the communion cup from laity

cards.front: What three sacraments did the Ten Articles (1536) keep as binding, out of the original seven?
cards.answer: Baptism / Eucharist / Penance

cards.front: Why did Henry VIII have ideological reasons, not just religious ones, for destroying Thomas Becket's shrine?
cards.answer: Becket had resisted royal authority in the twelfth century, so destroying his cult helped erase a symbol of defiance against the Crown.

cards.front: How did the role of the clergyman change between Henry's reign and Edward's reign?
cards.answer: Clergy went from being required to be celibate under Henry to being permitted to marry under Edward, as services shifted from Latin to English.

title: Reception, Active Audiences and Aberrant Readings
subject: media-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the three specialised active audience reading practices the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Fan reading / Queer reading / Feminist reading

cards.front: Why can a 1970s sitcom that seemed mainstream at the time produce oppositional readings today?
cards.answer: Because social values around gender, race and class have shifted, so contemporary viewers re-read it through a changed cultural context.

cards.front: Why is aberrant decoding said to be the norm rather than the exception in mass communication?
cards.answer: Because senders and receivers often do not share the same cultural codes, so unintended readings happen regularly.

cards.front: How does a queer reading of a media text work?
cards.answer: It looks for gender and sexuality subtext not necessarily intended by the producer but visible to audiences outside heteronormative norms.

cards.front: What are the three roles the Odyssey tests Odysseus's heroism in?
cards.answer: Leader / Husband / Father

cards.front: What four things does Athena do to help Odysseus and his family in the poem?
cards.answer: Inspires Telemachus to seek news of his father / Engineers his release from Calypso's island / Gives him his beggar's disguise / Tips the battle in Book 22
items: Inspires Telemachus to seek news of his father
Engineers his release from Calypso's island

cards.front: Why is physical strength (bie) useless against Polyphemus in the Cyclops episode?
cards.answer: Polyphemus is far stronger than Odysseus and his men, so only cunning (metis) — the Nobody trick and the stake — can save them.

cards.front: Why does Odysseus refuse Calypso's offer of immortality?
cards.answer: He would rather be a mortal man with a wife and home than an immortal without them, showing what he truly values.

cards.front: Name the four criteria the lesson says designers balance when selecting a fabric for a product.
cards.answer: Function / Aesthetics / Cost / Environmental considerations

cards.front: What two methods does the lesson give for making bonded/needle-punched non-woven fabrics?
cards.answer: Needle punching (mechanical entangling) / Thermal bonding (heat fuses fibres)

cards.front: Why does more twist make a yarn stronger but less soft?
cards.answer: The twist locks the fibres together tightly, increasing strength, but this reduces the yarn's softness.

cards.front: Why is thread count alone not a reliable way to judge bed linen quality?
cards.answer: Fibre type, yarn quality and finishing treatments also affect quality, and multi-ply yarns can artificially inflate the count.

cards.front: Why has the UK's ageing population created growing markets in areas like retirement living and mobility products?
cards.answer: As more of the population is older, demand grows for products and services suited to older adults' needs.

cards.front: Why might two people of the same age and income sit in different lifestyle segments?
cards.answer: They can have different values and ways of living, such as prioritising sustainability versus prioritising status and luxury.

cards.front: Why does Portia's disguise as Balthazar create dramatic irony?
cards.answer: The audience knows Portia is a woman in disguise, but the characters in the courtroom do not.

cards.front: Why is Portia's mercy speech considered ironic given her later actions in court?
cards.answer: She argues mercy should temper justice, yet she and the other Christians show Shylock no mercy once he is defeated.

cards.front: Why does Shylock refuse to accept three times the loan amount and insist on his bond?
cards.answer: He believes the law is the only protection he has in a society that despises him, so it must be upheld strictly.

cards.front: What three things does Shylock lose as a result of his forced conversion, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: His faith / His community / His wealth (kept only half)

cards.front: Name the four reasons the lesson gives for why historians' interpretations of the Crusades differ.
cards.answer: Historian's purpose / Evidence used / Time at which they write / Historian's perspective and background

cards.front: How does Ibn al-Athir's al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh frame the Crusades differently from Western chronicles?
cards.answer: It presents the Crusades as a catastrophic Christian invasion of Muslim lands, not a holy liberation, celebrating Muslim resistance.

cards.front: Why did Ibn al-Athir's account glorify Muslim resistance and downplay rulers who cooperated with crusaders?
cards.answer: He wrote when Muslim reconquest under Saladin was the dominant political reality, shaping his account to celebrate resistance.

cards.front: How did Carole Hillenbrand's approach shift the question historians asked about the Crusades?
cards.answer: She asked what the Crusades meant to those experiencing them, rather than whether they were justified or crusaders sincere.

cards.front: Name the three snap judgements made at or after the Meryton assembly that shape the novel's relationships.
cards.answer: Darcy judges Elizabeth as 'tolerable, not handsome enough' / Elizabeth judges Darcy as proud and disagreeable / Mrs Bennet judges Bingley as perfect son-in-law for his money
items: Darcy judges Elizabeth as 'tolerable, not handsome enough'
Elizabeth judges Darcy as proud and disagreeable
Mrs Bennet judges Bingley as perfect son-in-law for his money

cards.front: Why was refusing to dance at a Regency assembly seen as such a big insult?
cards.answer: Dancing publicly signalled interest, so refusing to dance was a public insult, and Darcy's refusal marked him as antisocial.

cards.front: How does the novel's ending overturn the first impressions formed at the assembly?
cards.answer: Darcy, first judged proud and disagreeable, proves honourable and generous, while charming Wickham later proves dishonest and predatory.

cards.front: Why does Austen use the Jane and Bingley subplot alongside the Elizabeth and Darcy story?
cards.answer: It mirrors their relationship, showing passive trusting Jane against active sceptical Elizabeth, arguing marriage needs both feeling and judgement.

cards.front: Name the first four of Heracles's twelve labours in order.
cards.answer: The Nemean Lion / The Lernaean Hydra / The Ceryneian Hind / The Erymanthian Boar

cards.front: Why did Hera's persecution of Heracles ultimately make him great?
cards.answer: By driving him to madness so he killed his family, Hera caused the twelve labours imposed as penance, which became his most famous achievement.

cards.front: Why did placing the twelve labours on the Temple of Zeus at Olympia matter?
cards.answer: It put Heracles's deeds on the holiest temple at the most important sanctuary, showing they were divinely sanctioned and linking him to his father Zeus.

cards.front: Name the three anthology poems the lesson compares with Baby Song, alongside the parent-child pairing point each makes.
cards.answer: You're by Sylvia Plath (playful tone vs baby's resentment) / My First Weeks by Sharon Olds (heaven vs regret) / Love by Kate Clanchy (frightened parent's view vs baby's own voice)
items: You're by Sylvia Plath (playful tone vs baby's resentment)
My First Weeks by Sharon Olds (heaven vs regret)
Love by Kate Clanchy (frightened parent's view vs baby's own voice)

cards.front: How does the steady rhyming couplet form of Baby Song create an odd effect against the baby's words?
cards.answer: The couplets sound like a soothing nursery rhyme or lullaby, which sits oddly against the baby's own angry complaints.

cards.front: Why is the gap between the baby's tone and its situation important in Baby Song?
cards.answer: Gunn gives a normally silent, powerless baby a confident, opinionated voice, so its helplessness clashes with its assured complaining.

title: Jobs, Work Experience and Future Plans
subject: french-aqa

cards.front: Name the three choices French students can make after le collège (age 15), given in the lesson.
cards.answer: le lycée général (academic sixth form) / le lycée professionnel (vocational school) / un apprentissage (apprenticeship)

cards.front: Name the three future tense structures the lesson says you should combine to show range when discussing future plans.
cards.answer: near future (je vais + infinitive) / conditional (je voudrais) / simple future (je serai, je travaillerai)

cards.front: How is the conditional tense formed in French?
cards.answer: By adding imperfect endings to the infinitive, or to an irregular stem if the verb has one.

cards.front: What happens to French workers on 1st May, la Fête du Travail?
cards.answer: They do not work but still receive their salary, and many join street demonstrations for workers' rights.

title: Manifest Destiny and the Pull of the West
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name three of the Indigenous nations the lesson names as already living in the West before Manifest Destiny.
cards.answer: Lakota / Comanche / Nez Perce / Cheyenne

cards.front: The lesson lists several consequences that followed the Gold Rush. Name three of them.
cards.answer: California became a state in 1850 / accelerated the Pacific Railroad debate / Chinese migration to California began / made overland routes across Plains territory a federal priority
items: made overland routes across Plains territory a federal priority

cards.front: Why does the lesson say it is wrong to describe Manifest Destiny as being about 'filling empty land'?
cards.answer: The Plains and Far West were already home to dozens of Indigenous nations, so the doctrine's real work was legitimising their dispossession.

cards.front: Why did most forty-niners not get rich from the Gold Rush?
cards.answer: The gold overwhelmingly enriched San Francisco's merchants and bankers rather than the diggers, leaving many forty-niners poorer than before.

cards.front: Name the two movements (parts) that structure 'Origin Story'.
cards.answer: The narrative of the parents' meeting / An extended reflection on what the story means for love
items: The narrative of the parents' meeting
An extended reflection on what the story means for love

cards.front: How does enjambment in 'Origin Story' mirror the poem's storytelling?
cards.answer: It lets sentences spill across lines, mirroring how a story keeps unfolding rather than stopping neatly.

cards.front: Why does Ewing include specific, unglamorous details about her parents before the comic-book imagery begins?
cards.answer: These details root the myth in real working lives, resisting the glossy simplicity of an actual comic-book hero's backstory.

title: Chapters 4–6: The Carew Murder and Dr Lanyon
subject: english-literature-aqa

cards.front: How does Stevenson's description of Soho's fog and darkness link to the novella's themes?
cards.answer: The fog mirrors the moral confusion surrounding Jekyll's double life, symbolising London's hidden, immoral side.

cards.front: Why is the broken walking stick significant as a clue in the Carew murder?
cards.answer: It was Utterson's gift to Jekyll, physically connecting Jekyll to the murder and foreshadowing that he and Hyde are one person.

cards.front: What signs in Hyde's Soho rooms suggest he left in a hurry?
cards.answer: Luxury furnishings / Ashes in the fireplace / A burnt cheque book

cards.front: Name the four groups of workers who walked out during the Winter of Discontent (1978-79).
cards.answer: Lorry drivers / Refuse collectors / Gravediggers / Public sector workers

cards.front: What three types of argument did opponents of EEC membership raise in the 1970s?
cards.answer: Sovereignty concerns / Economic/socialist objections / Fears over migration

cards.front: Why did Bloody Sunday intensify the Troubles?
cards.answer: The killing of unarmed civilians by British paratroopers caused outrage that surged Provisional IRA membership and support, escalating violence.

cards.front: Why did the SNP vote against Callaghan's government in the March 1979 no confidence vote?
cards.answer: The SNP's 11 MPs voted against the government in protest at the failure of the Scottish devolution referendum.

cards.front: Name the four addition polymers the lesson gives, with one use each.
cards.answer: Poly(ethene) — carrier bags / Poly(propene) — crates and car parts / PVC — pipes and cable insulation / PTFE — non-stick cookware coatings

cards.front: What two ways does condensation polymerisation differ from addition polymerisation? (HT)
cards.answer: Monomers need two reactive groups / A small molecule (water) is released at each bond
items: A small molecule (water) is released at each bond

cards.front: Why is PET chosen over glass for drinks bottles, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: PET is lighter, reducing transport energy, cheaper to produce, shatterproof, and recyclable compared to glass.

cards.front: Why is life-cycle assessment used to compare materials like PET and glass bottles?
cards.answer: It compares total environmental impact across the whole life cycle — raw material extraction, manufacturing, use and disposal — not just end-of-life.

cards.front: Why did Cromwell's cavalry give Parliament an advantage at Marston Moor?
cards.answer: Cromwell's disciplined cavalry returned after charging rather than pursuing off the field, unlike most cavalry of the period.

cards.front: Why did Parliament struggle to win the war quickly despite victory at Marston Moor in 1644?
cards.answer: Commanders Essex and Manchester proved reluctant to press their military advantages, slowing Parliament's progress.

cards.front: Why did Charles refuse to negotiate seriously over the Propositions of Newcastle in 1646?
cards.answer: He was playing for time, hoping to split Parliament from its Scottish and army allies rather than accept permanent subjugation.

cards.front: Name the four marriage models the novel presents.
cards.answer: Elizabeth and Darcy / Jane and Bingley / Charlotte and Collins / Lydia and Wickham

cards.front: Name the three assessment objectives this extract question is marked on.
cards.answer: AO1 informed personal response with textual references / AO2 analysis of language, form and structure / AO3 understanding of contexts
items: AO2 analysis of language, form and structure

cards.front: How does Elizabeth's prejudice against Darcy connect to her own pride?
cards.answer: Her prejudice against Darcy is rooted in her wounded pride after his insult at the assembly.

cards.front: How does the appearance versus reality theme link to Austen's narrative technique?
cards.answer: Free indirect discourse shows the story through Elizabeth's flawed perspective, so the reader shares her mistaken first impressions until the revelation.

cards.front: Name the four broad groups of solutions the lesson gives for reducing desertification risk in the Sahel.
cards.answer: Water and soil management / Tree planting / Appropriate technology / Rotation and reduced livestock

cards.front: Name the three factors the lesson gives for why the Great Green Wall has been slowed down.
cards.answer: Scale / Funding / Conflict

cards.front: Why does over-cultivation contribute to desertification?
cards.answer: Farming the same field continuously without rest exhausts the soil's nutrients.

cards.front: How does a drought trigger the vicious cycle of desertification in the Sahel?
cards.answer: Drought makes farmers move cattle to new land, which gets overgrazed, thinning vegetation so soil loses grip and washes away, forcing further moves.

cards.front: Name four Greek gods and their Roman equivalents given in the lesson (other than Athena/Minerva or Poseidon/Neptune).
cards.answer: Zeus → Jupiter / Hera → Juno / Ares → Mars / Aphrodite → Venus / Hades → Pluto / Demeter → Ceres

cards.front: Why did the Romans originally focus less on myths about the gods' personal lives than the Greeks did?
cards.answer: Early Roman religion was ritual-focused, believing correct performance of rites maintained the pax deorum and secured Rome's safety and prosperity.

cards.front: How does the breastplate on the Augustus of Prima Porta statue make a political statement?
cards.answer: It shows the sky god Caelus above and earth goddess Terra below, framing Augustus's military victory within a cosmic order under Roman rule.

title: The Trinity, Creation and Human Nature
subject: religious-studies-b-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four characteristics of God's nature that the Creation account reveals, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Creator / benevolent / omnipotent / eternal

cards.front: Name the three chapters of Genesis 1-3 and what each covers, as the lesson describes them.
cards.answer: Genesis 1: six days of creation / Genesis 2: forming of first humans / Genesis 3: the Fall

cards.front: Why does the Catholic Church read Genesis 1-3 mainly metaphorically rather than literally?
cards.answer: Because the six days are seen as a literary structure conveying theological truths about God and humanity, not a scientific timetable.

cards.front: Why does being made in the imago Dei underpin Catholic teaching on the sanctity of life?
cards.answer: Because every person bears God's image, giving them inherent worth, so every human life deserves respect regardless of ability, age or usefulness.

cards.front: Name the four steps in the model comparative paragraph structure.
cards.answer: Opening statement comparing themes / Named poem analysis (AO2) / Comparison connective / Chosen poem analysis then context (AO3)

cards.front: Name the four common mistakes to avoid in the comparison essay.
cards.answer: Writing about poems separately / Feature-spotting without analysis / Treating context as a separate section / Retelling the poem
items: Treating context as a separate section

cards.front: Why should context be woven into analysis rather than bolted on as a separate section?
cards.answer: Because AO2 (analysis of language, form, structure) is the main focus and worth more marks than AO3 context.

cards.front: Why is writing three paragraphs on the named poem then three on the chosen poem a mistake?
cards.answer: It produces two separate essays rather than sustained comparison, since each paragraph must discuss both poems.

cards.front: Name the four carbon allotropes described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Diamond / Graphite / Graphene / Fullerenes

cards.front: Name the three properties of metals the lesson says come from delocalised electrons.
cards.answer: High melting points / Malleable / Good conductors of electricity and heat
items: Good conductors of electricity and heat

cards.front: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water but not as solids?
cards.answer: The ions become free to move and carry charge once molten or dissolved, unlike in the fixed solid lattice.

cards.front: Why does graphite feel soft and work as a lubricant?
cards.answer: Its layers are held together by weak intermolecular forces, so they can slide over each other easily.

title: The Scramble for Africa & the Boer War
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three British presences in Africa that expanded together in the earlier 19th century, giving Britain its 'civilising mission' self-image.
cards.answer: Trade (palm oil) / Missionaries (e.g. David Livingstone) / Royal Navy West Africa Squadron

cards.front: Name the four ways the lesson says empire was sold to the British public through propaganda.
cards.answer: Cigarette cards / Music hall songs / Boys' Own and Girls' Own Paper / 1924 Empire Exhibition at Wembley
items: Boys' Own and Girls' Own Paper

cards.front: Why did the Berlin Conference's 'effective occupation' rule cause a rush of European activity in Africa?
cards.answer: Powers had to prove control by planting flags and signing treaties with African chiefs to keep claimed territory.

cards.front: Why did the guerrilla phase of the Boer War lead to British concentration camps?
cards.answer: Boer commandos kept fighting after Pretoria fell, so Britain burned farms and corralled civilians into camps to stop them.

cards.front: Why does a poet use personification, such as 'the wind whispered secrets'?
cards.answer: To make the object seem alive, usually to make it appear more powerful, threatening, or sympathetic.

cards.front: Why should you explain the effect of a sound device rather than just naming it?
cards.answer: Because simply noting a device is feature-spotting, while explaining its effect on the reader is genuine analysis.

title: Humanistic Theory, Identity and Free Will
subject: psychology-edexcel

cards.front: Name Maslow's five levels of needs, from the bottom of the pyramid to the top.
cards.answer: Physiological needs / Safety needs / Love and belonging / Esteem needs / Self-actualisation

cards.front: Name Erikson's eight stages of identity development, in order from infancy to old age.
cards.answer: Trust vs mistrust / Autonomy vs shame / Initiative vs guilt / Industry vs inferiority / Identity vs role confusion / Intimacy vs isolation / Generativity vs stagnation / Integrity vs despair

cards.front: Why does conditional positive regard lead to incongruence?
cards.answer: Children start valuing only the parts of themselves that win approval, creating a gap between real self and ideal self.

cards.front: Why does Maslow argue that people find it hard to pursue self-actualisation when facing poverty or unsafe housing?
cards.answer: Lower, more basic needs like safety must be satisfied before a person can focus on higher needs like self-actualisation.

title: Developing Recipes & Meals for Specific Needs
subject: food-preparation-and-nutrition-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three time-saving techniques the lesson gives for developing recipes for working parents.
cards.answer: Batch cooking and freezing in portions / Preparing ingredients in advance (e.g. mirepoix) / Choosing methods with shorter active cooking time
items: Batch cooking and freezing in portions
Choosing methods with shorter active cooking time

cards.front: Why does replacing dairy milk with oat milk change the sensory outcome of a lactose-free recipe?
cards.answer: Oat milk has a sweeter flavour than cows' milk, so it can alter the taste of the finished dish.

cards.front: Why can steaming and adjusting flavour with salt improve a dish that tastes flat during recipe testing?
cards.answer: Salt enhances and balances other flavours, so a flat-tasting dish often needs salt rather than more of another ingredient.

cards.front: Why does replacing chicken breast with chicken thighs help adapt a recipe for a low budget?
cards.answer: Chicken thighs cost less per kg than chicken breast, though they contain more fat and give more flavour.

cards.front: Name the four potential effects of climate change given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Rising sea levels / More extreme weather events / Changes in habitats and biodiversity / Disruption to agriculture and food supplies
items: Disruption to agriculture and food supplies

cards.front: Name the four mitigation measures for climate change given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Reducing fossil fuel use / Increasing renewable energy / Improving energy efficiency / Carbon capture and storage

cards.front: Why did carbon dioxide levels in Earth's early atmosphere fall over billions of years?
cards.answer: CO2 dissolved into forming oceans, was locked in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels, and was absorbed by photosynthesising plants and algae.

cards.front: Why does the build-up of oxygen matter for life on Earth?
cards.answer: Rising oxygen allowed complex oxygen-dependent organisms to evolve and led to the ozone layer forming, which blocks harmful ultraviolet radiation.

cards.front: How does shaping differ from forming in the way each process works?
cards.answer: Shaping fills a mould with molten or softened material using fluidity, while forming plastically deforms a solid workpiece using force or heat.

cards.front: Why is injection moulding classed as shaping rather than forming?
cards.answer: Injection moulding uses liquid polymer filling a mould, whereas forming requires a solid workpiece being plastically deformed.

cards.front: Name the five applications of electromagnets given in the lesson that changed everyday life.
cards.answer: Electric telegraph / Electric bell / Relay switch / MRI scanners / Scrapyard cranes

cards.front: How does winding a wire into a solenoid strengthen its magnetic field?
cards.answer: The magnetic fields produced by each turn of wire add together inside the coil.

cards.front: Why does increasing the current in a transformer's secondary coil reduce transmission heat losses?
cards.answer: Stepping up voltage reduces current, and since power loss equals I squared times R, lower current cuts heat losses.

cards.front: How does a current-carrying coil create sound in a loudspeaker? (Higher tier)
cards.answer: The coil's field interacts with the permanent magnet's field, so varying current makes the coil vibrate, pushing a cone to create sound waves.

title: Norman Government, Justice and the Anglo-Saxon Inheritance
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four elements of the Anglo-Saxon system of government that the lesson says the Normans kept largely intact.
cards.answer: Shires and hundreds / Sheriffs as royal officers / The writ / The geld land tax

cards.front: How did Norman tenants-in-chief differ from Anglo-Saxon earls and thegns in how they held power?
cards.answer: Tenants-in-chief held land formally from the king and owed forty days' knight service, making them the king's sworn men first, unlike semi-independent Anglo-Saxon earls.

cards.front: Why did William introduce the murdrum fine?
cards.answer: Because Norman lives were seen as under permanent threat from a hostile Anglo-Saxon population, so it made English communities responsible for protecting Norman incomers.

cards.front: Why did William's use of primogeniture cause political tension after his death in 1087?
cards.answer: Robert Curthose got Normandy while William II got England, leaving younger sons with less and fuelling the 1088 rebellion.

cards.front: Name the four phases of the genre cycle described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Establishment of conventions / Refinement and intensification / Self-parody / Decline or transformation

cards.front: Name the three forms of intertextuality the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Explicit / Implicit / Structural

cards.front: How does a low-angle shot affect how a subject appears?
cards.answer: It makes the subject appear powerful.

cards.front: Why are hybrid genres commercially appealing?
cards.answer: Because they can target audiences from two genre communities simultaneously.

title: Plot and Structure: A Four-Act Tragedy
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Name the three consecutive reversals Miller uses to structure Act 3 of The Crucible.
cards.answer: Proctor confesses his adultery / Elizabeth lies to protect him / Mary Warren turns on Proctor

cards.front: Name the four stages of the classical tragic sequence that map onto the four acts of The Crucible.
cards.answer: Exposition and catalyst / Rising action and complication / Climax and reversal / Falling action and catastrophe

cards.front: Why does Elizabeth's lie in Act 3 destroy Proctor's defence rather than save him?
cards.answer: By lying to protect Proctor's honour, she unknowingly destroys the one piece of evidence that could have discredited Abigail and saved them both.

cards.front: Why did Miller change historical facts, like making Abigail an adult, when writing The Crucible?
cards.answer: He deliberately altered and compressed history so the pattern of accusation and confession would resonate with 1953 McCarthyite America as allegory.

title: Placing a Track in Time: Rock, Pop, Broadway and Screen by Era
subject: music-aqa

cards.front: Name the two things Broadway songs did in the 1950s to carry the plot, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: An opening number that sets the scene / A song where the main character states what they want
items: An opening number that sets the scene
A song where the main character states what they want

cards.front: Why can grid-exact drumming not be used alone to date a track?
cards.answer: Drum machines appear from the early 1970s, and many tracks from the 1980s onwards still use a live drummer, so it must be weighed with other clues.

cards.front: What marks out modern film and gaming music from earlier orchestral scoring?
cards.answer: It blends full orchestra with synthesisers, electronic percussion, sound design and driving ostinato patterns under action scenes.

title: The Norman Conquest and William's Forest Laws
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four Anglo-Saxon institutions the lesson says William kept after the Conquest.
cards.answer: the king's peace / tithings / the hue and cry / the shire reeve and local courts
items: the shire reeve and local courts

cards.front: Name four activities the lesson says became crimes under Forest Law inside royal forest land.
cards.answer: hunting deer or wild boar / felling trees / gathering firewood / grazing pigs / owning an unclawed dog capable of catching game
items: owning an unclawed dog capable of catching game

cards.front: Why did William I introduce the Forest Laws and the Murdrum fine?
cards.answer: To protect the small Norman ruling minority and to enrich and project the king's power over land, hunting and movement.

cards.front: Why did the Murdrum fine give English communities an incentive to identify a killer?
cards.answer: Because if the killer of a Norman was not produced, the whole local community had to pay a ruinous collective fine.

cards.front: Why is Don John resentful and driven to villainy in Messina?
cards.answer: As an illegitimate brother he has no status, inheritance or prospects, so his villainy comes from resentment of legitimate social structures excluding him.

cards.front: Why does Leonato call Beatrice and Benedick's relationship a 'merry war'?
cards.answer: They never meet without a skirmish of wit, fighting each other with words the way soldiers fight with swords.

cards.front: Why does Don John's plot succeed despite him not being especially clever?
cards.answer: It succeeds because Claudio is gullible and the honour system makes men quick to believe the worst about women.

title: Kenilworth Castle: location and physical fabric
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four building phases of Kenilworth Castle given in the lesson, in order.
cards.answer: c.1125 Geoffrey de Clinton's motte-and-bailey / 12th century Norman stone keep (Caesar's Tower) / 1361-99 John of Gaunt's great hall / 1560s-70s Robert Dudley's Leicester's Building

cards.front: Why did King John's Great Mere make Kenilworth Castle so easy to defend?
cards.answer: It flooded the surrounding valley so the only land approach was from the north and east, cutting off other routes to attackers.

cards.front: Why can we now only understand the Great Mere through maps and archaeology rather than seeing it?
cards.answer: Because it was drained by Parliamentarians during the 1649-1650 slighting, removing the feature itself.

cards.front: How do the thick walls of Caesar's Tower and the huge windows of Leicester's Building each act as evidence of their purpose?
cards.answer: Thick Norman walls show a priority on military defence, while Leicester's large glazed windows show a priority on display over defence.

cards.front: Name the two things the star watches over 'for ever' in the octave of 'Bright Star'.
cards.answer: The tides performing their ritual washing / Fresh snow on the mountains and moors
items: The tides performing their ritual washing
Fresh snow on the mountains and moors

cards.front: Why does the speaker reject the star as a model for his own steadfastness, despite admiring it?
cards.answer: Because the star's constancy is solitary and cold, while he wants constancy combined with physical closeness to his beloved.

cards.front: How does Keats make the sestet's language perform the closeness it describes in 'Bright Star'?
cards.answer: The alliteration of 'tender-taken breath' and rhythm of 'soft fall and swell' mimic the rise and fall of breathing.

cards.front: Name the three end-of-life routes for waste materials given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Recycling / Incineration / Landfill

cards.front: Why might a nanoparticle drug-delivery treatment cause fewer side effects than a conventional drug?
cards.answer: The drug is attached to a nanoparticle designed to travel to a specific tissue, like a tumour, and release it there.

cards.front: Why does landfill waste the resource value of materials and also create extra pollution?
cards.answer: It buries materials instead of reusing them, and decomposing organic material in landfill produces methane.

cards.front: Why are platinum nanoparticles more effective as catalysts in catalytic converters than bulk platinum?
cards.answer: Nanoparticles have a far greater surface area than bulk platinum, making the catalyst more effective.

title: Catholic Social Teaching: Loving Our Neighbour
subject: religious-studies-aqa

cards.front: Name the four core principles of Catholic Social Teaching given as the Key Fact in the lesson.
cards.answer: Dignity of the human person / The common good / Preferential option for the poor / Solidarity

cards.front: Name the three global Catholic agencies named in the lesson that put Catholic Social Teaching into action.
cards.answer: CAFOD / Trocaire / Missio

cards.front: Why did the parable of the Good Samaritan matter for how Jesus defined 'neighbour'?
cards.answer: It made clear that 'neighbour' crosses ethnic, religious and social boundaries, not just people close to you.

cards.front: How did Gaudium et Spes change the Church's understanding of its role in the world?
cards.answer: It rejected the idea the Church was only sacramental and otherworldly, teaching it is within the world, sharing humanity's struggles and joys.

cards.front: Name the four tactics the lesson gives for how Chinese forces neutralised US firepower in Korea.
cards.answer: Night-time attacks to negate air power / Mass infantry infiltration to find UN flanks / Bugles and horns instead of radios / Operating without long supply lines
items: Night-time attacks to negate air power
Mass infantry infiltration to find UN flanks
Bugles and horns instead of radios

cards.front: Name the three things the lesson says MacArthur wanted to do that went beyond limited war.
cards.answer: Bomb China / Blockade China's coast / Deploy the Nationalist Chinese army from Taiwan
items: Deploy the Nationalist Chinese army from Taiwan

cards.front: Why did Mao decide to intervene in the Korean War despite Politburo opposition?
cards.answer: Hostile forces on the Yalu threatened Chinese industry and the revolution, and letting a fellow communist state fall would damage Beijing's prestige and Sino-Soviet relations.

cards.front: Why did Truman's sacking of MacArthur matter for civil-military relations?
cards.answer: It upheld the principle that elected civilian government controls the military, even at the cost of Truman's approval rating falling to 22 percent.

title: Puja, Pilgrimage and Hindu Rites of Passage
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four things a worshipper does during daily puja at the home shrine.
cards.answer: Wake the deity / Bathe and dress the image / Offer food, flowers, incense and light / Recite prayers or mantras
items: Offer food, flowers, incense and light

cards.front: Name the four forms bhakti practice can take, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Singing devotional hymns (bhajan) / Chanting God's name (kirtan) / Performing puja with heartfelt emotion / Reading or hearing sacred stories (katha)

cards.front: Why is the fire considered important during a Hindu wedding ceremony?
cards.answer: The couple walk round it seven times making seven vows, and the fire acts as the divine witness to the marriage.

cards.front: How does the mundan ceremony prepare a Hindu child for life ahead?
cards.answer: Shaving the child's first hair removes impurities carried from the previous life, purifying the child.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare put Shylock's 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech in prose rather than verse?
cards.answer: Prose strips away poetic formality, showing Shylock speaking from raw, unfiltered emotion rather than calculated rhetoric.

cards.front: Why did Jessica's elopement intensify Shylock's desire for revenge against Antonio?
cards.answer: The Christians took his dignity, his daughter and his wife's ring, leaving the bond as his only remaining source of power.

cards.front: How does the sequencing of Solanio's mockery before Shylock's own speech affect the audience?
cards.answer: It lets the audience absorb the Christian stereotype first, then Shylock's speech demolishes it, forcing them to confront their assumptions.

cards.front: Name the three things Shylock is stripped of by the end of the trial scene, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: His wealth / His forced conversion to Christianity / His identity and community

cards.front: The lesson gives four ways Napoleon appears surrounded by ceremony when he rarely appears in public — what are they?
cards.answer: Surrounded by dogs / Announced with a ceremonial cockerel crow / Eats from Jones's Crown Derby china / Takes meals alone with dogs waiting on him
items: Announced with a ceremonial cockerel crow
Eats from Jones's Crown Derby china
Takes meals alone with dogs waiting on him

cards.front: How does Squealer use Napoleon's cult of personality to explain good events on the farm?
cards.answer: Squealer credits every success, like harvests or eggs laid, personally to 'the leadership of Comrade Napoleon'.

cards.front: Why does Squealer deny that Animalism ever forbade trading with humans?
cards.answer: He insists no such rule existed and claims it was a lie spread by Snowball, so Napoleon's betrayal seems justified.

title: The Nature of God and Human Life in Sikhism
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three key contrasts the lesson gives between Sikh mukti and Christian afterlife belief.
cards.answer: Sikh soul merges with God, losing identity / Christian salvation keeps personal identity with God / Christianity teaches bodily resurrection through faith in Jesus
items: Sikh soul merges with God, losing identity
Christian salvation keeps personal identity with God
Christianity teaches bodily resurrection through faith in Jesus

cards.front: Why does the belief that God's light (Jot) is in every being lead Sikhs to reject caste discrimination?
cards.answer: If every person carries the divine light, all humans have inherent worth and dignity, so discrimination contradicts equality before the one Creator.

cards.front: Why is human birth considered a precious opportunity in Sikhism?
cards.answer: Only humans have the unique capacity to reflect on the divine and choose the path of liberation, ending the cycle of rebirth.

title: Changing attitudes to authority: the permissive society
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five legal reforms passed under Roy Jenkins between 1965 and 1967 during the 'permissive moment'.
cards.answer: Decriminalised homosexuality / Abolished the death penalty / Relaxed divorce law / Legalised abortion / Ended theatre censorship

cards.front: Why was the case of Derek Bentley (hanged 1953) controversial and used in the death penalty debate?
cards.answer: He was hanged despite doubts about his responsibility, raising fears about executing people unjustly.

cards.front: How did the 1968 student protests differ from what the Profumo Affair had exposed about the establishment?
cards.answer: The Profumo Affair showed the ruling class was not morally superior, while 1968 protests challenged whether it was politically legitimate.

cards.front: Why does the lesson describe the 'permissive society' as contradictory when it comes to drugs?
cards.answer: Laws liberalised private behaviour like sex and divorce, but drug law became more restrictive on public safety grounds.

title: Act 3: The Raid, Death & the Ending
subject: english-literature-edexcel

cards.front: Why does Stanhope become tender towards Raleigh in the play's final scene, after being furious with him?
cards.answer: His anger was grief and self-protection, not indifference, and Raleigh's death lets his buried love and grief for Osborne surface.

cards.front: How does the play's ending refuse to give the audience catharsis?
cards.answer: It ends with no final speech or reflection, just the dugout being destroyed, leaving the audience with loss and no meaning.

title: The Amicable Grant and the Limits of Wolsey's Power
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three consequences the lesson gives for the collapse of the Amicable Grant.
cards.answer: Planned invasion of France abandoned / Wolsey's reputation permanently dented / Principle of parliamentary consent to taxation reasserted
items: Principle of parliamentary consent to taxation reasserted

cards.front: Who did the leadership of the East Anglian revolt against the Amicable Grant come from, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Yeomen / Clothiers / Small employers / Supporting clergy

cards.front: Why did the Dukes of Norfolk and Suffolk negotiate with the East Anglian rebels instead of fighting them?
cards.answer: They recognised it was a tax strike, not a feudal rebellion against the king, so negotiation was more appropriate than battle.

cards.front: Why did taxpayers in Kent refuse to pay the Amicable Grant when commissioners arrived?
cards.answer: They cited Magna Carta and refused to pay without parliamentary consent.

title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect
subject: separate-sciences

cards.front: Name the three ways to increase the speed of an electric motor.
cards.answer: Increase the current / Use a stronger magnet / Add more turns to the coil
items: Add more turns to the coil

cards.front: Name the four magnetic materials given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Iron / Steel / Cobalt / Nickel

cards.front: Why is steel used to make permanent magnets rather than soft iron?
cards.answer: Soft iron loses its magnetism as soon as it leaves a magnetic field, but steel keeps it.

cards.front: Why does a d.c. motor coil keep spinning continuously instead of stopping after half a turn?
cards.answer: The split-ring commutator reverses the current direction every half turn, keeping the force acting the right way.

cards.front: Why can identical twins, who share the same genotype, have different phenotypes?
cards.answer: Because phenotype is influenced by the environment, such as diet or health conditions, not just genotype.

cards.front: Why can polydactyly appear in every generation, unlike cystic fibrosis?
cards.answer: Because polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele, so only one copy is needed to show the condition, so it cannot be hidden by carriers.

cards.front: In a cross between an affected heterozygous parent (Dd) and an unaffected parent (dd) for polydactyly, what are the offspring outcomes?
cards.answer: Dd genotype / dd genotype / 1:1 ratio / 50% chance per child

cards.front: Why is the fog symbolic when Dunsey steals Silas's gold?
cards.answer: It symbolises Dunsey's moral blindness, as he cannot see beyond his own immediate needs.

cards.front: How does the theft of the gold help Silas rejoin the community?
cards.answer: His desperate visit to the Rainbow Inn shows vulnerability, so villagers start visiting and bringing him gifts of food.

cards.front: Why are the villagers at the Rainbow Inn briefly terrified when Silas bursts in?
cards.answer: They have been telling ghost stories and mistake wild-eyed, distressed Silas for an apparition.

cards.front: The lesson gives four points contrasting the gold with Eppie — what are they?
cards.answer: Gold is inert, Eppie is alive / Gold is private, Eppie is public / Gold is circular, Eppie constantly grows / Gold kept Silas isolated, Eppie draws him into community
items: Gold is inert, Eppie is alive
Gold is private, Eppie is public
Gold is circular, Eppie constantly grows
Gold kept Silas isolated, Eppie draws him into community

cards.front: Name the four main areas the Treaty of Versailles' terms are grouped into.
cards.answer: Territorial / Military / Financial / League of Nations

cards.front: Name the four other Paris peace treaties (besides Versailles) mentioned in the lesson.
cards.answer: Treaty of Saint-Germain / Treaty of Trianon / Treaty of Sèvres / Treaty of Lausanne

cards.front: Why did Italian nationalists call the Paris settlement a 'mutilated victory'?
cards.answer: Italy was denied Fiume and colonial territories in Africa promised by the 1915 Treaty of London, despite receiving South Tyrol and Trieste.

cards.front: Why did General Ferdinand Foch call the Versailles settlement 'an armistice for twenty years'?
cards.answer: He believed the peace was too lenient to stop Germany seeking revenge, so war would return within twenty years.

title: The Celestial Sphere and Coordinate Systems
subject: astronomy-edexcel

cards.front: Why is an object below the horizon at altitude −5° not visible?
cards.answer: Altitude below 0° means the object is below the observer's horizon, so it cannot be seen.

cards.front: Why is a star best placed for observation when it transits the meridian?
cards.answer: At transit the star is at its highest altitude, so light passes through the least amount of atmosphere.

cards.front: Why do constellations have a 'season' when they are best placed at night?
cards.answer: Sidereal time gains four minutes per day on solar time, so objects transit earlier each night and the whole RA range cycles through transit over a year.

cards.front: Name the four key endocrine glands (or gland pairs) the lesson describes.
cards.answer: Pituitary gland / Thyroid gland / Adrenal glands / Pancreas / Ovaries and testes

cards.front: How does an electrical impulse cross the gap at a synapse?
cards.answer: Neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synaptic cleft, diffuse across, and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new impulse.

cards.front: Why does the fight or flight response involve both the nervous and endocrine systems?
cards.answer: It involves nerve impulses for fast signalling and adrenaline released from the adrenal glands for a widespread, sustained response.

cards.front: Why must you keep things like the ruler, catcher and hand position constant in the reaction time test?
cards.answer: So the only thing affecting reaction time is the variable being tested, reducing random error and making results reliable.

title: The Social Construction of Crime and Deviance
subject: sociology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three dimensions of the relativity of deviance given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Across time (historical variation) / Across place (cultural variation) / Across situation (situational variation)

cards.front: How does the interactionist perspective explain why an act becomes labelled as deviant?
cards.answer: No act is inherently deviant; it becomes so only when a label is successfully applied by someone with the power to make it stick.

cards.front: Why did Durkheim argue that some level of crime is normal and functional in society?
cards.answer: Punishing crime clarifies the boundaries of acceptable behaviour and reaffirms shared values, so a moderate amount is beneficial.

cards.front: Why can killing another person be treated as murder in one context but heroic or legal in another?
cards.answer: Situational variation means context, such as warfare or self-defence, shapes whether the same act is considered deviant or criminal.

title: Stalin's terror: purges, show trials and gulag
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: What four methods did the NKVD use to extract confessions during the Great Terror?
cards.answer: Prolonged interrogation / Physical abuse / Sleep deprivation / Threats against family members

cards.front: Name four groups of people targeted by the mass operations of the Terror, beyond party elites.
cards.answer: Ethnic minorities (Poles, Germans, Koreans) / Factory managers / Engineers / Academics

cards.front: How did the purge of the Red Army contribute to Soviet military failures when Germany invaded in 1941?
cards.answer: It removed most senior commanders, leaving the Red Army without experienced military leadership at a critical time.

cards.front: Why did some accused party members confess to crimes they had not committed at the show trials?
cards.answer: They faced NKVD coercion, but some also confessed out of a twisted sense of party loyalty.

title: Correlation, Causation and the Vocabulary of Association
subject: statistics-edexcel

cards.front: Why is writing 'X causes Y' from a strong correlation statistically wrong?
cards.answer: Strength of correlation says nothing about cause, so a lurking variable could explain the pattern instead.

cards.front: Why should you use 'associated with' rather than 'causes' when describing a correlation?
cards.answer: It states the pattern accurately without claiming proof, since a lurking variable could explain the link instead.

cards.front: Name the four pieces of evidence the lesson gives that current warming is human-caused, not natural.
cards.answer: Warming faster than natural cycles in ice cores / Rising CO2 correlates with industrial activity / Isotopic signature shows CO2 from fossil fuels / Stratosphere cooling while troposphere warms
items: Warming faster than natural cycles in ice cores
Rising CO2 correlates with industrial activity
Isotopic signature shows CO2 from fossil fuels

cards.front: Name the two physical consequences of a disrupted energy balance linked to sea level rise.
cards.answer: Thermal expansion of warmer oceans / Melting of land ice

cards.front: Why does CO2 absorb infrared radiation but O2 does not?
cards.answer: CO2's bonds have vibrational modes matching infrared photon energies, while symmetrical O2 has no such vibrational modes at infrared wavelengths.

cards.front: Why does warmer air from climate change intensify rainfall and droughts?
cards.answer: Warmer air holds more water vapour, which intensifies rainfall events and droughts.

cards.front: Name the six pieces of information the Domesday commissioners' fixed questions asked about each manor.
cards.answer: holder in 1066 vs 1086 / hides assessed / number of ploughs / number of peasants / mills, fisheries and woodlands / value then and now

cards.front: Who typically made up a Domesday commissioner team sent to each shire?
cards.answer: a bishop / a baron / a clerk

cards.front: Why did William need the Domesday survey completed so quickly in 1085-86?
cards.answer: He had hired a large mercenary army to defend against a threatened Danish invasion and needed accurate tax data to pay for it.

cards.front: Why is Little Domesday fuller and less summarised than Great Domesday?
cards.answer: It was effectively a draft covering Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex that was never compressed into the main volume.

title: Royal African Company and the slave economy
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four key dates in the arc of Britain's rise to dominance of the Atlantic slave trade.
cards.answer: 1672 - RAC chartered / 1698 - monopoly broken by Ten Per Cent Act / 1713 - Treaty of Utrecht, Britain wins Asiento / 1720 - South Sea Bubble
items: 1698 - monopoly broken by Ten Per Cent Act
1713 - Treaty of Utrecht, Britain wins Asiento

cards.front: Name the four forms of resistance by enslaved Africans described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Individual acts of sabotage / Slowing work pace / Preserving African cultural practices / Larger-scale rebellions

cards.front: Why did the number of enslaved Africans transported by British ships increase so dramatically after 1698?
cards.answer: The Ten Per Cent Act ended the RAC's monopoly, letting any English merchant trade in enslaved Africans by paying a 10% duty.

cards.front: Why did plantation owners rely on continuous importation of newly enslaved people?
cards.answer: Overwork and disease on sugar plantations meant life expectancy was short, so owners needed constant replacements for those who died.

title: Terror, Purges and the Cult of Stalin
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three Moscow show trials of the Old Bolsheviks, 1936-1938.
cards.answer: Trial of the Sixteen, Aug 1936 / Trial of the Seventeen, Jan 1937 / Trial of the Twenty-One, Mar 1938

cards.front: Name four groups beyond the Old Bolsheviks targeted by mass arrests in the Great Terror.
cards.answer: Ex-kulaks deported 1929-30 / Polish residents of the USSR / Germans and Latvians / Engineers, priests and teachers

cards.front: How did NKVD arrest quotas help drive the Great Terror?
cards.answer: Yezhov set regional targets for numbers of 'enemies' to find, which drove ordinary Soviets to denounce colleagues, neighbours and rivals to deflect suspicion from themselves.

cards.front: Why did Stalin use Kirov's murder to justify mass arrests?
cards.answer: He presented it as proof that hidden enemies were active inside the party, and a decree that day authorised summary trials and executions of suspected terrorists.

cards.front: What three things does the speaker in 'Love' admit she doesn't know how to do or understand about her baby?
cards.answer: How to keep him wrapped / How to give him suck / No idea about him

cards.front: What three high-value quotations from 'Love' carry the poem's arc from strangeness to love?
cards.answer: I hadn't met his kind before / I thought he was an emperor / I started there
items: I hadn't met his kind before
I thought he was an emperor
