cards.front: Why does Clanchy describe her baby's strangeness before showing love arriving in 'Love'?
cards.answer: It makes the poem's honesty feel earned, showing love begins in confusion rather than being assumed instantly.

cards.front: How does the poem's ending frame the way love develops in 'Love'?
cards.answer: 'I started there' shows love beginning from not-knowing and uncertainty rather than switching on instantly.

title: War Communism, the NEP and Society Under Lenin
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four features War Communism imposed on the economy from 1918–21.
cards.answer: Grain requisitioning / Full nationalisation of industry / Ban on private trade / Labour conscription

cards.front: Name the four events the lesson says pushed Lenin to abandon War Communism for the NEP.
cards.answer: The 1921 famine / Strikes in Petrograd / The Tambov peasant war / The Kronstadt Mutiny

cards.front: Why did Lenin replace War Communism with the New Economic Policy in 1921?
cards.answer: Peasant revolt after Kronstadt, Tambov and the famine had become more politically dangerous than any economic objection to retreating.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception to call the NEP 'a return to capitalism'?
cards.answer: The state kept the 'commanding heights' of heavy industry, banks, transport and foreign trade, only privatising retail, small workshops and grain trade.

cards.front: Name the four Inuit adaptations to living in polar and tundra environments given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Hunting seals and walrus through sea ice holes / Following caribou herds in summer / Building insulating igloos from compacted snow / Preserving meat in permafrost as a freezer
items: Hunting seals and walrus through sea ice holes
Building insulating igloos from compacted snow
Preserving meat in permafrost as a freezer

cards.front: Name the two types of cold environment the lesson divides the world into.
cards.answer: Polar environments / Tundra environments

cards.front: Why is Arctic amplification making the region warm faster than the global average?
cards.answer: As sea ice melts, the dark ocean surface absorbs more heat than reflective white ice did, accelerating warming further.

cards.front: Why are polar bears increasingly threatened by climate change?
cards.answer: They depend on sea ice to hunt seals, and a longer ice-free season gives them less time to feed and raise cubs.

cards.front: What are the three main brain scanning techniques described in the lesson?
cards.answer: CT scan / PET scan / fMRI scan

cards.front: Why might a stroke in the motor cortex cause paralysis on the opposite side of the body?
cards.answer: Because the brain's motor pathways cross over, so damage on one side affects the opposite side of the body.

cards.front: Why can a stroke affecting Broca's area cause difficulty producing speech?
cards.answer: Because Broca's area, in the left frontal lobe, is damaged and neurons there die and cannot regenerate.

cards.front: Why are fine details of brain function hard to detect using scanning techniques?
cards.answer: Because scans measure activity across thousands of neurons at once, limiting fine-grained detail.

title: The course of the war: Crécy, Calais and Poitiers
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Why did French cavalry charges fail repeatedly at the Battle of Crécy?
cards.answer: English longbowmen on a ridge fired dense volleys of arrows that French armour could not withstand at close range.

cards.front: Why did English commanders use the chevauchée strategy against France?
cards.answer: Burning towns and crops showed the French king could not protect his subjects, damaging his authority while also forcing battle on English terms.

cards.front: What three roles did Calais serve for England after its capture in 1347?
cards.answer: Supply depot / Military staging post / Commercial centre

cards.front: Name the three reasons Iago gives for wanting to destroy Othello.
cards.answer: Passed over for promotion in favour of Cassio / Suspects Othello slept with Emilia / Covets Desdemona himself
items: Passed over for promotion in favour of Cassio

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare introduce Othello through Iago's racist language before the audience meets him?
cards.answer: It forces the audience to confront racist prejudice first, so they can see how it distorts reality once Othello himself appears.

cards.front: Why is Roderigo's gullibility significant to the play's themes?
cards.answer: It shows people believe what they want to believe, so Iago exploits each character's own desires to destroy them.

cards.front: Name the four skills the lesson says the left hemisphere specialises in.
cards.answer: Speech production / Understanding language / Reading / Logical, step-by-step thinking

cards.front: Name the four skills the lesson says the right hemisphere specialises in.
cards.answer: Spatial awareness / Recognising faces / Processing emotion / Creative/holistic thinking

cards.front: Why could split-brain patients name objects flashed to the right visual field but not those flashed to the left visual field?
cards.answer: The right visual field is processed by the language-dominant left hemisphere, while the left visual field goes only to the non-verbal right hemisphere, which cannot share information across since the corpus callosum was cut.

cards.front: Why could split-brain patients still identify a left-visual-field object by touch with their left hand even though they couldn't name it?
cards.answer: The left hand is controlled by the right hemisphere, which had processed the object, so it could select the match by touch despite lacking language ability.

cards.front: Name the three points to make when commenting on an outlier.
cards.answer: State its approximate value / Suggest whether it is genuine or an error / Explain its effect on the mean compared with the median
items: Suggest whether it is genuine or an error
Explain its effect on the mean compared with the median

cards.front: Name the four characteristics that must all be true for a binomial distribution. (Higher)
cards.answer: Fixed number of trials, n / Only two outcomes per trial / Probability of success stays constant / Trials are independent

cards.front: Why is the mean greater than the median in a positively skewed distribution?
cards.answer: A few unusually high values in the right-hand tail pull the mean upwards, above the median.

cards.front: Why is the median usually reported as the 'typical' UK household income rather than the mean?
cards.answer: A small number of very high earners drag the mean above the median, so the median better represents typical income.

cards.front: Why does Act 1 of the play end where it does, structurally?
cards.answer: Act 1 ends when the truth about Christopher's mother begins to emerge, splitting the play along the revelation of truth.

cards.front: How does the play's continuous scene structure reflect Christopher's mind?
cards.answer: Scenes flow without blackouts or set changes, mirroring the speed of Christopher's thinking rather than realistic drama's pace.

title: Practitioner Application: Documentary Theatre and Brecht
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Why does The Great Wave use composite characters and shaped scenes instead of being fully verbatim?
cards.answer: Because as a dramatist, not a journalist, Turnly used dramatic art to communicate the truth of the abductions in ways a documentary record cannot.

cards.front: Why is it a misconception that using Brecht means the audience should feel nothing?
cards.answer: Brecht wanted audiences to feel but not be incapacitated by feeling, so his techniques interrupt total identification without prohibiting warmth or grief.

cards.front: How does a Brechtian approach honour the ethical responsibility of staging real victims like Hanako?
cards.answer: It positions the audience as witnesses who see clearly and judge, rather than fully immersing them in her captivity as pure emotional experience.

cards.front: Name the five varieties of love Shakespeare presents through different characters in Romeo and Juliet.
cards.answer: Petrarchan (Romeo/Rosaline) / genuine and mutual (Romeo/Juliet) / possessive (Capulet/Juliet) / physical (Nurse) / conventional (Paris)

cards.front: How does the public Montague-Capulet feud cause the private and internal conflicts in the play?
cards.answer: The feud stops Romeo and Juliet marrying openly, forcing Juliet to choose between father and husband and needing deception, causing internal turmoil.

cards.front: What does a model sentence combining quotation, analysis and context look like for an extract-based response?
cards.answer: It embeds a quotation, explains its technique's effect, and links this to social context all within one sentence, like the 'Beautiful tyrant' example.

title: Designing Logic Systems and NAND-Only Implementations
subject: electronics-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three-step algorithm for converting a circuit to NAND-only form.
cards.answer: Redraw with NAND equivalents / Identify back-to-back double inversion pairs / Cancel the back-to-back pairs

cards.front: Why must unused inputs on a CMOS 4000 series gate never be left floating?
cards.answer: Because a floating input causes unpredictable switching, so it must be tied to Logic 0 or Logic 1.

cards.front: Why does the final NAND-only version of the burglar alarm circuit (Q = AB + C) only need 3 NAND gates instead of 5?
cards.answer: Because two back-to-back tied-input NANDs between the AND and OR equivalents cancel out as double inversion, so they can be removed.

cards.front: Name the three 'king-becoming graces' Malcolm lists in his test of Macduff.
cards.answer: Justice / Verity / Temperance / Mercy

cards.front: Why does Malcolm pretend to be a worse tyrant than Macbeth when testing Macduff?
cards.answer: To check whether Macduff's loyalty is genuine before trusting him, revealing the truth once Macduff shows real despair for Scotland.

cards.front: Why does the Doctor say Lady Macbeth needs 'the divine' rather than 'the physician'?
cards.answer: Her illness is spiritual guilt over multiple murders, not a physical ailment, so only God or confession could help her.

cards.front: How does the imagery in Malcolm's final speech suggest order is restored to Scotland?
cards.answer: His talk of planting suggests growth and renewal, showing the natural order reasserting itself after the tyrant's destruction.

cards.front: Why does Shakespeare have Romeo and Juliet's marriage take place offstage in Act 2 Scene 6?
cards.answer: Withholding the ceremony reinforces the secrecy and fragility of a union that cannot be publicly acknowledged.

cards.front: How does the Queen Mab speech contrast with Romeo's view of love?
cards.answer: Mercutio calls dreams and love 'children of an idle brain', showing cynicism that contrasts with Romeo's sincere passion.

cards.front: Why does e-commerce push retailers' profit margins down?
cards.answer: Customers can compare prices in seconds online, increasing price competition and squeezing margins.

cards.front: Why can cloud file-sharing speed up work between distant teams?
cards.answer: It lets people in different locations, like Leeds and Vietnam, edit the same document at the same time.

cards.front: Why does light bend towards the normal when it enters glass from air?
cards.answer: Light slows down when entering the denser medium, which bends it towards the normal.

cards.front: Why does a prism split white light into different colours?
cards.answer: Wave speed in glass varies with wavelength, so different colours refract by different amounts.

cards.front: Name the two ways the lesson describes measuring the speed of sound in air.
cards.answer: Timing an echo from a clap near a wall / Two microphones with a data logger over a known distance
items: Timing an echo from a clap near a wall
Two microphones with a data logger over a known distance

title: Selecting Timber & Boards for a Purpose
subject: design-technology-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four common defects of timber caused by moisture movement and grain irregularities described in the lesson.
cards.answer: Cupping / Bowing / Twisting / Knots / Shakes and splits

cards.front: Name the four ways designers minimise timber movement given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Use kiln-dried timber at correct moisture content / Use manufactured boards / Use lamination / Frame the component to expand and contract freely
items: Use kiln-dried timber at correct moisture content
Frame the component to expand and contract freely

cards.front: Why is timber described as anisotropic in terms of its strength?
cards.answer: Its strength differs with the direction of applied force relative to the grain, being strongest along the grain and weaker across it.

cards.front: Why do short-grain sections in joints commonly fail?
cards.answer: Shear forces act parallel to the grain and can cause the timber to split along it, so short grain is weak there.

title: The Berlin Wall and Cold War relations
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name four features used to fortify the Berlin Wall, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: watchtowers / searchlights / dogs / trip wires / death strip of raked sand

cards.front: Why did Kennedy's 'Ich bin ein Berliner' speech matter for the Cold War?
cards.answer: It was a powerful symbolic statement of American support for West Berlin as a democratic outpost surrounded by communist territory.

cards.front: Why was the October 1961 Checkpoint Charlie standoff significant for the Cold War?
cards.answer: It showed Berlin could be the flashpoint where a local incident escalated into direct superpower confrontation.

cards.front: How did Brandt's Ostpolitik change travel between East and West Germany?
cards.answer: The 1972 Basic Treaty normalised relations, letting West Germans visit the GDR more easily and allowing some East Germans, especially pensioners, to visit the West.

title: Structure and Localisation of Function in the Brain
subject: psychology-aqa

cards.front: Name the four main lobes of the cerebral cortex.
cards.answer: Frontal lobe / Temporal lobe / Parietal lobe / Occipital lobe

cards.front: Name the two key language areas of the brain and which lobe each is in.
cards.answer: Broca's area - frontal lobe / Wernicke's area - temporal lobe

cards.front: Why does damage to the frontal lobe change personality and self-control?
cards.answer: The frontal lobe contains the prefrontal cortex, which is involved in planning, decision-making and personality, as shown by Phineas Gage's case.

cards.front: Why is brain plasticity used as a challenge to the localisation of function idea?
cards.answer: After injury, healthy parts of the brain can take over functions of damaged areas, showing the brain is more flexible than strict localisation suggests.

title: The Nazi economy — work, rearmament and self-sufficiency
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three currencies the lesson says ordinary German workers 'paid in' under the Nazi economy.
cards.answer: Real wages fell or stagnated / Working week lengthened / Consumer goods rationed in all but name
items: Consumer goods rationed in all but name

cards.front: Name the three synthetic substitutes the Four Year Plan invested in.
cards.answer: Synthetic oil from coal / Synthetic rubber (Buna) / Artificial textiles

cards.front: Why did Schacht break with Hitler over rearmament?
cards.answer: He warned that rearmament was outrunning what the economy could support without causing inflation.

cards.front: Why do historians argue the Nazi unemployment 'miracle' was mainly an armaments boom?
cards.answer: Job creation was largely a side-effect of rearmament, driven by military spending rather than genuine productive demand.

cards.front: Name the three main ritual responses to death compared across Theravada, Tibetan and Japanese Buddhism.
cards.answer: Merit-transfer, chanting and cremation / Bardo Thodol and 49-day ritual period / Obon ancestor veneration

cards.front: Why is cremation the norm in Theravada funerals?
cards.answer: It reflects the Buddhist teaching on impermanence and the lack of a permanent self.

cards.front: How does the Ullambana Sutra story explain the origin of Obon?
cards.answer: It tells of the monk Maudgalyayana using the power of the Sangha to release his mother from the hungry-ghost realm.

cards.front: Why is a well-practised mind trained in the Eightfold Path considered better prepared for death?
cards.answer: Because the mind travels through life and after death, so meditation in life has direct consequences for the experience of dying.

cards.front: Name the four factors of production the lesson lists as resources used to satisfy wants.
cards.answer: land / labour / capital / enterprise

cards.front: The lesson names two roles the government plays in the economy. What are they?
cards.answer: a consumer of resources / a regulator that shapes the rules
items: a regulator that shapes the rules

cards.front: How can a shortage of a good be resolved, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: A shortage can be resolved if the price rises or supply recovers, unlike permanent scarcity.

cards.front: Why does producing luxury cars create a trade-off for society's other wants, like housing?
cards.answer: The steel, workers and factory space used for cars cannot simultaneously be used to build affordable housing.

title: Creation and the Problem of Evil
subject: religious-studies-ocr

cards.front: Name the three persons of the Trinity involved in creation, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: God the Father as creator / Holy Spirit as agent hovering over the waters / the Word/Jesus through whom all things were made
items: Holy Spirit as agent hovering over the waters
the Word/Jesus through whom all things were made

cards.front: Name the three Christian responses to the problem of evil given in the lesson.
cards.answer: the Free Will defence / suffering produces spiritual growth / acknowledging mystery beyond human understanding

cards.front: Why do many mainstream Catholic, Anglican and liberal theologians read Genesis metaphorically rather than literally?
cards.answer: Because Genesis teaches who created the world and why, not how or when, letting them accept evolution and the universe's age.

cards.front: Why is natural evil harder to explain than moral evil, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Because natural evil arises from natural processes like earthquakes or disease without any human choice or sin behind it.

cards.front: Name the three aspects of availability considered when selecting a material.
cards.answer: Stock form / Lead time / Supply certainty

cards.front: Name the four lifecycle stages considered when assessing a material's sustainability.
cards.answer: Extraction / Processing / Product life / End-of-life

cards.front: Why is a higher material cost per kilogram sometimes acceptable for a one-off prototype?
cards.answer: A one-off can be hand-processed cheaply without tooling, so accepting a higher material cost avoids the manufacturing cost of precision tooling.

cards.front: Why does mass production of 100,000 units justify investing in precision tooling despite the upfront expense?
cards.answer: At high volume even a small saving in material cost per kilogram adds up to a large total sum, which recovers the tooling investment.

cards.front: Name the five useful contextual threads the lesson lists for writing about Refugee Boy in an essay.
cards.answer: Ethiopian-Eritrean war and mixed-heritage families / UK asylum process and its dehumanising bureaucracy / British media hostility towards refugees in early 2000s / Zephaniah's experience of racism and activist purpose / Sissay's own background in the care system
items: UK asylum process and its dehumanising bureaucracy
British media hostility towards refugees in early 2000s
Zephaniah's experience of racism and activist purpose
Sissay's own background in the care system

cards.front: Why does the stage adaptation make Alem's isolation feel more immediate than in the novel?
cards.answer: Because the audience watches his isolation happen in real time, rather than reading about it after the fact.

cards.front: Why is Juliet's idealism about names both her strength and the cause of her destruction?
cards.answer: She believes love can transcend social identity, but in Verona names determine allies, enemies and fate, so her reasoning fails.

cards.front: How does the herb speech foreshadow Friar Lawrence's role in the tragedy?
cards.answer: The flower holding both poison and medicine mirrors how his sleeping potion, meant to help, becomes poison when the plan goes wrong.

title: The Nature and Purpose of Marriage
subject: religious-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Why is marriage indissoluble in Catholic teaching once validly made and consummated?
cards.answer: Because Catholic teaching holds marriage is a sacrament, one of the seven outward signs of God's grace, so it cannot be dissolved.

cards.front: Why does Islam require the free consent of both bride and groom in an arranged marriage?
cards.answer: Because Islamic teaching requires consent of both parties for a valid nikah, so forced marriage is condemned as invalid.

cards.front: What are the four ashramas (stages of life) in Hinduism, with marriage marking entry into which one?
cards.answer: Student stage / Householder stage (grihastha) / Retirement/forest-dweller stage / Renunciation stage

title: Graphics: Pixels, Resolution and Colour Depth
subject: computer-science-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three colour depths (bit depths) the lesson describes, from lowest to highest.
cards.answer: 1-bit (2 colours) / 8-bit (256 colours) / 24-bit (16,777,216 colours)

cards.front: Why does ppi (pixels per inch) matter less for on-screen display than for printing?
cards.answer: On screen, pixel size is fixed by the display hardware, so ppi has less effect than when printing.

cards.front: Why is resolution alone not the same as image quality?
cards.answer: Resolution only measures the number of pixels, but quality also depends on colour depth, so a high-resolution image can still look bad with too few colours.

cards.front: Name the four things that make Shylock a victim, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Public humiliation / Economic persecution / Daughter's betrayal / Forced conversion

cards.front: Name the three things that make Shylock a villain, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Demands lethal bond / Refuses mercy / Pursues vengeance

cards.front: Why is Antonio's melancholy significant to the structure of the play?
cards.answer: His unexplained sadness opens and closes the play, framing it, possibly from grief over losing Bassanio to Portia.

cards.front: How does Jessica's assimilation into Christian society cost her something?
cards.answer: She gains a husband but loses her father, her faith and her culture by joining Belmont's world.

cards.front: What three couples are united by the end of The Merchant of Venice?
cards.answer: Bassanio and Portia / Gratiano and Nerissa / Lorenzo and Jessica

cards.front: Why might Jessica's silence in Act 5 suggest loss rather than contentment?
cards.answer: She has converted, betrayed her father and joined a society that despises her origins, so silence may hide unease.

cards.front: How does the play's ending formally satisfy comedy while still feeling hollow?
cards.answer: Marriages happen and fortunes are restored, but Shylock is destroyed, Antonio is alone and Jessica is silent.

cards.front: The lesson gives four reasons why Mao launched the Great Leap Forward — what were they?
cards.answer: Believed masses could leap past Soviet model / Wanted to overtake Britain in steel / Reassert authority over rivals like Liu Shaoqi / Fund industry without Soviet credit
items: Believed masses could leap past Soviet model
Wanted to overtake Britain in steel
Reassert authority over rivals like Liu Shaoqi

cards.front: The lesson names four historians who disagree on the origins of the Great Leap — who are they?
cards.answer: Frank Dikötter / Roderick MacFarquhar / Yang Jisheng / Mobo Gao

cards.front: Why did Lysenkoist farming methods wreck China's 1959 harvest?
cards.answer: Deep ploughing and overly close planting meant crops grew too thickly to ripen or rotted in waterlogged fields.

cards.front: How did inflated harvest reports worsen the famine during the Great Leap?
cards.answer: Local cadres passed up false huge harvest figures, so the state set procurement quotas too high, taking grain peasants needed.

title: Ethical Behaviour and Deviance in Sport
subject: physical-education-edexcel

cards.front: Name four forms of deviance at elite level the lesson gives, besides doping.
cards.answer: Match fixing / Deliberate physical assault on an opponent / Verbal abuse of officials / Racism directed at opponents
items: Deliberate physical assault on an opponent

cards.front: Name three consequences for an individual athlete caught committing deviance.
cards.answer: Bans / Fines / Loss of sponsorship

cards.front: Why is match fixing described as the most corrosive form of deviance?
cards.answer: Because it strikes directly at the authenticity of the result.

cards.front: How does weak enforcement encourage athletes to be deviant?
cards.answer: If detection is unlikely and consequences are manageable, the risk-reward calculation tips toward deviance.

title: Practitioner Application: Brecht and the Crucible
subject: drama-aqa

cards.front: Why does The Crucible already work in a Brechtian way, even before staging choices are added?
cards.answer: Dramatic irony makes the audience a jury, knowing the accusations are false while watching an institution destroy innocent people.

cards.front: Why would a Stanislavskian performer use emotion memory to play the linen scene rather than focus on the witchcraft plot?
cards.answer: The scene is really about two people seeking a way back after betrayal, so the performer needs the real texture of Proctor's guilt.

cards.front: Why does Danforth's gavel motion make his authority more frightening under a Brechtian gestus approach?
cards.answer: It comes down reflexively like a machine, showing an institution with no doubt that has automated its own moral responses.

cards.front: Name the six key features of the citadel of Mycenae listed in the lesson.
cards.answer: Lion Gate with lioness relief / Grave Circle A with gold treasures / Palace and megaron at the summit / Cyclopean walls up to twelve metres high / Sally port for covert exits / Underground passage to a cistern
items: Grave Circle A with gold treasures
Palace and megaron at the summit
Cyclopean walls up to twelve metres high

cards.front: Name the four features Mycenae and Tiryns share according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Cyclopean walls / A palace with a megaron / A controlled entrance ramp exposing attackers' right side / Grave monuments nearby
items: A controlled entrance ramp exposing attackers' right side

cards.front: Why was the site of Mycenae chosen for the citadel?
cards.answer: It was defensible, visible, and close to routes linking the Peloponnese to the rest of mainland Greece.

cards.front: Why does the Lion Gate relief show no human figures, gods or battle scenes unlike Egyptian or Mesopotamian art?
cards.answer: It makes its statement through symbol and scale alone rather than narrative imagery.

cards.front: How does the mask releasing Jack's savagery show what really keeps people civilised?
cards.answer: Removing self-consciousness removes the fear of being judged, revealing that civilised behaviour was only ever maintained by that fear.

cards.front: Why is Piggy punched with his glasses broken after his outburst about the ship?
cards.answer: Speaking truth to power is punished with violence, showing reason and intellect being attacked by force.

cards.front: How does Percival Wemys Madison's forgotten name and address show civilisation fading?
cards.answer: His name and address, standard identification linking him to the adult world, is remembered in Chapter 5 but completely forgotten by Chapter 12.

cards.front: Name the three questions Piggy asks the group in Chapter 5 about what they are.
cards.answer: Humans? / Or animals? / Or savages?

cards.front: Name the six material categories in design given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Papers and boards / Timber-based materials / Metal-based materials / Polymers / Textile-based materials / Electronic and mechanical systems

cards.front: Why did Alec Issigonis design the Mini with a transverse engine and front-wheel drive?
cards.answer: To maximise interior space in a tiny body, responding to the Suez fuel crisis's demand for a small, fuel-efficient, affordable car.

cards.front: How does Zaha Hadid's use of parametric design and advanced manufacturing affect her buildings and products?
cards.answer: It lets her create fluid, dynamic, curvilinear forms that seem to defy gravity, previously impossible to realise.

cards.front: Why does Viola's disguise as Cesario trap her in an impossible situation?
cards.answer: She falls in love with Orsino who thinks she's a man, while Olivia falls in love with her disguised self.

cards.front: How does Maria's forged letter deceive Malvolio in the subplot?
cards.answer: It is written in Olivia's handwriting and tricks him into believing Olivia loves him, instructing yellow stockings and cross-gartering.

cards.front: Why is the shipwreck described as the play's dramatic catalyst?
cards.answer: It strips Viola of her family, status and female identity, forcing the disguise that creates every comic complication.

title: Stalemate, Armistice and the Cost of Korea
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three changes in 1953 that broke the deadlock and led to the armistice, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Eisenhower took office and hinted at nuclear weapons / Stalin died in March / Prisoner deadlock broken by neutral commission plan in June
items: Eisenhower took office and hinted at nuclear weapons
Prisoner deadlock broken by neutral commission plan in June

cards.front: Why was a decisive UN advance impossible in Korea after 1951, despite UN technological superiority?
cards.answer: Rugged terrain, dug-in Chinese positions and China's willingness to absorb huge casualties stopped any breakthrough.

cards.front: How did Syngman Rhee try to sabotage the 1953 prisoner deal, and what happened?
cards.answer: He unilaterally released 27,000 anti-communist prisoners, but the US held the line and the deal went ahead.

cards.front: Why does the Talmud teach that a wronged person must forgive?
cards.answer: Because once the wrongdoer genuinely seeks forgiveness and makes reparation, the wronged person becomes obligated to forgive.

cards.front: Why do many Quakers register as conscientious objectors instead of fighting?
cards.answer: They believe there is 'that of God' in every person, so killing any human being is always wrong.

cards.front: Why might holding onto resentment be spiritually harmful in Hindu thought?
cards.answer: It may generate negative karma and bind the individual more tightly to the cycle of birth and rebirth (samsara).

cards.front: What three non-combatant roles did many Quakers serve in during the World Wars, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Ambulance units / Hospitals / Farming

title: Vietnam Before America: France, the Vietcong and the Cold War
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the seven parties that took part in the 1954 Geneva Conference on Vietnam.
cards.answer: France / The Vietminh / The State of Vietnam (Saigon) / The USSR / China / The USA / Britain

cards.front: Why did the French choose to fight at Dien Bien Phu?
cards.answer: They assumed Vietminh artillery could not be brought through the surrounding mountains, so a French garrison supplied by air could crush any attack.

cards.front: Why did Vo Nguyen Giap's forces succeed at Dien Bien Phu despite the French plan?
cards.answer: Thousands of porters disassembled artillery and carried it by bicycle and hand into the hills, with Chinese supplies crossing the border, defeating French assumptions.

cards.front: Why did the USA refuse to intervene directly to save the French at Dien Bien Phu?
cards.answer: Britain refused to support intervention and the US Congress would not authorise unilateral war, so requested airstrikes were declined.

cards.front: Name the four key divine attributes given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Omnipotent / Omniscient / Immanent / Transcendent

cards.front: Give the two broad paths the lesson describes for how humans gain knowledge of God.
cards.answer: Special revelation / General revelation

cards.front: Why does Buddhist enlightenment differ from revelation in theistic traditions like Christianity or Sikhism?
cards.answer: The Buddha gained direct insight into the nature of reality himself, rather than receiving a message from a creator God.

cards.front: Why do some religious thinkers argue that the beauty and order of nature is evidence for God?
cards.answer: Many believers hold that nature's beauty and order, such as seasons or the complexity of the cell, communicates something about its creator.

cards.front: What three factors combined to make immigration restriction broadly popular in the 1920s, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Racial prejudice / nativism / Economic anxiety over jobs / Fear of foreign radicals (Red Scare)

cards.front: Why did trade unions like the American Federation of Labor lobby for immigration restrictions after the First World War?
cards.answer: Returning soldiers found immigrants had taken their factory jobs, so unions wanted restrictions to protect wage levels.

cards.front: Why was the trial of Sacco and Vanzetti widely criticised as biased?
cards.answer: Witnesses who gave alibis were dismissed and the judge made prejudicial remarks about their anarchist beliefs and foreign origins.

cards.front: Why did the Palmer Raids target immigrants in particular?
cards.answer: The 1919 bombings were widely blamed on anarchist and communist immigrants, merging fear of radicals with anti-immigration feeling.

cards.front: Name the three sources of evidence scientists use to work out what Earth's early atmosphere was like.
cards.answer: Composition of ancient volcanic gases / Chemical signatures in ancient rocks / Comparison with Mars and Venus atmospheres
items: Comparison with Mars and Venus atmospheres

cards.front: List the five gases released by volcanic outgassing that formed Earth's early atmosphere.
cards.answer: Carbon dioxide / Water vapour / Nitrogen / Methane / Ammonia

cards.front: How did rising oxygen levels lead to the formation of the ozone layer?
cards.answer: High-energy UV radiation from the Sun converted some oxygen molecules (O2) into ozone (O3), forming the ozone layer.

cards.front: Why did the ozone layer allow life to colonise the land?
cards.answer: It absorbed most of the Sun's harmful UV radiation, preventing the DNA damage that would otherwise make survival on land very difficult.

title: Dracula and The Lost Boys: Vampires Across Eras
subject: film-studies-eduqas

cards.front: Name the three named sequences from The Lost Boys (1987) suitable for micro-analysis.
cards.answer: The boardwalk-arrival sequence / The cliff-hang gang initiation / The climactic house-fortification finale

cards.front: How does Karl Freund's staircase-descent lighting in Dracula (1931) construct the vampire as 'architectural'?
cards.answer: A single off-axis light source leaves only the steps' edges and a sliver of the figure visible, making Dracula seem part of the castle itself.

cards.front: How does the boardwalk-arrival sequence in The Lost Boys (1987) make the vampire's world seem seductive rather than threatening?
cards.answer: Steadicam movement, saturated neon colours and cuts timed to the rock soundtrack turn the vampire's world into an attractive spectacle, not a static threat.

cards.front: Why is naming a technique without anchoring it to a specific sequence a weak way to answer the comparative-study question?
cards.answer: Without a named sequence the technique cannot support a macro claim about meaning, so the analysis stays vague and unconvincing.

cards.front: Name the four paths of yoga the Bhagavad Gita teaches as routes to moksha.
cards.answer: Action (karma yoga) / Knowledge (jnana yoga) / Meditation (astanga yoga) / Devotion (bhakti yoga)

cards.front: Name the four purusharthas (aims of human life) in Hindu teaching.
cards.answer: Dharma (ethical duty) / Artha (material prosperity) / Kama (pleasure and love) / Moksha (liberation)

cards.front: Why does avidya (ignorance) keep the atman trapped in samsara?
cards.answer: Avidya is the mistaken belief that the physical self is the real self, which perpetuates the cycle of rebirth.

cards.front: Why can someone with a lot of harmful karma still reach moksha, according to Hindu teaching?
cards.answer: Karma is not fixed fate; through righteous action, devotion and wisdom a person can change their atman's trajectory.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says Emotional weight is carried by in 'Chemistry' rather than explicit statement.
cards.answer: The toy boat / The pond / The meals at the family table
items: The meals at the family table

cards.front: Why does Swift use pathetic fallacy 'in reverse' with the pond in 'Chemistry'?
cards.answer: The still, unchanging pond mirrors grief's frozen quality, contrasting with the turbulent family changes happening above it.

cards.front: How does the narrator's childhood status create tension in the story?
cards.answer: As a child he watches and senses events but cannot act, caught between loyalty to his grandfather and his mother's happiness.

cards.front: Why does the narrator suspect his mother caused the grandfather's death?
cards.answer: She sides with Ralph against her father, and the grandfather becomes marginalised and withdraws before dying, though Swift never confirms this.

title: Peter's Confession, the Transfiguration and Conflicts of Jesus
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the three key conflicts of Jesus with the religious authorities given in the lesson.
cards.answer: Healing the paralysed man (forgiving sins) / The Sabbath controversies / The cleansing of the Temple

cards.front: Name the three views the disciples reported when Jesus asked 'Who do people say I am?'
cards.answer: John the Baptist / Elijah / One of the prophets

cards.front: Why did the religious authorities find Jesus's claim to forgive sins so threatening?
cards.answer: Because forgiving sins was something only God could do, so it implied Jesus was claiming divine authority.

cards.front: Why does the Transfiguration show Jesus as the fulfilment of the Law and the Prophets?
cards.answer: Moses represents the Law and Elias represents the Prophets, so their appearance with Jesus shows Israel's scriptures point to him.

title: Network Protocols and the TCP/IP Model
subject: computer-science-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says protocols define about communication.
cards.answer: how data is broken into packets / how packets are addressed / how errors are detected / how the two ends signal they've finished
items: how data is broken into packets
how the two ends signal they've finished

cards.front: Why do Ethernet and Wi-Fi both use MAC addresses instead of IP addresses?
cards.answer: They operate at the Link layer, delivering data on the local network, unlike IP addressing which handles routing at the Internet layer.

cards.front: Why is organising the TCP/IP model into layers useful for design?
cards.answer: It keeps the design modular, so a new application protocol can be added without rewriting packet routing, and hardware can change without affecting applications.

cards.front: How does data move through the four TCP/IP layers when it is sent and received?
cards.answer: Sending data passes down Application to Link, each layer adding addressing; receiving data passes back up Link to Application, stripping each layer's information.

title: Religious matters: settlement, Catholics and Puritans
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the three groups Puritans split into over how to reform the Church.
cards.answer: Those working for reform inside the Church / Presbyterians who wanted bishops abolished / Separatists who left to form independent congregations
items: Those working for reform inside the Church
Separatists who left to form independent congregations

cards.front: Name the three Catholic-style features the 1559 Settlement kept in church services.
cards.answer: Priests wore vestments / Churches kept altars / Ambiguous wording on communion

cards.front: Why did the 1559 Settlement keep some Catholic-style features in services despite Protestant doctrine?
cards.answer: Elizabeth wanted outward conformity so both Protestants and many Catholics could attend, not enforce inner belief.

cards.front: Why were around 37 London ministers suspended by Archbishop Parker in 1566?
cards.answer: They refused to wear the surplice, the vestment required by the Prayer Book, which Elizabeth ordered enforced.

title: Mains Electricity, Power and the National Grid
subject: separate-sciences-edexcel

cards.front: Why is the live wire in a plug dangerous even when the appliance switch is off?
cards.answer: The live wire stays at about 230 V relative to earth at all times, so touching it drives a current through your body.

cards.front: Why are switches always placed in the live wire rather than the neutral wire?
cards.answer: So that when the switch is open, the appliance and neutral/earth wires are isolated from the high-voltage supply.

cards.front: How does an RCD circuit breaker detect a fault faster than a fuse melts?
cards.answer: It detects tiny imbalances between live and neutral currents, showing leakage to earth, and trips within milliseconds.

cards.front: Give the four voltage levels a step-down transformer sequence reduces mains electricity through before reaching homes.

title: Popular Music: Forms, Hooks and Textures
subject: music-eduqas

cards.front: Name the four types of instrumental backing the lesson gives for melody-and-accompaniment texture in pop.
cards.answer: Block chords / Broken-chord (arpeggiated) pattern / Repeated bass riff (ostinato) / Simple strummed chord loop

cards.front: Name the four exam checklist questions the lesson gives for labelling a pop extract's section.
cards.answer: Is the lyric repeating or changing / Is there a short repeated instrumental idea / Does it build tension or provide contrast / Is the texture thin or thickened
items: Is the lyric repeating or changing
Is there a short repeated instrumental idea
Does it build tension or provide contrast
Is the texture thin or thickened

cards.front: Why does the piano riff in 'Don't Stop Believin'' act as a unifying hook across the whole song?
cards.answer: It recurs as an accompaniment figure under the verses, so it repeats throughout and holds the song together.

cards.front: How does the texture change going into the middle 8 and final chorus in 'Someone Like You'?
cards.answer: Extra instruments and layered backing vocals thicken the texture without ever competing with the lead vocal line.

title: Themes: continuity and change in British entertainment
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: Name the five technologies the lesson gives as step-changes in entertainment access, in order.
cards.answer: Printing press (1476) / Steam railway (1840s) / Cinema (1896) / Radio (1922) / Television (1936)

cards.front: How did religion and changing attitudes shape entertainment across British history?
cards.answer: Religious authority and moral attitudes repeatedly reshaped what leisure was permitted, from Church feast days to Evangelical reform to secularisation ending Sunday trading laws.

cards.front: Why did jousting, falconry and the Grand Tour remain restricted to the wealthy in the medieval and early modern periods?
cards.answer: Access to leisure was shaped by income, so these activities required significant wealth that most people did not have.

cards.front: Name the four propaganda techniques Squealer uses, as identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Fear / Pseudo-science / Rhetorical questions / Rewriting history

cards.front: How does the pigs' teaching themselves to read and write help them gain power?
cards.answer: It gives them exclusive access to knowledge, letting them exploit the other animals' inability to read.

cards.front: Why do the other animals find Squealer's milk and apples argument 'unanswerable'?
cards.answer: Not because it is logical, but because they cannot articulate a counter-argument and fear Jones's return.

title: Work Done, Elasticity and Hooke's Law
subject: science-aqa

cards.front: Name the steps given for investigating Hooke's law in the required practical.
cards.answer: Hang spring from clamp stand / Measure original length / Add masses one at a time, record new length / Calculate extension by subtracting original length / Plot force-extension graph / Gradient of straight line gives spring constant
items: Add masses one at a time, record new length
Calculate extension by subtracting original length
Gradient of straight line gives spring constant

cards.front: How does a ruler with a pointer (set square) improve the Hooke's law experiment?
cards.answer: It reduces parallax error when measuring the length of the spring.

cards.front: What happens to a spring's force-extension graph and behaviour beyond the limit of proportionality?
cards.answer: The graph curves instead of staying straight, and the spring no longer returns to its original length when the force is removed.

cards.front: What happens to the 200 J of work done pushing a box against friction?
cards.answer: It is transferred to the thermal energy store of the box and floor, warming them slightly.

cards.front: Why does Ralph win the election over Jack in Chapter 1?
cards.answer: The boys vote for his size, attractive appearance, and his holding of the conch, not his competence.

cards.front: Why does Ralph's decision to give Jack control of the choir as hunters matter?
cards.answer: It gives Jack a private army loyal to him rather than the group, planting the seed of later conflict.

cards.front: Why does Piggy call the boys 'a crowd of kids' as the signal fire rages out of control?
cards.answer: Because their excitement and lack of discipline let good intentions become destructive, causing the fire to rage uncontrolled.

cards.front: What three things does Golding highlight about Jack's choir when they first arrive on the island?
cards.answer: Wear black cloaks / Carry a long silver cross each / March in step in two lines / Commanded with arrogance / Forbidden to break formation
items: Carry a long silver cross each
March in step in two lines

title: Stalinist economy: collectivisation and Five Year Plans
subject: history-eduqas

cards.front: The lesson gives three aims of collectivisation. What were they?
cards.answer: Make agriculture more efficient / Give the state control over food supplies / Free up labour for industrial cities
items: Give the state control over food supplies
Free up labour for industrial cities

cards.front: Why did Stalin believe collectivising agriculture was necessary in 1928?
cards.answer: Independent farmers could hoard grain and resist price controls, so the state needed control of food to feed workers and fund industrialisation.

cards.front: Why did dekulakisation harm Soviet agriculture at the time it needed to improve?
cards.answer: It destroyed the most productive, experienced and capital-owning peasants just as farming most needed their skills.

cards.front: Why did large numbers of women enter Soviet industrial work in the 1930s?
cards.answer: Mainly because of the desperate need for labour in a rapidly industrialising economy, not ideological commitment to equality.

cards.front: Name the four common omissions to look for when comparing a flowchart to its specification.
cards.answer: Missing decision diamond (condition never tested) / Missing output block (action never taken) / Loop arrow pointing to wrong step / Counter that is never reset
items: Loop arrow pointing to wrong step

cards.front: In the worked central heating example, why did the original flowchart waste energy?
cards.answer: It turned the boiler off at any temperature of 18°C or above, instead of running until 21°C as specified.

cards.front: Why can't an engine management system be built using an analogue circuit instead of a microcontroller?
cards.answer: Matching all the sensor variables simultaneously would require an impractically complex analogue circuit.

title: Questionnaires, Pilot Studies and Cleaning Data
subject: statistics-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four things a pilot study can catch before the main data collection, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: Ambiguous questions / Response categories not exhaustive/mutually exclusive / How long the questionnaire takes / Leading or loaded wording

cards.front: Name the four types of problem the lesson says data cleaning must tackle.
cards.answer: Missing data / Non-responses / Incorrect formats / Extraneous notation or outliers

cards.front: Why must genuine outliers be checked against the original source rather than deleted automatically?
cards.answer: Because they might be real, unusual values rather than errors.

cards.front: Why does asking about sleep on a Monday give different answers to asking mid-week?
cards.answer: Because timing affects responses, as answers change depending on when a question is asked, such as after a weekend.

title: Feudalism and the Norman Land Settlement
subject: history-aqa

cards.front: Name the four levels of the Norman feudal pyramid, from top to bottom.
cards.answer: King / Tenants-in-chief / Sub-tenants (often knights) / Peasants

cards.front: What four categories of peasant does Domesday Book list?
cards.answer: Villeins / Bordars and cottars / Freemen / Slaves

cards.front: Why could England's small Norman ruling class field thousands of armed knights on demand?
cards.answer: Great honours were sub-divided into dozens or hundreds of knight's fees, each owing fixed military service to its lord.

cards.front: Why did the feudal chain of obligation break down during revolts like 1075 and 1088?
cards.answer: Patronage bound loyalty to landholding, so when that bond snapped at one link the whole chain of obligation shook.

cards.front: Name the four shocks between 1947 and 1950 that deepened the Red Scare.
cards.answer: Soviet atomic test (August 1949) / 'Loss' of China to Communism (October 1949) / Conviction of Alger Hiss (January 1950) / Start of the Korean War (June 1950)

cards.front: Why did Truman issue the Loyalty Order in March 1947?
cards.answer: He wanted to head off Republican accusations that his administration was 'soft' on Communism.

cards.front: How did J. Edgar Hoover help build public hysteria about Communism before McCarthy?
cards.answer: He fed intelligence on suspected Communists to HUAC and journalists, shaping public anxiety over years.

cards.front: Why did the Alger Hiss case convince many Americans that Communists had infiltrated government?
cards.answer: A senior State Department official was found to have passed secret documents to a Soviet spy, showing infiltration at the highest levels.

cards.front: Name the seven characters/character groups and the response to moral crisis each represents in DNA.
cards.answer: Phil - control without conscience / Leah - conscience without action / John Tate - denial / Cathy - sadistic enthusiasm / Richard - discomfort without courage / Adam - dehumanised victim / Mark and Jan - detached narration

cards.front: Why does John Tate's leadership collapse when the group panics after Adam's apparent death?
cards.answer: He relies on denial and intimidation, banning the word 'dead', but controlling language does not control reality, so the group sees he has no plan.

cards.front: How does Kelly show that Cathy was never forced into cruelty by Phil?
cards.answer: Cathy follows Phil's orders with enthusiasm and escalates each act of cruelty herself, showing she was waiting for permission, not coerced.

title: Cuito Cuanavale, de Klerk and the negotiation begins
subject: history-ocr

cards.front: Name the four pressures the lesson gives that pushed de Klerk towards negotiation.
cards.answer: Economic crisis / International isolation / Internal unrest / Failure of 'total strategy' in Angola

cards.front: Why did South Africa's Defence Force get involved in Angola's civil war from the mid-1970s?
cards.answer: It supported UNITA rebels against the Cuban and Soviet-backed MPLA government, as part of its 'total strategy' to prevent a communist state on its border.

cards.front: Why did Mandela insist MK would not surrender its weapons after his release?
cards.answer: He committed the ANC to negotiation but said arms would only be given up once a new democratic constitution was in place.

cards.front: Why do historians describe de Klerk's decision to negotiate as a calculation of survival rather than a conversion to liberalism?
cards.answer: He had been a loyal NP minister, but recognised economic crisis, isolation, unrest and Angola's failure left no viable path except negotiation.

cards.front: Name the three inputs used to control the pick-and-place machine.
cards.answer: Position encoder / Component-present sensor / Placement-complete sensor

cards.front: Name the three outputs used to control the pick-and-place machine.
cards.answer: Vacuum gripper / X-Y positioning motor / Placement actuator

cards.front: Why can't a motor be connected directly to a microcontroller output pin?
cards.answer: The pin only supplies 20–40 mA, far less than a motor draws, so it would damage or destroy the microcontroller.

cards.front: How does a BJT transistor let a microcontroller switch a high-current load?
cards.answer: A small base current from the microcontroller controls a much larger collector-to-emitter current through the load.

cards.front: Why does the ascending order of the three prophecies make them so tempting to Macbeth?
cards.answer: It moves from what he already has to what is coming to what seems impossible, so each prediction feels more convincing.

cards.front: How does the natural order idea explain why Macbeth murdering Duncan is so wrong?
cards.answer: Duncan uses organic imagery of planting and growing loyalty, so Macbeth forcing power through violence rejects this natural, patient order.

cards.front: Name the three shallow reasons the poem gives for why the soldier enlisted.
cards.answer: Had drunk a peg after a football match / Told he'd look a god in kilts / Wanted to please his Meg
items: Had drunk a peg after a football match
Told he'd look a god in kilts

cards.front: How does the para-rhyme of 'hymn' and 'him' create meaning in Disabled?
cards.answer: It sounds similar but not identical, setting the boys' happy voices against the broken man and echoing his broken body.

cards.front: Why does Owen set Disabled in a park in the evening rather than on a battlefield?
cards.answer: The ordinary setting shows war's long, quiet aftermath rather than needing a battlefield to show its damage.

cards.front: How does the caesura-heavy ending of Disabled affect the poem's pace?
cards.answer: The repeated question 'Why don't they come?' creates halting pauses that slow the final lines almost to a stop.

cards.front: Name the four things the lesson says St Paul's Cathedral shows about Restoration England.
cards.answer: Disaster / Recovery / The new science / Alliance of Crown and Church

cards.front: Why was Old St Paul's already in poor condition before the Great Fire?
cards.answer: Its spire had been destroyed by lightning in 1561 and never rebuilt, and the nave had been used as cavalry stables under the Commonwealth, leaving the fabric cracked and patched.

cards.front: Why did the clergy reject Wren's Great Model design?
cards.answer: It was a radical centralised church under a dome, too unlike the long nave and choir of English cathedral tradition they insisted on.

cards.front: Why was the coal tax a shrewd way to fund the rebuilding of St Paul's?
cards.answer: It was broad, steady and collected at the port, paid in small amounts by everyone in London who burned coal for heat.

title: Human Life, Ethics and Worship in Buddhism
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the Six Perfections (paramitas) that a Bodhisattva develops, according to the lesson.
cards.answer: generosity / ethics / patience / effort / meditation / wisdom

cards.front: How does metta bhavana meditation develop loving kindness?
cards.answer: It deliberately generates feelings of goodwill, starting with oneself and gradually extending to all beings.

cards.front: Why is tathagatagarbha (Buddha-nature) considered compatible with anatta?
cards.answer: Because Buddha-nature is not a fixed self but a dynamic potential for awakening within beings.

cards.front: Why are mantra recitation and mala beads not the same as praying to a God?
cards.answer: They act as supports for mental training or transformative sacred syllables, not addressing an omnipotent creator deity.

title: Akhand Path, Gurpurbs and Sikh Ceremonies
subject: religious-studies-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five occasions the lesson gives when the Akhand Path can be performed.
cards.answer: Before and after a birth / At marriages / During gurpurbs / At the start of a new enterprise / During times of difficulty or as respect for the deceased
items: At the start of a new enterprise
During times of difficulty or as respect for the deceased

cards.front: Why do Sikhs light lamps on Divali (Bandi Chhor Divas)?
cards.answer: The people of Amritsar lit the Golden Temple with lamps to welcome home Guru Hargobind after his release from imprisonment.

cards.front: How is the first letter of a child's name chosen at Naam Karan?
cards.answer: A Hukamnama is randomly selected and the first letter of the first word of that hymn gives the child's first letter.

cards.front: Why do Khalsa Sikhs take the surname Singh or Kaur at Amrit Sanskar?
cards.answer: These names abolish caste surnames that marked social position, so all Khalsa Sikhs share one surname expressing equality.

title: Cardwell, professionalisation and the Victorian citizen-soldier
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the four main changes Cardwell made to the army between 1868 and 1874.
cards.answer: Abolished purchase of officer commissions / Introduced short service for soldiers / Linked battalions to county districts / Built recruitment depots

cards.front: Name the three later reform stages the lesson gives as part of the thirty-year professionalisation arc alongside Cardwell.
cards.answer: Earlier 19th-century commissions trimming flogging / 1881 Childers reforms finishing reorganisation / 1906–12 Haldane reforms creating Territorial Force

cards.front: How did short service benefit Britain's army without a large standing army?
cards.answer: Reservists could be recalled in an emergency, giving Britain a trained pool of men without the cost of maintaining a large standing army.

cards.front: How did press coverage help make Cardwell's reforms possible?
cards.answer: Russell's Crimean dispatches and Fenton's photographs created a politically active public opinion that demanded army reform.

cards.front: Name the four functions the lesson gives for why a pre-performance routine helps performance.
cards.answer: Narrows attentional focus to task cues / Raises arousal to optimal level / Triggers mental state of past success / Reduces impact of distracting factors
items: Narrows attentional focus to task cues
Triggers mental state of past success

cards.front: Why does internal imagery work best for skill execution while external imagery works best for analysing technique?
cards.answer: Internal imagery uses a first-person view suited to kinaesthetic feel, while external imagery's third-person view suits spotting technical errors and tactics.

cards.front: Why does a familiar physical warm-up help mental preparation, not just the body?
cards.answer: The predictable routine cues the brain into competitive readiness, narrowing focus and reducing distraction by signalling this moment is like past successful sessions.

cards.front: Why can too much arousal harm performance in a fine motor task like a golf putt?
cards.answer: Excessive arousal causes tremor, loss of coordination and poor decision-making, which impairs the precision fine motor tasks need.

cards.front: Name the four economic problems the lesson gives for the Soviet economy under Brezhnev.
cards.answer: Falling industrial productivity / Scarce, poor-quality consumer goods / Chronically inefficient agriculture / Dependence on oil and gas exports
items: Dependence on oil and gas exports

cards.front: Name the four privileges the lesson says the nomenklatura enjoyed.
cards.answer: Special shops / Foreign goods / Dachas (country houses) / High-quality healthcare

cards.front: Why did the Soviet Union struggle to defeat the mujahideen in Afghanistan?
cards.answer: Soviet forces controlled cities but could not pacify the countryside against guerrillas armed and funded by the US, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.

cards.front: Why did the rapid deaths of Andropov and Chernenko lead the Politburo to choose Gorbachev?
cards.answer: Two elderly, ill leaders dying quickly made the USSR look decrepit, so the Politburo could not risk another invalid leader.

cards.front: Name the three biographical links the lesson gives between Shelley's life and the novel.
cards.answer: Her mother died days after childbirth / Her own infant daughter died / She was surrounded by radical thinkers debating science and knowledge
items: Her mother died days after childbirth
She was surrounded by radical thinkers debating science and knowledge

cards.front: Why does nature fail to comfort Victor when he seeks solace in the Alps?
cards.answer: Nature is vast and indifferent to human plans, reminding Victor of his own insignificance rather than easing his guilt.

cards.front: Why does Shelley draw a direct parallel between Victor and Prometheus?
cards.answer: Like Prometheus stealing fire, Victor steals the secret of life from nature and is punished by losing everyone he loves.

cards.front: Name the four stages of the menstrual cycle in order, with their approximate days.
cards.answer: Days 1-5: menstruation / Days 6-13: uterus lining rebuilds / Day 14: ovulation / Days 15-28: lining maintained

cards.front: Why does menstruation begin if a released egg is not fertilised?
cards.answer: The corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone levels drop, so the uterus lining is no longer maintained and is shed.

cards.front: How does the combined pill prevent pregnancy?
cards.answer: It contains oestrogen and progesterone, which prevent ovulation and thicken cervical mucus so sperm cannot pass through easily.

cards.front: [HIGHER] How does progesterone prevent a second egg from being released after ovulation?
cards.answer: Progesterone from the corpus luteum inhibits FSH and LH through negative feedback, stopping another egg maturing.

title: The Nature and Functions of Sleep
subject: psychology-ocr

cards.front: Name the three core functions of sleep identified in the lesson.
cards.answer: Keeping the brain healthy / Physical repair of the body / Emotional stability

cards.front: Why can working night shifts or flying across time zones make sleep difficult?
cards.answer: They create a mismatch between the internal clock and external cues, so the endogenous pacemaker and exogenous zeitgebers conflict.

cards.front: How does bright screen light in the evening cause insomnia?
cards.answer: It suppresses melatonin production, which pushes sleep onset later.

cards.front: How does losing REM sleep affect a person's wellbeing?
cards.answer: Losing REM sleep can affect emotional stability, since REM is when the brain processes emotional experiences.

title: Pizarro and the Conquest of the Incas
subject: history-edexcel

cards.front: Name the five factors top-band judgements weigh against each other to explain the conquest of Peru.
cards.answer: Disease / Civil war / Surprise at Cajamarca / Spanish horses and steel / Indigenous allies

cards.front: Name the three groups the lesson says allied with the Spanish because Atahualpa had crushed them in the civil war.
cards.answer: The Cañari / The Huanca / Huascar's old loyalists

cards.front: How did Atahualpa's execution help the Spanish conquest of Peru?
cards.answer: It removed the empire's only recognised authority, leaving the Inca without unified leadership to resist.

cards.front: Why was the siege of Cuzco in 1536–37 finally broken?
cards.answer: Reinforcements arrived from Almagro returning out of Chile, and Manco Inca's Indigenous enemies switched sides.

cards.front: What are the four features that made up the design of the scaenae frons in Roman theatres?
cards.answer: Elaborate multi-storey backdrop / Made of stone / Decorated with columns / Decorated with niches and statues

cards.front: Why did Roman comedy performers use masks, costumes and exaggerated gestures?
cards.answer: So that audience members far from the stage could still follow the action.

cards.front: Why does Juvenal in Satires 11 show contempt towards chariot racing fans?
cards.answer: He prefers reading in peace and sees the crowd's faction loyalty as inferior to earlier Rome's sober, martial values.
